And again: To shave head and beard and become a shramana, to receive the Buddhadharma, to put away worldly goods, to be content with what is begged, eating once a day and lodging one night beneath a tree, careful never to do so twice. What makes people foolish and dull is love and desire. In such teachings he admonished with every kind of earnest and bitter word, all for the sake of those who are disciples of the Buddha: that at the very first, leaving home, they should make the leaving of desire their first practice. The descendants of later ages, though they leave home in body, are drunk in heart with the five desires, and do not know what affliction is the dharma of detachment, or what road is the road out of suffering. Tangled and confused, they do not wake of themselves; and further they counterfeit dignity and pretend to virtue, deceiving others outwardly and their own minds inwardly, harboring flaws without knowing it. To seek one of true mind and right mindfulness is hard to find. Vimalakirti said: The straightforward mind is the place of practice. Ruchang, since you have the will to seek the dharma of detachment, you should make the straightforward mind the foremost meaning. Take care.
Instructions for My Young Master Dezong

Since you began to follow this old man, more than twenty years have passed, and not only have you labored in your duties; you have also met with calamity and walked the land of miasma, and that three times now. Earlier I sent you back to the mountain home to serve your teacher, but your mad mind did not rest and you came back to me. Now I hear that your teacher has become a thing of the past, and you were unable to hold his towel and vase while he lived, or to lift his hands and feet when he died. Can you be called his disciple? You are going back now; do you not think how you will repay your teacher's grace in the unseen? The ancients called on teachers and visited friends precisely to accomplish the work of the Way. You have followed your teacher more than twenty years: where is your work of the Way? The ancients were ashamed to face their parents, teachers, and friends; since your work of the Way is not accomplished, fortunately you have no parents, teachers, or friends left, so you have no place to put your shame. The patriarch said: Sentient beings are no different from Buddha; it is only that sentient beings have many habits and the Buddhas and patriarchs are pure and stainless. You have served a good spiritual friend and heard his instructions with your own ears, and you are old now, yet you are still so drifting. Do you not know how, in the days to come, you will face this old monk? If by any chance this old monk were like your parents, I fear you would have no place to put your shame in this life either. I think of your loyal heart and righteous courage, which are not less than the ancients'. Yesterday I read the words of the great master Daguan, who compared you to Tian Guang. If so, how shall this old monk repay you for your life? It is said that among all offerings the Dharma is foremost. Now I make this a further offering to repay your life. Never again forget the words of today's parting. At the fork in the road I hold your hand and urge you earnestly: take care.
Instructions for the Attendant Hui

The Buddha appeared in the world for the sake of one great cause: to lead beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha's knowledge and vision. Yet the Buddha's knowledge and vision are the knowledge and vision of sentient beings, and the knowledge and vision of sentient beings are the knowledge and vision of birth and death. Hence it is said: When knowledge and vision establish knowing, that is the root of ignorance; when knowledge and vision are without seeing, that is nirvana. Thus the knowledge and vision of sages and ordinary beings are not two, and the difference of delusion and awakening lies only in whether one establishes or not. The patriarch said: If you establish a single dust mote, the country is destroyed and the family perishes. For knowledge and vision are fundamentally without sage or ordinary; but wherever there is establishment, there is a self, and where there is a self all obstacles arise at once; where there is no self, the ten thousand dharmas sink level. Thus we know that the self is the root of birth and death. Not only do ordinary people make greed, anger, and delusion and so become obstructed by self; even all the sages and cultivators, so long as their knowledge and vision are not forgotten, are entirely obstructed by self, and this is the root of birth and death that is hardest to pull out. Therefore among the two kinds of obstacle there is coarse and fine: the coarse is easy to dismiss, the fine hard to remove. Because knowledge and vision are deeply hidden and rooted in the mind, they are hard to pull out. Hence the sutra says: To preserve the self and to be aware of the self are both called obstacles. This is precisely the knowledge and vision establishing knowing, hidden as deeply as life itself, which one cannot cut off oneself. That is why the ancients spent twenty or thirty years in bitter study; and even if one awakens to the fact that one's own nature is complete, like the bright moon over a cold pool or the sound of a bell in the still night, undiminished however it is struck and undispersed however the waves touch it, this is still a matter on the shore of birth and death. This is where the ancients greatly did not deceive themselves; for to deceive oneself and others is to destroy oneself and others. The attendant Fuhui left home with this old man early. When I first saw him he was a dull lump; after ten years away he came back duller still. Yet I have always been glad that within his dullness there is a wakeful undull place. This attendant makes this dull-and-not-dull his root of life. Now five more years have passed; his dullness increases daily, and his undull part too grows secretly and silently. Thus people look at the attendant and see dullness, and the attendant looks at himself and sees himself duller still; but no one knows his own dullness. This summer the old man returned to the mountain from western Yue, and the attendant suddenly put on his dull look, and the old man laughed aloud: his dullness will never have its day. I said privately that this dull man makes dullness his own fault. If he can take this dullness as his own place of use, he will be quite content, and can end birth and death, and will not betray the matter of leaving home and wandering. But if he further establishes this dullness, then the illness is worse than knowledge and vision establishing knowing. Attendant, if you can push over this dullness, you need not worry that your eyebrows will not be tied together with this old man's.
Instructions for Deng Sizhi

The Buddhas and patriarchs appeared in the world and taught the dharma of prajna, teaching people to cultivate with prajna as the root. Prajna is Sanskrit; in Chinese it means wisdom. This wisdom is the Buddha-nature inherent in us, also called one's own mind, also called self-nature. This substance is fundamentally undefiled, therefore it is called pure; fundamentally undimmed, therefore it is called luminous; fundamentally vast and all-embracing, therefore it is called empty space; fundamentally without delusion, therefore it is called one truth; fundamentally unmoving and unchanging, therefore it is called true suchness, also called thusness; fundamentally perfect and illuminating all, therefore it is called perfect enlightenment; fundamentally still and extinguished, therefore it is called nirvana. In the Buddhas it is perfectly realized, and so is called great enlightenment, also called bodhi. The Buddhas use it, and so it is the wondrous function of spiritual power; bodhisattvas cultivate it, and it is named wondrous practice; the two vehicles attain it, and it is named liberation; ordinary people are deluded about it, and it becomes deluded thought and karmic consciousness. When it is aroused and used, it becomes greed, anger, delusion, craving, pride, flattery, and deceit; when it is made into karma, it becomes lust, killing, theft, and lying; and the fruit it reaps is knives, saws, iron, grindstones, and even cauldrons of boiling water and furnaces of coals, all kinds of instruments of suffering, all transformed from this mind. It is just like a waking man at ease, with all kinds of joyful states before his eyes; after a little while he falls into a heavy sleep and suddenly dreams he is in hell, where all the instruments of suffering and their agonies are borne at once, unbearable and unendurable, and just when he seeks help and cannot get it, the guests chatting in the hall outside have not yet fallen silent, and he wakes with a start, moaning as he rises. He looks and the scene of joy is still before his eyes, the wine still warm and the dishes still hot; the place on the pillow and mat has not been left, yet the states of suffering and joy are suddenly different. In short, joy comes from outside, suffering comes from within. From this we see that the doctrine of heaven and hell appears plainly within one's own mind; how could it be a mere phantom marvel? It is all just where one's own deluded mind has arrived. The sutra says: The mind takes what is of the mind, and the unreal becomes unreal dharma. It also says: The dharmas above and below in the three realms are made by one mind alone. Seen thus, it is not the Buddhadharma alone that teaches one mind; from the sages and worthies of old down to all the nine schools and strange arts, to speak at the utmost, even to sentient and insentient things, none is not established from this one mind. Only there is difference of great and small, many and few, good and evil, right and wrong, bright and dim, and the use each makes is different. Hence it is said: Mountains, rivers, and the great earth fully reveal the body of the Dharma King; creatures with scales, shells, feathers, and fur universally manifest the samadhi of the body of form. All this is the true light of prajna and the shadow matter of our own mind. The substance of mind inherent in us is thus vast, all-embracing, pure, and luminous; and the various states and forms of things that lie crossed and crowded around us are thus all manifested by our own mind. That we have this and do not know it is indeed pitiable. And worse, we mistake what comes from our own mind and take it as the happy ground of craving and love: the eye delights in beautiful forms, the ear in licentious sounds, the nose in scents, the tongue in flavors, the body in touches, and the mind in dharmas; and all these too come forth from our own mind. We take them further and make them joy, make them pleasure, make them greed, anger, and delusion, make them lust, killing, theft, and lying, and so make all kinds of illusory karma, and further invite the fierce suffering of the three evil paths in the future. It is like a man dreaming and not waking. Is this not greatly pitiable? Because this mind is one substance with all the Buddhas and not two, and because the patriarchs of every generation awakened to it and were no different from them, only we possess it fully and do not know it as illusion. The son ran away and forgot to return, and the parents thought of him and searched for him. That is why Śākyamuni appeared in the world, why Bodhidharma came from the west, and why what Caoxi taught for more than thirty years, and the seventeen hundred cases that flowed down to point people to, are all this matter. It is not old Lu alone: what this old man speaks to Sizhi today is also this matter; and what Sizhi and all those present who hear and see it share is also this matter. The sutra says: This is the one and only matter; the other two are not true. Thus we know that apart from this one matter, everything becomes the talk of Mara and idle discourse. If the Buddhas, who have fully realized it, did not appear in the world, they would fail sentient beings; if the patriarchs, who awakened to it, did not teach the Dharma, they would fail the Buddhas; and whoever hears it but does not believe, understand, accept, and practice it fails himself. To fail sentient beings is arrogance; to fail the Buddhas is downfall; to fail oneself is folly. Thus the Buddhas and patriarchs may be failed, but oneself must not be failed, since one has it inherently and does not seek it, possesses it fully and does not make good use of it. It is like holding a pearl and begging: is this not greatly pitiable? Sizhi, you now bear a body in the sea of dust and your mind has fallen into a deluded road; suddenly you wake with a start and turn back to seek this matter, like the son holding the pearl who is ashamed to herd with beggars, and mind after mind asks people for the way to be self-sufficient. This old man at once points this dharma straight at you, as if showing you the divine pearl at the hem of your robe: it was Sizhi's own all along, and it is not this old man handing it to you as a favor or a worldly courtesy. Yet this wish-fulfilling jewel responds to every request, and all kinds of undertakings and states of use are fully supplied by it. As for the way to make it respond as you wish, that again lies in Sizhi's own mind, in your skill, diligence, and strenuous effort. If you can truly consent and strive with all your might, and one day suddenly awaken, then you will swallow in a single mouthful the mountains, rivers, and great earth, creatures with scales, shells, feathers, and fur, the Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of every generation, and the undertakings of Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius, without borrowing another's strength. Otherwise you remain a sentient being of dream inversion; how then could you be called a true man? Sizhi, Sizhi, better to fail the Buddhas and patriarchs above and this old man below than ever to fail yourself, your ruler, or your parents. The prajna this old man speaks today is all the mind-ground Dharma gate of the Buddhas and patriarchs from of old, and it does not differ by a single character from what the Sixth Patriarch first taught. Only, of those who first heard it, you are the only one. Since one man now stands in place of the twelve hundred of old, this old man cannot contain his joy, and so he too teaches the dharma of prajna. As our Buddha and patriarchs said: as for one person, so for the many. If Deng holds this to benefit self and others, it may well become a broad and long tongue.
Instructions for the Chan monk Miaoguang Miao

The conditions for entering the Way and the roads into it differ for each. Following the prajna seed-nature of former habits, they are shallow or deep and not the same. Some first cast aside letters and simply raise the huatou of an ancient's karmic condition, and so awaken and enter. Some first study the various wondrous gates of practice within the teachings, and afterwards throw away the mixed poisons and rely solely on contemplation to awaken and enter. Thus the great master Yongjia, through the Tiantai practice of stopping and seeing, suddenly saw his own mind as clearly as a fruit in the palm; and when he met Caoxi, he was like a lion slipped from its ropes, and old Lu, exhausting all his divine power, could only say, Just so, just so. This is the first model among the teachers from of old. The Chan monk Xuan has traveled everywhere and long relied on lecture halls, and has already glimpsed a part of the Buddha vehicle's teaching eye. If, from what he has glimpsed, he can cut away all views and the habits of letters, and apart from letters single-mindedly raise and thoroughly investigate the Buddha's and patriarchs' upward road, inquiring day and night until he reaches the place where the Buddha had not yet appeared and the patriarch had not yet come from the west, a single cold place, and suddenly it bursts forth from within his own breast like a bean popping in cold ashes: then he will believe that all dharmas do not go beyond his own mind, and that all the mountains, rivers, the great earth, blades of grass, motes of dust, and hairs are all himself. Then he may let things take their course and, as suits the occasion, perform the conditions of giving the Dharma. This is what is called opening the gate of sweet dew and walking upon the crown of the Buddhas' and patriarchs' heads. But if the mind and will are narrow and base, and one takes the leftover tea and cold rice of the lips as the supreme wondrous flavor, then one cannot even save oneself; how would one dare to speak of the knowledge and vision of Buddhadharma?
Instructions for the Pilgrim Kuan Liang

People of old went on pilgrimage for the sake of birth and death; people today merely go on pilgrimage and do not know birth and death. This is greatly to be pitied; this is what is meant by using it daily and not knowing it. The fault lies in not knowing what one originally has. If a person knows what he has, he knows to value himself; knowing to value himself, he does not follow things and can turn things instead. The Book of Songs says: My heart is not a stone; it cannot be turned. You must know that unless it is a vajra mind-ground, nothing fails to be turned by things. Once turned by things, one follows them along. Can such a one be called a pilgrim monk? Kuan Liang came from the north to the south and has come to comfort me several times, and has not been turned by the hardships of the road, hunger, and cold. This old man only knows that his heels are strong, and so called him Iron Foot. Now, seeing that his mind does not shift, I further praise him with the words Iron Guts. Yet iron guts are what this old man knows; the matter of his pilgrimage is certainly not what you know. If you knew a little about pilgrimage, you would not go straight on like that. This old man pities his foolishness and fears for what he does not know, and so sends him off with this letter. Go on pilgrimage again. If after this you still cannot grope for your own nostrils, then on some later day it will surely be hard to meet as we meet today.
Instructions for the Chan monk Ruliang

The Buddha said: To shave head and beard and become a novice, to be free of desire and still, is the foremost of all. Thus we know that desire is the first and greatest matter at the head of the road of birth and death. Therefore the Buddha sharply rebuked it and warned against it. Apart from it, one gains peace and happiness. The reason sentient beings sink in the sea of suffering and cannot quickly reach the other shore is solely that desire is the fault and the affliction. The Buddha said: The root of all suffering is craving; if craving is extinguished, there is nothing to rely on. The three realms are the house in which all beings take their stand, and desire is its foundation; the clamor and noise of the toils of the dust are all this. If one wants to leave that reliance at once, then there is no question of breaking the three poisons, leaving the three realms, and breaking the net of Mara; then the Tathagata is greatly delighted. Thus we know that if the five desires are not left behind, the three realms are hard to break; how sorrowful the Tathagata must be. To seek stillness and liberation is then difficult. Ruliang left home young and went on pilgrimage in many places; now he has met this old man, brought forth the bodhi mind, been given the novice precepts, and resolved to practice the conduct of detachment from desire. This is the first wondrous practice of one who vows to leave birth and death. I fear only that his resolve is not firm and his practice not strong. The Buddha said: One must long endure bitter effort before it can be accomplished. You should have a decisive resolve, and not stop until you become Buddha. This is the true resolve to practice the conduct of detachment from desire.
Instructions to Zhou Yangru

Zhouzi asked for instruction on the essential purport of the Dharma-characteristics teaching. The Elder therefore brought up the Sixth Patriarch’s verse on consciousness and wisdom: “The great perfect mirror wisdom is pure in nature; the wisdom of equality has no sickness in the mind; the wisdom of marvelous observation sees without effort; the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done is like a round mirror. The five and eight, the six and seven, turn from effect and cause; but only the names are turned — there is no real nature. If at the place of turning one does not linger in feeling, then amid teeming activity one forever dwells in nāga samādhi.” In these eight lines he exhausts the heart’s marrow of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and lays bare the very root of nature and characteristics. Yet those who count jewels and tally sand, greedy for much and unable to chew what they bite off, generally look on this as idle furniture; there is never one who truly fixes his eye on it. How pitiable! Everyone says the Sixth Patriarch could not read and had no understanding of the teachings — how then could he speak thus? They do not realize that the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ wisdom-life is wholly contained, with nothing left over, in eight words: “The three realms are mind only; the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only.” Because they are mind only, the three realms are still, utterly without a single thing. Because they are consciousness only, the ten thousand dharmas are manifold — for the ten thousand dharmas are nothing but transformations of consciousness only, and when sought in one’s own mind and nature they are utterly unobtainable. Therefore the Buddhas and Patriarchs taught people only to say: outside the mind not a fragment of anything is obtainable. This is precisely what Huangmei revealed at midnight: “From the first, not a single thing exists.” In this one phrase all Buddhas of the ten directions and three times, and the Patriarchs of every generation, are packed so tightly that it cannot be broken apart. Hence the robe and bowl were entrusted with it. And the two schools and five houses all unfolded from this one phrase. Where was there ever a division into nature and characteristics? Now, looking at the verse on consciousness and wisdom, let me break it open a little. If we take it that the three realms are mind only, there is no place to begin speaking. It is because this mind is deluded that it turns into consciousness, and so loses the name of true suchness and is called only ālaya-consciousness, also named storehouse consciousness. This consciousness is the whole of true suchness transformed; it is precisely what is meant by “the conditioned and the unconditioned joined together to form it.” It is the root of the real and the deluded, of delusion and awakening; the basis of birth-and-death and of ordinary beings and sages. The Laṅkāvatāra says: “The ocean of storehouse consciousness is forever still; it is moved by the wind of objective conditions. Great waves surge through the dark abyss, and there is no time of ceasing.” Since it says the storehouse consciousness is the ālaya, and yet also says it is forever still, then it is fundamentally unmoved. What is moved is not the storehouse consciousness but only the wind of objective conditions. The verse says: “If the objective conditions before are not, the mind too is not.” So then what grasps at objects is not the storehouse consciousness but the mind of birth-and-death. This mind of birth-and-death is provisionally named the seventh consciousness, but in truth it is the stirring thought of the eighth consciousness — what is called the vital impulse. Once this impulse is stilled, the objects before one are suddenly empty, and though the sixth consciousness may still discriminate, it has nothing to lodge upon. As for the first five consciousnesses, they have no substance of their own; they are merely the storehouse consciousness functioning in response to conditions. They can illumine objects but cannot discriminate, and so it is said they are “like a round mirror.” What discriminates the five sense objects is not the five consciousnesses but the consciousness of mind that arises at the same moment; therefore it is said to have accomplishment. If discrimination does not arise, then seeing is without effort. Seen thus, the storehouse consciousness is fundamentally real, and so it is called “pure in nature.” Its fault lies in a single thought of giving rise to mind, and this is the sickness of the mind. Where there is arising there is ceasing. This arising and ceasing is like the flowing of water: there is no flow apart from water. It is only because of water’s nature of not abiding that a mark of flowing is seen; and where there is flowing, it is clear that it is not the still water of a deep pool. Hence the Laṅkāvatāra speaks of two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing: the arising-abiding-ceasing of marks, and the arising-abiding-ceasing of the surging stream. Both belong to the storehouse consciousness. If arising-and-ceasing is not extinguished, the first seven consciousnesses arise; if arising-and-ceasing is extinguished, only the one pure reality remains, and the nature of true suchness is thereby restored. Restored, consciousness is no longer called consciousness but wisdom; hence “no sickness in the mind.” What the Sixth Patriarch’s verse sets forth is the turning of the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms. The great perfect mirror wisdom is what the storehouse consciousness turns into; the wisdom of equality, what the seventh turns into; the wisdom of marvelous observation, what the sixth turns into; the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done, what the first five turn into. Because delusion belongs to the functioning of the storehouse consciousness, the real is likewise likened to a round mirror. But the sixth and seventh are turned first, in the midst of cause, while the five and eight, being one substance, are perfected only at the fruit. Seen thus, consciousness is fundamentally unreal, yet delusion has these two functions. Therefore it is said: “only the names are turned” — the name is changed but not the substance. Moreover this substance does not lie in meditation or cultivation, but only in all the affairs of daily use; sages and ordinary beings turn it at the same moment, and everything depends on whether one lingers in feeling or not. Hence the difference between sage and ordinary being, between delusion and awakening. Zhouzi, if you have set your mind on this, then earnestly fix your eye on the place of turning in daily use, and try to settle it for yourself.
Instructions to Shu Bosun

The scholar Shu Bosun had his mind set on the Way and asked for instruction. I therefore taught him, saying: Laozi said, “In pursuit of learning one daily increases; in pursuit of the Way one daily decreases. Decrease and again decrease, until one arrives at non-doing.” Students increase their knowledge and views and take this as progress; they do not realize that as knowledge and views increase, the view of self prevails. When the view of self prevails, the temper grows more arrogant; when the temper grows more arrogant, the feelings grow more reckless; when the feelings are reckless, desire blazes and the nature is dimmed. When the nature is dimmed, the Way recedes further. Therefore one who pursues the Way takes decrease as increase. Our nature is fundamentally pure, utterly without a single thing — this is what is meant by “the substance of the nature in which not the finest dust is established.” But because habitual defilement is thick, it issues as greed, hatred, delusion, and pride; and so one indulges feeling and material desire. The thicker material desire becomes, the more the nature is daily dimmed — this is what is meant by “the harm of having a surplus.” One who pursues the Way today should only decrease his surplus in order to restore what the nature lacks. If the substance of the nature is complete, the light of the Way daily shines. Issuing from it, one becomes loyal, filial, benevolent, and righteous; extending it, one governs the state and the family, and its benefit is widespread and its virtue great. To attain merit and fame that do not decay — all this is the gain of decrease. Hence in the hexagrams of the Changes, decreasing the upper to benefit the lower is called Increase, and decreasing the lower to benefit the upper is called Decrease. If one does not know what to decrease, and merely takes the increase of knowledge and views as learning, then increase and decrease are inverted; how could one then fully realize one’s nature? Therefore one whose will is set on the Way values decrease.
Instructions to Wen Zhen

Confucius said: “If wealth could be sought, even as a whip-holding groom I would do it. If it cannot be sought, I will follow what I love.” He also said: “Wealth and honor gained by unrighteousness are to me as drifting clouds.” Now if wealth could be sought, he would not be ashamed to hold the whip; yet having said it could be sought, he also said wealth and honor are as drifting clouds. Did he seek it, or did he not seek it? What he means is: wealth and honor that are unrighteous are like drifting clouds — a strong statement that they must not be sought. This is the teaching by which the gentleman endures poverty, and the reproach by which the petty man runs to excess. Our sage taught people this as the foundation for settling their destiny and steadying their will. Alas, alas! People today do not understand the foundation of the great destiny, but stand trembling in the field of success and failure; they have not understood the source of nature and life, but harbor thoughts of gain and loss. When gain and loss alarm the mind, taking and rejecting go divergent ways, and flying thoughts crisscross in the breast. To seek a settled will and clear principle, renewed virtue and advancing practice — can it be had?
Instructions to Liu Pingzi

It is not hard to turn toward the Way; what is hard is to give rise to the resolve. It is not hard to study the Way; what is hard is to seek outside. It is not hard to understand the Way; what is hard is to pick and choose. It is not hard to enter the Way; what is hard is to be content with oneself. It is not hard to awaken to the Way; what is hard is to seek the wondrous. A student of the Way who sees through each of these and is not deceived by others has a broad mind and a glad spirit, and walks alone, free and unconstrained — such a one is called a person of wondrous penetration.

“Natures are near to one another; habits carry them far apart.” These words point directly to the shortcut of cultivation through a thousand ages. If we only knew that our own nature is near, and that it is only through habit that it becomes distant, we would at once cut off the vital pass: inner habit would not be allowed out, outer habit would not be allowed in. With both ends cut off, what lies between is naturally alone. In that aloneness, this is precisely what is meant by “as though something were standing there, towering.” If one arrives at the ground where that towering thing alone remains, then the nature restores itself.

Ziyu said: “The way of learning and inquiry is nothing else than seeking back the mind that has strayed.” And yet there are those whose minds never cease seeking, and whose learning and inquiry remain unclear. Why? The fault lies in “releasing without releasing” and “seeking without seeking” — a vague, shadowy semblance that they regard as of no importance. If one knows what it is to release without releasing, then one is naturally not released; if one seeks without seeking, that is true seeking. Master Ziyu, who saw the nature and understood the mind, had nothing more than this in his single transmission and direct pointing. If you have the will to turn toward the Way, take this as your standard.

The Way lies in daily use, yet people do not know it; the Way is right before the eyes, yet people do not see it. Knowing daily use but not knowing the Way, seeing what is before the eyes but not seeing the Way — it is not that the Way is far from people; people themselves are far from it. Hence it is said: the Way is before the eyes, yet it is not what is before the eyes; the Dharma is likewise not apart from what is before the eyes, yet it is not reached by ear or eye. If you can pass through what is before the eyes — at the passes of favorable and adverse, in the realm of praise and blame — and are not ensnared, but stride straight through with your whole body, then with such an attitude the sage is not confined to the three dynasties, and past and present do not depart from a single thought. If you have the will to turn toward the Way, then from the first arousal of the resolve, enter right here.
Instructions to Ou Jiafan

The world takes the loyal minister and the filial son as the highest principle, and says that loyalty springs from filial piety and begins in serving one’s parents. The saying goes: “In thinking of serving one’s parents, one cannot but know others; in thinking of knowing others, one cannot but know Heaven.” Now Heaven is simply our own innate heavenly nature. In this world a person may feign almost anything, but the thought of serving one’s parents is the truest of all, because it comes forth from the heavenly nature. We who have received this nature and become human — if we do not know the original suchness of the heavenly nature, we do not know what is truly precious in being human. If one can truly know what is precious in being human, then toward all vain, mixed, defiled, and turbid affairs one will naturally not dare let them lodge in the breast and obscure the originally possessed emptiness and clarity. Once the original clarity is restored, the sage and worthy are within oneself. Hence it is said, “The Way is not far from man” — this is what it means.
Instructions to Li Zijin

Human nature is fundamentally clear, but is dimmed and covered by material desire and the dust of feeling; hence people do not know it in daily use. Therefore it is said, “Natures are near; habits carry them far apart.” If we have the will to work at restoring the nature, there is no need to seek outside; we need only take the places in daily seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing where habitual defilement and material desire weigh heaviest, and moment by moment overcome and remove them. When this overcoming has gone on a long time, things dissolve and dust vanishes, and the original clarity reveals itself of itself. It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is clean, the brightness appears. Yet the substance of the mirror was originally bright; it does not await polishing to have it. Whoever has the will to work at the Way should take the overcoming and polishing of bad habits as the first ground of entry.
Instructions to Li Zirong

The ancients said: “When cutting hair, one should reach the skin; when trimming nails, one should come to the flesh” — meaning that it must be done thoroughly. Therefore a student of the Way must first establish a long-range, unretreating resolve, and apply a solid, earnest, painful effort. It is like climbing a mountain ten thousand fathoms high: one does not stop until one reaches the very summit. Step by step exert yourself; thought after thought do not retreat. Do not be swayed by praise or blame, shaken or robbed by right and wrong, or crushed by hardship and obstruction. Be like one person fighting ten thousand. If you falter even a little, all your previous work is lost. How then could one reach the state of unretreating peace and joy without a firm and solid mind?
Instructions to Ou Jiake

It is said: “There is no one who does not eat and drink, yet few can know the flavor.” This says that the Way lies in daily use, very close at hand, yet those who know it are rare. The ancients said that apart from putting on clothes and eating food there is no other matter. So then, within past and present, those deceived by clothes and food are many. One who is not deceived by them may be called a hero. A student of the Way need not seek the wondrous elsewhere; if in all the conditions of daily use he is not deceived, and with one glance sees through the place of putting on clothes and eating food, that is true work that reaches upward. One who has his will set on the Way should do it amid daily use.
Instructions to Liang Tengxiao

When a gentleman lives in the world and has not yet met his opportunity, there is none who does not vow to assist his ruler, shelter the people, and establish an undecaying enterprise. But once he enters the registry of office, he sets his heart only on making a name, forgetting what it was that made for true merit. In time he is gradually stained by the customs of the age; his mind and spirit grow turbid, and before he knows it he has drifted onto the road of wealth and honor. In the extreme he no longer even scruples about his reputation, and his original resolve can no longer be found. Why? Because his first vow did not come from the fundamental reality, but was merely a vain admiration and a deluded thought. Since it was never a firm and unshakable resolve, how could it establish an undecaying enterprise? Master Liang Tengxiao is firm-boned and free in spirit — by no means a man of the dust of the world. Whenever he followed me, there was no word or phrase he heard that did not stir his heart to vigilance. Once he asked for instruction, and I told him: a student should indeed set his will on the Way and virtue; and whoever sets his will on the Way and virtue must first investigate our fundamental reality, and let it flow from the true nature. This true nature is vast beyond measure, bright and pure, swept utterly clean of the finest dust. This is the substance of our nature — what is called benevolence. Within this substance not a speck of dust is established; but if there is a single deluded thought, that already belongs to self. With self, one stands opposed to things; once thing and self are divided, self and other are set up; once self and other are set up, the substance of the great unity is blocked and dulled, and cannot be benevolence. When the original substance is blocked and dulled, all delusions arise; even if one has the will for merit and fame, it is all discharged from deluded thought, and whatever one does is not real. Since the root is deluded, one’s footing is unsteady; and so, once one enters worldly conditions, it is only fitting that one is at once stained by vulgar custom. From today, Master Liang, you should work at your own nature and investigate from reality. If you cannot yet thoroughly investigate the root of your own nature, then simply take the Sixth Patriarch’s saying — “not thinking of good, not thinking of evil; at that very moment, what is the Original Face of the Venerable One?” — as your huatou, keep it in your breast, and day and night earnestly investigate it. Investigate to the place where not a single thought arises; suddenly you will recognize your Original Face, and only then will you see that Old Lu did not deceive me.
Instructions to You Juezhi

The essence of prajñā is complete in everyone; it is only because habits are thick or thin that the obstruction is heavy or light, and so people differ as wise or foolish. Know therefore that when greed, hatred, delusion, and craving are present before you, it is the moment when the whole substance stands fully exposed — only it is turned about by turbid wisdom and is not noticed. This is what is called “daily use without knowing.” Alas! The sage is no different from the ordinary person; it is only that when the conditions before him in daily use are tangled and interwoven, he sees through them at a glance and is not deceived, blinded, or robbed by them. Seen from this, the wisdom of equality is present in every thought; like a great blaze, it makes all conditions transparent of themselves.
Instructions to the Upāsaka Wang Boxuan

The ancients often spoke of people amid the toil of the dust who have their will set upward and seek to escape birth and death — they called this “a lotus growing in fire,” because it is truly rare. For all living beings, through measureless kalpas, have wallowed in the five desires, burned by the fire of affliction, blazing day and night, never once turning the light around to gain a moment of coolness — and so it is even now. If amid the thicket of blazing flames one suddenly turns the head around and at once thinks of a way out, is that not a lotus born within the fire? Boxuan is a man of Min who came to trade in Yue, and came to pay his respects to the Elder and seek the Dharma of liberation. The Elder pitied him, gave him the five precepts, and taught him the method of Buddha-recitation, that he might devote himself single-mindedly to the Pure Land. The scripture says: “When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.” Since our own mind is the Buddha and mind alone is the land, purity and defilement are not two, and mind and Buddha are one suchness. Contemplate thus and think thus; thought after thought permeate and cultivate, and with the single mind pure, light shines forth and reflects, and the lotus Buddha-lands of the ten directions stand bright before you. Why speak only of a lotus born in a house of fire?
Instructions to the Chan Monk Jijue on His Pilgrimage to Putuo

The Chan monk Jijue was about to go east to pay homage at Putuo and begged a word to carry as the weight of his pilgrimage. The Elder instructed him, saying: The ancients left home solely for the great matter of birth and death; hence they traveled with staff in hand, visited and inquired of good teachers, climbing mountains and crossing rivers, and would not stop until they had brought about clear awakening. Those who leave home today bear the name of pilgrimage in vain: this year Wutai and Emei, next year Putuo and Funiu; with every mouth they say they are worshipping famous mountains and rejoicing in the monasteries, but in truth they do not know what a famous mountain is, or what a monastery is for. They do not even know who is a good teacher; they only remember how high and deep the mountains and waters were, and whether the gruel and rice in the monasteries was fine or coarse. They walk the whole world over and have not one word to bring home to their own mountain — is this not pitiable? The southern sea is boundless; it is the swell of the bitter sea of birth and death. The scenery of Mount Putuo is the eternal abiding of the Great One’s dharma-body. The tide resounding in the sea is the Great One’s universal gateway of teaching. If the Chan monk can truly cross the sea of birth and death, then he will behold the Great One at the universal gate and hear the sound of Dharma on the sea cliffs, turning back to hear his own nature — and he need not step outside the gate once. Why must he wait to reach Putuo before seeing? If he cannot, then the long road will be an empty going and an empty coming; even if the Great One appeared at his brow, he could not pull out the root of his birth-and-death karma. Let the Chan monk settle this for himself. And if the Great One has any words, then when you return you should repeat them to the Elder. Be careful not to waste your straw-sandal money in vain.
Instructions to Liang Zhongqian (Jiayin Year)

Liangzi, whose four marks were Zhongqian, had followed the Elder for years. The Elder loved him because his heart was upright and his spirit generous. Whenever he saw an injustice — whether or not it was his business, or wherever righteousness could be done — he would cast aside his body and life to stand in its way. The Elder often reproved him for being rough and flighty: he had the substance of the Way but lacked the work of containing and preserving it. He was like a fine horse without bit or bridle, and in the end could not avoid a fall. When the Elder was about to set out, Zhongqian escorted him to the boat at Shaoyang and asked for a word of Dharma to write on his sash. So the Elder wrote this and sent it to him. I say that Liangzi is a man of the Way: his heart is upright and not crooked — this is the root of the Way. His generosity is close to courage; his rushing to aid the urgent is close to compassion. But to forget his body and go to it is not to weigh his strength, not to examine what is fitting, not to probe the root but to attend to the branches. All this is driven by a rough and flighty temper, not issued from the power of the Way. The sages of old moved through the world with substance and function fully manifest, and so responded without missing the moment, like a bright mirror reflecting beauty and ugliness, like a balance determining weight — very far from recklessly following blood and temper. From now on, Liangzi, you should first wash away your habits and give your mind to the Way. Take the Sixth Patriarch’s huatou, “from the first not a single thing exists,” and lay it across your breast. At every moment watch the place where a thought arises; whether good or evil, give the huatou one thrust, and it perishes on the spot. Dense and unbroken, make this root huatou your own original spirit. When it has long been pure and familiar, mind and objects will naturally be empty and at leisure; in movement and stillness, in speech and action, wherever you meet anything, the huatou will be present before you — that is illumination and function clear and undistracted. Sustained by the power of samādhi, you will of yourself not fall into the realm of the rough and reckless, nor follow the heels of others. Even in reading books and writing essays this root investigation need not be hindered: when you have read and written, put it down and return it to “from the first not a single thing exists.” Then your breast will naturally be even and composed. After a long time you will suddenly see that this mind has no substance at all, as though you were within a treasury of light, and every pore of your body is the work of benefiting beings. What body or life would there then be to cast away? Working thus, containing and nurturing, the essence of mind will be present; reading a book, you will meet the sages’ minds mind to mind; writing an essay, it will flow from your own nature. This is the true accomplishment of a generous and manly person — what is called grasping the pivot at the center of the ring, to respond to the inexhaustible. Then even merit and enterprise will all become undecaying. Since Liangzi has this root, why should he fear and not do it?
Instructions to Liu Zhong’an (Winter of the Guichou Year)

I was staying at Wuyang, and for a time many followed me. I saw Liuzi: firm-boned and whole in spirit. I said that he had long planted the seeds of prajñā and that his vessel was near to the Way. I was about to travel to Nanyue, and Liuzi escorted me to the boat, where he especially asked for instruction, saying: “This disciple’s mind for the Way is most earnest, but because old habits are thick and deluded thoughts entangle him, he cannot escape straight upward. I beg the Master to instruct me.” The Elder said to him: “If you know deluded thought, then deluded thought cannot of itself entangle you. Since it is called deluded thought, it has no substantial reality; like a flower in the sky, how could it bear a fruit in the sky? Because you do not understand that deluded thought is fundamentally nonexistent, you take it as a real thing and set yourself in opposition to it, and thought after thought you wrestle with it, never having a single thought of rest. Thus you make deluded thought the master, and your own original substance is buried by it — that is why you find the Way so hard to reach. Have you not heard how a monk asked the ancient worthy, ‘What does one do when deluded thoughts do not stop?’ The worthy said, ‘Deluded thoughts are not evil.’ The Sixth Patriarch, in the assembly at Huangmei, managed only to say, ‘From the first not a single thing exists.’ From today, when you work, simply take the phrase ‘from the first not a single thing exists’ as your huatou, and day and night earnestly investigate it. Just watch where deluded thoughts arise, and on no account follow them along; give them one thrust on the spot, and they will naturally vanish without trace.”
The Dream Wanderings Collection of Elder Hanshan, Volume Five
Instructions to the Chan Monk Guanzhi Yun

One who studies the Way must first see through all the conditions of the world and not be turned about by deluded conditions. Second, he must rouse a single resolve for the great matter of birth and death, and settle it with an iron-and-stone heart, so that deluded thoughts and clinging conditions cannot seize away his will. Third, he must wash away all the bad habitual perceptions and views from before, leaving not a hair behind. Fourth, he must truly and truly let go of body and life, not allowing sickness, death, or evil conditions to obstruct him. Fifth, he must give rise to right faith and right view, and must not listen to the errors of false teachers. Sixth, he must recognize the place where the ancients applied their minds earnestly, and take it as his huatou for investigation. Seventh, in all places of daily use right mindfulness must be present before him, not deceived by illusions, mind after mind without gap, movement and stillness as one. Eighth, he must press straight ahead with his thought, and must not use the mind to wait for awakening. Ninth, he must be long-enduring: until his will reaches the field of the ancients, he will never be content to stop. He must not be satisfied with a little. Tenth, within the work, thought after thought he must let go and desist. Let go of letting go; desist from desisting. Let go until there is nothing left to let go; desist until there is nowhere left to desist — and he will naturally see good news. If a student applies his mind thus, he will come somewhat into accord with his own original matter. One whose will is directed upward should encourage himself with this.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Liaoxin Hai

We who leave home do so solely for the great matter of birth and death. To travel with staff in hand, to visit teachers and seek out friends, is only to decide the one road that goes upward from beneath one’s own feet — and not to be satisfied until it is clear. Hence the good teacher presents people with this matter alone. In recent times the Dharma gate has fallen desolate, and this spirit is seldom heard in any quarter. Wherever the pilgrim goes, there is nothing but the breath of gruel and rice. The Elder was lodging at the Linghu hermitage when the Chan monk Liaoxin came to consult him. Entering the gate, I saw that he had the nose of a patch-robed monk and seemed not to be an ordinary eater of gruel. Now he was about to return to Funiu, and so he offered incense and asked for instruction. The Elder said to him: In the Chan groves within the seas today, the first thing to rely on is the ascetic practice of Niushan; no other quarter can match it. If a student of the Way can risk and cast aside body and life, his one life will certainly not be passed in vain. As for the work of daily use, taking up a single thought of huatou is the most dense and unbroken. The reason you cannot transcend and attain great freedom is that you have been dead-set on guarding the huatou, never letting it go thought after thought, and do not know that in Chan investigation the first requirement is to shed body and mind inwardly and leave the world behind outwardly — the one point of detachment from thought. Therefore your tied-up thought becomes a bond of thought instead, and you cannot transcend into great freedom. This time, when you enter the mountain, you are fortunate to rely on the rules and the support of the assembly; it is just right to take hold of the situation and put your strength to work. Simply, within each thought, watch the place before the thought arises — this lies in the one point of detachment from thought. After a long time the thought will suddenly snap; mind and objects will both be forgotten, and you will be like a lion slipped from its rope, roaming at ease. When you next see the Elder, your eyebrows and eyes in movement and stillness will certainly not be as they are today.
Instructions to the Upāsakas of Xiangtan

While the Buddha dwelt in the world and taught the Dharma, there were the four assemblies who constantly followed him. The two who left home were the bhikṣu and the bhikṣuṇī; the two who remained at home were the upāsaka and the upāsikā. These are rendered as “male lay-server” and “female lay-server,” because, being at home and able to keep the five precepts, they can serve the Three Jewels closely and are fit to receive the benefit of Dharma. So when the Buddha-Dharma came east, people received its teaching as the times allowed, and each generation had such people. Some indeed understood the mind and saw the nature and entered the Patriarchs’ chamber. In recent times the Dharma way has long been buried, and the transmission has no eye; people bow three times at random, receive a name by routine, and call themselves disciples. In truth their fishy smell has not been spat out and their old conduct is unchanged, which gives rise to mockery and slander, brings no benefit at all, and is a great cause of destroying the Dharma. Therefore the Elder never dared to grant this lightly in his life. Now, observing the disciples of Xiangtan, their faith is sincere and deep, not the drifting of the common stream, and so I have with difficulty consented to their request. But I think that you have never before heard the Dharma; though you are called good people, you do not know what makes one good. Now, according to the Treatise on Consciousness-Only, the mental factors number fifty-one, and the wholesome dharmas are only eleven; the rest are all unwholesome mental factors. The eleven are: faith, diligence, shame, remorse, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, pliancy, non-carelessness, equanimity of action, and non-harming. With all eleven complete, one is a purely good person; lacking even one, one is deficient in virtue. If you can simply receive and keep these wholesome dharmas according to the teaching, investigate each one clearly, and at all times observe and keep them in mind — where a dharma is not yet pure and familiar, apply more of the work of grinding and polishing, and strive to make it perfectly good and only then stop — then such application of mind makes one a truly good person. What is called the good mind is simply the pure true mind. All living beings each originally possess the Tathāgata’s pure true mind, but it is defiled by evil thoughts, and so they follow feeling and create karma without knowing it. If one can now observe the good mind, then all evil dharmas will not appear before him of themselves, and the mind will be pure of itself. If you have the will to observe deeply step by step, then just investigate the Sixth Patriarch’s public case in which he taught Huiming: “Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil — at that very moment, what is the Original Face of the Venerable Ming?” Investigate it at all times; this is called the road that goes upward. Beneath your heels, who is there without a foot of ground? Press forward with effort, and you will certainly not be cheated. If you are willing to turn your hearts to the Pure Land, then rely on this method and recite the Buddha’s name with one mind; then in this life you may cut off birth and death and forever end your sinking. But I fear only that a thieving mind deceives itself and cannot do the true practice. The Elder has forced himself to speak to you thus — for pity of a three-year-old child, he does not spare his two eyebrows. On no account take this as a worldly saying to be bandied about.
Instructions to Fang Juezhi (Yimao Year)

Fangzi Juezhi was deformed in body, yet the heavenly impulse within him wondrously unfolded. He came to consult the Elder at Nanyue, and the Elder saw that his mind-light shone brightly, that he was one who had long planted the seeds of prajñā, and often showed him what lies upward. Fangzi received it in his heart as if drinking ice. Now he was about to take leave and offered incense to ask for instruction. So the Elder said to him: Fangzi, do not think that Heaven has made your nature whole while crippling your form, and count that a defect. I know that Heaven does not burden you with form, but in truth thickens your virtue. In the world those whose forms are whole are many, yet those whose forms harm their lives are more still. Who can leave form behind and put aside intellect to make his nature whole? The sage called form a burden to life and said, “The great trouble is that I have a body.” Therefore he extinguished the body and returned to non-being, so that with the form dissolved suffering ceased. Our Buddha taught living beings to take the breaking of self as the highest principle. The essentials of entering Chan do not rely on the bodily frame, nor on breath — all is left behind, and the mind is still of itself. When the mind is still, no joy can compare with it. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “You should contemplate this body as a false union of the four great elements. What is hard returns to earth, what is moist returns to water, what is warm returns to fire, what moves returns to wind. When the four great elements separate, where will this false body be?” From now on, Fangzi, day and night you should simply contemplate in this way. Contemplate to the place where not a single thought arises: then outwardly you do not see a body, inwardly you do not see a mind; body and mind are still, utterly without a single dharma. At that time you will first know that Heaven took away your false body only to make your true one whole, and your supreme joy will arrive at its utmost without waiting to forget form. Only press on and contemplate thus; one day it will be transparently clear, and you will believe that the Elder’s words are not false.
Instructions to the Secretary Zhi Hai’an (Yimao Year)

While the Elder was at Wuyang teaching the Dharma, for a time the disciples of the Dharma-nature, both monks and laypeople, who took refuge were many, and the sight of them was fine to behold — it was a matter of time and conditions. Before long, however, there was much trouble, and it was hard to gather the Dharma assembly. The Elder entered Caoxi, and many of those who had been in the assembly also withdrew. Only Zhi Hai’an, Xiu Liuyi, and Ruo Xingjiong, these three, did not leave off attending him. And when he retired in old age to Nanyue, the two, An and Yi, followed without letting go. This shows the depth of their feeling for the milk of Dharma, and their sense of duty was of the highest. The Elder dwelt in seclusion east of the lake, and before he knew it three years had passed. His daily living was extremely plain, yet the two were content; I think the followers in Chen and Cai were no better than this. Lately An, because his teacher was old, returned home to pay his respects; he offered incense and asked for instruction, wishing to beg a single word to hold in practice for life. The Elder thought to himself that he was old, and that in the Dharma which transcends the world it is truly hard to come together; the scripture says, “Like a one-eyed turtle in the great ocean meeting the hole of a floating log” — how could that be easy? Alas, you are going; you should listen carefully. The Buddha said that all living beings have realized perfect enlightenment; know then that the Buddha-nature is complete in each person, lacking not a hair. Yet living beings wander in birth and death, and for long kalpas revolve without returning, simply because they turn their backs on enlightenment and join with dust, following the stream of birth and death and pursuing the net of demons without knowing it. Because they do not know or awaken themselves, they suffer sinking in vain — exactly like a beggar holding a pearl who does not know that the wish-fulfilling jewel is in his own bosom, and casts it away, gladly enduring his loneliness. For this reason the Tathāgata called them pitiable. The Elder has always observed that your nature is straightforward, that you forget contrivance and are near the Way; but your habits are deep and thick and you cannot hold yourself, and you are often bitterly dragged along by old habits. Once you enter the snare of demons, you fall wholly, and in your suffering you do not know it; and when you suddenly recollect, you hate that you cannot leap out of birth and death. Then you busily pack up and prepare to practice, but the conditions of the Way are not yet gathered, the familiar state appears before you, habit rises again, and before you know it you follow the waves. By the time you turn your head to look after it, much time has passed. Rising and falling like this, leaning on the Elder for twenty years, in the end the great matter of birth and death beneath your own feet has no landing place at all. Why is this? Because though you have the makings of one who enters the Way, the remaining portion of this passage is corrupted in the source. In substance it continues the Elder’s instruction to Hai’an on the essentials of settling the mind, on the work of one who dwells in the mountains, and on the practice of the assembly, urging him to cut off the old habits that have kept him turning in birth and death.
Instructions to Liu Cunchi (Yimao Year)

When I had retired in old age to Nanyue, at the close of winter in the jiayin year, Liu Jizi of Chaling came from afar to consult me. On a snowy night we sat around the stove, a cold lamp shining between us. I asked how he had been applying his mind. He replied: “Formerly I received the Master’s verse: ‘A lotus is born in fire; the world calls it rare. It is not that fire bears the lotus — it is only that the mind is apart from defilement.’ Looking at this saying, I have gained some use from the last line.” The Elder was deeply pleased and instructed him, saying: That you have gained power from the line “the mind is apart from defilement” — these words are not empty, and are not easy to reach either. The scripture says: “Ordinary being and sage, worthy and saint, are equal, with no high or low; it is only that the defilement of mind is extinguished, and the attainment is like turning the palm.” Seen from this, living beings and Buddhas are originally without two; what is called mind, Buddha, and living beings — these three are without difference. But when the mind is pure, one is Buddha; when the mind is defiled, one is a living being. The distance between living being and Buddha is not far: it lies only in whether the defilement of mind is extinguished or not. This mind is originally pure, but because of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, the five desires, afflictions, and all the illusions of karma, it is sullied and obscured — hence it is called a living being. If this defilement is purified, it is then called Buddha. How could this depend on another’s power? But there is no helping it: all living beings, from beginningless time, have deep and thick karmic obstruction and firm afflictions, and it is hard for them to become pure; they must rely on the work of polishing. Hence there are the various skillful means of Chan investigation, Buddha-recitation, and looking into the huatou — all of them medicines for curing the mind. It is like the light of a mirror, bright by nature, darkened by grime; one must rely on the medicine of polishing. Yet the medicine is also grime: it is used to remove that grime, and so when the mirror is bright the medicine is no longer there. Again, true gold in the ore has sand and stone, defilement and filth; there must be a method of smelting, and when the gold is pure there is no use for the smelting. The mind-defilement of living beings is hard to leave; one must apply diligent effort to adjust and cure it. When the defilement goes and the mind is bright, it is said that living beings are originally Buddha — not that one should, while wholly within affliction and turbid defilement, falsely call oneself Buddha. The path of Chan investigation and looking into the huatou is the most essential for clarifying the mind. But in recent times few take it in hand: partly because their faculties are dull, and they lack the ancients’ dead-set mind; partly because they have no true good teacher to decide and choose for them, and so most fall into false views. Therefore the practice of cultivating Buddha-recitation and Chan investigation together is an extremely safe Dharma gate. If you take one recitation of the Buddha’s name and keep it in your breast, thought after thought pursuing and examining where it arises and where it lands, determined to see exactly where it comes to rest, then after a long time the defilement will suddenly be purified and the brightness appear, and the ground of mind will open through. This is no different from looking into a public case or huatou; but it requires pressing hard to succeed. If you bob along on deluded thoughts and pass the days idly, treating it as a matter of no importance, then even at the end of your years you will gain no use from it. If you take idly indulging deluded thoughts as your use, then you deceive yourself — not only for one life, but from now on, even to the end of kalpas, there will be no time when you are not deceived. You have a karmic affinity with the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation; try to investigate it earnestly. In truth, amid the turbid defilement of affliction, one recitation of the Buddha’s name is like a pearl that clears the water; but to use it thus is not yet to reach the very source. The scripture says: “It is like settling turbid water: the sand and soil sink of themselves and clear water appears — this is called first subduing the afflictions of guest-dust. When the mud is gone and the water is pure, it is called forever cutting off fundamental ignorance.” Simply test yourself silently with these Buddha-words, and there will be no mistake. If you can reach the place of truly leaving defilement, then, as the scripture says, “the mark of clarity is pure and undefiled, and one is not obstructed by the afflictions of guest-dust.” In that case not only will Amitābha come to welcome you; all Buddhas of the ten directions will praise you with one voice. I am fortunate to have spent this whole year’s snowy night with you; this cool and plain family style is rare in the world. If you do not betray this good meeting, then simply, from now on, never let a thought depart from coolness and plainness — this is the one path out of defilement. Press on step by step, and there will surely come the time of true liberation, of arriving home.
Instructions to Zhong Hengying

Zhong Mingsheng of Chaling came from a family of scholars of the Odes and Rites. In the past, because of trouble and hardship, he traveled to Yue and consulted me at Caoxi. The Elder enlightened him with the teaching of the retribution of good and evil and of cause and effect, and set his mind at rest so that he could return; and in the end his trouble was resolved. The resolution of it was not something that could be reached by thought and imagination; the time and conditions happened to meet, and it came of itself without intent. Thereby his old possessions were unharmed, and he trod a ground of peace and quiet, free of affairs. Yet in the end he was wholly unaware why this was so, and still thought to use his strength of mind to seek the things that in his life had not yet satisfied his heart — as though reaching into a bag for something, or picking up a mustard seed. On the last day of the jiayin year he came with Liu Cunchi from afar to comfort me and to keep me company through the turning of the year. The Elder sighed and said: What you have set your will on is like crossing the sea and fording rivers to seek sweet spring water: the spring may not be found, and the thirst will only blaze the more, and you will have the toil of the journey besides. Did I not once teach you the principle of cause and effect and retribution? Have you forgotten it? Good and evil answer like shadow to form and echo to sound; when the voice is harmonious the echo follows, when the form is upright the shadow is straight. Hence the sage did not speak of cause and effect, but only said that for the good a hundred blessings descend, and for the not-good a hundred calamities. He took settling one’s destiny and steadying one’s will as the admonition. Hence it is said: “One who does not know destiny cannot be a gentleman.” The sage teaches people to settle their destiny; the Buddha teaches people to follow conditions — the way is one. To settle one’s destiny is to have not the least need to force anything; to follow conditions is to allow not a single thought of deluded imagining. Therefore the Buddha-Dharma teaches people to take cutting off deluded thought as the root. Deluded thought is the root of all evil karma — greed, hatred, delusion, and the rest. Even a bodhisattva’s practice up to Buddhahood, and the recompense of the most excellent adornments and vast fields of merit among gods and humans, all begin from cutting off deluded thought. For when deluded thought is cut off, evil karma dissolves; when evil karma dissolves, a hundred blessings gather. This is what is called seeking much blessing for oneself. Therefore he taught him with a verse: “All worldly things from deluded thought arise; where the deluded mind dissolves, karmic bonds grow light. You need not seek a further road to bodhi — only step back, just where you stand.” Stepping back is the highest work of resting the mind and cutting off delusion. For the human mind is originally bright and vast, the source of ten thousand blessings; but it is screened by deluded marks and evil karma, and so calamity daily grows and blessing daily decreases. If now delusion dissolves and karma is cut, then the one nature is perfect and bright, and its enjoyment is boundless; to attain that place of enjoyment is true blessing. Know then that blessing is made by oneself, and truly cannot be brought about by cleverness, craft, or scheming. Moreover, by cutting off the deluded mind, the Buddha moved gods and humans to blessing. Zhong Mingsheng has the foundation for merit, fame, wealth, and honor; if he can directly rest his mind and, from the beginning, carefully examine one by one all the karma he has made in his life, then wherever there is a thought that wrongs the heart, injures principle, or is not in accord with the great Way — all of it is a root of suffering; let him spit it all out and establish a new foundation. Make a fresh effort, and take resting the mind, cutting off delusion, and awaiting the time as your single standard. Give your mind to the enterprise you already possess, and do not seek further the things of a single deluded thought. Thus you will remedy the faults of your former course; one day calamity will dissolve and blessing arrive, and merit, fame, wealth, and honor will press in upon you with no place to retreat. What need then for all kinds of deluded thought and clinging to seek elsewhere? If Zhong Mingsheng can truly believe without doubt and hold to this in practice, then even the fruit of Buddhahood may be expected — how much more the conditions of the world? Strive, strive!
Instructions to Yuan Datu

Scholars and gentry in the world who have their will set upward and give their minds to studying the Buddha often think deeply and raise themselves high, casting off worldly affairs from afar and imitating the withered-tree ascetic as wondrous practice. They do not realize that the Buddha already sharply rebuked such people, calling them scorched sprouts and rotten seeds, meaning that they cannot enter the world to benefit living beings. This is exactly what the earlier Confucians pointed to as nihility and extinction, and our Buddha would not have tolerated it long ago. What Buddhism values lies in benefiting self and benefiting others; only then is one called a bodhisattva. The Sanskrit word bodhisattva is rendered as “being of the great mind,” because such a one can enter the realm of living beings and can cut off affliction, and so earns this name. Apart from the world a bodhisattva has no practice to cultivate; apart from living beings he has no instrument for cutting off affliction. Therefore the bodhisattva relies on living beings to cut off the afflictions of his own nature. It is like the stone of another mountain, which can polish one’s jade. Affliction means greed, hatred, self-love, views, pride, and all kinds of bad habits, which obstruct the light of one’s own nature. Without all the adverse conditions and situations of living beings in the world, one cannot grind and cut them away. This is what the Odes mean by “cut and file, carve and polish.” Moreover, the Buddha’s five precepts are the five constants of the Confucians: not killing is benevolence; not stealing is righteousness; not committing sexual misconduct is propriety; not drinking wine is wisdom; not speaking falsely is faithfulness. Only because they come from the Buddha’s own mouth, the words differ while the meaning is the same. People today often make a vow to receive the Buddha’s precepts, yet of themselves neglect the five constants — they know two fives but not ten. They also exalt Chan concentration as the highest vehicle because it can clarify the mind and reveal the nature, not knowing that the Confucians have this too. When Yan Yuan asked about benevolence, the Master said, “To overcome oneself and return to propriety is benevolence.” The self is the grasping of self — is this not first breaking self-grasp as the essential of Chan cultivation? “One day overcoming oneself, and the whole world returns to benevolence” — is this not the wonder of sudden awakening? For the whole world consists of things set against oneself as opposing obstacles; if self-grasp is once broken, then all things are oneself — is not “returning to benevolence” the effect of sudden awakening? And when he asked directly for its particulars, the Master said, “Do not look, listen, speak, or move contrary to propriety” — because what one looks at, listens to, speaks, and moves among are all things and not propriety, and so they are one’s obstruction. To say “do not” means not to be turned about by sound and form; in all places not to fall into impropriety — is this not entering Chan with precepts first? But the Buddha mostly spoke in terms of leaving the world, yet what he practiced was never apart from the world; even what a bodhisattva dwelling in the world practices is no other than this. Buddha means awakened: to be able to awaken this mind is to be named Buddha; it is not that apart from this pure mind one seeks another Buddha. It is just that living beings’ bad habits and obstructions are heavy and their minds are hard to purify; therefore the skillful means of Buddha-recitation is established, and the Dharma gate of seeking birth in the Pure Land. And it is said, “When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.” Know then that Buddha-recitation is indeed a wondrous practice for purifying the mind. But Buddha-recitation is fundamentally for purifying the mind; if one recites the Buddha’s name and yet one’s mind is not pure, what is the use of reciting? If one keeps the precepts while turning one’s back on the five constants, what is the use of the precepts? Master Yuan has his will set on the Way and has formed a fellowship to cultivate the pure karma together — this surely issues from good roots long planted. He came to see the Elder and firmly asked to receive the precepts. The Elder instructed him, saying: The precepts are originally complete in one’s own nature. If you truly believe the Elder’s words and purify your own mind, then the precepts are already received, Chan is already cultivated, the Pure Land is already entered, and the bodhisattva’s wondrous practice, the worldly and world-transcending dharmas, and the two benefits are all complete — none of it goes beyond this. Strive at it, sir.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Shuanglun Zhao

The Chan monk Shuanglun Zhao came to consult me, saying that he intended to withdraw into the mountains and investigate the matter that goes upward alone, and asking the Elder for the method of dwelling in the mountains. So the Elder instructed him, saying: For the ancients, dwelling in the mountains was a place of great renunciation of body and life — by no means a small matter. It requires above all that one be good at using the mind. As for the method of using the mind: first, take up the single thought that goes upward and plant your stance firmly at the place where Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot allow you. Next, you must spit out all the knowledge and views and the wondrous words and wondrous sayings in your breast, as so much mixed poison. Next, you must recognize that the original substance is utterly without a single dharma, and must not let the shadows of deluded thought and habit produce all kinds of states that confuse and disorder right mindfulness. Next, you must look into your root huatou — such as the Sixth Patriarch’s public case, “not thinking of good, not thinking of evil; what is your Original Face?” — and hold it up with all your strength. Whenever any bad habit appears before you, at once see through it with the phrase “from the first not a single thing exists.” On no account follow it on in unbroken succession; clench your teeth, for here you must hold your ground, and only then will you not be shaken or robbed by it. Using the mind thus is the place of effort when you are alert. If you use the mind with too much effort, then laziness arises and drowsiness sets in. At such a time you must simply brighten up quickly and not fall into the pit of torpor. You must quickly recite a mantra: relying on the power of the mantra, you can match this demon. For in the storehouse consciousness there are bad habits from many kalpas, and now they are squeezed out by the huatou and transform into inexhaustible states. All demonic states arise from deluded thought; all torpor arises from scatteredness. Just when you are using the mind rightly, a single scattered thought at once falls into torpor — this you must know well. Yongjia’s fourfold criterion of stillness and alertness is the most essential. The ancients, in using the mind, simply leaned steadily on one phrase of root huatou, as if it were an iron wall and a silver mountain. If you reach the place where not a single thought arises, that too is a sign of power, but do not take it as the ultimate. Only when the work goes on effortlessly and no longer depends on thought, and with one thought it opens clear and body and mind seem to fall away empty — only that is the place where the work takes hold; and even that is not yet the ultimate. But if you can reach this, you will naturally be light and at ease and will give rise to joy. Yet this is only the original matter, not something extraordinary. If you give rise to the thought that it is extraordinary, you fall into the demon of joy, and you will start producing groundless wild knowing and wild understanding. This pass is the most dangerous; these are things the Elder has tested. The ancients said: “Before the withered tree and the cliff, wrong roads are many; travelers who reach here all stumble away their time.” This is no small matter. Even if you have the strength to fight through all kinds of states, that is just the time to practice and the time to protect; it is not yet arriving home.
