If you take this as enough, you will start giving rise to thoughts of all the worldly conditions of the five desires. This pass is hard to cross; of those who cross it, not one or two in a hundred. That is why one does not reach the ancients’ field — it is precisely the fault of being satisfied with a little. Even if a student works bitterly for a lifetime and reaches this ground, if he is dragged off by such bad habits he still falls into the pit of birth and death, and all his previous work is lost. Is this not lamentable? Sayings such as this are not few in the records of the ancients. The Elder has picked out a few, because in the Dharma-ending age it is hard to find a true student of the Way — it is also that, having once been a prodigal myself, I pity the traveler. On the whole, the ancients’ dwelling in the mountains was not to nurse laziness and seek comfort; it was solely for the great matter of their own birth and death. Therefore they went into ten thousand layers of cold cliffs and made their living without any device. If one dawdles away the days here and wastes the light of time for nothing, is that not still more pitiable? Nevertheless, the differences in using the mind you now know. As for the shifting conditions before you in the mountains — the water flowing, the wind moving, gibbons crying, birds calling, clouds rising, mist gathering, crowding before you, even more clamorous — Yongjia’s saying about seeing the Way and forgetting the mountain must be seen through. When the Elder first dwelt at Longmen in Wutai, beneath ten-thousand-fathom cold cliffs, in piles of ice and snow, I was like a dead man buried; the cold pierced to the bone and penetrated all five organs, and only a faint breath remained, and I watched it come and go through the ice. At this point, turning the light back, I sought the place where a single thought of my own mind arose and could not find it. This state is exactly a condition that aids the Way. Again, when the great wind blew, ten thousand apertures roared with rage, day and night without rest; and when the snow melted and the torrents ran, the sound was like rolling thunder, and again like a thousand troops and ten thousand horses galloping. Such confused states were hardest to bear at first. Then I thought of the ancients’ saying: “If one listens to the sound of water for thirty years without turning the faculty of mind, one may be permitted to enter the Way.” So the Elder made a furious resolve and sat and stood on a single-plank bridge, listening to the sound of the water all day. At first it was clattering and hard to dissolve; after a long time it was indeed suddenly stilled. From then on all states were stilled. What is called “the ten thousand states are originally at leisure; it is only people who make their own clamor” — this again is the first piece of work for a person of the Way dwelling in the mountains. Let the Chan monk remember it and not neglect it.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Zhuanyu Heng (Bingchen Year)

The road that goes upward is the original matter of one who has left home. When the ancients set out to surpass the ordinary, it was only to investigate this matter clearly. In recent times people generally do not know what leaving home is for; how can one expect them to be like the ancients? The Chan monk Zhuanyu Heng first relied on Master Kongyin of Wutai and studied the scriptures and treatises. After a long time he swept them all aside and took up the single thought, earnestly investigating his original matter. He traveled ten thousand li to the south, passed through Caoxi, and paid his respects to the Elder, asking for instruction. The Elder told him: If in this matter you do not put down body and mind and investigate with bitter effort to the place where the water runs out and the mountains end, there will in the end be no landing place. And even if you reach the place where the water runs out and the mountains end, the ancients called this “still, sunken, dead water,” and also “the wondrous nest.” If you do not turn your head and turn your brain around, then what is before you will be like an iron wall and a silver mountain — that is only the time of power, not the place of use. The ancients’ use of mind was not to die all the way to the bottom; one must be able to come alive within death. The essential is to turn the mechanism and shift the position. Therefore it is said: “The one who sits at the top of a hundred-foot pole has indeed entered, but is not yet real. Let him step forward from the top of the hundred-foot pole, and the whole universe appears in his body.” When a student reaches this, he must simply turn around and walk another road, and only then will it not become an obstruction to him. The Chan monk assented, bowed, and departed. He went to cut thatch at Nanyue. Before long the Elder too came dragging his staff, and asked after the monk, who had been harried by the demon of sickness and had already gone to Baoqing for medical treatment. Hearing this the Elder sighed and said: The Chan gate is in decline, and a student who truly works for birth and death is the hardest thing to find. Now this man has this illness — is it that the dragons and gods are weary of the Dharma gate? On the first day of the third month of spring in the bingchen year, at midnight amid wind and rain, the monk suddenly came, braving the rain and plunging through the mud. The Elder was overjoyed to see him and said: This is not something a sick man could do. Seeing the fresh, clear spirit in his brows and face, he knew that his illness was eight or nine parts cured. Then the monk again offered incense and asked for instruction. The Elder specially taught him, saying: Your demon of sickness is your great good teacher, a condition that aids the Way. Do you know this? Consider: the sickness of living beings lies in having a self. Because they grasp a self, all afflictions and all sicknesses arise from it. When sickness arises, suffering must follow. From ancient times to now there is no one who is not sick in this way; only the person who knows that sickness is sickness is not sickened by it. Moreover, this body is a false union of the four great elements; what is gathered must scatter. Even if you were not ill now, would you not in fact be ill? If you understand that the sick one is not sick, then sickness cannot sicken him. You know today’s illness, but you do not know that through many lives and kalpas, illness after illness has come down to today. If you do not settle today’s illness, then from now on you will not know where illness ends. You know the sickness of birth and death, but you do not know that you must escape the sickness of birth and death — and that is a much greater sickness than birth and death itself. Why? The ancients said that if Chan investigation does not get out of the realm of the aggregates but falls into the pit of consciousness and feeling, then even a wondrous awakening becomes the view of self. If one grasps the four great elements as self, the sickness can still be treated. But if one leaves the four great elements and still grasps a self, this sickness leaves even the king of physicians helpless; it is the hardest of all to cure. All Buddhas and Patriarchs came into the world expressly to cure this one disease of the vital organs. They spent how much effort, yet how many are there who are willing to take the medicine and be cured? The monk’s bodily illness is cured — on no account let him be invaded by the illness of Chan. Yunmen said the dharma-body has two kinds of illness. He said that one may pass through the dharma-body, but if the grasping of dharmas is not forgotten and one’s own views still remain, that too is illness — a strong statement about the illness of clinging and grasping. Let the Chan monk spit out all the wondrous words and wondrous sayings he formerly held, along with the merit he has accumulated in clinging to Chan investigation, until not a single bad perception or bad habit remains. Then it will surely not grow into a root of illness. It will even leave the Buddhas and Patriarchs with no place to stand. Have you not heard of the youth Sudhana, who traveled south through a hundred cities and consulted fifty-three great good teachers, each bestowing a different Dharma gate, and in the end came only to being equal to the dharma-realm, equal to space? Was there ever a real dharma to which he was tied? And have you not heard of Vairocana, whose dharma-body is no body, but who takes the wondrous practice of Samantabhadra as his body? Samantabhadra has no practice; he takes the practice of living beings as his practice. Therefore it is said: “What bodhi takes as its condition is living beings in suffering; if there were no living beings, there would be no bodhi.” This is the true model of how the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the lineage came into the world. Therefore the Elder said to the monk: Your body of four great elements is sick, and only the demon of sickness can cure it; the illness of Chan pierces the heart, and only living beings can cure it. From today on, simply make your body equal to the great earth, and the demon of sickness will hide its traces; make your mind equal to living beings, and the view of self will not stand. When the view of self does not stand, the illness of Chan dissolves of itself. For when the mind does not take itself as mind, it is fundamentally unborn; being unborn, not a single dharma is established. If not a single dharma is established, what dharma is there to become an obstruction of views? The ancients said: “It is easy to renounce feeling; it is hard to renounce dharmas.” When the monk renounces body he renounces feeling; when he renounces views he renounces dharmas. With feeling and dharmas both forgotten, will he not be a person of great unobstructed liberation? Alas, I am old, and to meet again will be hard. Strive, monk.
Instructions to Li Fujing

Li Yingzhen of Lingling asked for instruction on the purport of mind and nature. So the Elder taught him, saying: What are mind and nature? They are the great root of all sages and ordinary beings, of all living things. Because the substance is the same while the function differs, there is the difference between delusion and awakening, and hence the distinction between the real and the deluded. It is said that the three realms are mind only and the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only. Because one mind is deluded, it becomes consciousness; and consciousness is purely the functioning of delusion, pursuing objects and clinging to conditions, no longer knowing the true mind that is originally possessed. But if one knows that the true is originally possessed and understands that the deluded is fundamentally nonexistent, then one can return from delusion to the real, and from the realm of living beings one may at once enter the realm of the Buddha. When Bodhidharma came from the west, he transmitted only the mind-seal, the Dharma gate of sudden awakening — precisely awakening suddenly to this mind. This is the purport of the Chan school concerning mind, nature, the real, and the deluded. As for what our Confucians revere, the mind and nature transmitted by Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius: they say, “Only the refined, only the one,” taking refinement and oneness as the ultimate principle, and they distinguish the human mind from the mind of the Way — this too is a distinction between the real and the deluded. Only the teaching of the world does not go beyond this. What they call the mind of the Way is the nature that is not deluded and not false; what they call the human mind is the nature deluded into feeling. People in the world know only how to use feeling, not how to use nature; they know only the waves, not that the waves are originally water. Therefore Confucius said: “Natures are near; habits carry them far apart.” When nature is near, the water originally has no waves; when habit carries one far, one pursues the waves and forgets the water. One does not even know the water — how much less does one understand that the nature of wetness is without two? Take one body of water: mix it with salt, sour, bitter, and pungent, and its bland nature is lost, yet its wet nature is fundamentally without two. Know then that the many flavors are transformations of the deluded, while the wet nature cannot be transformed. What cannot be transformed is real; what can be transformed is deluded. If one understands that the wet nature is without two, then the many flavors cannot be had. This is what is meant by “Yao and Shun are the same as other people”: what is the same is the nature, what is not the same is the delusion. It is also said, “Everyone can be a Yao or a Shun.” What can be is the nature; what cannot be is habit. As for people’s habits, if one abandons the low and defiled and inclines to the high and bright, then daily one moves away from one’s habits and nearer to the nature — and it is by this habit too that one can become a Yao or a Shun. Habit nearing the nature is what the Chan school means by gradual cultivation. Because the learning of the worldly Confucians has not left the ordinary and near and is still far from the sage, without gradual advance one cannot reach the utmost. Therefore the sage established his teaching with only “habit,” “arriving,” and “overcoming”; his work of entering the Way lies in gradual restoration, and he did not speak of sudden awakening. But the Chan gate sets aside the love of wife and children and removes the desire for wealth and honor; with all burdens already released, one is close to the Way. Therefore the work of restoring the nature is easy to accomplish, and so it is called sudden awakening. Because the ground on which one stands differs, the cultivation is easy or hard. In truth, as for mind and nature in a person, there is fundamentally no difference of sudden or gradual; one speaks only of the thickness or thinness of habitual defilement. This is the essential of entering the Way. If one investigates the subtlety of mind and nature and traces it to its source: what Chan takes as its root is the unborn and undying; what the Confucians take as their root is birth and death. Hence it is said, “Generation and regeneration is called the Changes.” This is the distinction between the roots of Confucianism and Buddhism. The doctrine of mind and nature lies here. As for the one point that goes upward in the Chan gate, it transcends speech and language, and does not take mind and nature as a real dharma either.
Instructions to the Censor Jia Huanran, Who Asked for Guidance

The Buddhas came into the world, yet there is no dharma they could speak; the Patriarch came from the west, yet he had no real dharma to give people. It was only to smash, as was fitting, the various inverted and clinging feelings of living beings, to make them let go of clinging and suddenly awaken to what they originally possess. Because living beings’ minds of deluded clinging are firm and hard to break, and are further deepened by beginningless ignorance, affliction, and karmic obstruction, sudden awakening is hard to attain; hence our Buddha spent forty-nine years and measureless skillful means establishing the dharma of cutting off delusion and realizing the truth. From ordinary being to sage, he set up fifty-five stages of gradation. It is not that the World-Honored One liked to make such arrangements and spend his grandmotherly heart. Because the sicknesses of living beings’ minds are measureless, the prescriptions to match them are measureless too. When one arrives at ultimate reality, until knowing and seeing are utterly extinguished and not a single dharma is established, only then is it the ground of arriving home. If even a hair of knowing and seeing is not forgotten, one is still outside the gate, lodging in a thatched hut. Cast it away and cast it away until there is nothing left to cast away — and even then, this is still a matter on the side of the dharma-body, not the matter of the dharma-body going upward. It is only the utmost limit of the teaching schools, not the utmost limit of the Chan gate. Seen thus, is practice a careless thing, to be taken as attainment on the strength of a half-understanding? Moreover, in the Chan gate before the Sixth Patriarch the work of investigation was not spoken of; only sudden awakening here and now was valued. From Nanyue and Qingyuan onward, people’s faculties were not uniform, and most relied on investigation and nurturing. When the five houses were established, their gateways and arrangements differed, but the essential purport within them was originally without difference. As for responding to capacities and receiving people, they were like the Qin mirror on its stand, reflecting through to the liver and gall. As for loosening people’s adhesions and removing their bonds, pointing directly to the dharma-body and the road that goes upward, and wiping out the knowing and seeing of Buddha-Dharma — until the source was exhausted and the bottom reached, they absolutely would not let it pass lightly. In the time when the Chan way was greatly flourishing there were many clear-eyed teachers in the world, and students of the Way consulted and verified everywhere, so that those who awakened did not fall into false views. By the Song and Yuan, though teachers were many, students’ false views were not few: if they did not fall into birth and death, they fell into the view of emptiness, having substance but no function, like the two vehicles’ one-sided emptiness. Some even denied cause and effect and fell into the outsiders’ libertine nihilism. Or their awakening of mind was not thorough, and seeing a mere glimmer they were satisfied with a little, calling themselves bodhisattvas, talking of emptiness with every mouth while their minds clung to existence, and so creating the karma of birth and death without knowing it. In all such cases they had no clear-eyed teacher to examine and press them; hence the Chan gate withered. The ancients said, “It is not that there is no Chan; it is only that there are no teachers” — this is what they meant. On the whole, in the Dharma-ending age those who investigate Chan and are satisfied with a little are many. Even if there is a true student willing to work with a dead-set hand, unchanging in his will for ten or five years, and he comes to understand that his own mind is utterly empty, because he has no clear teacher to verify him he falls into the view of emptiness. Or his consciousness-spirit is not yet broken and he falls into the doorway of lights and shadows. Or his habits are not yet pure, and pressed by the work they manifest all kinds of states, which he takes for the wondrous functioning of spiritual powers. Or he sees Buddhas and bodhisattvas appear and teach the Dharma, or gains knowledge of others’ minds and of past lives and can see future events, or gives rise to all kinds of strange views. All these are transformations of habit; if one takes them as extraordinary, one falls into the demonic path. It is a pity that a whole stretch of work should do no small harm. All this comes from not meeting a clear teacher and not knowing the skillful means of cultivating the mind in the Buddha’s teaching, and so one falls into error. There are also those who truly investigate and truly awaken, clearly seeing that their own mind is utterly without a single dharma, but who cannot open the true eye at the crown of the head, and so sit in the place of bare nakedness, red and scattered, pure and clean and utterly without a point. This is called clinging to the top of the pole, still sunken dead water. Hence it is said: “The one who sits at the top of a hundred-foot pole has indeed entered, but is not yet real. Let him step forward from the top of the hundred-foot pole, and the whole universe appears in his body.” It is also said: “Where there is a Buddha, do not linger; where there is no Buddha, pass on quickly.” This is precisely to teach people that they must not sit inside the armor of no-affairs and then say there is no Buddha to attain and no living being to save — for this falls precisely into the view of annihilation and cannot leave this view of emptiness. Even if one reaches this, it is still a matter on the side of the dharma-body, not the matter of the dharma-body going upward. Have you not heard Yunmen say: “When you reach the side of the dharma-body, there seems dimly to be something there; this too is light not fully penetrating. Even if you penetrate it, to let it go is still not permitted”? These words are truly a mirror for cultivating the mind and seeing into the heart. Hence the ancients said: “The word ‘awakened’ must be spat out.” Know that the Buddhas and Patriarchs taught the Dharma with one flavor only: to dispel living beings’ clinging feelings. What is called simply exhausting ordinary feeling, with no other sagely understanding. If one makes a sagely understanding of it, one at once receives the host of demons. The fifty kinds of skandha-māras in the Śūraṅgama Sutra are not idle words. If practitioners today have no clear teacher to point the way and do not rely on the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ teachings for verification, what shall they use as their evidence? Originally, because living beings clung to existence, the Buddha broke their view of existence. Because the two vehicles and the outsiders clung to emptiness, the Buddha broke their view of emptiness. Because bodhisattvas clung to the two extremes of emptiness and existence, the Buddha taught neither emptiness nor existence to break the view of the two extremes. And when they entered the Buddha-Dharma, he further dispelled their Buddha-view and Dharma-view. Hence he dispelled until there was nothing to dispel. This is precisely “not seeing a single dharma is the Tathāgata.” Have you not heard of Sudhana, who consulted fifty-three great good teachers, entering the fifty-three Dharma gates and the Buddha’s realm, and who did not speak of the matter of becoming a Buddha, but only said “equal to space, equal to the dharma-realm, equal to Vairocana”? And when he met the bodhisattva Samantabhadra, the latter then taught him the ten kinds of conduct and vows. This is the great model of practicing the Way and learning Buddhahood: one does not treat post-awakening as a matter of no further affairs. If people today, though they can awaken thoroughly to the dharma-realm, do not learn Sudhana’s cultivation of Samantabhadra’s great conduct, in the end they cannot avoid falling into the outsiders’ view of emptiness. Should one not fear this? The tangled vines above are spoken especially for those who practice without much learning and wisdom, who apply their minds wrongly and cannot enter the Buddha’s knowing and seeing; hence I could not avoid wagging my tongue. If you regard them as idle words, you will not only betray this old monk but greatly deceive yourselves.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Yujue

The two Chan monks Huiyu and Huijue of Qiyang consulted the Elder at Ziyun Mountain in Huangmei. They said that in their minds birth and ceasing went on without a moment’s pause, like wild horses, and they especially sought instruction: how should they subdue their minds? The Elder taught them, saying: A student practices for the great matter of birth and death. Because thought after thought in the mind does not stop, birth and death are unbroken. If you truly want to end birth and death, you must let go of all ten thousand conditions utterly, until they are clean and gone. But there are seeds of beginningless habit that cannot be cleaned away; you must investigate a huatou. There are such things on paper, but you do not know the method for the difficulty or ease of taking it in hand; you must consult a good teacher, who will teach you the skillful means, because he has walked that road and knows the easy place to enter. For example, the Sixth Patriarch, hearing “let the mind arise without dwelling on anything,” awakened on the spot. People in the world do not understand this and take it as some wondrous principle. It was originally nothing wondrous: because he formerly had dwelling, and now heard of non-dwelling, he let go at that moment and so awakened. What is wondrous about it? Take Master Yongming: formerly he applied his mind to Buddha-recitation and could not enter; later, before Weituo, he drew lots and obtained Buddha-recitation. People in the world take Chan as a principle to be discussed, not knowing that Chan is one’s own mind. The scripture says, “unborn and undying” — this is it. If you want to understand the great matter of birth and death, know that the precepts are honored and you must never dare to transgress them. First you must have the strength of faith, a willing mind, and a firm resolve, and put down all wondrous words and wondrous principles, worldly affairs, and human feelings. This one point of Chan investigation is originally without anything wondrous or extraordinary. This matter is extremely simple — will you believe it? If you truly will, then simply put down all your former deluded thoughts at once and do not allow them to creep up. Slowly take up one recitation of Amitābha Buddha and lean on it steadily. You must watch where this thought arises, like letting down a fishing line into a deep pool. If deluded thoughts arise again, it is because beginningless habit is too heavy; you must let go again. On no account use the mind to cut off deluded thoughts; simply straighten your backbone, do not think east or west, and look fixedly right at the place where the deluded thought arises. Let go and let go again; slowly raise the Buddha’s name once more, and firmly watch where this one recitation of the Buddha ultimately arises from. After five or seven recitations the deluded thoughts will not arise. Then bring down the doubt: examine just who it is that recites the Buddha’s name. People in the world take this as a mere phrase; they do not know that only here, in bringing down this doubt, lies the place of power. If deluded thoughts arise again, then shout “Tut!” and just ask who it is — and the deluded thought will at once vanish without trace. The Buddha said, “Except when sleeping, always gather the mind.” When sleeping you cannot gather the mind; as soon as you wake, take up the huatou. Not only when sitting, but walking, standing, drinking tea and eating, in movement and stillness, do the same. In a dense crowd, do not see that there are people; amid all movements, do not see that there is movement. Thus you will gradually have a place of entry, and the seventh consciousness will not function here. Lean steadily on it day and night thus, not counting the effort, and one day the eighth consciousness will suddenly burst open and expose your Original Face — that is the time of ending birth and death, and only then will you not betray the resolve with which you left home. But when investigating Chan, do not seek awakening. Let the Buddha come, let the Patriarch come, let demons come — simply do not move. Take up the single thought and walk on; let there be no further doubt in between. Thus dense and unbroken, mind after mind without gap, put forth effort in daily use, and there will surely be a landing place.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Mingyi

A student does not know the road that goes upward, but seeks only to increase his knowledge and views. He does not realize that to establish knowing upon knowing is the root of ignorance. This is not knowing what one originally possesses, and rushing out to seek it elsewhere, wishing further to increase one’s clarity. But if one clarifies that clarity, then clarity too is not established — what increase is there? Hence it is said, “In pursuit of learning one daily increases.” Whoever speaks of learning looks for a nest of comfort in someone else’s house. Even if he finds it, it is in the end not his own. Since it is not his own, the joy is not true joy; and if the joy is not true, how can he be at peace in it? To seek peace outside oneself is the common disease of students since ancient times, not only today. The Chan monk Mingyi asked for instruction. Would he say there is no benefit, and wish to clarify it? Or that there is benefit, and wish to clarify it? If you say there is no benefit, then with no benefit there is no need. If you say there is benefit, then since there is already benefit, why need clarify it? Try to see from what clarity is clarified and from what benefit benefits. If you seek to clarify your clarity, you lose the original clarity; if you seek still more benefit, it turns into no benefit. Whoever seeks benefit is like a man already full who still craves the flavor, and so harms his digestion and brings on illness. If he can vomit up what he has eaten, he may recover without medicine. If he guards his illness and avoids the doctor, it will end in a lump and a stoppage. Whoever is sick in this way, even Bian Que and Li Zhu could not cure. Why? To crave food and not vomit it is the first illness; to nurse the illness and hide the disease is the second; when the illness is full-blown, to avoid the doctor is the third; to go further and hate the medicine is the fourth; to seek a quick effect, distrusting the prescription that cures the root, and so to doubt the doctor and abandon the medicine is the fifth; and to take poison by mistake from a quack doctor, so that life is harmed — this is the incurable category. A student who abandons his original clarity and rushes out to seek, increasing his knowledge and views, is mostly like this. How sad! When I was young, each time I read the parable of the physician I never failed to repeat the sage’s teaching three times. I observe that students in recent times, as soon as they become novices, can recite this — yet in old age they do not know the source, and so there is no limit to those who waste their lives for nothing. This is the fault of not understanding. There are also those who seek clarity but mistakenly force the unclear to be clear for them — truly the fault of not reaching the root. The Buddha said: “Rest the mind and reach the root; therefore one is called a śramaṇa.” If a student can rest the mind and reach the root, clarity need not be sought outside and benefit need not be much increased; the self-nature is complete — where has it ever been deficient? If the Chan monk Mingyi can truly know this and at once spit out all the many places he formerly sought, then, like a man whose food-injury has left no residue in his belly, his original vitality will restore itself. When a student scrapes away knowing and seeing, he may be called a person of the Way with no affairs. Try carefully to examine the bellyful of sour stuff you had before, and see what flavor it has. Investigate! Investigate!
Instructions to the Chan Monk Huileng

The Chan monk was born and grew up in the town of Xiu. When young he traded on the rivers and lakes, and because he wearied of the dust and vulgarity he went to Mount Kuang and took the tonsure under Master Xufang. The Elder came from Nanyue to spend the summer at Jinzhu. The monk offered incense and asked for instruction. So the Elder taught him, saying: You have been able to renounce the world’s affection and love; your body has left home, but your mind does not yet understand what leaving home means. Formerly our Buddha, the World-Honored One, gave up the golden wheel, abandoned the royal palace, entered the Snow Mountains, and practiced austerities for six years; seeing the morning star he awakened to the Way, accomplished perfect enlightenment, and became the teacher of the three realms, revered by the six paths, honored and supported by gods and humans, saving all living beings and bringing them out of birth and death together. This is the very first model of leaving home. Seen thus, is leaving home a matter of stealing ease and nursing laziness, prizing ready-made comfort? There must be an original matter in it. The Patriarchs of the lineage left home for the great matter of birth and death; as for traveling with staff in hand and consulting good teachers, it was especially to bring the mind-ground to clarity and to pull out by the root the plant of birth and death accumulated through measureless kalpas, so as to transcend the three realms and forever leave the bitter destinies — this is benefiting oneself. Afterward, when the dragons and gods pushed one forth and one established the Three Jewels, that is benefiting others. With the two benefits complete, this is the original matter of leaving home. Today, monk, you have left home — have you known of this matter? Have you known the great matter of birth and death? What is birth and death? It is this present body and mind of the five aggregates, gathered from beginningless kalpas with every kind of seed of habit — greed, hatred, delusion, pride, aversion, and craving. The mind that day by day gives rise to delusion and creates karma is originally the Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature, a seed of light; now it is covered by ignorance and affliction, and one does not know it in daily use. Thus to be deluded about this Buddha-nature is birth and death; to awaken to this Buddha-nature and at once cut off affliction and escape birth and death is to be a true child of the home-leaver. Seen thus, leaving home is a great man’s matter of ending birth and death, not the enjoyment of comfort or the prizing of ease. To refuse to practice, to not seek to clarify the mind and see the nature, is to consume the offerings of the faithful in vain and to invite in return the suffering of repayment in a future life. What leaving home is there in that? Monk, from what birth, by what conditions, by what fortune have you met a clear teacher to save and liberate you, and dwell at ease in a famous mountain’s monastery with Dharma companions in harmony? And again, how fortunate to meet a good teacher to guide and instruct you! If you do not give rise to deep rejoicing and great shame, and resolve with firm will to practice and seek to escape birth and death, then you abandon yourself — like going to a mountain of treasures and returning empty-handed. Is that not pitiable? Monk, if you are willing to rouse your will and practice, you must first cut off at once all your former afflictions, aversion, craving, and habits; single-mindedly seek only the one point of ending birth and death; and take the single phrase “Amitābha Buddha” and keep it in your breast as your own root of life, mind after mind unbroken. Recite until the flower opens and you see the Buddha: that is the true time of ending birth and death and truly leaving home. If you do not take the Elder’s words and rouse true faith, you will be avoiding drowning by jumping into fire; this life will be missed, and when will there be a time of getting out? Think for yourself and encourage yourself. Do not neglect it.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Banji Wen

The Chan monk studied the examinations’ learning in his youth, but had the will to leave the world. At forty he abandoned wife and children and paid homage to Master Guoqing Zhan, a disciple of Elder Zibo, and was ordained at Guizong. Guizong was the Chan cave where the venerable elders of old established the banner of Dharma, and the Buddha’s relics are there. Know then that the conditions of the monk’s leaving home were excellent and the place he dwells in is excellent; it is only that he has not roused an excellent mind. Guizong had long been in ruins. When Master Zibo passed that way he was grief-stricken and sorrowful; seeing a withered pine half broken by axe and bill, the Master in compassion chanted a spell and banked earth about it, hoping it would flourish again, and using it to divine whether the monastery would be rebuilt. Within a few years its bark and wood were whole again. Thereupon Master Zhan resolutely raised it anew. When people far and near heard of it, there was none who did not look up in wonder and follow. The layman Xing Laici vowed his heart to lead the way. A few more years passed, and the present Emperor was moved to bestow the imperial canon to glorify the famous mountain; and so the halls and pavilions were completed. Then the Elder Jianyin raised funds to make a great Vairocana image to settle and secure it. From this the Three Jewels had two of their number; only the Jewel of the Saṅgha was not yet gathered, and so it was not enough to spread the way of Dharma. In the eighth year since the monk left home, the Elder came from Nanyue on a visit and paid homage to the relics on the summit of the Golden Wheel Peak. He saw the excellence of its mountains and streams, and inquired into the hardship of its restoration: the halls and pavilions were built, but a Chan dwelling was not yet made, and it was still a desolate place. Laici had indeed labored bitterly to protect the Dharma, but the work of carrying it out is the business of our own followers. If the monks do not press forward to do it, they betray the intention of its founding; I fear that if Zibo and Jiguang have spirits, they will not close their eyes. Therefore he earnestly urged and encouraged the assembly, and Jianyin and the monk became its leaders. Hearing this, the monk at once roused an excellent mind, universally converted the great donors, and adorned the Buddha-land; then he shouldered his staff and left the mountain. As he was about to set out he asked for instruction. The Elder, wishing to firm his vow, joyfully taught him, saying:

Though you have left home, you have not yet heard of the practice that transcends the world. Formerly our original teacher Śākyamuni gave up the position of a golden-wheel king, hid his light in the Snow Mountains, and practiced austerities for six years, thereby accomplishing perfect enlightenment and becoming the teacher of gods and humans. In truth, through long distant kalpas he had broadly cultivated merit and wisdom. Hence it is said that in the three-thousand great-thousand world-system there is no place the size of a mustard seed where the bodhisattva did not give up body and life for living beings. As for giving away head, eyes, brains, and marrow as one casts off spittle — this was not for one or two kalpas, but through measureless kalpas, life after life, birth after birth, such bitter practice. Only then did he win a body and land of excellent marks and wondrous adornment. Even the single bowl of rice of a Dharma-ending disciple today was bought with the Tathāgata’s body, life, bones, and blood, and left for his children and grandchildren to enjoy. Seen thus, we who have left home, with clothing and food ready-made and dwelling at ease in comfort — how can we lightly consume it? If one does not think of repaying the Buddha’s kindness, embodying the Buddha’s mind, practicing the Buddha’s practice, and managing the Buddha’s household affairs, then though named a home-leaver, one is in truth provisioning the implements of suffering in the three evil paths. What is meant by embodying the Buddha’s mind? The mind of great compassion. By practicing the Buddha’s practice? The mind of patience and forbearance. By the Buddha’s household affairs? Widely practicing the six pāramitās, accomplishing the two adornments, establishing the Three Jewels, and spreading the transformation of Dharma. If one does not do thus, one is not a disciple of the Buddha but a thief, stealing the Buddha’s robe to nourish the root of one’s own suffering. What benefit is there in leaving home like that? As for the two adornments of merit and wisdom: to resolve to awaken the seed of prajñā, to understand and penetrate one’s own mind and wondrously accord with the Buddha’s mind — this is called wisdom. To broadly practice the pāramitā of giving, adorn the land, and bring living beings to accomplishment — this is called merit. Hence it is said, “Merit and wisdom both complete, one is called the doubly-honored one.” Therefore I now urge the monk, first, to resolve to seek prajñā, to understand and awaken his own mind, and so to escape the bitter sea of birth and death; and second, to broadly practice all practices, universally converting the ten directions and adorning the Buddha-lands, and so to accomplish the pure karma of the Pure Land. Apart from these two practices there is nothing to cultivate. Yet the Buddha said that teaching and converting living beings is precisely adorning the Buddha-land. For the living beings of the great earth are drowned in the bitter sea of greed and desire and all create the bitter karma of birth and death, sunk for long kalpas with no way out of themselves; hence they bring about the implements of suffering of the three realms and three paths. They depend on the Three Jewels as their field of merit, in which to plant the seed of prajñā as the cause and condition of their own enjoyment in other lives. But this must rely on the Jewel of the Saṅgha to open and guide them. Therefore we disciples of the Buddha, if we can convert one person to rouse an excellent mind and break his stinginess and greed, then one person purifies his own mind and adorns one person’s Buddha-land. Convert many, and one adorns many people’s Buddha-lands. If one can convert the whole great earth and make everyone rouse the mind, then one perfects everyone’s Buddha-land. This is to turn a defiled land into a Pure Land and transform implements of suffering into implements of joy — is this not the most excellent and supreme wondrous practice? The monk is going. Take a few words of the Elder and go; then you are a heroic man. At once rouse the vast and great mind. Like the butcher Broad-Brow, who put down his cleaver and straightway did the Buddha’s work; or like the eight-year-old dragon girl who, in the instant of offering her jewel, attained bodhi. There will surely be those who can break the bag of stinginess and give freely even of dung and earth, and so accomplish your vow. Strive, monk — by no means be idle.

Instructions to the Elder Jianyin Ci of Guizong, Who Went About Begging to Adorn the Buddha-Land

On the summit of the Golden Wheel Peak at Mount Kuang there are the relics of Śākyamuni Tathāgata — a place where the dharma-body ever abides. From of old the Patriarchs established the great banner of Dharma here; thirty-seven came before and after, and how many clarified the mind-ground and transcended birth and death among them is beyond knowing. Know then that the numinosity of this mountain is truly the Jetavana of China and the Vulture Peak of the Western River. As the Dharma’s fortune shifted and declined with the times, the jeweled palaces and Brahma halls fell away into wild thickets. Formerly Master Zibo walked this ground and resolved to restore it. His sincere spirit moved the hidden, and the withered tree flourished again — a strange omen indeed. Thereupon his disciple, the Venerable Fazhan Guo, set his mind on continuing the work and vowed to renew it, his resolve firm and unshakable, like Kang Senghui’s seeking of relics for Jianchu Temple. Before long the present Emperor was moved to bestow the imperial canon to guard the mountain gate; at that time the relics appeared and gave forth great light; mountains and rivers shook and roared, and grasses and trees showed auspicious signs. Truly a rare and excellent event in the Dharma-ending age. In the autumn of the bingchen year the Elder came from Nanyue to pay homage to the Tathāgata’s relics. Gazing up in reliance at the rare and surpassing sight, he was moved to feeling as he looked about. He saw only that the halls and pavilions were adorned but very far from complete; if one faltered midway, it would be no different from the former wild thicket — would that be the meaning of the dragons’ and gods’ protection? The original donor, the layman Xing Laici, has a great vow but weak strength; this is the responsibility of us śramaṇas, sons of Śākyamuni. Therefore he urged the Venerable Jianyin Ci to rouse a vast and great mind and to think how hard such a meeting is to encounter; he should spread his five limbs and give up the four elements to make adornment. Moreover, there are the vow-kings — officials and laymen who long ago received the Buddha’s charge on Vulture Peak — in the ten directions; why not universally invite them to gather and accomplish this excellent work? Then you will not betray the compassionate Father’s entrusting of the family estate to you. Hearing this, the Venerable Ci roused great courage and asked the Elder for a word to serve as his vanguard. The Elder laughed and said: There is no need for that. In the ocean-assembly of the dharma-realm, within the lotus-treasury, the boundless Buddha-lands with their wondrous adornment are all manifested within a single thought of the bodhisattva of the great mind, complete and full, with nothing lacking and nothing left over. It all lies in the power of a single thought of inspired resolve. It is just as the tower of Maitreya contains and holds measureless Buddha-lands, and so Sudhana came before it and did not see it; it required the power of the Great One’s snap of the fingers. Thus the Elder’s words are like one light snap of the fingers before the tower: as for adorning the Buddha-land, if you are but willing to open the door, it appears at once, all at once. What further strength is needed? Go, sir; do not be idle.
Instructions to the Layman Wang Ziju, Who Gave Up His Son to Leave Home

The layman Wang Ziju of Xindu had a son, Yingchen, who in childhood studied the Confucian books. One day he thought that the matter of birth and death is great, roused the mind to leave home, cut off his own hair, and went to Mount Kuang to pay homage to Master Jingtang of Yunzhong. In the summer of the bingchen year I came from Nanyue to this mountain. The layman visited me, and because the deepest affection of kinship is hard to sever, I therefore instructed him, saying: The hope that parents the world over place in a son is that he may bring honor to the name and glory to his parents; hence they take the support of three victims and five cauldrons as the fulfillment of filial piety. They do not realize that the richer the support, the deeper the suffering — it burdens one’s parents and is not true filial piety. Therefore our Buddha, the World-Honored One, thought little of the golden wheel and would not be it; he gave up father and mother, abandoned the royal palace, practiced austerities in the Snow Mountains, and after six years accomplished the Way, becoming the honored one of the three realms, revered by gods and humans. If he had not given up the most precious and cut off the greatest love, how could he have won an undecaying enterprise through long kalpas? Hence he is called “the greatly filial Śākyamuni, the Honored One, who through kalpas repaid his parents’ kindness.” Is this not to take the awakening to the unborn and the universal saving of living beings as the ground of repayment? When the Buddha taught the great precepts, he began with “filial piety is called the precepts” — meaning to be filial to father and mother, filial to teachers, monks, and the Three Jewels, filial to the ultimate Way, filial to all living beings. Therefore one who truly practices the Buddha’s practice will regard all living beings as his parents through many lives — how could he fail to repay the parents of this one life? It is only to be feared that one who leaves home does not know its root. Now if the son takes the resolve to awaken to the unborn as his root and ground, and if he truly settles his will, then not only will repayment be more than enough, but support will also be more than enough. What the world calls filial piety is to use merit and fame to win the support of victims and cauldrons and so please one’s parents. But merit and fame are controlled by the Maker of things, and the victims and cauldrons await what one encounters; to say nothing of the fact that obtaining them multiplies suffering, the whole world seeks them and not all obtain them, and those who obtain them may not be able to enjoy them. There are those who have merit and fame but no emolument; there are parents who cannot wait; and there are those who wait but are not glad — because all depends on fate and not on oneself. But one who has his will set on the great Way seeks within himself, and enjoys within himself too; he holds the strategy of certain attainment and cherishes the support of supreme joy. This cannot be compared with the world. If the layman can give up his son and let him follow his will, then from now on, since the son has hidden his form in the mountain valleys, the layman too may take leave of worldly conditions and follow his son in the mountains. Being able both to cut off love and to transcend the dust, he will have a ground of joy. Then though he wear grass for clothes and eat from trees, brocade and fine fare would be no exchange for it. Father and son, day and night, will think only of the Way; morning consultation and evening inquiry would not be surpassed by a child playing in colored robes to amuse his parents. Water flowing and wind moving, the sound of scripture and the Buddha’s name, are not to be wearied of as loud strings and urgent pipes are. Bright lamps and clear incense, unbroken from dusk to dawn, are not to be compared with the reek of blood and filth. A thousand-fathom cold cliff and a three-room thatched hut make lofty halls and broad mansions look mean indeed. Father and son saving each other and together accomplishing the unsurpassed Way, enjoying honor and fame not of this world — this is a thing that must be attained. Compared with the grant of one office and the praise of one word, which cannot be counted on, it is as different as cloud from mud, heaven from earth. What the layman gives up is small, and what he wins is great; what the son goes against is slight, and what he accords with is deep. Is this not the great filial piety of the world? The layman joyfully received the teaching and asked for a name, wishing to hold to it as a disciple. The Elder named him Fuzhi — “blessing arrives” — meaning that his blessing comes from now on. His style he named Dalai — “the great comes” — meaning that what is given up is small and what comes is great. So he wrote this as a document of the Dharma gate for the son.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Lingyuan Jue

The Chan monk had dwelt at Guizong on Mount Lu for years. He said he knew his faculties were inferior and that he could not enter at one leap, so he had made a vow to recite the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma ten thousand times in this life, and he asked for confirmation. He did not know whether this practice was the same as or different from the work of investigation, and wished to hear instruction. The Elder therefore taught him, saying: The Buddhas’ teaching of the Dharma is like eating honey: the middle and the edges are both sweet, fundamentally without difference of taking and rejecting. It is only because students rejoice in one thing and weary of another that differences arise. Therefore our Buddha came into the world expressly to open and show living beings the one great matter and its causes and conditions; and the Patriarch came from the west, pointing directly and transmitting singly, only to make people understand and awaken to this one great matter. What is called the one great matter is precisely the self-mind that living beings originally possess, named the seed of Buddha-nature. Know then that the scriptures are the road the Buddha opened and showed, and Chan is the wish that people walk along the road. To hold the scriptures without awakening the mind, and to investigate Chan without seeing the nature — neither is true practice. The Sixth Patriarch said: “When the mind is deluded, the Lotus turns the mind; when the mind is awakened, the mind turns the Lotus.” How could holding the scripture and investigating Chan be two? It lies in the student’s firm and long-unshakable resolve. Holding the scripture is investigation; investigation is holding the scripture. Therefore the Buddha’s meaning in the scripture, when he sought people in the final age to hold the scripture — was he seeking those who follow the lines and count the ink? The ancients’ investigation required the bitter heart of thirty years. Now ten thousand recitations of the scripture cannot be done in less than thirty years. If the monk can hold this single thought of thirty years of dwelling in the mountain without change, the Buddhas and Patriarchs will surely stroke his head and comfort him. Only discern a willing mind, and you will certainly not be cheated. On no account understand it as two dharmas.
Instructions to the Venerable Chang of Guizong, of the Zongyuan Hermitage in Qiyang

The Venerable Chang had his will set on the matter that goes upward and devoted himself to holding the Lotus Sutra. Hearing that the Elder had come to Mount Kuang, he crawled on hands and knees to see him at Donglin, and told him that in reciting the Lotus Sutra he doubted the passage, “In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions there is only the One Vehicle Dharma; apart from the Buddha’s skillful means, they are but provisional names to guide living beings.” He did not know what the One Vehicle is, or what skillful means and provisional names are, and asked for instruction. The Elder said to him: What is called the One Vehicle is the original mind of all living beings — the self-nature of awareness that is present before us in daily use. Because this mind-nature is the great root of all sages and ordinary beings, it is called a vehicle; vehicle means that which carries. Hence it is said, “The dharmas above and below in the three realms are made by one mind alone.” Outside this mind not a fragment of anything is obtainable. Even in our daily use, at the gates of the six faculties, seeing and hearing without delusion, clearly and constantly knowing, not obscured by the dust of toil and deluded thought, the light shines universally and the numinous awareness is luminous — this one mind is the realm of the Buddha, and so it carries one to Buddhahood. If with this mind one broadly practices the six pāramitās and gathers and converts living beings, without seeing any living being to save or any Buddha to attain, then this one mind is the realm of the bodhisattva, and it carries one to bodhisattvahood. If with this mind one contemplates the four noble truths, can cut off the cause of suffering, craving, and affliction, transcend the three realms, and realize the joy of cessation, then this is the realm of the two vehicles, and it carries one to the two vehicles. If with this mind one diligently cultivates the pure life, the four dhyānas and eight concentrations, then it is the realm of the four holy ones and four dhyānas, and it carries one to the Brahma heavens. If one can cultivate the ten good deeds and cut off the highest grade of evil, one is moved to the realm of the heavens of the six desires, and it carries one to the heavens. If one is deluded about this one mind and gives free rein to killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, cutting off the Buddha-seed nature, one is moved to the harsh retribution of the three paths, and it carries one into the three evil destinies. Therefore the Buddha said the three realms are mind only; apart from this one mind not a fragment of anything is obtainable. This one matter alone, and no other matter — therefore it is called the One Vehicle. It is not that apart from this mind there is another dharma to speak of. If there were a dharma outside the mind, that would be the false view of the outsiders, not right Dharma. If one understands this mind, then one knows that the three worthy ones and ten sages, and all living beings, are but shadows and echoes of the one mind, and that the Way is a provisional name. Then one knows that the three vehicles and twelve divisions of the teaching spoken by the Buddha are arranged according to capacity and are all provisional names to guide living beings; there was originally no real dharma to give people. All the various skillful means were for opening and showing this mind, not that there is another, different dharma taught to living beings. Not only is the Buddha’s teaching a skillful means; even the final twirling of the flower and Kāśyapa’s smile, and Bodhidharma’s coming from the west to transmit singly the mind-seal, are also skillful means. As for what is called “pointing directly at the human mind, seeing the nature and becoming Buddha” — to say “pointing directly” is already crooked. Students in the final age do not understand their own mind but seek only outside, and in the end have utterly no true benefit. And if they have the will to investigate the matter that goes upward, they do not know that fundamentally there is no dharma, and do not understand that their own mind is one flavor of reality, but want to seek the wondrous elsewhere. Applying the mind thus, not only is the true eye unclear, but they fall into the false views of the outsiders; though named students of the Way, they unknowingly become seeds of hell. Is this not pitiable? The Elder has often said that a student should above all apply his mind truly, and purify his own afflictions and habits and the seeds of karmic consciousness. Break one part of karmic consciousness, and one part of the Buddha’s knowing and seeing is exposed; understand one part of the Buddha’s realm. Cut off ten parts of karmic consciousness, and it is ten parts of the Buddha’s realm. How could there be a clever method outside the mind, patched together and brought in, that could be the Buddha’s realm? Chan monk, doubt no more. Simply understand that your own mind is the One Vehicle; if you awaken to the fact that all dharmas are but provisional names, that is true work. You must simply, in all places, not be deluded. Put your strength into the work thus, and do not make another kind of calculation and reckoning — all of that is the seed of false views.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Guyu Zhuo

The Chan monk Guyu came from Fuliang to consult at the Golden Wheel and asked for instruction on doing the work. The Elder asked him: How do you apply your mind in daily use? He answered: I contemplate that all is mind only. The Elder asked again: When you contemplate thus, do you still see objects? He answered: At this point I see no objects at all. The Elder said: Since you see no objects, what is it that is mind only? The monk said: I simply do not forget the subject. The Elder said: You say “mind only,” but you are doing the work with knowing and seeing; in truth you have not understood the state of mind only. The ancient worthy said: “Not yet understanding that objects are mind only, one gives rise to all kinds of discrimination; having understood that objects are mind only, discrimination no longer arises.” Do you still give rise to discrimination toward the objects before you? If when you contemplate you seem to forget objects, yet when you meet conditions you discriminate as before and give rise to mind in pursuit of objects, then to insist on saying “mind only” like this will in the end never yield real proof. Even if you can forget the objects before you, if you cling to “mind only,” then you cannot forget the mind; you have forgotten the object but not the subject. Therefore mind and objects cannot merge and fuse, and this is called the obstruction of wisdom. How much less, when you have not even forgotten objects, to insist on “mind only” and take it as a real dharma? The ancient worthy said: “If a hair’s breadth is not penetrated, it is as though a thousand mountains stood between.” Even if you reach the point where mind and objects are both forgotten and not a single dharma is established, that is still a matter on the edge of knowing and seeing — how much more to take the thinking mind as the ultimate? Is that not deceiving oneself? The monk is now going to the depths of the ten thousand peaks of Nanyue. Earnestly observe the water flowing and wind moving, birdsong and mountain light — filling the eyes and ears, utterly without the marks of body, mind, or world, beaten into one piece. Even these two words “mind only” must be thrown beyond the ten thousand worlds; there is something further. If you fall into the nest of “mind only,” you will still have no share in getting out.
Instructions to Yuan Gongliao

The Buddha said that even the wriggling and the sentient all have Buddha-nature; the tradition says that a person can be a Yao or a Shun. From this we know that the nature of numinous awareness is the root of things, and that there is no one who does not possess it. Yet observing the people born through past and present, heroes are not few, while sages and worthies are not commonly seen. Why? Because of the bias of habitual defilement: people follow feeling and chase after things without turning back. This is what is meant by “the common people use it daily and do not know it.” If one can seek to know oneself, then sagehood is not hard. Hence it is said, “One who knows himself is clear.” Because one does not know oneself, delusion daily thickens and the mind daily darkens. If there is a heroic person who blocks feeling and restores the nature, then sagehood may be expected, and his enterprise will surely be undecaying. The Buddha’s ten precepts, Confucius’s four noes, and Chan’s one mind are all essentials of restoring the nature. A person of will — can he not strive? Yuanzi Daosheng, now called Suling, once came to inquire of me at Caoxi, and I knew him to be a vessel of the sharpest faculties. When I passed Mount Kuang, he waited for me from afar; seeing what he had composed, his bones were extraordinary and his nature quick. But his habits are heavy and his temper high, and so he gives free rein to habit without seeing the nature. If he can strive to keep feeling at a distance and restore the nature, then he will not be proud, not contrary, not niggardly, not bent on success; then his vessel will be broad without overflowing, his will firm and unmoved, his mind cool and his temper dissolved, and he may sit and advance in this Way. Sagehood may be expected — how much more so worldly achievement? The Elder loved him and taught him the method of investigating the mind, much like the worn shoe on the bridge of Yishui. So he named him Gongliao, hoping that he would daily grow more indifferent to what is sweet to the palate.
Essentials of Chan Investigation (An Informal Instruction in the Chan Hall at Mount Jing)

The Chan school is one lineage, for transmitting the Buddha’s mind-seal; it is fundamentally no small matter. From Bodhidharma’s coming from the west, the purport of single transmission was established, using the four fascicles of the Laṅkāvatāra to seal the mind. Thus although Chan is a special transmission outside the teachings, in truth it uses the teachings for verification, and only then is the Buddha’s and Patriarchs’ non-dual Way seen. Its work of investigation also comes from the teachings. The Laṅkāvatāra says: “Sitting quietly in mountain forests, cultivating the upper, middle, and lower, one can see the surging flow of one’s own deluded thoughts.” This is truly the World-Honored One’s precise instruction on the method of doing the work. It also says: “Mind, consciousness, and mentation are manifested by one’s own mind; the states of self-nature are marks of the false. The ocean of birth and death, karma, craving, and not-knowing — all such causes are transcended.” This is the Tathāgata’s precise instruction on the wondrous purport of awakening the mind. It also says: “The holy ones of the lineage transmitted it one to another: deluded thought has no nature.” This again is the precise instruction of the secret mind-seal. This is the essential place where the yellow-faced old fellow taught people to investigate. And when Bodhidharma instructed the Second Patriarch he said: “Simply let outer conditions rest, and within have no panting; make the mind like a wall, and you may enter the Way.” This is the essential method by which Bodhidharma first taught people to investigate. When it was transmitted to Huangmei and the time came to seek an heir, the Sixth Patriarch simply said, “From the first not a single thing exists,” and received the robe and bowl. This is the precise purport of the transmitted mind-seal. And when the Sixth Patriarch returned south and instructed Daoming, saying, “Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil — at that very moment, what is the Original Face of the Venerable Ming?” — this is the Sixth Patriarch’s first precise formula for teaching people to investigate. Know then that the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the lineage only taught people to understand and awaken to their own mind and to recognize themselves; there was never any talk of public cases and huatous. From Nanyue and Qingyuan onward, the Patriarchs instructed as was fitting, mostly striking at the place of doubt, so that people would turn head and brain around and stop. Even for those who did not understand, though he applied the hammer and tongs, he simply left it to their time and conditions. It was Huangbo who first taught people to look into a huatou; and only with Chan Master Dahui was it strongly advocated, teaching students to investigate one public case of the ancients as a nose-hold, calling it a huatou, and requiring people to hold it up earnestly. Why? Only because in the field of the eighth consciousness of students the seeds of bad habit from measureless kalpas inwardly perfume, surging on in continuous succession, deluded thoughts unbroken, and there is no help for it. So he gave you a meaningless phrase to bite firmly on, first putting down all inner and outer mind-object deluded thoughts at once. And because you cannot put them down, he taught you to raise this huatou, like cutting a tangled skein of silk: one cut, and all is cut, no longer continuing. Block the consciousness and do not let it pass again. This is precisely Bodhidharma’s rule of “outer conditions resting, within no panting, mind like a wall.” Without taking it in hand thus, you will never see your own Original Face. It is not teaching you to ponder over the words of a public case and make them into a doubt, hoping to get an explanation from them. Even Dahui, who taught only looking into the huatou and used a poisoned hand, wanted only for you to kill the thieving mind. As he said in instructing the assembly: “In investigating Chan you need only empty the mind. Paste the two words ‘birth and death’ on your forehead, like a man who owes another ten thousand strings of cash. Three times by day, three times by night, in tea and in rice, walking and standing, sitting and lying, when exchanging courtesies with friends, in quiet and in noise, raise a huatou: ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature?’ Zhou answered, ‘No.’ Just look at it this way and that within; when it has no flavor it is like butting against a wall; when you come to the crucial juncture it is like a mouse entering a horn — and then you will see it cut off.” He wanted you to prepare a long-range body and mind and wrestle with it; then suddenly the flower of mind will bloom, illumining the lands of the ten directions, and one awakening will be thorough. These are the tongs and hammers that Elder Dahui customarily used. His meaning was only that you should use the huatou to block and intercept the deluded thoughts beneath the faculty of mind, so that their surging cannot proceed; and right at the place where they do not proceed, look into and take up your Original Face. He was not teaching you to ponder over a public case, to make it a doubt, and to seek an explanation. As he said, “How could the blooming of the mind-flower be gotten from another?” As the Buddhas and Patriarchs above have each pointed out, they want you to investigate yourself, not to seek from their mysterious and wondrous phrases. People today who investigate Chan and do the work all say they look into a huatou and bring down doubt, but they do not know to investigate at the root; they only seek on the huatou itself. Seeking and seeking, suddenly they think up a stretch of scenery and say they are awakened; then they compose verses and present odes, take it as rare goods, and think they have got it — never knowing that they have fallen wholly into the net of deluded knowing and seeing. Is not investigating Chan like this blinding the eyes of the people of the whole world for generations to come? Young people today, before their sitting cushion is steady, claim to have awakened to the Way, then show off their mouths, play with their spirits, and take it for the swiftness of the Chan mechanism; they think up a few groundless, wild, random words and call them verses on the ancients. That comes from your own deluded thought — when did you ever dream of the ancients being present? If awakening to the Way today were so easy, then the ancients’ practice — like Changqing, who sat through and wore out seven cushions; like Zhaozhou, who for thirty years did not mix his mind with anything else — by this comparison the ancients were the dullest-facultied people and would be of no use to you moderns even to carry your straw sandals. The person of overweening pride, who has not attained and says he has attained — should one not fear this? As for investigating Chan, looking into the huatou, and bringing down doubt — these can never be dispensed with. What is called “small doubt, small awakening; great doubt, great awakening; no doubt, no awakening.” One must simply be good at using doubt. If the doubt is broken, then the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ nostrils are naturally strung through on one thread. Take the public case of looking into the Buddha-recitation: just examine earnestly who it is that recites the Buddha’s name; do not doubt who the Buddha is. If you doubt who the Buddha is, you need only listen to the lecturer explain that Amitābha Buddha is named Infinite Light, and you would then be awakened, and compose a few verses on Infinite Light. If this were called awakening to the Way, then those who awaken to the mind would be as many as hemp and millet. Bitter, bitter! The ancients said a huatou is like a tile for knocking on a door: you only knock the door open to see the person inside; you do not do your business outside the door. This is enough to show that when doubt is raised from the huatou, the doubt is not on the huatou but must be at the root. Take Jiashan’s consultation with Chuanzi: he asked, “A line cast a thousand feet down, the intent is in the deep pool. Three inches from the hook — why do you not speak?” As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him with the oar and knocked him into the water. When Jiashan had climbed back into the boat, the Master said again, “Speak! Speak!” As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him again, and Jiashan was greatly awakened and nodded three times. The Master said: “The line at the pole’s end is yours to play with; not stirring the clear waves, your intent is of itself distinct.” If Jiashan had been doing his business on the hook and line, how could Chuanzi have given his life to get him through? This is the ancients’ quick and easy, skillful way of getting out. In the past, when the Chan way flourished, there were clear-eyed teachers everywhere, and students of investigation were many throughout the world, and everywhere there was opening and unfolding. Hence it was said, “It is not that there is no Chan; it is only that there are no teachers.” Now the Chan school has been silent for a long time. How fortunate that at one time many have roused the mind to investigate. Yet though there are teachers, some measure the capacity and weigh the advance, and verify according to feeling; the student’s mind is shallow and he thinks he has got it. He does not believe the Tathāgata’s holy teaching, does not seek the true road, but only does his work muddle-headedly, and then takes a winter-melon seal as the final decision. He not only deceives himself but deceives others as well — should one not fear this? Take the officials and laymen of old who were recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp: there were only a few. People amid the toil of the dust today do not cultivate even the coarse precepts; their turbid deluded thoughts run wild; relying on their own cleverness and having read a few karmic encounters of the ancient worthies, each one is self-conceited as a person of the highest faculties; seeing a monk, they at once contest Chan repartee, and also take themselves to be awakened to the Way. This, though a fault of the times, is truly a case of us followers, one blind man leading a crowd of blind men. The Elder now follows the true and essential place of the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ work and discusses it with you all. Those of high clarity and understanding will have their own way to correct it.
Instructions to Dong Zhiguang

The student Dong Sizhang grew up in a house of wealth and honor, and early roused the mind to seek escape from birth and death — surely the power of the inward perfuming of a surpassing affinity with prajñā planted in former lives. He first consulted Master Yunqi, who taught him the Dharma gate of the Pure Land. Then he consulted the Elder at Shuangjing and wished to receive the upāsaka precepts. He also of himself exposed his deep and heavy karmic offenses and asked for the essentials of escaping suffering, and by what cultivation he might extinguish his offenses. The Elder therefore taught him, saying: Since a student knows the root of his offenses is deep and heavy, the ancient worthies taught people to dissolve old karma as it comes and never to create new calamity. For living beings heavy in karma the Buddha opened the one gate of repentance, which is the most skillful means of escaping suffering. The verse says: “All offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dissolve them. If one wishes to repent, let him sit upright and contemplate true reality.” This is the correct practice; all else is auxiliary skillful means. The self-nature of living beings is equal to the Buddha’s, originally undefiled and without the marks of birth and death, coming and going. But because of the first non-awakening one is deluded about one’s own nature, and so it is called ignorance. Because of ignorance, deluded thoughts arise, all kinds of inversion, and one creates all kinds of karma, falsely taking the suffering of birth and death in the three realms. All this is ignorance: not understanding one’s own mind, one is turned about by deluded thought. It is like a person fast asleep who has all kinds of evil dreams, all kinds of states, all kinds of terror, unbearable suffering — and when he wakes he seeks the things of the dream and cannot find them at all. Thus living beings fall into the dream of ignorance, follow deluded inversion, create all kinds of karma, and take on all kinds of suffering for themselves. Seen with waking eyes, how could all those inverted conditions be found? But now, within the dream of ignorance, how can one dissolve old karma? One must use the light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and truly believe that one’s own mind is originally pure, not driven by deluded inversion. Then karma has no cause — for deluded thought is the cause of all karma. Why? Because from beginningless time one has been deluded about one’s own original mind, and life after life has created all kinds of karma with a deluded mind; the habit of karma accumulates within the field of the eighth consciousness and is watered by the water of ignorance, so that these evil seeds sprout the shoots of karma — this is the root of offenses. All evil karma arises from this. If you now wish to dissolve old karma, you must first rouse the great light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and not allow deluded thoughts to sprout and secretly grow. If you can cut off with a single thought the place where deluded thought arises, then the root of accumulated karma is dissolved on the spot. What is called “I do not fear the arising of a thought; I fear only that awareness is late.” If awareness and illumination are even slightly late, you will be turned about by it. If in daily use, at the place where mind stirs and thoughts arise, you are aware thought after thought and extinguish them thought after thought, this is what is meant by “all offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dissolve them.” For the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom — this is what is meant by wisdom being able to dissolve them. If day and night without cease you diligently observe and do not let it pass, but simply at the place where deluded thought arises investigate it to the point of utterly no mark of arising, looking and looking and in the end finding nothing obtainable — then after a long time, when it is pure and familiar, your own mind will be pure and without a thing. A mind without things is true reality. If you constantly contemplate this mind, what deluded thought can lodge in it, what accumulated karma can rest on it? Applying the mind thus is called the samādhi of contemplation. If your own afflictions are coarse and heavy and you are not aware at the place where ignorance obstructs, then the ancient worthies had people investigate: take the public case of examining the Buddha-recitation and put your strength right there. Raise one recitation of the Buddha’s name and lay it across your breast; then examine just who it is that recites the Buddha’s name. Thus as you raise it, so you examine it, never letting it go empty. Lay this mass of doubt across your breast like your own root of life, never letting it go. In all movement and stillness, leisure and busyness, coming and going, sitting and standing, this one matter alone, and no other. Applying the mind thus, as soon as you see a deluded thought arise, give the huatou one thrust, and it shatters on the spot; all deluded thoughts naturally vanish without trace. With this huatou, like the sun’s disk in the sky, there is no darkness it does not illumine. I fear only that the mind’s strength is lazy and you will not earnestly hold it up, and so cannot match the deluded thoughts. If you can match them, then the place where deluded thoughts dissolve is the time when old karma dissolves. Apart from this one point, to seek elsewhere outside the mind means that even were the Buddhas to appear in the world there would be no place for repentance. This lies in one’s own power; no other power can substitute for it. If bad habits are strong and your strength cannot match them, then in the past the Buddha gave clear instruction: if a practitioner’s habits are not removed, he should single-mindedly recite the mind-mantra spoken by me, the unconditioned Mind-Buddha. This is truly an extraordinary skillful means. Because each person’s storehouse consciousness flows secretly and his habits are deep and thick, and the power of wisdom does not reach there — at the place it cannot reach, one must rely on the Buddha’s mind-seal to break it secretly. It is like a hard-to-break rebel: one must request the sword from above. This requires that morning and evening you find your own skillful means. But take the work of investigation as the highest principle. The Elder instructs you thus, much like giving a blind man a staff. In truth, the practice lies with oneself; neither teacher nor friend can substitute.
