Because the layman’s will is set on the Dharma gate, he is named Fujue, “blessing-awakening,” taking awareness and illumination as the root of practice. His style is Zhiguang, “wisdom-light” — for without the light of wisdom, how could one break the darkness of delusion? Only you must let awareness and illumination be undimmed and the light of wisdom be present before you; then that is the time of ending karmic obstruction and escaping birth and death.
Instructions to Wen Rudong

The layman Vimalakīrti dwelt at home in the city of Vaiśālī, swept away all he owned, and lived alone in a single room, using illness as a way to teach the Dharma. Even Mañjuśrī and the thirty-two great ones exhausted their eloquence and could not match his one silent word. He is the first of all laypeople since ancient times to do the Buddha’s work well. Old Pang dispersed all his family wealth, received from Mazu the great meaning of the coming from the west, and said, “I only wish to empty what exists; never make real what does not.” He again is one who learned well from Vimalakīrti. Layman Rudong, take these two elders as your good teachers.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Huanyou Hai, Hall Master of Mount Jing

The Buddhas and Patriarchs are one mind; the teachings and Chan are one. The Chan school’s special transmission outside the teachings is not that apart from the mind there is another dharma to transmit; it only wants people to leave behind language and writing and awaken singly to the purport beyond words. Chan practitioners today at once disparage the teachings, not knowing that the teachings expound one mind, which is the root of Chan. But the Buddha’s exposition of one mind covers both the deluded and the awakened paths thoroughly; the Chan school points directly at one mind, which does not belong to delusion or awakening, and wants people to awaken thoroughly. In truth, ultimately there is no two. In the Tathāgata-garbha, coming and going, delusion and awakening, birth and death are utterly unobtainable — how could this belong to delusion and awakening? The Second Patriarch said, “Seeking the mind, it is utterly unobtainable.” The Sixth Patriarch said, “From the first not a single thing exists.” This is precisely prajñā without the five aggregates, faculties, dust, and consciousness-realms, and without the dharmas of the three vehicles that transcend the world. “Because there is nothing to be obtained, one obtains bodhi” and “seeking the mind, it is utterly unobtainable” — how are these two dharmas? Know then that the teaching’s exposition of one mind has only a surplus of ordinary feeling and sagely understanding. Chan investigation suddenly breaks ignorance — that is cutting off ordinary feeling. Even awakening is spat out — that is cutting off sagely understanding. Thus Chan rebukes knowing and understanding, and the teachings were never not rebuking it either. Those who today turn from the teachings to Chan but cannot forget knowing and cut off understanding, who take up the huatou but cannot forget feeling and cut off traces, are all rebuked. How can one slander the teachings and say they are not worth taking? Those who today abandon the teachings to investigate Chan: if they can first understand that fundamentally there is no ordinary being or sage and that it does not belong to delusion or awakening, that is their ground of view. Investigating according to this, if in one’s thought there remains the slightest feeling-view or wondrous knowing and understanding, it is all not yet penetrated and is a matter on the edge of birth and death — how can one take it as attainment? Today, with no clear-eyed teacher to verify, if one does not use the teachings to seal the mind, one will end in the false paths of demons and outsiders. But one must not take the Buddha’s spoken words and the Patriarchs’ wondrous phrases as one’s own knowing and seeing; one must investigate until one reaches the place of accord. As the scripture says, “All afflictions should, at a thought, be transformed into unsurpassed awareness.” This is what sudden awakening looks like. One must not mix afflictions and habits with knowing and seeing and take that as wondrous awakening. Nor is it anything separate in addition: it is only the dissolving of afflictions and habits and the exposing of the Original Face. Hence it is said, “After awakening, one is the same as before awakening; still simply the person of former times, not changing the place of former practice.” Have you not heard how Jiashan, before he met Chuanzi, entered the hall and a monk asked him, “What is the dharma-body?” Shan said, “The dharma-body is without marks.” He also asked, “What is the dharma-eye?” Shan said, “The dharma-eye is without blemish.” Daowu was sitting there and could not help laughing. After he had met Chuanzi, Daowu sent a monk to ask, “What is the dharma-body?” Shan still said, “The dharma-body is without marks.” He asked again, “What is the dharma-eye?” Shan still said, “The dharma-eye is without blemish.” The monk returned and reported this to Daowu. Daowu said, “This fellow has finally penetrated.” This is the model of a clever lecturer who abandons the teachings to investigate Chan. Hall Master Hai has long been intimate with the teachings; now he abandons what he has studied and seeks only the road that goes upward. Look at how Jiashan’s two turning words before and after are the same — why did Daowu approve the latter and not the former? Try to see where he did not approve and where he approved. If here you can settle it, I guarantee you will spit out the meaning of the teachings and the meaning of the Patriarchs all at once. Another day you will be able to drink up the whole canon in one gulp, and every word will turn into a treasury of light. Enough of these tangled vines. Take care, take care.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Lingjian Zhi, of the West Hall at Mount Jing

The teachings say: “All dharmas are unborn; I speak of the meaning of the instant. At the very moment of arising there is ceasing; this is not spoken for the foolish.” The ancient worthy said, “One who awakens to the unborn first sees the instant.” But having awakened to the unborn, what instant is there to see? If one sees an instant, then one has not awakened to the unborn. Now why is it said that one who awakens to the unborn first sees the instant? Then are the unborn and the instant one or different? The Buddha spoke of the instant in reliance on the unborn, so they are not different. The Patriarch said, “One who awakens to the unborn first sees the instant” — so the unborn and the instant are again not one. If one seeks it apart from oneness and difference, then the meaning of the unborn becomes a stake to tether a donkey. Weishan said: “People today who in one thought suddenly understand their own mind are said to be awakened. Then, with that which they have awakened to, they purify the present karma and its flowing consciousness — this is called cultivation.” Now the flowing consciousness means the subtle arising and ceasing, which is the mind of the instant. To speak of cultivating after awakening means that one sees it after awakening. And if one sees the instant only after awakening, then the earlier awakening was clearly not true unborn. Today, in Chan investigation one raises a huatou, and though this is called putting forth effort, the subtle arising and ceasing flows on secretly, like a stone pressing grass: it darkens and is not seen. If one does not cut off arising and ceasing, how can one awaken to the unborn? And if it is not the unborn, how can one match birth and death? If one sees it only after awakening, then the World-Honored One’s speaking of the unborn in reliance on the instant becomes a superfluous dharma. The West Hall master has eaten his fill of the teachings; now he abandons what he has studied and takes up the single road that goes upward. Settle this for yourself here. But you must not reconcile it by doctrine and principle, nor seek it in intellectual understanding. If you can, within the instant of a single thought, suddenly see the unborn, then the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ nostrils are strung through on one thread.
Instructions to the Hermitage Master Zhixi Xian

The hermitage master had long dwelt in the lecture halls, and then practiced with the Patriarchs’ karmic encounters at Shaolin. Now he has swept aside all he had studied and takes up the single road that goes upward, hanging his shadow at Shuangjing. Just then the Elder arrived, and he offered incense and asked for instruction. The Elder taught him, saying: In this matter everyone is originally without deficiency, complete and full. The reason they do not know it in daily use and gain no benefit from it is simply that the seeds of beginningless bad habit have been perfumed and dyed deep through accumulated kalpas and are already hard to pull out; and now they are newly perfumed with the words of the teachings, the Patriarchs’ public cases, and all kinds of knowing and seeing, adding another layer of obstruction. Though one wants to understand oneself, the more one seeks the farther away it goes. Why? Only because one is blind to oneself and seeks it from others. The afflictions and habits accumulated over lives are called the obstruction of affliction; the wondrous knowing and seeing are called the obstruction of the known. If the two obstructions are dissolved, the original substance appears of itself. In investigating the matter that goes upward today, one must first spit out utterly all the words and languages and wondrous principles one has learned before, naming them mixed poison. Take up the root huatou alone and bring down the doubt again; cut off the root of deluded thought and affliction, so that inwardly it cannot get out and outwardly cannot get in. With the former and latter limits cut, what lies between is naturally alone. Only one mass of doubt, as your own root of life. Doubt until you cannot doubt and cannot exert effort; then fix your gaze upon it and see what on earth it is. Look and look, press and press, and there will come a time of cutting off. But if the least knowing and seeing remains, then a thousand or ten thousand li lie between. Just look at the First Patriarch’s saying, “Make the mind like a wall, and you may enter the Way.” This is the first road home. If the mind will not die and the doubt is not keen, then for a thousand lives and a hundred kalpas you will remain on the road. Hermitage master, simply gather your spirit into this. I guarantee that the place you attain another day will certainly not be reached by “thus, verily, and the like.” Strive greatly.
Instructions to the Hermitage Master Songpu En

The ancient worthies taught people investigating Chan to first shed body and mind inwardly and leave the world behind outwardly, putting everything down and keeping not the slightest trace, and then to take up singly one public case as a huatou — such as Zhaozhou’s “Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhou answered, No”; or “The ten thousand dharmas return to the one; where does the one return to?”; or examining earnestly who it is that recites the Buddha’s name. Raise whichever one and lay it across your breast like a diamond king’s precious sword, cutting off all thoughts and deluded imaginings at once, like cutting a tangled skein of silk. Inwardly it cannot get out, outwardly it cannot get in; block the vital pass and seal the throat, allowing no breath to pass. Press hard thus, and fix your gaze: what on earth is this that takes up the huatou? Bring down doubt thus; doubt on and on, doubt until the mind is like a wall, and never allow a second thought to arise. As soon as a deluded thought secretly flows, see it at a glance, then at once raise the huatou with all your strength and bring down the doubt again; examine and doubt again, and press and block this mass of doubt. When thought does not arise and deluded thinking does not proceed, that is precisely the place of power. Lean steadily on it thus; in all walking, standing, sitting, and lying, amid movement and stillness, leisure and busyness, clench your teeth and resolve never to let it go. Even in dreams do not let it go. There is only the one thought of the huatou, which is the root of life of the person concerned — like a man dead though still breathing. Only by wrestling with a poisoned hand thus is one a person who works at Chan investigation. When your effort reaches its extreme, not counting days and months, suddenly the cold ashes will burst with a bean — that is the time of great joy. If you drift along as you please and work one day and freeze ten, I fear there will never be a time of power. Hermitage master, since you have your will set on the matter that goes upward, encourage yourself with this.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Chengmi Xian

In daily use a student contemplates the four great elements as a shadow, contemplates what is before him as a dream, contemplates the mind as a rushing torrent, contemplates movement as a mechanical puppet, contemplates sounds as echoes in a valley, contemplates objects as flowers in the sky. Contemplating thus, there is no self and no mine; nothing moves me, nothing acts. Coming and going, sitting and standing, there is no arising and no stopping; responding to thought, there is no birth. This is called entering the samādhi of non-contention.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Tanyan Zong

The Chan monk Zong in his youth frequented the lecture halls and habituated himself to the meaning of nature and characteristics. After a long time, because he had not seen his own nature, he roused doubt and investigated. One day, having gained no entry, he met the Elder when he came to Shuangjing, and offered incense to ask for instruction. So the Elder taught him, saying: The ancients said, “I do not value your practice; I value only your ground of view.” What is called practice is the work of advancing; what is called the ground of view is understanding and penetrating one’s own mind as the root of practice. If the root of practice is unclear, then one’s advance loses its aim. Therefore a student of investigation takes the ground of view first. What is called the ground of view is truly believing that one’s own mind is originally pure and utterly without a single thing, and that not only ordinary feeling but even sagehood is not established. It is only because of beginningless ignorance that one obscures one’s own wondrous clarity, and so gives rise to all kinds of inversion and deluded discrimination and creates all kinds of karma. It is like a waking man with nothing to do who suddenly, in sleep, has all kinds of dreams; the sufferings and joys of the dream appear plainly before him, and when he wakes and seeks them they are utterly unobtainable. This is called producing something from nothing — how could it be a real dharma? But the foolish, being inverted, cling to it as truly existing; this is not seeing thoroughly. When the Buddha appeared in the world and taught all kinds of dharmas, these were tools for breaking the dream, and had no root either. And students of the Buddha-Dharma again cling to them as real dharmas of their own — this is adding a dream within a dream. The method of Chan investigation today has no other wondrous formula: it is simply to break the dream-thoughts and inversion. If one understands that fundamentally there is nothing, and truly believes that one’s own mind is pure and without a thing, then one understands that deluded thought does not exist. Understanding that delusion does not exist, one knows that the Buddha-Dharma that breaks deluded thought is also fundamentally nonexistent. Buddha-Dharma is medicine; deluded thought is the disease. If medicine and disease are both not established, then the original substance is at peace. Understanding thus, one knows that both medicine and disease are diseases. The wordless public case of the ancients that one now takes up in investigation is the medicine for attacking the disease of medicine and disease. It is called using poison to remove poison. If one knows that fundamentally there is nothing, then the single word “investigate” is yet another poison laid down. How can one take this as something wondrous? If one does not believe one’s own mind, then even investigating is taking poison by mistake. Can the Chan monk believe this? You should investigate at the place where not a single dharma is established.
Instructions to Gu Shanzi

I was dwelling at Jizhao in Shuangjing when the layman Gu Shanzi came to consult me. I asked his profession; he said he practiced geomancy. Then he came to Huacheng, and because I pointed out the mountains and waters and spoke of the subtlety of the Maker’s transformations, which surpass form and energy, he grasped the essence and let go the coarse. I then questioned him, saying that I had once seen a piece called On Awakening, which my student Zhouzi had written and for which I had written a preface, saying: The One is the root of the ten thousand things, the storehouse of the Maker’s transformations. Hence it is said, “Heaven obtains the One and is clear; earth obtains the One and is at peace; the sage obtains the One and becomes the rectifier of the world.” When rectified, one does not slip into the crooked, and one firms one’s root. Now man and things, principle and energy, mind and form, are all one. Obtain the One, and all principles return to it. The saying goes, “Know the One, and the ten thousand affairs are finished.” Therefore we who investigate the wondrous always say, “The ten thousand dharmas return to the One; where does the One return to?” That the ten thousand return to the One can be known; where the One returns to cannot be known. Now man is bound by the entanglement of ten thousand affairs, and ten thousand cares assault his mind, a welter and a confusion, and in the end he is not at peace — this is the fault of not knowing the One. The layman can observe that heaven and earth and the Maker’s transformations return to the One, yet does not know that body and mind, nature and life, return to the One; this is to know two fives and not to know ten. If one knows that nature and life return to the One, then the ten thousand transformations are complete within me. Can one not attend to this?
Instructions to Tan Liangsheng

Tan Liangsheng’s faculties are the sharpest, for he comes from the habitual practice of prajñā in former lives. Yet prajñā is the Buddha-nature of living beings, complete in each one; that faculties differ as sharp or dull is simply because the habits of the five desires are thick or thin in unequal measure. The sharp-facultied, having long practiced prajñā and purified the habits of defilement, come to this life clever and bright. But people do not know to turn back; they use their sharp faculties and cleverness as provisions for defiled bad habits — this is called inversion. Because prajñā inwardly perfumes them, they now and then have the will to leave the dust, and they say, “At such and such a time, when worldly affairs are finished, I will go and study the Way.” Such a view is common to the whole world. Because they have the thought of a future, whatever conditions they meet before them, since they cherish a lofty ambition for the future, they regard as not worth doing and do not deign to do. By this empty imagining they instead increase their pride and arrogance, thinking that others do not have this mind and are all mediocre. And they themselves let the present pass by, so that both the worldly and the world-transcending are lost, and the light of time is spent in vain; and when the future comes, it may not be as their first resolve wished. Moreover their minds do not check their conduct in small matters, and their feelings remain rough; they take the view of self as high clarity — this is an even greater mistake. To call this having aspiration is rather not as good as the old farmer in a hamlet of three households: he has no other thoughts, and year after year his livelihood is not lacking. Should one not be ashamed? The sage taught people not to overstep their rank; hence it is said, “Act according to your station.” Laozi said, “He who straddles does not walk.” Since you now have this will toward the Way, then from today on be careful and meticulous; go on working according to the rules. Take one true mind and go forward with what is before you, learning the Way without defilement. If you do not let the present moment pass at any time, then the future will not be empty. But if you use empty imagining and a mere promise in the present and wait for the future, that is to cross a river and seek a well to quench your thirst — is that not foolish? Let Tan Liangsheng look directly at the one point of not letting the present pass in vain, and he will see where his life comes to rest.
Instructions to Cao Shiju

In daily use the common people never depart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and the sage is the same. Their function being the same, yet there being the difference of sage and commoner, lies only in knowing and not knowing. Hence it is said, “The common people use it daily and do not know it.” The student’s work of restoring sagehood lies only at the place of not knowing in daily use, seeking the knowing that he originally possesses. If he sees the knowing that he originally has, then toward all sounds, forms, goods, and profit he is clear and not moved by them; meeting conditions and encountering circumstances thus, he is like a mirror showing reflections, and not a single thing can move within him. This is the essential gate of entering the Way.
Instructions to Feng Yanling

In turning toward the Way a student must first fear birth and death. Second, he must know the root of birth and death. The root of birth and death is precisely the various kinds of aversion, craving, taking, rejecting, self-pride, greed, hatred, and delusion that appear before him in daily use. Since these are the bitter root of birth and death, he must resolve to cut them off. There is no other technique: simply, when they arise, illuminate them at once and allow them no rise. At the place where they do not arise, they are dissolved right there. When they are dissolved, do not let them continue. Applying the mind thus, not letting a single thought pass at any time, mind after mind undimmed, one’s knowing becomes numinous of itself. If the knowing is numinous, then when it touches objects the objects do not drag the mind, and when it contemplates the mind the mind does not adhere to objects. With mind and objects not reaching each other, birth and death have no place to lodge. Applying the mind thus, there is no need to seek the mysterious and wondrous elsewhere.
Instructions to the Novice Hanhui Qi on Dwelling in the Mountains (Bingchen Year)

Qi first paid homage to Master Daguan and sought the Dharma of transcending the world. The Master approved and sent him to consult the Elder, who had him ordained and dyed. He relied on the Elder for several years; then, for the sake of the work of carving the great canon, he returned to serve his original teacher. That great task was not a matter of one day. Now, in old age and illness, he sought a place of great rest, and his plan had come to nothing. When the Elder came to Shuangjing and saw Qi, his spirit was weak but his mind’s strength was stronger; for more than ten years he had gained the single road that goes upward and had a little grip on it, lacking only that one shout of sudden breakthrough. When they spoke of a place to retire, the Elder taught him, saying: The whole great earth is a place of stillness and cessation; it lies only in the place where a student is willing to put things down, and that is the place of rest. Why seek it elsewhere? The ancient worthy said, “Not apart from true suchness is the place of standing; the place of standing is itself true.” It is only because one’s own mind arises and ceases and one follows feeling in all kinds of taking and rejecting that everywhere there are obstructions. The Third Patriarch said: “The ultimate Way is without difficulty; it only dislikes picking and choosing.” He also said, “It is because of taking and rejecting that it is not so.” If it is not so, then throughout the ten directions there is no place of rest. The Elder observes that Shuangjing is the place where the eighty-eight Patriarchs taught the Dharma, and where Chan Master Dahui also came to rest. Even your own original teacher, whose heels covered the seas, had no place to plant his foot; in the end, because of the work of carving the great canon, his bones were buried in the same pit as Dahui’s. How much more you, who followed your teacher’s wheel of vow and carved the scriptures at Jizhao’s founding — these are all places where you spent your life, and are the place where you may give up body and life. The Elder knows that what you cannot give up is not laziness but the fact that the view of self is not forgotten. In the pure dharma-realm, Buddhas, Patriarchs, and living beings all have a share; only the one with the view of self cannot enter. If one sees that there is a self, then one looks on Buddhas and Patriarchs as human forms; human forms stand opposed to me, and thus in the end there is no person to be avoided and no place to rest. If you yourself do not rest, then there is no place to rest; if you are willing to rest, then you rest on the spot. Putting everything down is the great rest. When you rest, Buddhas and living beings alike hide their shadows, and there is no place to contain them. You seek the road that goes upward; though it is called extraordinary, it is not as good as putting it down and being level and at peace. The ancients said, “When the household and the land are level and at peace, people are few.” If you reach the ground of levelness and peace, then even a Buddha is not made — what further upward is there to seek?
Instructions to the Chan Monk Shijing Yi

Because the ancients had not clearly understood the great matter of birth and death, they went into the mountains and dwelt alone in solitude, hanging their shadows there, solely to investigate clearly the matter beneath their own feet. Hence it is said, “While the great matter is not yet clear, one is as though bereaved of father and mother.” It is not to nurse laziness and seek idleness and pass the time as one pleases. If you truly want to investigate this great matter, you may only carry dung out, never carry dung in. You must spit out deluded thoughts and bad habits and the knowing and seeing of letters all at once, and let your breast be clean and gone, not a single dharma standing before the mind, with only one huatou as your own root of life. The ancients’ thirty years of not mixing the mind is precisely this. But if you now dwell in the mountains and drift idly as you please, giving free rein to feeling, and when a deluded thought arises you must patch together a few lines of poetry and compose a couple of verses, taking them as the principle of awakening to pass the days — then you are only a lazy fool nursing idleness. How can you be called a person of the Way dwelling in the mountains? You not only waste the light of time but consume in vain the offerings of the faithful. When you come to the last day of the twelfth month, with what will you face Old Man Yama? You cannot get past him with a poem and a verse. The Chan monk should think about why he dwells in the mountains: in the end he must find a landing place, and only then will he not betray the excellent affinity of one meeting through a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives. The ancient worthy said: “Those who suffer in the hells of the three paths are not truly suffering; to lose the human body beneath the robe — that is truly suffering.” Can one not keep this in mind?
The Dream Wanderings Collection of Elder Hanshan, Volume Seven
Instructions to the Chan Monk Taisu Yuan

When a student has first studied the teachings and then turns his mind to the road that goes upward, though he has the will, there is no help for the fact that in his storehouse consciousness there are the newly perfumed habits of the mixed poison of letters, and the old habits of greed, hatred, delusion, craving, and affliction; inner and outer attack each other, and it is hardest of all to pack away. What he wants to put down he cannot put down; what he wants to cut off he cannot cut off; what he wants to stop he cannot stop. Therefore he must raise a huatou; but it is like a gourd on the water — he cannot press it under, and can only wrestle with it, and it is the hardest thing to take in hand. And when he cannot take it in hand, he beats the retreat drum. Such a one is a person without aspiration and without strength — what is the use of talking about Chan investigation to him? Beginners today should simply put down at once all the principles and knowing and seeing within and without the mind, along with deluded thoughts and imaginings — put down and put down again, until there is nowhere left to put down; and only then raise one public case as a huatou, such as Zhaozhou’s word “No,” laid across the breast. Why did he say “No”? Bring down the doubt again. If the doubt has power, deluded thoughts will not arise. If you see them just beginning to arise, on no account set yourself against them and try to cut them off with the mind; nor may you use the mind to stop them, nor may you continue them. Simply see them, and let them go; with one letting go they dissolve. Quickly raise the huatou and look deeply into it, and those deluded thoughts will naturally vanish without trace. This is the formula for a beginner taking the work in hand. When the huatou is pure and familiar, deluded thoughts will naturally be rare and will not become obstructions. After a long time, when the doubt has power and deluded thoughts are temporarily at rest, you will gain a single moment of joy. But do not take that joy as something extraordinary; from there simply work well. The Chan monk abandons the teachings for Chan; for a beginner this is the hardest thing. Therefore I teach him this. On no account regard it as a small matter.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Henghe Zhi on Holding the Lotus Sutra

The Chan monk left home at Fudu and long served Master Dan as an attendant, gaining the Dharma gate of endurance and maintenance. He dwelt at Huacheng for years; Huacheng is the place where the great canon was carved and a Dharma cave within the seas. The monk put his strength into the permanent dwelling and managed the hundred affairs. When the Elder came to Shuangjing, the monk bowed and asked for instruction, wishing to hold the Lotus Sutra. So the Elder instructed him, saying: For the sake of the one great matter and its causes and conditions the Buddha appeared in the world — that is, to open and show all living beings the Buddha’s knowing and seeing and cause them to awaken and enter. What is called the Buddha’s knowing and seeing is the Buddha-nature that living beings originally possess. Now it is sealed and covered by ignorance and has become deluded knowing and seeing; and so in daily seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing one follows feeling and creates karma, and so takes on the suffering of birth and death without knowing it. Our master Śākyamuni came into the world expressly once, solely to open and show this matter and cause people to awaken to what they originally possess, not seeking it outside. If one awakens to this original possession, then whatever functions in response to conditions at the gates of the six faculties in daily use is the Buddha-wisdom present before one, and is called the Buddha’s knowing and seeing, not the deluded knowing and seeing of living beings. If one awakens to this knowing and seeing, then everywhere and in every dharma there is true application of mind, and all movements and practices are true wondrous practice, all becoming the true cause of Buddhahood. Hence the scripture says: “Even raising a single hand, or giving a slight bow of the head, even one stick of incense or one flower offered to the Buddha — all have already accomplished the Buddha Way.” Slight causes and small good deeds all become the true cause of Buddhahood; how much more so to bear responsibility for the assembly’s affairs and give one’s life for the Dharma — is this not the true seed of Buddhahood? When our Buddha taught people to hold the Lotus Sutra, he meant entering the Tathāgata’s room, wearing the Tathāgata’s robe, and sitting on the Tathāgata’s seat. The Tathāgata’s room is the mind of great compassion; the Tathāgata’s robe is the mind of gentleness and patience; the Tathāgata’s seat is the emptiness of all dharmas. If the monk can honor these three teachings of the Tathāgata, he is truly one who holds the scripture. If he cannot enter these three Dharma gates, then let him simply hold the chapter on the Practice of Ease and Bliss, thinking of it thought after thought and wishing to enter it mind after mind, day and night without forgetting. Then the sixty thousand-odd words will be luminous word by word, appearing at the gates of the six faculties. If he does not enter this Dharma gate, then even if he can hold a hundred thousand myriad copies, he only makes an enemy of the meaning — is he truly one who holds the scripture? If you do not believe the Elder, then go and ask Mañjuśrī and Maitreya.
Instructions to Wang Lunian (Sixth Day of the New Year, Dingsi Year)

The student Wang Lunian grew up in Huaixi, came to pay homage at Mount Jing, and asked the Elder for a word. The Elder saw that he bore a righteous spirit and had a compassionate heart, and so said to him: Have you heard that in ancient times there were men of great strength? To conquer others is folly; to conquer oneself is wisdom. The fool is always weak; the wise are always victorious — this is the way of things. The sage taught people to use non-use as use; hence it is said, “The soft overcomes the hard; the weak overcomes the strong.” The Changes says, “Hard yet able to be soft — the way of good fortune.” Xiang Yu uprooted mountains and lifted cauldrons, his strength the mightiest of a thousand ages; but when he was defeated and parted from Consort Yu, he sobbed and shed several lines of tears. He could conquer others but could not conquer himself. The sage pointed this out directly to Yan Yuan: “To overcome oneself and return to propriety is benevolence.” Students past and present all know the words “overcome oneself,” but cannot do the work of conquering themselves — how is that wisdom? If Wang Lunian has strength in this, he should not fall among the ranks of ordinary men.
Instructions to the Attendant Zaiyong

The attendant Yong was born in Western Shu and in his youth was sunk in mean service. Fortunately his prajñā-cause was not obscured, and while still young he knew to consult Master Miaofeng and roused the mind to leave the world — surely the inward perfuming of seeds planted long ago made him so. It happened that Master Danju entered Shu, and at that time Yong was serving Mr. Xu. The latter had always admired his faith, and so ordered him to pay homage to Master Dan and seek the Dharma of escaping suffering, and he was tonsured as a novice. When the Elder came to Shuangjing, Yong served as his attendant, diligent day and night without slackness. The Elder at first pitied his dullness and constantly roused him; whenever Yong heard the Elder instruct the patch-robed monks, his brows would stir with animation. Know then that the seed of Buddha-nature in living beings waits for its time to sprout. When he asked for instruction, the Elder taught him the public case of examining who it is that recites the Buddha’s name and told him to investigate it. Yong could also receive and bear it. I fear only that he lacks the decided mind for birth and death and cannot risk his life to the very end; and I fear too that bad habits and bad knowing and seeing may obstruct him midway and carry him into the net of false views. Apart from these two faults, then with the single thought, tightly embracing the mass of doubt through the six periods of day and night, even twenty or thirty years without awakening he should not rest. Even if he does not awaken in this life, it will become a surpassing cause, and in a future life when he gets out he will know this matter; though many kalpas pass, he will never lose the seed of the right cause. But if his resolve is not firm and his application not keen, and he gives rise to false thoughts instead, then he will not only betray this life — through a thousand lives and ten thousand kalpas there will be no share in getting out.
Instructions to the Attendant Zaijie

Elder Zibo bore the great Dharma wholly on his body and wished to establish the enterprise of reviving the Dharma gate; therefore he devoted his strength to printing the great canon. This one great matter and its causes and conditions was no small thing. In the end he entrusted the whole burden to Master Dan to carry on one shoulder. Since the canon was carved but could not be stored in a fitting place, the work of restoring Huacheng was again no small thing. And Huacheng’s restoration was not the work of one hand or one foot. The attendant Jie took the lead with courage in every matter, not avoiding hardship or danger, and his merit was the greater part. This again was the hardest thing among the many. It has been said that in the world there is no one who gladly uses his strength for nothing — even the heroes of old were so, how much more others? When Emperor Gaozu of Han had settled the empire and the meritorious officials were not yet enfeoffed, he suddenly saw them whispering in the sand. He asked Zhang Zifang. Zifang said: “These are men who braved arrows and stones amid weapons and passed through ten thousand deaths and one life; all of them want a fief of a few feet. Now that they have not seen any enfeoffment, they are whispering.” Thereupon he enfeoffed them at once. This was the old rule for employing people. Now consider the attendant Jie: at first he had no other aim but to leave home. Now he has run about for seven years, and Huacheng is settled; the great Dharma has found its place. Among those who take credit for the work, would there be none who whisper? The Elder says that now one may reward him with the Tathāgata’s reward. The attendant Jie has, through the Elder, received the Tathāgata’s great reward. But if he cannot honor the Tathāgata’s Dharma, keep the Tathāgata’s precepts, and do the Tathāgata’s work, and if by any chance he breaks the precepts and destroys the Dharma, the Tathāgata too has his three-foot blade. Be careful!
Instructions for the Novice Monk Zaijing

The Buddha, among the twenty difficulties, said: To gain a human body is difficult; to be born in a central land is difficult; to encounter the Buddhadharma is difficult; to draw near a good spiritual friend is difficult; to give rise to right faith is difficult. Of these five, each is the difficulty of difficulties. The novice Zaijing already possesses four of them; what he lacks is only the arising of right faith. Now he has been fortunate enough to leave home, to meet a great good spiritual friend as his refuge, and to plunge body and all into the great ocean of the Buddhadharma. By what cultivation did he obtain this? By what causes did he arrive here? If he does not rouse himself with courage and give rise to great right faith, wash this whole phantom, deluded body and mind until it is utterly clean, stake his one life, resolve to escape birth and death, cultivate the ten thousand practices far and wide, and knit the supreme, unsurpassed connection with Buddhahood — will he not miss it face to face and lose the seeds of goodness planted over many lives? The ancients said: Those who suffer in the three evil paths and the hells are not truly suffering; to lose one’s human body beneath the kāṣāya — that is suffering indeed. The Buddha said: When the mind is straight as a bowstring, one may enter the Way. Straight as a bowstring means having no crookedness. What is crookedness? It is the contriving, scheming mind; the stealing mind; the perverse mind; the mind that conceals its faults; the mind without shame; the lazy, self-indulgent mind; the mind that seeks out others’ faults; the haughty, arrogant mind; the mind that exalts self and condemns others; the mind that gives rise to no filial devotion or compassion. In short, every unwholesome mind is a crookedness of one’s own heart. If you would now set your mind on the path, simply sweep away all the foregoing minds, examine yourself at every moment, watch over your thoughts from thought to thought, and permit no licence. Lest you be unable to cut them off at once, take one gongan of the ancients and set it across your chest. When habit-energy stirs, lift up that phrase and wrestle with it. With long familiarity it will become pure and ripe, and then the mind of itself will grow straight, the thought of the Way will daily increase, practice will daily advance, and the ground of the mind will daily brighten. A life such as this may at last be called not wasted. Otherwise, when birth and death arrive, with what will you meet them? The novice should ponder this himself, and on no account let it pass as a trifling matter.
Instructions for the Ascetic Haigeng, Disciple of Xing Tian

Looking through the ages at the heroes of old who waded through hardship and suffering and held to a long, unretreating resolve, one finds them, by and large, few. Men such as the five ministers of Jin, who went into exile with Chong’er and for nineteen years never slackened their hearts — even they, day and night, looked toward a fief a foot wide and a name preserved in the annals. That is fame and profit tugging at the heart, and so they forgot themselves in the task. Such has ever been the common feeling of the world. But as for the Daoist Tian: he followed Master Da for more than twenty years, forgoing sleep and food, never slackening for a single breath. For the slightest fault he was severely reproved and heavily caned; ordinarily both his legs were black as ink, yet he never once raised a resentful thought or spoke a resentful word. Even when he met with grave trouble, he gave himself to it as to death. In the silent, bitter, empty gate of the Dharma, what was he seeking after all, that he could be so vigorous, firm, and unshakable? Seen in this light, that which was rarest among the loyal ministers and righteous knights of old is now found in this Daoist. And when he died he was buried beside Master Daguan at Shuangjing. I say that this clod of earth is not easy for laymen to obtain — nor even for monks. In the land of the Dharma he has already received a fief of earth and title. Had he not given his body in bloody battle, how could he have come to this at his end? He entrusted this scroll to his disciple, the Daoist Zhu; Master Dan has now named him Haigeng, and this too is a deed of merit in the Dharma gate, a bond of family inheritance. How could it be a small connection?
Instructions for Zhu Suchen

Scholars who study the Way mostly take reading as an obstacle. The Old Man says: how does reading hinder the Way? It is only that when you are not reading, you are mostly disturbed by groundless deluded thoughts. If in your leisure you can gather the mind to one place and cut off deluded thoughts so they cannot proceed, keeping the mind on the Way heart to heart and never forgetting it thought to thought, then you will spend much time studying the Way and little time reading. The Old Man has often instructed students: you must see through a thought at the very place it arises, and not let things arise wildly before they arrive. If you can truly apply your mind thus, deluded thoughts will of themselves be cut off, outer affairs will of themselves cease to disturb you, the power of the Way will of itself grow strong, and your practice will surely come easily to completion.
Instructions for Shen Zhizhi

The Way does not want mixture. Mixture brings multiplicity; multiplicity brings disturbance; disturbance brings anxiety; anxiety brings failure to enter. The ancients said: In studying the Way, the resolve should be gathered into one. What I call one is simply the oneness of resolve. Since you already know the work of investigation, take the gongan you are investigating and set it across your chest. Whether at leisure or busy, in movement or stillness, receiving guests or entertaining visitors, in all the affairs of daily use, keep it before you and never let it go. Let it go, and you will be disturbed by circumstances; disturbed, you will grow weary; weary, you will have only a mind seeking idleness and no mind mindful of the Way. When mind and resolve are one, all things can be done. Wherever you apply the mind, apply it at the place where thoughts arise. As soon as one arises, see through it; seeing through it, it vanishes on the spot and no longer continues to toy with you. This is the secret of investigation. Hence it is said: Plan for the difficult while it is easy; do the great while it is small. Here, at the easy and the small, take hold, and you will feel the labour lighten. If you set this aside and wait for leisure and quiet before doing your work, then to the end of your life there will be no time for entering the Way. Mr. Shen: simply work at the single thought; there is no need to seek outside. Even bowing to the Buddha and reciting mantras are done only in the power of faith at a single thought. In sum, all these skilful means are but methods for gathering in the mind.
Instructions for Master Danju Kai

Among the loyal and righteous of old, none could bear great matters without great strength. Strength is of two kinds: strength of mind and strength of breath. It is said: Where the will arrives, the breath follows. And again: Hold fast your will, but do not abuse your breath. For when the body is overtaxed it withers; when the essence is overtaxed it is exhausted; when the spirit is overtaxed it comes to rest. Zhuangzi said: To follow the limitless with the limited — that is peril. And to go on acting on that knowledge is peril indeed. This speaks of overuse without knowing how to nourish. Therefore Laozi said: In governing men and serving Heaven, nothing surpasses sparing. Sparing means having and yet not using to the full. Nourishing the body is governing men; nourishing the nature is serving Heaven. What our Buddha called the six senses galloping among the objects of the six dusts, so that in time they become wearied — it is for this reason. Hence we know that when the ancients undertook great matters, none failed to work upon things from a surplus. Emperor Gaozu of Han took the empire by force; in a hundred battles he was beaten a hundred times, and with a single victory the great work was done. Was this not a case of one who was good at guarding his surplus in order to govern his insufficiency? The late Master laid the great matter of the Dharma gate upon your single shoulder, and you spared no strength. Amid a hundred breakers you brought every ounce of spirit and strength to meet them, because your will had surplus and you had no leisure to consider how easily the body wears out. But now the body is easily dissolved and time gone is hard to recover. You should rest and nourish in good season to preserve your heavenly harmony. This is what is meant by the root being established, whereupon the Way is born. Take the learning of your life and make the brightening of the mind its standard. If the mind is broad and the body slighted, then your strength will be whole and your charge will have surplus for unfinished work — like a journey of a thousand li reached after a brief rest. You will surely know how to place yourself. What say you?
Essentials of Buddha-Recitation — Spoken at Yunqi for Wen Zijiang, His Son, and His Mother

The one gate of reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking birth in the Pure Land was from the first meant for the great matter of resolving birth and death. Hence it is said: Recite the Buddha’s name and resolve birth and death. People today set their minds on it because they want to resolve birth and death, and only then are they willing to recite. They say only that the Buddha can resolve birth and death. But if you do not know the root and stem of birth and death, where after all are you reciting toward? If the mind that recites the Buddha’s name cannot cut off the root and stem of birth and death, how can birth and death be resolved? What is the root and stem of birth and death? The ancients said: Where karma is not heavy, one is not born in the Sahā; where craving is not cut off, one is not born in the Pure Land. Hence we know that the root of craving is the root and stem of birth and death, for the suffering of birth and death that all living beings endure is the fault of craving and desire. Trace this root of craving back: it is not something that came to be in this life, nor in one, two, three, or four lives. From the very beginning, since birth and death first existed without beginning, life after life, casting off one body and receiving another, has all been the turning of craving and desire. Down to this very day — look back and consider: was there ever a single thought that briefly parted from this root of craving? Seeds of craving such as this have been deep and thick for kalpas accumulated, and so birth and death are without end. Only today have you set your mind on reciting the Buddha’s name, and you merely gaze into emptiness seeking birth in the West, not even knowing the name of craving as the root of birth and death — how could you have cut off a single thought of it? Since you do not know the root of birth and death, then while you recite on one side, the root of birth and death only grows on the other. Reciting in this way has nothing whatever to do with birth and death. However you recite, when you come to the end of your life you will see only the root of birth and death and craving appear before you. Then you will know that the Buddha’s name was of no power at all, and you will complain that reciting the Buddha’s name is without efficacy — but repentance will come too late. Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha’s name today: you must first know that craving is the root of birth and death, and that in reciting now, thought after thought must cut off this root of craving. In the daily affairs before you — reciting at home — your eyes see sons and daughters, grandchildren, family connections, and property, and there is not one thing that is not loved. Then there is no affair and no thought that is not the business of birth and death, as though your whole body were in a pit of fire. You do not know that while you are reciting, the root of craving in your mind has not let go for a single thought. Just as, while reciting, you say only that your recitation is not earnest, not knowing that craving is the master and recitation the surface. Thus the Buddha’s name is merely recited while craving is merely allowed to grow. Again, when thoughts of sons and daughters appear, turn the light around and look: can this one recitation of the Buddha really hold off this craving? Can it truly cut off this craving? If it cannot cut off this craving, how after all will birth and death be resolved? Because the conditions of craving have been familiar for many lives, while reciting the Buddha’s name has only just been taken up and is very unfamiliar, and is not yet earnest, therefore it has no power. If you cannot master the objects of craving before you now, then at the moment of death you will certainly be unable to master them. Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha’s name: first, you must know that the mind seeking to resolve birth and death must be urgent; the mind to cut off birth and death must be urgent; you must cut off the root and stem of birth and death with every thought — and then every thought is the time of resolving birth and death. Why must you wait for the thirtieth day of the twelfth month to resolve it? That would be late indeed. It is as said: before your eyes all is the matter of birth and death; resolve it before your eyes and birth and death are empty. With such earnestness thought after thought, each cut drawing blood — if with this kind of application you do not escape birth and death, then all the Buddhas have uttered falsehood. Therefore, whether at home or having left home, whoever knows the mind of birth and death — that is the season of escaping birth and death. What other wondrous method could there be?
Instructions for the Attendant of Yunqi

When the Master had not yet entered cessation, for the nineteen years before, in rising and resting, eating and breathing, you attended him day and night. Every secret practice you saw; every subtle word you heard; every response to capacity you understood; every matter of his heart you knew. So it is that the Master’s whole body, form, voice, and sound were all vividly present between your mind and eye. Even the thousands and tens of thousands who drew near him were not your equal in truly knowing and actually seeing him. And now the great assembly — each one sees the Master passed into cessation, yet you alone do not entertain the thought of cessation. In the Dharma-ending age, those who practise the Pure Land all speak of visualizing Amitābha’s sublime marks. But since they have never seen his face, their visualization is not true. They wish to hear Amitābha preach, but their contemplation is not true either. I regard the Master as an emanation body of Amitābha. You have served and attended him long; how could you forget the Master and seek instruction in the Buddhadharma from another house? I tell you, attendant: you need not think otherwise at all. Simply think of the Master as in life — every manner and model, voice and speech, deportment in action, cultivation and contemplation, compassion in benefiting beings — carefully, from head to foot, all day and through the night, pass each one through your mind. Then, thought after thought as you think of him, that is the hour when Amitābha appears. The moment a single thought forgets him, that is the hour of betraying his kindness and entering birth and death. The Old Man has no Dharma to speak; he simply places the Master’s whole body within your mind, and you must not spit it out. This is this old fellow’s samādhi of hiding his body. Ponder it well.
Instructions for the Attendant Dengyu

Recite the Buddha with your own mind; reciting the Buddha is minding the mind. Mind and Buddha are not two. Thought after thought without abiding, the one who recites is not established; the object of recitation is empty by nature. With the nature empty and quiescent, both grasper and grasped are forgotten. This is called accomplishing the Buddha of self-nature right where the mind is. Lose it for a single thought, and you fall into the karma of Māra.
Instructions for Master Xuanjin He

You received your training at Jingci, the very place where Chan Master Yongming proclaimed the Way. When first you shaved your head, you bowed to Yongming’s stupa amid the wild thickets, and in all things you followed his bequeathed model. You copied out his recorded sayings by hand, and for your teacher’s sake you divined and moved his stupa to the Zongjing Hall. Afterwards you vowed never to solicit alms, and practised only the Lotus Repentance ritual, holding firmly to that vow, so that those who gathered were like clouds. When the stupa work was done, you restored the Zongjing Hall and built the Three Pools life-release pond — all of them Yongming’s original vows. When I went to mourn Master Yunqi and was about to proceed to Jingci, you arranged the Zongjing Hall as my lodging. I entered the gate and bowed to Master Yongming’s stupa, and saw how exquisite and meticulous it was, laid out according to the Dharma, every minutest detail conforming to rule. I stayed ten days; a thousand and more people gathered about, each filled with the joy of the Dharma; nothing within or without was neglected, all was in perfect order, and your direction of it was exactly right, as though you gave it no thought. From this I saw that your talent is fit to order the world, your compassion sufficient to benefit beings, and that you possess not only deep resolve and true endowment but inconceivable wondrous practice — which one could hardly achieve without riding on past vows. When I had gone, you escorted me and asked for instruction. So I told you: As a disciple of the Buddha, people are true or false, practices are principle or affair, talents are essence or function, minds are broad or narrow — and all are called monks, yet among them the difference is as between sky and earth. Therefore the Bodhisattva’s gates of benefiting beings are of many kinds. The Buddha rebuked the śrāvakas as arhats in name only, rejecting them as not genuine. What the Buddha valued most was one who protects the life of wisdom in the final age — for such a person is exceedingly hard to find. Living in a hard and turbid world, one cannot even save oneself; how could one act for the Dharma gate? If one cannot provide for one’s own body, how could one be willing to cherish living beings? In all the Mahāyāna teachings, whoever can protect the Dharma is called a true disciple of the Buddha, because he can bear his family’s inheritance. The Buddha grieved that after his cessation it would be hard to find those who hold the sutras. Yet the sutra is the Buddha’s dharma-body and the life of wisdom — not paper, ink, and words. Moreover, the dharma-body flows through the five paths and becomes living beings; hence we know that to protect living beings is to protect the Buddha’s life of wisdom. Therefore the Prajñā teachings of the Bodhisattva path make saving living beings the first thing, and non-abiding in the mark of living beings the wondrous practice. It is said: I save countless, numberless living beings, and yet in truth there is not one living being to be saved — this is understanding the mark of living beings as empty. But I am myself a living being among living beings. Since living beings are empty, what is there of me? When self and others are both empty, who is it in between that acts and receives? With thing and self both forgotten, the between is of itself still. If the three wheels are empty, then true reality is thusness, equally illumined in one light; bodhi and nirvāṇa are all like dreams and illusions. What Dharma is there to speak, what Chan to cultivate, what ten thousand practices to perform? That is why at the Lotus assembly, praising those who hold the sutra, he said: Raising a hand or bowing the head, all have already become Buddhas. This is to use the already-accomplished Buddha-mind to perform the present multitude of practices; therefore each practice is a Buddha practice, and no practice is more wondrous than this. Such a one is called a true disciple of the Buddha. The Buddha said: The object of compassion is living beings in suffering; if there were no living beings, there would be no bodhi. Therefore the Bodhisattva has the mind of the great earth, because he bears living beings; the mind of a bridge, because he ferries living beings across. Vairocana takes Samantabhadra as his body, and Samantabhadra takes living beings as his body. If you take living beings as your mind, you bear the Tathāgata. Consider my words, sir, and use them to seal and confirm your own mind. If you see your own mind and find it truly accords with the Dharma, then outside the Dharma there is no Dharma, just as outside space there is no space. If there is a single blade of grass or mote of dust that does not wholly return to the Dharma-nature, then there is a Dharma outside the mind and a mind outside the Dharma, self and others stand in a thicket, and right and wrong are not yet dissolved. Forsaking this Dharma gate, where else will you seek the path that goes beyond? The Buddha from the first had no Dharma to give to people, and the patriarchs too wished to save themselves. If you retain the view of a single Dharma, then your own mind is not yet saved; unable to save yourself, why seek the Buddhas and patriarchs to be your manure-carrying slaves? From now on, sir, you must raise your eyes higher and examine yourself. Do not say the old monk is garrulous.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Liaowu Shen

The Buddha said: When a bhikṣu’s mind is straight as a bowstring, he can enter the Way. Vimalakīrti said: The straightforward mind is the place of practice. The sages also said: Man is born straight. Hence we know that the Buddha-mind has no other wonder; it is simply the straightforward mind among living beings. Straight means having no crookedness. What is called straight is not establishing a single mote — only that is called straight. What can the straightness of a bowstring contain? As soon as one thought is not straight, that is a fault. If you can be straight thought after thought, then thought after thought contains nothing. Where things are not established, the original substance of itself appears. Therefore the Sixth Patriarch said: Always see your own faults. This one saying is the essential secret of becoming a patriarch. What is called a fault is not a mistake in what you do; it is the delusion of your own mind. Since this mind is originally without a single thing, level and even, as soon as one thought arises it is a fault. One thought is a fault — how much more the various evil habits that appear thought after thought without your being aware of them. How can you escape fault? If a student does not apply his mind at the single thought, then though he studies and inquires all his life he cannot obtain true benefit, for he makes floating thoughts and reflected images his practice and so errs to the very end. When this Chan practitioner first came to the Old Man at Mount Jing, the Old Man at once gave him the style Liaowu — wishing him to apply himself to the fact that originally there is not a single thing. Sending him off in the boat, I gave him this to encourage him.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Xueling Jun

One who studies the Way must first have a firmness of bone and spirit; second, a breadth of understanding; third, an urgent mind about birth and death. Firmness of spirit and breadth of understanding come from past habits and disposition. But if the mind set on birth and death is present before you, and you resolve to have these three complete, that is turning toward the Way. As for applying the mind in investigation: when the ancients taught people, the very first step was to investigate apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and to study beyond the paths of ordinary and sage. Students all know these words. But when it comes to applying the mind, as soon as a single thought is raised it falls into the rut of consciousness — how is one to leave it? Because through many lives habit has made its living entirely within the world of body and mind, one has fallen into the territory of the five aggregates and is enveloped by them, unable to escape. When one does the work, all sorts of strange things appear — all from this fault. You must have a broad understanding and a lofty point of view. First set aside body, mind, and world, then lift up your original huatou, like a peg in empty space. In time, the void will suddenly burst apart — that is the vision of a great person, and it is certainly not to be compared with the ordinary, silent-illumination false Chan. For this measure of strength you need a single block of hard bone, and only then can your footing stand firm. One who is soft, warm, pliant, timid, and steeped in the habits of rice and gruel — how would he dare come near a ten-thousandth of it? As for looking at the huatou, what is most to be feared is falling into the rut of abstruse and wondrous views and knowledge; that is the ghost cave of Black Mountain. As soon as the slightest abstruse view or knowledge hangs in your chest, or you hold the ancients’ words in your heart and will not let them go, you fall into the false views of outsiders. In this, not a mote may be attached; the place where nothing can be attached is the place of gaining power. You need only smash the lacquer bucket through and through — then it is real. Nor may you use the mind to wait for awakening, making of it a bar across your path. Just apply your strength thus, Chan practitioner; one day you will believe for yourself that this old monk does not deceive you.
Instructions for the Daoist Liu

You left home for the sake of birth and death and have sat alone on a lonely peak for ten years here — how earnest that is. I hear you have been assailed by Māra several dozen times and your mind did not move; all urged you to go elsewhere to avoid it, and you would not go. What a power of patience! Surely you have gained much power in the fundamental matter. Since you can be thus in a single thought, you should view the four elements as flowers in the sky and the moon in water, and view death and life as a dream, an illusion. If you truly attain liberation, then sit or stand and pass away. If you cannot, then simply keep one thought unmoving: let them cut you with knives or smear you with sandalwood, dismember you joint by joint — and still not move a single thought. Only that is right view and right practice. Now I hear you wish to stop eating and die. This is something Māra has seized upon; you should see through it at once, and on no account take that thought as something to hold to. Not only would it waste your own bitter resolve for birth and death, it would also, I fear, lead others into the net of false views.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Feishi Yu

Students in the Dharma-ending age mostly delight in superficial habits and do not reach what is true. Hence in the Buddha’s teaching they grasp only names and phrases, do not penetrate the ultimate purport, add to their views and knowledge, and give rise to great arrogance. Thus they bind the root of birth and death with the Buddhadharma itself. It comes of this: at the first arising of the mind they did not set foot on birth and death, nor do they know what birth and death are; they suppose it has nothing to do with them, and walk on blindly in the night, and so fail to find the right path of practice. Moreover, every word and phrase the Buddha taught is a Dharma for escaping birth and death — who would have thought people today would fall by it? This is not the Buddha’s fault; the fault is that the student lacks right faith and right view, and has never drawn near a true good spiritual friend to point it out and break it open for him. The student Fang Yu once interviewed the Old Man beyond the ranges; he is genuine and unadorned. When the Old Man travelled east to Wu and Yue and had cut the new commentaries on the Śūraṅgama and the Lotus, he ordered Yu to proofread them, to weigh and consider them, and Yu grasped the purport beyond the Old Man’s words. The Old Man now returns to Mount Kuang to rest in old age. If one day Yu can keep him company amid leisure and silence, investigating the matter that goes beyond, he will surely not be obstructed by the knowledge-obstacle of his old textual habits. The Old Man is going. On the peak of the Seven Sages, there is a cow-dung fire roasting taro, waiting for you. Bear it in mind.
Instructions for the Layman Shen of Wujiang

All living beings take self-attachment as the root of birth and death. Because there is a self, there are things; things stand over against the self, and so opposition takes shape. Because the self summons enemies, all contrarieties come home to it; and being contrary, they delude it. Thus the eye is deluded by form, the ear by sound, the nose by scent, the tongue by taste, the body by touch, the mind by dharmas. Deluded, one is disturbed; disturbed, one is disordered; disordered, one loses one’s uprightness. Having lost uprightness, one is wounded in many ways. The people of the world are deluded by these and do not know it; they are wounded by them and feel no pain — folly indeed. And they take them as enriching the self, and so love them, grasp them, and seize them — folly more foolish still. Only the wise know they do not profit the self, and so keep far away and avoid them. Yet avoiding them is not so good as forgetting the self. If you can truly forget the self, then toward all those enemies it is as with a shower of arrows shot into empty space: there is nowhere for them to lodge. Let those with resolve for the Way try beginning here.
Instructions for Wang Ziyong

People of the world make their living entirely upon the deluded, phantom states of body and mind; from birth to death they have never once turned to awaken to the original face of their own mind. Because they do not awaken, they do not know where the root of their illness lies. When water and fire oppose each other and the four elements attack one another, that is illness of the body. When deluded thoughts climb and cling, and love and hate, taking and rejecting arise, that is illness of the mind. Illness of the body can be treated with medicine and stone; illness of the mind has no medicine to cure it. The Buddha is the king of physicians for the world: in treating living beings’ illnesses of mind he used all manner of skilful means, yet in the end he used only the awakening that breaks through deluded thought as having no nature — that alone is the wondrous medicine that brings one back to life. If a student seeks a method of peace and joy, he must first see through the fact that the body is not his own. Just look: before your parents gave birth to you, was there ever this body of blood and flesh? And when the four elements separate, where will this body then stand? Observing thus at all times, in time a single thought will suddenly awaken and break through, and you will no longer be afflicted by this body. This is the wondrous medicine for illness of the body. All illness springs originally from the deluded mind. You need only observe thought after thought in daily use: wherever any thought, good or evil, arises, that is the root of illness showing itself. You must apply your strength to that very thought: observe it at the place it arises; see where after all it arises from, and who after all it is that arises and perishes. And when the deluded thought ceases, you must certainly trace where after all it ceases to. Tracing thus until arising has no place of arising and ceasing has no place of ceasing, this is called arising and ceasing having no footing; then the substance of mind is at peace and attains great freedom. Holding the vital gate shut in this way, before and after are not continuous, and the single thought between stands alone. At this place where the single thought stands alone, with long ripening the root of the illness of deluded thought pulls itself out, and all mental defilement has nowhere to lodge. This is the wondrous medicine for illness of the mind. Ziyong, your resolve for the matter that goes beyond is earnest, but your fault lies in seeking it in words and letters, not knowing to seek it in your own ground of mind. Your own deluded thoughts are already the root of illness; and then you take others’ words as real dharmas — this is called adding one more layer of obstruction. From now on, simply see through the deluded thoughts of your own mind and do not be dragged along by them. Just watch where deluded thoughts arise and on no account let them continue. The Buddha said: If the mad mind rests, that resting is bodhi. The supremely pure and bright mind is not to be obtained from outside. If you apply your mind thus without retreating, then this present mind of yours is itself the great gate of peace, joy, and liberation. Because he asked for instruction, the Old Man named him Fujue — Blessing-Awakening — since this awakening is the foremost, measureless blessing. Strive at it!
Instructions for the Layman Lübo, Shen Yuchang

The layman was born into a family of the ten wholesome deeds and dwells in a house of wealth and honour: Bodhisattvas are his father and mother, good spiritual friends are his kin, those of like practice and like vow are his servants, and compassionate manifestations are his sons and daughters. Yet he stands amid it all like a blue lotus rising from the water, erect in the mud. Having given rise to faith, he cultivates blessings and virtues, and everything goes as he wishes. About his dwelling lie lakes and ponds some li around, and the fish he keeps are as many as the sands of those lakes. When first he invited the canon to pass by Reed Island, the fish of the whole marsh, riding red light in the night, were all reborn in heaven. Such is the breadth and excellence of the blessed conditions he has met. Yet he is ashamed that his practice of the Way is not strong, and he asked the Old Man for instruction. The Old Man therefore told him: this is indeed something to be ashamed of. Why? Because outward giving is easy while inward giving is insufficient — it is that the mind is harder to relinquish than goods. Still, this too is hard for a true man. Because the root of craving from kalpas of birth and death is deep and firm and hard to pull out, unless one rouses a great, courageous, resolute will, to seek to practise according to the Dharma is truly no easy thing. Yet when the Old Man looks with the right eye, it is not hard at all. Layman, have deep faith. If you can truly view the body through things, the body becomes easy to slight. View the mind through the body, and the mind becomes easy to forget. View the affections through the mind, and the affections become easy to break. View the nature through the affections, and the nature becomes easy to illumine. View thoughts through the nature, and thoughts do not arise. When thoughts do not arise, the Way is in me and not in things. In that case, how is this different from the fish in the pond who, gazing at the shadow of the Dharma, at once escaped birth and death? If the layman can believe without doubt, then dwelling at home he enters the homeless; living in the world he can leave the world. All your wealth and kin enter the samādhi of illusion. What Way then is hard to practise, what root of craving hard to pull out? If the layman wishes to enter Vimalakīrti’s gate of non-duality, he should enter from here.
Instructions for Yan Fujian

The Buddha said that in the world there is not one dharma that is firm and enduring, meaning such dharmas as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and no-self, which are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, arising swiftly and ceasing swiftly. The impermanent, birth-and-death, corrupting dharmas are all like this. Only the seed of Buddha-nature, though it be within birth and death, is not destroyed through kalpas — that is truly firm. People of the world mistake the impermanent for the permanent and take the infirm as firm; this is called the inverted view. Yet the root of inversion is the nature of evil — what blessing is there in it? Now, if in a single thought you awaken within the dharmas of impermanence and birth and death, and set your mind on seeking the seed of Buddha-nature, then you can give up impermanent wealth and exchange it for the firm wealth of Dharma; give up the impermanent body and life and seek the firm life of wisdom. This is the blessing that transcends the world, the greatest of blessings. Therefore, in accordance with your faithful mind of taking refuge, I name you Fujian — Firm Blessing — only wishing to rouse in you a firm mind. It is what is called seeking abundant blessing for oneself. How could an empty name be worth esteeming?
Instructions for Gu Ruping

Ruping attended old man Zibo for the longest time. Long ago, when I was imprisoned in the capital on account of my troubles, I sent a letter in reply to Zibo. Ruping was at his side, and he handed the letter to him, charging him: Keep this; one day there will surely be a time when we meet. Let this be the tally. Twenty-two years passed. In the bingchen year, in the month of the summer solstice, I came from Nanyue to Shuangjing for the ceremony of installing Zibo’s remains in the stupa. Ruping met me at Songling and brought me to Mr. Yan’s house in a mean lane. There he bowed and asked for instruction, and brought out this scroll, and I saw Zibo’s own hand and my letter of former days. Alas! In the ocean of the Dharma-nature, sages and ordinary beings rise and sink like froth on the great sea, with no footing for their arising and ceasing, no place for their coming and going. Even birth, death, dream, and illusion are utterly ungraspable in the still quiescence. Moreover, my death of former days was not death, and so my life now is not life. Not dying and not living, still and single in one horizon. Hence we know that Zibo’s death now — is it truly death? His hand is vivid still; the dharma-body abides forever. What Zibo saw in former days is as close as the eyelash today. You now see the inch-wide heart of Zibo in those days, its lone radiance shining and displayed like sun and moon. Since in life he was not separated from you by bodily form, how can he be divided from you by the darkness of death? The Buddha said: He contemplates that far-off time as though it were today. Not only are Zibo and I like froth on the vast sea; all ordinary beings and sages are like lightning in the sky. Ruping, you have long entered Zibo’s room; in this one-horizon, equal Dharma gate, you must be like one who bathes in the great ocean, so that the waters of a hundred rivers soak through every pore of your body. Old man Zibo perhaps never touched on this, so I have specially broken it open for you, that you may believe in this Dharma yourself and gain great benefit. If not, then try looking toward the time before your parents gave birth to you. In time you will know that seeing me and not seeing me have no boundary of before and after.
Instructions for Yan Zhongxian on Reciting the Cundī Mantra

Laymen who remain at home have thick five desires and deep-rooted afflictions; day by day the active defilements cross and interlace before them like boiling water seething, so how could they gain a single cool thought? Even if they set their minds on practice, it is hard to set to work. Some, being clever, read the teachings, but they merely learn a few views and knowledge to stock their talk, with no practical use whatever. Reciting the Buddha’s name they likewise take as commonplace and will not settle their minds to death over it; and even if willing, they gain no power, for they recite only upon floating thoughts while the habit-energy in the storehouse consciousness flows on unseen — they never see it at all. Therefore in reciting the Buddha’s name they never see a single thought come to rest. If recitation had power, why seek a separate wonder? Nowadays there is a sort who love the lofty and admire the strange: hearing of Chan investigation and sudden awakening, they at once pride themselves on being of superior faculties, refuse to practise, and fear falling into gradual stages. From the ancients’ encounter dialogues they memorize a few ready-made phrases and rattle them off, seeking only a quick and clever repartee. These are the most pitiable of all.
