It seems to me that if one has truly set the mind on the path and fears birth and death, one had better enter by way of mantra recitation, for it begins with a whole heart of earnest resolve, and so is easily attained. The student Yan Fuchi asked about the essentials of practice at home, so I gave him this. Let readers on no account take it as devoid of principle, for principle has misled people too many; hence this Dharma gate surpasses even investigating the cypress tree or the dried shit-stick.
Instructions for the Master of the Śūraṅgama Hall at Jiahe

The sutra says: The seed of Buddhahood arises from conditions. That is, if you would know the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the season and its conditions. Hence we know that the Dharma realm takes dependent arising as its principle; look carefully at the world and beyond it, and there is not one dharma that does not arise from causes and conditions. The ancient monastery of the Śūraṅgama was founded in the Tang dynasty; Changshui wrote his commentary on the Śūraṅgama here. Its history is long. Standing amid the markets of the royal city, it had long been encroached upon by the powerful. Old man Lu of Wutai received the Vulture Peak’s bequest in this land and made the protection of the Dharma the purpose of his life. When Chan Master Daguan came forth in accord with the times, he had a great karmic bond with the old man; at a single meeting their minds sealed and matched, and at once they discussed restoring it. But one to shoulder the burden was hard to find. Master Kaigong of Mizang cast off the scholar’s gown and left home, becoming Master Da’s intimate disciple. Hearing of the plan to restore the Śūraṅgama, he took the whole burden upon himself. When the meditation hall was completed, they discussed printing the canon in fascicle form to spread the Dharma’s fortunes, and again received the imperial compassion in the bestowal of the canon. But the great hall was not yet finished. Unhappily Kaigong withdrew into seclusion and could not complete the work; and old man Wutai too passed from the world. Then the prefect Mr. Cai Huaiting arrived and it rose up in a single day; layman Bao Xinxian was obtained as leader, and in a moment people’s hearts gathered like an echo. Within less than a year the dark-blue hall towered high and the golden images blazed — how grand! Counting from the first proposal to restore it, nearly twenty years had passed; so in the season and its conditions there is surely something inconceivable. I came to Shuangjing to perform the cremation rites for Master Da, and on my way back passed by the Śūraṅgama. I saw its vast and spacious plan — truly a Pure Land within the dust; its meditation hall pure and clean — truly a Brahmā palace in the sea of illusion. And I met its master, Master Lin: a man upright, dignified, and refined, patient, kind, and harmonious — one may call him a leader of the monastery. I have privately grieved that in this evil world of the five turbidities, the Buddha’s work is entrusted to Bodhisattvas, who still dare not engage in benefiting beings here — how much less can ordinary beings of the broad earth? By Master Lin’s dignity and refinement, all who see him revere him; by his patience and compassion, all who turn to him are glad. With the hearts of all who revere and all who are glad, he accomplishes a work not yet complete: it is like sailing with a fair wind upon a calm stream — what difficulty is there in reaching the other shore? I say the lion’s string is about to fall silent, and it is fortunate that you continue it — this too is what causes and conditions have assigned. All depends on your firm, unshakable vow-power to guard a place of practice hard to build and hard to keep, and to make of it a Buddha-work infinite and imperishable. When the great Dharma flows abroad, that is your own heart-light spreading everywhere. How then could you not firm up this body of blood and flesh, which the Three Jewels cherish?
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Langya Yao of Eastern Chan

Eastern Chan Monastery at Jinsha was built by the grand scribe Mr. Wang Nianxi and is presided over by Langya Yao. When he heard that the Old Man was making a journey to Shuangjing, he specially sent his heir, Master Nanrong, to request sutras and arrange the summer retreat, intending to make it a forest resting place for the Old Man. In the ninth month, after the full moon, the Old Man arrived. He saw their sincerity and strict order, the assembly pure and solemn, devoted to reciting the Lotus Sutra as their work; the term had run only seven years and already more than thirty could recite it whole. This is a rare thing. He had not dwelt there long before going on to Mount Jing, and when his business was done he was about to return to Mount Kuang and bid farewell to the world for good. The Master earnestly urged the Old Man to stay, his feeling not yet exhausted, and at parting the Old Man gave him this instruction: In the nature of the Dharma realm, how could there be marks of coming and going? It is because the eye of wisdom is not yet open that the dust of passion divides; the view of parting and meeting cuts the heart, and the conditions of gathering and scattering bind the thoughts. Unless one penetrates the three periods as unchanging and the ten directions as without interval, one cannot easily reach the state of non-duality. Moreover, the Lotus Sutra takes true reality as its principle: the Many Jewels Tathāgata of the past still exists, and Śākyamuni of the present is not extinguished. The one mind abides forever, undimmed through endless kalpas. The cause of Prince Mahābhijñā endures to this day; the condition of Dīpaṃkara’s prediction is spontaneously and presently realized. Seen thus, how could there be the slightest mark of change or error? Just observe the single light of the white curl between the brows: it illumines all without obstruction, and all sages and ordinary beings, their beginnings and ends, their causes and fruits, are plainly before the eyes. The Old Man’s coming and going is like the bright moon on the long river: each goes its own way east or west, while this moon remains perfectly still. If a single thought is pure and true, then heart-lights interpenetrate. Do not take worldly truth and common feeling as the permanent view of birth and death. May you, sir, with the Lotus samādhi, carry it to its end in the future; then you will be knit brow to brow with the Old Man, returning together to actuality, leaning on one another for long kalpas, never parted through distant ages. Why then be so petty about this illusory, empty body, this image in water and mirror, giving rise to thoughts of self and other? The Old Man is going. Strive, sir.
Instructions for the Two Students Wang Shengchong and Yuanshen

Buddha-nature in a person is like water in a high plain: whoever digs for it will surely find it. It is only that our afflictions are deep-rooted and our feelings of love and hate are firm — no less than the soil of a high plain. If one can dig with force and seek deeply, working without cease, bent on pulling up the root of afflictions and tearing the net of love and hate, then the deep spring of the Dharma-nature will flow without exhaustion, watering the spiritual root and moistening the sprout of wisdom. Not only may the fruit of the Way be awaited; one will also open the hidden current to moisten the scorched and withered, benefiting gods and men alike, all returning to the ocean of Dharma, where a single drop becomes one with the vast sea. How could this be sought outside? The brothers Shengchong and Yuanshen have long entered Zibo’s room; the wise man has gone, and I fear the clear stream of the water of nature may be somewhat blocked. The Old Man has come in season and cleared it for them. Now the source is opened, and from this time it will never run dry. Do not let the dry soil of affliction be thrown in to muddy it.
Instructions for Sun Shenbai

The root and stem of ignorance and birth and death lies only in the single thought before you now. It is like a man who travels all ten directions, exhausting his life’s strength without cease, thinking he has covered a thousand myriad leagues of road, never knowing he has not moved one step from his heel. Hence we know that the deluded thoughts that shift and flow through kalpas and the turning of birth and death have in truth never left this person’s single thought. If in daily life before you, in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, you apply your strength at the very place each thought arises and see through it, so that the place of arising does not arise, then the root of craving of kalpas of birth and death is cut off on the spot. Truly this does not depend on any other power. The Buddha said: If the mad mind rests, when it rests that is bodhi — how could these be empty words? The Old Man points out to you the phrase, before your parents gave birth to you. Apply yourself and look into it; one day you will have a time of believing for yourself.
Instructions for Jiang Yanghui

The student Jiang is brilliant in his youth, with no ordinary spirit; had he not planted a spiritual root long ago and possessed deep seeds of prajñā, such fine substance would hardly be obtained. As a child he once met Master Zibo, who at once named him Xinguang — Light of Faith — meaning the light of the prajñā inherent in the nature. Now that he has come to the Old Man for instruction, I give him the style Yanghui — Nurturing the Shade. In our daily seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, the light of wisdom shines forth; but veiled by ignorance it turns into emotional consciousness and so is dark and undisplayed. If you can have faith in the true light that is originally yours, and not be blinded amid present circumstances — so that at the crossroads of love and hate, in the midst of darkness, the spiritual light shines alone, unclouded by the root of passion — then you nurture it in the shade, and the substance of that light grows brighter and the original source may be recovered. Use its light, and you bring no disaster on your body. If the student Jiang embodies this, then a vast and great light will appear amid all his movements and activities; whatever fame or achievement he establishes will be an imperishable and splendid work. How could he darken himself and not believe? Only let the banner of your arrogance be toppled, and the light will reveal itself.
Instructions for the Assembly

Lately among the young people of various places there are many with the will to investigate Chan; but when you meet them, they are all upside-down fellows. They take stubbornly guarding deluded thoughts as their vow; nurturing laziness as bitter effort; growing their arrogance as lofty solitude; playing with their lips and tongue as keen repartee; clinging to foolishness as the matter that goes beyond; turning their backs on the Buddhas and patriarchs as being right themselves; and relying on cunning cleverness as wondrous awakening. Hence whenever they come to a monastery, their bodily karma cannot enter the assembly, their speech and thought cannot be in harmony with the assembly; they give free rein to feeling and will and do not cultivate the three karmas. They regard bowing and recitation as inferior, practice as menial drudgery, the Buddhadharma as an enemy, and stock phrases as their own insight. Even those who can look at a huatou and do the work first want to use the mind to seek awakening. So before the cushion is steady, before their drowsiness has cleared, before they have even dreamed of it, they are already haughty and conceited, running off to see a good spiritual friend, talking of the wondrous and the sublime, presenting their awakenings and understandings, and using a few groundless, wild sayings to seek confirmation. If they have the good fortune to meet a clear-eyed good spiritual friend, he will break their rut for them — that may be called great luck. If they are unlucky and run into blind, pat-a-blind Chan, one stamp of the winter-melon seal and they are packed off into the pit of false views, falling for a hundred thousand million kalpas with no time of getting out. Are these not pitiable? Foolish folk such as these lose the right cause themselves and then take the poison of error; even if they met Linji or Deshan, they could not undo their deluded clinging. Are they not the most pitiable of all? The ills of the Chan gate have come to this. Look carefully at the ancients from the first: they were certainly not like this. Consider Baizhang serving Mazu, always working in the fields — the cases of planting the spade and the wild duck are the places where his practice was truly tested. For this reason he had the warning: a day without work is a day without eating. Yangqi served Ciming for more than twenty years, personally performing the practices and bearing a hundred thousand hardships as an officer, never shrinking from toil; hence his radiance was great and vast, illumining past and present. As for Lazy Rong carrying rice and Huangmei at the pounding shed — look through the ancients one by one: not one came by any other way than hardship. Why is it that young people today, as soon as they enter a monastery, take Chan investigation as the matter that goes beyond and merely seek to sit upright, enjoying what is ready-made, hands folded in their sleeves and never stretching them out, not picking up so much as a blade of grass? With such thin blessing and utterly no sense of shame, even if they had a wondrous awakening it would only make a solitary tune, with no offerings from gods or men; how much more those who have no true practice, who waste the faithful’s gifts and gladly fall into the depths? If you are a man truly set on birth and death, you should contemplate our teacher Śākyamuni Buddha: in the three thousand great thousand worlds there is not so much as a mustard seed’s worth that is not a place where he gave up head, eyes, marrow, and brain in quest of bodhi. Thus should you rouse your courage, stake your one poor life, and give this stinking bag of bones to the ten directions as an offering to the assembly, bearing all practices with a bitter heart, doing what is hard to do, enduring what is hard to endure. If in daily life you penetrate through and through at the gates of the six senses, then you will attain liberation in every dharma. The ancients said: One who enters by conditions accords swiftly. Apply your mind thus for thirty years without change: even if you do not awaken to the Way, when you next put forth your head you will surely be a man who props up heaven and stands on earth. With this the Old Man instructs you and announces it to all fellow practitioners.
The Dream-Roaming Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Fascicle Eight
Instructions for Zhijian, Superintendent of Guizong

Guizong was a place where the ancient venerable ones preached the Dharma. Master Daguan took the lead in restoring it; afterwards Master Zhan exhausted body and strength and at last recovered the old property. More than twenty years have passed since then; Master Zhan passed away, and his disciple Xiuzi took up the burden. In the summer of the bingchen year I came to bow to the Relic Stupa at Jinlun. I saw that this monastery’s plan surpasses the finest in Mount Kuang, and I reflected that a helper and support is truly hard to find. In the assembly I noticed the Chan practitioner Zaizhi, whose brows and bearing were fine and outstanding, with uncommon spirit. So I charged the abbot to appoint him superintendent. The Chan practitioner is skilled in secret practice: whatever the assembly’s business for the day remained unfinished, he would look to what must be done and would pass the whole night without sleep, personally attending to each matter one by one, so that by daybreak nothing was left undone. I sighed and exclaimed: Is it so indeed? I have often seen the young in monasteries wholly without shame, given over to nursing laziness, unrestrained in the three karmas, not practising bowing and recitation, sleeping even in broad daylight — would they be willing to forgo sleep the whole night and take the toil upon themselves to provide for the assembly’s needs? Of old, among the Buddha’s twelve hundred disciples, Rāhula alone was called foremost in secret practice, and so he became the Buddha’s eldest son. Among the patriarchs of this land, only Baizhang, with his rule that a day without work is a day without eating, became the model for monasteries through a thousand ages. Yongming performed a hundred and eight practices every day, and so his portrait is offered in Yama’s hall. The Buddha said that in the three thousand great thousand worlds there is not so much as a mustard seed’s worth that is not a place where a Bodhisattva gave up body and life for living beings; hence he is revered as the god above gods. So we know that from the first, Buddhas and patriarchs without exception built the world’s fields of blessing and merit through the gate of practice. If the Chan practitioner can with this mind give up body and life and shoulder the monastery, that is establishing the Three Jewels. If the Three Jewels abide forever, that is continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom. If the life of wisdom is unbroken, that is repaying the Buddha’s profound kindness. To know the kindness and repay it is to be a filial son of the compassionate father. Having taken up such a vow of practice, at all hours of day and night think earnestly, thought after thought: Since beginningless birth and death I have cast off bodies and bones piled as Mount Sumeru, and drunk mother’s milk as the waters of four seas; and all these castings-off and receivings of body have created the bitter karma of birth and death. Was there ever a single day when I used this body and life to practise the practice that transcends the world? If there had been, then in this life I would certainly not be standing thus on the ground of an ordinary being. Now I am fortunate to have this body; let me rouse a resolve hard to come by, and for a whole lifetime, to the end of my life, not abandon this fundamental practice — then one lifetime will surpass a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives. Only thus may one be said not to have been born in vain. From now on, Chan practitioner, rouse yet more vigour. At all times simply keep Zhaozhou’s huatou, Does a dog have Buddha-nature?, in your chest, and investigate it with your mind at whatever you are doing: why after all did he say No? One day, when you knock against it and brush against it, the mass of doubt will burst apart in a single thought, and the birth and death of former days will be resolved at once. This may be called accomplishing in one lifetime the twofold adornment of blessing and wisdom. The ancients said: Move the flowers and the butterflies come too; buy the rock and get the clouds thrown in. The thirty-six generations of patriarchs before will all, on the Chan practitioner’s eyebrows, turn the great wheel of Dharma.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Nian Zizong

The Buddha taught his disciples to cultivate the Dharma that transcends the world through only two wondrous practices: benefiting oneself and benefiting others. Benefiting others is called cultivating blessing; benefiting oneself is called cultivating wisdom. When a Bodhisattva rouses the mind, he diligently seeks unsurpassed bodhi. Though he knows the Dharma-nature is empty and still, he does not abandon the conditioned practices. Knowing the Dharma-nature to be empty is benefiting oneself; not abandoning the practices is benefiting others. From the first, no Buddha or patriarch has escaped birth and death except through these two practices. Therefore Śākyamuni, the World-Honoured One, diligently practised what is hard to practise and endured what is hard to endure through kalpas. We, through vast kalpas, have in the ocean of birth and death raised our heads and sunk them again, casting off and receiving bodies beyond reckoning — all of it vain living and wasteful dying. Was there ever a hair’s breadth of true practice? Had there been true practice, then we would certainly not be as we are in this life, with this face. Turn the light around and reflect, and think fiercely — is it not painful? The Chan practitioner is now fortunate, by virtue of past conditions, to have left the world early and departed forever from the sea of suffering, and further to dwell at ease on a famous mountain, a supreme place of practice where the patriarchs preached the Dharma. This is a condition hard to meet in ten thousand kalpas. It is exactly to meet a king’s banquet when starving, to meet the king of physicians when ill. You should rejoice beyond measure. Even if you give this whole span of life, staking one lifetime to accomplish this merit, it already surpasses a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives passed in vain and to no profit. The Chan practitioner should believe the Old Man’s words: from now on, rouse a firm and unretreating mind, hold a courageous, strong, and resolute will, use all your bodily strength, measure your own ability, muster a whole heart of willingness, follow conditions and your vow, be patient and bear annoyance, endure bitterness and toil. Then if in one day you accomplish a single kind of merit, it already surpasses a lifetime spent in vain. The Chan practitioner says himself that his body is weak and his spirit weary and that he cannot take on affairs. The ancients valued strength of mind and greatness of vow, not whether the body was strong. Though you now have a small ailment, it is no great suffering. But if you create evil karma and fall into the three evil paths, then even should you seek, with this body and mind of small illness and small affliction, to do the profitable work of a field of blessing, you will not be able to obtain it. The Buddha had living beings contemplate the suffering of the hells and give rise to the bodhi mind — this is exactly the banner of vigour to be raised today. The ancients said: Better to die with the Dharma than to live without it. Even if you give up this body and life to perform this wondrous practice, it is still the ship of prajñā that can reach the other shore. If you do not force yourself and strengthen your will, you may be said to have wasted this life — to have reached the mountain of treasures and returned empty-handed. Is that not a pity? If you can set your mind at peace in non-doing, then the mind is empty; the mind being empty, the spirit is not exhausted; the spirit not being exhausted, the body is not wearied. This is the wondrous practice of non-doing. Meeting conditions is itself the principle; you will certainly not be turned about by daily affairs, and in every matter you will accomplish the great gate of liberation. Ponder this well.
Instructions for General Lu — Shixian, Styled Zhenhu

The General is of an old lineage of Haoliang, by nature heroic and outstanding; his killing instinct was certainly inborn. In middle age he came to know he should turn toward the Way and entered the room of Mr. Zhou of Haimen, who lifted up the ancients’ words, I urge you, sir, to recognize the master, and showed them to him. When the Old Man retired to Mount Kuang, he came to pay his respects beneath Jinlun Peak. Knowing that his karma of killing was too heavy, he wished to seek repentance. The Old Man was glad that his nature is straightforward and without falsity — truly of the company of the loyal-hearted and righteous-spirited heroes of old. Yet through the ages many have been endowed with such a nature, and all have misused their minds, turning the seed of Buddhahood into an instrument of hell’s suffering. Buddha-nature is not two; between living beings and Buddhas not a hair’s breadth intervenes. One who penetrates the nature is a Buddha though a living being; one who does not penetrate it is a living being though a Buddha. It is like clear cool water: offered to the Buddha it is pure; used to wash filth it is foul. Hence the Buddha’s compassion is the living being’s killing instinct. The ancients said: To protect life one must use killing; only when killing is exhausted can one dwell in peace. And again: In Sanskrit, arhat; in our language, slayer of thieves. The sutra says: To do battle with the māra of the five aggregates, the māra of afflictions, and the māra of death, and to win great merit; to extinguish the three poisons, leave the three realms, and shatter Māra’s net — at that hour the Tathāgata is greatly delighted. This is the model by which the old man Śākyamuni urged people to kill. Because the Buddha can kill in this way, he is titled the Great Hero, the World-Honoured One. People of the world are foolish: endowed with the heroic Buddha-nature, they do not kill their own thieves but instead kill people, and kalpa after kalpa, life after life, repay it with the suffering of hell, while thinking their merit great. Are they not the most foolish and deluded, using their Buddha-nature upside down? It is said: One general’s success, ten thousand bones dried white. Since antiquity no crime has been greater than killing. To kill men and count it merit, to slaughter living creatures and eat their flesh, indulging the belly and taking it as pleasure — their folly is of the same kind. If the General can turn his mind toward the beyond and seek abundant blessing for himself, then from today let him use the courage of killing to kill his own desires. The Buddha said: Greed and anger surpass sworn enemies; to cut them off oneself is to slay the thieves. To shatter afflictions and escape the suffering of birth and death is to be a Great Hero. To seek thereby directly the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood is the great reward. Such is the profit of this killing; to cast it aside and not seek it — can that be called wisdom? Still, to kill others is easy; to kill oneself is hard. Hence it is said: Leaving home is the business of a great man, not something generals and ministers can do. The Old Man has tangled his vines to this extent; this is called the compassion of the gift of Dharma. If the General believes this, it is true repentance.
Instructions for Huicheng Xin, Chief Seat

Chief Seat Huicheng left home in middle age, casting off wife and bringing his son. He studied under the two great masters Daguan and Lianchi, and even sealed himself in retreat east of the lake at Nanyue. When the Old Man was about to choose a dwelling at Nanyue, Cheng broke open his retreat to welcome him and became his attendant. One day he bowed and said: I am fortunate, in the Dharma-ending age, to be a disciple of the Buddha and to have set my mind on escaping birth and death. I have personally seen the three great masters appear in this evil world of the five turbidities, guarding the Dharma gate, doing what is hard to do, enduring what is hard to endure, and training those hard to train. Whenever I read in the Tathāgata’s teaching the Bodhisattva path, I used to take it for empty words; now I have personally received the three great masters’ conduct and model. While they are present I can take refuge in them to the end of my life; truly it is hard to forsake this and seek a protector elsewhere. So he painted the likenesses of the three great masters and wore and honoured them all his life, resolving life after life to hold this wheel of vow, passing among gods and men and circling the six destinies without ever wearying. I beg the Master to attest it for me. The Old Man heard and laughed, saying: This is indeed your deep heart and original vow. Still, it seems close but has not yet reached the root. Try to contemplate our teacher, Vairocana: the dharma-body is not a body; it is made a body by the practices of the three great beings Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and Samantabhadra. Mañjuśrī is wisdom; Avalokiteśvara is compassion; Samantabhadra is practice. Set aside these three, and the dharma-body is empty and still, with nothing to rest on. Thus the Tathāgata’s dharma-body: if we speak of its wisdom, it penetrates the Dharma realm’s principle and phenomena, cause and effect, down to every blade of grass and mote of dust, exhausting the very bottom of each; and it penetrates the root of every thought and mental count throughout the realm of living beings. If we speak of its compassion, then all living beings without number are its own body: whatever hunger, cold, hardship, illness, or itching living beings suffer, even the fierce suffering of the three evil paths, the Bodhisattva’s whole body feels as one with them; hence he cannot forsake a single living being. If we speak of its practice, then throughout empty space and the whole Dharma realm there is not a blade of grass or mote of dust that is not a place where the Bodhisattva gave up body and life. Hence Samantabhadra’s ten vows each say: When the realm of space is exhausted, the realm of living beings exhausted, the karma of living beings exhausted, the afflictions of living beings exhausted — yet my vow and practice shall have no end. Therefore our teacher Vairocana, by these three dharmas, accomplishes one body. Remove one dharma and the dharma-body is not accomplished; let one living being be other than oneself and the dharma-body is not universal; and if even a mote or blade of grass is not penetrated, then ignorance is not yet exhausted — and if it were so to the very end of space, and practice and vow also ended, then the dharma-body would be annihilated. Yet within the nature of the Dharma realm, these three are seen as the three eyes of Maheśvara: they are one and yet three, neither three nor one; in the sea of quiescence they are like a bubble ceasing and a bubble arising. If there is an outstanding great man of immeasurable capacity who can walk upon the crown of Vairocana’s head and look back at these three practices, it would be much like calling a slave master. Their petty, trifling practices, compared with the three great beings, are no better than those of slave boys and serving girls; how could they exhaust the measure of the Buddha’s dharma-body? If from this you can rouse a firm mind, give up body and life, and establish the Three Jewels, then whatever in the least benefits the Dharma gate and living beings is the virtue and function of the whole Dharma realm — like extending from one mote to all motes, beginning with one hair and melting many hairs; from this life to the furthest future, kalpa after kalpa, life after life, never retreating from this mind, just as Samantabhadra’s realm of space is exhausted while his vow and practice are endless. Life after life, in eating and resting, rising and dwelling, walking, standing, sitting, and lying, you will never be outside a single pore of our teacher. The three venerable ones alike emerge and sink in the ocean of the Dharma-nature, never leaving the samādhi of illusion, playing a part as the scene requires, carrying their pole and props with them, speaking illusory Dharma to open illusory beings — that there is; but how could that make them your teacher? Do not, with a limited mind, narrow the Tathāgata’s dharma-body realm to yourself. That is enough.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Zijue Zhi

The Buddha said: You bhikṣus should every morning touch your own head. These words are most intimate and to the point. The Old Man has often reflected on them: our Buddha’s compassion pierces to the marrow. He often said that bhikṣus of the Dharma-ending age enjoy many things — dwelling at ease with the four requisites and all kinds of offerings, each supposing them his due, never thinking who I am, where things come from, or why I receive them. Hence those who know kindness are rare and those who repay it fewer — simply because they have never once touched their heads. Let them turn the light around and touch their heads once, and they cannot help starting in surprise: Why have I shaved head and beard and ceased to be of the company of laymen? If one knows one’s form differs from the worldly, then one dare not dwell near the worldly, dare not let the body enter the worldly, dare not let the mind think on the worldly. Then one delights in the practice of detachment and, without waiting for a teacher’s instruction, rouses courage of himself, and entering the mountains fears only that he has not gone deep enough. How then could he bear to mingle with the market crowd, giving loose rein to body and mind, becoming a shameless man and doing profitless things? The Chan practitioner Zijue lived among people and came to Mount Kuang to bow to the Old Man, wishing to wither his mind dwelling in the mountains and cultivate the practice that transcends the world. The Old Man accordingly instructed him in the practice of cultivating blessing and wisdom together. Cultivating wisdom lies in contemplating the mind; cultivating blessing lies in the ten thousand practices. For contemplating the mind, Buddha-recitation is foremost; for the ten thousand practices, offering is foremost. These two are the total retention. In all our daily use, every stirring of the mind is a deluded thought, the root of birth and death, and so it invites bitter fruit. Now turn the deluded mind to Buddha-recitation, and thought after thought becomes a cause of the Pure Land — that is pleasant fruit. If recitation continues unbroken thought after thought, deluded thoughts vanish, the light of the mind shines out, wisdom appears, and one accomplishes the Buddha’s dharma-body. As for why living beings are poor and lack blessing and wisdom: it is because life after life they have never once made an offering to the Three Jewels to seek blessing and virtue, but only for the sake of this suffering body of birth and death have they craved the pleasures of the five desires, feeding the root of suffering. Now turn the mind that craves for oneself to making offerings to the Three Jewels; with this limited body and life, according to your mind and strength, make offerings to the ten directions — even a stick of incense, a flower, a grain of rice, a stalk of vegetables. Then it is like a drop of water entering the vast sea, a mote falling upon the great earth: though the sea should dry and the earth be exhausted, that blessing is without end. Hence one is rewarded with the Buddha-fruit’s Lotus Treasury adornment as one’s own field of enjoyment in the future. Forsake this, and there is no wondrous practice of attaining Buddhahood. If the Chan practitioner grows weary, let him touch his head, and he will of himself rouse measureless courage.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Tai of Longhua

In former days when I went to Chang’an for alms, I passed beneath the Longhua trees. The abbot, Master Rui’an, was delighted to find me, and looked on me as one with many lives of kinship. I observed that of those who dwelt in monasteries in the royal city, most were given to superficial habits; this Master alone was solitary, hard, pure, and aloof, meeting things without lending them a word or a look. In my heart I knew he was no man of the dust. So we became friends who never thwarted each other and visited often. His disciples likewise all treated me as kin, so there was no distance between us. When the Master passed away, his heir Master Tan looked on me as he had looked on the Master. I was banished beyond the ranges and was ashamed that in all my life I had never found a way to repay his kindness. Lately, coming out from the ranges to Nanyue, the dharma-grandson, the Chan practitioner Tai, came from afar to inquire after me. When I saw him I could not help an aching in my vitals; the voice and countenance of the Master of former days stood plainly before my eyes. When I went to Shuangjing to settle the matter of Master Da’s karmic affairs, the Chan practitioner attended me. Afterwards, when I returned to Mount Kuang, I brought him back with me, thinking of your grandfather’s kindness and hoping to accomplish the Chan practitioner’s work of transcending the world, as a way of repaying it. He dwelt with me a year, but because of the toil of clearing wild land, body and mind had not yet been set down. Lately I was just pointing things out to the Chan practitioner and rousing his first resolve, and he had begun to have a direction, when his father sent a letter summoning him and assigned him other affairs. I tried hard to keep him, but could not. Now the Chan practitioner is about to take leave and asks for instruction. So I told him: We who have left home must first attend to what is great and slight what is small. What is great? Birth and death. What is small? Worldly ties. The ancients said: Except for birth and death, the truly great matter, all else can be deliberated. Living beings sink in the sea of suffering, drowned in worldly ties; from kalpas past down to today they have never once turned to reflect. Now you are fortunate to be a disciple of the Buddha, your body wearing the kāṣāya, and further to have met a teacher and the conditions for entering the Way — yet you do not stake and cast off worldly ties and apply your mind bitterly to investigating the matter beneath your own feet. I greatly fear this life will be missed; and when you next put forth your head, who knows whether all conditions will be as complete as they are today. The Chan practitioner now dare not disobey his father’s command; go then, it must be so. But you should make the thought of birth and death urgent, and not lose the conditions for pursuing the Way. When the matter is done, return at once. The Old Man is fortunate enough to be buried alive in an empty mountain; as long as a remnant of breath remains for one day, he will discuss the great matter with the Chan practitioner and there will be the merit of one day. The Old Man takes the end of his life as the term; let the Chan practitioner attend him with a mind dead to the world. If only the Chan practitioner’s single thought of the present person blazes with light, then not only will he resolve the great matter of kalpas of birth and death, but it will also be the Old Man’s way of repaying your grandfather — not betraying the karmic meeting of this life. The Chan practitioner is going. Do not linger long in a foreign land and add again to the accumulated karma of birth and death.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Cuilin

What the Buddhas and patriarchs taught was only a true mind and genuine practice, as the essentials for escaping birth and death. When the mind is true, then in all one’s movements, words, deeds, and undertakings there is not one thing that is not true. When practice is genuine, then in all one does there is not one act that is not genuine. Hence truth and genuineness are like good seed; all the other undertakings and established practices are the conditions for its growth. For this reason it sprouts, puts forth a stem, flowers, and bears fruit, and in the end is not in vain. Therefore the Buddha said that rousing the mind and practising is like sowing seed, and accomplishing bodhi is the fruit that results; fruit means the real. Because beginning and end are both true, the Buddha rebuked the two vehicles as scorched sprouts and rotten seeds — because their mind and practice were not true. From the first, the patriarchs taught that investigation must be true investigation and awakening must be genuine awakening. Hence we know that all living beings who live vainly and die wastefully do so because deluded thoughts and inversions run the show; kalpa after kalpa, life after life, there has never been a single true thought, and so they drift in the ocean of birth and death and find it hard to reach the other shore. This is what is meant by the karma-consciousness vast and vague, with no root to rely on. How much more for a disciple of the Buddha, whose body is beneath the kāṣāya: how could he wander one lifetime, thought after thought turning in deluded thought and karma-consciousness, never once reflecting, never seeking a practice of genuine walking? That is to lose one’s human body beneath the kāṣāya — the most pitiable of all. Since the Chan practitioner has not grudged a thousand li to come and consult the Old Man, he must have roused a whole heart of true faith. In this empty mountain’s silence — no place for plundering emptiness — for what did you come? Having roused true faith, it is not finished with one meeting; if you do not seek a stretch of genuine practice, it is all in vain. If you seek genuine practice, it must be discovered from a true mind. If you truly have a real and genuine mind for birth and death, you must take all the time from birth until now, and from leaving home until now, and think through and examine it point by point from the beginning: was there ever a single thought or a single act that was a genuine matter? The past has already been passed in vain. From today onward, rouse a whole heart set on transcending the world; set down at once all worldly roots of passion and deluded clinging; cast away this handful of bones at once; cast this one life into the empty mountains and great marshes, and let sun scorch and wind beat it. Cast aside entirely all thoughts of comfort, ease, fullness, and warmth. Hang nothing but the single thought of death and birth on your eyebrows; keep one gongan of the ancients in your chest and investigate it day and night. Watch: as soon as a single worldly thought arises, that is where you fall into birth and death — you must cut it off, allowing not a hair’s breadth. Investigating thus, do not rest until you awaken. This very act is the true mind for birth and death. With this mind, throughout the twelve hours, in all movements and activities and the various practices — bowing to the Three Jewels, making offerings to the ten directions, harmonizing the assembly, caring for the aged and sick — do all of it with your own body and all your strength, without a single thought of weariness, without a single thought of self and other, right and wrong, gain and loss, without a single thought of rest or sufficiency. Like Master Yongming, who performed a hundred and eight skilful practices every day, unchanged to the end of his life — that is genuine practice. Cultivating the mind and establishing practice thus, you will break through to the original light of the ground, and all the seeds of habit stained through kalpas — greed, anger, delusion, craving — will one by one melt away and be transformed into the genuine seeds of Buddhahood. Applying the mind thus, one may be said not to have lived this life in vain, not to have failed in leaving home, not to have wasted a long journey through wind and waves to consult a teacher. But if you remain as before, plundering emptiness and only tasting feelings, then the seeds of karmic and sinful defilement will simply follow deluded thoughts, and you will not only betray this life but truly take upon yourself the suffering of the three evil paths for kalpas without end.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Shunze Yi

A śramaṇa, a son of Śākya, is one who has gone beyond the dust; to draw near the Buddhadharma is a Dharma beyond feeling, in truth a tool for breaking the self. Students nowadays study widely and hear much, but only increase their self-view; few can savour the taste of Dharma and nourish the dharma-body and the life of wisdom — is this not inversion in the extreme? The Chan practitioner Yi takes wide learning as without benefit and sets his will on pure practice; that is already far. Yet if he merely makes pure practice his conduct, without bending his will to exhaust the root and stem of birth and death and penetrate deeply the ground the Buddhas and patriarchs never reached, then his founding resolve is not far-reaching, and he will take a single day’s price as his gain — how could he not betray what he originally has? What is rare among our kind is weariness with the world; what is rarest is weariness with birth and death. The Chan practitioner now knows the weariness but does not examine why he is weary; this is still the fifty steps laughing at the hundred. Alas, I am old; my remaining days are few; the great affliction of birth and death lies across my very eyelashes, and I fear my weariness is not yet complete. The Chan practitioner too is advanced in years. If he can make the Old Man’s weariness his own, and if he does not weary of the Old Man’s company amid a thousand cliffs and ten thousand ravines — cutting off shadows and forgetting words, cultivating the practice of detachment — then from this he will bow farewell forever to the five turbidities, depart forever from the four kinds of birth, and roam together in the vast land of Ultimate Bliss. Is that not the supreme connection? Why stop at a journey of a thousand li with provisions for three months? As for those who fly only to the elm and the sandalwood, or go only as far as the wild green — they are surely not worth speaking of the Way with.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Miaoji

The Chan practitioner takes mantra recitation as his exclusive practice and has pursued it for thirty years, yet his mind-ground has shown no brightening. He begged the Old Man for instruction, and the Old Man told him: The Buddha said that on the path of practice there are many gates of skilful means, but the return to the source is not two. Even investigating Chan and lifting up a huatou, and reciting the Buddha’s name or holding mantras, are not two dharmas. It is only that those who do not know how to use the mind do not know to use these to grind away habit-energy and shatter deluded thoughts; instead, with a clinging mind they feed ignorance — hence they use much strength and reap little. This matter is like using a tile to knock on a door: you only want the door to open, and need not reckon what the tile in your hand is like. Through measureless kalpas we have accumulated seeds of greed, anger, delusion, craving, and mixed defilement, hidden in the storehouse consciousness, deep, firm, dark, and far, so that no one can break them. The sages provisionally set up skilful means and taught people to lift up one gongan as a huatou, to lay on doubt heavily, and to cut off deluded thoughts at the pass without letting go a hair. With long effort it gains power, like pressing a dog until it leaps the wall, and suddenly the storehouse consciousness bursts open and the original face is revealed — this is called awakening to the Way. If one could simply press deluded thoughts until they do not arise, what need of a huatou? Even the old woman counting charcoal balls, single-minded and undivided, could awaken; how much more reciting the Buddha’s name or holding a mantra — are these two dharmas? That your thirty years of mantra recitation has brought no effect is not because the mantra lacks efficacy; it is simply that the mind reciting the mantra has never gained power. Ordinarily it is like pushing an empty cart downhill: the mind just lets it roll along — when did it ever exert strength? Applying the mind thus, not only will this life bring no proof; through endless kalpas it will be only thus. And when the dark realm appears before you and birth and death arrive, your eyes will still be dazzled and confused, and you will blame your practice for having no result. Is that not deceiving and erring yourself? From today the Chan practitioner need not change his practice: simply take the mind that recites the mantra and make it your huatou. Word by word, mind to mind, apply your strength and grind away, like pushing a heavy cart uphill, exhausting every ounce of strength in your whole body, not daring to slacken a hair, inch by inch, step by step, never letting the heel come down empty. When you strive thus, you press the deluded thoughts until they stream and cut off the very root of life, giving them no passage. At this point, at the very place you are striving, lay on doubt again and look deeply: ask, this effort of reciting the mantra — what after all is it? Look and look, doubt and doubt, like a mouse entering a cow’s horn, until you reach the place where you cannot turn around or breathe out. This is exactly the time of gaining power. On no account think of resting; nor take this as hard and give rise to thoughts of withdrawal. And when you press through to the place where a single thought opens up, that is the samādhi of lightning-flash — on no account take it as a wondrous joy. From there, gather yet more spirit and stake your life on it. Until the storehouse consciousness suddenly bursts and empty space shatters, never let go. If you can recite mantras thus, how are they two dharmas from investigating Chan? Hence it is said: Gutei merely recited three lines of mantra and became renowned as surpassing all others. This is proof enough. Even if you saw the Buddhas and patriarchs face to face, they would not alter the Old Man’s words.
Instructions for the Novice Monk Zhi

Nowadays among those who leave home, in this Dharma-ending age of firm contention, if one can resolve his will for the great matter of birth and death, lift up single-mindedly the one matter that goes beyond, and take awakening as his term — such a person of the highest faculties is truly rarely seen. There are also those who investigate this matter, but their evil perceptions and evil habits are thick; before the cushion is steady, false views spring up on every side and most fall into the way of Māra. This is the difficulty. The ancients said: If you cannot yet investigate the beyond, then at least set your heart on the teachings, and your time will not be passed in vain. Setting the heart on the teachings is also of two kinds. One whose faculties are somewhat sharp strives to exhaust the principles and tenets of nature and marks, penetrating deeply to their source; by the power of hearing much and permeating habit, he enters samādhi through hearing, thinking, and cultivating. Such a one not only illumines mind and nature for himself but can also be a teacher to others; this too repays the Buddha’s deep kindness and does not betray the resolve to leave home. As for one whose faculties are somewhat dull and who cannot broadly approach the teachings, then the single gate of recitation and holding is especially the essential practice. Therefore Master Tiantai made reading, reciting, receiving, and holding the foremost of the five grades of contemplation practice; and the Lotus Sutra says that the Dharma-master who holds the sutra, in this present flesh body born of father and mother, at once attains purity of the six senses. How could the merit of holding the sutra be an inferior practice? Since the novice knows to weary of the suffering of birth and death and has come to the Buddha to leave home, if he has no single practice to which he devotes his mind, will he not betray this life? Even the single practice of holding the sutra, if one can devote mind and will to it, as the ancients quietly ordered their minds in contemplation, will one day, words forgotten, bring accord and understanding and the attainment of the Buddha’s mind-seal. This is to gain total retention through letters — what is called the gate of the turning dhāraṇī. Entering realization through this, the root and stem of kalpas of birth and death is, by this Dharma gate, cut off at once. Is this not a direct road to unsurpassed bodhi? But if you let the years drift idly and waste the light of time, falling into the common stream of rice and gruel, will you not vainly consume the faithful’s gifts and add again to the burden of karma? What then is the use of having left home?
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Xingjue

Leaving home is originally for the great matter of birth and death. But those who leave home today do not know what birth and death are; they only know how to drift with the waves, their karma-consciousness vast and vague, with no root to rely on. The ancients travelled to practice places and wandered on foot, seeking out teachers, solely to investigate clearly the matter beneath their own feet. People today travel the whole world and pass through every monastery, yet only stir up the habit-energy of rice and gruel, and never come to know how a good spiritual friend deals with people. It is a pity to rush about a whole lifetime and in the end have no foothold at all. These are to be pitied. There are even those with a single thought for birth and death who do not know the essentials of practice, and take bowing, reciting, and Buddha-recitation as practice; after a lifetime of hardship, the matter beneath their own feet is like a black lacquer bucket — it has nothing whatever to do with birth and death. The Chan practitioner has roused a true mind for the great matter of birth and death. Only investigating the one matter that goes beyond is genuine work. First you must muster a long, settled, unretreating will. The ancients spent twenty or thirty years lifting up a single thought and would not rest until they awakened. Above all, do not hope for quick success. Old man Śākyamuni ground and refined body and mind for three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas — was he of dull faculties? The ancients’ opportunities for investigation are many, but only the one plain huatou, Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name?, is easiest to gain power with. The Chan practitioner has now roused his mind to investigate; simply lift up this one gongan at all times. First set down at once all deluded and cluttered thoughts within and without body and mind, until you reach the place where nothing more can be set down. Then deeply lift up one sound, Amitābha Buddha. The four characters are clear and distinct; look at them sharply. If you look and find little power, lift the Buddha’s name again. When there is strength, lay on doubt and ask: Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name? Ask again and again — who after all is it? If you see drowsiness or distraction appear, at once gather your spirit: lift again, look again, ask again, doubt again. Doubt until you reach the place where you cannot doubt; then in your chest it will be like a silver mountain and an iron wall standing between mind and eye. This is the time when the huatou gains power. If you reach this place of power, it is exactly right to lay on doubt again. At all times and in all places in daily life, let it not shift thought after thought, until after long practice even in dreams it is as when awake. If your effort reaches this, on no account retreat or fall away. Suddenly the mass of doubt will burst apart and you will of yourself suddenly see the original face. If you will rouse this settled will and hold this unretreating mind, then simply go straight on with a single thought. On no account seek quick results; on no account use the mind to wait for awakening. If your work is fine and close, there will naturally be a time of breaking through. Of all that is said above, this one matter of investigation is the easiest and most labour-saving. It requires that you can set it down, lift it up, lean on it steadily, and doubt it keenly. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whether in movement or stillness, at leisure or busy, all are times for applying the mind. The Sixth Patriarch said: As for this matter, one may do it even with swords wheeling in battle. That is what this means. If the Chan practitioner has the will and truly is for birth and death, then set foot on this one road.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Baozang Xiang on His Pilgrimage to Putuo

The Great Being Avalokiteśvara realized the perfect-penetration root and, with a dharma-body of the Dharma realm, manifests in response to conditions — how could he be fixed in residence at Putuo? The sea is a figure for birth and death, the mountain for nirvāṇa. The Great Being, with his dharma-body, responds universally within the sea of birth and death; even the ordinary daily life of living beings is the manifestation of the Great Being’s awe-inspiring spirit, still and quiescent, like a mountain of jewels. Hence Putuo in the sea is used to figure it. Because he is within the sea of living beings’ afflictions, and when living beings suffer, that is the Great Being’s own suffering, therefore at a single invocation of his name they gain liberation. It is living beings awakening the Great Being of their own minds; when the Great Being is present, quiescence is present, and where there is quiescence suffering cannot reach. Hence the mountain stands in the sea and the waves cannot shake it. Therefore it is said that the Great Being always dwells at Putuo — not that a fist-sized rock in the sea is narrowly pointed to as the Great Being’s abode. Living beings, deluded and confused, do not bow to the Great Being of their own minds, who sits in person upon the quiescent place of practice, towering and unmoved like a mountain in the sea; instead they trudge over mountains and rivers, must go thousands of li away, and wear themselves out in hardship, seeking him outside. Their delusion is extreme. Yet even so — the sutra says: The return to the source is not two, though the skilful means are many. Now all the living beings of the great earth believe in the Great Being at the Southern Sea; it fits to meet their capacity and lead them in, letting them cross the sea and climb the mountain, and at a single call to the Great Being suddenly awaken their own minds. Then the waves before their eyes all enter the gate of perfect penetration. One must bring them to believe for themselves and only then stop. Among those who practise thus, if even one person can believe these words of the Old Man, his pilgrimage on foot will not have been in vain. Otherwise he will have wasted the price of his straw sandals.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Minghui on His Pilgrimage to Shaolin to Venerate the Patriarch

As for this matter: before the Buddha appeared in the world, before the patriarch came from the West, it illumined heaven and earth, lacking nothing and with nothing to spare. Even when the yellow-faced old man appeared in the world and muddled about for forty-nine years, wagging lips and tongue all day, he never spoke a single word of it. And at the last, when he held up a flower and Kāśyapa broke into a smile, he said: I have the treasury of the right Dharma eye and the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa; now I entrust it to you. This is much like deceiving a child with an empty fist. From that came what is called the Way transmitted apart from the teachings — like fitting a handle to a bowl. One man transmits a falsehood, ten men transmit it as truth. Bodhidharma came from the West and it was again called the single transmission and direct pointing. Nine years at Shaoshi — he took in that foolish fellow Shenguang, who stood in the snow and cut off his arm. You would think there was something extraordinary in it; yet when all is said and done, it is simply that the mind cannot be found. From this, receiving falsehood and echoing it, everyone has built castles in the air and set up his own gate and yard — two schools and five houses — and in the end never brought it out for anyone. Down to this day the whole earth is black as lacquer, so that deluded and mad folk play with the ghost of their spirits in ghost caves, calling themselves heirs of Shaolin Chan and descendants of such-and-such a house. To deceive foolish people thus — is it not painful? The Chan practitioner comes today to consult this old monk. This old monk here has no Buddhadharma or Chan to give anyone — what dried shit-stick is there to speak of? And the Chan practitioner wants to go off to Shaolin to venerate the ancestral founder and seek Buddhadharma and Chan, forsaking the foot of earth beneath his own heel and searching instead beyond a thousand mountains and ten thousand rivers, in another man’s house. Is that wisdom? Let the Chan practitioner try to understand the matter beneath his own feet. Before he has taken one step out the door, and when he arrives at Mount Kuang — are these the same or different? Right now, one step from Mount Kuang, and when he has gone to Shaolin and come back again — are these the same or different? If they are different, then before he took one step out the door he had already gone astray — how much more for a thousand or ten thousand li? If the Chan practitioner does not believe the Old Man, then go to Shaoshi and ask the exposed pillar in front of the Single Transmission Hall: see what it is.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Fajie Yue

The Chan practitioner grew up in Jianchang. Since leaving the dust he has long wandered abroad, and once paid his respects to Zibo and to the Old Man in the capital — more than thirty years ago. Now he has come again to see the Old Man at Mount Kuang, and the Old Man told him: From the first, those who leave home do so for the great matter of birth and death. They climb mountains and cross rivers, seeking a good spiritual friend to decide and choose for them, so that beneath a single word or phrase they may cut off the root of life and sever at once the dust-toil and evil habits of a hundred thousand million kalpas, like a hawk slipped from its leather jesses, from then on never again bound by anyone, able to swing its arms free on the road of birth and death without a backward glance. Look carefully at the patriarchs in the Transmission of the Lamp: in the places where they drew out nails and pulled out wedges for people, what wonder or secret was there? It was only that the student had single-mindedly held the one matter of birth and death in his chest — unable to swallow it, unable to spit it out, choked and stopped up like one mourning his mother — until by chance, when conditions ripened, he suddenly met the tip of a good spiritual friend’s staff and was turned with a single poke. What doubt or hesitation remained? He simply believed that his own mind is originally complete. People today go on pilgrimage, travel to the ends of the earth, enter every monastery: wherever their eyes fall and it is warm and bustling, that is a good place of practice; wherever the rice and gruel is fine and clean and they can eat their fill, that is a good teacher. Even when they meet a clear-eyed teacher, they are deceived by the warmth and miss it face to face. Wandering and consulting in this way, not for the fundamental matter, is simply drifting in birth and death, wasting a lifetime’s time, squandering the price of straw sandals — is that not greatly to be sighed over? The Chan practitioner, for the sake of birth and death, left home and went on pilgrimage, consulted teachers, dwelt on famous mountains, practised austerities, and went through every kind of Dharma practice, one by one. Now tell me: the matter of birth and death right now — how is it after all? Tell me: seeing old man Zibo before, seeing the Old Man now, and not having seen them — what difference is there? Tell me: now on the ten-thousand-fathom peak of Mount Kuang in the depths of white clouds, and in the royal city amid ten thousand fathoms of red dust — are these states the same or different? If you say they are the same, then you are three thousand li apart with no connection. If you say they are different, then where are the eyes of a patch-robed monk on pilgrimage? If you can decide it here, then thirty years are today and today is thirty years ago; red dust is white clouds and white clouds are red dust; and all birth and death, affliction, and karmic action, and all the various differentiated states, are without exception quiescent before your eyes. If not, then go on pilgrimage again today: start over and go to Wutai and Emei, visit Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, and ask them what the Dharma gate of equal, single-horizon quiescence is. When you have something to say of it, come back and see this old monk.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Chongguan

The Chan practitioner Guan has travelled back and forth between Wu and Chu, and has come several thousand li to consult me. At first sight I knew he had the will but not yet the ability. The Old Man pitied him for coming so far, and having nothing else to point out, took his name and gave him the style Jianwei — Seeing the Subtle. It is because the root and stem of living beings’ birth and death flows on subtly and minutely, and deluded thoughts darken them so that they do not know themselves, that our Buddha, the great teacher, established contemplation to illumine it. Indeed, without contemplation and illumination one cannot see how great the power of birth and death is; and if contemplation does not reach the subtle, it cannot manifest the power of its illuminating function. If one can shatter the hidden and subtle, then birth and death can be escaped. This is, to be sure, the ultimate rule of the teaching schools. But for a patch-robed monk there is a hammer and tongs beyond the ordinary. If only he can make a single thought like an iron wall and a silver mountain, blocking the throat so there is no place to breathe out, until he dies and comes back to life — only then will there be a small measure of accord. The Chan practitioner is still drifting on the waves of the ocean of consciousness and has not yet cut off the root of life. Some other day, if he can spit out the mixed poison, set down body and mind, and come again to ask — then there may be a share for him.
Instructions for Master Liuru Kun

From the first, when the patriarchs taught people to investigate Chan, though they spoke of surpassing the Buddhas and going beyond the patriarchs, in truth they wanted people to become Buddhas and patriarchs. There has never been one who wished to become a Buddha or patriarch but did not follow the Buddha’s and patriarchs’ spoken teachings. To set aside the teachings and speak of practice is to set aside compass and square and seek for round and square. Moreover, when the Buddha taught Ānanda, he began by saying: You should have a straightforward mind. Vimalakīrti said: The straightforward mind is the place of practice. Master Aśvaghoṣa, in revealing the essentials of practice, said one must rouse three kinds of mind: the straightforward mind, because one takes right mindfulness of thusness as the Dharma; the profound mind, because one would gather all wholesome practices; and the mind of great compassion, because one vows to save all living beings from suffering. From the first, no patriarch failed to rouse these three minds. Students only know to go blankly along investigating a huatou, wanting only to crave wonders with deluded thoughts, not knowing that this is the patriarchs’ skilful means of the straightforward mind that rightly remembers thusness. If you speak the two words thusness, students will at once take them as a principle to be understood — who then would be willing to do the work to death? If you only tell them to look at the huatou, then when they look at the huatou and press the root of passion of kalpas, and it suddenly breaks, all the deluded thoughts and emotional calculations of former times vanish on the spot, and not one thought of arising can be found. Reaching this is the state beyond thought — what is called right mindfulness being no-thought. If you reach no-thought, then without seeking to unite with thusness you will of yourself accord face to face with it. This is the model by which the Buddhas and patriarchs taught people the straightforward mind. Hence we know that in investigating Chan there is no other clever method at all; it is only that people must truly work to death and work until they reach that kind of field. What secret or cleverness is there in it? This is the first, the practice of the straightforward mind. The second is the profound mind: to gather all wholesome merit and virtue. This wholesome merit and virtue is not an outward, conditioned affair. As Master Bodhidharma said to Emperor Wu: Pure wisdom, wondrous and perfect, whose essence is of itself empty and still — that is true merit. Hence we know that what Bodhidharma called pure wisdom, wondrous and perfect, is exactly Aśvaghoṣa’s straightforward mind that rightly remembers thusness; and the merit and virtue Aśvaghoṣa spoke of is simply doing it with the straightforward mind that rightly remembers, so that thusness pervades and completes all conditioned dharmas and affairs. If today you would realize and attain thusness, you must not seek it in a dead-eyed ghost cave; you must seek it in all the daily conditioned ten thousand practices. And seeking it in practices does not mean fishing out a wondrous thusness apart from things; it simply means taking the straightforward mind that rightly remembers and testing it upon all things, to see whether or not it accords with the straightforward mind that rightly remembers. If in every thing and every dharma it accords, then there is not one dharma or thing before you that is not the realm of thusness. That is why Mazu and Baizhang and their disciples, in daily life — carrying firewood, hauling water, hoeing fields, planting rice, tending fires, cooking meals — tested it face to face in every task; and every ordinary word or phrase, cold or warm, was meant to be for the disciples a gate of entry into realizing thusness. Only when one is tested and found truly undeluded in all places is one allowed a share in helping others. If a hair’s breadth in the chest is not penetrated and one has not reached the state of no-thought, then as soon as a thought stirs one is turned by karma and falls into the cave of birth and death; hence it was not lightly permitted or sealed. These seventeen hundred tangled cases in the Transmission of the Lamp are all words of true confirmation, not wondrous repartee. Students today all take them as wondrous and extraordinary sayings, store them in their chests, and count them as their own understanding, without ever seeing through a hair of what lies before them in daily life. Is that not a mistake? The third is the mind of great compassion: to vow to pull out the suffering of all living beings. Students today see pulling out living beings’ suffering as a Bodhisattva’s business, and wait to become Bodhisattvas some other day before saving living beings. They do not know that being able to save living beings is what makes one a Bodhisattva. To save living beings from suffering is not a matter of first having spiritual powers and wondrous function before going to save them; it is exactly the straightforward mind that rightly remembers, the gathering of all merit and virtue — that is the work of saving beings. Thus the World-Honoured One taught Subhūti to save all living beings, and yet in truth there is no living being to be saved; and to practise the six pāramitās widely, and yet not one dharma to be practised; and even to seek the Buddha-fruit of bodhi above, and yet to gain nothing. Now, is not saving living beings the gathering of all merit and virtue? And is not the fact that not one dharma is obtainable exactly the straightforward mind that rightly remembers thusness? Such wondrous function is one’s own daily spiritual power, which none can forbid you to take and which is inexhaustible — what dharma then is not a matter of merit? Since all the various affairs and dharmas of living beings’ daily life are the activity of affliction, if now with a single thought of thusness you seal and break through them in every affair and dharma, all are turned into the wondrous function of thusness — that is saving the living beings of your own mind. Investigating and learning thus is what is called true investigation and genuine inquiry. It is not sitting at ease in the ready-made, nursing laziness, and after three or five years boasting with a big mouth, saying, I have investigated Chan for so long and awakened to so many wondrous places. Insight such as this belongs to men who will eat the iron rod before old man Yama; they are worse off than a country fellow in a three-house hamlet, who at least escapes repaying the old debt to the faithful donor. In this old man’s view, the Buddhas and patriarchs taught people plainly and clearly from the first; it is only later people who misunderstand and so go astray. Since the Chan practitioner has turned his heart to the Old Man, he must believe the Old Man’s words. From now on, take the crystal bottle you have been clutching and smash it with one squeeze; move all your former investigation onto this one body and mind, and at the gate of accomplishing living beings, stake your life. Verify it truly one by one. Rouse a vast mind: to be able to lead one living being to rouse the bodhi mind is to pull out one living being’s suffering; to break one part of your own self-attachment and diminish one part of affliction, to dissolve one part of self-view and affliction, is to realize one part of the realm of thusness. If from there you rouse a long-enduring mind, then for three lives or ten kalpas, kalpa after kalpa, life after life, you will practise until affliction is utterly dissolved — and that is where all living beings are saved. If the afflictions of living beings were all exhausted at once, what Buddha or patriarch would there be left to become?
Instructions for Master Xiyin Jing, Who Devotes Himself to the Pure Land

In recent times scholars and officials mostly delight in mouth and ear, indulging in talk; they all honour Chan investigation as the matter that goes beyond and slight the Pure Land, refusing to practise it. This has led those of our kind who love fame to memorize many ready-made phrases of the ancients to furnish their tongues, and to esteem one another for it, until the Dharma gate declines day by day. Not only is genuine practice wholly absent, but they slander the Mahāyāna scriptures as mere letters and forbid drawing near them. With no clear-eyed teacher in the world, in the end no one can turn back that mad tide. This is greatly to be feared. It comes mostly from not going deep into the teachings and not knowing the purport that our Buddha, in saving living beings, has many gates of skilful means while the return to the source is not two. People of the world know only that under the patriarchs’ gate awakening is paramount; but the original intent of awakening the mind is to escape birth and death. Is reciting the Buddha’s name not a Dharma for escaping birth and death? Many who investigate Chan may not escape, while those who recite the Buddha’s name escape birth and death without doubt. Why is this so? Because investigating Chan requires leaving thoughts behind, while reciting the Buddha’s name is devoted to thought. Since living beings have long been sunk in deluded thought, leaving it is truly hard; but to turn defiled thought into pure thought is to use poison against poison, a method of exchange. Hence investigation is hard to awaken to, while Buddha-recitation is easy to accomplish. If one’s mind for birth and death is truly urgent, and one recites the Buddha’s name with the mind of investigation, what fear is there that one lifetime will not resolve birth and death? It is only this Pure Land Dharma gate that people of the world regard as provisional, never knowing that it is the most real of Dharma gates. Look carefully at Samantabhadra: taking the Dharma realm as his body and cultivating the ten great vows, he must point his way to the Pure Land. Aśvaghoṣa, the patriarch who transmitted the mind, based himself on a hundred Mahāyāna works and composed the Awakening of Faith, and in the end concluded by returning to the West. The patriarchs of the Transmission of the Lamp in this land, though they did not speak explicitly of the Pure Land, once the mind is awakened it escapes birth and death — and if they did not return to the Pure Land, would that not be annihilation? Yongming gathered the whole canon, pointed to the one mind, and also gathered it back into the Pure Land. When Chan reached Zhongfeng, the age was in decline, and he praised the West with all his strength. How much more is this Dharma gate one that our teacher spoke unasked, and that the Buddhas of the ten directions all praise — would the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and great patriarchs be less able than the karmic-defiled living beings of today, and speak wildly? Master Jing in middle age cast off his attachments and left home; he first consulted Master Zibo, who gave him the pointer for investigating Chan. Now, as to the one gate of the Pure Land, he wishes to practise but has not decided. So the Old Man told him: For this matter you need not ask others; just look at how your own mind for birth and death stands. If your mind for birth and death is like saving your head from fire, and your resolve is to accomplish it in one lifetime, it is like a man suffering a fatal illness: one person seeks a resurrection pill that might save him, and another gives him a single folk remedy from across the sea, enough to bring the dead back to life. It rests only with the sick man to have a settled mind and believe he can take it, and then he need not wait for the resurrection pill to be found — take this single remedy, and at once sweat breaks out all over his body, and he revives after seeming to expire. Only then does he know its wonder. Just deeply believe in this Dharma, devote mind and will to it single-mindedly, and at the end of your life you will know its effect for yourself. Why need you ask others? Strive and practise it; it will certainly not deceive you.
Instructions for the Novice Monk Xingkai

The novice monk Xingkai came to consult the Old Man and asked for instruction, and the Old Man gave him the style Jianren — Firm Patience. The Buddha instructed his disciples: Put on the robe of patience, called the armour of firmness. Armour is the means of guarding against harm. It is like a great general facing the enemy: he does not suffer the harm of arrows and stones, but preserves his body and life and wins the merit of certain victory — that is the power of armour. Now we śramaṇas, sons of Śākya, tread the field of birth and death and meet the great enemies, the five desires and the various māras. Without firm patience we are not able to overcome them. Hence it is said: endure forms, endure desires; endure what is hard to endure. Only then can one preserve the dharma-body and the life of wisdom and reach the land of Ultimate Bliss. Even our Buddha said: All kinds of hardship should be endured. How much more in the perilous road of the Dharma-ending age, full of calamities — without the power of firm patience, how could one accomplish the work of transcending the world?
The Dream-Roaming Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Fascicle Nine
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Yetai

The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī dwells on Mount Qingliang and, with a retinue of ten thousand, constantly proclaims the Dharma. Hence the śramaṇas of the Western Regions bow in veneration from afar to this mountain as the golden-hued world. The Avataṃsaka Sutra says: Mañjuśrī is in all places, coming from the golden-hued world in all places. Seen thus, does Mañjuśrī truly dwell forever on this mountain? It is that in the realm of living beings, wherever afflictions gather, that is a land of feverish affliction. If a practitioner can open the eye of wisdom, penetrate the root, forget feelings, and know the substance of mind in accord, then here and now it is cool. In that case nothing that meets the eye is other than Mañjuśrī’s field of transformation, and no step leaves the place of practice of coolness. This is what is meant by Mañjuśrī in all places and the golden-hued world. The Chan practitioner Yetai dwelt long on Mount Tai and wandered by night, and so got this name.
