Now he comes south on pilgrimage to consult teachers; surely he comes personally directed by Mañjuśrī. Like Sudhana’s inquiry in the south, though he passed through a hundred and ten cities he did not move one step from his heel; and as before, in travelling all the ten directions of the world he never left the golden realm. Every teacher’s gate of adverse and favorable means is none other than Mañjuśrī’s eye of wisdom. Now he sees the Old Man on the peak of Five Breasts — is this the same as the golden-hued world or different? If you can distinguish here, I grant that you have seen Mañjuśrī face to face. If not, then buy another pair of straw sandals and go on pilgrimage. Investigate! Investigate!
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Xingran Jue

The Chan practitioner Xingjue left home in middle age and came from afar to Mount Kuang to seek full ordination. Because he had a hidden ailment he could not attend long, and taking leave to return he asked for instruction. So the Old Man told him: The body is the root of the great affliction and the gathering place of all suffering. As to birth and death in the six paths, you must first know this bitter cause of birth and death. It is said: The cause of all suffering is craving, which is the root. If craving is extinguished, there is nothing to depend on. Therefore the Buddha taught the Adamantine Precepts and the Dharma gate of the mind-ground: they are the sharp tool for cutting off desire and the raft for escaping suffering. You are now fortunate to hear this Dharma; do not forget it thought after thought, do not slacken heart after heart — this itself is the essence of practice. As the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: You should contemplate this body as compounded of the four elements. I now contemplate its hardness returning to earth, its moisture to water, its warmth to fire, its movement to wind. Contemplating carefully, the four elements each have their destination — where then will this deluded body be? Observing thus, not forgetting thought after thought, not dulling heart after heart, with long ripening you will see this body suddenly fall away. When the four elements are empty, all suffering is at once released. This very work is the foremost wondrous secret for escaping birth and death. From the first, not one of the patriarchs failed to come from investigation; no one who awakened to mind and nature gained benefit without practising. You should reflect further: though this body suffers, while a breath remains you may still seek the means of escape. But if you lose this, and your body has worn the kāṣāya to no purpose, then the suffering of the three evil paths will come and last through long kalpas, and though you wish to escape you will not be able. Hence it is said: Contemplate the suffering of the hells and rouse the bodhi mind. Strive, and do not slacken.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Shuoming Dao

The student of the Way Dao once consulted the Old Man at Caoxi, and the Old Man specially revealed to him the purport of the Diamond Prajñā. In our practice, unless we rely on the fundamental wisdom of prajñā, birth and death are hard to escape. Yet this prajñā is not to be sought outside; it is the very substance of our own mind, complete from the first. Therefore in practice now, seek only your own mind and do not go looking for branches and leaves. What the Buddhas and patriarchs taught was simply to seek the mind within: hence it is said, Know the mind and reach the source, and so one is called a śramaṇa. And again: If a person knows the mind, the great earth has not an inch of soil. Our own mind is originally the light of prajñā, originally without a thing; only because of a single thought of delusion do we use it daily without knowing it. Knowing only this illusory, false self, we do not know the originally abiding dharma-body. If now you would awaken to the original dharma-body, then here and now in daily life, at the gates of the six senses, wherever a thought stirs and clings to a self, illumine and break through on the spot: originally there is no self. With no self there is no person; with no person there is wholly no living being. Since living beings are empty, the root of birth and death is cut off. Since birth and death are escaped, there is no lifespan. Thus with the four marks removed, the one mind has nowhere to lodge — is that not the wondrous practice of non-abiding? If you cannot awaken on the spot, then simply place the Sixth Patriarch’s one phrase, originally there is not a single thing, before your eyes. Whenever circumstances appear and a mind arises in opposition, that is self-attachment. At that very attachment, illumine once; illumined through, feeling is at once forgotten and the opposing mind is cut off — that is no-self. With no self there is no person; with self and person both empty, then in daily life body and mind have not the least hindrance. For the adverse and favorable states of daily life are all the road of birth and death; if the states are seen through and there is no hindrance at all, then the root and stem of birth and death is cut down from there. Is this not skill in cultivating the wondrous practice of prajñā’s non-abiding? If the Chan practitioner has the will to escape birth and death, he must take this as the first principle. To seek elsewhere is to fall onto the crooked path of the outsiders.
Instructions for Wei Shengqi

The layman Shengqi recently sent a letter asking for instruction, saying: Of late, though I am alarmed about the great matter of birth and death and wish to be liberated wherever I am, yet when adversity comes suddenly I cannot digest it on the spot. Though I soon become aware of it, the master has already been dragged along. From the tenor of his letter, he is one who truly has the will for the great matter of birth and death, only he has not met a good spiritual friend to point out the work of the mind-ground, and so has no handle. It is that we have always taken deluded thoughts as the mind and do not know the Buddha-nature we originally have; we have always only given rise to liking and disliking, hate and love, and all sorts of discriminating views upon the adverse and favorable states of worldly feeling, never knowing that these feelings of hate and love, anger and joy, are wholly the root and stem of birth and death. There is no one in the whole world who does not spend a lifetime tumbling about in them. The ancients, in teaching people to investigate Chan and resolve birth and death, did not mean that apart from this there is some other wonder; it is simply to see through the mind of hate and love upon just these states — that is resolving birth and death. Since these deluded thoughts of hate and love have from of old been thoroughly and deeply steeped in habit, without a skilful means how could one hold them off? Hence the teaching of investigating Chan and looking at a huatou is exactly the sharp tool for breaking affliction. The reason one is dragged along is simply that one has no huatou as master. Take the case of the monk who asked Zhaozhou, Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said, No. Take this one word No and hold it in your chest as a huatou; lay on doubt, not forgetting it thought after thought, not dulling it heart after heart. Amid all leisure and busyness, movement and stillness, in social intercourse and in sudden haste, simply lift up this one phrase, lay on doubt heavily, and question it. Doubt and doubt, until only one huatou stands before you. Even when reading a book, as soon as you set the book down, turn your head and look and at once lay on doubt. Let this doubt be firm, and on no account turn it into reasoning and understanding. You want only one thought of doubt to be keen; with long ripening, whenever you see a deluded thought arise in the mind, one question such as this and it melts like ice on the spot. The joy and anger that arise in the mind are only one deluded thought. With this huatou first as master, when a state arrives you see through it as soon as it comes, and it melts like ice on the spot with no effort at all. Doing the work thus, you will not only hold off states but also have a time of awakening. Only, on no account turn it into wondrous reasoning; I fear that would mislead you instead.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Fudun

A Chan practitioner from Xin’an came from afar to consult at Mount Kuang and asked to be given the precepts. He was named Fudun and styled Duru. Du means sincere and earnest, pure and single without falsity, the utmost of genuine devotion. Now we śramaṇas, sons of the Buddha, wish to transcend birth and death, realize the true and eternal, and seek the blessing and joy of unsurpassed nirvāṇa. Unless with a single thought of genuine devotion, pure and true without delusion, one forcefully breaks the māra of afflictions and at once pulls out the root of love and hate, it is hard to at once enjoy the blessing of non-doing. A journey of a thousand li depends on the first step. Take the precepts from here as your foundation, for they are the first step toward bodhi. Then with thought after thought pressing forward and heart after heart not retreating, seek only the single thought: the root of passion of birth and death — search and pull at its place of arising and in the end it cannot be found. Yet the place where it cannot be found is exactly the place where birth and death has no attachment. I fear only that your will is not firm and your practice not strong. If you fear it is not strong, then simply place the four characters Amitābha Buddha across your chest as a sharp axe, and in time the root and stem will be cut of itself. Striving thus is what is called Duru. Strive! Strive!
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Fuhou

A Chan practitioner from Xin’an came to consult at Mount Kuang and asked to be given the precepts. He was named Fuhou — Thick Blessing — and styled Jiru — Accumulating Thusness. For one who has left the world, blessing grows thick by gradual accumulation and is complete only at Buddhahood, like piling up motes of dust to form the great earth — thickness at its utmost. Our Buddha, the World-Honoured One, through measureless kalpas gave up head, eyes, marrow, and brain, accumulating merit and piling up practice, and only then attained bodhi. Bodhi is the peaceful dwelling of nirvāṇa, the utmost ground of blessing and joy. Without accumulation, how could one come to this? And thus means the thusness of Buddha-nature, which we originally possess. It is simply that through kalpas of accumulated affliction encroaching upon it, the dust of affliction and passion grows daily thicker, and the thusness of Buddha-nature grows thin. Now that you know Buddha-nature is originally yours and is not to be sought from another, from this day forth let every thought in daily life know its home. Whenever you see the dust of passion arise, illumine it with the light of wisdom; with long ripening, Buddha-nature will be thick and affliction thin, affliction thin and karmic obstruction light, karmic obstruction light and birth and death cut off. Thus by accumulating thusness you cut off birth and death, seek to realize bodhi, and enjoy the thick blessing of permanence, joy, self, and purity. Is this not arriving by accumulation? Hence it is said: If water is not piled deep, it has no strength to bear a great ship. Strive, Chan practitioner.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Tongchen Rui

The Chan practitioner Tongchen Rui of southern Dian came far to the capital and attended the lecture halls in person. Then he cast off all he had learned and went south to consult teachers. He wandered in the Yellow Mountains of Xin’an, loved their quiet beauty, and lived in seclusion there, going about with a single bowl and no fixed abode. He took the great Avataṃsaka Sutra as his daily recitation. In mid-summer of the renxu year he came to consult at Mount Kuang, seeking full ordination. He offered incense and asked for instruction, and the Old Man told him: You take the great Avataṃsaka Sutra as your constant recitation — do you know its guiding principle? Our Vairocana, in the cause-ground of vast kalpas, with a mind commensurate with the Dharma realm, cultivated Samantabhadra’s practice and realized the Dharma realm to its end. He is named the reward body and titled Rocana, possessed of marks and excellences as numerous as the dust of Buddha-lands: this is the direct reward. The twenty-fold Lotus Treasury World of endless adornment that he evokes is the dependent reward. Abiding in the ocean-seal samādhi and according with the wisdom of universal brightness, he proclaimed this sutra for the Bodhisattvas on the grounds, called the sūtra of the universal illumination of the Dharma realm — a Dharma gate commensurate with the nature, of every kind of subtlety, inconceivable. Such a Dharma gate is the state of the Buddhas’ own realization, and yet it is wholly present in the deluded mind of living beings’ daily use, appearing thought after thought. The sutra says: Suppose within a single mote of dust there were the scriptures of a great thousand worlds, recording all the affairs of the three thousand great thousand worlds; and suppose a wise man clearly saw these scriptures, broke open the mote, and brought out the great sutra to benefit others without end. Now the single mote of dust is the deluded mind of living beings; the scriptures of the great thousand are the virtue of the nature living beings originally possess, hidden and unmanifest — which is to say, living beings use it daily without knowing it. The clear-eyed wise man breaking the dust and bringing out the sutra is the Buddhas’ realization to the end, and the revealing of this Dharma to living beings for their great benefit and joy. Hence we know that what this sutra speaks of is the deluded mind of living beings’ daily use. How great! The mind of living beings possesses vast, inconceivable power and boundless wisdom and function, yet it is covered by a trifling deluded thought — is that not to be grieved? Our Buddha appeared in the world especially for this matter. Hence it is said: For the sake of one great matter, he appears in the world. Because the Buddhas realize this great matter, for this reason and on this account they appear in the world and speak for living beings, with no other business. Because living beings are deluded about this great matter and so have birth and death, therefore birth and death is called the great matter. Seen thus, what the majestic text of eighty fascicles reveals is simply the one deluded thought of our mind. Hence it is said: I now in the minds of all living beings accomplish equal and perfect enlightenment. That is, the living beings within the Buddhas’ minds accomplish the Way at every moment, and the Buddhas within living beings’ minds realize the truth thought after thought. Therefore the venerable Prajñātārā said: In-breath does not dwell in the aggregates; out-breath does not touch the conditions. Thus he always turned such a sutra, a hundred thousand million times. If one can with such an eye turn such a sutra to the end of the future without interruption, that is what is called dust proclaiming, lands proclaiming, blazing proclamation without pause. This is the great purport of the true sutra of the Avataṃsaka Dharma realm. If the Chan practitioner awakens to this Dharma, then before the scroll is unrolled he will see through to the boundless Dharma realm, and in the midst of poking the fire, lifting incense, clearing the throat, or snapping the fingers. Yet even so, one must still drill through the ox hide to get it.
Instructions on the Practice of the Pure Land Dharma Gate

A Chan practitioner from Haiyang came from afar to consult at Mount Kuang and asked to be given the precepts, and was named Shenyu — Deep Fool. Offering incense, he asked for instruction: I, your disciple, have made a vow to seek birth in the Western Pure Land and have gathered a number of Dharma companions to meet in one place and devote ourselves to the work of the Pure Land. I beg your compassion to point out the essentials of the Dharma. So the Old Man told him: Of the Dharmas the Buddha taught for practising and escaping birth and death there are many gates of skilful means, but only reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking birth in the Pure Land is the most swift and essential. Even such perfect and wondrous gates as the Avataṃsaka and the Lotus, and Samantabhadra’s wondrous practice, point in the end to the Pure Land. Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna, and in this land Yongming, Zhongfeng, and the other great patriarchs, all upheld the one gate of the Pure Land with all their strength. This Dharma gate is one the Buddha spoke unasked; it covers all three faculties and gathers in all four assemblies — it was not set up provisionally for those of lower faculties. The sutra says: If you would purify the Buddha-land, purify your own mind. In practising the Pure Land work now, you must take a pure mind as the root. To purify your own mind, you must first purify the root of the precepts. With three bodily, four verbal, and three mental — these ten evil karmas are the cause of suffering in the three evil paths. The essence of holding precepts now is first to purify the three karmas, and then the mind is of itself pure. If the body does not kill, steal, or commit sexual misconduct, the bodily karma is pure. If the mouth does not lie, speak idly, speak divisively, or speak harshly, the verbal karma is pure. If the mind is not greedy, angry, or deluded, the mental karma is pure. Thus with the ten evils cut off forever and the three karmas clear as ice, this is the essence of purifying the mind. Within this pure mind, weary of the suffering of the Sahā and vowing birth in the Land of Peace and Nurture, establish the right practice of Buddha-recitation. But in reciting the Buddha’s name the mind for birth and death must be urgent. First cut off outer conditions and lift up a single thought, taking the one phrase Amitābha Buddha as your root of life, not forgetting it thought after thought, not breaking it heart after heart, throughout the twelve hours — walking, standing, sitting, lying, lifting the spoon, raising the chopsticks, turning, bowing, rising — in motion or stillness, at leisure or busy, at all times, neither dull nor dark, with no other conditions. Applying the mind thus, with long ripening, even in dreams you will not forget or lose it, awake and asleep as one, and your work will be fine and close, beaten into a single piece — that is the time of gaining power. If your recitation reaches single-mindedness without distraction, then at the end of life the Pure Land appears before you, and you will of yourself not be detained by birth and death; you will evoke Amitābha Buddha to send forth light and receive and guide you. This is the sure proof of birth there. Now single-minded, devoted recitation is indeed the right practice, but it must also be aided by visualization to be more secure and close. The Buddha taught Queen Vaidehī the sixteen sublime contemplations, and so she accomplished it in one lifetime. The Contemplation Sutra still exists. If you gather Pure Land companions to practise together, let each follow his own vow: from the sixteen contemplations take any one — either contemplating the Buddha alone and the Bodhisattvas’ sublime marks, or contemplating the Pure Land’s states, such as the lotus flowers and jewelled ground described in the Amitābha Sutra — and visualize as you wish. If the visualization is clear, then throughout the twelve hours the Pure Land is present before you; sitting or lying, walking or standing, eyes open or closed, it is as if before your eyes. If this visualization is accomplished, at the end of life you are born at once in a single thought — as is said: Birth is certain birth, yet going is truly not going. This is the wondrous pointer of the mind-only Pure Land. Applying the mind thus and holding the precepts strictly, the six senses become pure. Cutting off evil karma and affliction forever, the mind-ground becomes pure. Contemplation and recitation following one another, the wondrous practice is easily accomplished. There is no true cause of the Pure Land outside this. But if one merely speaks of reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking birth in the Pure Land, while not holding the pure precepts, not cutting off affliction, and leaving the mind-ground defiled, the Buddha said such a person will never succeed. Therefore the practitioner must first take holding the precepts as the foundation, making vows as the assisting cause, and reciting the Buddha’s name with visualization as the right practice. Practising thus, if one is not born there, then the Buddha has uttered a falsehood.
Essentials of Buddha-Recitation and Chan Investigation

The gongan of plainly verifying Buddha-recitation is this: lift up single-mindedly the one sound Amitābha Buddha as a huatou, and at the very place you lift it, lay on doubt and ask: Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name? Lift again and ask again, ask and ask again: who after all is it that recites the Buddha’s name? Leaning steadily on the huatou in this way, all deluded and scattered thoughts are cut off on the spot like tangled silk severed, and no longer permitted to arise; as soon as one arises it vanishes. There remains only one thought, clear and singly bright, like the white sun in the sky. Deluded thoughts do not arise; confusion of itself withdraws; still and yet awake. Master Yongjia said: Still and awake is right; still with dullness is not. Awake and still is right; awake with scattered thought is not. That is, being still does not fall into torpor or dullness, and being awake does not fall into deluded thought. Stillness and wakefulness flow together; sinking and floating are both set aside. When you look to the place where not one thought arises, then before and after are cut off and the between stands alone. Suddenly the lacquer bucket is smashed and you at once see the original face; then body, mind, and world sink level on the spot like a flower in the sky whose shadow falls, and the ten directions are bright and clear, becoming one great treasury of light. Only then is it the season of arriving home; in daily life before you it is bright and perfectly clear, with nothing more to doubt. Only then do you believe that your own mind was always thus, and that the Buddhas and patriarchs’ own field of enjoyment is not two and not different. At this state you must not take it as an emptiness view; if you take it as emptiness you fall into the outsiders’ evil view. Nor may you make it a view of existence, nor a wondrous view and knowledge. Any view at all is a false view. If in the course of your work various states appear, on no account acknowledge them; one shout and they vanish. Evil states need not be feared; good states need not be rejoiced in. These are the māra of habit. If you give rise to worry or joy, you fall into Māra. You should contemplate that they are only what your own mind manifests and do not come from outside. You should know that originally it is pure, that in the mind there is utterly not a thing, that originally there is no delusion or awakening and no belonging to sage or ordinary being — how then could there be all these states? It is because we are deluded about this original mind that we must do the work, to wear away the habit-energy of ignorance. If you awaken to the original mind as originally without a thing, originally bright, vast, pure, and still, and pass your time thus at ease, what work is there left to do? People today believe only that this mind is originally without a thing; the reason they must do the work now is that they have not yet seen the original face, and so must once do the work to death before there is a season of arriving home. Go straight on from here, and there will naturally come a time of suddenly seeing the original face; then there is no further doubt whatever about escaping birth and death.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Haikuo on Writing Sutras in Blood

The Chan practitioner roused his mind to copy the five great divisions of the Avataṃsaka Sutra and came specially to Mount Kuang to ask for instruction. So the Old Man told him: Vairocana, abiding in the ocean-seal samādhi, manifests the ten Dharma realms and clouds of inexhaustible bodies and speaks the Avataṃsaka Sutra, called the sūtra of the universal illumination of the Dharma realm. If we speak of the direct reward body, he proclaims it with light from every pore; if we speak of the dependent reward world, then grass, mustard seeds, and motes of dust proclaim it — dust proclaims, lands proclaim. Proclaiming thus to the end of the future without pause or rest, such a sutra fills the Dharma realm. It is what is called the one-character Dharma gate, which an ocean of ink could not write out. Now you, with your limited body and mind and your drops of bodily blood, how will you write it all out? Yet if this sutra truly cannot be written, then all living beings are utterly cut off from it. And it is said: The sutra of the Dharma realm — whatever is within the Dharma realm is none other than this sutra. If you awaken to Vairocana taking the Dharma realm as his body, then your own body and mind are likewise the same as the Dharma realm. Then in daily life before you — in movement and stillness, speech and silence, lifting the spoon, raising the chopsticks, coughing, spitting, swinging the arms — all is the great function of the Dharma realm. How then could any time be other than the time of writing this sutra? If the body is the same as the Dharma realm, then every pore is all-pervading; and thus a single drop of blood let fall would dry up together with the ocean of the nature. That is why the great being Samantabhadra flayed his skin for paper, split his bones for pens, and pricked his blood for ink, its measure equal to the Dharma realm. Thus the whole sutra does not go beyond a single character, and the writing of one character is the same as the whole sutra — how much more so for a hundred scrolls of text. If the Chan practitioner can contemplate thus, then the one who writes, those who see and hear, those who bow and praise and make offerings of a stick of incense or a flower, and even those who lend their labour and strength, all alike return to the Dharma realm. Such merit — how could it be conceived or discussed? If the Chan practitioner lacks such an eye and does such a practice, he will not escape pressing his eye and seeing flowers in the sky — will that not only add to his inverted thoughts?
Instructions for the Novice Monk Nenghua of Caoxi on Copying the Avataṃsaka Sutra

The Buddha said: The seed of Buddhahood arises from conditions. Thus the direct cause of living beings, the Buddha-nature, is originally complete; but because ignorance is firm, if one does not meet good conditions it can never come forth — like a seed in the ground, which needs the conditions of rain, dew, and warming sun before it can sprout, put forth a stem, and even flower and bear fruit. Before the Old Man came to Caoxi, the novices there practised worldly trades and did not even know that there are Buddhas and monks — how could they know the Buddhadharma? Since the Old Man began teaching there, with all manner of skilful means drawing them in and instructing them, they first came to know they were monks. Then, because Buddha-nature is hard to illumine, he first taught them to copy the great Avataṃsaka Sutra, to make them know to draw near and accord with the Buddhadharma; once faith was roused, they could be led into the Buddha’s wisdom. At first there were only two or three; afterwards everyone looked to one another and roused the mind. Within ten years, those who have copied this great sutra have completed more than ten sets. It is a thousand years since the Sixth Patriarch entered cessation, and what is done today has never been done before. Buddha-nature is originally present in everyone; the merit of the sands of the Ganges is originally complete in everyone. But without a teacher to open and guide them, all use the virtue of their nature to create evil karma and invite the bitter retribution of the three evil paths. If one awakens to this Buddha-nature, one turns evil karma into the measureless adornment of the Pure Land. Now the novice Nenghua can turn the mind that creates karma into the adornment of the Pure Land, making the true cause of Buddhahood. This is what is called the seed of wisdom held within the mind-ground: meeting the conditions of the Dharma rain and the sun of wisdom, it can put forth the sprout of bodhi, grow the roots of goodness, send out branches of merit, and open the flowers of the ten thousand practices, and in the future will surely bear the wondrous fruit of bodhi. This is precisely what is meant by the seed of Buddhahood arising from conditions. The Old Man has often instructed the disciples at Caoxi: if from now on everyone is courageous, rouses the unsurpassed mind, sets his will on the Buddhadharma, and investigates clearly the great matter beneath his own feet, then as in the days when the Sixth Patriarch was in the world, those who illumined their own minds would number far more than thirty out of a thousand. It depends on the work of teaching one another in turn.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Xingchu Yuan on Copying Sutras

The Chan practitioner Xingyuan came to consult at Mount Kuang, and the Old Man gave him the style Xingchu — Awakening at the Beginning. He had vowed to copy the great sutras, and so the Old Man told him: In leaving home and practising, the Buddha said there are many gates of skilful means; it all depends on how each person rouses his mind. First and foremost is to investigate Chan and seek to illumine one’s own mind, with the will to resolve birth and death. Next is to penetrate deeply the ocean of the teachings, with the vow to make them widely known, to protect the right Dharma, and to continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom. Next again is to weary deeply of birth and death, devote the mind to the Pure Land work, and vow birth in the West. All these are practices of principle, and are the highest. As for the various practices of action, down to copying the scriptures: this is one of the six kinds of Dharma-master, and is praised by the Buddha. Hence the Lotus Sutra says that the Dharma-master who holds the sutra, in this present flesh body, attains purity of the six senses — how can this be compared with practices of action? And it says: Raising a hand or bowing the head, all have already become Buddhas. This is practice commensurate with the nature — how could it be achieved by tracing and dotting strokes? In former days, when the Old Man dwelt at Wutai, he once mixed gold with blood pricked from his body and copied the great Avataṃsaka Sutra. Throughout the copying, regardless of the strokes of the characters, their size and length, at every stroke laid down he recited the Buddha’s name once. Thus dotting and drawing stroke by stroke, the light of his mind flowed out, thought after thought unbroken and unforgotten, without error or omission; and in time it was no longer a matter of copying or not copying, until even in dreams it was all one piece. Thereupon amid all states, however turbulent and clamorous, his mind remained still, and he attained the gate of freedom and non-obstruction toward all states; and all that he saw and heard was nothing other than the true sutra appearing before him. Judging by this, the wonder of the practice of copying sutras lies in single-mindedness without distraction. How could it be like a child smearing vermilion, taking the copying of sutras as a way to seek merit? Let the Chan practitioner try this practice: copy thus and hold it thus, and there will be a small measure of accord. But if you take tracing as a wondrous practice and wide reputation as a means to seek offerings, then you are worse off than an ordinary monk of rice and gruel who does nothing.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Yong, Styled Zhaofan

The Chan practitioner Yong once consulted the Old Man at Wuyang, where the Old Man showed him the purport of non-arising. Lately he came to visit Mount Kuang, and the Old Man saw that his will for the Way was more earnest than ever, yet his work of investigation was not yet pure, because he had not taken it as one real, great matter. So the Old Man told him: When the ancients studied the Way, the first thing was that their minds for birth and death be urgent; it was not a matter of seeking wondrous principles. What is this birth and death? It is simply that in our daily life before us, amid all the states of dust-toil, when we meet states and conditions, adverse or favorable, the habit-energy within draws forth activity, and liking and disliking, taking and rejecting, and all sorts of deluded, discriminating minds arise. Thought after thought clinging to conditions, we give rise to good and evil and all kinds of karmic action, all of which become the root and stem of future birth and death. Because deluded thought is boundless, birth and death is without limit. Hence living beings turn through long kalpas in the bitter sea of birth and death with no time of getting out — all because they do not know the fault of their own minds. Hence it is said: If you do not understand your own mind, how can you know the right Way? Students of the Way, ancient and modern, who have the will to escape birth and death, need only seek to illumine their own minds. Because this mind has always been coarse and floating, like boiling water and leaping flame, never for a single thought cool and clear, the ancients provisionally set up a skilful means and taught students to hold up one gongan and investigate it thought after thought: as when a monk asked Zhaozhou, Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? or as Yongming taught people to verify plainly who it is that recites the Buddha’s name. This one word No, this one word Who, is the sharp sword that cuts the root of the life of birth and death. In this investigation and verification, simply look at this No or Who: where does it arise from, where does it fall to? Just look at this single thought’s arising and falling; you must see the root of its arising and ceasing. If you investigate to the ultimate point and burst apart the single thought of arising and ceasing, smash the lacquer bucket, and suddenly see the original face, then you will have the nostrils of the Buddhas and patriarchs above, all at once, in your own hands. From then on you will know the original person and no longer doubt whether he is Zhang San or Li Si — he turns out to be your own original spirit, your root of life. In that case what wonder is there to seek? Why need you seek it in another’s house? Yet this one matter: unless from the first arising of the mind you are urgent about birth and death, then however you exhaust your tricks, all is the ghost’s business; even if you have a bit of knowledge and half a view, it is all Māra’s talk, and whatever you do is Māra’s karma. It is a pity, for a matter of great import is hard to meet in a hundred thousand million kalpas. If the Chan practitioner truly has the will for this matter, he must take all the worldly truth, clever intelligence, views and knowledge, and all kinds of deluded thoughts in his chest and fold them all up, turning to work upon the single thought. Take one huatou as a sword sweeping the sky and cut off former deluded thoughts as one cuts tangled silk. If you can truly lay on such a ruthless hand and do such bitter, urgent work, and still find no true awakening, then the Buddhas and patriarchs from the first have all uttered falsehood. What is most to be avoided is simply the lack of a true mind, merely making investigation Chan a face to save and a fine-sounding phrase to speak.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Lüchu Chong

The Chan practitioner grew up in Yuzhang and had long had the will for the beyond. Hearing that the Old Man was resting in old age at Mount Kuang, he cast off worldly conditions and came with a pure mind to consult him. So he was kept and entered the assembly, coming into the Master’s room from time to time. After a while the Old Man observed that he had much of the soft and warm habit and that his bones and spirit were not firm, so his mind for entering the Way was not fierce. He often urged him on when he fell short. One day he offered incense and asked for instruction, and the Old Man told him: You have the will toward the Way but lack the spirit to rouse yourself, because the strength of your mind is not pure and so your bones are not strong. Your bones not being strong, you have no firm, resolute, courageous will; this is what is called having no master within, and so being unestablished. The reason there is no master within is that, first of all, you have no true mind for birth and death, and no settled, long-enduring, unretreating will. With no settled will, all your pursuits have no outstanding conduct; hence you follow old habits and let the days drift, keeping only to idleness and ease, taking wilfulness as freedom and lack of restraint. Since you do not know how to check your mind, you have no strength even to support the illusory body of the four elements; hence in daily life before you there is no true work at all and no true benefit. From today on, you must first rouse a whole heart truly set on birth and death and establish a settled, long-enduring, unretreating will, and for this whole span of life resolve to investigate clearly the one great matter beneath your own feet, determined to equal the ancients and only then not betray this life. To be like the ancients, you must take one gongan as your huatou for investigation. Master Yongming’s gongan of plainly verifying Buddha-recitation is the most secure. Then set down at once all the old habits, views, knowledge, deluded thoughts, and calculations in your mind from before, until you reach the place where nothing more can be set down. Then simply lift up one sound, Amitābha Buddha, and look at the place this thought arises, verifying plainly who it is that recites the Buddha’s name. Recite and verify, verify and recite; lean steadily on the single thought. At the place where your plain verification gains power, you will feel the mind to be like a wall. When you investigate to the place where investigation cannot go, that is the time of gaining power. Investigating thus for a long time, until the mind has nothing to use, like a mouse entering a cow’s horn, suddenly a single thought will burst apart — and that is the season of resolving birth and death. If you can apply your mind thus and strive thus, your bones will of themselves be firm and your spirit fierce, and you will be called a towering, outstanding true man. Compared with your former soft and warm condition, it will truly be a difference of a day against a kalpa. Strive, sir.
Instructions for the Chan Practitioner Huijing Xin

Our Buddha’s teaching takes the one mind as its principle. No matter how many hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates there are, none is other than a practice for awakening to the one mind. The most essential are simply Chan investigation and Buddha-recitation. Chan investigation was founded by the former patriarchs of this land as the method for awakening the mind. As for the one gate of Buddha-recitation, it is what our Buddha revealed to the Bodhisattvas of the three worthy ranks and the ten grounds, who all take Buddha-recitation as the essential for attaining Buddhahood. The Bodhisattvas of the ten grounds have already realized thusness — are they not awakened? Yet they all say they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha. When Sudhana consulted the fifty-three good teachers, the first, the bhikṣu Meghaśrī, gave him solely the gate of liberation by Buddha-recitation. And at the last, when he visited Samantabhadra, the good teacher who brings one into perfect enlightenment, he devotedly turned his merit toward the Western Pure Land, saying: I myself behold the Tathāgata’s measureless light, and before me he bestows on me the bodhi prediction. Seen thus, even the Avataṃsaka, the supreme single vehicle, in cultivating practice commensurate with the Dharma realm, never from beginning to end departs from Buddha-recitation. Sages of the ten grounds who have already realized thusness still do not depart from Buddha-recitation — and yet deluded people of the Dharma-ending age dare to slander Buddha-recitation as an inferior practice. Why doubt that Chan investigation and Buddha-recitation are different? It is a lack of wide learning, not knowing the Buddha’s intent, and giving rise to discrimination in delusion. If we speak in terms of the mind-only Pure Land, then when the mind is pure the land is pure. Hence when one first investigates Chan and has not yet awakened, without Buddha-recitation there is no way to purify one’s own mind; yet when the mind is pure, that is awakening to the mind. Since a Bodhisattva, having awakened, does not forsake Buddha-recitation, it follows that without Buddha-recitation there is no way to accomplish perfect enlightenment. How do we know the patriarchs did not awaken their minds by Buddha-recitation? If in reciting the Buddha’s name you reach single-mindedness without distraction, afflictions are dissolved, and you understand your own mind clearly — that is called awakening. In that case, Buddha-recitation is Chan investigation. And as with the Bodhisattvas, it is not forsaking Buddha-recitation after awakening. Hence all the patriarchs of old did not forsake the Pure Land. Thus Buddha-recitation is Chan investigation, and Chan investigation is birth in the Pure Land. This is a doubt unsettled through the ages; here it is broken open and exhausted, and the view that separates Chan and Pure Land is thereby wholly dissolved. Even should a Buddha appear in the world, he would not speak differently from this. To set this aside and give rise to other wild opinions is all Māra’s talk, not the Buddhadharma.
Instructions for Xiu Liuyi, Master of the Retreat

When I first crossed the ranges and came to Wuyang, beneath the bodhi tree, my disciple Xiu Liuyi and his companions at once led one another to take refuge. Then, from my leaving the ranges to Nanyue, and my travels in Wu and Yue, he followed me through hardship and suffering for twenty-five years from first to last, never once idle. When I returned to hide at Mount Kuang, the Master, always urgent in mind for birth and death and set on seeking the beyond, followed me also to the summit of Jinlun Peak and sealed himself in a death retreat for three years, lifting up a single thought, and was fortunate to have a place of self-confidence. Now, to visit his teacher, he has returned to his home mountain, and offering incense he asks for instruction. So the Old Man told him: Leaving home for birth and death and seeking the road that goes beyond is our proper business. The Chan practitioner’s three years in the death retreat — setting down body and mind, shaking off the dust of affliction, wearing away habit-energy — is the first step, and he has already gained confidence in it. But in investigating the root of the illness of birth and death he has not been able to pull it out at once, for in investigating Chan one must first recognize the root of the illness of birth and death before one can apply medicine to cure it. What is the root of the illness of birth and death? Greed, anger, delusion, and pride all take self-view as their root. The two kinds of birth and death of all sages and ordinary beings alike come from clinging to a self. But this self is established depending on views; such views are deluded views, and they are the root of self-attachment, called the thorn in the dharma-body. If the thorn of views is not pulled out, birth and death is hard to escape. Hence all ordinary beings cling to views of body and mind, self and others, right and wrong; all outsiders obstinately cling to false views; the sages of the two vehicles cling to views of birth and death and nirvāṇa, of delighting in and rejecting; all Bodhisattvas cling to the view that there are living beings to save and a Buddha to seek; the sages of equal enlightenment have not forgotten the views of Buddha and Dharma, and so there are the two ignorances. And even under the patriarchs’ gate, those who first learn to investigate Chan mostly first give rise to the view of waiting for awakening; in the midst of not having awakened, they deludedly give rise to the view of having attained what they have not attained. And when a single thought of the mad mind briefly rests, they cling to it as wondrous awakening and give rise to the view of being satisfied with a little; then they drag back the ancients’ words and phrases as their own understanding and cling to them as a wondrous view. Hoarding these in their bosoms and refusing to spit them out, in time they brew a poison and so wrongly fall into false views. Even if a single thought suddenly awakens to their own mind as originally without a thing, they fall again at the gate of light and shadow, taking it as the ultimate view. That is why Yunmen said: Even if you reach the dharma-body, because attachment to the Dharma is not forgotten and your own view still remains, you fall beside the dharma-body — this is called clutching the tip of the pole, and there is never a view of escaping. In short, if even a hair’s breadth of emotional view remains, it is gathered on the side of arising and ceasing, and all of it is the root of the illness of birth and death. Even if you awaken, you still belong to birth and death. Hence it is said that the word awakening too must be spat out — how much more when one has not awakened at all, but merely from vague, hazy impressions gives rise to views and knowledge and thinks he has attained, taking the ancients’ ready-made phrases as his own wondrous awakening. All this falls into self-deception and is no true investigation at all. Applying the mind thus is all the fault of not recognizing the root of the illness of birth and death. That is why the ancients said: You need not seek the true; you need only put a stop to views. If views and knowledge vanish, what need to wait for the true? That is why the Buddha told Ānanda: When seeing is seen, the seen is not seeing; seeing is apart from seeing, and seeing cannot reach it. This is the ultimate tracing to the source: it takes view alone as the root of the illness of birth and death, because deluded views arise from the dharma-body and see body, mind, and world, and so sink into birth and death. Hence now, detachment from views is taken as the ultimate rule for escaping birth and death and realizing the dharma-body. Master Aśvaghoṣa showed people that detachment from thought is true cultivation and genuine realization, because views exist owing to thought: if views fall away, thought is of itself detached and delusion of itself dissolves. Hence we know that the root of the illness of greed, anger, and affliction is shallow, while the root of the illness of the thorn of views is deep and hardest to pull out. Therefore in the work of investigation, afflictions are easily cut off but habit-energy is hard to remove. If habit-energy is not removed, deluded views secretly grow; and if deluded views grow, then even where one has awakened, it all becomes habit-energy and turns into Māra’s views. That is why the Śūraṅgama Sutra says the māra of views is the deepest, hidden and hard to know. If the Chan practitioner has the will for true investigation, he must simply see through it; on no account may he fall into the net of views and knowledge. Just when you are doing the work, take Zhaozhou’s word No and investigate it together with the Sixth Patriarch’s originally not a single thing. Before you lift it up, first set down body and mind, within and without, all at once; set down and set down again, until you reach the place where nothing more can be set down. Then look through to the bottom of this word No: what breath does it have after all? As soon as a single thought arises, give it one look on the spot; look steadily at it: what after all is it? Settling body and life thus and leaning steadily on the huatou, boring deep and stabbing painfully, not shifting a single thought, like a mouse gnawing a coffin — there will of itself be a time of breaking through. On no account keep the ancients’ gongans and phrases in your chest and use them for comparison, for as soon as the mind compares, it errs, and it is certainly not the ancients’ place of seeing. As for ordinary times when you meet conditions, simply lean steadily on the huatou, clear and singly bright, and you will of yourself not be shaken or robbed by the winds of circumstance. Even when talking with others, on no account take the ancients’ gongans as your own views and knowledge to furnish your talk. This one root of illness is the deepest, because just when you are speaking you aim only at brilliance and pleasure, quite unaware that this is not your own proper business; and so you give the mind free rein and let the mouth shoot off, never once turning the head to look, and therefore do not know it is an illness. If you let this illness grow, you will become a great māra of arrogance, held fast by the māra of madness. Among the monastics and laypeople fond of Chan whom I see before me now, it is so everywhere, and one cannot but be afraid. In the ancients’ investigation of Chan there was no other wonder: they were simply willing to sweep away worldly feeling and sagely understanding together, to let the chest be empty and bare, keeping not a hair of views and knowledge as master. When views and knowledge do not remain, the true view shines forth, and of itself there is not a single thing. When you set down in this way, the present single thought is like a great mass of fire: all the dust of passion and habit-energy is burned at a touch, like a flake of snow on a red-hot stove, with no trace left to remain. Looking back at all the affairs on the side of views and knowledge, it is like telling a dream. Hence it is said: In investigating Chan there is no secret method; you need only be able to set it down. If you set down one thought, that one thought is true; if you set down thought after thought, every thought is true; if you set down utterly, then to the end of the future you are utterly true. Go then, sir. If you do not forget these earnest words, then you will be knit brow to brow with the Old Man, with never a hair’s breadth of separation. Alas, alas! The Old Man is old. If you betray this connection and miss this life, then to seek again the connection of today — who knows how many thousands of millions of kalpas it will take.
Instruction to the Chan Monks Huimiao and Xinghou

In the land of the Eastern Sea the Buddhadharma does not flourish. Since Master Guifeng of Lingshan began to teach and convert there, no small number have been led to forsake the crooked and return to the upright. In former days the old man dwelt at Haiyin Temple and marveled at how richly that master's Dharma benefited others; most of his disciples were able to expound the Dharma. The student Xinghou of today is his direct heir. It is now twenty-eight years since the old man left Lingshan. In the year xinyou he came to seek instruction at Mount Kuang; after the turn of the year he took his leave to return to his old mountain, asking for the essentials of cultivating the mind. The old man therefore instructed him, saying: What the Buddha censures above all are the two obstructions, that of afflictions and that of the knowable, for they are the root of birth and death. The obstruction of afflictions is greed, anger, delusion and craving, the root of birth and death for ordinary people. The obstruction of the knowable is the knowledge and views of Buddhadharma, the root of birth and death for the sages of the three vehicles. If these two obstructions are not removed, there is no way to escape the mass of suffering. Alas, among the people of today those who do not know the Buddhadharma are hardly to be blamed; but even those who study the Buddhadharma do not cut off afflictions, and instead make the Dharma they have learned into an obstruction of the knowable, fostering arrogance and heaping up further afflictions. Their minds are defiled; the seeds are triggered and burst into activity, and they let themselves go. Body and mind are utterly unrestrained, and they follow their feelings in creating karma. Is this not a great error? Now that you, student, have heard the old man's instruction and know that this is the great matter of birth and death, you have aroused the mind to inquire and seek and to work at the ground of your own nature; this is the most excellent power of vow. Yet in your inquiry you need not seek anything else. Simply sweep clean, one by one, all the old seeds of habit in your breast, and permit none of them to burst into activity. In daily life, wherever you meet objects and conditions, at the very place where a thought arises, see through it on the spot and allow no continuation. As for the way to apply the mind, take the Śūraṅgama Sūtra's account of Guanyin's perfect penetration through the ear-faculty: turning the mechanism of hearing around, one hears back into one's own nature. This single gate of contemplation is the best way to apply the mind. If in daily seeing and hearing you can truly look back upon your own nature, you will not be carried along by outer objects. Turning the stream back thought after thought, every thought is a road home to the real. Apply the mind thus, yet if habits are not removed and burst into activity, your effort will surely lack power. All of it rests on this one point of turning against present karma, which is the highest practice. But you must also have a keen mind for birth and death; only then will you be willing to put in deadly earnest effort. Only when you truly work at it for the sake of birth and death will you have any benefit. It is not a matter of hearing it and letting it go, turning it into one more item of Buddhist knowledge and views.
Instruction to the Layman Jingxin

Formerly, when the old man passed through Wuzhong, the layman Jingxin came to pay his respects and ask for instruction, and the old man taught him the method of Buddha-recitation. Recitation is like the clear-water pearl that can purify muddy water; hence he was given the style-name Pure Mind. Several years have passed since we parted. Now he writes that his recitation finds it hard to become a single piece, and again asks for instruction. The old man therefore said: In practice the first requirement is a keen mind for birth and death. If the mind for birth and death is not keen, how dare one speak of recitation becoming a single piece? Moreover, through measureless kalpas beings have thought deluded thoughts moment by moment, their roots of craving firmly covered. Even in this present life, when has a single thought been painfully set on birth and death? Day by day, thought after thought follows feeling, and never once do they turn back and reflect. Now you wish, with a shallow and drifting faith, to cut off the birth and death of many kalpas; that is what is called saving a pile of firewood with a drop of water. How could such a principle hold? If your mind for birth and death were truly keen, every thought would be like putting out a fire on your own head; you would only fear that, once this human body is lost, a hundred kalpas may not restore it. You must clench this one recitation of the Buddha's name and resolve to stand against your deluded thoughts, so that all suffering stands present before you and is not screened off by delusion. Laboring thus with bitter earnestness, in time it becomes pure and familiar and naturally responds. Then, without seeking a single piece, it becomes a single piece of itself. This matter is like drinking water: cold and warm are known only to oneself and cannot be told to another. Everything depends on your own effort. If you merely make recitation a mask for your face, you will never in the year of the donkey have any benefit. You must be brave and fierce, and hesitate no longer.
Instruction to the Elder Rentian on Holding the Lotus Sūtra

The Great Virtue Rentian had recited the Lotus Sūtra for more than twenty years. As he was about to set out he asked for instruction, and the old man said to him: The Lotus is the Supreme Vehicle, the essential secret long guarded by our Buddha, and the writ of assurance by which he conferred on his disciples the prophecy of buddhahood. The Sixth Patriarch said: When the mind is deluded, the Lotus turns the mind; when the mind is awake, the mind turns the Lotus. To recite the sutra without understanding its meaning is to make an enemy of its sense. The Twenty-Seventh Patriarch said: The in-breath does not dwell in the realm of the aggregates; the out-breath does not touch any condition. Thus one constantly turns such a sutra, hundreds of thousands of millions of scrolls. Given what these two patriarchs said, how after all does Rentian hold this sutra? The sutra says: This Dharma cannot be understood by thought and discrimination. If so, then even the Sixth Patriarch, granting that he understood its meaning, still could not be said to hold it. Again it says: This sutra opens the gate of expedient means in order to reveal the true mark of all dharmas. If so, then mountains, rivers and the great earth, grasses, trees, tiles and stones are none of them other than the true mark; and even the Twenty-Seventh Patriarch, apart from in-breath and out-breath, still could not be said to hold it. Then how, after all, does Rentian hold it? As the Buddha said in the chapter on Holding the Sutra, even the fiftieth person in succession who transmits the teaching and has others hold the sutra gains merit beyond conception. From this we see that the merit of transmitting the teaching does not depend on whether one understands the meaning or not, nor on whether one is free of breath or not; one need only have a single thought of faith and know for oneself what is originally possessed, and the wisdom-life is not cut off. Therefore the old man praises the Blue Lotus Dharma Society above all, taking the holding of the Lotus as a wondrous practice. For as soon as one hears this sutra, one plants the true seed of buddhahood. If Rentian transmits this teaching to many people, as the Buddha praised, what other dharma could surpass it?
Instruction to Shen Dajie

Chan and Pure Land, these two practices, are from the outset not two dharmas; Master Yongming demonstrated this long ago. Chan is essentially free of thought — so be it. Yet the Pure Land has the highest grade of the highest rebirth, and that is never attained otherwise than by cultivation within freedom from thought. If one speaks of reciting the Buddha's name to the point of single-mindedness without distraction, is any thought retained there? Still, although in this there is no duality, when it comes to the actual work of application there is no lack of skill and clumsiness. For in inquiry the place where the mind is applied is most subtle and most close. When one is engaged in inquiry, it is a matter of not giving rise to a single thought; but if one speaks of reciting the Buddha's name, then a thought does arise. Thus there do seem to be two separate pieces. One must take the point of inquiry and the point of recitation and beat them into one line, so that what does not arise yet arises, and what arises is itself non-arising. Only this is the true practice of Yongjia's brightness and stillness flowing together. Why? If one discusses inquiry as the raising of a huatou, blocking off the root of the intellect so that not one thought arises, this is indeed the work of inquiry; but the ancients called it hugging the post while rowing the oar. That very thought of wanting no thought to arise is itself an arising; how could it be true non-arising? It is the same with recitation: if you hang the Buddha's name in your heart and never forget it thought after thought, how is that true single-mindedness without distraction? The ancients taught people to inquire into the living phrase, not the dead phrase; the very point is, in the midst of arising, to see the meaning of non-arising. As the sutra says: One who sees the instant awakens to non-arising. By this one saying, inquiry and recitation can at once become a single line. Practitioner, listen closely: in inquiring while reciting, it is easy to fall into confusion and error — do not take it lightly. How is inquiry itself recitation, and recitation itself inquiry? In your inquiry now, simply take the single phrase Amitābha as your huatou and do the work of examining it thoroughly. Put down all at once your own body, mind and world, together with all your former worldly conventions, habitual talk, and Buddhist knowledge and views. Then, from within emptiness and stillness, muster your strength and raise up one invocation of Amitābha Buddha, clear and distinct. Just as you raise it, look straight down at it and examine thoroughly: who is it that recites the Buddha's name? Bring up doubt again; examine and examine again, doubt and doubt again. Like a donkey gazing into a well, gaze on and on, doubt on and on, until you reach the place where the road of thought is cut off, like a silver mountain and an iron wall, with no place to turn the body or draw breath. Then suddenly you knock against it, touch it — the very meaning of non-arising — and it bursts forth before you; your whole body streams with sweat, as if waking from a great dream. Only then will you believe that arising is non-arising and non-arising is arising, that inquiry is recitation and recitation is inquiry. Looking back, you will know that all along you were like one searching for Chang'an while inside the Hanyuan Hall. In doing this work, the thing most to be feared is a mind that wants to awaken. The moment there is a mind that wants to awaken, that is a plank across your head. Just keep working straight on, with no reckoning of the schedule. When you reach the point where you cannot go on, rouse your spirits and start afresh. And you must never crave the mysterious and wonderful. Even if a thought subsides for a while and you feel still and joyful, never take that as something good; you must spit it out. Never take the mysterious sayings and wondrous words of the buddhas and patriarchs as your proof and call them Buddhadharma. Nor may you fall into the armor of do-nothingness and take that as attainment. In short, pay no heed to saint or ordinary being, delusion or awakening; single-mindedly seek where one thought comes to rest. Pursue it until it is hunted down and utterly cut off, and in time you will see your original face — like meeting your own father at the crossroads: you will not ask anyone where he is. Seen thus, this matter is from the beginning each person's own business, with nothing especially marvelous about it. If you, practitioner, would truly take the great matter of birth and death to heart, try starting from here; you will certainly not be cheated.
The Dream-Roaming Collection of the Old Man Hanshan, Volume Ten
Instruction to the Chan Monk Benhuaiyin

Long ago, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, our Buddha wished to entrust the Wondrous Lotus Sūtra to someone, charging him to uphold it in the final age and spread it abroad. Never mind the hundreds of thousands of gods and humans who received the prophecy of buddhahood; among all his disciples there was not one who dared to circulate this Dharma in the Sahā world. It had to wait for the host of bodhisattvas sprung from the earth before it could be shouldered. Is the holding of this Dharma so very easy? Because in the evil world of the five turbidities beings have scant merit and their natures are hard and violent, the most difficult of all to tame, our Buddha taught those who hold the sutra that patience must be the first practice. Hence he said: After the Tathāgata's extinction, one who wishes to expound this sutra to the four assemblies should enter the Tathāgata's chamber, put on the Tathāgata's robe, and sit on the Tathāgata's seat; then he may widely expound this sutra for the assembly. The Tathāgata's chamber is the mind of great compassion amid all living beings. The Tathāgata's robe is the mind of gentleness and patience. The Tathāgata's seat is the emptiness of all dharmas. Dwelling securely in these, and then with a mind free of indolence, one may expound the Lotus Sūtra for the assembly. Thus the Buddha recounted his own past practice in seeking the Dharma: how Devadatta in life after life wronged him, and how Never-Disparaging paid homage, and how the four assemblies even reviled him, or attacked him with knives, sticks, tiles and stones — all such sufferings he endured with joy, without one thought of indolence or retreat. This is precisely the Dharma taught to bodhisattvas, the supreme practice of holding the sutra in the final age. We who are sons of the Buddha — if we have no practice of patience, how shall we hold the Buddha's wisdom-life and keep it unbroken? And when he entrusted the sutra to the bodhisattvas who would hold it, he made them vow: All kinds of suffering we shall be able to endure. Therefore the Buddha said that if one surveys the three thousand great thousand worlds, there is not so much as a mustard seed's worth of space that is not a place where a bodhisattva gave up body and life in quest of bodhi; even head, eyes, marrow and brain were not spared. So he taught those who hold the sutra to begin with the practice of patience. Alas for this Dharma-ending age: without great power of patience, how can one protect the Buddhadharma and continue the wisdom-life? The old man has again and again expounded the practice of patience to Chan monks. This monk was able to believe the old man deeply and has sustained himself by the power of patience; now he has not only preserved the monastery to the end, but has also perfected his own practice. He must never be judged by ordinary worldly standards, nor should one seek the Dharma of birth and death anywhere apart from this. Moreover, this sutra is the one great cause for which our Buddha, the World-Honored One, appeared in the world. The one great cause is the Buddha's knowledge and vision, which beings inherently possess. The Buddha's knowledge and vision means the ability to see the true mark of all dharmas. Because beings are deluded as to the true knowledge and vision, they merely identify with the illusory and false body and mind of the five aggregates and do not see the true mark. If one sees the true mark, then throughout the three realms above and below there is not a single dharma to be found; where then could birth and death lodge? If this is so, can it be that only Chan inquiry can end birth and death, while holding the sutra cannot? Nanyue and Tiantai were both great patriarchs who awakened to the true mark. If among the companions of the Dharma Society who read and recite this sutra there should be even one who awakens and enters the Lotus samādhi as Tiantai did, then this very assembly on Vulture Peak is solemnly present and has never dispersed. Those who protect and uphold it will then be replete with Ganges-sands merit beyond conception. For this Dharma the Buddha, kalpa after kalpa, life after life, gave up body and life. If this monk can give up this one life and accomplish a great Dharma-benefit, why look outside and seek the Buddhadharma elsewhere? Even if today one cannot end birth and death, if one relies on this Dharma as a boat, upholding it with the power of vow, then in the sea of birth and death one will surely in the end reach the other shore; that is better than the former life of living in vain and dying in vain. Since this monk believes the old man's words, let him from now on rouse a great power of patience and a great power of diligence; this is called truly offering the Dharma to the Tathāgata and fulfilling Samantabhadra's great practice. Never give rise to a mind of arising and ceasing, set up views of self and others, and so conceive the thought of retreating and falling away.
Instruction to the Chan Monk Benyuanjue of Yangshan in Xin'an

Benyuanjue restored the Yangshan monastery over more than thirty years; the many splendors that appeared there like a conjuration all came from the power of his own mind. He also recited the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment and the Sutra of Brahma Conduct for more than twenty years, maintaining pure conduct with care; all this came from prajñā habituated in past lives. Now he came to pay homage at Mount Kuang, asked to receive the great precepts, and, holding up incense, requested an exposition of the great purport of the Perfect Enlightenment. The old man therefore instructed him, saying: The Buddha taught that all dharmas above and below the three realms are made by the one mind alone. It is said that from perfect enlightenment flow all pure true suchness, bodhi, nirvāṇa and the pāramitās, for the instruction of bodhisattvas. Therefore, as a son of the Buddha, if one penetrates the gate of mind-only, then all causes and results, defiled and pure, are right here before one and transform with every thought. Hence it is said: When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. Take the case of Yangshan: it was once all dangerous cliffs and craggy rocks, wild thickets and rank grass; now in a single day this monastery has appeared there as though fallen from heaven. All of it came from the first thought of firm faith, and so brought about such vast Buddhist work. From this we see that the Western Pure Land, too, is hardly to be obtained apart from the mind. Today the old man specially confers on this monk the Brahmā Net Vajra Jewel Precepts. These precepts are called Vairocana's gate of the mind-ground. The sutra says: If one receives the Buddha's precepts, one immediately enters the rank of the buddhas. Know therefore that a single thought of faith at once opens the Buddha's knowledge and vision, and all Buddha-lands appear before that thought. Hence all buddhas' Pure Lands are established from the vajra mind-ground. If this monk can truly understand this gate, then from now on, in every daily activity, clearly knowing that all is poured out from his own mind, each dharma will be a true cause of the Pure Land. If he can further hold the one invocation Amitābha Buddha, never forgetting it, never dulling it, reciting until movement and stillness are not two and waking and sleeping are as one, then every step before him treads the Pure Land; walking in procession on jeweled ground, this very body and mind already sits within the lotus calyx. When the time of death comes and he lets go this body, the flower will open and he will see the Buddha, as if waking from a dream. Only then will he know that birth and death are a dream and the Pure Land a conjuration, and in a single thought he will dwell forever in the stage of non-retrogression. What dharma besides this can deliver one from birth and death? This monk has long cultivated pure conduct, but he has not yet heard a good teacher in person to shatter the dream of former deluded thoughts. He has only to understand that every dharma is mind-only; what need is there to seek the Buddhadharma elsewhere? Strive on, and take care.
Instruction to the Good Man Chen

Chu and Mian are renowned prefectures, lands of ancient culture; yet teachers of the Dharma who have passed through and transformed them are rare. The Chan monk Guanzhi planted his staff here and kept retreat for three years, and for a time many turned to him. The good man who has lately come is an old disciple who took refuge in faith. He came from afar to consult the old man of Mount Kuang and asked for instruction to pass on to the people. The old man therefore instructed him, saying: Men and women in the household who can keep the five precepts — not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking wine or eating meat — when the Buddha was in the world, such people were always called upāsaka and upāsikā in the assemblies. This means near-serving men and women, because they are fit to draw near and serve the Three Jewels. What they practice is the careful keeping of the five precepts, by which they avoid falling into the three evil paths; this is the blessing of gods and humans. Hence it is said: If the five precepts are not kept, the road to the heavens and the human realm is cut off. In keeping the five precepts, the first thing is to understand and believe in cause and effect: good and evil retribution follow like shadow to form. Doing good creates a cause of blessing whose fruit is surely rebirth among gods or humans; creating evil brings an evil fruit, and one must fall into the three evil paths. Consider the high officials and noble ranks of the world, the rich and honored — such people must have cultivated blessings in former lives: offering to the Three Jewels, feeding monks, giving alms, printing sutras, making images, building temples and pagodas, relieving the poor and rescuing the suffering. Their long life and many sons, fathers kind and sons filial, husband leading and wife following, elder brothers friendly and younger respectful — all this must come from releasing living beings, not killing, and keeping fasts and precepts. If a householder can keep these five precepts, the five constant virtues are complete in him: not killing is benevolence; not stealing is righteousness; not committing sexual misconduct is propriety; not speaking falsely is trustworthiness; not drinking wine is wisdom. One who can do this in the Confucian school is a gentleman of accomplished virtue. How could keeping a fast be a matter outside one's duty? Among such people there are those of high intelligence and lofty understanding who, having kept these precepts, further reflect that the human world is impermanent, like a candle in the wind, and fear that once this human body is lost, ten thousand kalpas may not restore it. Reflecting thus and pondering the suffering of birth and death, their mind of renunciation grows keen; they should then arouse the mind to hold and recite Amitābha Buddha. Lay this one Buddha across your heart, never breaking it thought after thought, never forgetting it moment after moment; morning and evening bow to the Buddha and recite sutras, dedicating the merit toward the West and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. If recitation becomes pure and familiar and the mind is single without distraction, then at the time of death one will see Amitābha Buddha send forth light to receive and guide one; one will be received into a lotus and take it as one's father and mother. When the flower opens one sees the Buddha, and from then on one is forever freed from the suffering of birth and death and turning in the wheel; one takes final leave of the three realms. Such a one is called a bodhisattva. This work of recitation has been practiced by men and women in households in every age, accomplished in a single life, and many have been born in the West. Hence it is said: There is only the direct path of practice — simply recite Amitābha Buddha. To seek anything else is deviant view and deviant conduct. If the good man holds this and converts others of his kind, then one person, one family, and on to one village, one prefecture, one whole city, will become a Buddha-land. Only strive in your practice; if your faith is true and keen and you carry it out with a single thought, you need not seek any other wondrous Buddhadharma.
Instruction to Sheng Liansheng

Laozi said: My great affliction is that I have a body. If I had no body, what affliction would I have? The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: This body of mine is composed of the four great elements. One should contemplate that within the body hardness returns to earth, moisture to water, warmth to fire, and movement to wind. When the four elements each separate, where then is this false body? Contemplating thus in earnest, in time the mind becomes wholly familiar with it and the mark of the body suddenly becomes empty. All kinds of afflictions arise from deluded and inverted thought; like the inversions of a dream, they were never really there. When affliction arises, look directly at this mind's deluded thought: where does it arise from? Pursue it to the place where it was never born, and deluded thought no longer arises. When deluded thought does not arise, affliction is empty. When body and mind are suddenly empty, all afflictions are at once extinguished, and with that thought one enters the cool land of ultimate bliss. This contemplation is of the essence; it is the wondrous medicine for escaping suffering. Yet for a beginner the contemplation is not easily accomplished. Simply take Amitābha Buddha as your huatou and examine it truly, never letting it go. When a deluded thought arises, raise the huatou and press it — the deluded thought will vanish of itself. Because ordinarily you have no right mindfulness, you follow deluded thoughts wholly and are carried along, clinging without pause and so feeding your suffering. All dharmas arise from the mind; outside the mind there are no dharmas. If one does not contemplate the mind but seeks a road of escape from suffering, it is like stepping backward and hoping to go forward. You need only rouse a brave and fierce mind; never say you cannot — that is drawing your own limits.
Instruction to Wu Qigao

Qigao had long taken refuge in the Three Jewels and had kept a vegetarian mind for years. Now he came to Mount Kuang to seek the conferring of the precepts and to become a disciple of the Dharma gate, so as to form a bond for future transcendence. He was therefore given the name Fuchang and the style-name Layman Pure Mind, and the upāsaka precepts were conferred on him. Again he held up incense and asked for instruction. The old man therefore said: All the various karma-activities of the world are impermanent and are wholly causes of suffering; hence beings are born in the Sahā land, a place where beings are gathered, which is why it is called Endurance. Foolish and deluded people take suffering for joy, and so increase craving and add further to the root of suffering, not knowing what is essential for escaping it — this is inversion. Therefore, if anyone in the whole world has but a single thought recognizing that all is impermanent, suffering and empty, and arouses the mind to seek transcendence, that person is a person of great wisdom. If he has but a single thought of turning back and reflecting, arousing a mind that wearies of suffering, that is the road out of suffering. If he has but a single thought of the vow to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, that is the root of buddhahood. This is why the Buddha taught the precepts, instructing people to stop evil and cultivate good: when evil is stopped the mind is pure; when good is cultivated suffering ceases. When suffering ceases blessing increases. A pure mind is the cause of the Pure Land; the ending of suffering is the root of ultimate bliss; the increase of blessing is the fruit of everlasting joy.
