Seen thus, the great meaning of this sutra is that one single-mindedly investigates the mind, advances to break ignorance, and defines the stages to show the depth of realization — not comparable to cutting off and realizing in parts. That one first breaks the aggregates and afterwards enters the eight stages clearly shows that it is not a matter of matching the breaking of the five aggregates to the stages. How could one insist that breaking the aggregates runs parallel with the arranged stages? As for the teaching on breaking the aggregates, the Buddha, fearing that practitioners would be content with a little and would practice in confusion, specially set it forth to guard against error; it is not that he used it to explain the stages. Moreover, that one who has not broken the consciousness aggregate falls into the two vehicles can be known. If one in the Chan gate suddenly awakens to one's own mind and suddenly leaves birth and death, one does not fall into ranks — that is, within the three gradual stages one suddenly breaks the eighth consciousness and naturally transcends the stages. Yet though the patriarchs speak of transcending, they speak only of the plain dharmakāya Buddha, who does not necessarily possess the adornment of marks and radiance, spiritual powers and wondrous function. Even the buddhas and tathāgatas: none became a Buddha without awakening to his own mind. If one awakening finished everything, why should the buddhas have had to pass through three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas? People today, before their cushion is steady, use worldly cleverness to plunder the koans of the ancients, flaunt their own knowledge and views, and falsely claim to have realized sagehood, thinking themselves to surpass buddhas and patriarchs. Such are arrogant and conceited persons who claim to have attained what they have not and fall into great false speech — should one not fear it? How could such people be mentioned in the same day as true practitioners, whether they break the aggregates or not? Yesterday, traveling east, I saw many Chan practitioners, and not a few had fallen into such conceit. This rustic specially brought up the breaking of the aggregates to seal and correct them, and those who heard were ashamed and submitted, and their deviant views were considerably broken. I have seen laypeople discussing Chan fall into this sickness often. For true cultivation today, one should take as the urgent task the practice of the three gradual stages, the sudden awakening to one's own mind, and the sudden transcendence of birth and death. If one's own mind is once clear, the consciousness aggregate breaks of itself, and the four earlier aggregates break of themselves without needing to be broken. It is like bringing one's head to the white blade — like cutting the spring wind: how could the form aggregate obstruct it? Again it is said: The old monk can turn the twelve hours; and again: The in-breath does not dwell in the realm of aggregates, the out-breath does not touch any condition — how could he be within the feeling, perception and formations aggregates? The Sixth Patriarch knew his destination at death — was that not going wherever his vow wished? Such a one is hardly to be compared with those who falsely claim to have realized sagehood. We should prize only the clear investigation of our own mind and the single matter of escaping birth and death, and need not debate whether the breaking of the aggregates accords with the stages. Weighing it by principle and proving it by the holy words, such is my dim and inferior view; let the learned instruct me.
Guangzhi of the West Hall Asks About Six Doubts Concerning the Teaching Vehicle

First question: The ancients, in classifying the teachings, said that the two forms were both projected and the two beginnings were simultaneous; that the Buddha first taught the Avataṃsaka, intended for the Great Vehicle, with the two vehicles wholly excluded; and that when he turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths at Deer Park, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had not yet abandoned their deviant teachers and left home. Why then in the concluding passage of the Avataṃsaka are there śrāvakas such as Śāriputra? If we go by the concluding text, the two vehicles did hear the Avataṃsaka; why then is it asserted that the two vehicles were wholly excluded? Text and meaning contradict each other. I beg you to distinguish and explain.

Answer: The teachings say that the buddhas of the ten directions have one body and one wisdom; therefore in the buddha-lands of the ten directions only the One Vehicle Dharma is taught. Hence at the site of bodhi, immediately upon attaining perfect enlightenment, he taught the Avataṃsaka as the Supreme One Vehicle Dharma, intended solely for beings of great faculties; this is called teaching according to real wisdom. But since beings' faculties are not uniform, those of middling and inferior understanding neither see nor hear it, and so are wholly excluded. Therefore, in response to inferior faculties, he manifested a small transformation body, accomplished the Way through the eight phases, and at Deer Park taught the three vehicles' dharmas. It is said that the Buddha's true dharmakāya is like empty space, appearing in form in response to things like the moon in water; because he merely responds to faculties, he manifests a body, and what he teaches is expedient wisdom. At the Avataṃsaka assembly, in the Jetavana Grove, when Mañjuśrī, king of elephants, turned about, Śāriputra and six thousand bhikṣus attained the Way at his words; these too were bodhisattvas of the grounds, named great arhats. Now since the Buddha manifested a small response body and showed himself born among humans, and the various outsiders clung firmly to their view of self and were not easily gathered and converted, Śāriputra and the others likewise appeared as śrāvakas to assist and spread the conversion of the Dharma, becoming an echoing assembly — the sort who are inwardly hidden and outwardly manifest, not real śrāvakas. The assertion that the two vehicles were wholly excluded refers to real śrāvakas who cling to marks; and the reproof that Śāriputra and the others received was precisely to strike the drum of the Dharma's conversion. It is much like a stage play, where each takes a part to stir up feelings of sorrow, joy, parting and reunion, and when the play breaks up there is no involvement at all. So the bodhisattva's benefiting of beings is like play: responding when tuned, meeting by chance — how could it be a literal dharma?

Second question: In the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Universal Eye did not see Samantabhadra. Three times he entered samādhi and surveyed the three thousand great thousand worlds without seeing him, and then came and told the Buddha. The Buddha taught him that in the samādhi of stillness, if he raised a thought he would see him. Universal Eye had but to raise one thought and at once saw him in empty space. If Samantabhadra's body is the one true dharma-realm, he should be seen within samādhi — why was he not seen? If Samantabhadra is a body of form and marks, he should have been seen before entering samādhi — why did the Buddha teach that he was seen only when a thought was raised?

Answer: The dharmakāya is without marks; even Universal Eye could not gaze upon it. That he sought it in samādhi and did not see it is because the dharmakāya has no mutual seeing of this and that. Know therefore that what can be seen belongs to the second approach; hence it was seen only when a thought was raised.

Third question: In the Awakening of Faith, true suchness perfumes from within, and so there is deluded mind; wearied of the suffering of birth and death, one seeks nirvāṇa. The deluded mind is of two kinds: first, ordinary beings and the two vehicles perfume and cultivate relying on the consciousness of things; second, bodhisattvas perfume and cultivate relying on the karmic consciousness. Students today inquire relying only on the consciousness of things and cannot rely on the karmic consciousness. Chan inquiry is originally a Great Vehicle gate; if one inquires relying on the consciousness of things, it becomes instead the practice of ordinary beings and the two vehicles. And if in inquiry one uses both consciousnesses at once, that contradicts the ancients' saying: Inquire apart from mind, intellect and consciousness. I beg you to open and decide this.

Answer: The teaching that ordinary beings and the two vehicles cultivate relying on the consciousness of things and that bodhisattvas cultivate relying on the karmic consciousness refers to arousing the mind and attaining realization in dependence on consciousness. Now when a Chan student arouses the mind, though it be the consciousness of things, his resolve aims directly at smashing the lacquer bucket of the karmic consciousness and penetrating straight to the one point above, before delusion began, not falling into the nest of the two consciousnesses. If he is content with a little, then he cannot be free of mind, intellect and consciousness.

Fourth question: The ancients said: I do not prize your conduct, only your insight. And again: If insight is not clear, one falls into a pit. Nowadays explanations in various quarters are of two kinds. One says that broad learning in sutras and treatises, with understanding based on them, is called insight. Another says that only after awakening clearly is there insight. If learned understanding is insight, why does the Chan school not permit the reading of the teachings? If insight comes only after awakening, then what dharma should a beginner take as insight in his practice, so as to avoid the calamity of falling into a pit?

Answer: Understanding as insight is of three kinds: there is understanding by learning, understanding by faith, and understanding by awakening. If one understands from the teachings or from the patriarchs' koans the ultimate point of the buddhas and patriarchs, not falling into side branches, this, though it is named insight, is understanding based on a ground. If one has not personally met with the spoken teachings but simply resolves with certainty to believe in one's own mind, in which there is not a single thing, that is understanding by faith. If through inquiry one one day clarifies what is originally possessed, that is understanding by awakening. All three are named insight. But understanding based on another mostly falls into the obstruction of knowledge and views. Understanding by faith, even so, still requires practice to reach true realization. Understanding by awakening, though it be a single thought of sudden awakening, still has beginningless subtle obstructions of delusion which must also be purified. Though these three kinds of insight are prized, without conduct one can in the end hardly reach the ultimate. The insight prized by the ancients was based on faculties; it is not that conduct is not valued. The occasional words of the ancients must not be taken as literal dharmas.

Fifth question: The ancients said that inquiry should be carried on while carrying firewood and drawing water and while traveling on foot. Students today hold that one should sit quietly, for then the work of inquiry has power; but in the four dignified postures, when in contact with things, thoughts fly in confusion and the huatou sinks away. If one only sits quietly, that again contradicts the ancients' conduct; if one engages with things, the mind is scattered all day. How can a student be made to be without conflict between movement and stillness in daily life?

Answer: When the ancients did their work, they wanted it observed in walking, standing, sitting and lying, in the four dignified postures; they did not teach you to sit rigidly like a dead thing. Because one who first enters Chan has a mind much scattered and stirred, one provisionally takes to quiet sitting to gather the mind; but in truth one must take what is done in stillness and test it in the midst of movement, to see how it fares. If the mind is applied closely and continuously, movement and stillness are naturally as one and are beaten into a single piece. That thoughts now fly in confusion before objects means that the huatou has no power at all — can such a one be a true practitioner? What matters now is only that the huatou gain power; then, regardless of movement or stillness, one will naturally not be turned about by them.

Sixth question: The sutra says that mind, Buddha and beings — these three are without difference. It also says that the realm of the buddhas is equal and the realm of beings is equal. It also says that only when all beings are saved does one accomplish the buddha-way. If beings and buddhas are equal, then the Buddha has no meaning of saving beings; how is it that only when all beings are saved does one accomplish the buddha-way? And if the buddhas and bodhisattvas save all beings, the realm of the buddhas would seem gradually to increase and the realm of beings gradually to decrease. How then can beings and buddhas be called equal?

Answer: Mind, Buddha and beings are from the beginning equal. Because beings are the beings within the Buddha's mind, the Buddha saves the beings of his own mind. If the mark of beings is empty, that is the saving of all beings, and one accomplishes the Buddha of one's own mind. Even if one mind were wholly made into beings, that would be beings making themselves into the beings of their own minds, and the realm of the buddhas would not decrease. Even if the realm of beings were exhausted, it would only be the dissolving of each one's own realm of beings; because the mind is equal, the Buddha does not increase either. The Buddha sees the realm of beings as empty; but if beings' own minds are not empty, then beings do not decrease either. It is like the vast sky when clouds gather and mist darkens it: the sky does not decrease; when the clouds scatter and the mist clears, the sky does not increase. Though it be darkened all day and cleared all day, the substance of the sky remains limpid. How then could there be increase or decrease in the realm of the buddhas?
Reply to Dajie's Six Questions

First question, on keeping the precepts: A beginner does not know how to keep the precepts and fears that every movement is a fault; receiving them has its order, and one must certainly not be reckless. Yet within them the great and small vehicles are distinguished and the expedient and the real have their applications; though faculties differ in sharpness and dullness and capacities vary in depth, there are inevitably abuses. I beg you to set out the rules of conduct, so that the sharp may look up and follow them and the dull may broaden their scope.

Answer: The precepts established by the Buddha are recorded in detail in the Vinaya. His original intent was that because beings have eighty-four thousand afflictions, he set up eighty-four thousand rules of discipline as medicines matched to the illness, wishing to cure the illness of affliction and make the dharmakāya pure. Because faculties are great or small, the precepts have three grades: the ten precepts of the śrāmaṇera, the two hundred and fifty precepts of the bhikṣu, and the bodhisattva's ten major and forty-eight minor precepts. The two kinds of precepts, those of the śrāmaṇera and the bhikṣu, were established according to circumstances and are called preventive precepts, meaning that they block and stop transgressions. Though great and small alike observe them, they belong mostly to the Lesser Vehicle: one merely restrains the body from acting. One who can restrain the mind from arising is of the Great Vehicle, yet this too remains within the precepts of marks and affairs. As for the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts spoken of in the Brahmā Net Sūtra, they are called the precepts of nature; they were spoken by my original teacher, the reward-body Buddha Rocana, as the mind-ground gate of all buddhas, named the Vajra Jewel Precepts, and he commanded Śākyamuni to transmit and spread them in turn. What is meant by the precepts of nature is this: to understand and penetrate that one's own nature is pure and from the beginning undefiled, and to awaken suddenly to the originally existing pure dharmakāya, whose nature is inherently complete — this is called the precepts. The sutra says: If a person receives the Buddha's precepts, he at once enters the rank of the buddhas. Hence all that Śākyamuni taught in forty-nine years was but the transmission of this precept-dharma; and what he showed at the end by holding up the flower was but the showing of this nature of the precepts. What the patriarchs of every generation awakened to was but the perfecting of this light of the precepts. Therefore, when one contemplates all beings, the seed of buddha-nature is from the beginning equal, because all alike possess the equal dharmakāya. If one contemplates beings by way of buddha-nature, then whenever a single thought of killing, stealing, lust or lying arises, or one speaks of the faults of the four assemblies, praises oneself and disparages others, or slanders the Three Jewels, one cuts off the Buddha's wisdom-life, no different from killing a Buddha; hence the ten major items are set out. If one contemplates beings by way of the equal dharmakāya, then there is nothing to kill, steal from, lust after or lie about, nor anyone to disparage, for these are the perfect and sudden precepts. What they chiefly value is the seed of buddha-nature alone, which is the Buddha's wisdom-life. Not only those of sharp faculties can receive them; even paṇḍakas and the two-sexed, men given to lust and women given to lust, and even ghosts and spirits — anyone who understands the master's words is fit to receive them. One need only believe that the seed of buddha-nature in all beings is the equal dharmakāya. If one can contemplate thus, then in every state encountered in daily life one is wholly within the ground of the light of the precepts. Then not only does one not restrain the body from acting; in killing, stealing, lust and lying, with every glance and every thought the buddha-nature appears before one and is instantly transformed into a mass of light. How could it be merely that the mind does not arise? Yet as to the way of keeping them: with the preventive precepts it is indeed hard, for it lies wholly in restraining the three karmas and subduing transgressions. But the precepts of nature are truly hard: one must hold them with a single mind of vajra and not lose them. A single thought of dullness, and the whole body falls — is this a small matter? Hence the Avataṃsaka, for those at the beginning of the ten faiths who keep these precepts, sets out the Chapter on Pure Conduct with its one hundred and twenty great vows, so that in daily life there is no place of leakage; yet this still follows marks and affairs. As for those at the beginning of the ten dwellings who keep these precepts, there is the Chapter on Brahma Conduct: examining and contemplating the transcending of marks is precisely the method of keeping these precepts. A beginner who constantly keeps these two chapters will in time naturally accord. As for the abuses mentioned: in the preventive precepts there is the abuse of clinging to marks, and hence of arrogance and self-exaltation and of hating and disparaging those who keep the precepts. Among those who keep the precepts of nature there is the abuse of claiming to have attained what one has not, of indulging oneself and letting feeling run loose, of taking a thief for one's son. Remove these two extremes, and whether one is sharp or dull, one is called a true keeper of the precepts.

Second question, on Chan inquiry: To keep the precepts without according with one's own nature is in the end muddled. To seek to see one's nature, nothing surpasses inquiry. Yet within it doubt and awakening interlock, and the son and the thief are hard to tell apart. I beg you to hand down an enduring mirror, so that I do not fall into the pit of delusion.

Answer: The Buddha spoke of what a renunciant practices: the three studies of precepts, concentration and wisdom. Now the Vinaya is the study of precepts, and inquiry is the study of concentration. But the study of concentration as set out in the teachings is the wondrous gate of the three contemplations, the shortcut to awakening to the mind. Later, when the way of Chan came east, the weight was laid on direct pointing, the single transmission, and seeing one's nature as Chan, without speaking of concentration; yet Chan is concentration. At first Bodhidharma showed the Second Patriarch merely that seeking the mind it is utterly unobtainable, which is called sudden awakening. Even the Sixth Patriarch only taught people not to think of good or evil, and asked which is your own original face; this turning back to seek one's own mind is the work of inquiry. Originally there was no talk of watching a huatou and bringing up doubt. Only later, from Huangbo onward, did people teach the watching of huatous, taking one koan of the ancients as the root of inquiry, and this was transmitted as a literal dharma. Down to the present, masters teach people to inquire into koans only and not to investigate their own minds, and because of this many have been misled. Hence there are many who inquire into Chan today, but none who have gained right knowledge and views; moreover they use Chan inquiry to disparage the teachings, which shows that theirs is not true Chan inquiry. They do not realize that the ancients, because students found it hard to enter, used it as an expedient for a time, wanting only that people recognize their own original mind. How could the buddhas and patriarchs have two minds? They do not realize that raising the huatou, blocking off the root of the intellect, and permitting no arising and ceasing or flowing of a single thought, is precisely the essential gate of entering concentration. People today make of it something strange and special, and so mostly ruin themselves. In inquiry today one cannot do without a huatou, because the beginner's mind is scattered and hard to control and needs this as a handle. Before raising it, one must first steady body and mind, put down inside and outside all at once, put them down until there is nowhere further to put them; then, slowly, muster your strength and raise the huatou, looking back at where it arises — from where does it arise? What after all is it? Because one has not clearly seen one's own mind, one brings up doubt, saying: What is my own original root of life? Seeking thus is called inquiry. One must be undimmed thought after thought and unwavering mind after mind, leaning on it day and night, forgetting sleep and food, until suddenly the bean pops in the cold ashes and the original substance appears before one thought: this is called awakening to one's own mind. When you reach this, you are still just the same person as before, with not the least thing strange about it. If a single thought of joy comes and you take that as enough, that is called taking a thief for your son — how much worse to fabricate all kinds of knowledge and views and utter verses and hymns as rare merchandise? Never fall into this net of māra.

Third question, on koans: After the huatou is shattered, the seventeen hundred tangled vines fall like splitting bamboo. Yet if one case is slightly mistaken, all becomes cloud and fog, and only when the former shattering is undone does one come to believe in the ghost's gate. Not to recognize this fault, but to play with one's spirit and soul, is to lie hidden in the three evil paths.

Answer: If a student can truly see his own mind clearly and reach the place of no doubt, then he breathes through one nostril with the buddhas of the ten directions and the patriarchs of every generation; what need to speak of koans or no koans? This matter is not the business of a beginner; set it aside for now and do not keep it in mind.

Fourth question, on sealing with the teachings: One who does not seal and verify by the teachings does not gain right knowledge and views — this was the Master's former instruction. But the road of conceptual meaning is an old habit, and old habits are hard to dissolve, like oil mixed into flour. If by any chance, in the place of sealing, there is a thread of consciousness, then the awakened one falls instead into skandha-māras, and deviant views are fostered, doing no small harm. I beg you to expose the critical point.

Answer: When the old man ordinarily requires practitioners to seal the mind with the teachings, he means that for what one knows and sees oneself, having never had a clear-eyed person to point out the deviant and the right, one should seal and verify it by the Buddha's sutras. In the Śūraṅgama, the Laṅkāvatāra and the Perfect Enlightenment, what is spoken is all the work of meditation and the essentials of awakening to the mind; one compares one's own mind against them to see whether it accords with what the Buddha said or not. Hence it is said: Take the holy teachings as a bright mirror to illumine one's own mind — not that one takes the mysterious and wondrous phrases of the sutras and turns them into one's own understanding. As for your question, it is precisely that you do not know where the huatou lands. As for the various sicknesses of our mind, only the Buddha has exposed them fully: the rising and sinking of the seven destinies in the Śūraṅgama, the forms of the fifty kinds of skandha-māra, the deviant views of outsiders and the two vehicles in the Laṅkāvatāra. Had the Buddha not spoken in detail, how would we know to fear them? This is what I mean by sealing the mind. One should only illumine the mind by the teachings; it does not consist in the road of conceptual meaning, nor should one take that road as the end. As for old habits of all kinds, they are more than the road of meaning.

Fifth question, on expounding the teachings: The gift of Dharma is great, and the offering of Dharma is supreme. From awakening one seals the teachings, and from that sealing one expounds the teachings; this seems to accord with the Buddha's knowledge and vision and to turn the great Dharma-wheel. Yet if the awakening is not true awakening, one seals by self-confidence; if the sealing is not true sealing, one takes expounding as one's own office, erasing all commentaries and flaunting only one's own clarity. Whether one is a lion or a fox is easy to confuse in oneself; whether one expounds or slanders is hard to know for oneself. I beg you to hand down a precise judgment, and I shall forever consult it as an oracle.

Answer: As a son of the Buddha, one finds the Buddha's grace hard to repay; only by transmitting the Dharma in the Buddha's place is one truly repaying it. Hence among the ancient masters who spread the Dharma there were three kinds. First, those who awakened to their own nature and wondrously accorded with the Buddha's mind, so that the Buddha's words flowed out as if from their own breasts, with the four unhindered eloquence, and who further entered deep into the ocean of the teachings with vast and billowing waves — such as Qingliang, Guifeng and the great patriarchs of Tiantai. Second, those who, though not yet awakened to their own minds, relied on the Buddha's words to seal and settle their minds, broadly exploring the ocean of teachings and expounding as they understood, without erring from the Buddha's intent — such people, though not yet beyond words and images, did not presume to discourse wildly according to their own views but expounded according to the teachings, as the great Dharma-masters of former times. Third, those who had seeds of prajñā from past lives and had the work of meditation, who clarified their own minds and wondrously accorded with the Buddha's intent, but had not broadly engaged in much hearing; their right views were not mistaken. Though they had the fault of taking the shallow for the deep, they had not the crime of slandering the Dharma; what they spread was always with the mind of the gift of Dharma, not seeking worldly fame, profit or respect — such as the venerable Wenling and Jiyin of old. These are all great in the gift of Dharma. As for those who, though clever and of sharp faculties, rely on their own views as attainment, reject ancient and modern alike, let their tongues run wild, and spread the Dharma only for profit — such people not only destroy the Buddhadharma but also mislead and ruin later generations. How could they be called expounders of the Dharma? This is plainly evident and needs no asking.

Sixth question, on versifying the ancients: After awakening, the ancients' verses on the old cases were like painting empty space, not falling into form or mark. People today, whose awakening is not yet thorough, lightly take to versifying the ancients; their lines come from poetic fancy and their repartee resembles buffoonery, yet they take these as words of awakening and states of awakening, and they are on everyone's lips. One turn and they fall into the fox state, and they are placidly unafraid. Is this not a corruption of the Dharma-ending age? We are apt to lose our footing in this pit. I beg you to apply the needle, and I shall everywhere receive your deep compassion.

Answer: Versifying the ancients has existed from of old; it does no more than bring out the ancients' manoeuvres and casually display the arrangements of the house, to manifest the great function and great capacity, and to bring forth one's own hand of letting go and seizing, killing and reviving. It is not merely letting the mouth run and feeling run loose, or composing for the sake of attainment. These two matters, versifying the ancients and expounding the teachings, are not urgent for a beginner; why should one undertake them in advance? The old worthies said: If one but awakens to one's own mind, one need not worry about being unable to expound the Dharma. Thus for a beginner the only urgent thing is to investigate the mind and seek clarity in the great matter of oneself. Never harbor such a view. If we can awaken to our own minds, then even without expounding the teachings or versifying the ancients, ours is a true leaving of home, and we do not disgrace the kāṣāya we wear.
The Dream-Roaming Collection of the Old Man Hanshan, Volume Twelve
Master Jizhao Kai Asks for Instruction on Eight Points

Question: The sutra says that unhindered pure wisdom is born entirely from meditation. How is it then that Nanyue said to Mazu: If you learn sitting meditation, know that Chan is not sitting or lying; if you learn to become a Buddha, know that the Buddha is not a fixed mark. In the Dharma of non-abiding one should not grasp or reject? Which of these two statements is right and which wrong?

Answer: In the patriarchs' gate one does not discuss sitting in meditation or becoming a Buddha; one prizes only seeing one's nature. If one sees one's own nature, clearly and distinctly, there is naturally no grasping or rejecting. The moment there is grasping or rejecting, one falls into right and wrong.

Question: The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: This body of mine is the four great elements — hardness, moisture, warmth and movement — which each return to earth, water, fire and wind; hence it is said that the four elements each separate. Where then is this false body? I do not know whether the elements separate while the body is not yet dead, or separate after death?

Answer: What matters is that before death one can let it go, so that at the time of departure one is not burdened by it. If one waits until the moment itself, to separate is like a live turtle shedding its shell — difficult beyond difficulty. The ancients said: What is done in leisure is used in haste — precisely this.

Question: The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says that Ānanda asked the Buddha: In the road of the original arousal of the mind, from what does one gather and subdue it, to enter the Buddha's knowledge and vision? The Buddha said: If you wish to enter the Buddha's knowledge and vision, you should examine carefully whether the mind aroused on the causal ground is the same as or different from the enlightenment of the fruit ground. If on the causal ground one takes the mind of arising and ceasing as the ground of practice and yet seeks the Buddha Vehicle's non-arising and non-ceasing, there is no such possibility. I do not know whether the mind with which one now inquires into Chan and studies the Way in order to escape birth and death is a mind of arising and ceasing.

Answer: When a student inquires into Chan, he first cuts off the mind of arising and ceasing; when it becomes clear, he then sees the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing. If one inquires with a mind of arising and ceasing, one merely follows deluded thoughts in their flow; that is not inquiry.

Question: Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai said: To visit good teachers and seek a bit of knowledge or half an understanding is the māra of the good teacher, because it gives rise to views of words. To make the four great vows, vowing to save all beings and only then become a Buddha, is the māra of the wisdom of the bodhisattva Dharma, because one does not let go of the vow. To keep fasts and precepts and cultivate meditation and learning and wisdom is a root of good with outflows; even if one sits on the bodhi seat and attains perfect enlightenment and saves beings numerous as Ganges sands, all realizing the fruit of pratyekabuddha, it is the māra of good roots, because one gives rise to greed and clinging. If toward all dharmas one has no greed or defilement, and the principle of Chan alone remains, with most profound meditation and no further advance, that is the māra of samādhi, because one long indulges and plays in it. How can one who now inquires into Chan and studies the Way escape these māras and enter the right road of practice?
Answer: All practitioners, simply because their mental views are not forgotten, move along with the net of māra. If mental views are dissolved and forgotten, then even the Buddha is not established.
Question: In breaking the clinging to the four elements and the five aggregates, is there a before and after?

Answer: The teachings say that the five aggregates are broken gradually and that the form aggregate must be broken first. But if in Chan inquiry one smashes the lacquer bucket, then the consciousness aggregate is broken first. Once the consciousness aggregate is broken, the four elements have no support, and so it is like cutting water or blowing on light — no contact at all.

Question: As for the four phrases of the Diamond Sūtra, from ancient times to now no one has spoken of them clearly. Some point to form, sound, scent and the like as the four phrases; some point to eye, ear, nose and tongue; some to all marks being non-marks; some to the truth of existence and the truth of non-existence. As for Vasubandhu, he said: I ascended to the Tuṣita heaven and asked Maitreya for instruction, and he said: No mark of self, no mark of a person, no mark of a being, no mark of a life. The Sixth Patriarch said: Mahāprajñāpāramitā. And Master Shanhui of Shuanglin said again: Holding the four phrases in the sutra, one should not be apart from one's body; the foolish see it as a dream, the wise see only the real. From ancient times to the present there has never been a settled wording — why is this?

Answer: The Buddha's teaching of prajñā is like the many herbs of the snowy mountains: every one of them is medicine, and picked up and used it will certainly cure the illness. So when the ancients pointed out what the four phrases are, each was plucking one stalk of grass from the snowy mountains.

Question: The ancients said: Even when one reaches utter purity without a speck, it is still the outflow of true permanence. Even when one reaches the point where not one dharma stands before the mind, one is still subject to Yangshan's inspection. Even when one reaches the state where the whole body is illumination, one is still within the monk's letting down of the hand. Even when one realizes that which is before the seven buddhas and beyond Sound-Voice, it is still a matter of understanding words. Do students today really reach these states?

Answer: The ancients' handed-down words were only out of fear that people would fall by the roadside. Even if a student reaches this, it is still a matter of the roadside; how much more so, not having reached it, to open one's mouth and talk of Chan — that is always deceiving one's own mind.

Question: Master Yuanwu said: Since there have been patriarchs, their sole concern has been the single transmission and direct pointing: using words to drive out words, using the mechanism to seize the mechanism, using poison to attack poison, using function to break function. Hence the branches and schools divided, each mastering its own style. One must be of supreme faculties and have the will to perpetuate and prosper the buddhas and patriarchs; only then can one enter deeply into the inner chamber and only then be sealed and verified. Apart from this, one should treasure and keep it secret and not take it lightly. Now I see students who mostly do not examine their own faculties but want to inquire into the matter above. Is faculty truly not to be discussed?

Answer: The patriarchs' selection of people takes faculties into account; this is the same as the Buddha's discussion of lineages in the teachings. If one is not of such a lineage, one remains stuck to skin and bone. People today, whose faculties are impure, are certainly wholly excluded from this matter. If one is willing to give one's mind to this matter and from then on not retreat, in time one may be permitted to advance. Such a one falls within the category of the undetermined lineage.
Wang Jie'an and Zhu Baimin Ask for Instruction
Question: The Buddha taught the sudden teaching and the gradual teaching, and Chan opened the sudden gate and the gradual gate. These two teachings and two gates — are they the same or different?

Answer: When the buddhas and patriarchs appeared in the world, they fundamentally had no dharma to speak. And since the Dharma is fundamentally without speech, how could there be distinctions of sudden and gradual? The talk of sudden and gradual is set up solely for the sake of faculties and has nothing to do with the Dharma. Now as to the teachings having sudden and gradual: when Vairocana first attained perfect enlightenment and at the site of bodhi taught the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, he suddenly revealed the gate of the mind-ground of the equal dharma-realm, directly showing it without remainder, like the sun newly risen that first illumines the high mountains. Those who later classified the teachings called it the perfect and sudden gate; this is the Buddha's sudden Dharma. Yet this sudden Dharma was bestowed only on one class of beings of great faculties on the grounds; within it the forty-two stages are arranged — that is the gradual within the sudden. The remaining beings of inferior faculties in the assembly were as blind and deaf, wholly excluded. Thus, though the Dharma was great, the faculties it gathered were not broad; it is what is called there being only one gate, and that one narrow. Would the Buddha teach the Dharma for one person alone? Therefore he manifested response bodies and transformation bodies, established according to the three kinds of faculties, and taught the three vehicles' dharmas, beginning with gradual cultivation and realization — what is called the gradual of the teachings. Later, in the Laṅkāvatāra, the Lotus and the Nirvāṇa, he suddenly revealed the seed of buddha-nature; this is the sudden coming from the gradual. This is how the teachings are divided into sudden and gradual. As for the one gate of Chan, it is spoken of everywhere in the teachings. Among the bodhisattva's six pāramitās there are the two of meditation and wisdom; the classifying of the bodhisattva teachings opens from these two the two gates of calming and contemplation as the ground of practice. Here the teaching uses the sudden while cultivating gradually, so that Chan is the gradual within the sudden. As for Bodhidharma's Chan: it was the World-Honored One's holding up of the flower at the end, and Mahākāśyapa's breaking into a smile; the Buddha then showed him the treasury of the true Dharma-eye and the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, and so it became the purport of the special transmission outside the teachings. Twenty-eight transmissions in the Western regions, then Bodhidharma came east, and six transmissions to Caoxi; and the patriarchs recorded below in the Transmission of the Lamp are the Chan of the single transmission directly pointing to the one mind, which cannot be compared with the Chan of the six pāramitās. For this singly shows the one mind and no other dharma, directly seeing one's own mind at once, not belonging to cultivation, realization, delusion, awakening, cause or fruit; it specially reveals the one point of the Buddha before he appeared in the world. This is called the path above, and named the sudden teaching of the Great Vehicle. This is the sudden of Chan. As for the patriarchs of every generation who suddenly awakened to this mind: though it be under a single word or phrase, a single blow or shout, they awakened directly — this is because of practice through many lives, with deep roots of prajñā, when causes and conditions ripened and matured today; there are also those who in this life inquire for twenty or thirty years before they awaken. Thus, though sudden, it also comes from the gradual. As Weishan said: If a student can in a single thought awaken clearly to his own mind and recognize what he originally possesses, this is called awakening; yet there still remain beginningless ignorance and subtle outflows, and so with what he has awakened he purifies the outflowing consciousness of present karma, and this is called cultivation; there is no other cultivation apart from this. Seen thus, within the sudden there is never a lack of the gradual. I have observed that the Laṅkāvatāra divides sudden and gradual into four gates: first, sudden-sudden; second, sudden-gradual; third, gradual-sudden; fourth, gradual-gradual. Know from this that one cannot hold to one and speak of all. Though one awakens suddenly, gradual cultivation is not abandoned; the minds of the buddhas and patriarchs are from the first not two.

Question: The Buddha's various sutras are all talks according with nature and purport of definitive meaning. Why is it that Bodhidharma praised the Laṅkāvatāra repeatedly, saying, This sutra is the essence of my mind, while Huangmei pointed to the Diamond? What difference is there in the other sutras?

Answer: The Buddha's various Mahāyāna sutras, though they are talks according with nature and of definitive meaning, in their gate of establishing conversion do not depart from delusion and awakening and from the mutual opposition of nature and characteristics; they insist on returning from the false to the real, and all have their harmonizing before the one real is revealed. As for the Laṅkāvatāra, it directly points to the one mind. Though it speaks of the real and the false, it shows that the storehouse of consciousness is itself the tathāgatagarbha, and no harmonizing is needed; it reveals only the state of the holy wisdom of self-awakening. One need only understand that the deluded thoughts manifested by one's own mind are without nature, and that is holy wisdom; no further turning is required. As for its practice, one simply contemplates directly the flowing of one's own mind and the present measure of deluded thought, and penetrates one's own mind at once, without establishing stages or ranks. Hence those who classify the teachings name it the gate of the sudden teaching. Therefore Bodhidharma took it as the mind-seal, using this sutra to show the essential key of the Chan school; and because this sutra is hard to understand and difficult for inferior understanding to enter, when the transmission reached Huangmei he used the Diamond to seal the mind. The Diamond is one of the eight divisions of prajñā, whose text runs to six hundred scrolls; only this scroll alone accords with the patriarchs' mind-seal. For prajñā is the initial gate of entering the Great Vehicle, exactly as the Śūraṅgama says: the bodhisattva takes the mind of non-arising and non-ceasing as the ground of practice. And prajñā is the Buddha's fundamental real wisdom, which is precisely the mind of non-arising and non-ceasing. This sutra takes non-abiding as its principle and the cutting off of doubt as its function. Because the two vehicles falsely give rise to views of beings, of a Buddha and of dharmas, and to all kinds of abiding and clinging, and bring up doubt layer upon layer, this sutra plucks out the root of doubt entirely and brings one to the place of no doubt, where knowledge and views perish and not one dharma is established, dispelling all clinging minds. This is exactly the same as the Chan school's method of loosening the glue and removing the bonds, cutting off the discriminations of intellect and words — precisely the Chan school's not permitting deliberation, not attaching to thought, withering consciousness and emotion, and penetrating above the dharmakāya. Hence Huangmei's sealing the mind with this sutra was well founded. The other sutras all have some stickiness; this sutra alone is clean-cutting. If one understands this in Chan inquiry, one enters easily.

Question: It is said that there is Tathāgata Chan and patriarch Chan. Do these two Chans really have sameness or difference? When Xiangyan, on hearing the pebble strike the bamboo, had an awakening, he presented to Yangshan the verse beginning Last year's poverty was not yet true poverty. Yangshan said: I am glad that my brother understands Tathāgata Chan, but patriarch Chan — you have not yet dreamed of it. By these words one sees that Tathāgata Chan and patriarch Chan are different. Yet if from Mahākāśyapa it was transmitted to the First Patriarch who came from the West, and patriarch succeeded patriarch, the first patriarch of all the schools is Śākyamuni himself — how could there be any difference?

Answer: Tathāgata Chan and patriarch Chan are from the first not two. Only, Tathāgata Chan speaks of awakening within delusion and requires cultivation before entering; patriarch Chan directly points to the one point that does not belong to delusion or awakening and does not depend on cultivation, requiring a person to awaken at once to his own mind directly. Whoever falls into the juncture of delusion and awakening is already in the secondary meaning. Hence the old worthy said: Cultivation is indeed not absent — but what of defilement? Therefore the Chan school's path above requires one who is a man of that ilk before one can attain it. Among the four kinds of Chan in the Laṅkāvatāra, the supreme one-vehicle Chan is precisely patriarch Chan. In truth there is from the first no difference. If one's faculties are impure and one recklessly flaunts cleverness and knowledge and views, taking that as understanding patriarch Chan, then one has not even dreamed of Tathāgata Chan. It is like a poor man falsely claiming to be a king and bringing execution upon himself. Should one not fear it? Should one not fear it?
Instruction to Xiao Xuanpu, Minister of Rites (from the sixth day of the tenth month in the winter of the guihai year of the Tianqi era, his brush here fell still)

In entering the Way one must first awaken clearly to the mind-substance of this person, which is from the beginning luminous and vast, embracing all without exclusion, filled and pure, in which saint and ordinary are not established and which is not confined or obstructed by body, mind or world. This is the path above, the mind-seal of the coming from the West — this and nothing more. Once one can awaken thoroughly to this mind, then in daily life, responding to conditions, all states are like images in a mirror: nothing sticks when they come, no trace remains when they go. In this way whatever one does flows out from the true mind and the real, and each act is a true and deathless undertaking — one that not only vies in brightness with the sun and moon. Compared with the petty contrivances of deluded people's deluded thoughts and schemes, how can it be mentioned in the same breath? This radiance is complete in everyone, from the first without lack. But because the view of self is firm, whatever one does one takes as one's own merit and holds one's own view to be certainly right; right and wrong interlace, and in the end there is no settled conclusion. The reason for this is that without a mind vast and greatly impartial, one wishes to establish an undertaking that will not decay for a thousand autumns — that is hard indeed.

Our mind-substance is from the beginning perfect and luminous; that we cannot now awaken suddenly nor enjoy it before us is because through measureless kalpas greed, anger, delusion and craving and all kinds of affliction have obstructed and covered our own minds. Hence the work of gradual cultivation cannot be dispensed with. Weishan said: If a student can in a single thought suddenly awaken to his own mind, he has only to take what he has awakened and purify the outflowing consciousness of present karma; this is called cultivation, and there is no other cultivation apart from this. If a student of the Way seeks only sudden awakening as the end and supposes there is no work to do, then his habits lie deep and secretly break out when he meets conditions, and in time he flows into the realm of māra. Yet the work of gradual cultivation is also without stages: in daily life, at the place where a thought has not yet stirred, plant your feet firmly and turn the gaze inward; at the place where a thought arises, pursue and examine that thought — from where does it arise? Pursue it to the place where the thought arises and find that it was from the first unborn; then all deluded thoughts and feelings melt like ice on the spot. What is to be avoided is lacking the power of bravery, so that one cannot grip the throat and, unaware, lets it continue, and so flows on and never returns.
Instruction to Zhou Ziyin (the following is appended from Haiyin's drafts)

Today in the mountain dwelling the assembly begins its retreat, and Haiyin takes the seat to expound the Lotus Sūtra. At that moment your handwritten letter arrived, along with fine fruit. This is enough to divine that you too are a man of the Dharma assembly, one who has already attained the fruit of the Way. This is no earthenware divination. What your former letter said, and my daily practice, are exactly in accord; you may also gradually enter the gate of non-duality. But in your daily life, every matter and every thought is a mind of arising and ceasing; how can you take quiescent extinction as joy? If you seek a measure of benefit in the mind-ground, you must all the more, when your reading and writing are done, at every place where you meet conditions, be firmly grounded on the spot and suddenly turn the gaze inward, contemplating where these various doings and this mind of arising and ceasing arise from, and where they now cease. Contemplating deeply thus for a long time, you will gradually enter into subtlety and closeness. Further, wherever the habits secretly flow and afflictions arise without cause, look steadily and firmly at it: see what it finally is and where it arises and ceases. Pursue it to the place where its traces are swept away and extinguished — like dropping a flake of snow into a cauldron of boiling water. In daily life thus, not a thought may be let go. The moment the least thought of laziness, sloth or indolence arises, the mind that seeks ease and comfort and enjoyment — that is precisely the root of the illness breaking out. Then at once raise your eyebrows and glare; do not let it bind you. The moment you see the binding, never let yourself fall over with it and roll about with it in the dust. Most strictly avoid this. For the most part, one invocation of a bodhisattva or one invocation of a Buddha, clung to with desperate urgency, is what you press against it with. When various evil habits arise, then with all your strength raise up this huatou and swing it at the sky: no matter whether it be māra or Buddha, affliction or habit, good or evil deliberation, all the dust of feeling is cut off at once, like slicing through tangled silk. Doing the work thus, it does not hinder your reading or your writing. As for reading, see where the book you read is lodged; as for writing, see from where that writing flows. Nor does it hinder receiving guests and entertaining visitors, drinking tea and eating rice, or relieving oneself. In every place there is no need of the slightest crack or gap. Settle your mind thus. Then compare it with what Yongjia said: Just when the mind is applied, precisely no mind is applied; no mind precisely applies, constantly applying yet precisely nothing. Is this the same or not the same? I do not know whether you can believe the old man Haiyin and not be deceived. Try it and see for yourself. If you find the faith not mistaken, then you will know how very laughable Yan Hui's three months of fasting the mind was. As for the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, read it until familiar and take it as your daily lesson morning and evening, and when we meet in the spring we shall decide it together. My ordinary letters to you inevitably carry a little emotion and consciousness; I am ashamed that I have not brought you to thorough penetration. It is not that I am not thorough; I fear that your faith is not thorough. Now I see your faith gradually increasing and drawing daily nearer purity. If at this moment I do not cut out this bare heart and give it to you, when will you be thorough? If you dawdle and are not thorough, then Haiyin will go on being thorough by himself. What do you say? What do you say? The human world is pitiable; this Way is pitiable; but the mind I hope for in you is more pitiable still.

Your letter asking for instruction is most sincere and earnest. But you have not yet got the two words empty and illusory exactly right, and hence there is obstruction in regard to mind and objects, which is why the work is hard to do. Now I shall speak it out plainly for you, and then it will be clear and you will have no further doubt. What is called empty is not the emptiness of utter nothingness; it is like the vulgar saying, as if there were no one beside him — could it be that there really is no one beside him? It is only that, raised high in his eyes, there is no such person. What is called illusory is not the illusory of weird transformations; it means existing yet not real. It is like a conjuror at a fair pulling many figures out of a tube: the tube contains nothing at all, yet suddenly there they are; though they exist, they are not real. Since they are not real, they are fundamentally not there; because they are fundamentally not there, it is said to be empty. Hence it is said: It is like a conjured man — it is not that there is no conjured man, but the conjured man is not a real man. Since the man is not real, is he not empty? The Buddha's word empty was spoken to break the world's clinging to things as truly existing; it does not mean utter nothingness and annihilation. Truly fearing that people of the world would sink into annihilation, he spoke further the word illusory to dispel their view of annihilation. Thus all dharmas of body and mind are empty because illusory, and because empty they are said to be like illusions. Observing these two words as depending on each other, one at once sees their wonder. What is called empty is contemplating emptiness by way of illusory existence, and is named true emptiness; what is called existence is the illusory existence of what is fundamentally not there, and is named wondrous existence. Because of true emptiness the mind is not annihilated; because of wondrous existence objects are unborn. Since objects are unborn, what can the mind grasp? Since the mind is not annihilated, how can deluded thoughts remain? If deluded thoughts do not remain, with what mind will one grasp objects? Objects are themselves illusory; with what objects will they pull the mind? Thus the mind does not grasp objects, yet the mind is not annihilated; objects do not pull the mind, yet objects are just as they are. When mind and objects are thus, wherein is one not joyful? This is what is meant by: The mind is fundamentally unborn and exists because of objects; if the objects before it were absent, the mind too would be absent. One need only see through their illusory unreality and call it as if absent; then the numinous mind shines alone and the deluded mind suddenly rests, and that is called also absent. What is absent is the deluded mind — how could the true mind be utterly absent? What is the deluded mind? It is the one that clings to objects without dissolving. What is the true mind? It is the one that does not grasp the marks of body, mind or objects, that clearly and constantly knows, numinous and silently illumining. Applying the mind thus, what obstruction is there? Hence it is said: When the mind grasps the mind itself, the non-illusory becomes illusory dharmas; when there is no grasping, there is nothing that is not illusory; since even the non-illusory does not arise, how can illusory dharmas stand? It is precisely as said: Objects and conditions have no beauty or ugliness; beauty and ugliness arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcibly name them, how can love and hate arise? Thus, if feeling does not adhere to things, how can things obstruct a person? Since things cannot obstruct a person, how can a person obstruct things? The reason people of the world have no freedom is only that they do not understand that mind and objects are unborn and unreal, like illusions. If one understands that a single thought is unborn and like an illusion, then all suffering and joy, care and trouble, gain and loss, love and hate, grasping and rejecting, melt and dissolve like ice on the spot. Hence it is said: Knowing the illusory, one at once departs, without using expedients; departing from the illusory, one is at once awake, and there are no stages. This is what is meant by reaching the Buddha's house in a single thought — no empty saying. You have only to observe that wherever deluded thoughts arise and cease, wherever states arise and cease, they are nothing but illusory and unreal; then the mind will naturally not run after objects, and objects will naturally not pull the mind. Coming and going, responding to conditions, one thought is empty and bright, numinous and shining alone, illumining the body and mind before one as illusory and conjured, like the moon in water, like an image in a mirror, like a cloud in the sky, like the shimmering of heat waves. Holding it thus with the vajra eye, move it no more. Let whatever states come — touched, they dissolve; let whatever deluded mind come — glanced at, it perishes. Applying the mind thus, what delusion is there that could trouble you? What deluded state could assail your mind? These words are Haiyin's utmost, laying himself bare wholly for you and overturning everything to the bottom. Do not doubt further. Above all, do not think ahead and reckon behind; all such deliberation is evil perception and evil habit, and all of it is a cause that obstructs the Way. If you follow this old man's words, you are this moment a man of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Writing freely as the brush comes, I have not noticed how clumsily I have babbled; such a grandmotherly heart, leaking and dripping thus. Take care.

It is several months since we parted, all in a blur; the flowing light is swift and the sun and moon cheat one. Whenever I hear that you are twice as diligent as usual, joy pours into and irrigates my mind-field. At first I intended that after your honored father had gone, you would surely come into the mountains for a meeting, so that we might seal and verify your past work and decide it together. This hope was so real that it took shape in a dream — laughable, that a man of the Way should fall into such sentiment and views. Your letter says: By sitting I seek stillness; by stillness I seek the mind. This is the initial gate of entering the Way and is most apt. But within sitting you have not yet understood the crucial point; hence you grow weary from sitting long. Because you have not penetrated the wonder of the mind-substance, after being still for long you wish for some news; and you are also doubtful and adrift, as if with nowhere to return. It is truly because the mind that seeks has not obtained the secret key, and so the very thought of seeking feels instead like toil. Thus you seek the mind with the mind — exactly like a thirsty deer chasing the heat shimmer. The transmission says: Knowing where to rest, one then attains stability. Because your mind does not yet know where to rest, you do not attain stability. You ask for a list of methods for governing the mind, such as the four noes and the three reflections, to lead this mind in and hold this mind steady. This is where your refined and bitter earnestness lies, and it is what I greatly hope for in you. Now that you are willing to pledge yourself in your own heart, how could I instead be secretive and stingy? My only fear is that you, having begun in our Buddhadharma without having heard much, may in the midst of its names and phrases mostly turn them into the stale habits of your former seeing and hearing, so that the medicine of ambrosia cannot take effect near at hand in restoring your countenance. The methods by which the buddhas and patriarchs of old taught people, though their roads are many, do not go beyond the three studies of precepts, concentration and wisdom — what is called: from precepts arises concentration, from concentration arises wisdom. As for the detail of their items, among the sutras none surpasses the Śūraṅgama; as for the patriarchs' words, none surpass the single book of Yongjia's Collection. Read it until familiar and savor it. As for the key to entering concentration and applying the mind in it, as it says: Just when the mind is applied, precisely no mind is applied; no mind precisely applies, constantly applying yet precisely nothing. And again: After conditions are forgotten, still and silent; the nature of numinous knowing, clear and distinct; in the darkness of dull blankness, brightly shining; according with fundamental true emptiness, perfectly certain. This is the divine talisman for applying the mind. As for the four noes and the three reflections, these are precisely the precepts; all is contained therein. In truth the items of the work of cultivating the mind do not go beyond the three gates of calming, contemplation and even holding. In that Collection, śamatha is calming; vipaśyanā is contemplation; and yuganaddha is the twin operation of calming and contemplation and the even holding of concentration and wisdom. Let this serve for now to answer your request. The passages circled in red in the Collection — give them your attention for news of the matter. If there is anything you do not understand, do not hesitate to send questions again and again. As for the shortcut method of calming and contemplation, allow me to write another page later, to make up for today's deficit.

This matter of causal conditions — the transformation of what is most difficult into what is most easy — comes about because through measureless kalpas, life after life, we have flowed along in mixed defilement, and our habit of it is deep and thick. Even when a single thought of faith arises today and we begin to cut it off before evening falls, if we would stem the long current of endless kalpas, the task is truly far from easy. Even this single thought of turning the head back is exceedingly hard to bring forth. It is the wondrous sprout of good roots accumulated over kalpas; meeting its season, it first pushes out its shoot — yet its flowering and fruiting depend entirely on constant tending and protection. Otherwise it withers in an instant. Meeting circumstances and conditions, handling affairs with the Dharma, in time it becomes thoroughly familiar; add to that the work of calm and insight, and you may gradually arrive at liberation. Yet we are liberated from the very beginning. So the reason affliction is not liberated is no fault of the Dharma: it is that the mind binds and clings to itself, and so is not liberated. This is because our worldly feelings have long been thick and our habitual defilement thoroughly familiar; what is familiar is hard to forget, and so it flares up at the slightest touch. Hence the saying: I have never seen one who loves virtue as he loves beauty. If you exchange the one for the other, then what was unfamiliar becomes familiar of itself, and what was familiar becomes unfamiliar. Unfamiliar, it thins; thinning, it recedes; receding, it grows faint; faint, it is forgotten; forgotten, there is no leisure left to seek release — and of itself it no longer binds. In time the mind settles into peace, and the thousand forms and myriad shapes before you are seen as flowers in the sky and the moon in water, as heat-haze and frozen river. There was never anything to bind or cling to — so what release is there to seek? You say Sengzhao’s words on the immutability of things have served you well. Were you not a vessel of great capacity, you could not enter that old master’s gate. Yet the single line, “The sun and moon shine across the sky,” remains unclear to you. If this is unclear, then you do not understand Sengzhao; and if you do not understand him, then his words have not truly served you. This line the old man doubted for several years, until at last, within his own mind, he came to see it for himself, alone and clear. From that time on, wherever I have met conditions and found strength, it has mostly been through this old master’s words. That you believe at once upon going out the door is truly no small connection. The old man does not hesitate to speak it out plainly for you — only I fear that one day you will curse the old monk. Just take this line and lay it across your mind. In every movement, every action and undertaking; in every place of sound and form, wealth and profit; in every condition of adversity and favor; in every stirring of joy, anger, sorrow, and delight; in every choosing and rejecting, loving and hating — wherever there is any flowing, moving state, seal it at once with this seal. Apply the one seal and it is settled. Watch how it is that there is nowhere immutable; how it is that there is a place of constant stillness; how it is that there is a place that does not flow; how it is that there is a place that does not move; how it is that there is a place that does not reach around. Look and look in this way, and suddenly, with a crash, you will see through this line. Then you will know that the old man has not deceived you, and only then will you believe that the original truth does not deceive itself.
Instructions to Huang Weiheng

Though you say you aspire to the Way, the eye within you has not yet become clear. You constantly take worldly Dharma and Buddha-Dharma, the Chan school and the teaching school, and inevitably speak of them as two separate halves. If here you speak of them as two halves, then all your hating and loving, adversity and favor, choosing and rejecting, liking and disliking, success and failure, movement and stillness — fittingly, every one of them will be split into two halves as well. Haiyin has told you again and again: the buddhas and patriarchs from the first have no substantial Dharma to give to people; they only point out and expose, for each person, the matter that is originally present in his own portion. The Zongjing says: take the one mind as the source, and illumine the ten thousand dharmas as a mirror. It is precisely because we cannot know the one mind that the Buddha spoke teachings to point it out; and because we cannot see our own mind that the patriarchs borrowed Chan to show it. Both were acts of last resort. Now you say that studying the teachings leaves you mentally weary, while following Chan is like riding a favorable wind. This is only the depth of your prajñā-habit from many lives. Yet in this whole matter, from Haiyin’s side, both are empty deceptions: there is simply no talk of difficult and easy. If you do not penetrate your own mind, then Chan becomes deviant understanding and deviant defilement, and both fall into the pit of consciousness and feeling; while the teachings become deluded knowing and deluded seeing, and all come down to a handle for words and talk. Neither is the ultimate true ground. You do not realize that the teachings are the Buddha’s eye and Chan is the Buddha’s mind; the two are not two different things — how could there be this and that? When Haiyin teaches people to read the teachings and investigate Chan, it is never with views of that kind. To form such an interpretation today is not only to betray Haiyin, but to betray your own inherent spirit as well. I recall an ancient asking: the ancients ate when hungry and slept when tired, and that was the Way; people today eat when hungry and sleep when tired — why is that not the Way? The answer: the ancients, eating, simply ate; sleeping, simply slept — and so it was the Way. People today, eating, do not eat; sleeping, do not sleep; they think wildly and reckon at random — and so they turn their backs on the Way. From this we see that in your daily life you need only raise your eyebrows, give a shout — let gods be startled and ghosts afraid, let the heavenly māras’ courage shatter and the shades of the dead dissolve — one shout and they are driven back, leaving you on your original ground, silent and still, not a thread hanging, stark and bare, utterly naked. Take this one style of household. When you want to read, then read; when you do not, set it aside — do not allow a single word to hang there. When you want to write, then write; when you do not, set it aside — do not allow wild thinking and reckoning. Even in drinking tea and eating rice, simply drink tea and eat rice. When you want to sleep, then sleep; when you must relieve yourself, then relieve yourself. Meeting it, it is finished — and afterwards you must not allow a single thought of recollection, like a wandering ghost. Clean and pure, spotless and white — and yet you must not sit down inside that cleanness and purity either. Thus, single-bladed, you go straight in, one thought pressing forward: then in reading you meet the ancients face to face, and in writing you simply spit it out in one breath from your own breast, with no before and no after. The time of storing is the time of pouring forth; the time of pouring forth is the time of storing. In this way you are not turned about by movement and stillness, by light and dark, nor shifted by any of the myriad tricks. This is what is called a towering great man, a fellow beyond measure. Do you believe this? If you truly believe it, then hike up your robes and enter here. Take care, take care.
Instructions to Layman Ma

One who studies the Way must, first, be urgent in the matter of birth and death. Second, he must know that the body is the root of suffering and that the mind is the root of deluded thought and karmic creation. Third, he must truly and genuinely see through it: the fame, rank, wealth, and honor of the world, its sounds and forms, goods and profits, are all vain blossoms, unreal. Fourth, he must fear that in this life he may create evil karma and hereafter fall into hell, undergo every kind of suffering, with no one to rescue or protect him. Fifth, he must know that the root of life now present is no more than the space of a single breath: if this breath is cut off, then to seek again today’s business of investigating Chan, studying the Way, and making merit will be forever impossible — how much less the enjoyment of wealth and honor? When one who studies the Way has these five minds, and hour after hour, moment after moment, stores and piles them in his breast, then all the vain and flowery states before him grow naturally cold and faint, and the ground of his mind becomes naturally pure. What he has learned in the past, his views and knowledge, his learning, his clever talk and tricks — he sets it all down. He brings forth the bodhi-mind, forever cuts off wine and meat, coveting nothing and loving nothing, keeps the precepts and cultivates merit, performs every kind of good work, and takes these as the foundation that carries the Way. He further reads the Mahāyāna scriptures to help bring forth his own mind and open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; only then may he undertake contemplation. He contemplates only this mind: vast, perfect, and bright, pure, empty, and still, not a single dharma to be obtained. Deluded thoughts were never there, and neither is there birth or death. As for this body of faculties, all its movements are like those of a phantom man who never had a mind or consciousness; all the states before him are like flowers in the sky, suddenly arising and suddenly ceasing, originally not existing. There is only the one bright thought, perfectly clear, never obscured — and even this thought is not there. This is called right mindfulness. With the mind used in this way, throughout the six periods of the day, in movement and stillness, at leisure and in business, he is thus, unmoved. In adversity and favor, in like and dislike, foe and kin are equal. Following worldly conditions, whatever merit he performs, each act and each dharma becomes perfect and wondrous pure practice. One who practices thus is named a bodhisattva in action. If a man of the Way can truly use his mind in this way, he may be said to engage in the Buddha’s work without leaving the dust of affliction, to manifest the body of a magistrate and yet speak the Dharma; and this is what is meant by repaying the Buddha’s grace and repaying the grace of the state. Your nature is spiritually clear, and you have resolved your mind toward the Way; therefore I have specially given you these instructions, and I bestow on you the name Pure and Wondrous Layman. Do not be false to your own inherent spirit; do not forget these words. Take care.
Instructions to Wang Sheng on Seeking the Precepts and a New Style-Name

The young man Wang is named Tingzuo, styled Zizhan. He feels his given name is commonplace and his style-name trespasses upon the ancients, and asks the Phantom Man to renew them. The Phantom Man, delighted, told him: How extraordinary, your substance! The tradition has it: if you can renew yourself daily, renew day by day, and renew again each day. Now your vow is to expel the old self and make it wholly new. Not only would you renew your name; you would renew your mind. The name is the guest of reality; the mind is the reality of virtue. If you do not devote yourself to the real but prize an empty name, that is not virtue. From this we see that you are not only commonplace in name but commonplace in mind. What is meant by commonplace is not a matter of clothing, cap, speech, or appearance; it means what has been tainted and stained by long familiarity in one’s inherent virtue. Our inherent virtue is originally bright, but as day by day we steep ourselves in cravings, the eye is obscured by deviant forms, the ear by licentious sounds, the nose by foul and fragrant scents, the tongue by rich flavors, the body by false contacts, the mind by deviant thoughts. These six obscure one another and churn and darken what is within; smoked and steeped, dyed and habituated, habit becomes nature, and we call it what we originally have, call it what is naturally so. Thus we gallop far into the realm of confusion, and the virtue of original brightness is turned around and seen as something alien — how should we know there is an old self, an old self? This is what the sages grieved over; their grief lay precisely here. Therefore they cast one into the water of the precepts to wash it away. And the precepts are nothing else: they are the light of wisdom inherent in one’s own mind, which the Confucians call the bright virtue. Now, a person’s wisdom-light is not bright, and so the bright virtue darkens day by day. To restore the bright virtue and return to innate truth, one must brighten the wisdom-light and shatter the darkness and obscuration. When darkness and obscuration are broken, the original substance appears; when the wisdom-light is bright, all hindrances dissolve. This is why our Buddha established the precept against killing to perfect humaneness; the precept against stealing to fulfill righteousness; the precept against sexual misconduct to establish propriety; the precept against false speech to deepen trustworthiness; and the precept against drinking wine to brighten wisdom. When the five precepts are complete, the five constants are fulfilled; when the six senses are restrained, the three karmas are purified. This is what is called washing away old defilement, advancing in daily renewal, forsaking the old self, and creating a new transformation. Therefore the Phantom Man also changes your given name to Yan, and your style-name to Zilun, so that you may receive the Buddha’s precepts as you would a ruler’s command. Strive at it.
Instructions to Zhou Ziqian

The five colors make the eyes blind; the five notes make the ears deaf; the five flavors spoil the taste; galloping and hunting make the mind run wild. These are Laozi’s warnings. Look not at what is contrary to propriety; listen not to what is contrary to propriety; speak not what is contrary to propriety; move not in any way contrary to propriety. And again: in youth, when the blood and vital breath are not yet settled, the warning lies in matters of desire; when grown, when the blood and breath are at their fullest, the warning lies in strife; when old, when the blood and breath have declined, the warning lies in acquisitiveness. These are Confucius’s warnings. Not to kill, not to steal, not to commit sexual misconduct, not to speak falsely or with ornate words, not to speak with a double tongue or harshly, not to be greedy, hateful, or deluded. These are the Buddha’s warnings. Ah — our own nature is originally spiritually clear and pure, but because of the stains of habitual defilement it grows daily more turbid and darkened, and we sink into confusion without waking. This happens only in the space between ear, eye, mouth, nose, body, and mind as they face sounds, forms, scents, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas: stuck fast and entangled, contriving and struggling in the mind, long deluded and never turning back. Therefore the sages, in pity, earnestly made these warnings for us; and further, they wished to expel old defilement, cut off the habits of the dust, and restore our originally pure true mind. From this we see that the precepts are in me and are complete in the mind; cultivate them with the body — this is what is meant by the Way not being far from man. Hence it is said: Is the sage far off? Embody him and he is spirit. If we would reach the source of the great Way, it lies only in reverently upholding this. Master Zhou is young and has set his will earnestly on the highest; he has turned his mind to this, and so I have written these words to show him.
Instructions to the Novice Zuding
