But when I read the words in your note and learned that the Grand Censor’s last stretch of radiance shone wholly from the tip of your staff, sending forth the great matter of a hundred thousand million kalpas, how fortunate that in the body of an official one should see it once more; I could not but turn grief to joy. Yet though this matter rests on a lifetime’s strength in the Way, it leans heavily on the hand of a good friend. Your heart is true toward the Way, and now you have this example before you; it is proof enough that the Buddha-Dharma works. Formerly Lord Ouyang Wenzhong asked a monk: the ancients, at the brink of death, would sometimes depart laughing and talking; why is it so silent and empty today? The monk said: the ancients kept thought after thought in concentration and wisdom, so how could they be confused at the end? Men today keep thought after thought in distraction, so how could they be settled at the end? Wenzhong was greatly startled. This saying is exactly the mark for us who study the Way. You tell me that ordinarily you examine yourself well enough, but when the situation arrives the habitual thought rises again. This is precisely where your power of thought is true and earnest, that you can see the truth thus. The Master also said: by nature men are close together; by habit they draw far apart. And again: to learn and constantly practice it. This word practice is not merely the study of letters; it means practicing the nature. The nature is originally without things, pure, empty and bright; it is because things and desires stain and habituate it that it grows turbid, dark and unclear. Think: from the time we gained awareness until today, we have practiced worldly ways and been stained by things and desires, rushing like fire day and night without a moment’s rest. Compare the time and nearness of that habit with the work of keeping the Way in mind since you repented and knew your fault, and how do the rawness and ripeness, the slackness and tightness, compare? The Master, discussing his disciples, said that only Yan Hui could go three months without departing from it; the rest reached it for a day or a month at most. Seen thus, to pit a day’s or a month’s work against the desires and habits of many lives and hope to overcome them is like using a drop of water to save a fire of piled brushwood; by its nature it cannot. The ancients said plainly: in studying the Way there is no other trick; you must make the raw places ripe and the ripe places raw. When after long familiarity they are pure and beaten into one piece, then of themselves thought after thought is Amitābha and head after head is the Land of Bliss. You ask me for a piece of writing on the paper you sent; I respectfully record two Pure Land poems. I pray you set your heart on the one gate of the Pure Land. If you are willing to gain power in the public case of Buddha-recitation, in time you will have your own ground of benefit. Formerly, whenever I sat in the Grand Censor’s company, I saw that even while lifting his cup he never let the Buddha’s name leave his lips; even in spitting, sighing and laughing he did not notice that the Buddha appeared on his tongue. This shows that this old man made it his secret practice in life. Right in the midst of the blazing flames of the five desires he cast in this one thought, and at once his five viscera were cool, as though sweet dew had sprinkled his heart. I observe privately that men who study the Way in these days only know to crave the mysterious and wondrous, and do not know how to lay a dead hand to work at the root. In ordinary times, when nothing happens, they talk pleasantly enough; is that not delightful? But when honor and disgrace, calamity and the brink of death arrive, then they are all flurry and confusion. This is not another man deceiving them; they deceive themselves. In this matter not the least pretense is possible, just as brass and true gold show themselves in the fire. Your spiritual root was planted in former lives and now has blossomed; I pray you water it constantly with the water of the Buddha-recitation samadhi. When after long familiarity it is ripe, it will flower and bear fruit in its own season. I am moved that you believe this poor monk truly and deeply, and I regret how hard a good meeting is; I have not noticed how much I have spilled out. This poor monk is nearing sixty; a body with outflows is hard to bear, and after ten years buried in the miasmic smoke my beard and hair are now white and I am no longer my former self. The thought of rest never leaves a single thought, but the rope of karma is not yet untied, and I dare not lie down at ease in the mountains and forests. I have a mind to pass my old age at Caoxi, to borrow a handful of earth to cover these dry bones and so finish this life; I do not know how the conditions will be. Thus a meeting with you is the harder. But whenever there is a wind to carry it, we may as well send word to each other often.

Formerly, through a bond at the sea, I was fortunate enough to meet your countenance once; seeing your features pure and your bone firm, I knew in my heart that you were of the highest capacity. But the time and conditions were not ripe, and I had only a loyal heart, not daring to speak out rashly. It is like a seed long planted; its season has simply not come, and it must wait for the timely rain to water it before it sprouts. This is a matter of course. After that this humble one, driven by the power of karma and without freedom, fell into the sea of miasma, and in a flash eight years have passed. From time to time I think privately that in this life I may never again form a bond beyond the world with you. Yet this humble one’s habitual tendency of compassionate vows seems deep: whenever I meet one who has the seed of prajna, at a single sight I am like a magnet drawing iron, and if I would free my own mind of it, I certainly cannot; how then could I forget you? After the full moon of the seventh month in the xin-chou year, the two students Feng and Wang returned from the capital gate bringing your letter. I could not but be overturned with joy, sobbing and wetting my collar. For in human life a friend who knows one is hard to meet, and in the conditions of the Way a teacher is even harder to meet, while the root of faith is hard to arouse, and harder still than meeting a teacher. For teachers do exist, but to seek one who greatly arouses a true root of faith, who takes the matter of birth and death as urgent, and who is as bitter, earnest, fierce and keen as you, is one in ten thousand times ten thousand that is hard to find. Yet this seed of prajna is the very mind-light we already possess; once deluded, it becomes the karma-consciousness, entangled in this shell of a body. From the first we know only that there is this body of blood and flesh, and it is buried under all manner of sounds, forms, scents, flavors and dust-realms, like a vast racing sea without a far shore, ever wider and deeper and ever more savory; who would be willing, in the swift current, to rouse himself sharply and turn his head to look at the other shore? From ancient times those who are doubly deluded among the deluded have never been otherwise. Since you already know the ten-thousand-age numinous bright nature beneath your own person, this nature is in you already and is not to be sought outside; why then fear you cannot attain it? The only fear is that your faith is not firm, your seeing not true, your seeking heart not keen. Rank and wealth are sought from others; this matter is sought within oneself. Confucius spoke of one who has not thought about it; how could it then be far? Yet though it is sought in oneself, the first thing is to know it truly, speak it through and see through it, and only then will your effort not be misdirected. If by any chance your knowledge and views are not right and your grasp of principle not true, and you have no teacher or friend to explain point by point the matters that puzzle you; or if the mind that reckons self and other, right and wrong, praise and blame, gain and loss before you is not forgotten; or if the old habitual stains are thick and cannot be cleansed at once, and meeting conditions you are stirred and mistake it all for sound principle: this is the hour when you fall into the net of doubt and breed discouragement. Our own nature is originally pure; it is only that from measureless ages, life after life, evil habits have stained us down to today, and familiarity does not obey the man. And as for the time one has set one’s heart on this matter, how can it compare with the familiarity of reading, working, and the daily use of food, drink, man and woman, sound and form, goods and profit, from childhood to this day? Therefore one who studies the Way must make the raw places ripe and the ripe places raw; this is the first step of entering the gate and setting to work. Next, to wear away habitual tendencies, one must surely make the power of thought the master, whether it be an ancient’s phrase or the single holding up of one mantra: engrave it on the mind, keep it in thought at all times, and when after long practice this thought is pure and there is a master within, then in meeting conditions and encountering circumstances nothing comes out and nothing enters, and the single thought in between shines alone, bright and clear. In all dealings with affairs and people it is like a mirror showing images: neither welcoming nor sending off, coming it does not stick, going it leaves no trace. This is the first place of gaining power. If subtle feelings and imaginings secretly grow and lengthen while you do not notice; or if, knowing your own views, you begrudge the pain and protect it and will not cut clean in one stroke: this is dawdling, soft warmth, self-forgiveness and self-deception. Here of all places you must keep a tight eye and never let it pass, nor let it deceive you. To let it go lightly and forgive it is self-deception; hence Confucius said: do not deceive yourself. This is teaching us to walk with a hand pulling each step. Because our feelings are muddled and our wisdom dark, we have always played the clever man at the threshold of light and shadow, in the shadow of the consciousness-spirit, wholly unconcerned with the true ground of this place. If you recognize it here, it is washing sand to pick out gold: when the sand is gone the gold is pure of itself, and you need not fear failing to reach the season of refined radiance. You set your heart on this matter, and it is easier for you than for others, because your faculties are sharp and your hardships already many; all worldly thoughts have been worn down by your many disappointments, and you have gained no small advantage. What the world counts as loss you must count as gain, as Laozi says of rejecting that and taking this; this too is what Heaven has made. And take this humble one, who has dwelt in the land of miasma these eight years: in truth I have penetrated a great deal of the Dharma-gate I had not certified before, and this is hard to speak of to worldly men. As for the method of practice, all the sutras contain it; only do not turn it into a mysterious phrase. To turn it into a phrase adds one more layer of obstruction. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch is the best guide to the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground, but men of middle and lesser faculties cannot reach it, because they have no practice. The Yongjia Collection is in truth a footnote to the Platform Sutra. If your understanding follows the Sixth Patriarch and your practice follows Yongjia, what fear of not leaping in at one bound? Only beware of turning it into a phrase. The Lankavatara is the most direct of all, only it is hard to read. These two books alone can serve as wings. I pray you set your heart on them and keep them in mind.
To Chen Jiannan, Second Master

You tell me that in these days you have been investigating the Lankavatara and the Platform Sutra, and that your practice has advanced considerably. This is a great cause for congratulation. The ancients said: the countless heart-breaking things of a lifetime, where but in the gate of emptiness can they dissolve? Since all suffering is born of existence, the Buddha spoke of the suffering realms of the three worlds as the three existences. What is called the gate of emptiness is not the emptiness of nothingness but the emptiness of hollowing out. Layman Pang said: only wish to empty what there is, meaning to empty all thoughts within and all conditions without; when inner and outer are both empty and mind and conditions both vanish, then all suffering ceases of itself. This is the shortcut of the Chan gate out of birth and death. What you call the Pure Land writings are likewise a key crossing out of the sea of suffering; how can you look on them as shallow and near? Let me speak to you briefly. Buddha means awakened, that is, the numinous bright nature we already possess; our mind is originally Buddha, as the Sixth Patriarch said: originally not one thing. If you understand this original nothing, you at once see the Buddha-nature that is originally your own mind; this is called the sudden teaching of attaining buddhahood, beyond which there is no other Buddha to attain. As for the Pure Land, there are two kinds: the land of phenomena and the land of principle. In phenomena it involves cultivation with marks and all manner of practice-gates, as set out in Longshu’s Pure Land writings, a secret method for drawing in men of middle and lesser faculties. The land of principle is the realm that the Buddhas and patriarchs enjoy for themselves; it is named the Land of Eternal Stillness and Light. Eternal means unchanging, still means unmoving, light means undimmed; it is the very substance of our own nature. Hence it is said: the Pure Land is mind only, Amitābha is self-nature. Again: when the mind is pure the Buddha-land is pure. Again: born, yet truly not born; gone, yet truly not gone. This is the realm certified by those of the highest faculties, and this is what the Platform Sutra means by the Pure Land. As for cultivating the Pure Land, it takes Buddha-recitation as the main thing, for it is the method of purifying one’s own mind. In our daily use ten thousand sufferings cross and tangle, defiling the original mind like muddy water, like a swift current and a fierce flame. Recite the Buddha’s name once, and the five viscera are cool and all suffering rests at once; this is the Buddha saving living beings from suffering. By reciting the Buddha the mind’s grime is at once removed, and with one pure thought every circumstance met is none other than the Land of Bliss; wind and moon, sound and color are none other than the true realm; whatever the eye lights on is the Pure Land, and every thought raised beholds Amitābha. Why wait for the three-inch breath to cease and to cross the distance of a hundred thousand million Buddha-lands? In this Dharma-gate the first requirement is a decided will; the second is to be able to put things down; the third is to be able to follow conditions, and following conditions is simply accepting one’s lot; the fourth is to know it truly, which is to be without doubt; the fifth is to loathe suffering keenly, for when the loathing of suffering is keen the thought of desire is removed of itself and one does not turn back. With these five keys, simply hold one thought as a great general surrounded in the midst of a heavy siege, resolved to break out, one man with a single blade against ten thousand. With such courage and decision, the bandit of birth and death and the demon-armies of suffering retreat without battle; this is what is called a true general. The sutras say: doing battle with the demon of affliction and the demon of death, one wins great merit, leaves the three realms and breaks the net of Mara; then the Tathagata greatly rejoices. This is what is meant by dissolving the hero’s spirit within the gate of emptiness. This poor monk left home young and set his heart on this matter. In my life I have met many fortresses of Mara and fought them all off; though I have not yet broken out of the siege, I may now call myself a great general of the Buddha-gate, no less than Li Guang on his flying horse. This matter is like drinking water: only the one who drinks knows cold and warm; how would I dare speak of it to worldly men? In this matter a minister cannot present it to his lord, a son cannot present it to his father; how then would I dare make it a matter for worldly friends? Now you have suddenly roused this faith; the seed must be there from former lives, waiting only for its season to sprout. That you have now seen this one book on the Pure Land is the spring rain: a fattening moisture wetting the sprout of a scorched banana. The mechanism of the maker of things is very subtle here; it is also the beginning of your good fortune. This poor monk has often said that in this world our daily use is no more than one full meal and one sound sleep; all else is superfluous. Now since you cannot even eat your fill or sleep soundly, and must strive to the death to please men’s eyes and ears and add to your own sea of suffering, can you be called a wise man? Since you do not gain the enjoyments of the world, and the joy of leaving the world you do not know at all, you are truly to be pitied. Worldly matters are sought from others; the matter of leaving the world is sought from oneself. To abandon what one can surely gain within oneself and not do it is the height of folly. What I have said is all the realm I have truly certified in this life since leaving home; it is hardly to be compared with the lips and tongue of the common run. Reckoning now from leaving home at nineteen to fifty-eight, for forty years it has all been this one thought; and that I now gain a cool place amid this great punishment, this blazing fire of great suffering, is by no other method. This matter I would not dare speak of unless you had this great bond; I fear you would cover your mouth and laugh. For instance, all the letters and words of past years have flowed out from within this, and though I know the wonder within it, I cannot speak it. The world regards them as letters, which is very shallow. Throughout the world those with the eye of Dharma are few. These years this poor monk has mixed with the world and blended his light; these four words I knew to be wondrous from childhood, and I have studied them hard all my life, but only in the last ten years have I taken them bitterly to hand, and only in these last three years have I gained some accord. Thus one sees how hard it is to move through the world, and how the highest man is not easily studied and not easily reached. This I speak to you alone. Compared with this matter, all lies in working it out amid adverse conditions; then the benefit is seen the more and the merit greater, a day for a kalpa. This requires a man of great strength to do it. Someone of old said: there are bones for a general or a minister, but no blessing for leaving home. These words are not shallow. Yet the hardship of leaving home is no small matter either. This poor monk’s lifelong suffering is no less than ten thousand times yours; but the will with which I bore it is as far from yours as sky from earth. Since leaving home, whenever I have addressed anyone, I have never used the words brother or brethren. Why? Because my will was to walk alone and step alone, not to be a companion of the world; this is the upward will that leaves the world. Only in these three years have I begun to associate and call men brother; this is precisely the first step of gaining power in mixing with the world and blending the light. Hence one knows that the mind of a bodhisattva answering the world is wondrous in having no fixed direction and no abiding, and that this is the highest vehicle. When the Sixth Patriarch heard only that one should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere, he awakened at once to the original and the wheel of suffering of kalpas of birth and death ceased at once. Was he a small man? This much I know for myself: formerly I dwelt in the withered, empty place of one-sided stillness, which is no different from the worldly man dwelling in a sea of affliction. You formerly dwelt in existence, which is no different from my dwelling in emptiness. Now you can turn over and trample it through at once, and so leap past thirty years of my practice in one bound; you may be called one who leaps in at a single step. This is not to cast aside the realm before you and seek a way out elsewhere; to abandon what is before one and seek liberation elsewhere is either folly or madness. Yongjia said: the illness of rejecting existence and clinging to emptiness is the same, like fleeing drowning and leaping into fire. This is exactly it. Because meeting you face to face is hard, my last letter was written beforehand; at the sealing I read your letter again and was moved beyond measure, so before the messenger I wrote hastily at my desk, and did not notice how much creeper I had trailed. It is only that one who has often been a companion pities the guest. You have brought forth this supreme mind; it is a bond for leaving the world. How could I answer it with the common and shallow? Therefore I have poured myself out thus. Take this letter and use it to pass the days; it may well prove a cooling powder.

Your letter that came before spoke of turning your heart to the Pure Land. Since you are so keen, I wrote hastily at my desk before the messenger until the page was full, not knowing what I said. In the main I spoke at length, urging you to settle down in the midst of what is not to your liking and seek a ground of peace there. Whatever difficult conditions you meet, right in the difficulty put down body and mind and let men call you ox or call you horse; for me there is nothing that cannot be. This is a benefit only Laozi could manage; even the Master had not gained this Dharma-gate, and so could not avoid finding the world difficult. But after he met Laozi and was jabbed by him at the sore point, straight through to the bottom, he gained measureless benefit at once. As for what he later said to his disciples, do not be willful, do not be absolute, do not be obstinate, do not be self-centered, and being wholly empty: all this is talk after awakening, by no means the talk of one still wearing the scholar’s cap. The impurity in our minds is only these matters of self and other, right and wrong; the clinging feeling cannot be put down. Willful, absolute, obstinate, self-centered, insisting that things must go my way before they are good. Yet if I insist on my way, will others not insist on theirs? All this belongs to the sea of suffering and the land of filth. Just put down this mind, and the mind is clean and spotless, happier than words can tell. Why would that not do? Broad and open, this very mind accords with the Buddha-mind. Recite the Buddha with this mind, and thought after thought is Amitābha and thought after thought is the Pure Land.

On the point of leaving the provincial capital, the various matters of my dream, as he related them, were clear before my eyes. Though I did not wholly believe them, beyond the words I had already grasped their subtle purport; this was a great delight. Since ancient times, men of disciplined conduct worry that their character is not yet settled; those who meet calamity fear their merit and fault are not clear. This poor monk has now gained both; how fortunate, how fortunate. Even if I die in a ditch, what regret is there? Therefore my resolve to pass my old age at Caoxi grows firmer. If by the spirit of the Sixth Patriarch I may borrow a handful of earth to cover these dry bones, what more could I wish for? In this undertaking of restoration the merit is great, and I do not reckon its quick completion by months and years; this mind of mine feels rather at ease. And Buddha-work in the Dharma-gate is like a cloud in the sky, without fixed marks at all; like praying for rain in a drought, when sincerity is complete nothing fails to answer. Heaven’s seasons and men’s affairs come to the same thing. Master Xiao’s nature is honest and steadfast, a loyal and true gentleman, hard to find even among the upholders of the moral order; it is a pity his temper is too hasty and his heart too kind, so that at a petty man’s words he is easily moved and cannot decide. This poor monk, touched by the meeting with one who knows me, and wishing to make merit for the place, set his body across a hundred bending blades and removed a great harm from the people; happily he barely escaped himself. Now my small strength is exhausted, yet the affair has no end; how can I use limited spirit to float on a boundless sea of poison? Would any wise man be content with that? Had I not been here last year, there would have been much to fear in this place. This autumn they were eager to invite me to go; that is why I declined with all my strength. This poor monk regards this body as bound up with the Dharma-gate, and would borrow the spirit of the Buddhas and patriarchs, trusting to it for merit through ten thousand ages; that is a far greater thing than this. How dare I not love myself? Now after many turns I have at last accomplished the plan of hiding my traces. Moreover, looking from now on, my former self is not far off; how could I bear to be stained with impurity and again defile the Pure Land? Birds do not weary of height, fish do not weary of depth; Caoxi shall be my corner of the hill. You who know me, what do you think? You tell me that in reciting the Buddha one should hold a rosary; this is the most intimate practice of keeping thought. Formerly I did not dare mention it, fearing you had a sense of shame about it. Now that you need it, I respectfully offer a string of galingal-wood beads that I have carried myself. Though I have held them long and their fragrance is gone, their spirit is full; I know that when you receive them you will at once enter the treasury of joy.
Reply to Yang Yuanru, Military Commander

The ancients said: in the field of heat and confusion it is hard to keep a cool eye. Since the three realms are without safety, like a burning house, all who come and go within it are scorched and boiled. If one would find a patch of cool ground amid the blazing flames, none but a cool-eyed man can find it. If one can make a single thought cool at once and suddenly see the whole earth as ice, then one no longer makes a home in body, mind and world. This is how the men of great strength from of old, playing in the field of birth and death, could turn the dust of toil into Buddha-work and affliction into bodhi: they relied only on one cool eye and one stretch of cool heart and entrails. What other spiritual powers and wondrous functions were there? These words are very easy to know and very hard to see. Take the case of the Buddhas and patriarchs: they took the single saying that all dharmas are like a dream as the essential road out of the world. Yet among the wise and foolish of the world, all alike can say that life is a dream. Their words are similar but their meaning is not; in truth they have never really, with one glance, seen through life as a dream. If one truly saw through it, then one would naturally walk away with swinging arms from every pass of honor and disgrace, profit and harm, gain and loss, right and wrong; who would then dare cross his edge? In truth there is nothing very mysterious in it, though as for the first step, there is after all a method. In dealing with the world, one should first take the things of the dream and set them before one’s eyes, observing them in fine detail, insisting on certainty, until one sees to the point of unknowingly breaking into a great laugh. Then one suddenly feels that the ordinary talk of things being like a dream is utterly different. Then, taking the same place, with one thought turn the realm before you and set it within the dream, observing it in fine detail, until in the heavy, sunken, upside-down state one suddenly wakes with a start. Then looking back over one’s whole life and all the various realms one has passed through, and seeking them truly, they are utterly ungraspable; and that place where they are utterly ungraspable is the first pass at which all Buddhas and patriarchs leave birth and death.
The Dream-Wandering Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Fascicles 16 to 20
The Dream-Wandering Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Fascicle Sixteen
To Zhou Haimen, Inspector

This ascetic has been favored with the sprinkling of your sweet dew, which cooled heart and bone and at once lifted a long illness. This bond is truly no shallow thing. My feelings since we parted are much like those of Empty-Born sitting at ease in his stone chamber, seeing the Dharma-body never leave eye and ear. I have often said that the matter within this must belong to a man within this. The Way of Dharma in Lingnan has long been buried, and happily the hand and eye of great compassion have raised it up, so that the icchantikas at once brought forth supreme roots of goodness. Though those who enter the chamber are few, those who know of it are many, and those who take refuge grow daily more numerous. Even at the Bodhi tree, and among the monks of Caoxi, the hardest of all to tame, those who have turned their hearts and believed of late are already two or three in ten. This whole stretch of true wind flows from the great treasury of light; it is proof enough that this official journey of the layman was the dragon-devas pushing you out, riding the wheel of great vows. The Gazetteer of Caoxi has now at last been printed; be so good as to let fall one word and place it at the head of the volume, to bring out the Sixth Patriarch’s radiance and open the eyes of gods and men, so as not to fail this excellent meeting.

I met the recommended scholar Ke in the provincial capital in the fifth month, like a man born again. His faculties are keen and sharp, and at the pass of sorrow and illness he could suddenly shatter the nest of birth and death; a true hero. I recall your words, layman, that everyone has the highest faculties, only there is no great forge and bellows. Had it not been for you, how could this man have opened up like this? And had he not the highest faculties, how could he have been so fierce and brave? Hereafter the life-line of the true Dharma in the lands beyond the sea will truly depend on this man. May the Buddha’s power bless him with health and strength of body, so that he need not fear falling short of the ancients. When this wild monk teaches the Dharma these years it is like speaking to wooden men. Among my disciples outside the world I have lately gained one or two who can bear a little hammering; among the worldly truth those who have faith for a time are many, but the one who truly walks and practices is Feng Changli of Shunde. This young man has deep spiritual roots; the whole countryside honors him at once, and old and young alike who come to his door treat him as their teacher. His sincerity moves others, and so his teaching wins such trust. Seeing this young man’s resolve, he will not retreat hereafter and can carry on the Jiangmen succession; this is the turning point of the Dharma’s opportunity in Lingnan. I hear lately that he has been associating with the Grand Scribe Tao Shikui. This gentleman has a heart of ice and snow and does not come from one lifetime of pure precepts; when he met this mountain monk, it was a pity the opportunity was not deep. If he could be brought along, it would be a still greater delight. Tu Changqing has lately shared the same aspiration as Deyuan, and should also be guided into this upward road. Censor Zheng Yunya is truly a man who lives for birth and death; lately in retirement I know him well and find him congenial, but when he met this mountain monk this one opening upward had not yet been revealed. If you, layman, could find a way to inquire after him and comfort him, your compassion would be no shallow thing. The Dharma-conditions here are gradually opening; as for the disciples ripe for transformation, I have already reported them in a former letter, and there are still two or three not yet ripe. If Heaven grants me three years, perhaps some may be brought to accomplishment, enough not to fail this journey. This is what the Buddhas protect, what the Tathagata sends, and what those who know me in the Dharma hope for.
Reply to Ren Yanghong, Inspector

This practice lies only in the swift current, in the spark of flint and flash of lightning, where the hand is quick and the eye is fast; that is great strength. You tell me that in this you have gained great coolness and peace; this is precisely the first meaning of certifying bodhi at once. I only fear that the power of illumination is not firm and that you are carried along without knowing it. If you know it, then the clouds scatter and the rain stops, the breeze is clear and the moon shines; the joy of it cannot be described.
To Zhu Xingcun, Inspector (courtesy name Yibin)

I have heard the Buddha say that all conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow. I remember how I once received your teaching and attended you; now it is all vague, like a dream. After we parted, Caoxi went as its fate decreed, and all things were like illusory matters; now I look on them as a bubble, and in the mind of idle thought they are but a shadow. Seen by great wisdom, is it other than this? As for the one bond of Caoxi’s revival, every hair of it came out of the samadhi of compassionate mind; even this wild monk’s measureless bitter toil was all upheld by compassionate vows. Though the work is not finished, its general plan may serve as the one-age undertaking of reviving the ancestral Way. For this wild monk it is not worth recording, but your honored compassion, that one stretch of the radiance of guarding the Dharma, can never be erased. Now my disciples have written out by hand the actual events of the past and arranged them in ten articles; I venture to beg your Dharma-giving in the form of an essay, to serve as an adamantine banner. It shall endure with the Sixth Patriarch’s Dharma-body without end; truly it is the one great matter of the revival a thousand years hence. I only pray you send forth your broad and long tongue to cover the great thousand worlds, so that all who see and hear may enter the great treasury of light.
To Ding Youwu, Grand Counselor (courtesy name Juefei)

The bond between you, sir, and this wild monk is in itself most strange, and those in the world who know of it all call it strange. It is because we both fell into the two kinds of knowledge and views, worldly and world-transcending, and into the great obstruction of self-conceit, whose habitual seeds covered over our original wisdom-light. Because you fell into it, your wings were clipped midway and you could not spread the wings that beat the wind; because this wild monk fell into it, the Dharma-banner broke in the middle and I could not raise the good name of the Buddhas and patriarchs. Leaning on the vast true compassion of all the Buddhas and their inconceivable spiritual power, we were struck and shattered together by the swift thunder of Dharma. Our human affairs differed, but the forge and bellows we met were the same; then the realms of suffering into which we were cast were the same; and at the last even our lives depended on each other, the same. Would we not wish to leave birth and death together and certify bodhi together? So we bound it all in one strip of bamboo and cast it together into the Eastern Ocean, wishing only that we might at once wash away to the last drop the coarse and floating habits of kalpas, the self and other, right and wrong, grudge and kindness, gain and loss, every kind of filth. Otherwise, how could our dying together and living together have come to this? I have often said that for this public case, the ancients used this same one turning for those hard to tame; men like Changli and Dongpo, and Juefan of our own gate, were all such stuff. If not for Dadian, Changli’s obstinacy would not have melted; if not for Danzhou, Dongpo’s self-conceit would not have been dissolved; if not for Qiongya, Juefan’s habitual views would not have been erased. Yet these several gentlemen met the same smelting but different circumstances, and so are not called rare things of a thousand years. You, sir, are certainly not Changli, and this wild monk dares not look to the old masters Ya and Dian; though I am ashamed before Juefan, you do not yield to Dongpo. As for today’s bond, it far surpasses the former worthies; truly it is a thousand years in one hour, and my rejoicing is great. Had you, sir, no joy in Chan to show your resolve, and this mountain monk no Lankavatara to seal the mind, we should have gone back by the old road; would that not have failed this good bond and betrayed what Heaven made? That is why, dwelling together for years, I did not dare let a single faint glimmer of this one matter of going beyond appear: because with your highest faculties and sharp weapon you could of course leap in at one bound, exactly like the broad-browed butcher at the Nirvana assembly, who put down his cleaver and straightway did Buddha-work, by no means to be compared with triflers. For entering the Way has its own season and conditions. I never thought you would suddenly speak of parting; truly I think such a meeting is hard to find in a hundred kalpas, and now that we have met by fortune, how could I let it pass lightly? Therefore this wild monk, not knowing his own rusticity, at the end of wind and wave, hopes to receive your joy and settle death and life once for all. Without the fierce self-awakening of the three waters and the firm oath of Huiqi, this wild monk will not yield a single step but will chase you to the source at Caoxi, to where water runs out and mountains end, and only rest when there is great rest and great repose. The reason is this: you, sir, believe this wild monk’s mind with a bodhisattva’s faith and treat this wild monk’s body as flesh and blood; and all who know us in the world count the meeting of you and this wild monk a wonder beyond the world. If this wild monk did not lay out this one great matter, gouging out heart and liver to present it to you, how could he comfort the hopes of those who know him and repay your extraordinary love? And for you, sir, not to take shouldering the Tathagata as your own true and earnest business is likewise not the way to love this wild monk and repay one who knows you. This practice is by no means hard. Only your true mind’s substance, the light of prajna, stands openly revealed, so that your breast embraces the stars and your spirit covers heaven and earth; but the coarse, floating habits of anger and conceit keep appearing and obstruct your own wondrous clarity. Thus though I pour out heart and liver, men may not believe; though I spend all my compassion, men may not feel it. Think well, sir: beyond this, what have you to be ashamed of before others? Our Buddha said: when a single thought of anger arises, a million gates of obstruction open. This is the great taboo of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra in benefiting living beings, for anger and compassion cannot both stand. Now I only wish that you dissolve one part of habitual tendency and reveal ten parts of light, remove one part of anger and conceit and establish a hundred parts of merit. The ancients said: no need to seek the real, only cease your views. Again: no need to seek elsewhere; letting go is it. Again: see through it, and even buddhahood can be done. Yongjia said: let them slander, let them wrong me; burning the sky with fire only wearies oneself. I hear it as though drinking sweet dew, melting at once into the inconceivable. From this one sees that the ancients had no other strength: they were simply willing to put down together whatever in their breasts was displeasing, and simply to endure within themselves where others cannot endure. At first it is the patience of the ordinary; when patience reaches the unborn, one suddenly ascends the Buddha-ground. What subtle tricks are there besides, to daub at men’s eyes and ears? An earlier couplet of mine runs: at the arising of a thought, see through it; before an affair arrives, do not rashly give rise to it. Small as these words are, they can illustrate great things. From now on I wish you, sir, first to enter the gate of patience, do the work of examining the mind, and take up the business of letting go. Look back on half a lifetime of pilgrimage: it is all dream-work; spew it out in one mouthful and leave not a hair. Spring up with all your raw strength, rouse your spirit, overturn the nest and burrow, uncover brand-new sun and moon, and establish another livelihood; only then are you a great man, a spirit that covers heaven and earth and does not fail a lifetime. Of themselves dragons and gods will fold their hands and the specters will hide their tracks. This is precisely nurturing the heavenly nobility, whereby human nobility comes of itself. Compared with empty, drifting imaginings, this is as far as earth from sky from doing true and imperishable merit. Thus you may be named the layman Juefei. I have run on wildly to this extreme; how does your discernment see it? If one who knows me does not take this for deceit, then orchids and thoroughwort cannot match this accord, nor metal and stone equal this oath. This is the adamantine seed, not worn away through kalpas; I wish with you, life after life, to be a ford and bridge out of the world, to be kin in compassion, to save all living beings and never part from one another. What I say today has laid bare my heart and liver and cut through ordinary feeling; here I set the oath of going beyond the world. If you truly believe it, I beg you to burn to ashes all the letters I have written you, leaving not a word; then a hundred thoughts become ash. From now on, whenever I write to you, nothing shall be sent unless it is medicine, and every word I wish to follow the Buddha’s precepts of true speech and real speech, not false, not flowery. As for your teaching me, I only wish that we may spur each other on with our daily practice since parting, where it is easy and where hard, where it goes smoothly and where not, to accomplish the great work of one age. And I wish you first to set yourself as a gatekeeper at the pass of birth and death. Once this pass is penetrated, you may swing your arms and play in the field of spears and halberds, in the heaps of right and wrong, everywhere and at every point sending forth light and shaking the earth, manifesting the body of an official and doing great Buddha-work. Thus may you be called a bold and mighty man gone beyond the world, hardly to be compared in the least with the world’s heroes, ancient or modern. Our parting is not far off, but the feelings of birth and death are long; I gaze on each of us in our separate skies, creeper trailing everywhere. May the sword of wisdom strike once and leave not a hair. Only strive on with your discernment.

Day after day since we parted there has been no word at all. The farther the messenger, the deeper the longing. Whenever I see Weiwu, I cannot but ask in astonishment by what bond the news should be cut off thus. Then your letter suddenly came, drifting to me through the clouds. Opening it, I seemed to glimpse your countenance, and every character flowed from the true heart and the real. Joy and sorrow met together. And when I read those few phrases, that the mind of illumination is ever present and that walking, standing, sitting and lying are never apart from it, I could not but be overturned with joy. I never thought that today I should suddenly hear this rare Dharma. I have often said that this Way is complete in every man; faculties are not divided into sharp and dull, awakening is not bound to slow or swift; it rests only on a man believing himself and consenting to himself. What is called one thought turning back its light is the same as what one already has; how could it be sought from another? Only its opening has its own season and conditions. In letters I had from old friends in the three Wu, I looked eagerly for you, layman, to enter this Way at once; because I felt our one-body bond keenly, I had many worries, thinking that your habitual tendencies were rather strong and that this would be hard for you. But this wild monk sees the layman wholly transparent and pure, like a rhinoceros horn that startles chickens; whatever bias there is belongs to the invasion of external afflictions, not to your original nature. To enter the Way is like a single arrow piercing three gates. Once the mind is truly aroused, one man holding the pass can hold off ten thousand; how would I dare measure its slowness or swiftness, divide its sharpness or dullness? Then my worrying about the layman is like one who worries that the man learning to walk at Handan will not succeed in the walk. From of old there have been extraordinary men beyond measure; how can they be compared with the ordinary? In the main, this matter truly values courage: one step through to the bottom. When habitual tendencies suddenly arise, simply press hard once, like the Hegemon’s strength uprooting a mountain and lifting a tripod, all spent at once, or like one shout that lays a thousand men low. Then what habitual tendency cannot be worn away? The moment a single thought arises that it cannot be worn away, one falls into cowardice and already feels the spirit of no true man. This matter lies precisely where love and hate are bound up, at the place hardest to break; strike there with one blow. If it breaks there, then a hundred thousand million gates and locks break all at once. If the hard place does not break, then though you swallow in one gulp all the Buddha-Dharma, knowledge, views and principles, there is not half a point of real use, no benefit in the world or beyond it. Why? Because the root of the disease is not pulled up; like rat-poison, it erupts when thunder comes. When the root erupts, no matter how many famous or meritorious deeds you do, every skill is diseased action, far from the action of a fierce and mighty man. If the action is not that of a true man, how can you be called one who bears a transcendent measure? I sigh for the layman: character, talent, achievement, natural endowment, learning: every one surpasses others. But if the root of the disease is not pulled up, you can only trample one generation, not a thousand ages. If you are willing to gather up all the intelligence and strength you have carried through life, concentrate and gather your spirit, and press it all together onto this one great matter, then once you break through, all the grudges, honors and disgraces, right and wrong, gain and loss, afflictions and karmic obstacles of a million kalpas and a thousand lives transform at once into the supreme bodhi, the seed of light. From this one emergence, whatever you do, the least undertaking, all flows forth from this seed of light, and every matter and dharma becomes imperishable. This is what our Śākyamuni won by abandoning the palace, cutting off love and affection, and practicing austerities in the Snow Mountains for six years; for the layman to roll it up and tuck it in his bag in a single morning, is that not a great fierce and mighty man? I have often laughed at Goujian, who for the shame of Kuaiji slept on brushwood and tasted gall for more than twenty years, yet his ambition stopped at swallowing Wu. How narrow! This wild monk has often said that the bandit of affliction has invaded our right faith through kalpas, and not just one Wu; it has destroyed the pure land of Dharma, breached the city of nirvana, and placed us in a sea of suffering, drifting without bound, more than the shame of Kuaiji. If we could grit our teeth and establish Goujian’s resolve to avenge the grudges of birth and death through kalpas, we should not need twenty years of effort. Their work lay with others; ours lies with ourselves. Since it lies with ourselves, what hesitation could keep us from doing it?

You tell me that in this adverse circumstance you have gained great benefit; I am exceedingly glad. In the main, to gain great benefit in adverse circumstances is the capability of a great man; it is only everyday living, nothing very extraordinary. The real difficulty is this: in daily life, in favorable circumstances where habit makes things easy and smooth, it arises without your noticing and you are deceived by it. Here is where it is hard. Take what is before you now: no matter whether great or small, whatever is not to your liking is an adverse circumstance. Touch it and you are angry, so you are stirred by it; once stirred there is suffering, and you gain no benefit. This is precisely the difficulty of the familiar place. The mechanism of birth and death turns entirely on this one pivot. If you can turn it here, you are at once a sage; if you cannot, you fall back into the nest and burrow of affliction. At this swift current, to turn the lock with one motion is the strength that turns the gate of heaven; only a man of great strength with an adamantine mind like you, layman, could bring it off. What the ancients called the Buddha-Dharma being no great matter means exactly this. In the main, only when you gain benefit and joy in the midst of affliction is it true benefit. In your life your afflictions have been very great, and your joy has been great too. If you can now smash the nest of affliction to powder with one blow and leap with your whole body into the field of joy, then looking back on the shadows of habitual tendency from a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives and spitting them all out in one mouthful, you will truly be the freest, most boundless and happiest man in all of heaven and earth. Would you, layman, call this reckless talk? Today the practice-ground is complete, and there are countless joyful things before me; how I wish I could share them with you. I send this only to report that all is well.

On this journey of ten thousand miles, this poor monk, leaning on the compassionate power of all the Buddhas and the great grace of the sage lord, has sat in this land of miasma and attained this one great matter: truly the supreme bond of a hundred thousand million kalpas. I think only that the layman has shared these sweet and bitter things with this poor monk; how could he not share this taste of Dharma? The proverb says: the sun rises and affairs arise again. The dusty sea is vast and without end; where one can steal leisure, steal it. Think: this body of a true man props up heaven and earth; beyond worldly affairs there is the endless joyful ground of going beyond the world. How could one take the illusions before one and the world’s idle thoughts for the ultimate? Two years since the layman and I parted; I think at the place where you have seen through, one step of the heel must be gradually entering a better state. It is but a single cough or spit in your adamantine heart. How goes it?
To Tang Hairuo, Ministry of Rites

A single parting at Changgan, and in the blink of an eye ten years have passed. The bodily radiance of the relics stands before my eyes as ever; and all the various bonds of illusion are but empty-flower Buddha-work. This mountain monk sits in this land of miasma, leaning on the power of the Three Jewels’ true compassion to receive and uphold him; he is free of afflictions, and passes the months and years with Dharma-conditions, the watch-gongs no different from a broken-legged cauldron. But there is no help for the literary habit-tendencies of many lives bursting forth in the armor of nothing-to-do. Over a thousand days, apart from the leisure of running about in the ranks and serving my duties, my various writings amount to no less than several hundred thousand words; though of no help to the supreme Way, they at least show this single thread of solitary light undimmed in the land of rakshasa demons. Those who know me will not take this for foolishness.
To Liu Cunchi

We men, through many lives and piled kalpas, have our five desires like mud and our seven emotions like fire, deep and blazing; not one of the heroic has escaped being drowned and scorched by them, and to seek a single thought of turning the mind back is utterly impossible, let alone to hope that one may bring forth a mind of detachment, seek the way out of suffering, and set the mind wholly on the Pure Land. Here it is not only the lotus emerging from mud, but its root sprouting from fire as well. What joy could equal this? One who would leave birth and death must know the root of birth and death; one who would seek the foundation of the Pure Land must know that the foundation of the Pure Land is precisely the root of birth and death. It lies in the turning of this one thought of mind, sparing no effort. I pray you examine closely in the circumstances that stand before you daily: when wife and children gather, when friends come and go, where righteousness and profit attack each other, before joy and anger have arisen. Look ahead and fix your gaze there, truly and surely, and see what the root of birth and death is, and then pull it out with all your strength. Yet our mind is originally pure; what makes it defiled is truly the fault and grime of this root and stem. If you can pull the root out with strength, then the Pure Land will come without being sought. What is called, once one root returns to the source, the six senses are all liberated, means exactly this. If you see through the one thought at the root, then every point of daily life is a ground of liberation, all returning to the realm of ultimate bliss. Truly, though the body has not yet reached within the lotus, the mind is first sent home to the heaven of ultimate bliss.
To Zheng Jinwu

This poor monk is inferior beyond compare, nothing but a withered stump. Yesterday, when the thunder shook and startled, those who looked on stood as if beside a kalpa-fire; yet you, sir, threw body and mind wide open, rolled up your sleeves and pulled me out, using every kind of skillful means to rescue me, your will set on my living and nothing less, no different from the elder toward the children in the burning house. Since we parted I have sat stiffly in the land of miasma, often growing weary; then I think of you, sir, and unknowingly a measureless, courageous vow to save living beings springs up. Now, by the sage’s grace, the remaining years granted me, together with whatever Dharma I have spoken and whatever living beings I have benefited, all come forth from your adamantine mind-ground; your practice and vows are without end, and your merit is endless too. This inferior one has walked into the land of miasma and in a blink more than a thousand days have passed; I am ashamed that a cause with outflows cannot repay a gift without marks, and I would make my thanks by Dharma. I respectfully offer the several kinds of Buddha-work and Dharma words I have lately produced, to comfort your compassionate thought and repay one who knows me. Read them over again, and you will glimpse the tracks of a bird in the air, and trace the pilgrimage of a man of the Way, never apart from the dust of carts and the feet of horses.
To He Jinwu

I recall how the ancients spoke of men whose hair turned white together yet who remained as strangers, and of men who met for the first time beneath a tilted carriage canopy and were as old friends. Indeed there are those with whom no word is spoken and yet the Way abides of itself. But when it comes to the hour of calamity and of life and death, to look about for one who understands the heart without a word, even amid bonds and fetters — such a one is rare indeed. Why? Because men are readily moved in the mind that knows, but kindness is hard to bestow where it can never be repaid.

In former days, for my own misconduct, I brought down the emperor's wrath and was delivered to the provincial judge for interrogation. Thunder rolled above me, and cauldrons stood before me, so that my clear and steadfast heart could find no way to make itself known. You, sir, holding your commission, oversaw the punishment, and yet you lingered and hesitated amidst the rods and lashes. Even had my body been of metal and stone, how could it have borne that furnace and bellows? Yet by good fortune I relied on a single word from you, and the matter was settled. Truly it was as if copious rain had been showered upon a blazing fire, as if sweet dew had been poured into parched entrails; at once my whole being was cooled and I brightened into life, and I did not even know that I was amid knives and saws.

The law of the court, three cubits long, showed me no slightest leniency. Yet as I looked aside I saw your unwillingness to harm, rising plainly in your brow and eyes, and I knew well that you were a man of benevolence and a noble gentleman. I could only engrave my gratitude upon my heart, not knowing whose son you were. Now I have gone deep into the land of miasma, at the tail end of famine, on the brink of nine deaths, and my thoughts of your lofty righteousness have never once left my breast. Not long ago I asked a colleague of yours, and so learned that you are Master He. I respectfully write this brief letter to lay before you the private feelings of one who cherishes your virtue.
Reply to Zheng Kunya, Grand Coordinator

From afar you have graciously let the white-hair light shine eastward over ten thousand and eight thousand lands; and in that radiance the ascetic of austerities seems to stand before me, so that I bow to your compassionate countenance as if in person and hear the wondrous meaning with my own ears. Again I have been sprinkled with sweet dew, and the dust of habit is suddenly emptied away. The joy that leaps in my breast cannot be conveyed in words.

I have heard that the wondrous practice of the bodhisattva lies in testing the mind in every circumstance one meets. Where afflictions are emptied, there is no need to seek prajñā elsewhere; where the dusts are penetrated, just this is the gate of mystery. As I recite and revere that one phrase, the Ultimate Reality, it is truly a golden lancet for a film-covered eye. I have received in person your vow, though the hour for bowing at your feet has not yet come. Deluded feelings cling and cling, and my admiration only deepens. I only pray that true compassion will gather me in and not forsake the one who has affinity. When the wind is fair, I hope all the more that you will let down a hand from afar. This is what I thirst for.

Wuyang has long been called a land of the uncouth; the walled barracks where I dwell are no monastery. I rely on the sacred compassion and take ten thousand li as my taming and discipline, working cautiously at the forge and hammer. Fortunately I purge poison with poison, and my mean and narrow habits seem gradually to melt away. Truly it is like drinking water: only the drinker knows the warmth or chill. Yet in the end I am still like a fish on dry land blowing froth.

Caoxi in Lingnan is the place where the Sixth Patriarch unfolded his teaching, the Zhu and Si of the Chan gate; his flesh body is still there. I venture to wish to carry one handful of earth to seek blessing in the stillness and light, quietly dissolving old karma. From the first I have not dared to slacken body and mind, only fearing to fall out of step; from time to time I come and go amid the ranks. Now, relying on the indulgence of the authorities, it seems I may rest my shoulders.

Recently, while begging for food at Lingjiang, I suddenly received your jade-like letter descending from heaven like the sound of a celestial drum. Three times over I recited your compassionate intent: truly it is boundless great compassion, which does not forsake those with affinity even in a mote of dust or a pore of the skin. That one phrase about the hidden and the hidden hunter is truly a needle thrust into the sore place. Gratitude suffuses my heart, and I bow in thanks beyond measure.

You instruct me to settle my mind wherever I am; this is precisely liberation in every mote of dust. I pray you will skillfully tame and subdue, to widen the ship of deliverance. This is my utmost hope.
Reply to Ge Zixiu

From your letter I learn that even as a child you knew to ask yourself what the mind is: you took the lump of flesh to be the mind, and yet when the body still lies there after death, why is it no longer aware? At these few words about seeking the mind and not finding it, I could not help exclaiming in astonishment again and again. Since I entered the Dharma and turned toward the Way, and went into the mountains to practice, more than thirty years have now passed; yet among the black-robed and white-robed I have met in all the land, among those who first set their minds on the Way, I have never seen anyone make such a discovery of the novice's mind as this. The reason is that the buddha-nature of all living beings is the same, but the conditions of prajñā carried from former habits differ in depth, and the seeds of hearing and perfuming received from the good teachers one has drawn near in many lives differ in being false or true, sudden or gradual; hence the resolve to enter the Way differs in being crooked or straight, sincere or feigned, slow or swift.

What you describe all comes from having drawn near true and genuine teachers in many lives and from the unsurpassed prajñā seed of hearing and perfuming: the habit-energy has issued from within, and so from childhood you spoke it out unawares. Moreover, this seed is deep-rooted, and so it presses and presses, lying across your breast, lodged and blocked so that you cannot set it down even for a moment. Therefore you cannot swallow it and cannot spit it out, very much like an object stuck in your chest, only you cannot find it. Because you take it for an object, you cannot find it; and all your life your thoughts and deliberations cannot believe in themselves or decide themselves, so whenever you meet someone you go searching for it in him. When you are shown empty space, you take it as empty space; when you hear a shout, you take it as a shout. Yet empty space is form and a shout is sound; because in many lives you have flowed and turned in sound and form and grown practiced in it, you are now carried off by it again. And the reason you are carried off is only that you take this mind as an object and take sound and form as sound and form; hence in daily use, seeing form and hearing sound, you set them up as enemies of the mind. This is precisely what is called seeking Chang'an from inside the Hanyuan Hall: how could you ever escape the cage?

Have you not heard the ancients say: call it a thing and it is already missed? Again they said: never seek it from another; far, far it grows distant from me. Again: seeing form is not to be concerned with form; hearing sound, it is not sound. Again: in the place of sound, hearing is complete; outside seeing, there are no dharmas. Sayings such as these can kill a man, and they can also bring him to life; broadly speaking, they kill the living and bring the dead to life.

You say of yourself that the mind cannot be found. This is the most intimate point of all. Why will you not believe your own mind, but instead give rise to all sorts of thoughts and seek elsewhere? Have you not heard how, when Bodhidharma sat facing the wall, the Second Patriarch Shenguang said, My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to pacify it. Bodhidharma said, Bring me your mind, and I will pacify it for you. After a long while Shenguang said, Seeking the mind, it is utterly unfindable. Bodhidharma said, I have pacified your mind for you. From then on this saying spread through the world, and was called the single transmission and direct pointing. From the Sixth Patriarch down through Nanyue and Qingyuan to the five houses and the seventeen hundred koans, throughout heaven and across the earth, those who spoke of Chan and spoke of the Way and brought life and death to an end cannot be counted. All of them come from Shenguang's one phrase, seeking the mind, it is utterly unfindable.

If you insist that the mind is an object that can be sought from others and that teacher and disciple can hand to one another, then look: what object did Bodhidharma hand to Shenguang with his own hand, and what did he receive with his own hand? And when men look at Shenguang's phrase, seeking the mind, it is utterly unfindable, it is the same as your own words; why was Shenguang right, and why do you not believe? If you say your aspiration differs from Shenguang's, then the buddha-nature of living beings must differ too; if it is not different from Shenguang's, why was Shenguang free of doubt while you doubt the more? If you say that this very unfindability is itself awakening, why did Shenguang awaken once and awaken forever, while you, after hearing the shout, said that the knot of doubt had gone you knew not where, and yet today you are still not through the ancestral koans, and the words have become a further obstruction?

Just look and see where the fault lies. In the very moment when the shout of no-thought was truly heard, how did the knot of doubt suddenly fall away? What did you see that made you so free and easy? Why are you not free and easy today? Look at the place where you are not free and easy — who is it that binds you? At the place where the text does not open — who is it that obstructs you? You need only put forth your strength; drill right at the sore spot. When you have drilled to the place where there is no place left to land, suddenly you will see through it with your own eyes, and only then will you believe that this mind is not a thing and needs no seeking outside. Only then will you know that all your former error was error to the very end, and that this no-error is no-error to the very end. At such a time you will believe that what I say today is very much like raising the voice to stop an echo, or painting legs on a snake. Since words cannot reach the meaning, I have written carelessly as the brush ran, and unwittingly the rattan vines have spread over all the ground. When you have read it, spit it out and burn it; and do not leave it for later men, to make of it a topic that breeds fresh knots of doubt.
To Hu Shun'an, Censor

As for your plan of returning east, I know your courage and loyalty; there can be no miscalculation in it. This too is my humble wish. But the fortune and emolument of a life are all fixed beforehand from former lives; how can man prevail over Heaven? If by some chance it cannot be so, how can one then sit and wait for liberation before one may advance in the Way? Even now, outwardly seated among the carriages and caps of office, inwardly harboring the Buddha's mind, when you meet things and face occasions, rousing kindness and exercising compassion, then all that meets your eye is a seed of buddhahood and a field of blessing without end. If you but give it a little attention, the merit you make in a single day of leisure will be a thousand and ten thousand times greater than that trivial effort. Moreover, your authority is like heaven and earth; life and death lie in your hands. The springs of good and evil you can surely perceive clearly, and the subtlest turnings of events hang upon it in the greatest degree. The strategy of planning and of bringing peace to the realm is, within your great wisdom, no more than a glance.

Only take compassion as the root and use compassion to aid others; practice skillful means widely, and take your ease within the great samādhi. This is to manifest the body of a magistrate and perform the Buddha's work. How can such a man be spoken of in the same breath as one who seeks only the glory of a single body? By means of these very fetters you will turn them into a vehicle for victory. Why then be so anxious, hiding your traces and fleeing from form, while you sit and let the days and months gallop by? A thousand li away in thought, I have nothing to offer you; I take this stale talk to provoke a spit from you. What do you say?

All my life my one thought has been to bring life and death to an end directly. For more than twenty years, if I set my will on the mountains and forests, then even if I cannot penetrate to full realization and match the ancients, still at the crucial juncture of life and death I have good reason to trust: all demonic foes are in the end bodhi, adorning the fruit of buddhahood. As for other calamities and gains and losses, right and wrong, blame and praise, I leave them to nature. Why then strive to be at peace? Therefore since the day I fell into trouble, this single thought of a cool mind and ground has not shifted even for a moment. From last winter in the tenth month, I set my horse's head southward from Jicheng, through bone-piercing ice and snow, and in the twelfth month reached Baixia, where I met my old mother on the river and took joyful leave of her. On the eighth day I raised sail and went west. What I rely on is that feeling is withered and wisdom exhausted, the phantom shadow wholly dissolved, a bright mirror and still water, by which I may amuse myself. This stretch of karmic circumstance has been forged and tempered in the great furnace; do not let it entangle your heart on my account. I only wish you to quietly nourish the harmony of Heaven and await the highest joy. If Heaven grants me to return alive, I still hope to finish the unfinished karma between us and keep you company in my remaining years.

Since I fell into trouble, I have truly been at the brink of nine deaths; yet looking at it now with the true eye, I do not see the slightest mark of movement or stillness. Though ten thousand li lie between us, in truth we are not apart by so much as a half-step. I think of how you and I forgot all forms for half a lifetime; surely you have long since entered this Dharma gate, so how could you fall back into the common way, galloping in thoughts of coming and going, and wearing a dreamlike look of grief? This circumstance of mine not only surpasses thirty years of pilgrimage, it is enough to surpass the practice of vast kalpas. In Leiyang the heat steams like a cauldron, and those who die of miasma lie thick as on a scorched marsh. I sit alone in the charnel ground, drinking the miasmic smoke as if it were sweet dew, enduring hunger and emptiness as if filled with fine ghee. Were it not that feeling is withered and wisdom exhausted, how could I savor it? Recently I have gained the Great General as a protector of the Dharma, and have borrowed a branch among the walled barracks of the provincial capital. In the leisure left from bearing arms I sit withered behind a closed door; all conditions are suddenly cut off, and I read only the Laṅkāvatāra, inquiring into the mind-seal that came from the West and finishing the koans not yet finished. That the goodness of merit and the vajra mind have already become a banner of light — surely I am not unworthy of the gate and wall. The ancients once said that when the ancestors are not clear, the calamity reaches the sons and grandsons. My good fortune is that I have not fallen into that saying. The Buddha said that to give away seven treasures enough to fill the Ganges' sands is not equal to upholding four lines of this sūtra. Knowing that you do not forget the poor child, I venture this to comfort you. What else is there to say?

I sit amid the barbarian smoke and miasmic fog, and I am glad that the conditions for living grow daily thinner and the conditions for the Way grow daily thicker. The more the body suffers, the happier the mind. Then what place is not the sovereign's grace, and what thing is not the Buddha's power? This may be spoken to one who knows me; it is hard to speak of to common men. How is your Dharma body, I wonder. Vimalakīrti has said: would you know how to rid yourself of old age and sickness? There is only the study of the unborn. And a hundred years of light and shadow pass as between pinched fingers — how much can there be? Your years, sir, are daily higher and the prospect before you daily narrower. The flavors of this turbid world you have tasted all but to the dregs. As the proverb says: in the end salt is this salty and vinegar this sour — and to what end does it all come? The ancients said: when you come it is all very well; I fear only that when you go it will not be as when you came. This is no empty saying.

Think carefully, sir. Your former fame and career, together with your plans for sons and daughters — all are another man's business. What is your own business? If a single thought is sharply awakened to this, you will cry out unawares, and of yourself grow urgent, and set your own feet in order for the great matter of life and death. If you do not grow urgent and set it in order, then you have still not sharply awakened; and if you do not awaken once, sharply, then you are greatly not the man I take you for. Such is the business of a hero and true man. Twenty years ago I already knew that you would speak of this one thing, and so I did not spare body or life but wished to walk with you. But though half of it is piling up hidden merit and half is nourishing the body, and so we muddle on to today, yet within it there is one small red heart, very much like Zhang Liang's resolve to be for Han from first to last. For more than ten years I have talked and laughed with you — all of it a realm of empty bloom, mere human sentiment and Buddhist business; in truth we never once broke open liver and gallbladder together. Yet with you I have a single inch of heart and intestine that shines clear and mirrors clear, and you have never failed to know this inward song of mine. I had hoped we would return together with white heads and finish this matter together. How could it be that in a single morning we are torn apart and scattered even to this? From this very thing one may contemplate life and death. And now, though we dwell within the same heaven and earth, and though ten thousand li divide us, seen with the heavenly eye we are still next-door neighbors; yet we cannot once receive your countenance and take in your color and be glad as in former days. How much less along the long road of life and death, once parted into the dark and distant, when shall we meet again? If I cannot return alive, then it is a long farewell from you; and when I put forth another head, I do not know whether it can be as in this life and on this day. To speak of it brings great grief and bitterness. I have received from you the righteousness of one who knows me; without this I cannot repay you. And if you believe that I have not come to this place, then again I have no way to answer one who knows me.
To Zhou Lizhai, Court Historian

Formerly, though in my heart I secretly admired your noble forbearance, I never had the chance for deep speech. Yesterday, carrying my bowl into the royal city, I was fortunate to meet you beneath the dragon-flower tree; seeing how genuine and pure your resolve for the Way is, my joy penetrated to the very seat of my heart. The ancients made light of a thousand pieces of gold and heavy a single promise; a true scholar values only one who knows him. Henceforth I, a mountain monk, shall give my whole life to the mountains and seas, and covet nothing else. Since your Dharma eye is perfect and bright, how could you ever again fault the blind and blear-eyed? I privately think that the literary fortune of the East begins with you, and that the fortune of the Dharma may perhaps belong to this unworthy man. Worldly and world-transcending are of mutual use to each other; this too is a strange thing between the two realms. This is no mad speech; it is truly what I hope for from you, that you would take the Way as your own weight.
Reply to the Zhou Brothers, Ziyin and His Elder

In the world, gathering and scattering, arising and ceasing, formation, dwelling, decay, and emptiness — in the conditioned dharmas this is the way of things, and what is there in it to grieve over? What is truly grievable is that in the long night of darkness this torch of wisdom should be lost, so that the sons of the Buddha have nowhere to turn for refuge, and the seeds of wisdom and the sprouting seedlings of the spirit are daily scorched and withered by the blazing flames of the five desires, unable to come to the perfect fruit of victory. The six dusts darken the heaven of the nature; the weeds of craving lay waste the ground of the mind; afflictions blot out the grove of merit; greed and anger storm the house of nirvāṇa; they fell it with the axe of wine and lust and let it be trampled by the monkey and the horse, until day by day it lies waste and at last becomes a wild tangle.

I pray that in thought after thought, mind after mind, you will take this to heart with sorrow, and nourish and cultivate, weed and tend it, guard and fence it round, so that the flower of awakening spreads fresh and you adorn the jeweled ground. I hope that all gods and men may each harbor the seed of wisdom, and that creeping things and wriggling things and all that lift their heads may together ascend the shore of awakening. Thus you will not only raise your family's name through all ages, but will be enough to wash away the shame of the Dharma gate today. Without this, what hope could I place in you and your brother? On a journey of ten thousand li, if you take this to heart, we are still neighbors.
To Jiao Congwu, Court Historian

I reflect that in this age of the Dharma's decline, when all is thin and few, the dragons and gods have pushed you forward to manifest the body of a magistrate and raise the great banner of Dharma, to serve as the eye of gods and men in this age. This is no small matter. We were parted for many years, and yesterday we met beneath the tree, as if in another life. A human life drifts on and on, and is as dreamlike as this. And when I behold your countenance of the Way and your heavenly form, truly you are one who, without rising from the samādhi of cessation, manifests all manner of dignified conduct. Were it not that the light of your mind secretly returns, how could it illumine so perfectly? How could it be measured by sound, voice, form, and appearance? My joy is beyond measure.

I am ashamed that my faculties are dull and inferior; for twenty years I have worn my heart out in the mountains and forests, and still I sit atop the pole, with nowhere at all to let go. Yet the cause of the great matter is truly not easy. At parting I received one word of instruction from you, and my gratitude is boundless. Returning, I sat stiff and still in a hollow cliff, mind after mind shining alone; how dare I fail one who knows me? At times the sea is limpid and the sky clear, and the Dharma body suddenly appears — is this not the meeting of stimulus and response?

In my leisure I have opened the Zhuangzi with its wings and found that it gathers the great achievements of the various schools. Though the commentaries are often severe, every man has his own Zhuangzi; it is not Zhuangzi's own Zhuangzi. Only you have entered this samādhi very deeply — why not overturn it completely? I have often argued this: Laozi came forth in an age without a Buddha, and I would venture to class him with the pratyekabuddhas.
