His body measures with the Dharma-realm, the fountainhead of the ten thousand practices: what land or dust-mote does not fit within a single pore? The elephant king roams and wanders, unobstructed through the ten directions. I bow to him who is like space — vast, at ease, and free.
Eulogy for the Picture of Samantabhadra Bathing the Elephant

With the Dharma-realm as his body, where does he not go? Turning his back on this elephant king only brings toil and fluster. The elephant’s body is pure white, originally undefiled; washing it for no reason but adds specks of dust. Water does not wash water, white does not stain white: seek the two, and there is no distinction at all. Why then put the servant boy to such wasted labor? Where he does not reach, it becomes only more obstructed. As I see it, what is already complete is best: man and elephant both forgotten, saints and common folk swept away together.

The elephant’s body is spotless white — where could dust have stained it? A speck in the eye defiles the whole body. Wash it with water and the defilement only grows; leave it unwashed and it is clean of itself — no one knows why. Water adds nothing to purity, purity has no use for water; the two never meet. Such is the original state. The Great Being’s samādhi is the perfect fusion of the Dharma-realm: how could this dust-mote become a hindrance to him? To keep it is not defilement; to remove it is not purity. This phantom Dharma-gate is called non-contention.
Eulogy for Samantabhadra Riding the Elephant

With great practice and broad strides he treads the ten directions through: what pore, what dust-mote is there where he does not appear? Walking alone, sitting alone — how light and swift that is! To borrow another’s strength only brings confusion and disgrace. A lotus beneath his feet, the reins curled through the trunk — were it not for all this, he would be dragged down by it. Body and life lean on each other; coming and going, they have long grown familiar. Though it burdens him, it sets my feet at ease.
Eulogy for Samantabhadra, the Great Being, Empowering the Elephant

Our Great Being takes the Dharma-realm as his body: to any who uphold the sūtra he at once reveals his form. This is no display of supernatural power, no love of showing off; he would have living beings wake abruptly, here and now.
Eulogy for the Image of Great-Compassion Avalokiteśvara

I hear the Great Being is fundamentally without abiding, dwelling only in the thoughts of living beings. Since living beings are themselves the Great Being’s mind, why, being inverted, do they not see him? If one says the Great Being’s mind is inverted, how could he transform inverted people? And if living beings were not inverted, why should the Great Being labor to teach at all? Alas, people lack the light of wisdom: they lie drunk in broad daylight, dreaming all manner of dreams on fearful roads, terrified and panicked, unable to escape; they gallop and flee and cannot get away — like a thirsty deer racing after the heat-haze: the faster it runs the thirstier it grows, its strength and heart exhausted, and still it does not know it is inside a dream. The one who watches with waking eyes is moved to pity and shouts with all his might, yet the other does not feel the pain; and not only does he not feel it, he grows angry. Then he dreams again of pursuers, dreading those ahead and fearing those behind, and cries out with all his strength; at one cry he suddenly flings out his arms and starts up. From that one awakening he looks back at the dream and only then believes that his own mind gave rise to the inversion. Thus the Great Being can save from suffering; but he is much like the man with waking eyes. Though he may ever accord with living beings, the doubting grow only more frightened; yet if the person himself would but turn the light around for a moment, that would surpass the Great Being’s thousand hands and eyes. Good indeed, son of the Buddha — why be so inverted? If you do not seek within yourself but hunt for it in another, and if at the very place you hunt you see your own mind, then I too am named Avalokiteśvara.

The perfected one has no name; the name lies with people. He sees forms with the ear, hears sounds with the eye; the six functions are but one, and that one does not stand either. Pervading every realm and all space, there is no place he does not enter. The bright moon in the sky prints its light on a hundred rivers; like dew on grass-tips, every drop is round. At the tip of a single hair he manifests a wondrous body; sitting within a mote of dust he turns the great Dharma-wheel. In the blazing fire, on the mountain of knives, on the iron bed and the bronze pillar — one cry of utter distress, and suddenly it becomes a Pure Land. He chooses neither pure nor foul, makes no distinction of man or woman; if you would seek him, it is only within yourself.

I hear the Great Being divides his body into a trillion forms; eyes see and ears hear, yet none can tell which he is. When suffering comes they cry out, and crying out they are at once received; no coming or going is seen, no one knows who saves them. I now reflect: the Great Being is without self. At the gates of the six faculties he is like fire to whatever touches him: fire does not burn fire, dust does not stain dust. Because there is no this or that, he is named the Perceiver of the World’s Sounds.

The Great Being’s body is within the minds of living beings: intermingled yet not confused, apart yet not divided. Therefore when I have a request, he answers to the sound — not that the Great Being comes, but that I myself bear witness. If I did not know suffering, how could I make my plea? To know the very place of suffering: that is turning the stream back. Once my stream has turned, the Great Being is myself; seeking myself through myself — what could be amiss?

I contemplate the Great Being’s body: it is originally free of all marks. Because it is free of marks, it can manifest every kind of body — like the maṇi pearl, which shows all colors according to conditions. Thus Buddhas and bodhisattvas, the beings of the six paths, and even forms of other kinds: into all of them he enters. How then should one make distinctions of male or female body? If one sees the Great Being’s body as equal, without the mark of two, and understands that Dharma-nature is empty, then its radiance is like the full moon, and it can clear away the darkness of affliction, all at once, here and now. Therefore I take refuge in the Great Being and leap free of the suffering of birth and death.
Eulogy for Water-Moon Avalokiteśvara

His body like a drifting cloud, his mind like water and moon: unmoving yet responsive, wordless yet speaking. Call him and there is a sound; seek him and he is not found. Whatever suffering seeks him is wholly freed.

A water-moon bearing, an empty-flower surface, a valley-echo voice, a maṇi jewel. Wherever one meets him he shows his form; he comes and goes through the six paths with no dusk or dawn. His whole body and mind are only for others — where will you seek such a master?
A mirror image, water and moon, lightning in the vast void: touched, it stirs, and in a flash the shadow appears.
Not stained by a single mote of dust, openly displayed through the ten directions: a body covered with hands and eyes, needing no turning to and fro.
The mind is originally without affairs — for whom then these bitter thoughts? If someone comes asking, one does not know oneself.
The Great Being has no mind, yet answers like an echo to a sound: whoever has a request is answered as soon as he calls.
With a body without marks he answers the mind that seeks: nowhere does he fail to appear — he is named the Perceiver of the World’s Sounds.
The water flows into the sea, the moon never leaves the sky: responding without thought — this is the Chan of freedom.

The mark of no-mark: the mark is not in me. Appearing according to response, like fire meeting firewood — the thirty-two responses are still mere trifles; a billion and a trillion more — what should prevent them?
The Great Being’s body and mind are just living beings; therefore when vows are made, he comes as the response arises.
The perfected one has no form; true compassion makes no sound. Response and stirring meet in the Way: the sands are white, the water clear.
Taking wisdom as his life and beings as his mind, he seeks out the sound and saves from suffering: he is named the Perceiver of the World’s Sounds.

Body and mind transparent, like crystal; within and without made pure, like the moon upon a pool. He responds without being stirred, arrives without being sought; therefore my Master is called Inconceivable.

Speaking without sound, answering every request, like the echo answering the valley, like a precious mirror set before one — this is he who is named Avalokiteśvara; the samādhi he cultivates is called True Purity.

With a mind of quiescence he manifests wondrous marks: the full moon in the cold sky, its radiance measureless. I, with a refined mind, am like turbid water settling clear: the water clears, the moon appears, and no calculation is needed. The moon does not leave the water, the water does not leave the moon; since there is no coming or going, both are quiescent. My mind being still, the Great Being is myself; therefore what I seek is fulfilled as the thought arises.

Like an image in a mirror, like the moon in water: look, and it seems to be there; reach for it, and it cannot be grasped. With the sound of the ocean tide he puts forth his broad and long tongue — this is my Great Being’s rule of teaching the Dharma.

His Dharma-body is like a cloud filling the ten directions, born from emptiness like the light of water and moon. Because his body has no outside, his mind has no obstruction; hence in responding to things he attains great freedom. The thirty-two responses people call real are, for my Great Being, a single drop in the ocean. The afflictions of living beings are like a mad fire: let ambrosia be sprinkled, and at the thought they are cool.

I contemplate the Great Being as the moon in water, a branch of willow in hand, called the ambrosia of cessation: throughout the ten directions the world is moistened, and he can relieve living beings of the fever of the three poisons.

He responds without deliberation, pervades without thinking: spring comes and flowers open, the water clears and the moon appears. Hand grasps, foot runs; eye hears, ear sees. Far off, he is the more intimate; bland, yet never cloying. If a true man will but set his heart to bitter effort, the meeting will fulfill his life’s wish.

The Great Being’s body is originally without marks; it appears in response to the mind — a shape without shaping, a lightning flash, an empty flower, a mirror image, water and moon. Contemplate it thus, and suddenly one transcends.

In the ultimate void hangs the cool moon; its shadow sinks into many waters and admits no distinction. Thus the Great Being’s body is not two with things: wherever one sees or hears, there is no place it is not.

The Great Being is originally without body; his body appears according to living beings, as the moon reflects in many waters without distinguishing foul from pure. Dullness or brightness lies in clarity or turbidity, not in any choosing by the moon. Therefore, when the Great Being appears, one should contemplate with a pure mind; the contemplator’s mind being pure, all sufferings are emptied. If you would know the mind that saves from suffering, it is none other than the one who contemplates.

The Great Being does not think; his thinking is compassion. For living beings’ sake he sits dumbly, as if besotted. This besottedness and living beings cling together like glue and lacquer, and the two joined are past knowing. Thus he can save from suffering, shadow and echo at once. Therefore the Great Being’s compassion is deep and his vows heavy; but when the realm of living beings is emptied, his besottedness has no use.

I contemplate the Great Being as the moon in the sky: wherever there is water, it appears therein, choosing neither pure nor foul, for originally there is no this or that. Because the nature of water is empty, it has no dregs; the mind-water of living beings is likewise. Therefore whoever seeks has only to think, and he arrives. Because there are many waters, the moon shines everywhere; because there are living beings, the Great Being’s wonder is seen.
Eulogy for the Image of Avalokiteśvara Manifested as a Bhikṣu

Acting with purpose, responding without fixed direction — why forsake those others and manifest this one in true purity? Because the Buddha is no fixed thing, and without the Dharma who could transmit it? Were there no transmitter, the deaf and blind would all lie sleeping. Therefore the bhikṣu is the Dharma itself, the Buddha itself: his mind like space, like an echo issuing from the valley. Because space has no form, the blind can see; because the echo has no sound, the deaf can catch its meaning. Seeing and hearing do not abide; sound and form are both forgotten. By the power of samādhi he wakes the foolish and crazed: master within the dust, a lotus born in fire. Call his name and bow in reverence — he appears before you as the thought arises. Only then is my Master named as one who has attained the Chan of freedom.
Eulogy for Lotus-Leaf Avalokiteśvara

The sea of suffering has no shore — who will be the far bank? A single leaf of red lotus drifts along with the current. With this as boat he goes everywhere, missing no place. When creatures of every kind seek, he answers the stirring as the thought arises; therefore when his name is called, he appears through the universal gate.

The sea of suffering has no shore, the stream of desire never runs dry; what the perfected one relies on is a single leaf of green lotus. The far bank is not distant — no road is traveled. His body is like cloud and space, his mind like water and moon. Could one contemplate thus, what Dharma would there be to speak?
Eulogy for the Auspicious-Lotus Avalokiteśvara Carved by the Empress Dowager Cisheng

They say the udumbara flower appears but once in a thousand years; when a sage arises, it is taken as the sign. It is the Imperial Mother alone in whose palace this flower has grown: by this her virtue is attested — what more could be added?
Eulogy for Lotus Avalokiteśvara

The perfected one responds to things like the udumbara flower: few are they who see it, and so it is made much of. The green lotus rising from the water has its root in the mud; many see it, and so it is thought nothing remarkable. Therefore I say: the Dharma-body is all-pervading, praised throughout the ten directions, appearing through the universal gate. Thus complete and encompassing, why do people not know it? It is only before their eyes, raising the great Dharma-banner. Were it not true purity, this could not be brought about; and so the Great Being’s body is simply as it is.

The three realms have no safety — they are like a burning house; yet the perfected one dwells in them as in a land of coolness. The mire of the five desires is like a dung heap, yet the lotus rises tall, its stems and leaves growing of themselves. The maṇi pearl, pure and round in substance, fallen into a privy, loses nothing of its radiance. Buddha-nature in the midst of entanglement is soiled but not defiled: the lotus in the mud, the pearl in the latrine. In daily use, in action and rest, it is bright and undimmed. The lotus in the fire — therefore it is called auspicious.
Eulogy for Avalokiteśvara in Samādhi

With a mind of reflection he enters the thoughts of living beings: striking water he leaves a trace, knocking on space he makes a sound. Intermingled yet not confused, apart yet not two: an egret in the snow, a phantom in a pearl. Contemplating thus, he is named the most honored among the honored.
By the contemplation of illusion and the effortless power of wonder, through hearing, reflecting, and cultivating, he enters samādhi.

The Great Being has no mind — how could there be stillness or confusion? Living beings have no fixed nature — how could they be entangled at all? He ferries them in accord with conditions, yet originally has no such intention; suffering has no abiding place, like a sound in an empty valley. Therefore the Great Being’s compassion is the broadest: like space meeting space, like an echo answering an echo. Originally without coming or going, without arising or ceasing — the Great Being’s spiritual power is therefore beyond words.
Eulogy for White-Robed Avalokiteśvara
His robe is white, his heart is red; himself he has not, but only others. He causes all people to keep his name ever on their lips.
Originally undefiled, now likewise unstained: could one contemplate thus, the ten directions open clear.
A form without form appears with each stirring; in a single hair-tip its light is everywhere.
A broken bamboo branch serves as the auspicious grass; sitting, he cuts off the ten directions — the seas dry up, the mountains fall.
The seas run dry, the lotus withers; dust dissolves, awakening is verified — all by the willow branch that sprinkles and sweeps them clean.

I contemplate the Great Being’s mind: he would cleanse the defilement of living beings and so wears white himself, shielding their shortcomings. As water only washes away dust, and water does not wash water, so the Great Being and living beings in truth know no this or that. If you see your own mind, you know the Great Being’s face; split open a single mote of dust, and the Great Being’s radiance appears.

Within red, without white, the Great Being is in no way separated from the minds of living beings. Call, and the answer appears at once, like the bright moon held in turbid water. The mind’s stains of living beings are not easily removed, so the Great Being makes his own body their cleansing. If you would see the Great Being’s countenance in your daily life, seek it as form and it cannot be found: it lies only in one phrase, clear before the sound arises — heard by the eye, seen by the ear, past all speaking.

The Great Being is pure white because originally unstained; therefore he enters living beings, and his mind is not shallow. Like a water-clearing pearl cast into turbid water, the pearl keeps no shadow, yet the water clears to the bottom. The bright moon is in the sky: the water clears and it appears at once — uninvited it comes, unsummoned it pervades. Therefore the suffering of living beings is the Great Being’s body, and whatever is sought is the Great Being’s mind. Body and mind have no outside; this and that are not two. Appearing as the thought arises, he is named Inconceivable.

Deep and clear the cold sky, limpid the autumn water: the Great Being’s Dharma-body is truly like this. The moon does not leave the sky, the sky does not leave the water; they seem two, yet in truth there is no this or that. The mind is originally undefiled; the robe is not worn from love of white, but because those who are not white are made clean by gazing on him. The Great Being has no mind; living beings have thoughts, and the mark is born from the thought, like the moon in the palm. Therefore when there is a seeking, the response follows the thought: originally there is no coming or going — one’s own mind bears the witness.

The suffering of us living beings is itself the Great Being’s compassion; because suffering and compassion meet, my vows are never thwarted. Were there a hundred billion seeking, they would all be answered at once — how much less would he begrudge a wise man. Like quicksilver fallen to the ground, every drop is round: the one thing I seek, and every thing besides. I contemplate the Great Being’s body as one seeking an echo in an empty valley; the Great Being contemplates my mind as a thing seen in the palm of his hand.
Eulogy for Fish-Basket Avalokiteśvara
The basket is in her hand, her feet never stop walking; at the crossroads she would have people know that she is there.
One thing in her hand she can never put down; her true heart in every shred is spent for others without pretense. Therefore I say: she is one of true compassion.
Fish in hand, she hawks them in the street; her eyes search out people, seeking only to be quick. In her heart she cares not for half a coin — most likely she would settle compassion’s debt.
Eulogy for Purple-Bamboo Avalokiteśvara

The purple bamboo grove, the ground of seven treasures, the rock of Putuo, the vajra realm: sitting, he cuts off the ten directions, ever calmly at leisure. Whoever seeks him comes at the sound of his name. Were he not my Master Avalokiteśvara, who could grant every wish to each?
Purple bamboo is no grove; the Great Being is no body. What is seen now all comes forth from one’s own mind.
Eulogy for the Great Being Avalokiteśvara of the Southern Sea

Green sea and grey cliffs, yellow flowers and emerald bamboo, fish and turtles, dragons and yakṣas, dens of ghosts: he appears in form according to kind, emerging and sinking along the stream. Like space resting on the earth, there is no place where he is not complete. This is Avalokiteśvara’s body of freedom — not in vain is he called a Buddha of the past.

He sits upon the flat rock, contemplating the mind of quiescence; from all that stirs he brings forth a wondrous sound. The Dharma is free of marks; the true sūtra has no words. It is our Great Being who manifests bodies like clouds: every request is answered, no kind is left unvisited. With a mind of great compassion he is wholly one with deluded thought.
Eulogy for the Great Being in the Cliff Shrine

A slab of grey rock, sealed by moss and guarded by cloud: the Great Being’s Dharma-body is revealed within it, plain to the eye, with no concealment at all. Yet people seek him elsewhere — why is that?

A slab of rock, a lone peak, a clear pool, a white moon: the Dharma-body of freedom is originally without arising or ceasing. Form does not form itself; it is originally like an illusion — an empty flower before a filmed eye, lightning in a clear sky. It is not that the Great Being intends to do anything; it is the deluded who calculate in false thought. If you would see the Great Being’s true, original face, simply do not deliberate — the whole body appears of itself.
Eulogy for the Great Being Avalokiteśvara in Rock and Tree

Look at that grey cliff, towering and unmoved: it is truly my Great Being’s Dharma-body, standing alone and far. Look at the trees on the cliff, their branches and leaves spread thick: it is my Great Being’s shade of compassion, opening wide. He sits at ease within them, without speech or seeking, showing the thirty-two responses, wondrously answering everywhere. The sleeping multitude starts awake, yet he does not leave great samādhi; he pulls out every suffering and makes all pure. I contemplate the Great Being as thoroughly free of marks: in an illusory body he is named the most honored among the honored. He puts forth his broad and long tongue — mountains high, waters deep; day and night he ever teaches, and is named the Perceiver of the World’s Sounds.
Eulogy for the Responsive Transformations of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara

The Great Being’s body is like a maṇi jewel: the five colors appear in turn, and all is understood according to conditions. In heaven as a god, among humans as a human — since he is called the answerer of requests, why should he not show his form? If a son is sought, he answers as a man, adorned with merit, virtue, and wisdom beyond compare. It appears only in the seeker’s single mind; therefore it is named the inconceivable transformation.
Eulogy for Avalokiteśvara of Freedom

I bow to the Lord of Great Compassion, whose body of freedom is complete: a mirror image, the moon in water, doing deeds past thought. In the subtle dust of the Dharma-realm, one mote holds all lands, and every land as many beings as dust — nowhere does he fail to show his form. When a living being’s single thought is at leisure, he answers all at once and equally. As the chapter on perfect penetration says, this is still a matter of measure and number; only my own mind knows it — the Great Being is wholly unaware.
Moon-shadow and bell-sound, wondrous voice and form: the ear sees, the mind hears — merit beyond measure.
Eulogy for the Imperial Carving of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara

Our Great Being’s Dharma-body answers everywhere: through the gate of the ear-faculty he wondrously attains perfect penetration. Beat a drum in the ten directions and the ten directions hear it at once. In the emptiness of the Dharma-realm he manifests forms like clouds; in heaven above and the world below, no kind is left unentered. Therefore whoever seeks is fulfilled according to his mind. It is our gracious Empress Mother, endowed from former lives with the vow of compassion — like the Great Being’s mind, she practices wide skillful means, and by this wondrous image universally bestows on living beings, causing their wishes to be answered like an echo to a sound.
Eulogy for the Great Being Avalokiteśvara of Putuo

I hear the Great Being pervades without thinking, answering in lands as numerous as dust, practicing wide skillful means. Living beings are the mind; the mind is living beings. Therefore whoever seeks has only to call, and the sound is answered. As the water rises the boat floats higher; the more the mud, the greater the Buddha. The sharper the suffering, the deeper the compassion, with no leisure to receive and respond to all. He sits upon the rock of Potalaka, dwelling in the sea of birth and death: though space itself should melt away, this mind does not change.

He sits upon the Potalaka rock, contemplating the ocean of quiescence; everywhere he shakes the sound of the tide, and is named Avalokiteśvara Who Observes Freely. He puts forth his broad and long tongue, pervading the ten directions. Therefore whoever seeks appears at once as the thought arises. Living beings are already complete — why labor to go and save them? The water clears, the moon appears: neither before nor after.
Old Man Hanshan’s Dream-Wandering Collection, Fascicle Thirty-Four
Eulogy for the Great Being Avalokiteśvara in Celestial Robes

I bow to the Lord of Great Compassion, the perfectly complete and full Honored One, who sits at ease in the emptiness of the Dharma-realm, bright as the moon among stars, answering universally the minds of living beings, like the moon come over many waters. In the daily life of living beings his power is unknown; wishing to manifest a wondrous body, he borrows the painter’s hand. Painter and Great Being together enter the inconceivable: the shadow appears at the tip of a hair, like spring within a hundred flowers. In the most subtle and wondrous, the whole body appears at once, adorned with utmost beauty: necklaces of a hundred treasures’ light, celestial robes covering his form like thin mist shrouding the moon, as if within the white hair-mark. Seeing this rare mark, I bow and take refuge, and at once enter the ocean of quiescence. Know then that the seeker’s mind, pure as still water, stirs this wondrous body, and all is accomplished as the thought arises. By the vow from which this was born, may we together realize the vajra body, forever abiding to illumine the world, and be freed from every bond.
Eulogy for the Great Being Avalokiteśvara in Straw Robes

The Great Being is without marks — why then does he show himself so plainly? Straw robe and rush mat, complete just as he pleases. Beard and hair unkempt and scratched — not that he cannot cut them, but deliberately he leaves them, to pierce the eyes of the worldly. The Great Being is not worldly; the worldliness lies in the beholder. Like a flower in the air, it is the fault of the filmed eye. If one can remove the view of self, the Great Being is myself. Since he answers according to kind, what could be amiss? Again, like a place that hurts, only the one in pain knows it. If you would know the Great Being, neither the real nor the conventional will do.
Praise of Great Being Guanyin of the Sea Tide

The myriad forms are universally sealed; the sea of nature is profoundly still. One gust of circumstance-wind, and the waves surge to the sky. The perfect Dharma body abides unmoved, serene and ever present; within the waves its radiance shines forth all the more. Therefore, when beings’ waves of consciousness do evil, the Dharma body lies hidden yet still becomes seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving. Therefore the wise, amid seeing and hearing, turn back their gaze in a single thought, and the sea of karma is suddenly emptied. The Great Being saves from suffering, yet comes not from without: it is the self-mind made manifest, wrought without contrivance. Since it is only the self-mind, why seek outside? Simply hearing the nature of hearing — this is named Guanyin.
Praise of Guanyin, the Sea Moon — a Great Being Seated Within the Full Moon in the Midst of the Sea

The Great Being alone, perfect and wondrous in penetration, enters the sea of birth and death and seals it everywhere, like the moon. Within the pure radiance the Dharma body is profoundly still; the waves of affliction may surge to the sky unchecked. The more affliction flourishes, the more the Dharma body is revealed; and so toward living beings it accords and stays near. As water holds the moon, and the moon does not leave the water, light shines upon light — there was never any this or that. I contemplate the Great Being as never apart from this mind; therefore whoever seeks responds as echo answers sound. The constant light is not obscured; death and life are not divided. Quiescence stands before one, and of oneself one transcends. (The Great Being abides as moon and water, as mind and realm: no duality at all.)
Praise of the Great Being of Empty Sea

Birth and death are like a sea; the world is like empty space. A single piece of body and mind is let go within them. Space and water mingle and merge; the waves are no longer terrible. This alone is my Teacher: true liberation.
Praise of the Manifestation in the Body of a Great Heavenly General

The gate of perfect penetration realized by all Buddhas truly enters through the six sense faculties of living beings. Though the six faculties are one and the same, they differ in depth; the ear alone is the most perfect of all. Therefore the Great Being entered by the ear gate, and, both faculty and object forgotten, even contemplation was let go. When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescence stands revealed; in a single thought one equals the Buddha and all beings. The Dharma body is equal and nothing fails to merge within it; bodies of the ten Dharma realms appear all at once. Yet each sees according to his wish, as an empty valley answers every sound. Know then that the body of a Great Heavenly General responds at once when the seeker has the mind. One body contains every body, as the sea holds the taste of a hundred rivers. The wise can contemplate apart from form and appearance, and all faculties and objects are utterly still.
Praise of the Great Being Who Subdues the Six Demons

I contemplate the Great Being, inconceivable, ever present in the bitter sea of birth and death. Body and mind alike enter every sentient being, subduing demon foes and benefiting conscious creatures. The demons are not merely eighty thousand; all take the six faculties as their bellows. When the six gates are still, the wondrous function is complete — and this is the Great Being’s awesome spiritual power. Demons and the Great Being are fundamentally not two, like empty space and the light of the sun. If space and light were different, the Great Being would be seized by demons. Therefore to bow and to call the name brings the inconceivable power forth at the very thought. The green cliff, the emerald bamboo — these are his Dharma body; thusness unmoved is true liberation.
Praise of the Great Being Who Subdues the Twelve Demons

Before the Buddha appeared in the world, the demon realm was empty; once the Buddha appeared, demons came to be. Buddha and demon are fundamentally without difference; it is only from the inverted views of living beings. When faculty and object stand opposed, the demon ramparts seal one in; when mind and realm are both forgotten, the demon hordes are destroyed. Therefore Guanyin’s wondrous power of wisdom subdues demons only by purifying faculties and objects. When the six gates stand open and the Dharma realm is empty, Buddha and demon alike no longer appear. I now bow to the Inconceivable One, praying that he bestow fearlessness on living beings, that I may at once enter the gate of perfect penetration, and that all demons may ever be my Dharma companions. When demons can raise the Dharma banner at a thought, only then is the Great Being’s awesome spiritual power felt.
Praise of the Great Being of Perfect Penetration

The Great Being’s body is nowhere absent; therefore the Great Being’s mind is perfectly penetrating and unobstructed. Living beings of the ten directions were never outside it. Blue pigment within color, a clod of earth within water: since there is no this or that, boundaries are hard to draw. So when one responds to seeking, just so is one gladdened.
Praise of the Embroidered Great Being, with a Preface

The mother of the Xia family of Jiahe, née Fan, was fifty-two years old and had kept the vegetarian fast for thirty-five years, reciting the Diamond Sutra day and night. She happened to fall ill with a fistula, and her suffering was severe. Her daughter-in-law, née Feng, was by nature perfectly filial, and vowed to take the illness upon herself. So she embroidered an image of Guanyin, for three years without slackening, and completed more than twenty scrolls. The mother’s illness indeed was cured, and her step was better than before; the daughter-in-law, however, fell ill and died. The mother thinks of her daughter-in-law’s words and laughter as if she were still alive. Her son Xishu begs that a praise be made for her. The praise says:

With unconditioned compassion his body is everywhere, entering the minds of living beings as a needle draws thread. The daughter-in-law took on her mother-in-law’s illness and embroidered the Great Being’s body; it answered as her hand moved, like shadow and form. The mother-in-law’s illness was cured, and the daughter-in-law died. This is enough to show that the essence is one: there was never any this or that. The daughter-in-law relied on the Great Being, and in death too she is not extinguished — thread by thread, line by line, she puts forth the broad and long tongue.

The Dharma body is originally without form; form follows living beings and comes to be. When the delusive thoughts of living beings arise, the Dharma body at once appears. Therefore this person of mind, recalling no other matter, fixes wholly on the wondrous Dharma body, bright and pure as undyed silk. Then with the needle of contemplation he draws along the thread of delusive thought: thought after thought pierces the Dharma body, thread after thread completes the wondrous marks. When sincerity enters the subtle and minute, not a hair’s breadth leaks away. Solemnly, upon the ground of the one true, he conjures forth the formless body, perfects the pure mind, and accomplishes the faculty of perfect penetration. Therefore I look up and rely on him, and at once enter the inconceivable.
Praise of the Embroidered Great Being Crossing the Sea

In the sea of the three poisons, when the waves are at their worst, he walks upon the crown of his head and his feet stay perfectly dry. Entering the minds of living beings, he is nowhere absent; from a thread of delusive thought the Dharma body appears. Thought after thought is not in vain, mind after mind must pierce through. The universal gate reveals itself, and of itself it is accomplished.
Praise of the Thousand-Armed Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, with a Preface

The layman Zheng Fa of Goulou, through the conditions of past habit, bowed single-mindedly in reverence to the Thousand-Armed Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, holding the sacred mantra in his heart, diligent and unwearied for many years, hoping to rely on the awesome spirit and accomplish it within one lifetime. He reflected that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas save living beings by no fixed method: as one drowning in the great sea, whatever he finds to cling to, he will surely reach the farther shore; and as the many grasses of the snowy mountains are all of them medicine. Know then that if a living being can wish to escape birth and death, whether he practices Chan, recites the Buddha’s name, holds mantras, or reads sutras, so long as he can truly believe in his own mind and stand firm without retreating, there is none who will not escape birth and death — how much more when he relies on the power of the Great Being’s same-essence great compassion and the power of the sacred mantra? How could it not be accomplished in one lifetime? The layman came to Mount Kuang to consult this old man for instruction; since there was no Dharma to speak, I made this praise and gave it to him. If one understands the purport that light and darkness are not two, then the paths of sage and ordinary being are cut off, and the feelings of birth and death wither. Then, in daily use, in every instance and in every hair’s pore, all is the time of the Great Being’s hands and eyes, blazing with radiance. The layman should contemplate in this way: the one mind is complete in itself and borrows nothing from outside. The praise says:

The afflictions of living beings number eighty-four thousand; because of darkness they revolve through the six paths. In the Great Being’s body they become hands and eyes; the radiance of every hair’s pore turns along with the darkness. Therefore when living beings have suffering they must call out; the answer comes with the call, and the darkness is suddenly gone. Living beings and the Great Being were never two things: light comes and darkness goes, and it appears at the very thought. All the wise seek only within themselves; the two paths of ordinary being and sage were never this or that. As a lamp breaks the darkness, neither reaches the other; because they are not two, one sees the wonder. If one can contemplate thus, the Great Being is oneself; to bow and hold the name is as water entering water. Only take the suffering of beings at its utmost and lift it up: radiance shines forth, undiminished day and night.
Praise of the Four-Armed Guanyin

Hands and eyes filling the whole body — why only four? Within the inexhaustible he lets it be merely thus. The jewel scepter empties demons; the true sutra has no words. All of it is spiritual power, an inconceivable matter.
In Reverence to the Great Being, the Tathagata in the Sky

The Tathagata in the sky, whence does he appear? Just at this moment he stands face to face with the Great Being. Having become Buddha long ago, why bow to another? By revealing him one reveals oneself. After all, how is it? Manifestation is not one; bowing and mindfulness are not two. He universally manifests a physical body — truly inconceivable.
Praise of the Great Being of the Fire-Light Samadhi

The light of prajna is like a towering blaze; within it the Great Being enters the ground of coolness. The afflictions of living beings are themselves this prajna light; therefore the Great Being’s wondrous response is without fixed direction.
Praise of Bodhisattva Jeweled Palm

Asked who he was, he called himself Jeweled Palm; he stretched his hand and brushed the sky, and suddenly it gave a sound. What is heard in an empty sound? What is touched when the hand brushes? Should he meet a venomous dragon, he could not draw his hand back in time.
Praise of Cundi Bodhisattva

I have heard that the place where all Buddhas are born comes from the subtle and secret seal. The secret seal is the mind of all Buddhas, scattered into the delusive dreams of living beings. If the dreams are shattered, the Buddhas appear, as sunlight is seen in the cold sky; if the clouds of living beings’ afflictions are shattered, it is revealed by reliance on the Tathagata’s secret mantra power. To hold the mantra is to hold the mind of all Buddhas; my own mind was originally the secret mantra. The meeting of the three conditions is fundamentally not two; therefore a single thought is wholly complete. If only one can keep it ever present in daily use, like a child who, having found its mother, will not leave her — the Buddha-mind has already entered the mantra-holding mind, and one need not seek the Buddha to be liberated of oneself.
Praise of Bodhisattva Sunlight, with a Preface

Guangfu Temple on Guanyin Mountain, east of the town of Qu’e, was founded by a divine monk of the Song, who was named Bodhisattva Sunlight. The Bodhisattva first appeared as an elder monk of contrary conduct who paid no heed to the precepts, and his contemporaries despised him; when they further reproached him for building a monastery, he appeared in body in place after place and gathered alms all at once, so that those who went looking for his traces found he had still not left the temple gate. All quarters were moved and thought him strange, and so a precious monastery was completed. At the end of his life he revealed his own name, and to this day he is called Bodhisattva Sunlight. The temple fell into ruin; its abbot Tong Ta restored it anew, set up an image and enshrined it, and asked me for a praise. The praise says:

The sun alone in the sky shines bright and clear; mountain and river, deep valley — there is no place it does not light. Defilement cannot muddy it, fair weather cannot dim it. It is like a reflection in water, like a trace within a shadow. The mind that dwells in living beings is supremely divine and spiritual; it is not two with the Buddha — how much less so in a monk? The lotus rises from the mud, fragrant and pure, unstained; the mani jewel lies in filth, its radiance undiminished. Therefore the perfected one transcends and is utterly free of defilement; he does not dwell in the body — how could he be bound by ordinary or sage? He breaks the rules of deportment and shows himself at play. Fleshly eyes cling to appearances and do not know who he is. He does not leave his courtyard, yet his body fills the ten directions; he was never coming or going — like the light of the sun. Even one born blind relies on it to do his work. Adornment of form and appearance is still but spittle; his traces are like space, his response like the wind. He reveals himself wherever he is, and without appointment all is the same. One day is a thousand ages; one mind is ten thousand kalpas. Therefore the Great Being’s spirit is never exhausted.
Praise of Vimalakirti at Play in the Garden

He does not see a Pure Land, and so does not love to dwell there; he does not see a defiled land, and so does not loathe to live there. Monk or layman? A form to be seen: is it real or empty? Men and women mingled together: is it so or not? His mouth is vast as space, his tongue vast as his mouth; he does not know how to preach the Dharma, so he hides his shame in silence. His body is not ill, yet by illness he makes his body ill. Were this not borrowed play, it would be enough to make one die of laughter. Manjushri had not yet come, and so he arranged and waited; when at last he arrived, it was a whole debacle. For a thousand ages he has been duped, and those who see him measure and reckon. It is not the World-Honored One — hard indeed to grope for. The thirty-two were all made sport of. Luckily there was Manjushri, idly tearing and teasing. I do not know him, and he does not know me; let us wait until Maitreya is born, and when it is seen through, only then will the crowd disperse.
Praise of the Venerable Kaundinya

The elephant king roams abroad, and the elephant calf follows after. Like calls to like; meeting conditions, they gather. Though the enmity between them was heaviest, in the Way they are the closest kin. As two carts make the same ruts, surely there is a cause.
Praise of the Portraits of the Thirty-Three Patriarchs
The First Patriarch, the Venerable Mahakasyapa

A golden-hued form, a diamond heart; he upheld the wisdom-life and ever turned the Dharma wheel. When the World-Honored One twirled the flower, he broke into a smile — and to this day it leaves people unable to conceive or speak of it.
The Second Patriarch, the Venerable Ānanda

His vast learning was like the sea, drinking in and drawing up the stream of Dharma. All Buddhas, as they come and go, never leave his tongue. He blows the reed-pipe of Dharma transformation, and beat by beat it becomes a command. Therefore my Teacher is the one who is the true within the partial.
The Third Patriarch, the Venerable Sanakavasa

His prajna root had been realized in a former life; therefore when the Master was about to appear, the auspicious grass first answered. Mind seals mind, as fire casts into fire; meeting on a narrow path, there is surely nowhere to hide.
The Fourth Patriarch, the Venerable Upagupta

When one man’s mind becomes empty, the demon palaces tremble. Grasping the diamond blade, who dares trifle with him? If he would but turn the light around, the wild mind is stilled in an instant; bowing in refuge, all his transgressions are wiped away.
The Fifth Patriarch, the Venerable Nadi-Daśika

He had already awakened to the original mind, as sunlight shines through night. He shows the dream of birth and death, and his radiance surpasses it. The Master’s Dharma was originally nothing; my mind does not exist. As space meets space, his tongue never leaves his mouth.
The Sixth Patriarch, the Venerable Michaka

For this alone he came; for no other matter. Meeting in the bustling market, he reveals his own vessel of himself. The prefect saw what had not yet come to be, and knew this day beforehand. When one is to do business, one does not haggle over the price.
The Seventh Patriarch, the Venerable Vasumitra

He came by a familiar road and suddenly met a friend and kin. In a single word they discussed the truth, and at once he knew what he had not had before. He begged for the taste of sweet dew, and the Master showed him the Dharma of emptiness. If one claims to have gained something, he falls in with seven, falls in with eight.
The Eighth Patriarch, the Venerable Buddhanandi

It is not that he does not speak — it is that speech cannot reach it. It is not that he does not act — there was never any trace. Now that he has met the right man, only then may he open his mouth. From there he simply goes on, and does not fall into the old ruts.
The Ninth Patriarch, the Venerable Buddhamitra

He dwelt in his mother’s womb for sixty years, waiting only for the Master to come and so fulfill the former cause. The radiance on his crown was originally his own; let it be scraped once and it shines through — like a lion’s roar.
The Tenth Patriarch, the Venerable Pārśva

He pointed at the ground and it turned to gold, appearing at the movement of his hand. The sage at once drew near — what ease, what swiftness! He is like an empty valley that answers every sound with an echo. Know then that my own mind was never coming or going.
The Eleventh Patriarch, the Venerable Punyayaśas

The Buddha does not know the Buddha; the eye does not see the eye. To seek further from another — and so he met with reproof. He thought himself whole and complete, but was seen through long before. Waking with a start, only then did he know his words had fallen flat.
The Twelfth Patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa

The horse’s mournful cry had a cause of its own. The woman who rose from the earth was not the right person after all. The demon was never a demon, nor the Buddha a Buddha. Looked at with the true eye, what thing is he in the end?
The Thirteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Kapimala

He came from among the heterodox and attained right knowledge and view. Meeting a venomous snake on the road, his compassionate mind appeared. When further he questioned the venomous dragon, both were brought to submission. What the eye sees and the mind knows is like an echo issuing from the valley.
The Fourteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Nāgārjuna

A dragon among dragons, meeting poison with poison. The Venerable Master’s wondrous hand subdued them with a single word. The samadhi of Buddha-nature is in essence like empty space; a hundred thousand Dharma gates all enter within it.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Kanadeva

He dropped a needle into the bowl, wondrously matching the wordless. He revealed the meaning of Buddha-nature, and the full moon appeared before him. Coming to the elder’s house, he used the needle to draw thread: borrowing another’s causal conditions as expedient means for himself.
The Sixteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Rāhulata

Following the stream, he found the source; where the water ended and the mountains ran out, he suddenly met the man and knew him for a sage. Fragrant rice was lifted up and offered, and they shared seats and food. The great assembly drank together, and the sweet dew was like honey.
The Seventeenth Patriarch, the Venerable Saṅghanandi

He took no delight in the royal palace, and heaven opened a single road. Going straight to the exhausted source, he did not know the reason why. Beneath the purple clouds was where the sage dwelt; and in the end he found the boy, who met the profound intent of all Buddhas.
The Eighteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Gayāśata

Born after seven days, he did not fall into the aggregates. His body was fragrant and pure, originally clean. At a single word spoken at the door — “Who is it that answers nothing?” — he was suddenly startled awake, and in that instant knew where to return.
The Nineteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Kumāralāta

Having been born in heaven, he should not have given rise to desire. One thought not yet forgotten, and he was no longer at ease. By the power of prajna he rose again to the Brahma world; so he came to transmit the lamp — that was his family affair.
The Twentieth Patriarch, the Venerable Jayata

The unborn is inherently complete; there is no need to seek the truth. It arises when it meets conditions, as a flower meets spring. Seek it too urgently, and you turn farther from the Way. Know where to return in this instant, and come back along the very road.
The Twenty-First Patriarch, the Venerable Vasubandhu

Light and darkness share one essence; sage and ordinary being are one road. His place of coming was hidden and subtle, and none knew the reason. What is familiar is hard to forget, so he sought a companion further. Suddenly they met, and his willing mind gave its own consent.
The Twenty-Second Patriarch, the Venerable Manorhita

From the time of his prediction he came for no other matter. Like joins with like, and meeting conditions they must encounter each other. Alas, those cranes — they had flown and cried for long; at a single word, he knew at once what he had always had.
The Twenty-Third Patriarch, the Venerable Haklenayaśas

From the summit of Mount Sumeru he brought a golden ring. Alas, those cranes — their plight was pitiable. He got himself a lion cub who gave a great roar; its spirit pierced the heavens, and by it his heirs were tested.
The Twenty-Fourth Patriarch, the Monk Simha

When they met he asked for the pearl, and with an open hand it was there. What had been entrusted before had not long been parted. Knowing there was an old debt, he came expressly to repay it. With his head laid on the blade, white milk flowed out.
The Twenty-Fifth Patriarch, the Venerable Vasiṣṭha

Wielding the sword of prajna and holding the wish-fulfilling pearl, though he came only for a while, this journey was not in vain. By chance he met a wicked man and found in him a fine companion; through the crooked he struck the straight, and both had their advantage.
The Twenty-Sixth Patriarch, the Venerable Punyamitra

From the kshatriya caste he continued the transmission of the lamp’s flame. His true heir was not clear, and he nearly came to ruin; in the bustling market he suddenly met his old friend, and case fitting lid, he got the true one.
The Twenty-Seventh Patriarch, the Venerable Prajñātārā

Do not say there was no cause: meeting, he saw at once. His place of coming was natural, without resort to expedients. Now by means of that pearl he found the right man — digging a pond, he got the moon; buying stones, he got more than clouds.
The Twenty-Eighth Patriarch, the Great Master Bodhidharma

The Master’s mind was in great haste, and he came too early. Not a single word struck home, and his mind was not yet settled. He sat coldly in Shaolin; then he was fortunate to get Shenguang, who lost an arm — and his Way has flourished ever since.
The Twenty-Ninth Patriarch, the Great Master Huike

He came by sea expressly, with how much bitter toil. Within the land of the Great Tang he found only one man. Seeking it, one cannot find it; it is as water taking the shape of the vessel. By this he passed on the family tradition, and so he is the Second.
The Thirtieth Patriarch, the Great Master Sengcan

His whole body was an illness, and he did not know whence it came. Then he suddenly met the King of Physicians and woke with a start to its cause. With mind empty and bones firm he simply took to the road; meeting one of great strength, he handed over the whole load.
The Thirty-First Patriarch, the Great Master Daoxin

He left home while young, of sharp and swift faculties. For more than sixty years his side never touched a mat. Students gathered like clouds; why wait for a child? Because there was a former agreement, though those who looked on did not know it.
The Thirty-Second Patriarch, the Great Master Hongren

His origins were unclear, yet his birth was just right. One matter left unfinished, and both families were settled. In the mountains of Potou, on the road to Huangmei, he came and went freely, bearing the marks of a great man.
The Thirty-Third Patriarch, the Great Master Huineng

He had just thrown down the woodcutter’s axe; a stone was tied to his waist. The root of wisdom had long been planted, and from this it put forth shoots. Its source flows out from Caoxi and runs across the whole earth; to this very day there is no place it is not.
Praise of the Eighteen Arhats, with a Preface

In former days Li Longmian drew the eighteen arhats in fine ink outline, exquisite and inspired, dazzling the eyes of all who saw. Only Zhao Songxue could imitate them and come close to life. In recent times Ding Nanyu of Shexian painted the portraits of the patriarchs and did not yield to the ancients, and his fine outline work too was reckoned excellent. I once asked him to paint a “Crossing and Lifting the Robe” picture, but never obtained it. Lately, in Wuyang, Lord Hou of Nanhai and my friend Wang brought out this scroll and asked for a praise. Unrolled, its radiance dazzles the eye and its spirit and manner surpass the ordinary, as though one were sitting within the Lotus Treasury, hearing the Tathagata teach the Dharma gate of self-nature. On asking who the painter was, it proved to be the student Wang Boyu of Huangmei. Reverently burning incense and bowing my head, I made a praise for the whole of it. The praise says:

Within the realm of purity all wonders are born; the great earth and its mountains and rivers all return to perfect illumination. Fish and shell, feather and fur universally manifest samadhi — why should the arhats alone be thought a rare matter? All the arhats are phantom bodies; seeing them without recognizing them, how can one get their truth? At play in spiritual powers, they cough and spit, shake their arms; they bow and lift, bend and stretch — all are Buddha-work. A lion yawns and groans, or gathers his spirit in wall-gazing; beneath the trees, beside the water, his livelihood is beyond reckoning. Clenching a fist, the hand grows sore; subduing a dragon takes effort. Only let the deluded mind rest, and of itself all is silent and still. Hugging his knees and gazing fixedly, watching the other play his tricks — better to hold the beads and recite the Buddha’s name at ease. Belly bared and beaming, a palm-leaf scripture in his hand; he waves a whisk and talks in silence, striking emptiness so that it sounds. The listener is as though deaf, the speaker as though mute — not like the ordinary man with all his “thees” and “thous.” Weary, he leans on a tall pine, nodding and dozing; he stretches out his hand into space and is suddenly startled awake. Bones thin, brows long, waist bent, legs straight — every step he takes depends wholly on the power that bears him up. Sitting at ease in the quiet of the woods, his mind is idle beyond measure; now and then he looks at a sutra, and at once his words fall flat. One bowl, seven scrolls of the lotus — just this is the treasure; what need of other things? Where he finds his own use, this and nothing more. Dragons and gods revere him, and he takes no joy in it. Let others love or hate, let them bind him as they will: he savors one flavor of following conditions, and his self-nature is liberated. Only at the tip of a hair he manifests this spiritual power: the trace of a fish in the depths, the track of a bird in the air, a form in a mirror, a flower in the sky, a castle in the clouds, the moon in water. Contemplate thus — its wonder cannot be spoken.

The karmic consciousness is not dried up, and they drift upon the sea of poison — fish and turtle, crocodile and dragon, yaksha and ghost and monster. Laughable, you lot! You ride on emptiness with one flavor, not daring to fall in with their kind, and call it spiritual power. Bitterly you are rebuked by the Buddha, and afraid to face Vimalakirti; luckily for you, here you are at leisure and have dodged Huangbo. Vast the long swell, surging the mighty waves — you will not let your body go. What manner of thing is that? You take the dry land for yourself and make others go into the water; even if that is a bargain, how long can it last? Though called a game, in the end it turns to emptiness and deceit. Called and called, you will not turn your head back, and my melancholy only deepens. I shall watch you struggle on until the Dragon Flower Assembly comes. What sort of nose will you show when you meet my own Teacher, the monk?
Further, a Combined Praise in Sequence

Each holds a single sutra, and all of them lie before the eyes; the roads differ, but supporting a household is the same. Squatting on the ground he sits, both eyes staring into space. What has he seen, to set up this style of gate? Beneath the cliff he takes a stump for a bench; the incense spiral rises into the void like clouds making rain. His bones are thin as firewood, his spirit already spent, and still he must read the sutra, and his mind will not rest. His back itches and is hard to scratch, so he idly borrows a hand; where it lands is just the right place, and its wonder cannot be told. What spiritual power has he, hiding a dragon in a bottle? Loosen the hand and let it out, and let it soar as it will. A fierce tiger crouches on the ground, its majesty not to be touched; he exhausts all his strength, like a cat catching a mouse. The sutra is not words, and no few bear it: do not say that the eyes are weary and drowsiness is no good. A sound is made in the ear, as though there were some thing; and when you reach for it, you cannot get it out. The bright moon is in the sky, and he sits hugging his knees. Such leisure — what joy! His long brows hang heavy and keep veiling his eyes; his old hands have no strength, and turning the scroll costs him dear. His belly is too big to hide, and a fine sloven he looks; only let it go, and he is light and quick. In a patched and faded robe, he takes pains to mend it piece by piece; every stitch and every thread, such hardship. Holding a bright mirror, he sees his own ugliness; then he meets a lion, and it gives a single roar. They cross the water together, heels to the very bottom — what need is there to burden others, to burden ghosts?
Further, a Combined Praise on the Picture of Play in the Garden

My Teacher’s spiritual power — of himself he has limited store, and relies wholly on everyone, heads together and faces gathered. A dragon cannot be tamed; on this one bowl they rely — were it not for these, they would draw in hand and foot. The hand counts the prayer beads, and by this feigns reciting the Buddha’s name; giving up oneself to follow others only shows up the muddle. Holding a single stick of incense, whom does he make offering to? Conditioned merit is not as good as the unconditioned. Raised fists and clasped palms exchange mutual respect; facing the mirror he sees a head, and empty sound answers the valley. His hand holds the wish-fulfilling jewel — it was not without intent; look at what there was before he held it. Turn the head sharply — why keep looking back? To wait for a companion to walk with one is no longer a bold stride. Within the water vessel no pouring is seen; one thinks it must be glass holding sweet dew inside. In youth he did not strive, in age his mind is not at rest; he raises his brows and still must read the sutra. Seen from my side, all of this is a display of folly: though he can ride the clouds, he has not left the old nest. Those before have gone, those behind have not yet come; unable to keep pace, he cannot help but brood. He walks quickly and cannot move — fearing the sky will rain, he first puts on a bamboo hat, adding hardship to hardship. The palm-leaf leaves are without writing, the true sutra is without words; he only understands reciting with the mouth and does not know the mind’s awakening. Because the other has dust, he holds the white whisk; that one is pure and this one defiled, and both are wanting. Raised fists and clasped palms, walking together or going alone — look at his wish-fulfilling jewel: it is just right for scratching an itch. The head of the white feather fan is pure as snow; he has already cut off affliction, so why is he still hot? Let him ask the bowl whether there is any rice in it: if hunger comes, the donor will provide. A fierce tiger’s claws and fangs open a bloody mouth; fortunately it met my Teacher, and was tamed and went off. A single scroll of the true sutra holds immeasurable meaning; before it is unrolled, he has already seen the truth. All these many games are empty and deceitful; just look at empty space — what manner of thing is it?
Further, a Praise on the Picture of Crossing the Sea

The sea of suffering is boundless, and the wicked waves beat the sky; he crosses straight over, body laid across — who dares be first? Only the Venerable Ones, at ease in their spiritual powers, stake their lives without a thought and go on and take no harm. Because I am empty, nothing harms me; within and without there is nothing, and so there is nothing to cast off. They look on the abyss as a ridge, and tread the perilous as level; they arrive as their minds wish, and their eyes rest on it unalarmed. Though there be crocodiles, yakshas, ghosts and monsters, all are used by me, because I am utterly beyond opposites. Know then that the perfected one, dwelling amid birth and death, does not contend with things, and no thing fails to receive him. Seen in this light, the Dharma is fundamentally quiescent: only do not give rise to a mind, and it is called perfection beyond compare.
Further, a Praise of Each According to His Posture
One figure raises a vajra tower in his right hand, while his left palm is held upright as though engaged in contemplation.
With the vajra tower he gives some token of this mind; the upright palm and close contemplation — the thought and remembrance are profound.
Two old men, ill, lean on a staff; a boy pounds medicine
If this body were not, where could sickness rise? / The remedy for it—I know not its name.
Three: holding the ruyi scepter, sitting calm and at ease
He holds the ruyi; the ruyi burdens his hand. / Silently he looks within—what is there, after all?
Four: lifting the bowl and reaching into space, as if to take something
Nothing was there to begin with; in emptiness he seeks in vain. / Seeking what cannot be found, is he not ashamed?
Five and six: old men so gaunt they seem too frail for their robes, leaning on a youth who drags them along
Old and thin, too weak to walk; he should rest. / Why burden the boy, who tugs and strains?
Seven: holding pattra leaves, walking fast, looking back at the old man as if waiting for something
Walking alone is quick and easy, yet he frets for another. / The pattra leaves in his hand were nearly dropped.
Eight and nine: old men going ahead on staves, a boy carrying incense behind them as an offering, a ghost nearby in a posture of refuge
His steps are hard; his reliance is the boy. / This one stick of incense is not for the mountain ghost.
Ten: flying through the air on his staff, startling the mountain god; the Elder walks slowly, turning his head to look back
His staff flies up through empty space; the mountain god starts up. / Stay a while, Master—the Dharma banner stands here.
Eleven: Taming the Dragon
Because the dragon's nature is fierce, the Master showed his rougher art; / he only tames its nature—he does not take its pearl.
Twelve: Old and strengthless, his hand resting on a lone pine
A lifetime of pilgrimage; now he is old. / His body like a withered pine, his mind like still water.
Thirteen: Subduing the Tiger
The fierce tiger in the hills shakes the woods with dread; / our Master's Way is high—of itself it tames and bows him.
Fourteen: Reading the Sutra
The true sutra has no words; cowhide covers the eyes. / Pierce it through—till then he cannot be bold.
Fifteen: At ease in Chan, a macaque offers fruit
Still and plain, with nothing in his breast. / The macaque is wildest of all, yet even it knows to yield.
Sixteen: Mending his robe in the morning sun. Seventeen: belly bared, facing each other, they only smile and look
The needle-and-thread craft is indeed fine and close; / but seen with a wide eye, it is still a strain.
Eighteen: Sitting upright in Chan samādhi
The place of great rest—calm and free. / Looking on with cool eyes, all of it is conjuring.
This monk is laughable—he cannot bear to stay idle. / Both hands grope and rub; no one knows why.
The Buddha's precepts and deportment are grave and dignified; / with fists flailing and feet kicking, it is most unseemly.
Dry sitting and wall-gazing are his own true calling; / stretching and yawning like this, one thinks his heart is dull.
Fierce courage has come to this: bow broken, arrows spent. / Still he clenches an empty fist—rage wasted in vain.
The kāṣāya is on his body, free from the first; / to add massage to it looks like conjuring.
Hands stretched out, feet drawn in, groping left and right. / There is one thing that was there all along—yet he cannot grasp it.
Begging in the street, he lost a thing. / He searches and cannot find it, beating his breast and stamping his feet.
He will not lie down to sleep, but goes to play with stones. / If he cracks his hand, he will have a heap of trouble.
Beating his back with a backward hand, he must have a pain in his spine. / The young feel nothing; in old age it grows heavy.
Upright as a lone pine—that is a monk's true model. / Carrying on like a child at play, what manner is this?
Both hands clasp his head—old age is doddering. / If not palsy, then it is deafness.
The Elder's countenance is most refined and grave, / yet his heels show—these little things fall short.
Waking from a doze, the dream not yet shaken off, / eyes wide open, he drives a peg into empty space.
Who is chasing him, with anger filling his belly? / Hurrying in a fluster, afraid of being caught.
He is unskilled at walking meditation; on level ground he stumbles. / Though he leaps up, the loss is already done.
Four limbs drawn in like fists, a hundred bones like cotton— / he must have met cold weather, frozen and starved.
May I ask the Elder how many years he has seen? / Just look at his two brows—few in the world have such.
He was steady to begin with, yet he seeks work for himself, / like a boat in the waves—whose fault is that?
One: A pair of sutras and incense in the censer, sitting upright and still
Sitting still, conditions forgotten, without thought or care. / Sutras and censer incense are idle furnishings.
Two: Reading the Sutra
Holding one scroll of sutra, his aim is to cover his eyes. / If he pierces the cowhide, he will patch the long with the short.
Three: Walking with his staff slung across his shoulder
His staff slung across, he walks alone, he steps alone. / Just go straight on—why look back?
Four: Leaning on his staff, gazing at the waterfall
Leaning on his staff, idly watching a thousand-fathom waterfall. / Ask where it comes from—he does not know the reason.
Five: Stroking a deer, sitting to watch butterflies
The deer has forgotten its wariness and comes to sit beside him. / The butterflies flutter on—his fevered dream is not yet broken.
Six: Holding the ruyi scepter, sitting with belly bared
Belly bared and slumped, having nothing at all. / A pity he has not forgotten the hand that holds the ruyi.
Seven: Walking with a sutra scroll in hand
Having entered liberation, with no hindrance and no tie, / this little thing in his hand becomes mere talk.
Eight: Sitting beneath peach blossoms, turning his head to read the sutra
Under the blossoms he looks closely—surely not for anything else: / he would have people know that emptiness itself is form.
Nine: Reaching into the bowl to scoop the moon
There is water in the bowl, and in the water a moon. / He reaches out to grab it—and in the end gets nothing.
Ten: Bowing to the distant sky
Bowing on level ground, with nothing before his eyes. / Do not take the void to be the Dharma-body Buddha.
The dragon among the clouds transforms at will. / Why subdue it, and turn it into conjuring?
Twelve: Stroking a tree and gazing at the spring
Alone he strokes a withered stump, quietly watching the flowing water. / Of all the idle folk in the world, none is idler than he.
Thirteen: Looking up at high mountains and flowing water
Flowing water and high mountains—few are those who understand. / Our Master has grasped it, beyond all expectation.
Fourteen: Leaning on his staff, walking at leisure
Leaning on his staff he strolls, stepping freely along. / In this world there are few such monks with nothing to do.
Fifteen: Riding a tiger
A fierce tiger is hard to tame; all who see it flee. / Our Master straddles it as if it were child's play.
Sixteen: Sitting to watch the moon in the water
Bright moon on the cold pool, its light shining through and through. / To plant a foot in this turns into mere dust.
Seventeen: Pointing at the sky with his finger
He points at the sky with his hand—what is there in the sky? / Though he points it out, it seems to air the family shame.
Eighteen: Holding his staff, sitting on a great rock
He has come to forgetting altogether, happy beyond compare. / The staff in his hand—why not put it down?
Also: Eulogy on the Golden-Line Painting of the Eighteen Elders Riding Beasts at Play

The three poisons are cleared away, birth and death no longer bind him; / thus he gains spiritual powers and sports at ease. / Fierce beasts and glaring dragons, each and every one is tamed; / he rides them as he pleases and lets them gallop where they will. / Because he himself has forgotten contrivance, creatures too forget him; / both are forgotten together, like fire entering fire. / He wanders through the ten directions, coming and going without hindrance; / those who do not know him are startled when they see. / This deceives only the foolish—it cannot escape the eye of wisdom. / Should he meet Vimalakīrti, he would surely be taken to task. / To give rise to false discrimination in the midst of emptiness— / even if it be gold dust, it is still a speck in the eye.
Eulogy on the Picture of the Sixteen Elders, the True-Being Arhats
About to go, yet not going, as if pondering something. / For whom does he ponder? Our Master himself knows.
His staff slung across, his bundle carried on his back, / suddenly he turns his head—just this is it.
Standing with a hollow ring of footsteps, gazing as if something were lost. / Lifting a hand toward the distant sky—who is it facing him?
Bones thin as firewood, robe loose as a sack. / Were he not forgetful of form, who could bear such a wrap?
The water in the bowl, the dragon in the sky, / the hand that seizes the clouds—another display of spiritual power.
Sitting there stiff and still, half resentful, half pondering. / The bowl's water is clear and calm—who is it that drops in a needle?
Drifting as if mad, startled as if angry. / Even if he is without intent, he still falls to watching and waiting.
A fierce tiger is easy to tame; a deluded mind is hard to unloose. / Were it not for our Master, it would nearly come to ruin.
Bones thin, spirit weary, his long brows a great burden. / All day he pushes at them, his arm aching and strengthless.
Shrinking from the cold, he pulls his robe about him, hugging his knees as if in thought. / He turns his head away—what is there to think about?
Things that are in emptiness contend with you for nothing. / To seek them without cause—can that be called sage?
Bending low, head bowed, palms joined toward the sky: / because he sees the Dharma-body, he pays homage to the true form.
His bamboo hat like emptiness, his staff like a dragon, / he roams beyond all things and in an instant sheds the cage.
The vase holds nothing to begin with—where do these strange lights come from? / He lets them out and gathers them himself, with no one to tend them.
Both hands wrestle empty air, both feet hurry along. / Though he bustles for another, he displays his own shame.
Hooded under his patchwork quilt, he steals a cold-eyed glance. / Where the incense smoke rises—just that is it.
Eulogy on the Fourteen Elders
One: Hooded in a patchwork robe, palms joined, head bowed
Hooded in one robe, he sits through all conditions. / Palms joined and head bowed, thus he receives in faith.
Two: Subduing a lion, holding its cub, urging it to spring
The lion springs with mighty power. / To snatch its cub—will it not leap back?
Three: Planting his staff, raising his fist, walking alone, stepping alone
One staff props up the sky; two fists grip bone. / His Dharma power is boundless—he chants Namo Buddha.
Four: Three men sitting together, as if preaching the Dharma
Speaking without a tongue, hearing without ears. / The sound of Dharma is like thunder—no one will believe it.
Five: Sitting upright in silence
Delusions from kalpas past are unseen in the bustle; / but when he sits in silence, they all appear at once.
Six: Chan Samādhi
His robe is like emptiness, his spine like iron. / Sitting through the ten directions, he ends up with a branded brow.
Seven: Lifting the Bowl
Both hands lift the bowl, offering up the whole tray. / Look closely, all of you—what is there inside?
Eight: Great belly, bare midriff
A great belly is hard to hide; long feet are hard to draw in. / You have taken a dislike of your own—it is no fault of mine.
Nine: Reading the sutra under the moon
The moonlight is bright as day; old eyes are not sleepy. / He rises to recite the sutra, taking it to relieve his gloom.
Ten: Spreading his sitting cloth and taking his seat
He unrolls his sitting mat and loosens his robe a little. This is no sitting meditation — he stretches and yawns with his whole body.
Eleven: Wandering with a Cloth Bag
A cloth bag dangling from his shoulder, a staff gripped in his hand — wandering about like this, he is a sight both hateful and absurd.
Twelve: Holding the Ruyi Scepter
His hand grips the ruyi scepter, yet the scepter only burdens the hand; he wears the sangha robe merely to cover his ugliness.
Thirteen: Holding the Beads and Reciting the Buddha's Name
The Buddha recites the Buddha's own name — where can one hide? Seeking the self by means of the self — why should that be impossible?
Fourteen: Snapping a Reed to Cross the River
The sea of suffering has no shore, and the feet find no firm ground; leaning on a single leaf, he reaches the other shore.
The sea of suffering is boundless, and a lotus leaf becomes his boat; trusting his very life to it, he is old and knows no shame.
The aggregates are empty, yet he clings to the body; the mind is empty, yet he grasps at a solid form — so upside down as this, do not say he does not know it.
In his hand a ruyi scepter, beneath his feet a reed leaf; bustling and fretting, when will he ever rest?
He fears the monsters in the sea and treads upon a vajra club; fists clenched and eyes glaring, as though he had met a tiger.
Light streams out in empty space, scriptures lie beneath his feet; he laughs at the faults of others — how could he be called a monk?
Measuring the sea with a shell, seeking spring upon a branch — the truth stands before his face and he does not see it; how could he be named an Arhat?
Pouring out the sea and moving mountains, stretching out a hand and drawing back a foot — such sovereign powers of miracle: who would dare dispute them?
Let him plant his own feet on solid ground and watch where he steps down; steady and sure as he is, no one is craftier than you.
The nature of the divine dragon cannot be touched; but first seize its pearl, and so it dares not resist.
Here in the great ocean he has found the shallows; calling to mind Bodhisattva Guanyin, he is rescued in time.
Bliss he will not accept, so he lets others drag him along; old as he is, he still knows nothing of ease.
Head covered by a patched quilt, so blissful he could die; let others have their miracles — none of them comes close to you.
Verses on the Twelve Arhats Wading and Lifting Their Robes
1. Gathering His Robe to Cross the Water
Wandering on foot he meets a river, and his road has gone wrong; with nowhere to turn aside, he simply has to cross.
2. One Who Can Wade Carries One Who Cannot
The bold one knows no fear, the timid one fears a fall; but since he is willing to shoulder the other, both come off well.
3. The One Who Reached the Shore First Offers His Staff to the One Who Cannot
Nine parts of ten are crossed, only a single step remains; thanks to that staff, he has no small support.
Already on the far shore, he turns back to look at his companion; pulling him up at the very last — how skillful a means.
5. Robes Soaked from the Crossing, a Boy Wrings Them Out
Not knowing the water's depth, he strides in carelessly; soaked through his clothes, he ends up burdening someone else.
6. Reaching the Tree, He Takes Off His Robe and Ties It Up
His clothes are a tangled mess, sunk in mud and water; though he only dragged them across, he must weary himself tying them up.
7. Sitting Barefoot beneath the Tree, He Sneezes and Shakes Off Drowsiness
All his strength is spent, so he sits at ease and dozes; his nostrils turn up toward the sky, and one sneeze wakes him at once.
8. Tired in Spirit and Weary in Body, He Looks Up at the Dozing One
Though his spirit is weary, his two eyes are still open; he watches that drowsy fellow, who is quite muddle-headed.
9. Tying His Skirt
Just as he was wading, he feared the skirt would wrap around him; having taken it off and then put it on again, his effort was all in vain.
10. Leaning on His Staff, He Sits with Legs Spread Wide
Sitting with legs spread wide upon the rock, his spirit is open and expansive; fatigue is forgotten, and he is wholly at ease.
11. Sitting at Leisure, He Scratches an Itch with His Ruyi Scepter
