The place where he itches, no one else can know; with the ruyi scepter in hand, he scratches it as he pleases.
12. Sitting Upright on His Staff, He Turns to Watch a Younger Monk with Bundle and Bowl
Now that he has come to the place of rest, why not simply put it all down? But he keeps the other burdened with a bundle — how utterly muddled.
Verse in Praise of the Arhat Mending His Robe
Torn and tattered all over, it must be mended anew; to the craft of needle and thread he does not begrudge his toil.

One worn-out robe, a hundred patches and a thousand mendings; stitch by stitch he labors hard. Every stitch must pierce through — if it does not pierce, he will not stop. Yet even when the mending is done, it serves only to cover his head.
The Arhat Reading the Sutras
He has not yet understood himself, yet he burrows into old paper; within the realm of purity he turns up nothing but dregs.

Born unable to read a word, he forces himself to study the sutras; deaf of ear and dim of eye, to whom can he tell what he finds? The Sanskrit leaves have lain for years, bored through by worms; the strokes of the letters are untrue — all of it is a leaking of secrets.
Verse in Praise of the Arhat Who Subdues the Dragon
That creature so full of wrath cannot be seized by force; with wholehearted compassion alone, he fixes his contemplation upon it.
The black dragon lies fast asleep and its pearl is stolen by the master; were it to wake, how could it let the matter rest?
Verse in Praise of the Arhat Who Tames the Tiger
Its fierce nature is hard to tame, its power and ferocity unmatched; the master gives up his whole body and spends all his spiritual strength.
Claws and fangs are already bared, its savage temper not yet spent; were it not for our master, the town would have been terrified.
Verse in Praise of the Arhat Who Trains the Lion
Claws and fangs of the Dharma cave — who would dare lay a hand on them? Our master's spiritual power treats them as a plaything.
Verse in Praise of the Arhat Who Floats upon the Sea

The sea of karma is boundless, surging without cease; straight across he climbs to the other shore on a single blue lotus leaf. This body is no body, yet it shoulders the khakkhara staff. Empty water joins the sky, and the mark of no-mark is shown. Emptiness is not outside the existent; beyond the water there is no flowing. Who can give one shout and cut off both ends? Trample the vast void, kick over the ocean; the thread snaps at the heel, and the mind has no hindrance.
Verse in Praise of the Arhat Who Crosses the River
He crosses the stream of ignorance, yet is still halfway along; his deluded thoughts are not yet cut off — a gourd bobbing on the water.
Cutting off the current and passing over, he could surely transcend; why then must he rely on a single pattra leaf?
The banana tree's trunk is hollow stuff, quick to rot though it is; had he not borrowed another's aid, he would almost have been shamed.
His footing is not yet firm, the clay vessel is not strong; rocking and swaying, he is fortunate to come through whole.
Going on alone would have been the end of it; why turn his head? If he must wait for a companion, he will only grumble and mutter.
A pattra leaf rests in his palm, blue eyes prop up the sky; striding high and walking alone, our master is still a dragon.
Verse in Praise of the Arhat Burning Incense

The old do not rest their minds, the young do not strive; he pokes the fire and burns incense, never letting a single breath go idle. Nothing was ever the matter, yet he seeks out busyness himself — how will he ever arrive in the land of no-birth?
The Dream Wanderings of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Thirty-Five
Verse in Praise of Master Bodhidharma Crossing the River

He came west ten thousand li — for what matter, truly? When old Emperor Wu first saw him, doubt still lingered in his breast. Not one word struck home, so he swung his sleeve and took his leave. Snapping off a single reed, he meant to stretch it across the great earth; nine years sitting facing the wall, silent and without a trace of interest. He won but one arm of Shenguang, and his whole body was transformed into a mass of light. Meeting thus, no need to ask about the road ahead — a true man has his own ambition to pierce the heavens.

He did not come for nothing; there was a matter in his breast. Meeting no one who could receive it, he swallowed his voice and held his breath. Brushing off his robe, he went his way without a single backward glance; across the surging Yangtze he cut the current and crossed. Snapping a reed in two, five leaves floated in the sky — a mere substitute for walking, how could it be a miracle? His road ahead was undecided, and he knew not where he was bound; who would have guessed that before the Shaoshi cliff he would fall into nine more years of idle fancy?

He came seeking one who would understand, but met without meeting. Not one word struck home, so he withdrew and went his way. Snapping a reed, he crossed the long river, his feet never touching the ground. Had it not been for the Shaoshi cliff, he would have suffered a great loss. Fortunately he found a true-hearted one to cover his shame a little. He has cheated those who came after into calling it the meaning of coming from the West.
Another: Verse on the Half Shadow
In form he resembles a gray hawk; in mind he is like one seizing a hare. It is not that he has no body — he simply will not reveal it all.
Another: Verse on His Return to the West

He came in too great a hurry and returned too swiftly, his spirit worn and his face ashamed. All he left behind was one broken shoe, with skin but no bone. See him go back to face his venerable mother — what words will he bring her in report? Ah, ha ha. Was it unjust or not? He has set his descendants to weeping at the empty sky.

This matter is every person's own portion — why trouble to come specially from the West? He thought only to bring his capital and seek profit; who knew he would instead meet with doubt and suspicion? Returning home, he is desolate with boundless longing; only on reaching home does he regret coming back empty-handed.
Another: Verse on the Embroidered Portrait

Fundamentally he has no face, so the needlework is wasted effort; yet stitched through and through, not a hair is missing. Even so it is only his whole body, and one gets but half of him. On the Liang king's hall, by the Shaoshi cliff — surely there was nothing like this, with all its calculations. People say it is the first patriarch come from the West; I say it is a grandmotherly heart appearing in the world.
Another: Verse in Praise of Master Bodhidharma

One heart and one loyal gut, he came from afar for the great matter. Meeting no one of the true kind, he found little to interest him. Nine years sitting facing the wall, ice withered and snow grown old; without the man who cut off his own arm, this mind would never have been settled. It was only because he himself had hurried at the start that today he knows he came too early.

He came from very far, his heart bore very great bitterness. Meeting no master of the craft, he met with much scorn. Once his Way shone forth, its grace spread ever wider. His life hung by a thread on a single reed, yet he won descendants beyond counting. The whole heaven and the whole earth all take refuge in him — this is our master, the true first patriarch.

A matter lay in his heart, and he could not hold back his laughter. Ten myriad li from the West he came — who was there to understand him? Not one word matched, and so nine years facing the wall. Had it not been for Shenguang, he would nearly have come to ruin. The sea of suffering has no shore, its waves churn up the heavens; think of it and you fall, tread on it and you perish. Five leaves float in the air, one flower unchanged — from this we know our master is still present today.

His spirit covered heaven and earth, his mind embraced the six directions. Ten myriad li to the West he came, expressly for this one matter. It was not that he would not shoulder it; he simply had no taste for groping about. Not one word matched, so he crossed the river — and crossing water, how could his feet stay dry? Nine years facing the wall, cold and joyless, until he tricked Shenguang into dropping an arm. To this day the great earth runs with blood, and boundless family treasure has been cast away. People say it is the direct pointing and single transmission; I say it is the idle man making his living.

Blue-eyed barbarian, blue-eyed barbarian, ten myriad li you came — for what? Not one word matched, so you snapped a reed in haste and turned away your head, shaming me to death. On Songshan's stone chamber the ice and snow have withered; nine years facing the wall, your lips protrude in silence. Neither joy nor care, how lonely is your heart? Suddenly you open both eyes, and both are blurred. Asked who this stander is, a disciple of whom — he means to open his mouth and loses his life. One arm falls, and his heart and gall revive; the dripping blood runs across rivers and lakes. And tell me, who is there who does not have this matter? I ask you, why did you not finish it?

He came expressly for this, and found no one though he sought. Hastily he snapped a reed and withdrew at once. Before the Shaoshi cliff there was no flavor at all; thanks to Shenguang, he breathed out a little of his spirit. He barely left behind one stinking leather shoe, and his descendants complain that it is broken. How much better had he never come at all: the long sky's bright moon without the least film of cloud.

His going was too swift, his coming was too early; few there are who know him, and he only adds to his vexation. Had it not been for the Shaoshi cliff, this mind of his would nearly never have been settled. Though it is called the direct pointing and single transmission, in the end it only circled outside the gate. His descendants down to this day spread it abroad, and the family treasure has been scattered without stint. Hm! The east wind blows open the spring upon the trees; fallen blossoms cover the ground, and no one sweeps them.
Another: Verse in Praise of Master Bodhidharma in the Stone Chamber

In the gray-blue stone chamber he sat nine years facing the wall. It was not that he had no mind; he simply did not know. Utterly bored, with nothing certain to grasp. He waited until Shenguang's snow reached his waist, and out of empty space one word brought ruin. Five leaves bloomed and spring covered the earth; to this day the eyes are filled with thorns.
Another Verse of Praise
Since he came empty-handed, what is in his bundle? Take it for stolen goods and it becomes a smear of poison. Unable to explain himself, he bears the grievance to this day.
Verse in Praise of the Flesh Body of Master Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch

One yang returns, and warm breath gradually arrives; three yangs are complete, and all things are spring. One yin first comes, and flowing fire congeals within; three yins begin to interact, and grass and trees at once fall bare. The mighty force of creation can still make things wither and bloom; how much more the unborn, steeped and steamed in every thought. Through the existent he enters emptiness, and the four elements all melt; through emptiness he enters the existent, and the existent is then deathless. Existent and empty both forgotten, he is one with vajra. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all the light of tranquil extinction. Therefore our master is king within the Dharma.
Verse in Praise of Master Yongming Yanshou (with preface)

In my youth I read the Essay on Mind and the Formula of Mind Only, and knew at once that the master was a banner of light. Later I followed my late teacher Yungu and heard that the master each day performed one hundred and eight practices of skillful means; I took them for ordinary labors. Secretly admiring them, I put them into practice, and thereby took in every dharma without exception, thinking I had made good use of my mind. When I grew old and came to Jingci Monastery by West Lake, I entered the Hall of the Mirror of the School and bowed to the shadow of the master's stupa, inquiring into his life and deeds. His disciple Dahe brought out the Record of Conduct. I unrolled it and fell silent, losing myself. I sighed and said: This vast, boundless, subtle and wondrous practice of dharma truly cannot be upheld in even one ten-thousandth part without a vajra mind and Samantabhadra's vows. How much less to uncover the school of mind and melt the ocean of doctrine, to reveal the Dharma nature and gather in all beings — without the three wheels of the Dharma realm, how could one reach its threshold? I marveled and sighed at what cannot be conceived, bowed my head, and made this praise:

I bow my head to the master, banner of light, whose pure treasury illumines the whole Dharma realm. Riding the wheel of great vows, he reveals the three karmas, expressly opening the true eye for living beings. He personally transmits the secret seal of buddhas and patriarchs, blending the ocean of doctrine into one mind. He shapes sages and worldlings beyond all measure and enters at once the sea of samādhi of true reality. A hundred thousand wondrous practices reveal mind only; ten thousand virtues return to the one truth. Since the coming of the Three Treasures, in this land only the master could protect the Dharma; therefore Chinese and barbarian alike all look up to him, all entering the embrace of his compassionate mind. Flying, swimming, moving, growing — none is left out; he takes their suffering upon his own body. Were it not for the contemplation of tranquil extinction and equality, how could he see no mark of self or other? How sad that the deluded multitudes in this final age do not know they are all embraced by his vow-power. He hangs up this Mirror of the School to illumine all dharmas; before his eyes, what dharma is not a Buddha deed? This one virtue of releasing living beings alone enters the gate of Vairocana's Dharma realm. When one's own mind first enters the minds of living beings, how can living beings escape the Pure Land? I take lakes and mountains for brush and inkstone, yet cannot write one pore of the master. I vow that all who rejoice and hear or see may together realize our master's power of mind.
Brief Biographies and Verses on the Portraits of the Patriarchs
Verse in Praise of Kang Senghui, the Patriarch Kang

The Dharma-body relic pervades the whole great earth; its light shines everywhere, and there is no place it is not. Then came a man of the highest order, who followed the light and came seeking its manifestation; thus the Brahma monastery was first opened.
Verse in Praise of the Indian Monk Fotucheng

The man of the highest order hides and reveals himself, his conduct beyond reckoning; his whole being is light, and his workings are naturally distinct. He came and went in the emperor's court as one fondles a gull, then lightly took his leave — such was his timely Way.
Verse in Praise of Master Huiyuan of Donglin Monastery on Mount Lu

Vast in aspiration and lofty in heart, he roamed his mind in the Pure Land; he founded Donglin Monastery and made it his first step. The clear sound of the lotus water-clock has carried its cadence down to this day; all who hear it turn their hearts to him without fail.
Verse in Praise of Master Baozhi

The man of the highest order moves in hiding, his traces unknowable. From where did he come? He was the child of an eagle. Wandering through the world, no one could fathom him; having torn apart his own face, what need was there to speak?
Verse in Praise of Mahasattva Fu

The Way does not lie in the Daoist cap, nor Confucianism in the shoe, nor Buddhism in the robe — there is no self and other. If only you can keep from giving rise to discriminating mind, then you yourself are the master of the three teachings.
Verse in Praise of Master Zhang'an

Like echo and shadow he spread the Dharma's transformation, a dragon amid clouds and a tiger amid winds; whoever raises a banner must have his company. The doctrine and contemplation of one house flourished greatly under the master; he entered the ocean of much hearing, its source far and its flow long.
Verse in Praise of Master Fazhi

The one house of Tiantai took Nāgārjuna of old as its distant patriarch; doctrine and contemplation were clear and distinct, and many who touched them awakened. For five hundred years its bonds were not drawn tight, until in truth our master was born and greatly raised its guiding cord.
Verse in Praise of Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra

The abhiṣeka of Vairocana — this is the mind seal; the true command wholly raised, buddhas and demons obey. Dragon spirits run at his bidding, and a hundred monsters vanish in hiding; therefore the wise one attains great sovereignty.
Verse in Praise of Master Xianshou

In the great net of the Dharma realm, sages and worldlings are arrayed; there is one chief cord alone, and only the master could lift it. Drawing in the currents of ten thousand streams, they all return to the sea of nature; the five teachings are gathered as one, unchanged through all ages.
Verse in Praise of National Master Qingliang

Bearing the great seal of wisdom, he encompasses the Dharma realm; entering the gate of total retention, he possesses the four unhindered wisdoms. Nine feet tall of body, a hundred years in the world; teacher to the gates of seven emperors, his deeds beyond conception.
Praise of Chan Master Guifeng

To win a marquisate ten thousand li away, he cast aside his brush and took it up. Our master cast aside one thing and passed straight out of birth and death. Together they roam the sea of nature; his is the seal of a true son. He entered the gate of the dharma-realm, and so is called the Second Sage.
Praise of National Master Fazhao

The Great Being Mañjuśrī, whom he longed to see but once, therefore appeared beforehand in his alms bowl as the golden realm. When he came to the gate it was as if returning to a place long known. Pointing straight to the Land of Ultimate Bliss — that is where he took refuge.
Praise of Tripitaka Master Xuanzang

The great teaching flowed east, yet its dharma was not yet widespread. Then came a true arhat who gave up his life to go and fetch it. The light of prajñā streamed forth, and the school of Dharma-Characteristics opened wide. A boat upon the sea of suffering, bestowing benefit without end.
Praise of Master Kuiji

The profound doctrine of consciousness-only, its meaning deep and dark: only the master made it shine, like the sun in the sky. Surely he came from Tuṣita, having received the charge from Maitreya beforehand. Had he not come from there, who could know its secret?
Praise of Vinaya Master Daoxuan

The Tathāgata set up the teaching with the three trainings as its master. What samādhi and wisdom bring forth has the precepts as its base. When the great dharma flowed east, this teaching had not yet shone; then the master of Nanshan arose and roused its guiding line at once.
Praise of Chan Master Yixing

The exoteric and esoteric schools, the lore of omen and calendar: once the Great Expansion was complete, yin and yang fell into measure. Worldly and world-transcending dharmas alike he mastered and refined. The conduct of the fifth ground was seen in the master.
Praise of Chan Master Nanyue Huairang

His spirit soared to heaven, his mind empty beyond measure. He scooped up the waters of Caoxi and raised up waves and billows. The colt that lay asleep he roused with a single brick; then it kicked and trampled where it would, and all it touched fell dead.
Praise of Chan Master Qingyuan Xingsi

Naturally noble, he fell into no grades or stages. One word struck the mark, like a bee finding honey. From the single stream of Caoxi branch split and channel spread; from then on his heirs rolled on like thunder and lightning.
Praise of Master Wuxiang of Yongjia

His golden staff stood alone as a mark, a living dragon and a leaping tiger. Had it not been for old Lu, he would have been slighted again and again. He understood before a word was spoken and set out after a single night. Yet even such transcendence leaves him still a son and heir.
Praise of Chan Master Daoyi of Xijiang

The colt was a dragon: he walked like an ox and glared like a tiger. One hundred and thirty men — one stamp of the foot. The dharma flowed to the West River; a hundred streams poured east. A single drop spread everywhere and slaked the parched and barren.
Praise of Chan Master Shitou Xiqian

The barbarian's buddha-nature had its cause from the first. At a single word to go and reflect, he straightway got the truth. He sat perched on a rock, and that road is very slippery; even one who can walk it takes a tumble.
Praise of Chan Master Dazhu Huihai of Yuezhou

Holding the treasury himself, he yet sought it from another. One word pointed it out, and in response and function he was free. Yuezhou had a great pearl, round and bright, clear through and through; it shines wherever it turns and never falls into the old ruts.
Praise of Chan Master Tianhuang Daowu

He did not dwell on that shore — from where then did he come? One meeting with Shitou and the gate flew open. With this he showed people, prizing only that they know what they have. Picking it up upside down, he was like a man juggling balls.
Praise of Chan Master Weishan Lingyou of Tanzhou

Baizhang stood like a wall, and those who came gazed up from the cliff. Only the master went straight in; poking the fire, his mind opened. He took birth as a water buffalo and moved among the different kind; Yangshan saw through him — the family name of father and son.
Praise of Chan Master Niaoke Daolin of Hangzhou

He came riding the sunlight and dwelt according to his own nature. So when he first appeared, his awakening was naturally wondrous. He nested in a tall pine; people called it perilous, but he only watched others and never checked himself.
Praise of Chan Master Huangbo Xiyun of Hongzhou

Beneath Mount Daxiong there was a great beast; one roar and all who heard were deafened. His pivot was the swift thunder, his eye the flashing lightning. The style of the coming from the West grew perilous indeed from him on.
Praise of Chan Master Linji Yixuan of Zhenzhou

A lion of Huangbo, barely showing claw and fang. His pivot with Dayu was like an eagle seizing a hare. Three blows under the ribs, one slap on the cheek — he merely chanced to cross its edge; it was no crude rashness.
Praise of Chan Master Dongshan Liangjia Wuben of Duanzhou

His original face — one touch and it was seen. That insentient things expound the dharma still seemed to fall short. After meeting Yunyan he overturned the old nest; crossing the water he saw his shadow, and only then was he clear through.
Praise of Chan Master Caoshan Benji of Fuzhou

His capacity overleapt the norm and left no trace of name. With an eye beyond the ordinary, one glance and he knew. The five ranks, empty and dark; the essential teaching, fine and close-woven. Therefore to this day it is still black as lacquer.
Praise of Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun of Fuzhou

What is familiar is hard to forget — the habit of vegetables and bamboo shoots. Bell, chanting, and the sound of sutras: hearing them, his heart grew drunk. The master's staff was like a dragon, his friend's mouth like iron; hence his emergence in this life was naturally transcendent.
Praise of Chan Master Yunmen

No sooner had he met Muzhou than the door was shut and he was pushed out; pressing in, he was squeezed, and his leg was snapped off. From that turning he covered heaven and covered earth. Before he ever met Xuefeng, his mind had already chimed.
Praise of Chan Master Fayan

All is ready-made, with no hesitation at all. Amid the ten thousand forms he stands out boldly alone. One flavor, an even mind — it is right before the eyes. The moment thought stirs, one falls to the second.
Praise of Chan Master Shoushan Shengnian of Ruzhou

The seven scrolls of the Lotus Sutra he had long upheld; at one word he let them go and knew at once what he had always had. The teaching that is no teaching — bring it up and it appears. He shook his sleeve and went his way: what briskness, what ease.
Praise of Chan Master Tianyi Yihuai of Yuezhou

Compassionate by nature, he came to settle an old debt. Seeing a fish, he at once let it go. Once out of the dusty net, he straightway climbed the ground of awakening. The carrying pole snapped, the bucket fell away, and empty space shattered.
Praise of Chan Master Shishuang Chuyuan Ciming of Tanzhou

The Western River's counter-pivot none who saw could recognize. He himself had his mouth covered and lost his nostrils. His pivot shot out swift, breaking free beyond all tether. The clear-eyed praised him: a true lion's cub.
Praise of Chan Master Huanglong Huinan of Longxing Prefecture

A lion of the Western River, the family style of father and son. Gripping the Tai’e sword point-down, who dared face its edge? The master crossed it once, and the feelings of sage and ordinary were spent. In his room, three barriers; he raised the true command in full.
Praise of Chan Master Yangqi Fanghui of Yuanzhou

He shouldered the great dharma and held the monastery's net together. Meeting on a narrow road, one word revealed the mind. In later days his heirs filled the whole world: the source far, the stream long; the roots deep, the branches great.
Praise of Chan Master Shouduan of Baiyun Monastery, Shuzhou

Long he held a bright pearl, hoarding it as rare goods. When at last he met an expert, one laugh and it dropped. Seeing through the place of that laugh, he too fell over laughing. Whatever he picks up at random is nothing but treasure.
Praise of Chan Master Wuzu Fayan of Qizhou

He set out ill-starred and at once ran into a plank-carrier. Meeting anyone he questioned them, but it only served to screen his eyes. Luckily he met an expert, and one blow of the mallet broke it open. Turning his head back, he knew his words had fallen flat.
Praise of Chan Master Zhijue Yanshou of Huiri Yongming, Hangzhou

Riding the power of great vows, he appeared as an auspicious sign of dharma. The gate of dhāraṇī opened, and all practices were complete. He hung up the mirror of the one mind, brightly lighting all things. The Buddha-sun at midheaven leaves no darkness unlit.
Praise of Chan Master Gaofeng of Tianmu

The peril of Snow Cliff, a wall standing ten thousand fathoms — only the master climbed it and found the shortcut. The peril of the Death Pass exceeds the cliff itself; so those who gaze at it feel they are climbing to heaven.
Praise of Chan Master Zhongfeng of Tianmu
In the lair of Tianmu, a true lion's cub: barely showing claw and fang, and a hundred beasts fled. Lone peak, austere; dharma ocean, vast. Therefore our master is called king among monks.

He perched on the high peak of Tianmu and pierced the iron wall in empty space. He shattered the heavy barriers of buddhas and patriarchs and made light of the learning of a dust-mote world. He showed a body and mind like an illusion and displayed the samādhi-power of the nāga. He smashed the nest of living beings' birth and death — meet him though you may, there is nowhere to find him.
Praise of Chan Master Qianyan

He asked where the Buddha was; he sought but did not see. A rat upset the dish, and suddenly it appeared. He leapt up like space itself, answering sound with echo. Had it not been for this turn, he would have nearly drowned in idle thought.
Praise of Chan Master Foyin

The habit of letters leaked out from birth; with a mouth askew he spoke of Chan and never fell into old ruts. He painted his smiling face beforehand, none knows why; laughing aloud, he passed away. That very thing is it.
Praise of Chan Master Wuzhun of Jingshan

One word struck the mark, and the ten directions were clear through. From his tongue-root thunder ran; monks gathered like clouds. Twice he entered the inner court and guided the ten-thousand-chariot sovereign. He borrowed no other's power but relied wholly on the true command.
Praise of Chan Master Jizhao Yuanming

As the ways of the world rose together, the true man answered the times. Clouds and dragons, wind and tigers — none could hold him back. True gold comes out of the ore; an ancient mirror gives forth light. Once the bright essence is released, its shining function has no fixed direction.
Praise of Chan Master Baiyun Jue

He sat on White Cloud Peak with a tongue of crashing thunder. The sea of nature heaved its waves; the sky of meaning arrayed its stars. Dragons and spirits ran at his bidding, and demon hordes melted away unseen. One drop of coolness broke the fever of the miasmic air. A fine master indeed, of the fullest measure — were it not for that beard covering his mouth, people would surely take him for Kāśyapa on Vulture Peak.
Praise of the Vajra Stupa

I bow to the Vajra Banner, bright gathered light of prajñā, the mind of every living being, and so the mother of all buddhas. It enters every dust-mote and can do the work of benefit. How good, this man of wondrous wisdom, who from a subtle, fine-grained thought raised up this banner most supreme, like a lotus treasury. The banner stands upon a dust-mote; in one mote a single word is written. Mote within mote, worlds complete; word within word, light appears. And in this single banner, every mote assembled, the full conditions of prajñā are met, neither added nor diminished. Know then that the minds of living beings are each and all complete. I look upon this body of mine and find it no different from this peerless banner. The subtle mind of daily use rests wholly on the power of prajñā. If for a single thought one gazes in reverence, all is complete; thought after thought never apart from mind, and every merit is perfected.
Praise of the Painting of the Three Teachings

One yet three: a newborn child dressed in a flowered cloth coat. Three yet one: a tuneless tune blown on a holeless flute. He lies without a blush and hides his heart black as lacquer. Do not say his heart and soul are of two kinds; who can see through the true message? A heart full of matters it is hard to tell — the cuckoo's blood dyes the spring hills wet.
Praise of Emperor Wenchang

The essence of creation, blazing forth as pattern and letter, shining through the long night while sun and moon take turns to give light. Nothing but your utmost; silent, you are still. When one knocks, it sounds like a bamboo flute — deep, deep, never exhausted, like a valley that yet seems full. The Lord comes forth at the trigram Zhen: this is what is called utmost spirit.
Praise of Laozi Riding the Ox
The purple vapor came from the east; the black ox passed away to the west. He was not looking for anyone — what was it all for?
Praise of Laozi Passing the Pass

His mind dwelt in the most ancient; his Way turned from the shallow world. He shone without dazzling, was empty without bending. He reached emptiness and kept stillness, thought little and desired little; calm and tranquil, he gladdened the spirit, utterly without possessions. While the rival lords struggled and raced one another, while the tripods boiled in the Central Plain, he turned his longings toward the West. No sooner had he mounted the black ox than the purple vapor rose. The Keeper of the Pass knew beforehand that the True Man was coming; he bowed to his command and gazed up in reverence, begging him to unlock the hidden mystery. He left behind five thousand words: the Way complete, the virtue full. He did not place himself before things, nor begin any calamity. Humble in the Way, without self; knowing contentment, knowing when to stop. He blended with the world and softened his light, and none could take his measure. Therefore he was called like a dragon, and served as Keeper of the Archives.
Praise of Confucius

Teacher of a hundred kings, mandate of a thousand sages, the moral order of all ages, the true nature of every living being. He bore it all on his single strength, leaving nothing over. Had our master not been a man beyond measure, who could keep human relations upright forever?
Praise of Pengzu

His complexion like an infant's, his breath like a babe's; he drank the wind and supped on dew, and dined on cloud. Once in three thousand years the flat peach ripens — he was already a boy, and still he plucked the flowers.
Praise of Lü Chunyang

The universe within his hand, the ten thousand transformations born of his body. He received the purest essence of the three powers and won the fine purity of the two breaths. Bearing the green serpent sword, he sported without hindrance; meeting Huanglong, his wondrous awakening was made true. At dawn he roamed the isle of Penglai; at dusk he lodged on Kunlun. His years are as heaven and earth, his virtue like the spring sun. This is what is called a sage among men — or rather, a spirit among immortals.
Praise of the Marquis of Hanshou

Austere, as if alive; bright, as if present. A loyal heart glowing alone, a bearing majestic and grand. Spirit on his face, a heap of rock in his breast. Everywhere he meets people he loves to show himself — most likely his hero's debt is still unpaid.
Praise of the Half-Portrait of Master Yufeng of Mount Qingliang

A half-round moon, a single drift of cloud; snow grown old, ice dried up, water clear, sand shallow. People say he is a son of the first patriarch; I say he is Mañjuśrī's companion. Eighty years of ascetic practice without end, a hundred thousand kalpas fulfilled in a single thought. Who knows from which life came the old foe who came to this world to repay a former debt? Late he got a son neither lay nor monk, who put on a face neither true nor false. Yi! Today we meet again with a laugh, and wait only for the first assembly beneath the Dragon-Flower Tree.
Praise of Master Baofeng

True yet not true; no mark, and yet no lack of marks. Like color within a pearl, like an image in a mirror. He wandered the whole trichiliocosm and left no trace; the ten directions fell away with no obstruction. To strike the iron ox of Shaanfu, he snapped the bamboo staff of Qiongzhou. In the north the mountains are cold and snow is flying; in the south the earth is warm and flowers first open. Meeting you, he will not reveal the whole pivot, but says only that both is and is not are slander. Ask where that elusive master whom no one can lay hold of may be — people say he is Master Baofeng before the Son of Heaven's gate.
Praise of Master Zibai

The net of the dharma-realm was torn and its cords no longer drawn taut; then the master was born and by his strength pulled its main line up. He sat in the lion's den and felled the sandalwood tree. Before his spring was spent, claw and fang already showed. He beat the drum smeared with poison and poured out the sweet-dew draft; those who drank were drunk, those who heard went mad. In the stillness of extinction, his tongue crashed like thunder; rushing storm and coiling lightning — all it touched lost their souls. With the mind of the great earth, with bones firm as diamond, sinew in his eyes and nothing in his breast. Linji did not die, Huangbo still lives. Who knew the master would not accept their names? Broad and open his stride, keeping no rule or track; he turned and flung himself over Mount Sumeru and shattered the land of no-birth with one blow of his fist.

He sits alone on the lonely peak, his robe open to the hidden sea. A shout wakes the fish and dragons; ghosts and monsters melt away unseen. Propped on his ruyi staff, both eyes empty; the worlds of the ten directions have no cover. Do not say the spring wind is the same everywhere: ice is dried and snow grown old, yet the cold cliff remains.

An eye that settles heaven and earth, like a precious mirror hung on high: whoever stands before it, fair or foul cannot hide. Grip the Tai’e sword point-down and give it to others without grudging. Māra and the outsiders who cross it lose body and life. A fist struck by no hand — the fist is not in the hand; speech understood with no tongue — the words are not in the mouth. Brows and beard slightly shown, his form seems to exist; but knock at what is within, and he cannot split it open himself.

His face like the moon, his heart like iron; short hair and long beard, his bearing wholly apart. One clench of the fist and both eyes are empty; the spine straightens and all conditions cease. He smashes the diamond ring and perfects the extinction of sweet dew. The worlds of the ten directions have no barrier; a single ray of spirit-light is never idle through. Meeting him suddenly, the nose aches — there is a pain in the heart that is hard to tell.

Blood and sweat over his whole body, like a lion bursting its bonds. He snaps the root of affection and lays down the heavy burden. Without, he seems walled and guarded; within, he has no cliff or bank. Two eyes wide open — and there is only this fellow to see.
Praise of Master Yunqi

He came riding the power of his vows and dwelt in this world of endurance. He opened the gate of the Pure Land and settled the debt of compassion. He raised the banner of light and kept the diamond precepts. For more than eighty years, half of it spent in benefiting beings; at the end he left with only emptiness, without hindrance. If you would know the mind with which our master dwelt in the world, this is what is called Avalokiteśvara.

I look upon the master: lively in every part; through all his pores the light shines clear. His face and eyes are not seen — how then portray them? Even if one paints him well, in the end one does not hit it. He sits calm as space and speaks the dharma like the wind. To chase the wind and snatch at shadows, one cannot find their track. Hearing wind in the air, seeing shadows in water — how many foolish people sit dozing with their eyes open.

He dwells in emptiness and lives by wisdom; he enters the minds of living beings and practices Samantabhadra's conduct. Whether scaled or feathered, all alike enter the one equal dharma-nature: one flavor of compassion, fully pure. If you ask what dharma-gate our master used, the samādhi here is clearly without contention.
His mind like the moon in the sky, his form like an image in a mirror: this is our master through forty years, a true model of accord with living beings.

His countenance still, his mind close-held; no inside or outside, no going out or coming in. A hundred thousand samādhis are flowers in the eye; all gates of practice are bird-tracks in the sky. If you do not believe he divides his body among the ten thousand forms, the fool goes looking for him at the tip of a hair. Yi!
Praise of the Circle Portrait of Master Wuming

Long have I heard the name of Wuming, but never seen Wuming's face. Then a great mountain stood out, and we met across a thousand li. His livelihood was in his hoe; he taught the dharma like running lightning. He draws the stringless bow and is used to the arrows of Shigong; he only wants to shoot a man, and the man flees at the twang. But when he strikes a stubborn rock, head and feather both sink in. He flings out the iron lump, and all who see it are left without a reckoning. This is our master's old skin of a face: look at it, and you may only understand it before a word is spoken. If you ask about the upward pivot in broad daylight, cloud-wrapped mountains fill the eye and are hard to tell apart.
Praise of Master Wubian

The sea of lands is boundless, and not one dust-mote stands. Wherever his heel lands, conditions gather. A monastery that follows him about; tea and rice as plain as home; all who come are filled, and he does as he pleases. One stamp at the Wu River, and the dharma-pole is set up; dragons and elephants come galloping with no turning back. Clouds rise on the Twin Paths; the single transmission's moon is bright. Who is it that shouts aloud? The master answers as its echo. At the tip of a single hair he manifests the jewel-king's realm. Through eighty-eight generations none has closed the case. The whole pivot of the Way's fortune depended on the master's one flick. Half a nostril — who ever touched it?
Praise of Master Kongyin of Mount Qingliang

In the golden realm he ever followed the great assembly; only the master led the disciples and quietly wielded his great function. The five peaks stand high; as he walked in practice he looked and paused. Through ten thousand gorges the wind howled, and the sound of dharma spread everywhere. He roamed the sea of extinction and sat in the grove of sundry flowers, sporting like a lion, glancing, yawning, stretching often. His fame reached the ninefold court; his pure wind cleared the world. The ten directions took refuge in him, like the sea drawing in water. His form did not mirror his mind; the true does not mix with the common. One sees only his skin — who has gotten his bones? When the dharma banner toppled and the teaching net was no longer tight, the master pulled up its main cord like silk woven in heaven. The wise man has gone; a thousand years of stillness. Heaven truly gave him birth, and his bearing is unchanged. A thousand feet of cold cliff, ten thousand years of ice-cave: I sit before him, the master treads behind. I am driven by karma, he sustains by vow; heat and cold differ, but in this there is no shifting. When the kalpa-fire blazes, ice dries and snow grows old; once the phantom film is removed, the sky-flower is finished too. The floating clouds scatter and the blue sky is high; one round bright moon hangs clear in the void. Let me ask the man in the Vajra Cave: before and after, three and three — how many does that make?
Another Half-Body Portrait

This old fellow — where does he come from? No one knows why his face is covered with dust. A thousand feet of ice and snow could not freeze him to death; half of him remains, setting everyone guessing. How strange: the bell beneath the lion's neck — he tied it himself and untied it himself. Truly marvelous!
Praise of Master Shaojue

He takes the dharma as his body and wisdom as his life; the three realms as his home and living beings as his nature. His frame is a withered tree; his samādhi is without contention. The burning house is cold ashes; the toils of dust are a pit of ice. He makes the city his mountain forest and enters right samādhi through speech. So it is no wonder that he is ever speaking, blazing and unceasing, since the sea of wisdom runs across and he cannot himself hold it back. No wonder the master's mouth-gate is never straight.
Praise of Master Lingche

Bones like jagged peaks, mind vast and empty. Nostrils proud and noble, brows jutting like locks. Pure as a green lotus in a jade pond, tall as an ancient pine or a solitary crane. His tongue-root never stirs, yet his words crash like thunder — let no one say he has nothing to say.
Praise of Elder Ziguang

From the Vajra Cave he came to Rajagrha. He had no other business — only living beings. One body in the assembly, rice and gruel for all ten directions; whoever comes eats together, with no dividing host from guest. With a selfless mind he performs the Buddha's work. Meeting conditions, he takes them as the teaching; equal and without duality. If you seek the true, the true is not here — only look at what stands before you. He is a true son of the Buddha.
Praise of the Venerable Daxie in His Later Years

In his early years he already knew to leave the worldly life, and only in old age could he truly leave home. He made bubbling, blended practice his wondrous conduct and the Buddha's work his livelihood. In the five turbid worlds he holds not the least hindrance; in the pure realm there is only one lotus flower. This is the foremost master among the lay followers.
Praise of the Old Adept Dingzong

In youth he entered Thousand Buddha Cliff and dwelt in reliance on the Thousand Buddhas. Rising and sitting he never left them, and no one knew why. Though more than eighty years have passed, he is still at the very first step; only on entering the Vairocana grove does he begin the road home.
Praise of the Master of Xuejiao Peak

He sat and cut off Twin-Knot Peak; he squeezed juice from a pestle's weight. He smashed the vajra circle and bit through iron chestnuts and thorns. How many times did he freeze and starve, die and live again, barely winning a bit of idle breath. He is no parricide with a blood feud, so why is he so desperate at the point of death? He has salvaged a single life, and yet he casts it east and flings it west. He walks to the head of Twin-Path Peak and does not understand how to sweep away his tracks. To expose this face of his is to get grit in the eye. Even if you pile snow on frost, you must know the blazing sun of summer. Look closely at what he really is: brows across, a turtle's nose. In the cuckoo's call the rain falls like mist; the east wind blows the fallen blossoms into disarray. Barefoot and tousle-haired he descends the green heights — among those he meets, who truly knows him?
Praise of Master Fanhuai Hui of Lingxiao Peak

He came from emptiness and sought to dwell in the real, and so he turned toward Lingxiao and opened a road of his own. His body is already in the void, yet his feet have not left the ground. If you would rise utterly free, you must be utterly shattered. Cloud-wrapped mountains fill the eyes; the tangled vines are not few. Though he has no stake in them, still they wind around him. Taking up not a single thing, he need only put it all down. Where no smallness remains, greatness appears. He does not seek outside or beg from others; what is originally his stands before him, and all is real. Knowing and seeing dissolve; the mysterious and wondrous find no footing. One thought pierces straight through — a wall of silver mountains and iron cliffs.
Praise of Master Nayun

His backbone is like iron, his mind like emptiness. One robe like a cloud, ten thousand things like wind. Early he entered the house of Fangshan; late he bore the tradition of Qingliang. The older he grew, the stronger he became; the plainer he lived, the more inexhaustible. Had he not been one among the ten thousand in that cave, how could he have raised up such a lofty trace? Therefore when I think of him I cannot see him; when I write of him I cannot describe him. Dimly, faintly — he is like the old cowherd by the pond.
Praise of Master Xugu

Outwardly like floating clouds, inwardly like the valley spirit. His mind is the permanent dwelling, and so he makes it his body. Seventy-nine years pass like a dream; a hundred thousand billion kalpas are like a single life. Reclaimed, he has won one pure field, to pass on to sons and grandsons. Ah — a coral tree props up the bright moon; the Persian of the sea chews ice at night.
Praise of Master Yue'an

When he appears, he does not come; when he vanishes, he does not go. All his life face to face with people, yet no one can find where he is. Clouds race, the moon moves on; the boat sails and the shore gallops away. Ah — one long whistle in the autumn of sea and sky; at midnight the golden crow cries and heaven dawns.
Praise of Master Xueling

His face like the full moon, his bones like ice and snow. Gazing at him, he is craggy and layered; within him there must be jagged heights. Ah — white clouds cut across, the dawn peak is green; the cuckoo cries out all the blood of the spring hills.
Praise of Master Danju Kai

Bones craggy and layered, mind vast and empty. Spirit proud and noble, working lively and quick. That other half cannot be traced or drawn. Buddhas and patriarchs are slovenly; living beings are a tangle. He throws his life across his body and carries it all with one strength, never betraying the one stroke handed down in the family.
Self-Praise

I never penetrated the teachings; I never caught a glimpse in Chan. Entirely foolish and dull, in all ten directions clumsy and slow. Limitless as space, my temper hard as iron. I am glad I entered the cold cliffs early and threw my whole body down to rest. Then suddenly a black wind blew up and I tumbled into the land of raksasa ghosts. I was flung into a great furnace of red fire and pitched into a blazing house of flame in the burning south. Leaning on the Buddha's power for aid, I picked up this one life again. My face is covered with dust; my breast is full of ice and snow. It is not that I wandered practicing the path — mostly I was paying off old karma. Within it all, one piece of bitter heart is hard to speak of to anyone. Only at the Longhua Assembly will it at last become clear. And even then, whatever is drawn of me will not be the flesh and blood my mother bore.

I sat on Mount Laṅkā and perched on a firm stone, hearing the sound of the tide, entering the land of the unborn. Early I came from the golden realm; in old age I was mistaken for a guest of Leiyang. Behind horses, before donkeys, feeding on wind and dew. I passed through the whole furnace of fire and the mountain of knives, and I am glad the spears and shields have come to rest. Grateful for the ruler's grace, I was released and sent back, and picked up this one life. Turning over, I went straight up to the head of ten thousand peaks and slept day and night without a moment's idleness. All demons' minds are empty; all Buddhas' ears burn hot. If people today ask what the mechanism within is: on Mount Dinghu the clouds are forever white.

His form is like a patch of cloud, yet he does not dwell in the vast void. Coming and going without mind, he drifts once with the wind. He sits on the high peak of Dinghu and laughs at the exposed pillar of Caoxi. Let the bitter sea's waves churn as they will; he trusts his own liver and guts are cast of iron. Looking back at the blazing house of fire, how does it compare with the depths of the white clouds?

Long accustomed to being a monk, he fell short when he returned to lay life. Old habits are hard to forget, and practice goes unfinished. Fortunately he entered the great furnace of the sage emperor and was cast into an iron arhat, flung into the burning wilderness of the fire house, as though into a cauldron of boiling water and a bed of coals. Smelted until the bones and flesh of his whole body ran molten, he was left with one piece of compassionate heart. He knows well that so great a grace can never be repaid; to repay it he must rely on true vows alone.

His mind is no longer in the household, yet his form still blends with the world. He has a jewel in his eye and nothing at all in his breast. When people hear of him they argue yes and no; when they meet him they clamor and shout. Let them describe him in a hundred thousand ways — there is one small point that can never be drawn.

Neither layman nor monk, neither true nor false. His liver and guts are ice and frost, his body a clod of earth. Entirely foolish, in ten thousand ways free and easy. Had the sage emperor not broken the rule with hammer and tongs, how could he have ridden beside the general's warhorse? See how he has another kind of spirit, one that has nothing to do with literary flourish.

A walking staff and a long spear, a bowl and a cooking-pot — a single kind of livelihood, so what divides the fair from the ugly? Look only at the moon in water and the flower in the sky; beyond that, what have I to do with anything?

In youth I loved leaving home; in old age people urged me to return to lay life. Had I not gone along with worldly conditions, they would say I harbored something within. So I briefly stepped through the gate of light and shadow and let bare a glimpse of my original face. My whiskers and hair are a nuisance to scratch, but I take delight that my body knows no restraint. One turn of the Laṅkā scripture, one stick of incense — wherever I go, my livelihood is enough as it is.

The mind is not in the hair; the form is not that of a monk. The man is unworthy of mention; the name is unworthy of praise. There is not one thing worth taking, nothing but what is detestable. The gate of patience — only this can he master.

He loves mountains but they are not high; he loves water but it is not deep. As a monk he does not shave his head; as a layman he wears no cap. In letters he knows no characters; in arms he speaks no tactics. Truly there is nothing to be taken from him, only an empty name. This useless old teacher should simply be banished to the ranks of Leiyang, set before the donkeys and behind the horses — in that one thing he excels.

Walking alone, sitting alone, happy beyond compare. With a mind set on nothing, he does not even become a Buddha. Ten thousand miles to Leiyang he crossed in a single throw. If someone meets him and asks who he is: the first seat in the hall of Tusita.

His mind is not in the Way; his form does not enter the common world. His feet have no entanglements; his mouth has no restraints. He moves like wind through emptiness, responds like echo in a valley. Entirely foolish, in a thousand ways buried and forgotten. Fortunately he has borrowed one branch of the bodhi tree; in this life he has a thousand feet and ten thousand feet.

In youth he left home; in old age he returned to lay life. He feigns folly and plays the simpleton, all skin and no bone. He knows nothing of cultivation, entirely without restraint. One day he happened to offend the dragon countenance and was banished to Leiyang as a beast of burden. Now he has idled his way to Caoxi, learning to mind the stone and pound the rice.

This old man has no decorum — what kind of appearance is this? Strike him and he feels no pain; scratch him and he feels no itch; scold him and he feels no shame; slander him and he takes no hurt. He sits rigid and knows nothing of investigating Chan, lost the whole time in wild fancies. To become a Buddha he has no share; to become a patriarch he is blocked. Best to send him off into the ranks of the idle and make him an old squad leader.

The laity do not know his name; among monks he is not counted. In the ranks of Buddhas and patriarchs he is not admitted; in the realm of living beings he does not dwell. With bare hands he grips a spear; stripped naked he goes to battle. Afraid of death, he finds no gate into the earth; wanting to live, he finds no road to heaven. Everyone says he is a teacher with no skills at all — who would guess he is a great fool who cannot read a single character?

Frosted temples tousled and loose, an icy heart cold and plain. His mouth clamped shut, his tongue tied; he gallops like thunder and rolls like lightning. He has been a man of east, west, south, and north, and has borne a hundred thousand billion hardships. He is called a foolish monk and hailed as an iron man. Form and shadow keep each other company by the pestilential sea. Let no one say this man has no companion.

Sixty years since leaving home, three thousand days as a soldier, twenty autumns dwelling in the mountains — in the end there is no handle to grasp. As a monk he does not understand cultivation; in worldly life he keeps no scruples. What kind of karmic bond is this, to make him such a creature? What he loves best is one piece of foolish heart that takes the Buddha's and patriarchs' household affairs as his own family business. Affliction is boundless, the bitter sea without shore. He has weathered every storm and followed the ranks along; he throws himself across bramble thickets and plays among spears and halberds. And now he still will not turn his head — will old Yama not be angry? Perhaps he waits for Maitreya to be born, and only then will he understand. Ho! Spring hills, night rain, the cuckoo cries — voice after voice telling him to go home.

His bearing is doddering, and within him all is empty. In the realm of Buddhas and patriarchs he does not dwell; among living beings he is hard to accommodate. He understands no conditions and penetrates not a single dharma. He simply takes ordinary tea and rice and makes them the upright style of the house. In vain he spends a bottomless foolish heart and is left with endless affliction. Better to banish him to the land of the unborn, to lie high pillowed on white clouds and embrace the bright moon forever. Caring for nothing at all, he dimly becomes a truly foolish old man.

He came for the Sixth Patriarch and departed because of Master Rang. Coming and going may look like rushing about, but the Dharma gate is by nature without dwelling. He only meant to prop up the father-and-son household; he did not stir up idle temper. He passed through every hardship and wore through the bamboo clappers, and was left with a face full of dust, which he took as the ancestral meaning from the West. In the end, one piece of vajra mind still remains to spread Caoxi's ground once more.

Dull and unknowing, with a hundred things unthought. Utterly without skill, entirely foolish and dull-witted. How could he be an eye for gods and men? He is, after all, a rice-gruel teacher. He has only one marvel about him: bright moon on the coral branch.

Once in his bowl he saw a multitude, and asked whether it was Mañjuśrī who was toying with him. He went all the way to Mount Wutai and personally received its veneration. When he heard the teaching of the Pure Land, it was like dreaming with his eyes open. I think this old man's former body has come again today to make sport.

For seventy years he wandered through the human world in a dream — a following assembly, sky-flower Buddha-work. He cared nothing for danger and kept no taboos. One day he offended the dragon countenance and was squeezed until empty space shattered. Flung into the burning wilderness ten thousand miles away, he went on playing his part on every stage. Only when the bow snaps and the arrows are spent will he at last rest his breath. And looking now with the true eye, all he has won is one deep sleep.

The moon hangs on the tall pine, its shadow sinks in autumn water. There is a form to glimpse, yet nothing can compare with it. It cannot be approached, and how could it be seized? It draws the long wind of ten thousand miles and sets a single reed adrift on the vast waves. Most like the front of Shaoshi Rock — and yet not within the city of Vairocana. Clear beyond all dust, utterly without dregs. A mud ox bellows, a flower blooms on the pounding pestle. Though those who know him fill heaven and earth, how few can take it up whole.

Like a mirror showing reflections, like clouds floating in the sky. A sound in the empty valley, a fish's trace in still water. He has eyes but does not see; he has ears but is as though deaf. Since he cannot be praised, how can he be described? Call him a thing and you miss it at once — this is why he is the foolish old man.

Majestic and imposing, limpid and clear. He sets up no walls of the heart and has no cliffs or banks at all. His spirit covers heaven and earth; his gaze props up the Milky Way. Cast adrift at the gate of present-day affairs, he never stirs from the far shore of Wuyin. Whether layman or monk, a carrying pole never leaves his shoulder. If he is not a slave of the Buddhas and patriarchs, he is surely a peddler in the field of awakening. Had he not entered the great furnace of red fire, who would know he is an iron man? Only when Maitreya is born will this case be settled.

The ice and snow of Mount Wutai have withered; the waves of the Eastern Sea are fierce. The pestilence of the burning wilderness runs deep; the karmic bond at Caoxi is thin. Only when heart and strength are spent does he walk barefoot home to Mount Nanyue. On the head of the seventy peaks he sleeps most deeply; waking, his two eyes are utterly empty. He sits leaning on the tall pine, gazing alone, as one white cloud rises from the dark ravine.

Belonging neither to sage nor to ordinary, his original face — from where does it come? It issues from the tip of a brush. The water is clear and the moon shows its face; the clouds part and the mountain bares its bones. Know the thunder in the silent deep: most like an echo carried through an empty valley. If someone asks the meaning of the coming from the West, just tell him: this very mind is Buddha.

A broad face and a narrow mouth, brows set level, nose straight. Depict him as you will, there is no breath in it at all. Before the pattern and color are revealed, who knows the truth of him? He does not come on the road of gods and men — where, sir, have you ever known him?

This old man — within him there is nothing at all. Neither sage nor ordinary, neither mind nor Buddha. He fishes the moon's reflection with a rabbit-horn staff and binds the bones of empty space with a tortoise-hair rope. Call him Hanshan and you turn your back on him; do not call him Hanshan and you collide with him. Examine him carefully and he is a withered stump of root and knot — only he has a kind of wakefulness that in the end cannot be drawn. Ho, ho, ho! The moon sets but never leaves the sky; the bird returns to roost in the tree.

He sat in the ice and snow of Mount Wutai and listened to the waves of the Eastern Sea. He drank the pestilential poison of the burning wilderness and lay on the high peaks of Mount Nanyue. He picked up the bamboo clappers of the Twin Paths and blew on the cloth hair of Yunqi. Look at these wanderings of his — just like the moon on a pine tip. If you ask after the great man's conduct, there is not the least bit to it. Seek the mark of a monk and there is not a hair. He has only one set of liver and guts, whose pain and itch lie not in skin or fur. Scrutinize him again and again, scratch and probe: you cannot find it, and the tenderest spot cannot be clawed. But tell me, after all, what is it? Ah — gibbons wail in Wu Gorge under the frosty night moon; the heart-breaking sound melts away the dream soul.

Forty-seven years ago I once dwelt at Jiangxin. Now past seventy-two, I have come a second time. Like clouds in empty sky I come and go, and no one ever knows why. Meeting people I knew long ago, I ask the road home. To see through this dream-body is the very first step. If you ask for the final phrase: look at the lantern and the exposed pillar.
Another Praise on the Sea-Viewing Portrait

Great boulders and tall pines, vast waves and dark ravines. Look up to him and he is higher still; gaze at him and he is wider still. Within there is a man whose spirit is open and expansive. At times he hears the sound of the tide proclaiming the Universal Gate, and personally realizes the true liberation of the ear-faculty.
Another Praise of the Pilgrim

His ringed staff has no rings; his straw sandals have no straps. Through the ten directions he comes and goes, wherever his feet arrive. In the world and beyond the world, the two do not resemble each other. A monastery of water and moon, Buddha-work of sky-flowers. If you ask after his livelihood — thus, thus.
Praise on the Portrait of Hu the Censor

Not quite a monk, not quite a layman. One kind of heart, two manner of bearing. If you ask whether he is magistrate or bhiksu, he is like raw rice cooked into gruel. Today we meet on a narrow road, and still it comes to two and three make six. He is bound by neither south nor north, east nor west; touch him and he is like a nail driven into wood. Coming and going on the road of birth and death, he does not know where he will finally rest. May we together be born in the Tusita heaven — that would satisfy this heart a thousand and ten thousand times over.
Praise on the Portrait of Wang the Minister

A bosom of water and moon, an eye of sky-flowers. Liver and guts of iron and stone, a spirit of wind and cloud. Remember that before he entered the womb, he was not this slovenly fellow. Within him there is nowhere to draw a likeness; he looks a little odd. He should not have shut his mouth at Vaiśālī back then; now he has come to repay old debts. In the dust of toil he turns the inexhaustible Dharma wheel; on the tip of a hair he reveals a hundred thousand samādhis. He gives up himself for others and trades gold for a clod. Everyone today says he is a magistrate — I say his name is Avalokiteśvara.
Dream-Wanderings of Old Man Hanshan, Volumes 36-40
Dream-Wanderings of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Thirty-Six
Buddha and Patriarch Karmic Encounters (Thirty Cases)

When Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One, was first born, he pointed one hand to heaven and one hand to earth, walked seven paces around, and looked in the four directions, saying: "Above heaven and under heaven, I alone am the Honored One." Later Yunmen said: "Had I seen him then, I would have struck him dead with one blow and tossed him to the dogs to eat, all for the sake of peace in the world." Langya Jue said: "This may be called offering body and mind to the dust-lands; this indeed is named repaying the Buddha's grace." The verse says:

No sooner out of the womb than he was all in a flurry; / He opened his big mouth wide to tell of what he'd done. / He only thought to pour out what lay in his heart, / Yet stirred the bystanders to weigh his short and long.

Because Devadatta slandered the Buddha, he fell alive into hell. The Buddha sent Ānanda to ask him: "Are you at peace in hell?" He answered: "Though I am in hell, I enjoy the bliss of the Third Dhyana Heaven." The Buddha again had Ānanda ask: "Do you still seek to come out?" He said: "I will come out when the World-Honored One comes." Ānanda said: "The Buddha is the Great Master of the three realms; how could he have any share in entering hell?" He replied: "Since the Buddha has no share in entering hell, how could I have any share in leaving it?" The verse says:

What difference is there between hell and heaven? / Where grace is deepest, there he makes his home. / When life contents a man, that is his joy; / Why waste idle feelings picking at another's faults?

A brahmacārin named Black Teeth once exerted his spiritual powers and carried two twin-trunked parasol trees in his left and right hands to Vulture Peak, where he offered them to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "Brahmacārin." He answered: "Yes." The Buddha said: "Put it down." He put down the tree in his left hand. The Buddha again said: "Put it down." He put down the tree in his right hand. The Buddha again said: "Put it down." He said: "Both my hands are empty — I do not know what else you would have me put down." The Buddha said: "I do not tell you to put down the flowers. You should put down the six sense faculties within, the six sense objects without, and the six consciousnesses between. When there is not one thing to be cast aside, that is where you escape birth and death." The brahmacārin was suddenly greatly awakened. The verse says:

He carried them here and raised spears on level ground; / He told him to put them down, and left him helpless. / He went on till the water was dry and the mountains ended — / And even with nothing at all, he found it too much.

Long ago the World-Honored One came before the Stupa of Many Children and had Mahākāśyapa share his seat and sit upon it. He wrapped him round with his saṃghāṭī robe and then told him: "I have the treasury of the true Dharma eye; I secretly entrust it to you. You must guard and uphold it, handing it on to those who come after, and never let it be cut off." The verse says:

Clear and plain the whole earth lies open and bare — / How could a patch of robe cover and hide it? / The moment he called it secret, it was never secret at all; / His tongue sprawls over the ground in utter disarray.

Mañjuśrī was at Vulture Peak where all the Buddhas were assembled when he saw a woman seated in samādhi near the Buddha's seat. Mañjuśrī asked the Buddha: "How is it that this woman may sit near the Buddha?" The Buddha said: "Just awaken this woman and make her rise from samādhi; then question her yourself." Mañjuśrī circled the woman three times and snapped his fingers once, and even lifted her up to the Brahma heaven, exhausting all his spiritual powers, yet he could not bring her out. The Buddha said: "Even a hundred thousand Mañjuśrīs could not bring this woman out of her samādhi. Forty-two Ganges-sand buddha-lands below, there is a Bodhisattva named Wuming who can bring this woman out of her samādhi." In a moment Wuming arrived where the Buddha was, and the Buddha told him to bring the woman out of her samādhi. At once Wuming snapped his fingers before the woman, and with that the woman rose from samādhi. The verse says:

The woman before the Buddha had taken the wrong road; / It was not that Mañjuśrī's power fell short. / Though you have the hands to seize dragons and catch tigers, / You are no match for beating a drum and plucking a lute.

When Bodhidharma first arrived at Jinling he met Emperor Wu. The emperor asked: "What is the highest meaning of the noble truth?" Bodhidharma said: "Vast and open — nothing holy." The emperor said: "Who is it that stands before me?" Bodhidharma said: "I do not know." The emperor was not in accord, and so Bodhidharma crossed the river on a reed and sat facing the wall at Shaoshi for nine years. The verse says:

He came from far away with a heart full of warmth, / Thinking a foreign land would be his home. / He never guessed that meeting, they would not know each other; / He turned his head and sat in the cold — most desolate of all.

The Second Patriarch came to Shaolin to attend upon Bodhidharma. Standing in the snow, he cut off his arm and asked: "May I hear the Dharma seal of all the Buddhas?" Bodhidharma said: "The Dharma seal of all the Buddhas is not obtained from another." The Patriarch said: "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to set it at peace." Bodhidharma said: "Bring me your mind and I will set it at peace for you." The Patriarch said: "Seeking the mind, it is utterly ungraspable." Bodhidharma said: "I have set your mind at peace for you." With that the Patriarch awakened. The verse says:
The snow waist-deep, his arm cut and broken; / He came especially to force his mind to peace. / He borrowed your fist to batter your own mouth — / When did it ever add so much as a hair?

When the Sixth Patriarch came to study under Huangmei, the Fifth Patriarch set him to pounding rice in the mortar room. One day, because the Fifth Patriarch asked for verses, intending to transmit the robe and Dharma, the Master wrote a verse on the wall: "Bodhi is originally no tree; / the bright mirror is no stand. / Originally there is not one thing — / where could dust ever cling?" The Patriarch silently took note of it. At night he called him into his room and secretly showed him the mind-tradition and the Dharma eye, transmitted the robe and bowl, and had him cross the river south to return to Caoxi. The verse says:
What difference between a pestle head and a firewood axe? / Again he saw flowers in the clear sky. / He was firm that originally there is not one thing — / So why did he still pick up a torn robe?

He knew it already before he reached Huangmei; / Then why enter the room at the third watch? / Only because he made the robe and bowl a precious thing / Did he leave sons and grandsons, every one of them fools.

One day National Master Zhong of Nanyang called his attendant. The attendant answered. Three times he called and three times the attendant answered. The Master said: "I thought I had failed you — but it is you who have failed me." The verse says:
Three calls, three answers — all too clear. / Where in failing was there heavy or light? / Try breaking through to the moment before the call: / The long wind roars through the pines day and night.

When Chan Master Nanyue Huairang first came to study under the Sixth Patriarch, the Patriarch asked where he had come from. The Master said: "From Mount Song." The Patriarch said: "What thing is it that comes thus?" The Master said: "To say it resembles a thing misses it at once." The Patriarch said: "Can it still be cultivated and realized?" The Master said: "Cultivation and realization are not absent, but defilement is impossible." The Patriarch said: "It is this very non-defilement that all Buddhas protect and remember. Since you are thus, I am thus too." The verse says:
He came from afar with spirits soaring high; / When questioned, he was frost laid over snow. / Had he stood long since beneath the gate of the sun, / Why poke the fire and pour on hot water besides?
One day Master Ma ascended the Dharma seat, and Baizhang rolled up the mat before him; the Patriarch at once stepped down. The verse says:

A great general mounts the altar, winds from all eight sides; / Banners rolled, drums silent, the four ramparts empty. / Such is the clear and peaceful scene — / Only now is seen the king's army's greatest victory.
Master Ma was unwell. The temple director asked: "How is the Master's health these days?" The Patriarch said: "Sun-face Buddha, Moon-face Buddha." The verse says:

The illness lies in the marrow, beyond all cure; / He shuts the door and secretly ponders in the dark. / Others cannot understand that unendurable place — / And no sooner do they ask than the moment is already lost.

A monk was traveling to Mount Wutai and asked an old woman: "Which way leads to Mount Wutai?" The old woman said: "Just go straight on." The monk set off. The old woman said: "What a fine teacher — and off he goes just like that." Later a monk told Master Zhaozhou about it. The Master said: "Wait till I have gone and tested her." The next day the Master went and asked her: "Which way leads to Mount Wutai?" The old woman said: "Just go straight on." The Master set off. The old woman said: "What a fine teacher — and off he goes just like that." The Master returned to the monastery and said to the monk: "I have seen through that old woman of Mount Wutai for you." The verse says:

Slanting sunlight, fragrant grass in lush array; / Idly he lets the traveler lose his way. / How many, lost, still linger as a guest for the night? / At the fifth watch the dream breaks with a single cock's crow.

Zhaozhou asked a newly arrived monk: "Have you been here before?" The monk said: "I have been here." The Master said: "Go drink tea." He asked another monk, who said: "I have not been here." The Master said: "Go drink tea." Afterwards the temple director asked: "Why did you say 'Go drink tea' to the one who had been here, and also say 'Go drink tea' to the one who had not?" The Master called the director, who answered. The Master said: "Go drink tea." The verse says:

Zhaozhou's whole livelihood was plain and mild; / Whoever crossed his path was asked to drink tea. / If you would seek the plum blossom and its spring, / One branch leans over the wall into the neighbor's house.
You come from far, your road long and remote; / Caked clods fill your breast, your temper proud. / No need of a wondrous pill or a wonder-working drug — / Only one bowl of hot water poured over it.

A monk asked Zhaozhou: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West?" The Master said: "The cypress tree in the courtyard." The monk said: "Master, do not point to a scene and show it to people." The Master said: "I am not pointing to a scene to show people." The monk said: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West?" The Master said: "The cypress tree in the courtyard." The verse says:

The scripture of the great chiliocosm is split from a mote of dust; / The year's end turns, the yang returns, and all the earth is spring. / He holds up the cypress tree in the courtyard — / The ancestral meaning from the West is new again.

At Nanquan's place the monks of the east and west halls were quarreling over a cat. The Master came upon them and said to the assembly: "If any of you can speak a word, you will save the cat; if you cannot, I will cut it in two." No one answered, so the Master cut it. Zhaozhou returned from outside, and the Master told him what he had said. Zhaozhou then took off his straw sandals, put them on his head, and walked out. The Master said: "If you had been here just now, you would have saved the cat." The verse says:

Tai'e is drawn from its sheath, utterly without mercy; / Whatever it touches must be cut off from life and death. / By chance a white ox boasts a fine hand — / And trades a heap of donkey dung for a pair of eyes.
Muzhou addressed the assembly: "When the great matter is not yet clear, it is like mourning father and mother. When the great matter is clear, it is like mourning father and mother." The verse says:

The long river stretches boundless, faint its wind and waves; / Let the light sail come through with the rain as it will. / Reaching the shore, he looks back at the whitecaps — / His sorrow, turning, is more than when aboard.

One day Deshan was late for the meal, and came down from the hall carrying his bowl. At that time Xuefeng was the rice cook, and seeing him he said: "Old fellow, the bell has not sounded and the drum has not been struck — where are you taking your bowl?" The Master went back to the abbot's quarters. Xuefeng told Yantou about it. Yantou said: "Great or small, Deshan does not understand the final phrase." The Master heard of it and had his attendant call Yantou in, asking: "So you do not approve of this old monk?" Yantou secretly conveyed his meaning, and the Master let the matter rest. The next day when he ascended the seat, it was indeed unlike the usual. Yantou came before the monks' hall and clapped his hands, laughing loudly: "I am glad the old fellow understands the final phrase. Even so, he has only three years." And in three years, indeed, he passed away. The verse says:

Idly watching a lion as it romps with its cub, / It yawns and pants, spending all its strength. / Touched, it turns over and makes one throw, / Then bows its head and goes off, setting forth the whole. / The final phrase — do not be in doubt. / Free to roam, to whom would it yield? / Through all ages the long sky, wind and moon remain; / Three years is not likely to be the date of return.

At Deshan's place the attendant Kuo asked where all the sages from of old had gone. The Master said: "What are you doing?" Kuo said: "A flying dragon horse is given the command; a lame turtle puts out its head." The Master said no more. The next day, when the Master came out from bathing, Kuo brought him tea. The Master stroked Kuo's back and said: "What of yesterday's case?" Kuo said: "Old fellow, only today have you caught a glimpse." Again the Master let it rest. The verse says:

Long used to war, he hides deep the tiger-trapping snare; / How would a hot pursuer dare break into the ring? / Even if he saves his whole body and gets away, / His banners and spears are broken, his might already gone.

Once when Mazu, Baizhang, Xitang, and Nanquan were enjoying the moon, the Patriarch said: "At just such a time as this, what is it?" Baizhang said: "It is the very time for cultivation." Xitang said: "It is the very time for making offerings." Nanquan shook out his sleeves and walked off. The Patriarch said: "The sutras return to the storehouse; Chan returns to the sea. Only Shanyuan stands alone beyond things." The verse says:

The moon at mid-autumn shines surpassingly bright; / In how many homes do songs and flutes not cease? / The old fisherman goes home to lodge among the reeds; / Deep asleep on river and sky, no dream can form.

A scholar named Zhang Zhuo was at Changsha's place, reading the scripture of the names of the thousand Buddhas, when he asked: "Of the hundred thousand Buddhas I see only their names; I do not know what lands they dwell in. Do they still transform living beings?" The Master said: "After Cui Hao wrote his poem on Yellow Crane Tower, has any scholar written one there?" He said: "No." The Master said: "Take your leisure and write one." The verse says:
