Before Yellow Crane Tower the river water runs deep; / Wind and waves roar with thunder day and night. / A hundred thousand Buddhas wag their tongues together — / Why seek elsewhere when it is right before your face?

Jiashan came to study under Chuanzi. No sooner had they met than Chuanzi asked: "Virtuous one, what temple do you dwell in?" Jiashan said: "Dwelling is not dwelling; dwelling would not be like it." Chuanzi said: "Not like it? Like what?" Jiashan said: "It is not a dharma present before the eyes." The Master said: "Where did you get that?" Jiashan said: "It is not something the ear or eye can reach." The Master said: "A single phrase that fits the head is a donkey-tethering peg for ten thousand kalpas." The Master also said: "A line hung a thousand feet down aims at the deep pool; three inches from the hook — why do you not speak?" As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, the Master knocked him into the water with a stroke of the oar. When Jiashan had just climbed back into the boat, the Master again said: "Speak! Speak!" As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him. Jiashan was suddenly greatly awakened and nodded three times. The Master said: "From the pole's tip the line and silk are yours to play; not touching the clear waves, the meaning is of itself distinct." Jiashan then asked: "What of the time when one casts away the line and stops fishing?" The Master said: "The silk hangs in the clear water — floating, it settles the meaning of having and not having." Jiashan said: "Words carry the mystery yet there is no road; the tongue speaks and does not speak." The Master said: "The whole river's waves are fished out; at last the brocade-scaled one is met." Jiashan covered his ears. The Master said: "Thus, thus." The verse says:

He leans alone on the orchid-wood oar, guarding the ford; / Idly he lets down hook and line to catch the brocade scales. / By chance he meets a fierce dragon and gives it one bump — / In heaven-high waves he knows how to turn himself free.
A monk asked Zhaozhou: "Does a dog have the Buddha-nature or not?" Zhaozhou said: "Wu — No." The verse says:

One gaze down the long river — vast and faint the cold mist; / Gazing to midstream, my thoughts drift vague and lost. / How pitiful, deep in the night beneath the bright moon: / There is no one to ask about the boat at the ferry landing.

A monk asked Zhaozhou: "The ten thousand dharmas return to the One; where does the One return?" The Master said: "When this old monk was in Qingzhou I made a hempen shirt that weighed seven catties." The verse says:

The road comes to a cliff where there is nowhere to walk; / He turns his body one step and his footfall is light. / If you would seek the tracks of the antelope that hangs by its horns, / Though you had eyes, I fear you would be like the blind.

The Third Sage asked Xuefeng about the golden-scaled fish that has broken through the net: "I do not know what it feeds on." The Master said: "Wait until you are out of the net and I will tell you." The Sage said: "A good friend of fifteen hundred people, and you do not even know a huatou!" The Master said: "This old monk's duties as abbot are many." The verse says:

A little boat has spent the whole of one sail's wind; / Having reached the shore, why labor to turn the sail again? / If you ask where the old fisherman lodges — / He sings aloud and goes home in the bright moonlight.
A monk asked Yunmen: "When not a single thought arises, is there still any fault?" Yunmen said: "Mount Sumeru." The verse says:

The cold sky, the frost falling, the moon sunk in the west; / The clear night stretches long, the crane's dream wanders lost. / On the ocean floor the sun-wheel glows red as fire — / The traveler still listens for the fifth-watch cock.

When Yunmen ascended the hall he said: "There are two kinds of illness in the light that does not penetrate through. When all places are unclear and something stands before you — that is one. Again, even if you penetrate through the emptiness of all dharmas, and dimly there seems to be something resembling a thing — that too is the light not penetrating through. The Dharma body likewise has two kinds of illness. Having attained the Dharma body, if attachment to the dharma is not forgotten and your own views still remain, so that you sit beside the Dharma body — that is one. Even if you penetrate through the Dharma body, to let it go is not permissible; examine it carefully and see what breath remains in it — that too is an illness." The verse says:

A bright moon trails her shadow down the heavenly street; drunk in the east wind, I lean alone upon the rail. When court is done and the ninefold palace falls to silence, the six palaces still array their caps and gowns.

Master Luzu, whenever he saw a monk approach, would simply turn and face the wall. When Nanquan heard of this he said, “I am always telling monks and teachers: grasp it before the Buddha ever appeared in the world — and still you do not get one half of one. If he carries on like that, he will wait till the year of the donkey, a year that never comes.” The gāthā says:

Beneath the snow on the cold cliff lies one branch of plum; its boundless spring light it will not open wide. Yet the east wind lightly lets the secret slip, and hidden fragrance drifts into my dream.

Weishan addressed the assembly, saying, “A hundred years from now I shall be a water buffalo down the mountain. On its left flank five words shall be written: The monk of Weishan, so-and-so. Then if you call it the monk of Weishan, it is a water buffalo; if you call it a water buffalo, it is the monk of Weishan. What, then, will you call it?” The gāthā says:

In the belly of a horse, in the womb of an ass, lies the house of buddhas and patriarchs; where the great man walks, the road stretches far. If the water buffalo is measured against old Weishan, its horns stand high — and still it yields to him.
A monk asked Yunmen, “What is Buddha?” Yunmen said, “A dried shit-stick.” The gāthā says:

Mountains, rivers and lands stand openly revealed; rubble and thickets all give forth their light. But let a single mote of dust stand before your face, and buddhas countless as the Ganges sands are hidden quite.
Gāthās on the Diamond Sūtra (Eighteen Poems)
The World-Honored One Puts On His Robe and Takes Up His Bowl; Subhūti Sighs That This Is Rare
To put on the robe and take the bowl is just like this; to eat and walk in mindfulness — what is so wondrous there? Why then did Subhūti sigh that it was rare, leaving people all the more perplexed?
Thus Should One Abide
At the road's end, cold looks and desolation; then all at once you meet the great resting place. Let go, and this becomes the land of peace — why trouble yourself with grief and long debate?
Thus Should One Subdue the Mind

On the wall the lamplight plays at children's shapes; in the black night you suspect a ghost is at your heels. Wait for daybreak and see through it for yourself — all that alarm and delight, to whom will you tell it?
In Truth Not One Being Attains Deliverance

Last night I dreamed I came to the Ghost Gate Pass; countless rākṣasas thronged the Iron Mountain round. The cold cock crowed, the sky broke into dawn — I turned, and one smile scattered all my grief.
Not Abiding in Marks
A gandharva city fallen into a mirror; towers and halls and pavilions fill the void. Only look at the countless visitors who climb there, leaning on the rail, robes thrown open, seeing off the geese.
Giving Rise to the Mind That Dwells Nowhere

Seek not at random the tracks of birds and fish; lightning and flint-spark allow the mind no room. People today hear only the clamor of spring birds — who believes the note within the kalavinka's egg?
No Self, No Person, No Being, No Life-Span

The puppets mount the stage and wait for drum and gong; everyone gathers round to hear the loud song. You do not know whose hand the strings are in; when the strings snap, what shame and confusion follow.
The Four Fruits Form No Such Thought

A wayside inn on a long road, briefly welcoming travellers; one night of rest — how could it last? In a dream I suddenly climbed to the Tuṣita heaven; turning my head, all that fine thinking was spent for nothing.
Before Dīpaṃkara Buddha, in Truth Nothing Was Attained

Young, I took up book and sword and went to a far country, meaning in time to enter the examination hall. By chance in the street I met a diviner, who told me I should be the topmost scholar of them all.
To Hold Four Lines of Verse Brings Blessings Great

Year after year ghosts haunt us and shamans are called in; driven off, they come again and leave their filth behind. By the statute of the Most High Lord Lao, from this day let all evil spirits be driven away together.
Subhūti Is Moved to Tears

Who knows the place where the heart aches? A kingdom in mourning, a family ruined — and to whom shall I speak? I turn my head; from my old home no word comes. I cannot bear to hear the wild goose's grief again.
King Kali Cuts His Body Limb from Limb
King Mu loved the man made by Yanshi; the singing and laughter seemed so truly real. One burst of anger and it was torn apart — only then did he know it was glued and lacquered into a body.
A Single Thought of Faith Attains Bodhi

Say not the dog-butcher was unworthy of the Yi Gate's recommendation; one word of promise and he pledged his golden self. Hammer in hand, he walked straight into the commander's tent and seized the tally from the general's elbow.
The Three Minds Cannot Be Attained

Through the cold, vast sky a lone wild goose journeys on; the straining eye grows dim and miles are heaped on miles. Its traces were cut off from the very beginning — I urge you, do not reckon up the road.
There Is No Dharma That Can Be Spoken
In the house of illusions the tricks are many; the singing never stops, the dancers whirl. Pity the watchers, who only add to their grief and joy — have you ever seen the single thread behind it all?
The Tathāgata Says They Are Not Beings; Therefore They Are Called Beings

The painter follows his fancy, drawing forms and faces; features, robes and caps all differ one from another. Fair or foul, let him sort them all he likes — in the end not one of them is the true master.
The Tathāgata Says the Ordinary Being Is Not an Ordinary Being

High and low were never fixed by any rule; from a white-walled cottage ministers have always come. Once the Son of Heaven proclaims the edict in person, you are there and then the first name on the list.
The Tathāgata Comes from Nowhere and Goes Nowhere
I dreamed I wandered in the land of Huaxu; joyful on arriving, sorrowful on turning back. One cock-crow and the frosty sky grows light — empty flowers fall from my pillow into both eyes.
Gāthās on the Sixteen Sublime Contemplations of the Pure Land
1. The First, the Sun Contemplation: Behold the Setting Sun as a Hanging Drum
The white sun sinks in the west, and there I lodge my longing; where the sunset ends, the mind knows. Since we parted no word has come — and yet from then on it is ever as if we were face to face.
2. The Second, the Water Contemplation: Behold the Great Waters Clear and Still, Frozen to Ice and Radiant; Form the Perception of Vaiḍūrya
The cool mind-ground, blue and crystalline; translucent as water turned to ice. One shining field of pure vaiḍūrya — let it not bury the old barbarian monk.
3. The Third, the Ground Contemplation: Behold Ice and Vaiḍūrya; Accomplish the Perception of the Ground
Where can the roaming mind walk? The jewelled ground of vaiḍūrya is level as a palm. Before the foot moves, the step ahead is already taken — and yet it never travelled any road at all.
4. The Fourth, the Tree Contemplation: On the Vaiḍūrya Ground, Form the Perception of Jewelled Trees

Row upon row of trees, a forest of the seven jewels; arrayed before the eyes, solemn and deep in shade. The flowers hold countless maṇi gems within; when the wind stirs, they ever proclaim the wondrous Dharma sound.
5. The Fifth, the Pool Contemplation: In the Seven-Jewelled Pools, Form the Perception of the Water of Eight Good Qualities

The king of wish-fulfilling pearls wells up as a spring; the water holds eight virtues and flows among the flowers. On the diamond pool's floor the golden sand is spread; thought after thought the seven-jewelled lotus opens in the mind.
6. The Sixth, the Comprehensive Contemplation: Form the Perception of Jewelled Pavilions
Jewelled and adorned, the pavilions rise in tier on tier; countless devas assemble within. Unstruck, the heavenly music sounds of itself; the Dharma fills the ear and the joy is without end.
7. The Seventh, the Seat Contemplation: Within the Seven-Jewelled Lotus, Form the Perception of the Diamond Throne
The seven-jewelled flower holds a seven-jewelled throne; maṇi stamens and pistils knit the womb. As the mind wills, one field of radiant light — and one's own golden form appears therein.
8. The Eighth, the Image Contemplation: Form the Perception of One Buddha and Two Bodhisattvas

Marks and excellences, radiance, a body like water and moon — just as a lost child sees his kind mother again. From today, once you know the face you had before your mother bore you, you will no longer be a wanderer on the long road.
9. The Ninth, the Buddha Contemplation: Form the Perception of the Buddha's Marks and Excellences

The white-hair curl is Sumeru, the eyes are lotuses; mark upon mark of excellence, all without bound. Every pore of the whole body gathers light, illumining the three thousand and the great thousand worlds.
10. The Tenth, the Contemplation of Avalokiteśvara: Form the Image of the Great Being, with a Buddha Standing in His Crown

The great being's body, vast and without bound; in the light of his crown, transformed buddhas numberless as dust. Look closely: in each pore lie the lands of living beings; whatever meets the eye is clearly an old friend.
11. The Eleventh, the Contemplation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta: Form the Perception of Him Seated Upright, Holding a Lotus

Light, form and feature are all without fault; on his head a heavenly crown of a hundred jewelled flowers. Within those flowers pure buddha-lands are held — and no one knows who the master of the house may be.
12. The Twelfth, the Universal Contemplation: Form the Perception of Oneself Reborn, with the Lotus Opening and Closing
The mind conceives a lotus vast as space; reborn deep within, in a secrecy none may pierce. When the light shines through and the flower opens — waking eyes still find it like a dream.
13. The Thirteenth, the Miscellaneous Contemplation: Form the Perception of the Buddha in Bodies Great and Small, Not Fixed

A hundred rivers hold the moon, its shadows uneven; it goes and comes with each person, wherever he may go. You would say the two ends make two separate roads — who knows that in all its moving it never moved?
14. The Fourteenth, the Contemplation of the Three Highest Grades
The mind imagines climbing far to the Tuṣita palace; adorned and wondrous, realm upon realm. I hear Maitreya speak the truth myself — only I fear the meeting is a dream.
15. The Fifteenth, the Contemplation of the Three Middle Grades

The Son of Heaven seeks talent, choosing the filial and upright; village verdicts, great and small, all call them worthy. One day they climb the golden hall by special grace — that a white-walled cottage yields a minister is no accident.
16. The Sixteenth, the Contemplation of the Three Lowest Grades

Sword-trees and knife-mountains stand before the eyes; one turn of the light, and they become golden lotuses. To rise to general from a grave-robber is a hero's deed; only then you believe that office is not bought with coin.
A Gāthā on the Dharma of Original Abiding, in Celebration of the Eightieth Year of Chan Master Wunian of Mount Huangbo (with Preface)

In the third year of His Majesty's reign, in mid-spring of the guihai year, on the seventeenth day of the second month, fell the day of the four hundred and eightieth jiazi of Chan Master Wunian of Mount Huangbo. From his youth the Master set his will on the highest; he awakened early to his own mind, opened the true eye upon his brow, and raised the banner of fearlessness. The Dharma gate looks to him with reverence, and monks flock to him like the wind; all are guided to the supreme meaning and brought to enter the ground of self-confidence. Truly he is a ford and bridge in the age of the Dharma's decline, a torch of wisdom in the long night. The Chan school has fallen into decline, and it is owing to the Master alone that its family voice is still sounded. I, unwise as I am, have never beheld his countenance, yet the light of our minds shines upon each other with not a hair's breadth between. In the Dharma we forget feeling and hold no mark of self or other — and this has been so for many a day. Alas, I am old now, and I am ashamed that I cannot once take up the fly-whisk with him to seal a bond of Dharma joy. Now, happily, I meet the day of the Master's manifestation in birth; officials and laymen of the ten directions, black-robed and white-robed alike, each bring offerings and raise their praise. Hearing of it, I rejoice, and say to myself: one who awakens to the unborn is free of the mark of a life-span and cannot be moved by the four marks — how could one measure him by worldly truth? So I speak a gāthā on the Dharma of Original Abiding, and respectfully send an attendant to carry incense and flowers afar, to express my praise. It is to measure the great ocean with a drop of water, to view the vast void through a crack; I would not presume to exhaust his bounds, but only to show a little of my sincerity, in the spirit of offering the Dharma. And the gāthā says:

The self-nature of all dharmas is ever quiescent and extinguished, still and unmoving as empty space. The world's dense array and all its myriad forms are sealed by this one Dharma alone. Before the Buddha appeared, before the patriarchs came, this Dharma of original abiding lacked nothing. Blades of grass and motes of dust have their essence complete; even the white ox and the dark slave know it is there. How much more do living beings, each fully endowed, share a nature equal with all buddhas. This equal self-nature knows no birth or death — how could the four marks ever move it? It neither comes nor goes, has no beginning or end; therefore it is called the Dharma of original abiding. If one awakens to this and embodies suchness, in one leap he cuts off the views of ordinary being and sage. When the true eye opens, birth and death are empty; the two gates of delusion and awakening fly open on the spot. One who has passed the gate swings his arms and walks, treading the great square alone with no hindrance, like a lion roaming at ease — no jackal may follow in his tracks. He tears away the thatch that seals the five aggregates and sits openly on bare ground, robe thrown back, at peace. This is called the fearless, liberated one; from then on he ever abides in this Dharma. It is the Master alone who has understood this Dharma of original abiding, sitting alone on Huangbo's highest peak, lofty and unmoved as Sumeru, while all the myriad forms bow their heads to him. Sun and moon move on like flashes of lightning; the world's mountains and rivers are shadows in a mirror. Indeed, since mind is empty, body too is empty, blending all dharmas with no rising or ceasing. Thus one mote of dust joined with emptiness becomes one body with all space, and so with every mote of dust: body and dust are equal, not two. Once body and dust enter the emptiness of the Dharma realm, the essence of self-nature equals space. This emptiness is itself the Dharma of original abiding; one who enters it has a life without measure. Within space, worlds may rise and cease as they will; all sages and ordinary beings come and go. This Dharma is unmoved, its mark ever abiding; it is the life-span of all beings on earth. Since living beings are one with all buddhas, how could my Master differ from living beings? May my Master ever manifest and be born among them, realizing and entering the measureless life of all beings.
A Seat-Side Admonition, Shown to Master Huang

Desire must not be indulged; the will must not be unsettled; the nature must not turn perverse; the mind must not run loose; the body must not grow slack; learning must not be shallow; principle must not be obscured; thought must not be wild. Do not let idleness carry you outward; do not let craving destroy you within. Dwell in calm and quiet, and all your limbs will come to no harm; be not seduced by things, and your spirit will be king of itself.
An Admonition on Settling the Will, Shown to Master Jiang

Be not restless in the mire of worldly desire; be not sullen in disordered thought; be not proud as a floating cloud; be not chasing after the nets of the world. Rather, settle your will and dwell in simplicity; seek to gather your spirit and nourish it in stillness. Feed on wild greens with contentment; enjoy clear hills and waters alone. Open the Dark and the Changes to fathom transformation; read the Spring and Autumn Annals to mirror the past. Recite the Nanhua to dissolve your cares; knock at the Western scriptures to break through your hindrances. See the world's ways as a heat-haze; hear praise and blame as echoes in a valley. Look on all things as a worm's arm; regard this body as a rat's burrow. What do riches and honor ask of me? Gain and loss in others' hands turn like a palm. Bright before you, shining above you — be not reckless, be not scheming: what confusion, what blur? In form like a wooden cock, in mind like Xiangwang, blank and unknowing. Confucius said, “Free from envy, free from greed — what course could fail to be good?” This is what is called excellence enduring.
The Admonition on Self

All love and hate arise from the hindrance of self. If the hindrance of self is emptied, the light is measureless. When mind arises chasing objects, when thought stirs following feeling — forget both mind and object, and things and self are undivided. Things have no beauty or ugliness; it is the self that makes them right or wrong. If my mind does not arise, what can those things do? View motion and stillness as equal; see high and low as one; level ordinary beings and sages alike — this is called the inconceivable.
The Admonition on the Body

Reverently I ask you, body: what are you? A compound of the four elements, false within and without — gathered foam, a plantain trunk, dust and heat-haze; a dense forest of many sufferings, a vast wilderness of birth and death. Many are blind to it; few understand. When one breath fails to come, you are a wen, a clod of earth.
The Admonition on the Mind

What are you, mind — dim and unfathomable? You are the norm of things, the spirit of man; bright and undimmed, clear and ever awake. You are the storehouse of good and evil, the court of sages and saints. Let not desire obscure you; let not delusion entangle you. In calm and quiet, your spirit finds its own peace.
The Admonition on the Nature

Your essence is perfect and bright, your form subtle and profound; unmoved and unchanging, without mark or feature — as water is wet, as fire is dry. Through all transformation it does not shift; words and names cannot reach it. Gone or abiding, coming or now; at leisure or busy, still or restless — it stands alone, and this is called the true Way.
The Admonition on Destiny

I ask you, whence do you come? Truly by Heaven's favor. Long life or early death, poverty or success — let them come as they will. Be not envious, not greedy; bear no grudge, no hatred. Dwell like a quail, eat like a fledgling; be dragon-cloud or leopard-mist. Trust your spirit: rise and fall have their number. Be at peace and wait, and allow no longing for what lies outside.
An Inscription on Mother and Son (with Preface)

Because he spread the Dharma, Qing brought trouble upon himself and provoked the anger of the sage Son of Heaven; the voice of it was like thunder. Privately I thought of my old mother: hearing it, she would surely be frightened out of her wits. Yet by grace I was spared from death and sent into exile at Leiyang. Passing through my native place, I welcomed my old mother on the river. At the first sight of me she laughed and talked, her voice clear and bright, with not the slightest tangled thought in her breast. So I asked her, “Mother, when you heard that your son stood between life and death, were you not worried?” She said, “Life and death are allotted; I do not worry even for myself — why should I worry for you? It is only that people's words differ, and one cannot be certain how things stand; that is what makes one doubt.” We sat together in attendance, and toward dawn we made our final parting. My old mother charged me, “Take good care of yourself in the Way; do not worry about me. Now I too take my long farewell of you.” She set off on the road joyfully, without one backward look. I was moved that under heaven there are mothers such as this — does she not in one stroke exhaust all the feelings of birth and death? So I made this inscription for her, saying:

The love of mother and son: a lodestone drawing a needle. The wondrous nature is natural, perfect from the first. I see my mother as fire comes out of wood; the wood is burned away — the fire was never a self. Born, yet unattached; dying, as if unaware: only then do you see that this body of mine is the child of a stone maiden.
An Inscription on Clarifying the Mind, Shown to Ding Youwu

True nature is deep and still, like clear standing water. Love and hate strike it, and the waves of affliction rise. Rising without cease, the self-nature grows turbid; affliction and ignorance only deepen the unawareness. To grasp at the other with a self is like putting mud into water; to let the other stir me is like pouring oil on fire. The other troubles my truth, but the trouble is truly born of me. If I do not arise, the conflagration's burning turns to ice. Therefore the sage first empties the mark of self. If the mark of self is empty, from what can the other obstruct him? The work of forgetting the self lies in firm patience. The moment habit-energy stirs, suddenly give a sharp awakening; at the very place of awakening there is illumination — one thought turns the light back, sweeping away tracks and cutting off traces, and at once it is cool. Cool and still, standing alone, calm and joyful in spirit, nothing can stand against him.
An Inscription on Contemplating the Mind

Contemplate the body as no body — a mirror's image, the moon in water. Contemplate the mind as without marks — luminous and pure. When not one thought arises, it is empty, numinous, still and shining; perfect as the vast void, containing all wonders. It neither goes out nor comes in; it has no shape or feature. The hundred thousand skillful means all return to one pore. Do not rely on form and breath, for form and breath obstruct. Do not take deluded thought as real, for deluded thought breeds monstrosities. Contemplate this mind closely: it is hollow and empty, with nothing in it. In an instant feeling arises, and at once you feel dazed. At the critical moment turn the light back, and with all your strength shine upon it; the clouds scatter in the clear sky, and the white sun blazes. If the inner mind does not arise, outer objects are not born. Whatever has marks is not the original truth. When a thought arises, be aware; awareness at once shines through it. When an object comes, sweep it away; sweeping, let it go. The realms of good and evil transform with the mind; the forms of ordinary being and sage appear in response to thought. To hold mantras and contemplate the mind is like the medicine that polishes a mirror: once the dust and grime are gone, this too is not clung to. Vast and great spiritual powers are fully present in one's own mind; the Pure Land and the heavenly palaces — roam in them at will. You need not seek the truth: the mind itself is Buddha. If it is born in a place of heat, it ripens of itself in that place. Through the twelve hours of the day, everything is wondrous; wherever you touch, you are not deluded. This is called the essence of mind.
An Inscription on Mastering the Mind

Human nature is originally great, beyond form and vessel; it is only because there is a self that hindrances arise of themselves. When habits and defilements are thick, one is burdened by things; when learning is not broad, one is full of self-opinion. When principle is not clearly seen, one grows proud and leans on temper; one makes light of the inner and prizes the outer, chases things and loses the will. Cravings wound one's life, and one does not know what to avoid; one casts away oneself and forgets the truth — who would call this wisdom? The man of understanding keeps his heart empty, meets conditions without obstruction, yields with the times, plays in the world as dragon or snake. Gain and loss do not alarm him, high and low do not touch him; calm and tranquil, he gladdens his spirit, cutting thought short and stinting care. He strives at what he cannot yet do, is careful where he has not yet arrived; he learns non-doing, practices non-affairs, hears the unheard, sees the unseen. Turning back to look within, thought after thought he does not dwell; all delusions vanish, and the pure one is not two. This is the sage — the secret of mastering the mind. Seek it within yourself, and there is ample room; not to contemplate thus is called self-abandonment.
An Inscription on Awakening to One's Faults

A journey of ten thousand miles — every step is wrong; yet because the man is unaware, he does not shift an inch. A human life of a hundred years — thought after thought does not abide; the deluded press blindly on: who sorts the new from the old? Good and evil shift in turn, like a ring without an end; no one knows its limit, or who makes it so. The one who makes it does not know, and the newer it grows, the more deluded. The heels have nowhere to stand; lifting a foot brings weariness. When weariness has lasted long, one loses what one had; monstrosities come forth in hundreds, and one does not see their ugliness. Taking delusion for awakening, the whole earth goes astray; Momu apes a beauty's frown and is placidly pleased with herself. But let her come to the mirror for an instant and she will suddenly, sharply awaken: just still the mad mind — no need to apply powder. Natural beauty, brows and eyes clear and bright, the original face with not a hair's difference. Never mind fair or foul; no carving is needed. Leave it just as it is, and it returns to simplicity of itself. Awakening is not yes; unknowing is not knowing wrong. Spit out both right and wrong, and all things return as one.
An Inscription on Dream and Awakening

Good and evil have no beginning; it is one mind that turns and turns again. Sages and ordinary beings are not divided — only dream and awakening remain. To enter dream with awakening deepens the inversion; to enter awakening with dream brings liberation on the spot. Dream and awakening are both not it: still, numinous knowing, unborn and undying — what care, what thought? The hundred thousand illusions and transformations lie in a single thought. When a thought arises unawares, it is lightning in the vast void. If affliction does not knot, karma is not born. Love and hate, firm and hard, are truly the root of birth and death. Cause and effect, retribution, follow swift as shadow to form. If the root is not born, from what can the branches grow? Karma has many kinds, and killing stands first. All things love life and hate death — this is so for every one. Though the shells differ, the buddha-nature is the same. Only contemplate them equally, and the thought of killing empties itself. When the mind-mirror is buried in dust and habit is thick, wear it away with awakening, and the light will shine through of itself. As you grind, it falls away bit by bit; when a thought arises, be aware. When awareness reaches the unborn, mind and objects are empty and vast. Deluded thoughts racing after things are of no profit in the end. Examine and ponder this well: death and birth are swift. Birth and death come and go in a great, dark dream, turning only with karma — as if there were no birth. Born, yet unattached, one must wake from the dream. Seen with waking eyes, one binds oneself with no rope. Thought after thought, turn the light back; mind after mind, shine within. Simply do not follow feeling — this is called the essential wonder.
An Inscription on Forgetting Conditions

Feeling has wise and foolish; the nature has no brightness or dullness. The division between ordinary being and sage lies truly in turning toward or away. It is like a minister serving his lord, like a son attending his father: a single thought of pure truth allows no looking back or lingering. Linger, and it shifts; shift, and delusion is made. Once delusion has lasted long, the spirit grows weary day by day. Do not shift, and you awaken; awakened, you do not look back. Standing alone, deep and still, wondrous function ever abides. Responding to conditions like an echo, dwelling in the world like space, roaming free as things transform, in an instant you slip the cage. Neither going out nor coming in, no departing and no arriving. The world's marks are empty flowers; the breast holds the moon in water.
An Inscription on Contemplating the World

This illusory body of the four elements holds nothing at all; the foolish cling to it, shackled by love and hate. The wondrous, perfect, awakened mind is everywhere, pure and complete. Deluded thought piles up delusion, and inversion deepens the sickness. The thirsty deer chases the mirage: the more it chases, the thirstier it grows. See through it and rest — then you know it was a mistake. Playful spiritual powers never leave the daily round; high and low, fair and foul, let them tumble as they will. The man of understanding takes the great view and sees through it all: parting and meeting, sorrow and joy, are utterly unattainable. The realms of the six dusts are like treasures gathered in a dream; measureless greed and seeking end at a single awakening. Sound, voice, form, appearance — wind and moon moving through the sky: if you do not cling to them, are you blind and deaf? With this to meet the world, what hindrance can there be? The body is an ordinary being's, but the name is Avalokiteśvara, the Freely Contemplating Lord.
An Inscription on the Six Faculties

The body is the matchmaker of karma, the mind its seed. From the six roots of feeling come rushing greed and surging love. The eye flows out to forms and loses its true brightness; the ear flows out to sounds and loses its original hearing. The tongue misses no flavor, yet in truth it speaks many false words. Indulging will and feeling, the wind of consciousness stirs within; habit rises and the apertures hum, like a reed-pipe with a sound, no one knowing whence it comes, and the listener is shaken. Out of the mouth, into the ear — and love and hate arise. The sound has already died away, and the disaster is only beginning. Like thunder striking dung, suddenly poisonous fungi grow; the fool eats them and is accidentally killed. Nose and body together are one awareness — all are floating dust. The body has many faults and evils; the intellect is the pivot. Drifting on the waves of the poisonous sea, carried off by them, one muddles one's true lord. Therefore people in the world, though alive, are not alive. If you can look back, each faculty regains its pure truth. When the pure truth is restored, the six faculties hold nothing — like clouds floating in the sky, like an echo from the valley. Unbound by form, unhindered by mind, utterly beyond the dust of feeling, supremely at ease.
An Inscription on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation

Recite the Buddha, recite the mind; recite the mind, recite the Buddha. The Buddha is not outside the mind; the mind is not a thing. The self-nature is bright, mind after mind illumining. Deluded thoughts hide their tracks; the body is an empty valley. The Pure Land is never apart from what is before your eyes; lotuses ever line your two feet. Why wait for the life after this to be born there? Right here and now, neither going out nor coming in — this is precisely the Samādhi of Universal Light, and it lies in a single call from the man himself.
An Inscription on Rectifying the Mind

The mind is originally bright; obscured by desire, it grows dark. Its natural essence is dissipated as it follows feeling. To rectify it now, drive out desire and master feeling; once the one truth is restored, no delusion arises.
An Inscription on Making the Will Sincere

Thought is the root of delusion, which bores through emptiness each day. Search out its source with care: it hides in unawareness. Once aware, one is no longer deluded; delusion stilled, reality appears. In utmost sincerity without pause, one's goodness deepens and grows.
Inscription on Cultivating the Self

Desires that merely serve the body are the root of self-indulgence; the bewitchment of wine and lust is a pitfall that ruins the self. If one is lost to desire and does not turn back, body and mind will find no firm ground, and this life will have been passed in vain.
Inscription on Ordering the Household

The key to ordering a household lies in thrift and diligence alone. Where righteousness and propriety abound, quiet simplicity grows mellow of itself. Thrift and diligence are handed down through the family; quiet simplicity steadies the will. This is the secret by which sages and worthies conduct themselves in the world.
Inscription on the Six Wondrous Sites, with Introduction

The master of Snowy Peak built his hut beneath the Chaoyang Peak of Shuangjing. The thousand peaks stand like fingers, so he named the place Thousand Fingers. The peak before it clasps the hut closely, curving round like a horn, and I named it Qilin Horn, meaning also that it stands alone. Before the hermitage lies a pool that the local people call Inkstone Washing, for Dongpo thrice roamed this mountain; hence the name is attached to him as a hidden tribute. I changed it to Coming Moon, for the ancients likened the Way to this: once the pool is made, the moon comes of itself. Above the pool stands a studio, which I inscribed Washing the Moon, as a likeness of mind and object. Behind the studio is a spring whose flavor is sweet, cold, and mellow, and I titled it Surpassing Milk. For the ancient sages said that the water at the beginning of the kalpa tasted finer than milk, since it came from the vajra ground; the water on this summit must rise from a deep source, and so it may serve as a likeness of the lineage of the Way, by which one may know its root. Behind the hermitage stands a rock that I named Great Rest, meaning this is a true aranya, a place of genuine practice, a field of quiescence, a site of great repose. These scenes are natural, and so I titled them the Six Wondrous Sites; and at the head of the scroll I wrote: Six Penetrations, Four Reaches, wishing that those within these scenes, however old, might not be bound by wonder. One must simply take away both sides; hence I said reaching and penetrating. Then I made an inscription for each by hand, to record that they be not forgotten. They are not to be met as mere scenery, nor do they fall into words or thought; the host and guest must each attain them for himself.
Thousand Finger Hermitage

A thousand peaks stand erect, pointing straight at this hut; the hut is like space, utterly without a screen. Ask the master within the hut: he neither leaves nor enters. Should one come to call on him, there is only a shout in the void.
Qilin Horn Peak

A herd goes galloping and leaping, yet one qilin is content by itself. What the qilin prizes above all is its single horn, standing alone. A slab of rock is like a qilin, ten thousand trees like its fur; how laughable are those who ride it, never moving a hair.
Coming Moon Pool
The moon never came, nor does the water go; all at once they meet, and no one knows why. The sky beneath the water, the moon within the pool: the marks of coming and going cannot be spoken of at all.
Washing the Moon Studio

The moon has no dust to begin with, the water is clean of itself; from what place should it be washed? Seek it and you cannot find it. The moon falls into the water, the water holds the moon's reflection; a pity that the beholder, in his fevered dream, has not yet awakened.
Surpassing Milk Spring

To pick milk out of water, one must be a goose king; here no picking is needed, only skill in tasting. It is not yet permitted to enter the mouth; one must first know the flavor. Only those who know the flavor drink and are drunk in heart.
Great Rest Rock

A rock is not skilled at running, so why should it need to rest? The greatest rest is rooted in quiescence itself. Sit cross-legged here, unmoving, unshaken, and put forth the broad, long tongue while the pine wind howls through the night.
Inscription on the Prajñā Pavilion, with Preface

The pavilion takes its name from the reading of this sutra. It was the dwelling of the Wumen laymen Zhu Lu and Wang Zaigong. Lu was a remarkable scholar; Zaigong passed the provincial examinations and served as commandant of the prefecture, yet he scorned carriage and cap, abandoned wife and children, and went into retreat on Mount Tianmu. Before long he came again to Shuangjing and stayed in this pavilion, reading the Prajñā Sutra, and greatly awakened. I came from Mount Nanyue and, through the final karmic circumstances of Master Dahui, arrived at this mountain. When the layman saw me he rejoiced and took up the duties of a disciple. I sighed and said: without great strength and a delight in the joy of quiescence, how could one cast off the dust of entanglement at once and come to this? So I named Zhu Great Strength, and Wang Great Cover, and inscribed his pavilion Prajñā. Then I made an inscription to record it, saying:

How startling, this pavilion: bright and utterly transparent, inside and out laid bare, with nothing at all to bind or cling to. At the gates of the six senses all is perfect and void, and world and beyond-world are cast aside together. The flavor of this pavilion is calm, still, silent, and vast; its master within is at ease in body and mind. All the dust of feeling is a bonfire of tiny embers. Ask what this Dharma gate is called: its name cannot be spoken.
Inscription on the Vaiśālī Chamber, with Preface

The layman Guan Juexian grew up in Wumen. He took refuge in the Three Jewels early, kept no wife or children, and gave no thought to livelihood; he built only a single room and named it Vaiśālī, that he might welcome the ten directions. Since there was no Dharma he could speak, he made fragrant rice his Buddha-work. The old monk passed by his chamber, and so he asked me for an inscription. The inscription says:

The city of Vaiśālī is firm and densely sealed; though he dwells amid the marketplace, no trace of dust remains. Within it is a layman who keeps to a single room alone; the door lets in no wind, the six windows are empty and still. Only the ten directions gather like clouds from time to time. To those who ask the Dharma he gives only silence. The fragrant rice is not invited, but eaten as conditions come; no seat is borrowed, the open ground serves as a mat. All that exists is screened away, not a speck of dust is set up. Body and mind are both forgotten, the world is tossed aside together. Ten thousand burdens are all relinquished, all conditions suddenly stilled. To be in the dust and yet beyond it: this is foremost.
Inscription on the Iron Ruyi, with Introduction
When I took leave of Shuangjing, the master of Snowy Peak offered an iron ruyi together with an incense casket. Moved by this, I wrote an inscription.

This ruyi here speaks in place of my mind and mouth; since I cannot speak, I borrow your fine roar. Your words are not nonexistent, my Dharma is not existent; the two being apart, not even the one is held. Only the fragrance of the Dharma-body is paired with you. Trusting to this vajra, it is handed down unperishing.
The Collected Dream Wanderings of Old Master Hanshan, Volume Thirty-Seven
Verses on Mind-Only

Pure, wondrous, beyond conception, the perfect and true mind is vast and endowed with awesome power, manifesting immeasurable things. Its essence is free of every stain, yet it does not forsake the conditions of defilement and purity; in the world and beyond the world it brings all good karma to fulfillment. All karma is like a flower in the sky, from the first having nothing whatsoever; because there is nothing whatsoever, it is said to be true and eternal. One who understands well that the nature of karma is empty is not deluded by magical tricks, clings to nothing and rejects nothing, and contemplates reality in accord with the truth. Where it arises is the unborn; at the very thought it is empty and still, utterly without before or after. A single thought may be Mount Sumeru, yet motion and stillness are equal and thus. The wind of circumstance does not move it; quiescent and wondrous is its constant bliss. Pure as a lotus flower that enters deep into the mire yet is unstained by the dust of the world, one who holds this wish-fulfilling pearl lacks nothing whatever he seeks. Its divine light illumines the darkness, awakening all sentient beings everywhere.
Verses on Dwelling in the Mountains

I ask the people of the mountain: what joy is there in dwelling here? Three bowls of gruel a day, and stretching out both legs to sleep; a flat rock for a Chan bed, cloud and mist for a coverlet; a light breeze stirs the secluded pines and discloses the meaning of the coming from the West. I brush away the flowers in the clouds and scrape off the film from my eyes. A single thought cuts off center and edge, utterly without before or after. Waking, both eyes are empty, and I look back on the things of dream. Scooping at the moon beneath the water only turns to dull obstruction. Cast off both ordinary and sage, and one is freed from the burden of a mother's birth. To bring not a single thing along is still the second principle. Break through the barrier of no-affairs, and only then is the plan to dwell in the mountains fulfilled.
Shown to the Chan practitioner Daze, who thrice crossed the mountains and seas to pay his respects

For whom have you come ten thousand li, and what is it you have come for? Fumbling for your toes inside your boot, you find them nowhere but where they are. If you seek outside yourself, you will walk to the ends of the earth. Coming and going, coming again: this Dharma has never abided anywhere. Ask the monks of Caoxi whether bodhi can have a tree; if you do not gain a single branch, you have wasted the cloth you sold.
Shown to the Chan practitioner Dao Maiyuan

In Chan practice there is no secret formula; what matters is that birth and death be urgent. Birth and death hang at your eyebrows, and thought after thought must never lapse. Lift up the vajra ring, and make your spine strong as iron. Strive onward and press ahead, until the root of the life-force is cut off. Deluded thoughts suddenly vanish, and body and mind are cast aside on the spot. To see the original person is like driving a peg into empty space. Shatter the black lacquer barrel: only then is there great rest.
Inscribed on a Picture of the Ganges, shown to the Chan practitioner Hengyi Lin

The Buddha dwelt on the bank of the Ganges and constantly taught the Dharma facing the river; when he came to a point beyond thought, he used the river's sands as a likeness. Yet even the vast number of those sands does not exhaust the Buddha's meaning; only this Dharma-body reveals the true sense. The Dharma-body never changes, and its nature does not shift as it flows along. Though all manner of filth surrounds it, its essence is forever pure; even when the fire at the kalpa's end burns, its ultimate substance is not destroyed. Therefore the Dharma-body is constant, and self-nature has neither birth nor death. When a son of the Buddha understands this sense and awakens to the body of self-nature, then like the sands of the Ganges his nature is forever one through endless kalpas. This is called the vajra ground; may the Buddha's children dwell there well.
Verses on Contemplating Conditions

Contemplate closely: this body, from beginningless time, arises wholly from inverted deluded thought; it turns through the six realms amid the painful paths, and its nature returns to the human and heavenly states for measureless kalpas. Deluded thoughts never cease, and suffering has no shore; deluded objects are not emptied, and karma is like the sea. If for a single thought one turns the light back for a moment, that very instant one is set upon the other shore. Accumulated deluded karma rises like Mount Sumeru; self and other, right and wrong, are hard and solid in their suffering, forming the iron encircling barrier of birth and death, from which a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives cannot escape. The cauldron of boiling water and the furnace of coals were never there at all; they arise only from a single thought of anger. If at the point where it arises one dissolves it, then in the fire the golden lotus is true liberation. The states before one are like flowers in the sky, not to be likened even to mirror images or water-moons. The people of the world, deluded and confused, lack the eye of wisdom and mistake them for real, seeing them inverted. They foolishly take the four elements as the body and the six consciousnesses and three poisons as their masters, never knowing their own greed and anger and pride, but wildly chasing after the painful paths. When self-nature is pure, that is Amitābha; when the six dusts do not stain, that is the lotus land. When not a single thought arises, birth and death are empty, and in daily life before one's eyes is the true Land of Utmost Bliss.
On Reciting the Buddha's Name

Reciting the Buddha's name is meant to transcend birth and death, yet first one must know the mind of birth and death. Foolish craving is the very root of birth and death; unless that root is pulled out, liberation is hard. Foolish craving is itself the mind that recites the Buddha's name, so use that recitation to cut off foolish craving. If foolish craving can be cut off thought after thought, then mind after mind Amitābha appears in full. This very practice is true diligence, and not a single thought may be forgotten for a moment. The Pure Land lies within the pure mind; do not look for it elsewhere.
Verses on Perfect Brightness, shown to Bi Yisu, who had lost his sight

The mind's light, perfect and bright, is boundless by nature; it is only that the eye is blocked by floating dust. Across a sheet of paper one cannot see outside things, yet turning inward, who has ever seen his own organs? It is like the white sun shining in the sky while a man sits in a dark room as though born blind; the man in the dark also has two eyes, so why do they not meet the sunlight? These four elements of mine are like a thatched hut, and the mind within the body is a bird in a cage. Who can tear away the thatch and seal, when the light shines without end? If one can see for oneself that the mind's light is full, then clearly and constantly bright, one need not use the eyes. This is the light without birth or death, which does not turn and flow with the four elements. How fortunate you are that Heaven has taken pity on you, specially drawing out the obstruction so the heavenly light is whole. You need not complain in broad daylight that you cannot see; it is only like sleeping at night with eyes intact. With eyes intact in night's sleep it is just so: the mind's light, perfect and bright, is simply itself. If one is free of bright and dark and sees one's own mind, this perfect brightness bursts forth at once and transcends birth and death. Who in all the world knows the good of having no eyes? People of old once regretted that they had not gone blind sooner: casting off the four elements at once, the light is whole, and this is our family's wish-fulfilling treasure.
Climbing Kunshan, shown to the companions of my outing

In the city of Kunshan stands a fist of rock, very like Sumeru held in a mustard seed. I came with my staff and climbed it once, and entered at once into the eye of a gnat. When people of the day look up, suddenly it is gone, and the four assemblies all cry out in alarm. Hurrying over to question the man in the void, he simply points out what was there before.
Tan was crushed by a falling beam, and this verse was shown to him

A roof beam collapsed and crushed Tan; yet crushed by it, why did Tan not die? Had the beam reached the body, the body would have shattered; had the body reached the beam, the beam would not have been spared. Since the two did meet, why were they not at odds? Let me ask the reason why they were not at odds. The states before your eyes are not like that beam; why should Tan first be so frightened? And if he would not be frightened, let him watch a cornered dog leap the wall.
Shown to Fu Zhi, styled Benming, who cultivates the Pure Land

Simply contemplate the single phrase Amitābha Buddha, keeping it unbroken in the mind thought after thought. If each thought can be most clear, then you meet Amitābha face to face. Only think that the Pure Land is before your eyes, and in daily use nothing whatever is lacking. The Buddha land is wholly gathered within a single thought, and that is the true skillful means for rebirth there. Only, in the moment of clear awareness, one must not give rise to views of difference.
Contemplating the Body

This body is like a water bubble, briefly appearing and not for long. The foolish child takes it for a pearl, yet cupping it in his hands he cannot fill them. How much more, within it, does much greed become a swamp of sin. Only when seen with the eye of wisdom is it found to hold nothing at all.
Contemplating the Mind

This mind has no form at all; look for it and it cannot be seen. Arising and ceasing have no beginning or end, swift as lightning in the sky. Deluded thoughts chase after the toils of dust, like a thirsty deer racing toward a mirage. How one sighs for the people of past and present, who all suppress what is noble and make it base.

The sea of illusion is shoreless and without end; when will the toil of dust and deluded thought ever cease? Know that the marks of the world are lightning in the sky, and believe that human life is foam upon the water. Only gather the one mind and return to the Pure Land, relying wholly on the ten thousand practices as true cultivation. Whatever lies before you is the road of bodhi, and thought after thought you ever board the boat of prajñā.
Shown to the old monk Wuxiang

When I first met you, you were past sixty; ten years have passed since we parted, and how do you fare now? Time is limited, so awaken again and again; deluded thoughts are boundless, so cut them off thought after thought. The lotus of the Pure Land is watered by the water of Chan; the weeds of craving in the mind's field are hoed by the knife of wisdom. A hundred thousand kalpas have all been passed in emptiness; do not let this life drift into vanity again.
Shown to Shen Shengchengde: Two Poems
A man who sleeps in damp must sicken, yet the loach thrives only there. Each creature's nature has what suits it; why grieve or rejoice at pain and joy?
Things hold nothing to be desired; it is people who desire them of themselves. Sweet and bitter differ in flavor, yet the addict thinks his is wondrous.
Shown to the Layman Liuyi: Two Poems
The affairs of the world are suddenly like a dream, and human feelings are empty as clouds. Who knows that within the dusty marketplace, a still mind is already apart from the crowd?

Though one's traces draw near, how could one go against the world? When the mind is empty, what does it matter whether one is at home? Only look at the muddy water: from it, clear and bright, the lotus rises.
Shown to the Chan practitioner Puwen
You did not shrink from the hardship of a pilgrim's road, crossing mountains and rivers for ten thousand li. Now you have come to the road of Caoxi: who will repay you the money you did not borrow?
Shown to the Chan practitioner Gui of Jinshan: Three Poems
White hairs come, and care is hard to undo; the red dust road does not open. Though the body dwells within the realm of men, the mind is among ten thousand mountains.
Day after day amid the toil of dust, morning after morning in the field of like and dislike, I know not for what affair I busily labor for others.
The sea of suffering is deep beyond a bottom, and the affairs of this floating life have their limit. I know not, within the three realms, where my true home lies.
To Benhun, a Chan Practitioner
Sitting alone among a thousand peaks, too idle to don the hundred-patch robe, I quietly listen to the sound of flowing water and watch the white clouds drift at leisure.
Shown to Ben'ang, styled Fuwu
Where there is a self, one is sure to exalt oneself; pride leans upon temper. Bow down until you reach no-self, and you enter at once the land of coolness.
Shown to Huishan, styled Sea Moon
The great sea gathers all treasures, yet what holds it up is coral alone. The bright moon comes and goes in its time, cool and bright together with the night pearl.
Shown to the Chan practitioner Jingtang
One bowl and a lone staff; across three mountains he forms many conditions. A single drop of water from Caoxi repays the whole price of his straw sandals.
Shown to the student Liu on the Four Rests
To savor one flavor and always be content: much seeking is always a fault. Eat greens and drink water; in this alone one's life is complete.
The Eight Scenes of Bodhi Hermitage, with Introduction
The hermitage stands at Shimen in Jiahe, built by the layman Yan Shengsheng as a quiet dwelling for Master Zhihe Xing. Passing this way on my road to Mount Jing, I therefore wrote these inscriptions.
Bodhi Mountain
Without coming to Bodhi Mountain, how could one know the Bodhi realm? Only the people of the mountain, forgetting words, examine themselves in silence.
Jade-Green City
Verdant green encircles the Dharma city, just like a vajra ring: neither buddha nor māra may enter, and within it all is utterly empty.
An Ancient Image of Guanyin
Guanyin has her before and after, but the Dharma-body has no present or past. Because her mind is cut off from coming and going, she can forever relieve suffering.
Arhat Pine
Tall and upright stands the solitary pine, stately as an arhat's true form. If you would ask about the mind of nirvāṇa, look to the bright moon rising on the branch.
Lotus Bay
The lotus grows in a bay of mud, yet its nature is fragrant and pure by itself. Behold the one within the flower, sitting upright, speaking no word.
Life-Releasing Pool
A single mind of the unborn fully reveals the place of releasing life, causing all the scaly and shelled kind to tread the path beyond birth.
Bubble-Born Stupa
The bubble born was never born; the bubble burst was never destroyed. There remains only the seamless stupa, lighting the bright moon in the cold sky.
The Soap-Berry Tree
By affliction one can remove affliction; the soap-berry tree loves to grow. Seeing these soap-berry beads, one at once gives rise to the thought of leaving affliction behind.
Dwelling in the Mountains, Shown to the Assembly: Twenty-Five Poems
Sitting alone with a censer of incense, free and untroubled, ten thousand cares forgotten; quietly I watch the ants below the steps and wonder for whom they busy themselves after all.
Still and silent, apart from knowing and perceiving; bright and clear, with seeing and hearing dissolved. In the third watch, the moon beyond the sky; a single patch of cloud on the ridge.
The affairs of the world are a game of chess, every move contending for victory. Before black and white are divided, how many can be awake to it?
Within the treasury of pure brightness, a single thought suddenly arises, and the boundless sea of birth and death all comes into being from it.
The road of red dust is longer still; the green mountains are never idle. I ask those who come and go: who knows the good of the mountain?
The deep blue lotus, dwelling in mud yet unstained; the mind that clearly transcends the world is snow within a crystal cup.
The puppets come on stage at night, and the audience sighs with delight. Only in the heart of drunkenness could one bear it; it is hard to keep a sober eye upon it.
The four elements gather as conditions meet, and delusion divides them into fair and foul. Look at this phantom man: where do his feelings and consciousness come from?
A mote of dust contains a world; if you do not believe it wholly contains one, do not say the mote is small, but know that the world is empty.
On the road before the withered-wood cliff, the traveler comes and loses his way. He should climb another peak and rise one more rung of the ladder.
The bank tree splits the sheer cliff, the withered vine hangs over the ancient well. How can it bear the gnawing of the two mice, much less the assault of the rushing stream?
In the blazing house of fire there is no avoiding the heat of affliction. In the moment a single thought is set down, one attains at once the land of coolness.
The whole world wants much and seeks it; the more one seeks, the more affliction is born. Only the mind content with enough is the wish-fulfilling treasure.
The Pure Land appears from mind alone; the lotus is the fragrance of the nature-ground. If before your eyes it is never obscured, then this very place is the West.
Deluded thought is the realm of sinking and drowning; the purified mind is the place of liberation. When the light is turned back and shines within, face to face one bows to the King of Emptiness.
Chasing and racing after the mirage, step by step one enters the pit of fire. If one can open a single eye, in that instant one is the unborn.
The roads of the world are full of entanglements; empty fame is what binds a man most. Only when the thread at one's heel is cut is one permitted to leave the red dust.
In mountain forests there is much to delight the spirit; yet how many can savor the stillness? Until one reaches the place of true rest, it all ends as talk on the lips.
The mark of self is truly hard to break; the faults of others are very easy to find. A whole life spent in idle fault-finding comes in the end to nothing at all.
The self-nature is the buddha of innate suchness, yet it is all entangled by deluded thought. If one can but see through it once, on the spot one realizes the Golden Immortal.
All dharmas are wrought by mind alone; one thought astray, a thousand roads diverge. Know not the place where no thought has yet arisen, and the sea of suffering stretches without shore.
In the still place where conditions are forgotten, in the hour when thought after thought lets go, the coming from the West held no other meaning: it lies only in knowing it for yourself.
A single drop of the great ocean holds the taste of all a hundred rivers. The nature of dharmas is one from the first; only the deluded see it as many.
Men reckon a hundred years long; I reckon a hundred years short — a dream on the pillow at midnight, while the awakened man has not yet turned his eyes.
A patch of idle ground is mostly overrun by weeds; if you but cut them back in time, that is already the mind that leaves the dust.
Ten Verses Shown to the Assembly (Six-Character Lines)
Kill to the last the thieving heart and all its busy schemes; make of your life a trade that profits nothing. Gather up the endless delusive thoughts, and trade them all for a single lotus flower.
The four elements prop up a standing frame of bone; the inch-square mind is desolate as cold space. Only a thread of breathing, unbroken, remains — a tortoise-hair cord tethering the long wind.
You say a hundred years are like a dream — but who has ever opened both eyes? Though you use up every scheme and device, in the end you are a fool still.
Pity the cool and limpid ground of mind: for no reason greed and anger burst out from it. Like a thunderbolt a fire starts in the heart, and burns away the innocence of your own nature.
The body is a false union of many conditions; the four elements enclose a single emptiness. Its movements you call the true master — yet you know not who is within.

Pitfalls and snares you make yourself; who will bear the forest of knives and the cauldron of fire? You think only of the joy of the present moment — how should you know the long suffering that follows?
Your looks are a bearing beyond the dust; your robe, a lotus rising out of water. Look and see what thing is in your breast, and let no idle thought lightly veil it.
The silkworm spins the cocoon that binds itself; who made the moth singe its wings in the lamp? You thought to seek the light by cleverness, and never knew the pull of karma’s power.
A name is but a borrowed name, not a reality; blame and praise fall on the ear like wind. Hear them called thieving weeds — it is a man cursing empty space.
Swing your arms free in a forest of thorns; draw your body out of the field of right and wrong. What you win is a boundless cool indifference — such a one spares no one at all.
Gāthās, Part Two (Three Hundred and Eight Verses)
Reading the Four Marks Chapter of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment in Prison
The Mark of Self

Bells, drums, gongs and cymbals raise unending sound; sound upon sound, day and night, preaches the unborn. Pitiful are the drunk and dreaming who wound their own lives: gazing at one another in a mirror, their tears pour down.
The Mark of Person
Jagged peaks tower like an iron city; the forest of knives and the trees of swords are cold as ice. Who knows that fire breaks out from the iceberg? Burn up the iceberg, and the fire is gone.
The Mark of Beings
The iron gate is shut fast, too far to open; bar upon bar — what misery it is. How strange, those who groan through the long night know not for what they came in here.
The Mark of a Life-Span
A single rod of blood is utterly without mercy; once it touches you, it must cut off birth and death. When the pain reaches the heart and stings the nose, then you know the king’s law is very clear.
Leaving Prison and Passing Through the Market of Chang’an: Four Poems
Chang’an’s wind and moon are the same in every age; along the purple lanes and red dust the road never ends. What calls a man most intimately is a single cock-crow and the bell at the fifth watch.
When the body is like space, all is at ease; not a speck of dust divides ten thousand mountains. Pitiful is the traveler under the clear blue sky, eyes wide open, sighing that the road is hard.
Wild winds and gathered rain come all at once; countless travelers cannot open their eyes. Then of a sudden the rain stops and the clouds scatter — the great void was beyond dust from the very first.
A gandharva city and its phantom horsemen in the air; before the eyes it seems a village in the mist. You must walk straight into the city and look: sound and form were never real at all.
Passing Wu Mountain, at Jingtang Temple Meeting the Chan Monk Mingtong as He Venerated the Avatamsaka Sutra, and Thereby Instructing Him

Wherever you go, mountains and rivers are the original truth; the sutras of the great chiliocosm are a single mote of dust. In an idle hour split it open and lightly hold it out — do not say Mañjuśrī is the wise one.
Passing the Iron Buddha Hermitage: Presented to Zou Erzhan, Supervising Secretary

Green hills above the river, spring unbroken; the stream before the gate is pure, without a grain of dust. Opening the door, suddenly I meet the master of the hermitage: it is exactly the indestructible vajra body.
Instruction to the Novice Zhaoli
For what matter did you leave home at all? To cut off love and take leave of kin is no small thing. If you do not seek liberation in the robe itself, the pine gate turns into an iron-walled prison.
Written on the Wall of East Mountain Temple

East Mountain lies close at hand, green and faint; deep in the woods on a clear day the rain drifts fine. Market and stream blend their sounds together — whatever meets the eye is plainly the upward working.
Seeing Master Da’s Gāthā on the Wall of an Inn at Zhongpan, and Writing One in Response
You came to Caoxi when I did not come; I came to Caoxi when you had gone. Coming and going were never in the mind — who would have guessed we should meet where the road runs narrow?
The Rock of Refuge

For no reason a single thought drew in the rank smell of blood; from that time the body’s burden was no light one. Ten years in the hunter’s thicket where the nets are spread — the stones fill the eyes, and all of them are unborn.
Ordering My Young Disciple Dayi to Read the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra

A jade thread is not easily passed through a golden needle; do not question the blue sky through the bright moon. The mysterious pass is cut off and no news comes — go, and when you meet people, do not idly pass it on.
Inquiring After the Illness of Ding Youwu, Counsellor

Who in the world knows this body within illness? Vimalakīrti sat alone and saw the truth the partial reveals. Let great wisdom pour out its torrent of eloquence — a single silence turns back the spring of ten thousand forms.
Instruction to the Two Attendants Guohong and Futang on Returning to Their Home Mountain

A thousand rivers and mountains — to ask others is vain; a single step beneath your heel is closest of all. Do not let your foot slip over the cliff: though you thrust your head out afterward, you have already lost the truth.

Vast misty waters, how lonely the prospect; why ask everyone you meet whether it is or is not? Turn your head: ten thousand mountains, clear to the bone, and spring still brims across the level plain.
Presented to the Venerable Yinting, Who Requested the Canon and Returns to Yanxiang Temple in Nanxiong

Ever since Neng of the South crossed the ridge, the imperial ink at Caoxi still runs wet. Now once more the jade caskets of scripture arrive — wait and watch the rain and dew fall on this burning wilderness.
Farewell to the Chan Monk Gao, Returning to Cihua

A single leaf floats on a cup of boundless water; through misty floods you labor to find the ford. Go home to your mountain, where life runs full: deep among a hundred flowers the birds sing of spring.
Instruction to Zha Ruding

To wade rivers and climb mountains — that too is splendid; your straw sandals came far from Jingting. Enter the gate, and one smile forgets host and guest — do not say Vimalakīrti never opens his mouth.
Inscribed on the Ascetic Buddha of the Snow Mountains
Ten thousand mountains of ice and snow frozen to the root; body and mind in one piece, cold to the bone. Unless you come alive again within death, how can you ever dry up knowing and feeling?

For no reason he cast away the golden wheel of kingship, and by that very act let doubt arise in all the earth. It is a matter hidden deep in the ninefold heaven, never permitted to be known by outsiders.

Lightly he left Tuṣita and entered the royal palace; one glance back, and thought has no end. He walked into ten thousand mountains of a thousand fathoms of snow, and buried his body where no wind blows from the eight directions.

His mind like ice and frost, his bones like firewood; six years of cold and hunger, his mouth could scarcely open. Who would have thought — suddenly he saw the morning star rise, and was left with a brimming smile on both cheeks.
Reply to Magistrate He of Dingzhai

One phrase covers heaven and earth and is ever new; a thunderbolt from a clear sky sweeps the smoke and dust away. Where the arrow’s point presses there is no turning aside — meeting on a narrow road, they are old friends.

Green lions and white elephants ride through the clouds; gold light and silver radiance issue from the same place. If you ask the true meaning of the unborn, it is wind and rain in the empty hills roaring through the tall pines.
Instruction to the Scholar Ou Yuzhong, Who Teaches the Sutras at Helin
This Way is subtle as a single thread, and is kept whole only by the power of faith. Without one patch of vajra ground, it is hard to make every leaf of bodhi shine.
Farewell to Dharma Master Letian, Returning to Mount Kuang
Mountain hues and lake light open like a single mirror; Mañjuśrī has strayed and fallen in here. Do not let the lion lightly flick its tongue, lest it shake the old preaching seat of former days.
Presented to a Sanskrit Monk Who Came from the West

From the West came a blue-eyed barbarian of a hundred thousand li; crossing the river he once snapped a single reed. Even now his shadow lingers in the stone chamber — ask, then: in a former life, was he or was he not?
Mourning the Monk Benlai

Five years, three times I knocked at the gate of Chan; today I seek my teacher, and he has gone and will not return. It is not the white mallet in the Tuṣita court — most likely he is hearing the Dharma on Mount Wutai.
Farewell to the Chan Monk Ruzheng, Who Has Carved a Sandalwood Image and Returns to Mount Wutai
Fire clouds and a red sun fill the burning wilderness; golden light is held within the ancient way-place. Had Mañjuśrī not appeared in person, who would know that coolness is wherever one stands?

Sandalwood from the ocean shore, a pure dharma-body; boundless marks and excellences hidden in a mote of dust. Clearly split open for all to see — face to face, at the point of the moment, one phrase is new.
Sent to Dharma Master Daqian

Thirty years ago we shared the dharma seat; since we parted, no news has come from that far country. Suddenly I hear you now dwell among a thousand peaks — I think your mind is empty and you smell the wondrous incense.
Instruction to the Keeper of the Caoxi Stupa

A thousand autumns of incense seem as one morning; sons and grandsons keep the vigil all night, so still. Tea and broth are offered as though he were still alive — thus they fail not the year the stone hung at his waist.
Ten Poems Encouraging the Disciples of Caoxi

A thousand monks in harmony, like Vulture Peak; that the great assembly takes refuge here is no small matter. Had you not once received his own charge, how could you pass through the Patriarch’s gate?

The flesh body is still present, just as in life; morning and evening the tea and broth are offered with sincere hearts. Bell and drum plainly preach the Dharma without cease — no need for me to urge you again with a bitter tongue.

Seeds in the field of merit must be planted deep; cause and effect are like standing before a bright mirror stand. You have come to the jewel mountain a thousand times — this time you must not go back empty again.

Toil diligently at your work, do not shrink from labor; remember the stone that hung at his waist in that year. When one breath fails to come, a thousand myriad kalpas pass; if the roots of goodness are unplanted, suffering is not ended.
Do not let your whole life slip by lightly; time like an arrow is truly alarming. I fear only that after the last three inches of breath are gone, when will you again walk to the jewel mountain?
The garden of merit must not be taken lightly; every step beneath your heel must be clear. Do not let your footing slip and drift along with others, lest the blind walk in the night again.
A foot of rafter and a tile are made by many conditions; the fat and marrow of the faithful’s gifts must not be taken lightly. Never covet that stake of donkey dung, idly trading away a pair of eyes.

The fat and blood of faith outweigh Mount Sumeru; a grain of rice or a stick of firewood cannot be cheated. Only look at those wearing fur and bearing horns, repaying old debts in the bitter mire of hell.

Fortunate to be born in the Middle Land and to have left the dust early; your body wears the robe and is far from all six kin. You enjoy the pure blessings of the empty gate — how can you repay the Patriarch’s grace?

If from youth you keep the upward mind, a hair’s tip will grow at last to a thousand fathoms. Only after passing through all the bitterness of ice and frost do you become timber fit to leave the Deng forest.
Instruction to the Caoxi Novices Nengxin, Zhirong, Dayi, Jingxi, Tongwen and Fangjue, Who Copy the Avatamsaka Sutra: Seven Poems

Split a mote of dust and the great sutra comes forth; boundless seas of lands take shape one from another. Pine wind and birdsong speak it out plainly — it waits only for the man himself to listen with care.

Buddha-realms upon Buddha-realms, beyond all measure; a samādhi on the tip of a hair is no common thing. Know that when the hand is raised the whole body appears, and wherever it touches, the light of the ocean-seal shines forth.
Line after line, wild-goose shadows fall through the cold sky; upright or slanting, they simply trust the wind. Do not ask Samantabhadra for wondrous practice — first you must know the master within.

When will the pavilion of Vairocana open? The snapping of the fingers must await Sudhana. Then he suddenly sees within the tower an inexhaustible treasury — Buddha-realms upon Buddha-realms, how wondrous indeed.
East of the City of Blessings he bowed to Mañjuśrī; from afar he sought the good teachers to the ocean’s edge. Fifty-three of them sing a single tune — no need to travel far and wear out the road.
If the ocean waves were ink, they too would run dry; a brush like Sumeru is not hard to lift. To depict the lotus-treasury realm of Vairocana — the very first word, who is permitted to see it?
Paper, ink and written words are never the truth; the true sutra lies wholly in splitting a mote of dust. If you can make every word shine with light — do not say Mañjuśrī is the wise one.
Mourning the Monk Yishan of Wangu Temple
Twenty years ago I asked after your health; when we met it was as though we had just been born. Now I gaze far off at the moon over Zhongtiao — only its clear light still shines upon the bamboo hut.
Sent to Gao, Attendant Gentleman
I remember the day we parted in Chang’an, arm in arm in the snow where the roads divide. Now I am ten thousand li away in the burning wilderness — one thought of coolness, and only you know it.
Presented to Master Yi of Helin

Long have I lingered beneath the bodhi tree, and time and again walked in meditation around it. I think back to the day the tree was planted — I once pressed a handful of earth upon it with my own hand.
Presented to the Physician Yan Xingyuan
On the snow mountain the many herbs grow lush and green; plucked offhand, they are used with skill. You are no common healer of the realm — would you let them lie in waste and blame the spring wind?
Presented to the Old Man of Taihe
In the Vajra Cave we met of old; snow-white hair, loose and unkempt, and a spirit all the bolder. One cup of crystal tea and I am still drunk — dimly I remember the old cowherd.
Farewell to the Attendant Xian, Who Travels to Mount Wutai, with an Inquiry After Dharma Master Kongyin
From afar you go from the burning house into the cool; do not speak of ten thousand li of road as long. If you meet Mañjuśrī, ask him for news: in the cave now, how many Chan groves stand empty?
Passing Faxing Temple and Venerating the Sixth Patriarch Beneath the Bodhi Tree

Beneath the bodhi tree we met of old; a thousand years later I come again, and the spirit is still the same. Bell and drum, incense and smoke, unbroken — why then should his descendants hunt for a mysterious trace?
