Farewell to the Chan Monk Liji, Setting Out to Visit the Good Teachers
You carry a bowl of Caoxi water and sprinkle it over the five-flavored Chan of every quarter. Do not say old Hanshan has no dharma to speak — these days it is not worth half a penny.
Farewell to Master Jiong of Ruoxing, Pilgrimaging to Mount Putuo

On White Flower Mountain the waves flow without moving; the full moon in the cold sky is the Great Being’s face. If you would meet him there before the rock, look up in reverence and hear the Universal Gateway answer.
Rejoicing That My Dharma Nephew Xingguang Has Arrived
I remember the year I left home and parted from the Patriarch; you must still have been unborn then. Now, meeting after ten thousand li, one smile traces back a bond from a former life.
Inquiring After the Illness of You Shiyang

Let me ask after this body of illness in Vaiśālī: examine it closely — which of it is real? Only when the last layer of yin is stripped away do you first see the gentle warmth and the spring of the whole earth.
Seeing Off the Reverend Xinglai as He Sets Out on Pilgrimage

The misty waters stretch, and stretch, and have no end;
A hundred folds of hill-towns lie behind.
All this to seek a teacher and ask the matter through —
Meghaśrī is not on Wondrous Peak to find.
Remembering the Thousand-Buddha Temple of the Great Capital

I recall that seven-jeweled terrace of a thousand flowers,
Where every bloom and leaf a Tathagata showed.
I wonder whether he, at leisure among the flowers,
Still thunders Dharma as in the days of old.
To the Chan Monk Nengzhe

Your road to Caoxi has not gone astray;
The pilgrimage before your eyes is not far away.
Think of the view when first you stepped past the gate:
Fragrant grasses everywhere — and where is home?
Sent to the Layman Wang

On a snowy night at Qingliang we talked of Chan;
Since we parted, twenty years have gone.
I often think of your true Vaiśālī face —
How many times has the cold moon grown round?
Again Passing Faxing Temple, Glad That Master Jiong Returns from Pilgrimage to Putuo

Three years have passed, and under the bodhi tree he has not sat;
One thought forever hangs the lamp of prajñā bright.
Do not say the dhūta monk does not preach the Dharma —
His bond with the Way is not a thicket-hunting monk’s.
Singing of the Lankavatara Room, Sent to the Laymen Tianyu and Kong

The surging sea of poison spreads without a shore;
Night yakṣas and rākṣasas make their home therein.
Only the Lankavatara’s priceless jewel
Shines day and night across the Ganges sands.

Eight-faced and luminous, its substance perfectly round;
Though vajra be keen, it cannot pierce it through.
Ever enshrined within the mind-king’s hall,
It shines through the three thousand and the great thousand worlds.
Caoxi Snow Tea, Sent to Master Zhen of Jinshan

I plucked one branch of leaf that comes before the spring
And send it to the crane-boned master in his illness.
Brew up a cup and taste it for yourself —
Is it as when you first called upon old Zhao?
In the Spring of the Jiachen Year, Ordered Back to the Garrison, My Boat Moored at the Zhijiang; Masters Yi and Jiong, Qinan, Yuzhong, and Zhongqian Came to Inquire, and So I Instructed Them

Awhile I moor my lone boat by the willow shade;
In quiet sitting it is like Jetavana’s grove.
Beneath the bodhi tree I ever keep the assembly —
No wonder you can come and ask the Dharma’s sound.
To Liang the Geomancer

Mountains, rivers, the great earth — one mote of dust;
Only a perfect, clear Dharma eye sees the truth.
Of course one must seek out the place where one belongs —
Would you consent to lie buried among the world’s idle folk?
To Yinzong, Abbot of Luofu Mountain

Beneath Luofu Mountain the Ganges circles round;
The grove beside it seems Putuo’s own ground.
If you would seek the Lord who watches within the flower,
Look at the bright moon falling into clear water.
To Zhou the Physiognomist

Drifting through rivers and lakes with a hempen-hilted sword,
Your wondrous art of reading hearts from Huqiu came.
Should a man ask you of flourishing and decline,
A band of true light lies within his two eyes.
To the Chan Monk Xingru Ji

Why journey south to imitate Sudhana’s road?
Seeking good friends, you long have wandered to and fro.
Upon the Wondrous Peak’s summit there is no trace —
Do not say Mañjuśrī pointed you there wrong.
To the Chan Monk Shenglin of Putuo

Below Putuo Mountain lies White Flower Village;
Day and night the tide’s voice preaches the Universal Gate.
Ask what the dweller of the hut can call his own —
Only parrots telling him the day is done.
Hearing That the Reverend Xinglai Has Received Full Ordination at Yunqi and Returned, I Send a Verse to Inquire After Him

One staff that lives and moves just like a dragon,
Your companion when you climbed Tianzhu’s crest.
Since at Yunqi you heard the Dharma taught,
Are all your karmic conditions laid to rest?
Summer Days in the Mountains

A bamboo bed, a tile for pillow, pine wind enough;
At noon I sleep so deep my dreaming thoughts run dry.
These four limbs and this hundred-boned frame are all but guests —
I do not know which one among them is the host.
The Bell in the Still of Night

The bell rings out through the cold sky of the clear night;
One stroke is like wind through ten thousand hollows blowing.
It does not idly urge the dragons to hear Dharma —
It comes to waken the true master, all unknowing.
To Mr. Zhou of Taihe

The great Way has always been before your eyes,
Yet you seek withered Chan where all is dead.
Who knows that every daily, ordinary thing
Is the supreme condition of the birthless ground?

How weak the power of the Way beside the power of karma!
Consider well which of the two is ripe, which raw.
If when you meet a state you can turn back and interchange,
At once the mad flight ends — Yajñadatta’s flaw.
To the Elder Zongchi of Yuantong

The West River’s stream flows down from Caoxi’s source;
Mazu’s headache — who has power to heal it?
If you would seek a living herb at Yuantong,
Ponder most of all the words: a dead cat’s head.
To Mr. Gong Boqi

A thousand li you traveled seeking one who knows,
Only to seek this mind from someone else’s hand.
But when you meet and see him face to face,
You learn how all your former searching was in vain.
To the Chan Monk Ciming Xian

With a single staff you came from far Duobao;
South you wandered, mist and water, one floating cup.
If on your homeward road you pass by Caoxi’s way,
The path is slick — do not tread the moss after rain.
Written at Random on Again Passing Through Yangcheng in the Summer of the Wushen Year

Thirteen years have passed since I crossed the immortal town;
In this human world I now have passed my sixtieth year.
Looking back on the dusty realm, it all is like a dream —
I do not know to what, in the end, it all belongs.

With one bowl I passed through every quarter then;
Each famous mountain served me as a place of practice.
I ate my fill of the benefactors’ rice, unpaid —
And still today the reckoning takes thought.

On Wutai, a thousand feet of snow buried my head;
I thought to be cold ash and, dying, be done.
Who would have guessed one single spark of fire
Would burn the whole great earth and sweep it in flood?

Once on the Eastern Sea I rode ten thousand li of waves;
Thunderous breakers shattered rock, the crests rode high.
Lightly on a single leaf I go with the wind,
Straight to tread the three isles and hook the six great turtles.
To the Attendant Zhengwei

At the very top of the hundred-foot pole on the cliff,
To shift a single step is hardest of all to do.
Just let go your hands and turn your body over —
And do not take it for a cat or a white ox.
To the Chan Monk Yue, Who Recites the Avatamsaka Sutra

A hundred cities, mist and water, seem like sky;
Where shall we meet to question Samantabhadra?
I think of you passing the Wondrous Peak’s summit —
I wonder whether he then told of this causation.
To the Rice Cook

When will Deshan come bearing his bowl?
Do not idly guess at his going to Changsha for rice.
Borrow nothing from the fragrance-kitchen above —
The matter by the stove is wondrous in itself.
Sent to Master Miaofeng of Wutai

A world of crystal, a palace of limpid glass;
Gold light and silver shine are everywhere the same.
Alone you stride astride a golden-haired lion —
Walking the eight directions, no wind can enter in.

Bones like frost and crane, your hair as silver-white;
Who knows you for Mañjuśrī’s final form?
Since in that cave we took our leave of one another,
Not even a mote of dust has come between.

My staff across my shoulder, I roam the sea of lands;
Boundless Buddha-fields are gathered in a single mote.
At leisure I split that mote of dust and look:
The phantom flowers have fallen, and but two eyes remain.

A thousand fathoms of cold cliff, a hundred feet of ice;
In those years we sat facing one another on the crags.
And now the burning house has turned a realm of cool —
One Vimalakīrti here, and here one monk.
Sent to Master Kongyin of Wutai

Afar I think of you at play in the flowered grove,
Sitting alone in shade of sandalwood and jeweled trees.
Your tongue’s root never stirs, and yet you preach the Dharma;
Ten thousand men now hear the sound of ocean tides.

Since I cast this body into the miasmic sea,
Barbarous smoke and poison mist have been my food.
Returning, I drink my fill of Caoxi’s water —
No less than Qingliang’s cold that pierces to the bone.
To the Master of the Purple Bamboo-Shoot Estate at Caoxi

One night of east wind fattened the purple bamboo shoots;
Boundless spring color reached my brushwood gate.
Peach blossoms fill the eye, and no one asks —
Who will present the upward turning, plain as day?
Sent to Zhiyin

Deep hidden at Baimen, at rest upon one branch;
Mountains and waters please the heart, world thoughts wear thin.
You once have entered Vimalakīrti’s little room —
A hundred thousand samādhis on a single hair’s tip.
To the Chan Monk Gao, in Seclusion

The six windows tightly closed, no wind can enter in;
For what matter do you hide your body here?
Just try the place where Mañjuśrī snapped his fingers —
It will press and crack the vast emptiness apart.
To the Chan Monk Rong, Abbot of the Zhongxiao Temple Built by Grand Marshal Guo of Taihe

Freed of the body, you came from the land of plague;
Three lives over, again you weave a magistrate’s tie.
In Vimalakīrti’s ten-foot room there is no word at all —
Do not say that wordlessness is not Chan.

The three mysteries of the upward way — each step a doubt;
The single phrase before all words — who may it know?
Unless you let your hands go at the cliff’s edge,
You throw away the two brows your mother gave.
Sent to Master Guifeng of Lingshan

The assembly on Vulture Peak still stands as then;
Pines and cypresses and cloud-dwellers fill the Deer Park.
It is the Dharma body that forever preaches —
Bell and drum clearly tell us that the dusk has come.
Sent to Master Jiewai of the Eastern Sea

Having yourself received the Vulture Peak’s entrustment,
Today you open the Dharma seat beside the sea.
The hosts of Māra on the Laṅkā summit —
How often have they come to hear you teach?
To the Chan Monk Nan

I ask about the ailing body there at Vaiśālī;
I do not know who it is that lies sick within.
Two times of gruel and rice, three times of medicine —
Eat them with clear knowing: that is closest to the truth.
Sent to the Layman Lai Guxuan

Long keeping fast, in one room you serve the King of Emptiness;
Within the mind-ground you ever burn the incense of prajñā.
Afar I think of your long days of cross-legged sitting,
Quietly hearing birdsong come out of the mountain light.
Sent in Thanks to the Layman Qinglian

I often think upon the layman Qinglian;
In dreams my soul keeps facing the man within the mirror.
I know you have deeply won the birthless meaning —
Sure that one may dwell in dust and not be stained.
Dwelling in the Dinghu Mountains

Having passed through every wind and wave of right and wrong,
This mind has long been used to forgetting all contrivance.
I turn about and go straight in among a thousand peaks,
Sitting to watch idle clouds fly through the bright day.
Sent to Master Mingzong

You once came from Tuṣita with the white gavel in hand;
Once the golden needle touched you, the Dharma eye opened.
Now will you spread the proclamation far and wide,
Only to leave the level ground swept clean of dust.
Sent to Master Yun

At the river’s head we sat knee to knee when we took leave;
Turning my head, green mountains enter my dreams.
I ask about the thousand hundreds on the flower terrace:
The single phrase before all words — how many know?
Sent to Master Chao

Wrapped in cloud and bearing the moon, full-fed on wind and frost;
Through the long clear night the crane’s dream stretches far.
You finish reading the Lankavatara, the incense spiral thins —
I know there is nothing left for you to ponder on.
Sent to Master Yu

Long have you appeared from Vulture Peak as the right vessel;
Who bothers to ask if clouds rise or flower rain falls?
Do not say the Dharma seat today is desolate —
In that cave you have become the multitude’s refuge.
To the Chan Monk Zhongfu Biao

Seeing through the ties of the world, you understood and returned;
A lotus in the midst of fire does not easily bloom.
Wash utterly clean the senses and their objects —
Do not let yourself enter that womb again.

Clear and bright, the Buddha-nature has no veil at all;
It was only one thought gone astray in times before.
You slipped and long sank down in the sea of birth and death —
This time, do not betray the lotus any more.
To the Chan Monk Weimi

Your bowl and bag have come from distant Funiu;
Crossing the ridge, the cold plum blossoms are opening.
If you would ask the intimate phrase of Caoxi:
Bodhi has no tree, and the mirror has no stand.
To the Chan Monk Ningzhi Han

With rounded crown and square robe, a body of eight treasures;
The first intent of leaving home is to transcend the dust.
If for the sake of afflictions you let yourself be lightly buried,
When next you raise your head the truth is already lost.
Sent to the Chan Monk Zhan, Dwelling on Funiu

You once took up a single bowl and came to Caoxi;
Would you refuse the road with only a thorn staff?
I hear that in the deep, hidden place of ten thousand hills,
The setting sun slants low and birds contend in song.
Sent to Inscribe the Rushi Cloister of Guo Cigong

At Shravasti the Jetavana grove was once laid out;
Now you would again take up the mind that spreads out gold.
Where the Dharma King thus fully raises it aloft,
Only Mañjuśrī is allowed to know the tune.
Reply to Guo Yunshu

You once came to Caoxi to ask about the supreme;
The secret meaning of the West belongs to Neng of the South.
Do not say that Vimalakīrti, who sealed his lips,
Was not the long-haired monk of former days.
Sent to Inscribe the Nangquan Pavilion at Taiyi, for Guo Shuzi

A clear pool, a bright moon, shadows deep and still;
Water in a pouch holds rivers and lakes, a heart of ferrying.
Ask where the swimming fish most truly flourish —
The Hao bridge is not necessarily the one who knows.
To the Chan Monk Hongfan

Having bowed in thanks before the thousand-flower jewel seat,
You then would seek the three mysteries from Linji.
And now you come to ask again the road to Caoxi —
Clouds fill the green hills, and the moon fills the sky.
Sent to Master Nayun

In broad daylight you split a single mote of dust;
Idly lifting your staff, its use is intimate.
Deep in the night of the bright moon, the tiger beneath the cliff
Takes refuge still as the man of former days.
Seeing Off the Monk Who Made a Sandalwood Image, Returning to Chaling

A branch of sandalwood from the Southern Sea;
The Dharma body shows its brows wherever it may be.
Welcomed home beneath the silent shade of pines,
It is as when the flower was held, and nothing said.
To Mr. Guo Lingxi

Long keeping fast, embroidering Buddhas, bowing to the King of Emptiness;
The burning house is turned into a ground for choosing Buddha.
At night you trim the bright lamp, the mind all still and quiet —
No need to think of lotuses away in the West.
Ten Poems Left in Farewell to the Brethren of the Lingnan Dharma Society, About to Depart for Nanyue

Once fallen into the world’s dust, twenty years have fled;
That we meet thus, you must believe, is karma from before.
Ever since the robe and bowl came to the south,
Today I take up once again the Chan of direct pointing.

The matter is plain and clear within your own person;
No need to ask outside about failure or success.
If only wherever you touch you turn the light around,
The toils of dust will never trap the master within.

The great Way from the first is beyond the true and false;
It is our discriminating that forces far and near.
You must see through the face your mother bore —
Then you are one set apart among the dusty world.

I have drunk the miasmic smoke to the dregs, and still my teeth are cold;
I do not remember now the hardness of the roads behind.
This time I go into the deep, secret place of ten thousand hills,
To watch the five-hued clouds and glow from where I sit.

Twenty years I galloped through the land of plague;
These years I never noticed my temples turn to frost.
Now I take a single leaf of boat and go —
My traces shall be hidden in ten thousand ravines.

Long have I mixed my traces in the dust and dimmed my light,
Only because I am busy raising up this matter.
The thousand-foot fishing pole is almost hewn away;
I turn to sea and sky, and all is vaster still.

Since first I took refuge and circled the Dharma altar, I have begged at every hour for this mind to be at peace. Do not say we are parted by three thousand li — the moon stands at mid-heaven, and we meet face to face.

Now and then I take up rod and line and see my plain and simple heart; the bamboo-branch song done, how few are the listeners? The little boat goes home through a frosty night — where shall one seek the bright moon and the reed flowers?

In the cold sky the wild geese cry one by one, each voice alone; from today my traces fall among the Five Lakes. Boundless misty waves carry my sorrowful thoughts; a single sail on the horizon is the road home.

For the Dharma, how could I decline a distant road? How could I call this land of miasma the world’s end? Again and again I take one drop of Caoxi’s water to irrigate the five-petal flower that came from the West.
The Dream Wanderings Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Scroll Thirty-Eight
Gāthās, Part One
Elucidating Zou Sheng Ziyin: Ten Verses

This matter is utterly clear, with nothing hidden at all;
it stands revealed and magnificent through all heaven and across the earth.
If a true man does not pierce through with the vajra eye,
he faces a wall though he looks straight at it.

Seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are all flowers in the air;
while the film is not yet removed, one’s seeing only worsens.
Only when the eye is clear and pure as the open sky
does one come to know a different and better life.

In the realm of sound and form, how could it be by chance?
One takes up thorns and brambles and bitterly questions Heaven.
Who is it that casts all aside, turns over, and comes out?
Only then does he believe in the free and easy Chan that follows conditions.

The wondrous nature, perfect and bright, is true from the first;
from of old it is pure and bright, never stained by the finest dust.
Do not let deluded defilement lightly cloud and obstruct it:
just this is to be a man of great power who transcends the ordinary.

The mind of the Way was never apart from the ordinary;
why be so busy welcoming guests and greeting visitors?
Just look at the pivot within it all:
has it ever stirred by a single hair?

Deep and clear, the light of the mind is never deluded;
it is only that feeling and thought estrange it from itself.
Just see that where they rise there is no tidings at all,
and let the monkeys cry out by day and by night as they will.

The clouds of the nature-sky are clear, the moon’s disk alone;
why should body and world ask whether they exist or not?
Only let the traces of worldly ties be cut off,
and one need not labor to hang a name on rivers and lakes.

Worldly ties pursue us on and on — when will they ever cease?
One casts away one’s own home mountain and seeks outside.
The bright pearl lies buried in the hem of the robe,
while on the long road one vainly hugs one’s poverty and sorrow.

The lightning of the vast void spares nothing in its flash;
how could like and hate be allowed to march in file?
Split open the true face you were born with:
how could you let it pass your whole life buried?
To Yuan Sheng

Long ago I sent a letter south to Neng;
asking the Dharma, I paid court from afar to the supreme vehicle.
I know that samādhi may be entered through words —
I wonder, do you still recall the monk of former days?
To the Chan Monk Shuitian

How hard it is for a true teacher and a student to meet!
Within it the hidden message is hard to put into words.
On the summit of Wondrous Peak, along the track where you walked,
Sudhana was not taken in by empty talk.
To Tan Fuzhi

You once received the prediction at Vulture Peak;
today you come again and give one knock at the gate.
I ask you about the matter of the twirled flower that day —
the ascetic is no easy man to please.
To Zhong Sheng Hengying

Ten years have passed since you visited Caoxi;
to meet a true teacher is all former affinity.
Why should Ruan weep at the end of the road?
The supreme Chan that came from the West is yours already.
To the Scholar Fang Juezhi

The light of the mind shines out alone beyond the body;
you can fathom the Patriarch’s intent before a word is spoken.
I think you have heard Mount Kuang’s lotus water-clock till it ripened,
and so you come to renew the old affinity.
To the Chan Monk Changda
To the Chan Monk Zongxuan

Illusorily formed, the five aggregates are empty from the first;
to insist on seeking them is to catch the wind.
Just try, once body and mind have wholly dissolved,
to recognize and take hold of the master within.
To the Hermitage Master Yongzhi of Nanyue

Deep among ten thousand mountains, one thatched hut;
morning and evening the clouds and rosy light serve as my little assembly.
Above all, the voice of the stream cannot be shut away:
with its broad and long tongue it murmurs day and night.
Dwelling in the Mountains at Nanyue

Seventy years have passed like a dream;
my traces on rivers and lakes are all squandered and astray.
Now I am glad to have gained this idle field of ground —
ask nothing of how things were before.

My heels have trodden every water-and-cloud land,
yet I have never left the ancient place of the Way at Qingliang.
My strength fails and my mind is already weary:
to sleep well and eat my fill is my whole way of living.

The place of great rest and cessation is nothing ordinary;
when deluded thought subsides, the world is already forgotten.
People all seek the true Land of Ultimate Bliss elsewhere —
who knows that this very moment is the West?

One only sees the unborn, still and extinguished mind;
deluded thoughts find no way to invade it.
The senses and their objects are all shadows of flowers in the air —
why seek the Buddhas and Patriarchs outside?

Watch where the mind arises: it is utterly unborn.
In the flash of lightning the eye grows doubly bright.
I ask what the coming from the West was meant to accomplish —
the people of today understand only how to hurry on their way.
To the Monk Mijie of Luling

How stands the price of rice in Luling these days?
When you are asked, do not just repeat what others say.
If you can lightly chew and break a single grain,
you will know the Buddhadharma is no great matter.
To the Chan Monk Duyan

The Chan of Master Ma, one stream of the Western River —
I hear its transmission has long been lost.
Do not say a brick can be ground into a mirror;
of itself it will not fall to the byways of the road.
To the Chan Monk Dingshui

For long I have relied on the flower throne to seek the true meaning;
bell and drum are clear, and phrase by phrase is profound.
If you ask the precise purport of the coming from the West —
from of old the Buddhas and Patriarchs have never transmitted it.
To the Chan Monk Liangkong, Who Receives Guests at Wuchang

I hear a Brahma monastery has opened by the river’s edge,
just when the coming and going winds and sails are crossing.
I ask the fisherman who casts his line at Huating:
how many know the three inches between hook and bait?
Inscribed on Fang Juezhi’s Hut of Freedom from Defilement

In a hermitage the size of a mustard seed, not a speck of dust;
from the first there has been nothing one could draw near to.
In quiet contemplation, the cool ground of stillness and cessation —
suddenly one sees the Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma-body.
Inscribed on the Kṣānti Hermitage

Self and things are empty as space and cannot be sought;
they are a single floating bubble on the boundless sea.
Just look: where they rise there is no trace at all —
let suffering and joy come to rest right where they are.
To the Chan Monk Tianyuan

The matter beneath your own body and mind is perfectly clear;
no need to seek a teacher and wear yourself out in far travel.
Only take it up intimately right before your eyes —
who is it that sees forms and hears sounds?
To the Chan Monk Liuyi
Sent to Dharma Master Ruomei

One who dwells in a hut below Lotus Peak,
day by day befriending the Five Elders in the clouds.
The waterfall scatters jade dust through the air,
as if host and guest were sitting in talk together.
To the Chan Monk Changyuan of Yunju

Leaving the world is at root for the sake of fathoming this mind,
not for the sake of hanging a name in the monastery groves.
When the huatou is pressed to the place of no-mind,
one does not seek it outside in another’s house.
Sent to the Master of the Haihui Hermitage
Reply to Dharma Master Yu, Who Sent a New Commentary on the Lotus Sutra

The one assembly at Vulture Peak required much deliberation,
and for more than forty years it lay covered and hidden.
Today the whole body is utterly exposed —
clearly it lies in a single hair’s tip.

The gate is shut fast, and no wind passes through;
how many pace and sigh, lamenting that the road is ended?
It is not that a light snap of the fingers is much trouble —
how else would one know that what lies within is vast as space?

When the poor son came home and saw his father,
he entrusted his heart to him and believed without doubt.
Yet even if the whole treasury were handed over to him,
unless he overturn it, he will never know it at all.

The boundless ocean of Buddha-lands is all lotus flowers;
one may sigh that in former days they were counted as grains of sand.
If you point it out for yourself at the tip of a hair,
from today you will always drive the white ox cart.
To the Chan Monk Supu (with a preface)

This monk once came to consult me at Caoxi, and afterwards returned to Wumen. Not long ago the two Dharma Masters Chao and Yu, because I and his own teacher Xuelang were brothers in the Dharma gate, had this monk carry a letter and travel far to Nanyue to invite me to spend my last years there. Moved by the lofty friendship of these two masters, and mindful of this monk’s long toil, I composed two gāthās to record what was in my heart.

I once bowed at Caoxi and walked the land of miasma,
circumambulated three times in reverence, and circled the Chan bed.
The single phrase of the unborn was perfectly clear —
do not say that anything was concealed then.

From afar I bring a letter from an old friend,
and come especially to these empty hills to ask where I might dwell.
This whole body and mind I entrust to you entirely;
there is no need to ask what my remaining years will be.
Reply to the Two Dharma Masters Chao and Yu

The righteous spirit of the Dharma gate is truly beyond the ordinary;
of itself the green mountain has the fragrance of bone and flesh.
I mean to go up to the summit of Tongxuan Peak,
and there face you wordlessly on one rope bed.

The mountains and waters of Wumen are the most secluded and clear;
the twin peaks of Erlang have long been famed.
If only we might share the mist and rosy clouds and grow old together,
sleeping well and eating our fill would see out the rest of our lives.
To the Chan Monk Fucha

From afar I ask after Lanzan among a thousand peaks;
the cold tears at the corner of his mouth have never dried.
The yellow yam in the fire has just been roasted through —
to set it before you is no easy meal.
To the Chan Monk Dazhi

With bamboo staff and straw sandals I crossed ten thousand mountains,
coming from Nanyue to knock at the pine gate.
On Shitou’s road, slippery, it is hard to move a step;
do not say that travelling to seek instruction is a light matter.
Inscribed on the Scroll of Meeting at Biefeng
Inquiring After the Illness of Zhuan Yu, Master Heng

The four great elements I have long seen as bubbles and shadows;
where could the demon of illness hide its traces?
The ancients had their own way of resting at ease:
it lies in a single thought of the unborn.
To the Chan Monk Ruozhuo

You have walked to the ends of the earth seeking this mind,
yet from the first you have always sought it outside.
Even before you take a step beyond the gate,
trust that the grass grows deeper the farther the road runs.
Sent to Xu Beng’e

From time to time I ask after Vimalakīrti in his illness;
the door opens on non-duality and reveals the natural truth.
Having eaten the fragrant rice to the full, words forgotten,
one only then believes that with feeling put aside, the Way at last draws near.
To the Chan Monk Xinwen

The original self-nature is vast as space;
seeing forms and hearing sounds is a tree passing through wind.
Only let the floating clouds be wholly scattered,
and when has a single thing ever lodged within it?
To the Chan Monk Sanmei Zhen, on His Pilgrimage to Emei

You have travelled through all quarters; it is well to let the mind rest.
It was no vain thing to hang your name in the monastery groves.
When you return, your face will be covered with Emei snow —
white clouds and green hills, where shall they be sought?
To the Master of Jing Mountain

Lightning flash and flint spark — how could these be real?
A glance of meeting is not yet something to draw near to.
If the original tidings are truly cut off,
the whole great chiliocosm appears in your body wherever you stand.
The Chan Monk Yeyin Went from Huangmei to Nanyue and Then to Consult at Shuangjing; I Showed Him This Gāthā

You travelled far to Nanyue seeking your traces,
and I am glad that one thread of Huangmei has come through.
Elsewhere, at the place of meeting on the Five Peaks,
snows of ten thousand mountains surround a white-haired old man.
To the Chan Monk Wuxia

With staff in hand you came from afar to the deep places of Shuangjing;
to meet at a separate peak is to meet a kindred spirit.
If old friends ask about the rest of my life:
ten thousand folded ranges of cloud, and one single heart.
To the Lay Buddhist Nianxi

You have travelled south over misty waters through a hundred cities;
to meet a true teacher — what did it come to?
Seek still deeper in the Five Peaks:
you should know the Buddhadharma is no great matter.
To the Chan Monk Qinru, on His Pilgrimage to Emei

From Shuangjing far away you bow at Emei;
you cross waters and climb mountains — for whose sake?
If you see Samantabhadra’s true face,
do not fail that pair of brows.
To the Hall Master of Jing Mountain

At Shuangjing the single transmission of the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ mind;
grey cliffs and green bamboo, an ancient monastery grove.
You should know that where the true command is ever new,
bell and drum proclaim the wondrous sound of the Dharma.
In Memoriam: Master Huanyu

On the cold cliff, frozen and starving — who knew of it?
After seeming death you were revived again, and I owe it to you, Master.
Today, gazing at the pagoda’s shadow on the Five Peaks,
it is as if we still sat talking face to face.
To Dharma Master Ren’an

Body and mind are one piece, like a jar of ice;
try to see whether anything is there within it.
When deluded thoughts do not come and the tidings are cut off,
why seek your practice anywhere beyond this?
Passing the Bodhi Hermitage, I Happily Met the Chan Friend Zhihe

You were originally a man beneath the bodhi tree;
when you arrived, in a flash I seemed to see my former body.
The voice of the stream always preaches the unborn Dharma —
pity that the people of today do not hear it truly.
To the Chan Monk Xunnan, Who Tends the Sick

What is the most excellent cause for leaving the world?
To see through, right before your eyes, this body in illness.
Know the place where his pain and itching are bound up with yours —
of all ten thousand practices, none is truer than this one thought.
To the Chan Monk Demen, Who Collates Sutras

The eye of the sea has never held a speck of dust;
the great treasury of light is a place where one may rest.
Only look carefully from the very beginning:
the moment a fine mote clings, the truth is lost.
To the Chan Monk Feixuan Xiao

You once studied the teachings at Cien and ordered their framework;
then you threw away the fishing rod and travelled through all quarters.
If today you recognize the face you were born with,
there is no need to ask the Dharma King with your mind.
Passing the Sweet Dew Reception Temple

Climbing mountains and wading waters, all is a road gone astray;
who knows whether there is a village ahead or not?
Then straight on I suddenly met the sprinkling of sweet dew —
but one drop touched me and my scorched dryness broke.
To the Chan Monk Chengzhuo, Who Holds the Vidyā and Practices in Secret

Fierce flames blaze, and deluded thoughts pour forth;
the clarified butter must be poured upon the crown of the head.
When a single drop has reached every pore,
only then is it the secret cultivation of holding the vidyā.
At the Danbo Studio, Shown to the Lay Buddhist Yunshan
Instructions for the Layman Lianxi

When a deluded thought arises, still it on the spot; / let no single thought be left to hang upon the heart. / To forget all contrivance is the true Land of Peace — / why seek the Pure Land outside, somewhere apart?
Inscribed at the Ink-Light Pavilion Where Master Da Copied the Sutras

They tell how a lotus blooms beneath his brush; / the ink’s own light still shines in the empty brightness. / Idly I ask the master within the flower — / my ears are filled with autumn waves preaching the Dharma.
Instructions for the Student Cao Xiqing

A true man’s resolve is not of the common kind: / thigh stabbed, hair bound to the beam, all hardship tasted. / Only let the six senses stay undefiled, / and light will of itself rise in the ground of mind.
Inscribed on a Wall While Roaming Mount Fu, Having Heard the Chan Monk Zhideng Recite the Lotus Sutra Below Miaogao Peak
A lotus on the water, the sutra on his tongue; / one hut is locked deep in ten thousand green peaks. / Pine winds by day and night are preaching still — / a pity that the people cannot hear.
Instructions for the Novice Monk Zhensi

Birth and death, impermanence, rest on a single breath; / better to set your heart’s will on the green hills. / Only do no karma of the dusty world, / and you win a whole life’s leisure beyond all things.
On Mount Kuang, Pleased by the Visit of Chen Chishi, Grand Councillor

Ten thousand folds of green hills, one single mind; / wherever the eye falls, cloud-forest everywhere. / No need to ask again the meaning of the West’s coming — / water-birds now and then proclaim the wondrous Dharma.
Instructions for the Elder Xiu Liuyi, Who Kept Retreat at Golden Wheel Peak

When you sit alone atop a peak ten thousand fathoms high, / to drop both body and mind is to raise the whole affair. / The silver mountain, the iron wall, must be bored through: / utterly clear throughout — yet no knowing may enter there.
Seeing Off Chief Seat Wuxin Rong, Returning to Jingkou

In the empty hills I meant to spend my last years with you; / why should you sail eastward on the Dharma boat? / Wait until the lone moon rises over the sea-gate, / then round off one huatou for this old monk.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Daben

Pierce through the dusty world and the mind of ten thousand kalpas; / come home into the deep white clouds. / Below Golden Wheel Peak the pine billows race — / day by day hear the wondrous Dharma of the unborn.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Benhuai

Your body and mind have long dwelt in the white clouds; / why let conditions blow you about like tumbling weeds? / Gather yourself home and lay everything down; / lie high in the ten thousand hills, with the sun red overhead.
Instructions for the Attendant Xingsu

Cast off body and mind and bow to the Dharma King; / no need to ask the road ahead, to stay or go. / Only know the face you had before your mother bore you, / and grasses, trees, and thickets all give forth light.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Dunli on His Pilgrimage to Mount Wutai
One staff in hand, one gourd slung along; / do not shrink from ten thousand miles of pilgrimage. / If you meet Mañjuśrī on the day of the feast, / take care no bucket of foul water douse your head.
Instructions for the Two Chan Monks Jizhi and Huilin
A student need not strive and seek in pain; / when delusions melt away, you are free. / Just throw on your robe and watch in idleness — / whose stream is it that follows thought on thought?

The empty hills are still, all conditions cut; / I do not learn the five-flavored Chan of other places. / One who inquires need not seek what goes upward; / simply let go, and all is natural as it is.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Hengyi

This matter has never been sought outside; / seeing, hearing, knowing have their ground. / Know only that in daily use it shows at every turn; / do not fall into the second rank of following conditions.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Kewen

Flowers in the sky rise and vanish without a cause; / yet how each one stares with a film-shrouded eye. / Trust that in the clear sky it is nowhere to be found: / a true man must never be fooled by it.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Juhe

Sitting through a thousand peaks, I do not ask about Chan; / incense in the censer and sutra scrolls are my livelihood. / If beyond this there is nothing else to do, / then this dusty world is the heaven of Extreme Bliss.
Instructions Given When Chief Seat Ruoxing Jiong Came from Afar to Inquire

In the sea of suffering we followed one another twenty years; / once more from Mount Lu you come to bow to dry-bones Chan. / Look at me and ask nothing of the years that remain: / the Five Elders’ cloud-haze is there before our eyes.
A Verse for the Chan Monk Nianyun on His Sixtieth Birthday, He Having Served as Host at Wujiang by His Patriarch’s Command

In the dust of the world the road of awakening opens a cloud-hall; / body and mind spread out, filling the ten directions. / One patch of the Patriarch’s ever-abiding ground — / may it serve as ford and bridge through endless kalpas.
Instructions for Meizi

The burning house blazes; it is not easily cooled. / How pitiable that the six senses are scorched away. / But if a single thought can be cold as ice, / that is the first stage of passing beyond the ordinary.
Seeing Off Dharma Master Mei, Who Goes to Lecture at Weiyang

By chance you ride a single reed and cut across the river; / the Dharma drum thunders at the farther shore. / Countless beings wake from the great dream — / and you return, your bright mark never once withdrawn.
Instructions for the Layman Zheng Baisheng

When this one piece of body and mind is laid down, / let it be within and without like crystal. / There is no place in it for the least dust to cling; / in daily use, each turn is known to oneself alone.
Instructions for the Elder Fuwu Ang, Hall Master of Caoxi

I often think of the long-haired monk of Xinzhou; / he knew not a single word — what power was his? / A load of firewood on his shoulder, a stone at his waist, / and he won the endless lamp that came from the West.
The place of practice need not be sought elsewhere; / it lies in a single thought of the one before you. / If self-nature can appear in full, / why fear the Dharma-sea will not flow across the world?
Instructions for the Chan Monk Jiankong

To leave the dust, my first intent was the mountain woods; / at forty still unheard of, I am shamed before this mind. / Now I rejoice the silken thread at my heel is broken; / deep in ten thousand peaks, deeper still is best.
Instructions for a Chan Monk on His Pilgrimage to Mount Emei
Take the boundless Dharmadhātu as your body; / wherever you meet it, the intimacy is closest. / But if you go to the summit of Mount Emei, / cloud and glow fill the eyes and bewilder you more.

Westward I gaze on Emei, its snow like silver; / Samantabhadra sits upright in a single mote of dust. / The boundless ocean of lands is held within — / appearing as conditions call, the body that joys to be seen.
Instructions for Master Ye on the Casting of a Bell

Heaven and earth the furnace, all things the bronze; / melted into many openings, it roars in the long wind. / One note rings through the three-thousandfold world / and wakes the world from its great dream.
Instructions for the Student Li

In this floating world the light of day is bitterly brief. / What of the matter beneath your own feet — how goes it? / If in this life you do not seek a place of rest, / you will drift with conditions into the river of love.
Instructions for the Ascetic Pu, Who Begs for His Food

The market far, the hills deep, the begging road is long; / you carry only one bowl along the endless way. / Do not weary of the windings of the road: / remember Huangmei, and the stone that dragged at his waist.
Instructions for Dharma Master Wuyin

Once you circled the King of Emptiness by the flower throne; / from letters and words the fragrance of prajñā rose. / Now on a single hair you behold the ocean of lands: / meeting others, there is no need of fine deliberation.
Instructions for the Old Monk Huanzong, Who Printed the Avataṃsaka Sutra

Split a mote of dust and the great sutra comes forth; / the Dharma-gates are a net of pearls, each shaping the next. / Clearly it holds up the Lotus Treasury whole — / wherever it touches, it wakes the dreaming eye.
Presented to the Old Monk Xiangshan, Master of Geomancy

Mountains and rivers of the great earth are empty in his eye; / his one staff is alive as a dragon. / Clearly he points out the road of the unborn, / straight through to the one stream that came from the West.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Tiju
Zhaozhou’s “no” is the pass of birth and death; / the iron wall and silver mountain, seen with cold eyes. / Only see through it before your birth, / and no tongue will ever deceive you.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Yue, Who Gives Tea at the Qingliang Hut

With a willow spray he sprinkles sweet dew on the scorched and withered; / one drop touches, and fevered anguish revives. / Pointing straight at the true meaning of the West’s coming — / when we meet, he only asks: have you taken tea?
Sent to Wuyi Yuanlai of Mount Bo

Our hearts’ accord is not parted by a hairtip; / across a thousand miles of cloud-hills we meet face to face. / Most intimate of all when I long for you: / deep in the night, the bright moon chills the one it shines on.
Instructions for the Elder of Shouchang

Tiles and rubble turn into a great place of practice; / let not the Patriarch’s field lie fallow. / Remember the words: braving rain and piercing cold — / a grain of rice, a stalk of firewood can break the heart.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Qu Ranmi of Shouchang
The lion in his pit has long been trained in play; / his turning and leaping are not easy to know. / Do not let the wild fox’s tracks draw near; / the bared fangs — remember them at the moment.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Wanshi

Bury the body where no wind blows from any of the eight sides; / only when the thieving mind is dead does the work show. / Put your strength on the place before your birth, / and you will know the sun reddening beneath the sea.
Instructions for the Old Monk Bixia

You have traveled every other land and long since come home; / the temple, your native hills, opens where you sit. / A monk who enters the gate has nothing else to do: / to drink tea and wash the bowl is wonderful enough.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Xuanshu
The matter beneath your own feet must be clear; / raise one thought alone and do not count the miles. / Where delusive feeling is wholly spent, / the waters of mind will of themselves run clear.
Instructions for the Old Monk Guizong of Qiyang

Whatever meets the eye is plainly prajñā’s light; / the six gates ever shine, never concealed. / If in a single thought sense and object are cut off, / then in daily use, sitting still, you are in the great place of practice.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Huijing
The light seen by the mind is not in the senses; / darkness has never been able to dim it. / The three-thousandfold world is like a fruit in the palm — / Aniruddha himself entered by this gate.
Instructions for the Elder Liuru Kun, Who Kept Retreat

Gather in body and mind and shut the gate fast; / amid the dust it is no different from the deep hills. / Cast away all delusive thoughts, / and from now on seek diligently the leisure beyond the world.
Instructions for the Attendant Jieshen Jun

I recall how once, bottle in hand and following a staff, / time and again for the Dharma I came to Caoxi. / Now you come straight into the thousand peaks / and ask before the hall to be pointed past delusion.
Instructions for Youming Liaozhong on His Pilgrimage to Wuru

In years past, having finished your pilgrimage, you bowed at Qingliang; / one glimpse of Mañjuśrī and you returned home. / Not knowing how many are in the three-three assembly, / you come again to ask that it be expounded.
Instructions Given When Zheng Baisheng Came Again to Consult Me at Wuru

Yesterday you came past Mount Kuang to ask the Dharma; / did you understand the one phrase raised in full? / Only do not forget the road by which you go home, / and you will of yourself pass beyond the paths of sage and ordinary being.
Sent in Reply on Hearing That Shen Langqian Had Entered Retreat in the City
One room amid the market, open as space; / ordinary and sage mingle and fall within it. / Only the host is ever still and silent, / sitting through the ten directions where no wind blows.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Huikong of Guanyin Mountain in Danyang

Outside the Jetavana gate lies the ford of delusion; / wind and waves come and go, and passing travelers are many. / Hold high the lamp of wisdom, never dimmed: / it must shine right through a single mote of dust.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Andu

The sea of illusion is boundless, its waves not yet stilled; / trust wholly the oar of wisdom to steer the boat of compassion. / Midstream, hoist the light sail high and go, / straight on to the farther shore of bodhi.
Sent to Jin Zhendu
When we sat together at Jetavana at the meal, / since we parted I often recall your good contemplation. / Your Dharma bond must be like Vimalakīrti’s: / who lately has talked with you of non-duality?
Sent to the Chan Monk Yuguang of Mount Putuo

Long have you sat cross-legged below White Flower Mountain; / in the light of water and moon, one thought stands alone. / Even should you sit through all the ten directions, / seas dry and rocks rot — it is as though nothing were.
In Reply to Dharma Master Xinguang

In the empty hills one room is sealed by white clouds; / a bird’s path, subtle and fine, leads into ten thousand folds. / Were it not a road running straight beyond the heavens, / how would you know each step erases all trace?
Instructions for the Attendant Shenguang, Who Goes Home to Visit His Parents

Twenty years have passed since you left your kind mother; / you must clarify the state before your parents were born. / And now again you dream of going home: / this time you should cut the bonds of love.
Instructions for the Layman Yao Xingyang

Your mind is in the dust, yet you vow to leave the dust; / you must simply not be blind to the original person. / Ever and again recall where you take refuge: / among the eight-jewel flowers a latter body waits.
Instructions for the Old Monk Liaoci on the Increase of His Monastic Years

In this turbid world of floating life, do not ask the years; / the dharmakāya is not moved by the three times. / Only let one thought of constant light appear, / and the Lotus Treasury’s adornment is before your eyes.
Instructions for the Attendant Who Guards the Retreat Gate

Lifting the tea, offering water, you must truly know; / in movement and stillness, in turning about, see who it is. / You must look to where the three calls come before your eyes; / do not let those two eyebrows be wasted.
The rhinoceros fan is whole in bone and hide; / called for in haste, it cannot be picked up. / One word stings like three strokes of the rod — / how few can catch the fist beneath the ribs?
Instructions for the Chan Monk Benyuan of Yangshan in Xin’an

Cutting off love, know it is the cause of leaving the world; / would you let a speck of dust settle on the ground of mind? / Each thought must turn the light back and shine within; / be not blind to your own pure dharmakāya.

One thought of perfect clarity, hidden nowhere; / wherever it meets conditions, all is the light of stillness. / Pick up one mote of dust and the Dharmadhātu is held there — / where else would you look for the Western Land?
Sent to the Venerable Chongxu of Jiming Temple

Lake light and mountain colors shine before your bed; / the towers seem lotuses rising from the water. / Afar I recall where my old friend takes his joy: / sitting in Chan at white noon among the flowers.
Sent to the Venerable Liaoxin of Mount Huangbo

Chan from Huangbo is hardest to inquire into; / no sooner touched by words than it falls to second and third. / Only the wind and light are held up in one palm; / and to this day the hills and waters murmur on.
Sent to the Master of Fan Mountain

Manifesting as a princely body, wherever karma calls.
A mind like a lotus, unstained by the dust.
Enthroned in the deep palace, ever turning the Dharma,
That the original person in each be never obscured.
Sent to Layman Yuan

All along this body has been but a guest;
Today, swinging my arms free, I first go home.
Looking back at the red-dust roads where I hurried —
How much better to rest the mind in the white lotus.
Instructions to the Chan Man Minghai

Beneath the cassock, how could this be an ordinary thing?
Not to seek out one's own mind — that is what most deserves grief.
Drifting through kalpas of vast eons down to this day,
This turning back is truly worth discussing well.
Instructions to the Chan Man Xinwu, Nine Years in Seclusion

Shut in, sitting like a withered tree, nine years the term —
Much like the nine years of wall-gazing at Mt. Song.
Even though the snow may pile three feet deep around the waist,
How many know the one phrase that sets the mind at rest?
Instructions to the Practitioner Xingtong

Treading the pestle with a stone at his waist, as at Huangmei;
In the midnight hour, how could he ever open true eyes?
Only trust that from the first there is not a single thing —
Then you will know the bright mirror is no stand at all.
Seeing Off the Chan Man Kewen, Who Goes to Shaolin to Pay Homage to the Patriarch

Before the rock of the severed arm the snow is red still;
Who is fit to inherit the single vein come from the West?
On this journey, if you but obtain the Dharma of pacifying the mind,
You will revive the very spirit of the first patriarch.
Mourning Dharma Master Chaosong

You came at first from Tushita, summoned by the white mallet;
Now that you have gone, you should once more mount the preaching seat.
If we wait for the Compassionate One's next birth in the world,
We know you will take up again your former embryo.
Sent to Rong, Chief Seat

Boats come and go upon the West River without end;
Since we parted, word and letter have fallen wholly silent.
Only the moon above the pine before your bed —
Deep in the night its shadow falls before you still.
Sent to Layman Sun Tunan

Long have I drifted the rivers and lakes with no fixed trace;
Since we parted I have lain among a thousand peaks.
Who knows I have broken through every dream of men?
Only the empty mountain and the still night bell.
Instructions to Shenyu, Whose Courtesy Name Is Yine (Slow of Speech)

The great Way come from the West is beyond words by nature;
Best to trace the true source back through simplicity and silence.
You must press your inquiry to where conditions are forgotten —
Then you will trust the non-dual gate of Vimalakirti.
Sent to the Chan Man Sanbai

When will you carry your staff and bowl across to Donglin,
And enter my room to speak again of the mind that leaves the world?
Do not betray the autumn-night moon over a thousand peaks;
Its clear light shines alone on the deep, deep shadow.
Instructions to the Attendant Guangkai, Who Upholds the Lotus Sutra

Ever since I heard it myself before the kalpa of ink,
Even then a great karmic bond was already formed.
From now on, taking up again these words from many lives,
Each syllable opens the mind, a lotus on the tongue.
Instructions to the Practitioner Haizang, Who Pays Homage to the Lotus Sutra

Prabhūtaratna Tathāgata, the ancient Dharma-body,
Welled forth out of empty space and showed himself to all.
If in the very place you stand there is no birth or death,
Then every dharma, just as it is, is altogether true.
Instructions to Zuo Funian, a Filial Son of Jiangzhou

The Buddha was, through many lives, a man of filial piety;
With a single thought he always served his loving parents.
If you would seek to become a Buddha through the way of filial devotion,
Among the myriad practices none is truer than this thought.
Instructions to the Chan Man Mingming

You came from afar for the Dharma, clear to Mt. Kuang;
How often, dawn and dusk, you knocked at my gate.
If you would ask the true purport of what came from the West —
White clouds drift away, and then drift back again.
Instructions to the Chan Man Minghua, Whose Courtesy Name Is Daoguo (Fruit of the Way)

On a single reed he came from the West, and five petals bloomed;
From that time the seed of the Way has sprouted of itself.
Only water it diligently with the water of wisdom —
The fruit of bodhi will surely not be amiss.
Instructions to Elder Jianyi of Guizong

To shoulder the true Dharma in the ancient groves,
You must use a diamond-hearted resolve to guard it.
When the light shines forth and the whole body appears,
Each thing and every being is a kindred voice.
Instructions to Layman Wang

Father and son, the family has passed down the Chan of Pure Karma;
Once I sought the true teaching amid the miasmic seas.
And now, re-entering this blessed ground of Mt. Kuang,
We meet as though we had never parted at all.
The Chan Man Mochu of Wuyi Came from Afar to Request Instruction; Being Ill, I Did Not Go, and So Gave This

You came from afar for the Dharma, clear to Mt. Kuang,
Gazing after me with earnest care, coming and going again.
Do not say the old monk is too idle to teach the Dharma —
The white clouds will not let anyone out through Pine Pass.

A splendid lotus throne, thronged about by all the heavens,
Only waits for your light to come and open the Dharma feast.
Do not say the Dharma-body has never stirred:
The tongue's root long since has filled the three thousand worlds.
Sent as Instruction to the Chan Man Guanzhi Yun

Bearing a single bowl, you travel far to other lands;
Wherever you go, following conditions, there is the practice ground.
Do not say the dust of toil is no Buddha-work:
From the sea of suffering you launch a ship of compassion.
Instructions to the Chan Man Jingxuan

This very substance, perfect and bright, is the light of prajñā;
At the portals of the six senses it is never hidden away.
If in every thought the unborn appears,
Then wherever it touches, the mind is free — a field of liberation.
Eight Instructions to Chan Practitioners

The single thought before you must be held with care;
Lucid and alone it shines, never clouded over.
Only that one stroke before birth ever came to be —
It has never been permitted that old Hu should know it.

Coming and going through birth and death, long wretched and forlorn,
Never once halting until one awakens to the unborn.
I vow that in this very body I shall win release —
Do not let me turn my head and sink into the dark again.

One nature, perfect and bright, free of the faintest dust —
It was only that we mistook it for something before.
Let a man but cut off the hindrance of afflictions,
And he will naturally see the original person.

Waves surge on the sea of desire, an endless stream —
Who will turn his head back toward the other shore?
You must hoist the light sail high and be gone;
Until you reach the source's end, you will never rest.

Worldly ties are endless, and suffering has no shore;
One thought of turning back, and you are home.
Recognize the true face you have always had —
Then you will know your cassock was not worn in vain.

This mind need not be sought outside;
It rests only in the single thought before you.
Body and world — look at them from the side of emptiness:
They are but a floating bubble on a calm sea.

At the portals of the six senses, the six dusts are many;
Through the whole world, no one can do anything about it.
But if the mind will shine through them, thought after thought,
Then in daily use you will naturally not follow them.
Six Verses on Pure Land Practice

When all conditions are spent, close and distant ties are gone;
How could these old eyes endure the least mote of dust?
Let not the lotus water-clock of the six periods run dry —
Within the flower there is already a body to come.

At first it was craving thought that drew us into Sahā;
From the Pure Land one must surely emerge from the river of love.
If you would have the lotus flower for father and mother,
It all depends on thought after thought seeing Amitābha.

Seeing, hearing, knowing, perceiving — all are the everlasting light;
The lotus in the ground of mind gives off its fragrance unseen.
If the six senses but hold no stain or clinging,
Then everything before your eyes is the West.

Between the brows, a single thread of white-ray light —
Buddhas and living beings are wholly veiled within it.
If only it stays unclouded before you,
The lotus of the mind's ground gives fragrance unseen.

The toil and dust of the five turbidities is fit to be loathed and left;
The Pure Land of the West is the appointed place of return.
Only let thought after thought bring forth the light,
And you will see the flower open in the pool of seven jewels.

The Pure Land was never something to seek outside;
The single thought before you must know how to rest.
Turn and look where deluded thoughts dissolve —
That is the Pure Land's foremost prize.
Great Snow

Ten thousand mountains, ice and snow frozen to the root;
One whole body and mind chilled to the very bone.
Remembering the six years of hunger and want —
It makes a man's nose sting before he knows it.
Reply to Liu Sanwei, Grand Counselor

Clouds and mountains a thousand li away — here is this mind;
Let me send a single word to Donglin.
If you do not betray the lotus covenant,
The White Lotus Society's quiet tryst may still be sought.
Layman Huayu Upholds the Avatamsaka Sutra and Sent His Nephew Juezhi to Request Instruction, So I Send This

The Flower Treasury's adornment is wondrous beyond compare;
Boundless Buddha-lands are a single mote of dust.
If in thought after thought the light appears,
Then you are one who is freed by following conditions.
Instructions to the Novice Zaizhen

On the road of birth and death, suffering lasts the longest;
Best to seek a good remedy from a teacher.
If you can swing your arms and go in peace,
You must bow to the Dharma King in the gate of emptiness.
The Chan Man Yunzhen Came from Wutai to Visit Shuangjing

Old footprints in the Vajra Pit remain;
Since we parted, cloud-mountains have barred us a thousandfold.
Tonight, across the vast sky, snow for a thousand li —
In that year I sealed the cave's mouth fast.
The Dream Wanderings of Old Man Hanshan, Fascicle Thirty-Nine
Miscellaneous Discourses

The red dust rolls on; the world's road stretches far.
How many heroes have been wholly undone by it!
Delights that please the heart, poetry and wine that make one forget care —
the zither and books are elegant, yet still they yield a step.
Golden Valley and Orchid Pavilion are wastelands now.
Though a hollow name remains, it is gone along with the men.
To meet a monk beneath the bamboos, with no regard for the eyes of others —
is this merely stealing a moment's leisure? It is a mere excuse.
Thus one knows that leaving the world is the highest move of all;
pity that people of the day are blind to it and do not awake.
Amid the five desires, all kinds of evil conditions
are like boiling water and splitting flame.
To bring forth a single thought for the sake of birth and death
is like a lotus growing in fire — exceedingly rare.
If one does not deeply rouse loathing and fear, and seek the way of renunciation,
one can hardly escape being boiled.

Clever people of the world know from birth only worldly fame, wealth, and honor,
and the pleasures of loving wife and children, and think that a human life holds this and no more.
They do not know there is something far greater than this.
The heroes of old who passed straight beyond birth and death had no other means —
they simply saw through this.

What the sages of old knew, they passed on one to another:
deluded thinking has no nature of its own.
If delusion had a nature, then Buddhas and patriarchs would have no way to emerge.
Moment after moment — this is the name of arising and ceasing.
Only one who awakens to the unborn can see the moment.
These words confound everyone in the world.

The samādhi of illusion, the jewel-enlightenment of the diamond king —
in the snap of a finger one transcends the stage beyond learning. So swift is this dharma.
Yangshan dreamed he rose to Tushita Heaven and struck the white mallet;
and the case of Mañjuśrī being banished to the Iron Ring Mountain — are these the same or different?
The World-Honored One deliberately taught the mind-ground Dharma-door in the palace of Mara —
how laughable to say there is no other Pure Land.

All illnesses arise from deluded craving.
When deluded craving is not produced, inverted thinking ceases; this is called nirvāṇa.
All dharmas are unborn — I teach the meaning of the moment.
Arising is itself ceasing. This is not spoken for the foolish.
Can it be spoken to the foolish?

Dream, illusion, bubble, shadow; dew, lightning, the shimmer of heat;
mirror-image, water-moon, mirage-city, plantain.
These ten similes are the foundation for entering the Way.
Those who know them are few.

When the three inches of breath are gone, who is the master?
A hundred years on, what is left behind is an empty name.
The Tathāgata's twenty years of teaching on breaking attachment
has nothing that surpasses this.

Chan Master Zhenxie Liao, in a poem written while sick, said:
Only after illness does one know the body is suffering;
while healthy, one busies oneself mostly for others.
Truly, these are the right words.

The nature is fundamentally neither water nor fire, yet cold and heat arise of themselves.
This is a poem from the days when I lived by the sea, written while ill.
Now, lodging overseas, my old illness has suddenly come on, just as of old.
The illness does not change with the place, nor does feeling shift with circumstance;
yet its savor is quite different — hard to put into words for another.

Su Dongpo said: Whatever one is fond of, one is sure to be blinded by.
Reading his collection from Dan'er, I felt that Juefan, who later came overseas,
visited the old lodging to inquire into his traces, and an old woman answered him:
Master Su could not help his fondness for writing poems.
How could even an old woman know his fondness? Is that not precisely a blind spot?

When Dongpo was first banished and came beyond the ranges, he ate lychees and found them delicious, and so said:
Three hundred lychees a day — no harm in being a man of Lingnan forever.
When I first read this, I thought it mere pretense.
I have lived here nearly six years now; whenever a new season comes round,
I find myself reciting it a hundred times over without knowing it.

All my life I have loved the calligraphy of the Jin and Tang masters, and at times I made a refined pursuit of it;
the four masters of the Song I had not yet taken thought of.
Only when I was banished overseas did I often recall the flavor of Dongpo's thatch hut at Dan'er,
and before I knew it my brushwork drew near to his.
Xianzhi said: Outsiders — how could they ever know of this? These words have a rare savor.
The marvel of calligraphy is truly not easy to speak of.
Those who copied calligraphy in ancient times were many, but none of their words goes to the ultimate.
Only I have said: like a wild goose crossing the long sky, its shadow sinking into autumn water.
This is what the Chan school calls the one phrase that overturns everything to the bottom.
If a student can see through here, he may inquire into the highest vehicle of calligraphy.

When men of old discussed poetry, they always compared it to Chan.
They little knew that poetry is true Chan.
Tao Jingjie wrote: Plucking chrysanthemums by the eastern hedge, I gaze at leisure on the southern hills;
the mountain air is lovely at day's end, and the birds return together.
And at the end: Here there is a true meaning; I would tell it, but have forgotten the words.
Lines such as these, taken as poetry, are like a child reciting the first primer.
Among the Tang, only Li Taibai's words create the wondrous of themselves —
he could speak it without knowing Chan.
As for Wang Wei, whose words are mostly Buddhist,
later men vied in praising his skill in Chan; but was it Chan?
It was only literary Chan, not like Tao and Li, who reached beyond words.

When I was young, I read Prince Chen Si's Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luo:
Graceful as a startled swan, gentle as a sporting dragon.
I took it only as describing the goddess, and often said privately that a startled swan could be seen,
but a sporting dragon I did not know.
Long ago, when I lived by the sea, one early dawn the clouds were red though the sun was not yet up,
and for ten thousand li there was no cloud; sea and sky were one color.
Suddenly I saw a wisp of cloud spring up in the vast void, and the seawater flow backwards into the sky,
as though the Milky Way were hung across the nine heavens. I thought it a great marvel.
Then in a moment I saw a dragon coiling in the clouds, head and horns, scales and shell
as clear as something in the palm of my hand. It fell from the sky into the sea,
and the grace of its coiling was too wondrous for words;
nothing in the world could be compared to it.
Then I knew that the ancients did not speak at random.
Reflecting further, this is not true of dragons alone: the Buddha's benefiting of living beings,
his awe-inspiring deportment fully complete, is therefore called the conduct of a great one — like dragon and elephant, as they say.
Knowing Where to Rest

My teacher, the Buddha, the sage, left home to study the Way and rested at the Snow Mountains to practice;
when he attained perfect enlightenment, he at once took his seat in the field of bodhi and taught the Dharma.
The Snow Mountains are a place of coolness.
His meaning was that living beings share the five desires and are all burned by the fire of affliction,
boiling day and night without cease; and if we alone wish to leave it behind,
unless we place ourselves in a place wholly cut off, burying body and mind
amid ten thousand fathoms of ice and snow, letting the cold pierce to the bone,
freezing and starving there, dying the great death and then coming back to life —
how else could we stop the fierce flames and escape being melted away?
Thus my teacher rested here to practice, in the field of bodhi's enlightenment.
And it is said that this ground is made of diamond, the place of utmost firmness.
What he taught was the Dharma-door of the ocean of nature.
The ocean of wisdom has no nature of its own; deluded, it becomes karma and consciousness,
and so it is called the ocean of storehouse consciousness, moved by the wind of the ever-abiding state.
Awakened, it becomes enlightenment and wisdom, and so it is called the ocean of enlightenment,
whose nature is clear and perfect; perfect and clear, enlightenment is originally wondrous.
The meaning is to show that living beings share this same source of Dharma-nature,
and only deludedly have the distinctions of stillness and movement, delusion and awakening.
He wished to let us, by means of movement, contemplate stillness; by means of delusion, illumine awakening;
not to be toppled by the bewilderments of Mara and outsiders,
not to be moved by the winds of circumstance.
Unless one takes one's stand on the most utterly firm ground,
how else could one crush the heterodox, establish the great work?
Therefore my teacher took his stand here and taught the Dharma.
Seen in this light, the ground my teacher took is the ground he wished us all to take.
Hence my interest in Narayana. Narayana means firm and solid.
It stands facing the great sea, majestic as a Dharma-gate; its dwelling is named Ocean Seal,
bright as samādhi. It is said: In resting, know where to rest.
If we rest here, we may be said to rest where we should rest.
It is also said: To dwell in benevolence is beautiful. If one chooses not to dwell in benevolence, how can one be wise?
And again: The little yellow bird rests on the slope of the hill.
In resting, it knows where to rest — can a human being be less than a bird?
I shall repeat these words three times over.
Contentment in Poverty

It is said: Poor yet not flattering, rich yet not arrogant.
Arrogance loses one's wealth; flattery offers up one's poverty.
Therefore it is better to be poor and happy.
Poor and happy, then nothing is not a joy.
Thus Yan Hui's mean lane, Yuan Xian's bare walls, Zilu's padded gown, Rong Gong's plain belt —
did they rejoice in nothing, and yet rejoice? If one gains this joy,
then even the whole world could not be exchanged for it.
Ah, no wonder Xu You and Wu Guang, Nie Que and Pi Yi
bore the conduct of absolute renunciation.
Confucius also said: With coarse rice to eat, water to drink, and my bent arm for a pillow,
joy is there as well. Wealth and honor gained by unrighteousness are to me as drifting clouds.
The Essentials of Learning
Tending the Mind

Setting the mind at rest lies in emptiness; maintaining the mind lies in evenness;
employing the mind lies in illumination; awakening the mind lies in forgetting.
The substance of the mind is originally empty; when desires cross and mingle,
and deluded thoughts pile up, there is not a single gap left.
Thus the vital breath steams and the body grows dim, flickering and burning, and there is no peace.
Therefore it is said: Clear away things and it is bright and open; if you do not clear them away, it is not empty;
if not empty, not bright; if not bright, not at peace.
Thus setting the mind at rest lies in emptiness.
The mind is originally thusness; within and without are equal.
Its unevenness comes from weighing light and heavy.
Thus the foolish weigh the outer heavy, the wise weigh the inner heavy, the sage forgets both.
He who weighs the outer heavy falls; he who weighs the inner heavy strains;
he who forgets both is even. Even, then nothing is not centered.
Thus maintaining the mind lies in evenness.
The substance of the mind is originally bright and illuminates all;
it is only because of its muddy dimness that there is anything it does not illumine.
Look at people in the world: day by day their muddiness increases,
and even in action they have no means to mirror themselves.
Thus employing the mind lies in illumination.
The mind is originally undeluded; it is deluded because illumination is lost.
When delusion is dispelled, illumination too dissolves.
Thus awakening the mind lies in forgetting.

Contemplating the mind is the first and most subtle of Dharma-doors.
The mind is the master of the whole body and the root of all practices.
If the mind is not clear, those who would have the body upright and conduct correct are few.
Therefore all the various sufferings of the world arise from deluded and inverted thinking.
If inversion is not produced, then arising is itself non-arising.
Non-arising, then though there is arising, there is no arising;
arising without arising, then thought too is without thought.
Without thought, how could inversion arise? If anything arises, it is not correct contemplation.
Correct contemplation is never not correct.
Reading Zhuangzi

The true Lord has no form at all, transcendent beyond the dust of the world.
Then in a flash a single thought goes astray and breaks into this bag of skin —
like a monkey wrapped up tight, ill at ease on every side.
To rise or sit one must be attended; for hunger and thirst one begs to be served.
For fame and profit one busies oneself, selling off fields and gardens.
There is a further kind of folly: one wants one's face admired by others,
powdering and rouging a stinking skin — no different from a specter or a goblin.
Every one of them lives for the sake of others, and so drags down a debt for the next life.
Alas, men ancient and modern — who is willing to be startled by this?
Only the master of Qiyuan had some small understanding of this flavor.
Discourse on the Round Fan

In the summer of the jichou year, having been slandered by a madman,
I lodged in the eastern quarter of Mo. When someone came out with a fan and asked for my writing,
I spoke off the cuff and recorded it.

The great fire sweeps across, melting metal and shriveling stone;
of those who sit idle by a broken window, few escape being boiled by it.
Alas, a human being — if only he takes my skin and bone to sustain himself,
then for food and rest, rising and sleeping, he simply obeys its command.
It makes the joy of coolness spring up at once at his elbow,
and the misery of sweltering heat dissolve from his skin;
the swarming of mosquitoes is waved away and they retreat;
the torment of their stinging is brushed aside and quietly vanishes.
Why then boast of growing wings to ride the cool wind,
or mount the flying clouds and roam the six directions?
How sad! Once a cool breeze comes, it is cast away as refuse;
when frost and dew first rise, it is looked on as so much clutter.
Is this not to act without dominating, to succeed without claiming credit?
How could one speak of such a one together with this?
Discourse on Solitude

To speak of solitude is easy; to walk in it is hard.
And to be inwardly at ease with it is harder still than walking in it.
Even amid the churn of worldly affairs, without debating high or low,
the great men of old, whether they went forth or withdrew, acted openly while their minds remained hidden.
Truly it is hard to judge them by outward traces.
Unless one has eyes that can see beyond and holds a perfect mirror of illumination,
how could one give full measure to their countenance?
Ah, no wonder the madman of Chu sang as he passed Confucius,
and Xu You turned his head away from Yao and Shun.
Yet was it that these two were right and the three sages wrong?
Each affirmed his own as right; and to take one's own as attainment
is at root no more than shadow and echo before the great Way.
One who hates the shadow and joins in the echo is hard put to hear the purport of solitude.
Let the gentleman who faces the Way take his rest here.
Discourse on Sincerity of Mind, Given as Instruction to Tanzhi

If the mind is not sincere, it is not clear. If the nature is not still, it is not settled.
If the essence is not gathered, it is not complete. If the spirit is not concentrated, it does not roam free.
If the will is not single, it is not firm. If the vital breath is not nurtured, it is not harmonious.
If anger is not checked, it is not calmed. If desire is not blocked, it is not made few.
If learning is not discussed, it is not broad. If inquiry is not debated, it does not penetrate.
If the standard is not set, it is not firm. If conduct is not upheld, it is not strong.
Therefore the learning of the gentleman lies in valuing what others make light of,
in increasing what others diminish, in taking what others discard, in gaining what others do not have.
Thus his Way is great and his virtue vast, his person ample and his name honored —
transcendent and without peer.
Discourse on the Marsh and the Mountain

I have heard that Master Zhuang said:
To hide a boat in a ravine, to hide a mountain in a marsh, is called secure.
Yet a strong man can carry them off on his back, and the deluded do not notice.
His meaning is that where there is something hidden, there is something shouldered;
where nothing is hidden, nothing is shouldered.
Yet if one takes no hiding as the highest, I would suggest that to have something hidden
is better than to have nothing hidden.
Therefore it is said: When the mountain cherishes jade, the grass and trees flourish;
when the river stores pearls, its banks do not wither.
Is this not to have something hidden within and something shining without?
Therefore the gentleman values storing his vessel within himself, waiting for the time and only then using it.
Moreover, the mountain's accumulation is thick, and so it is high and all beauties are complete;
the marsh's accumulation is deep, and so it is low and all virtues return to it.
In taking its image from the gentleman, there is further meaning here.
Discourse on Awakening from a Dream

The Phantom Man was just then riding a single leaf and mooring on the shore of the phantom sea.
He was about to dwell in the vast emptiness with the teeming multitudes of the shimmering deep, and rest there.
It happened that Mr. Wandering Drifter came by, and touched him and asked:
Ha, how strange! I see that you cannot be fathomed.
Gazing at your form, it is drifting as a cloud; looking at your countenance, it is chill as ice;
tapping within you, it is wholly empty; drawing near, you are warm;
tracing you out, you are deep and profound; sealed, you seem shut in; floating, you seem to ride.
Comparing you, you seem a man and yet not a man. Where do you dwell, what do you do, that you have come to this?
The Phantom Man had no reply. He only murmured assent, silent and still,
without knowing, without recognizing, without showing, without speaking.
He slept and rested with him, sat and lay, ate and drank, rose and reclined, waking and sleeping,
for ten days without a break. Mr. Drifter's heart blazed and his will melted, and he was about to be wholly transformed along with him.
As Mr. Drifter was about to go, he made a request of the Phantom Man:
I am a man of wind and waves; I beg to borrow boat and oars,
to ride the drifting and reach the other shore as my support. Has the Master no intention of this?
He said: Stay. What words are these? Have you alone never seen a dreamer?
When he sleeps through the long night, he must sink into deep drunken stupor, head reeling,
his essence and spirit muddled and dim, his soul and thoughts shaken with dread;
his body seems to lie dead, his mind seems a specter.
He does not shift from his mat, yet a hundred monsters appear;
no more time passes than a moment, yet a thousand years stretch far away.
