Below it says: you still doubt the bodhi-mind by means of worldly deluded imaginings. This precisely breaks the habit of names and phrases; hence it says he doubts bodhi by worldly deluded imagining — what is meant by using the mind of arising and ceasing to discuss perfect enlightenment, so that the nature of perfect enlightenment likewise seems to flow along. Hence this knowledge and vision must be dissolved before one enters the one mind's true source. Because the true mind and true wisdom are hard to put into words, he specifically borrows the essence of seeing to break it by analogy. And since conjunction has been broken while Ānanda again forms the view of non-conjunction, he doubts again: as I consider it, is this wondrous source of awakening neither conjoined with all conditioning dust and mental thought? Observe this: one must directly forget both mind and realm and cut off the path of words and thought before entering the wonder of the one mind.

Question: In the earlier gathering of the five aggregates, the aggregate of form is raised first as arising through deluded view, and so it is said that because the eye is fatigued one deludedly sees flowers in the sky. Now in teaching the six entrances it again takes up the earlier combination of eye and fatigue as the eye-entrance. What is the intent? Answer: This is the most extremely subtle and cannot be compared with the earlier simile. For here it speaks of the very origin of the six faculties. Because the seeing-part grasps marks and absorbs habit inward, it conjoins and binds into the five pure form-faculties, which are what the defiling dust depends on; originally there was no entrance, and only now does it first exist. The eye together with fatigue — the eye is the present eye-faculty, which is the mark-part, and fatigue is the seeing-part. Because these two parts are fundamentally nonexistent, alike the fatigue-sign of bodhi staring, the intent is to show that the consciousness-substance is deluded in dependence on awakening; hence it says the two parts are the fatigue produced by bodhi. They are manifested in dependence on consciousness and are the marks of activity of consciousness, not apart from self-realization and originally without a second substance; hence it says they are alike. Thus he takes their forming the self-substance of the six faculties as the simile, meaning that originally there are no six faculties, and only because seeing and marks first conjoin do the pure form-faculties come to be; hence he raises both together, to clarify the very beginning of the six faculties' first binding. This is why it is hard to grasp.

Question: What is the meaning of 'entrance'? Answer: The mark-only school says it is the mark-part having substance and reality, form being the place where the seeing-part relies in its thinking; regardless of near or far it is the objective condition, because all have duality and all have something depended on. Now it is said that both are without substance, being only one true suchness; hence they are originally the Tathāgatagarbha.

Question: The Awakening of Faith's three subtleties are karma, turning, and manifestation, in that order; but in this sutra the three subtleties take seeing as the mark of turning and place it third, so that manifestation comes before turning. Does this not lose the treatise's meaning? Answer: It does not lose the treatise's meaning; each has its own emphasis. The treatise's meaning speaks solely of the arising of mental dharmas: within the true realm, at first because of a single deluded movement, the perfect luminous true mind is turned into ignorance; from this ignorance the marks of discrimination and continuity appear; and if one can be free of thought one realizes the one mind. This sutra emphasizes the living being's origin of arising: because of the initial single deluded movement, the markless true mind is turned at once into deluded marks that have marks, so that empty space and the four elements take shape from this — this is having what is possessed and having marks. Because there are possessed marks, the originally possessed light of wisdom is turned into deluded seeing, a deluded knowing that grasps marks. Thereupon seeing and marks share the same one luminous awakened substance, but now mixed and undivided they become a sentient being — what is called the conjunction of form and mind becoming the living being of the five aggregates. Its emphasis is on deluded seeing and grasping as the root of the sickness of birth and death — what is called the taker of rebirths. Hence it says: the self-mind grasps the self-mind; the non-illusory becomes illusory dharmas; not grasping, there is nothing that is not illusory. Hence the patriarch said: no need to seek the true; one need only put an end to views. The treatise turns mind alone, so true cultivation lies precisely in freedom from thought; this sutra turns objects, so it says that if one can turn things one is the same as the Tathāgata, and true cultivation lies precisely in not grasping, which cuts off the root of birth and death. Hence in breaking delusion it goes straight to selecting conditions. The sutra emphasizes the grasped, so it puts marks first; the treatise emphasizes the grasper, so it puts seeing first. Thus the gateways differ and cultivation and severing also differ. Examine this deeply.
The Dream-Roaming Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Scroll Forty-Four

blocks.text: Prefatory Words on Resolving Doubts about the Great Learning, Its Outline and Items

inline.s: At nineteen I abandoned brush and inkstone; at thirty I entered the mountains and cut off letters; at fifty I was censured and, by imperial grace, exiled beyond the passes; and it is now fourteen years since. Coming and going with my bowl in Wuyang, the young men wrongly esteemed me as one who knows how to speak, and came time and again to ask about the Way; yet I had nothing at all to answer, and for empty comings and substantial goings I am ashamed indeed. Sometimes someone would look on me as a Chan man, and I was like a mute eating huangbo — nothing but bitterness. One autumn day in the jiyou year I happened to come begging, and the young men prepared an incense-offering vegetarian feast at the Dharma society. I could only hold my belly with laughter that these young men truly understood me. When the meal was done they asked for instruction, and I could only breathe out the breath of gruel and rice; so I took my shame and departed. Returning by boat to Caoxi, I reflected that these young men had fed me for no short time, and that I had never yet repaid them. When one of them asked about the chapter in which Yan Hui asks about benevolence, I could only mumble. Even when I had words, they could not be complete, and complete they could not be exhaustive; and to seek to please the minds of the many is no easy thing to speak of. Because the young men's food was hard to digest, my belly still felt full. Sleeping enough in the boat, I heard my attendant reading the Great Learning, and its clamor raised doubts in me. So I took the one chapter of the classic and, following the outline and items, set up questions and answers to settle it for myself, and further cited the chapter of Yan Hui's asking about benevolence to join and compare it. It was like wielding a butcher's knife: in two half-meals I finished it. Read aloud, it did not form sentences — it is not literature. Thinking deeply, I recalled that from childhood I had read the books of Confucius seeking the Dharma of mind directly pointed out, and that he bestowed on Yan Hui alone the true transmitted secret; for the rest he drew the bow but did not let the arrow fly. I had never known that the sage's mind-seal was fully laid bare within two hundred and fifty words. How subtle, how subtle! Was I blind? Alas, I am now sixty-four years old, and only now do I know — one may call it late. I feared that when I died it would end in obscurity; hence I hastened to tell the young men. Some of them are past half my age, some not yet half; fortunate are those who hear this — one may call it early, like a good horse seeing the shadow of the whip and going a thousand li in a breath, or like the goose-king choosing the milk. Would they not take this as the breath of gruel and rice? This was stirred up solely by the feeling of one meal. May the young men take this and feed the hungry of the world; I dare not speak of broad charity. Written two days before the Mid-Autumn of the jiyou year by the outsider Deqing, in a boat on the Xu Yang Gorge.
The Way of the Great Learning Lies in Manifesting the Luminous Virtue, in Loving the People, in Resting in the Highest Good

'The Great Learning' means the learning of the immeasurable great person. The word 'way' is like 'method.' Because what people of the world see is small, they are all petty persons and cannot be called great persons, since what they learn is all petty method. Even the various schools and the hundred thinkers, with their strange stratagems and unusual arts, are no more than the view of one bend; even if their learning succeeds, it only makes a petty person. If one is willing instead to seek within himself his own original mind-nature, then once he awakens he is at once a great person; because what he learns is great, it is called the Great Learning. The method of the Great Learning is not much at all; it does not require much knowledge or much seeing. Only three things and it is done. First, one must awaken to the substance of one's own mind; hence it says 'in manifesting the luminous virtue.' Second, one must cause everyone in the world to awaken just as I have, so that all alike are no longer of the old knowledge and vision but make a brand-new career, with no self and no other, sharing great peace; hence it says 'in loving the people.' Third, whether for oneself or for the people, one must not hastily stop halfway; everyone must reach the thoroughgoing place before letting go; hence it says 'in resting in the highest good.' If one can truly learn these three things, one is a great person. The two characters 'luminous' must be understood distinctly. The second 'luminous' is the luminous of brightness and light, pointing to the substance of one's own mind. The first 'luminous' has two meanings. If one speaks of one's own work in respect of the luminous virtue, it is the luminous of awakening to clarity: the luminous virtue is the nature I originally possess, but I have always been deluded and unaware of it, exactly like a confused man who says his own head is lost and seeks it everywhere in vain; one day he suddenly comes to himself and at once knows the original head was always there and was never lost. Everyone's self-nature is originally luminous, vast, and free, lacking not a hair; but being deluded, they all seek understanding outside in the houses of others, learning their every word, thinking that what is learned is useful. If one day one awakens to one's own nature as luminous and bright, lacking nothing at all, this is to have awakened to and made clear the luminous virtue one originally possesses; hence it says 'manifesting the luminous virtue.' To awaken to the luminous virtue is at once to be a sage. This is spoken in respect of one's own portion of the work. If one speaks in respect of the portion of loving the people, the first 'luminous' is the luminous of making bright, the meaning of proclaiming and instructing, and again the meaning of displaying and revealing, like raising the sun and moon in mid-heaven; it is the luminous of great brightness. Both meanings must be thoroughly understood. Question: what is the highest good? Answer: from ancient times everyone's knowledge and vision only knew how to walk the two roads of good and evil, and only taught people to change from evil and turn to good — this is the old knowledge and vision, and what is so extraordinary about it? They did not know that the two ends of good and evil are external dharmas of duality, having nothing whatever to do with the substance of my own nature. Hence one who does evil in the world can be changed to good, and thus a good person can be changed into an evil one — enough to show that good is not reliable. Because good does not reach the utmost, even good is not good; hence the student cannot stand firm, because it is not the place of arrival and not a place where one may rest. Seen in this light, all of it is the habit of old knowledge and vision. Now when we speak of the highest good, it is awakening to and clarifying the true substance of the self-nature, which is originally neither good nor evil. It is only a stretch of luminosity, without inside or outside, without past or present, without self or other, without right or wrong — what is called standing alone and unchanging. Not one point can be attached to it; it is swept clean of the least mote. If one uses good to break evil and, evil gone, good remains, this is still separated by a layer, for this one character 'good' is originally guest-dust, not the original host; hence it is not the ultimate place where one may rest. One need only forget both good and evil and cut off the traces of self and thing, without reliance, without light or dark, without coming or going, unmoving and unshaken; only then is it the hour of arrival. Reaching this, in oneself one sees no virtue to be made luminous, and in the people one sees no people to be renewed; merged in one whole, this is the realm of the great person. With no good to name it, it is named the highest good. To know this is first to be said to know where to rest.
The Section: Knowing Where to Rest, and Then There Is Stability; with Stability, One Can Be Still

The character 'stability' points to the substance of the self-nature, quiescent and unmoving, limpid and ever stable, not something that becomes stable after practice. But students do not penetrate the substance, which is originally ever stable, and instead go off to practice and force themselves to become stable. They only take the knowledge and vision they have acquired in a lifetime and seek stability on the two ends of good and evil, on the mind of arising and ceasing — like a monkey put into a bag, like pressing a gourd under water. Seeking stability in this way, one will not be stable to the end of one's years. Why? The fault lies in using the mind of arising and ceasing, in harboring views of good and evil, in not penetrating the substance, and in wrestling solely with deluded thoughts — what is called taking a thief for one's son, being greatly ignorant of where to rest. If one can penetrate the substance, one is at once quiescent; this is the stability of the self-nature, not a stability that can be forced. Take the Sixth Patriarch's instruction to students on how to use the mind: not thinking of good, not thinking of evil — what is the original face of the venerable one? The student at that moment cuts clean in two, and at once sees the self-nature, and the mad mind suddenly rests, never again seeking elsewhere; only then does he awaken to the fact that his own self was never moved at all. This is the very picture of knowing where to rest and then having stability. He also said: you need only not think of either good or evil, and you will naturally see the substance of mind. This is the very picture of knowing where to rest. Hence the student values knowing where to rest; knowing where to rest, he is naturally stable. The character 'still' differs from the character 'stable.' Stability is the stable substance of the self-nature; this stillness is spoken in contrast to outward disturbance and unrest, and is far indeed from the substance of stability. Why? Because the student's deluded thoughts have always been flying in confusion, and his mind cannot rest for a moment; he only strains to suppress and press down on his knowledge and vision, using the mind to enforce stillness, not knowing that the more urgently he seeks stillness the more fiercely his disordered thoughts blaze, so that he certainly cannot be still. Why? Because he uses the mind to seek the mind: the more he seeks the farther away it is, and how could he obtain a single thought of rest? Seeking to enter from outside is like a man who calls at the gate and finds it unopened, and instead falls to quarreling with the gatekeeper; the quarrel goes on to the very end, and if the true master does not appear, the brawling can never rest. But if the master opens the double gate from within, the gatekeeper flees without a trace, and the one seeking entry truly sees the master, so that the mind of seeking to see also ceases and is no more. This is what is meant by the place where the mad mind rests being stillness. If one does not truly see the substance, in the end one can never be still. Hence it says: with stability, one can be still. The character 'peace' is the meaning of steady and level, and also like the peace of accepting one's lot: being self-sufficient and seeking nothing more. Because one has always sought stillness without attaining it, with mixed thoughts in confusion and seeking that never rests, this mind has not one thought of peace. Now that the substance is awakened, the seeking mind rests, and the self-nature is complete, lacking nothing and with nothing left over, steady and level, happy and free. This peace and leisure and happiness are obtained at the place where the mad mind rests. Hence it says: with stillness, one can be at peace. The character 'consideration' is not the consideration of deluded thought or pondering, nor the consideration of anxiety; it is the consideration that does not consider. Hence it is said: the Yi is without thought, without consideration, quiescent and unmoving, yet responsive and thereby penetrating the affairs of the world. And again: a hundred considerations return to one. And again: without considering, it pervades. This is precisely this character 'consideration.' It means that before awakening one sought solely on deluded thought and pondering, so that even for a single matter one had a thousand thoughts and ten thousand considerations, and in the end it was useless and could not be considered. The more one thought and considered, the more the mind became unpeaceful. Now that one has awakened and made clear this mind, which is peaceful and free, then as thought arises and the mind stirs, all is perfect and penetrating, and the affairs of the world are clear before one's eyes. This realm is not something that clever knowledge and vision can calculate; it is the radiance of the substance of one's own mind, naturally complete. Hence it says: with peace, one can consider. The character 'attainment' is not the attainment of gain and loss; it is the meaning of without leakage. The sage responds universally and aptly, illumining all dispositions; not a hair is mistaken, the very bottom is seen through, and each thing hits the mark; hence it is called attainment — it is not that there is something attained. When one had not yet made the luminous virtue clear, one used solely deluded thought and pondering, calculating and measuring, and even when right one did not attain it, because it was not real. Now with the radiance of the self-nature one contemplates all alike and illumines all together, and the manifold dispositions and differing states all return to one principle; hence one can accomplish all in detail without omission. This is not to have attained something, for it is the consideration that does not consider and the attainment that does not attain. Hence it says: with consideration, one can attain. It means it is not an occasional hitting of the mark; it is precisely by consideration that one hits it.
The Section: The Ancients Who Wished to Make the Luminous Virtue Clear throughout the World

This explains the preceding sequence of root and branch, before and after, so as to verify the actual effect of manifesting the luminous virtue and loving the people. Spoken in terms of the work of accomplishing oneself, manifesting the luminous virtue is the root and renewing the people is the branch — this speaks from the root up to the branch. Now, spoken in terms of accomplishing things, it therefore speaks from the branch back down to the root. Previously, from the knowing where to rest of the one mind one worked up to considering and being able to attain; reaching this, all the affairs of the world return to my square inch. Now one wishes to take the luminous virtue one has awakened to and reveal it to the people of the world, wishing to make everyone awaken together. The character 'wish' is precisely the power of vow: since I have now awakened to this nature of luminous virtue, and this nature is what all people in the world equally possess and share, how could I bear to know it myself and abandon others? Therefore I vow to reveal it to the people of the world and cause them to awaken and realize together. But I fear that one who bears this vow will be thought impractical and will find it hard to obtain quick results; and the world is so vast that it cannot be covered at a single step. Therefore for the time being one begins with one's own state: what is meant by knowing the far by means of the near. If one state takes effect, the world is easily transformed. Formerly Yao made his capital at Pingyang, Shun held the hundred offices, Tang had seventy li, and King Wen a hundred li; all were ancient rulers who wished to make the luminous virtue clear throughout the world, and who came from the power of vow? Hence I say the 'wish' is the power of vow. The person is the root of the world, the state, and the family. The sutra text afterward always comes back to rest in cultivating the person; hence it is clear that cultivating the person is the essential matter. Yet this one matter is the hardest to understand. Could it be that taking this body of blood and flesh and binding it into caution and dignity, like a boy in the presence of his teacher, is enough to govern a state? Could it be that making every matter on the body look well, like a player on a stage, is enough to bring peace to the world? Hence cultivating the person is spoken of entirely in terms of the mind. Take Yan Hui's asking about benevolence: Confucius told him that to overcome oneself and return to propriety is benevolence; this is precisely the true picture of cultivating the person. Then he told him: if for one day one overcomes oneself and returns to propriety, the world will return to benevolence. This is precisely the true business of governing the state and bringing peace to the world. If one does not believe that this overcoming of oneself is the true business of cultivating the person, how could it be that when Yan Hui asked for its particulars Confucius told him the four prohibitions? Moreover the four prohibitions are all matters of cultivating the person: overcoming oneself is the work of benevolence in the ground of mind; to overcome oneself for benevolence is to manifest the luminous virtue; the world returning to benevolence is to renew the people. 'Benevolence proceeds from oneself' — this self is the true self, namely the place of the highest good. Hence Yan Hui destroyed his cleverness, dismissed his limbs, and practiced the fasting of the mind and sitting in forgetfulness; all these came from the actual effect of the self and are the place of the highest good. What obstructs a person's one body is nothing but seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving: the seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting that are the old knowledge and vision of everyone from ancient times to the present. For benevolence one must cut away utterly all the old knowledge and vision and begin a wholly new life; one cannot enter by carrying along the views of old habitual habits. For the old seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are all contrary to propriety, disordered and inverted, and of no use whatever. Hence, gouging out the heart and plucking out the gall, he brought forth the single character 'do not.' 'Do not' is a word of prohibition, expulsion, and driving out: it means that the old seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting are all to be wholly cut off, with no transgression permitted; to transgress again is to be a thief. This is the strictest of prohibitions. Yan Hui heard it and understood at once, and thereupon destroyed his cleverness, dismissed his limbs, and did away with all of it; he simply sat, and sitting he forgot, until he forgot to the place where there was nothing left to forget. Then he turned over and leaped up, and all his seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving were wholly unlike those of the man of former days, as though he had newly built and made for himself another human body. Is this not a new person? Being new himself, he then extended this newness to transform the people, and none of the people failed to be transformed and renewed. This is what is meant by: if for one day one overcomes oneself and returns to propriety, the world returns to benevolence — precisely the effect of cultivating the person. Were it not so, how could cultivating the person be the root of governing the state and bringing peace to the world? The mind is the substance and the host; intention is deluded thought and pondering and is the guest — this is the distinction between mind and intention. Now to rectify the mind one must first cut off at once all the pondering and deluded thought beneath the root of intention, like cutting tangled silk; when not a thought arises, the substance of mind is pure and one without delusion. Hence it is called the thief: the mind's crookedness comes from the intention's insincerity; now that the ground of intention is without delusion, the mind is rectified of itself. Hence it says: wishing to rectify the mind, first make the intention sincere. Knowing and intending are again the distinction between the true and the false. Intention is deluded thought; knowing belongs to true knowing. True knowing is the luminous virtue of the substance, which has always been obscured by deluded thought so that it cannot show through; hence true knowing is dimmed and wronged while deluded thought holds sole power — like a treacherous minister holding the Son of Heaven hostage to command the feudal lords. Now to behead the treacherous and depraved, one must request the sword of the imperial presence; without the true mandate one cannot break the usurper. Hence it says: wishing to make the intention sincere, first extend the knowing. Knowing is the true lord, which has always been confused and unaware. Now the word 'extend' is like 'reach': as when a loyal minister, resolved to remove a traitor, dares not act on his own, but must first bring the traitor's crimes to the knowledge of his lord and awaken him — hence it is called extending. If the true lord once awakens, the treacherous and depraved cannot allow themselves to work their mischief. Hence it says: wishing to make the intention sincere, first extend the knowing. Things are outer things, what has always stood opposed to me — the objects grasped by seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, by seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting. Knowing is true knowing, the originally luminous light of wisdom of the self-substance. This single character 'knowing' is the source of delusion and awakening: because of delusion, inwardly true knowing is transformed into deluded thought, and so the intention is insincere; being insincere, there is no clarity. Outwardly one grasps the true realm as desirable, and so things are not transformed; not being transformed, they become obstructions. Thus this single character 'knowing' is the root and source of inner and outer mind and realm, of the true and the false, of delusion and awakening. The ancients said: the one character 'knowing' is the gate of all wonders and the gate of all calamities. Now, to set aside disorder and return to order, one must inwardly rely on the power of true knowing to break deluded thought, and outwardly use the illumination of true knowing to melt deluded realms. 'Investigate' is the investigate of Yu's investigating the Sanmiao: I move them by utmost sincerity, and they are transformed and return to me — what is meant by utmost sincerity piercing metal and stone and moving pigs and fish. Moreover knowing has true and false, differing, so its use also differs, and investigation likewise has two kinds. Using deluded knowing with deluded thought, things and I stand opposed and obstructive: this investigate is the investigate of grappling and opposition, as when it is said one forms schemes with what one meets and daily does battle with the mind. Using true knowing with utmost sincerity, things and I respond and communicate: this investigate is the investigate of responsive investigation, as when it is said to investigate what is not the mind. Take the donkey's braying, the frog's croaking, and the grass before the window: all are realms of sound and form that stand opposed to me as obstructions. Yet among the Song Confucians there were those who awakened on hearing the donkey bray and the frog croak, or on seeing the grass before the window. Sound and form are one and the same; what formerly stood opposed to me as an obstruction has now been transformed into the wondrous realm of my mind. Things transformed into knowing and made one with me — as a responsive investigation, what doubt remains? Question: true knowing has no thing to oppose it; how does it respond to and investigate things? Answer: true knowing is in fact thoroughly clear within and without, with no thing to oppose; and the principle of responding to things is the hardest to put into words. The Yi says: quiescent and unmoving, yet responsive and thereby penetrating the affairs of the world. Quiescent and unmoving is the substance of knowing; the affairs of the world are outer things; being responsive and thereby penetrating is investigating things. 'Responsive penetration' does not mean that true knowing drills into things, because true knowing is utterly empty and no thing stands before it. The true and false mind and realm cannot both stand: outer things are like darkness, true knowing like the white sun; when the white sun rises, all darkness is at once extinguished. It is spoken of at the point of dissolution and transformation as responsive penetration. When darkness responds to brightness, brightness becomes darkness; now when brightness responds to darkness, darkness departs of itself and brightness stands alone; hence though there is response, the two fundamentally do not meet, and the weight lies with the brightness. The substance of things is originally empty, and only because of deluded grasping do they become obstructions. Now with true knowing illumining alone, the place of release is thoroughly clear, and no thing can confront the feelings. With the quiescent unmoving true knowing one penetrates the illusory things that are originally nothing; thus knowing illumines itself without waiting to respond, and things melt of themselves without waiting to be penetrated; the two do not dissolve each other. How subtle, how subtle! Hence the student values true knowing alone: once true knowing stands, the luminous virtue is luminous of itself, with not a hair of fabrication. This is why the work of the Great Learning speaks of making luminous and of knowing, while cultivation, regulation, governance, and peace are all its things.

Question: In the opening outline you explained manifesting the luminous virtue, loving the people, and resting in the highest good, which are plainly three matters; now in the items you only explain making the luminous virtue clear throughout the world, and it ends by returning to extending knowing and investigating things, as though it were one matter. What does this mean? Answer: This intent of the sage is most wondrous, and no one in a thousand ages has understood it. Among these eight matters, weight is placed solely on the one character 'knowing.' This knowing is the luminous virtue; it is the substance. It was said above that the first 'luminous' has two meanings. What I earlier explained as extending knowing and investigating things uses the former meaning of awakening to clarity, and the work already lies within knowing where to rest: the character 'rest' is the quiescent unmoving substance of knowing, and the 'knowing' of knowing where to rest is the first 'luminous,' which is the work. This passage has already known to the utmost extreme; once the substance of knowing is ultimate, the full business of making the intention sincere, rectifying the mind, and cultivating the person is finished. Thus manifesting the luminous virtue and renewing the people are plainly two matters. Now, wishing to make the luminous virtue clear throughout the world uses the second meaning of displaying and making bright; hence extending knowing and investigating things may also be spoken of in terms of renewing the people. Moreover, knowing where to rest and then having stability is already standing: knowing where to rest, one's own footing is already set firm. Considering and then being able to attain is already reaching: one has penetrated all affairs and things without omission, and before one's eyes there is not a hair of obstruction, so that every dharma is true — is this not already reaching? The reason for standing and the reason for reaching both rely on the power of true knowing. Therefore, in doing the work of renewing the people, one extends the true knowing one has awakened to into all things; and once all things receive the single illumination of my true knowing, they are like snow touched to a red-hot furnace, like frost melted by the blazing sun, transformed without being expected to transform. Hence it says: extending knowing lies in investigating things. Things transform of themselves, and so it is called investigating. Once those things are investigated, my luminous virtue naturally shines throughout the world, and the people renew themselves without being expected to renew. This is what is meant by establishing others and reaching others. Thus manifesting the luminous virtue and renewing the people are but one matter: the three guiding principles are one and yet three, three and yet one. Hence these eight matters only complete the single sentence about making the luminous virtue clear throughout the world. And that one proceeds from family and state and afterward reaches the world is knowing the far by means of the near; this is most clear. Question: how can investigating things bring peace to the world? Answer: just say what the things investigated are. They are heaven, earth, and the myriad things, all contained therein. Could one set aside heaven, earth, and the myriad things and seek out another thing to investigate? If investigating things could not bring peace to the world, why did Confucius say that if for one day one overcomes oneself and returns to propriety the world returns to benevolence? And just say what the world is as a thing, and where returning to benevolence ultimately returns to. Investigate this. Question: how are extending knowing and investigating things reconciled with overcoming oneself, returning to propriety, and the world returning to benevolence? Answer: overcoming oneself is extending knowing; returning to propriety is investigating things; the world returning to benevolence is things investigated. Question: the student does not understand. Answer: the self is the thing; overcoming is extending knowing; returning to propriety means the self is transformed — is transforming the self not investigating things? The world returning to benevolence is a scene of peace beyond compare; this is called things investigated. Question: how are rectifying the mind and extending knowing distinguished? Answer: rectifying the mind is the four prohibitions: first cutting off all that is contrary to propriety in seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting. But it can only cultivate the person and rectify oneself; it cannot transform things. If extending knowing lies solely in investigating things, then one reaches others, and its merit is the greatest; hence the Great Learning places weight on extending knowing. Question: what is the purport of the sequence of investigating things and things investigated? Answer: in the preceding eight matters the character 'first' is used, and the weight altogether falls on the last, extending knowing, which speaks of the work. Now, speaking from things investigated up to bringing peace to the world, the character 'after' is used, and this too raises the character 'knowing,' to show that the seven matters that follow are all the effects of the character 'knowing.' The student must fix his eye on this character 'knowing.' What was said above, that extending knowing and investigating things means responding to things so as to reach one's knowing, uses the investigate of responsive investigation; and what is now said, that when things are investigated the knowing then arrives, means using things to verify the substance of knowing. The meaning is that if those things have even one hair that is not dissolved, then knowing has not reached the utmost; only when things are wholly dissolved is this true knowing brought to its utmost. Thus the investigate of things investigated is the investigate of coming to investigate — the investigate of what is called the coming of the spirits — and is precisely the meaning of the world returning to benevolence. That all things come to investigate is then the effect of knowing. Therefore, with investigating things and things investigated, the student must seek clarity. If all things have come to investigate, then one investigates all the way along until the world is at peace before letting go. The sage's intent is luminously clear; it is only that one must put forth true work before the outcome is seen. Question: from the Son of Heaven down to the common people, all alike take cultivating the person as the root. Since it was said there is only the one character 'knowing,' why does it return to cultivating the person? Answer: if one did not begin the work from cultivating the person, one would not be doing it in empty space. Hence the sage clearly showed you: overcome oneself and return to propriety, and the world returns to benevolence. For the self is one's own person, the thing closest to me, unlike outer things. Overcoming oneself means that in extending knowing I first extend it to the one thing that is my own person. If one investigates this thing that is oneself, and afterward investigates heaven, earth, and the myriad things, what difficulty is there? Hence it is altogether said that cultivating the person is the root. Question: investigate has three meanings: grappling opposition, responsive investigation, and coming to investigate. Answer: the three meanings all issue from one person. Pray let me make it clear by simile. Formerly the wife of Qi Liang was a good weeper. When her husband died she wept for him. At first, when she wept, the neighbors hated the sound and disliked the person, so that hearing her weep they covered their ears and seeing her they shut their eyes, because her weeping was unlike the weeping of others. Yet she did not stop weeping because the neighbors hated and disliked her. After she had wept a long time, the neighbors without realizing it grieved with her and wept too; and weeping, they forgot their dislike. Once dislike was forgotten, their minds turned to pity her. Nor did she stop weeping because they pitied her, but wept on without cease; and after long, everyone in the whole lane was a good weeper. When everyone was a good weeper, they forgot their grief and no longer noticed that anyone was weeping. When everyone weeps well and weeps long, the whole lane makes a custom of it; and once the custom is formed, everyone says he can weep himself. When everyone can weep himself, they look on the wife of Qi Liang as an ordinary woman, no different from themselves, and go about with her in close familiarity, and all is forgotten. Now the wife of Qi Liang wept not for her husband but for her heaven. Heaven is what she depended on all her life; losing it, she could not but weep. Her grief was the regret of a whole heaven. Knowing that heaven would not spare her, her weeping also would not cease; how could it cease because people disliked it? Even if everyone in the whole lane had asked her day after day, her weeping would only be more sorrowful. It was by no means that she meant to have people pity her; how could questioning stop her? Even with a blade before her and a cauldron behind, threatening to stop her, it could not be done. Why? Because beyond this heaven there was nothing to weep for. That at first people hated her was because the pain of her weeping was utterly unlike others': this is grappling opposition. That after long weeping everyone was in pain was because the pain of her weeping cut into people's minds, so that everyone was in pain for himself and not in pain for Qi Liang: this is responsive investigation. And when after long the whole lane became good at weeping until it was a custom, they no longer knew that the pain of weeping came from Qi Liang, and instead looked on the wife of Liang as simply one of themselves: this is coming to investigate. These words, though small, may illustrate great matters.

This is the Resolving of Doubts on the Outline of the Great Learning written by Master Hanshan. The Master dwelt at Caoxi, and scholars with tablets and robes often came with their brushes to ask about the Way. The Master manifested the body of a candidate and taught the Dharma. This year, passing through Wumen, he showed it to Qian Qianyi and said: this old man's playful brush still has a child's heart in it; it is after all not a matter beneath the patched robe. What do you say? I, Qianyi, have heard that Zhang Zishao in his youth studied under Guishan and caught a glimpse of the unarisen middle; and when he came to Jingshan, he was questioned and struck on the purport of investigating things and things investigated, and at once received its subtle meaning. Those who in the late Song were praised for moral integrity all put Zishao first. Seen from today, Zishao's bold arguments at the imperial lecture mat and his late banishment to Hengpu, where he held his book and stood leaning with his legs crossed in hiding — his youthful integrity appears like a goose's footprint in snow and mud. Had he not attained something deep from Jingshan, could he have been so? Those who play Zishao today have different vows, but in proclaiming the right Dharma by means of worldly truth they are one. Bian Que, hearing that the people of Qin loved little children, became a physician of little children. The world today esteems candidates; hence the Master manifests the body of a candidate and teaches the Dharma. How can this be called not a matter beneath the patched robe? Zishao once said: whenever I hear the causes and conditions raised by old man Jingshan, it is like a thousand gates and ten thousand doors opening at a single step. If candidates today can contemplate in this way, the Master's vajra eye will be pointed out one by one from the tip of his brush.
Reverently inscribed with incense by the Yushan silk-capped disciple Qian Qianyi in the fourth month of the dingsi year of Wanli
The Dream-Roaming Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Scroll Forty-Five

blocks.text: A Treatise on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi

inline.s: Statement of Intent

The patriarchs of the Western Regions composed treatises to break the non-Buddhists' attachments, and they had to be well versed in their own and others' schools. From ancient times the masters of the sutras and treatises in this land have all been well versed in their own and others' schools; but the last students of our school rest content in their narrow ignorance, are blind to the sameness of substance, look on other teachings as alien things, and cannot interpenetrate the teachings and contemplations, so that they find it hard to benefit the worldly. As for those of initial faith who cannot deeply exhaust the scriptural canon, they suffer from the fragmentation of names and marks and find it hard to comprehend; and as for those who are passionately fond of Laozi and Zhuangzi as a reservoir of style, when it comes to the destination of their words, none fails to gaze at the ocean and sigh. Then, looking at the various commentaries, each follows its own view and is hard to reconcile. And when one sees the Oral Meaning and the Supplementary Ink deeply citing Buddhist sutras, so that every phrase hits the mark, and even saying that the whole great canon issued from this, while the deluded take it as certainly so — one is deeply moved to sigh. Dwelling by the sea, in the leisure left by dry sitting, as I read through the Śūraṅgama and the Lotus, there were those who asked for instruction on the purport of Laozi and Zhuangzi; so the matter ramified to this, and I settled it for myself — not daring to seek understanding from a true man or to make of it a thesis that must be so. Moreover I sigh that those who from ancient times have defended the teaching and broken the enemy mostly dispensed medicine yet seldom opened up the sickness that lies beneath the heart and diaphragm: not that they did not apply it wondrously, but that they had not felt the pulse of the source of the illness. Therefore I have sealed and settled it with the contemplation of mind-only consciousness, like a maṇi jewel's perfect illumination in which the five colors are vividly distinct, like an empty valley transmitting sound to which every echo responds. If one contemplates all dharmas by mind-only consciousness, then they of themselves do not go beyond shadow and echo. Hence the treatise is named after this.
On the Source of the Teachings

I have observed that when the hundred crafts and arts of the world reach their utmost refinement and attain the wondrous, it cannot be transmitted in words; and those who imitate it cannot obtain it in words either. How much less can the wonder of the great Way be conveyed by mouth and ear, by language and letters? It lies in the wonder of the mind's awakening. Thus not only does Chan value wondrous awakening; even worldly cleverness and dialectical acuity, the language of governing the world, and the means of livelihood — there is no single dharma whose wonder is attained without awakening, and what is wondrous cannot be reached by words. Hence when our Buddha, the sage, taught the Lotus he discoursed purely on the true mark; and as for the wondrous dharma, he did not set forth a single word, saying only 'thus.' As for those who awaken to the wondrous dharma, he said only that one who teaches well — the language of governing the world and the means of livelihood and so forth — all accord with the right Dharma. And the sage of the fifth ground in the Avataṃsaka is well able to penetrate the learning of the world; as for yin-yang, the arts of number, charts and writings, seals and tallies, medical prescriptions and verse — there is nothing he does not master. Only then can one enter the world to benefit beings. Hence the great being of Equal Enlightenment manifests forms throughout the ten realms: according to what body and what dharma ought to be used for deliverance, he manifests that body and that dharma and delivers them. Seen in this light, is the Buddha-Dharma utterly without worldly truth, and is worldly truth wholly other than Buddha-Dharma? It is only that people do not awaken to the wonder of the great Way and so draw for themselves the difference of inner and outer. Is the Way really so? I privately observe that those who from ancient times to the present fence off the Way say of this one, 'he is a non-Buddhist,' and of that one, 'he is a heretic.' Seen broadly, they are like prizing and disdaining puppets, drawing boundaries across the great void, or judging the sun and moon by right and wrong. All of them fail to awaken to the wonder of their own minds and merely add to their idle disputation. For the sages of old were nothing else: they were simply those who had awakened to the wonder of mind. All their words and teachings flowed out from the mind of wondrous awakening and were shown according to capacity, shallow or deep. Hence it is said: nothing does not flow from this Dharma-realm; nothing does not return to this Dharma-realm. Therefore, if we do not awaken to our own minds we do not know the mind of the sages; and not knowing the mind of the sages, to imitate the words of the sages is like a player's joy and sorrow: though he rejoices he does not rejoice, though he grieves he does not grieve, for the joy and grief do not come from what he has himself. That joy and grief do not come from oneself yet one takes them as one's own — this I see in those who explain the sages' words.
On the Dharma of Mind

In youth I took Confucius as my teacher without knowing Confucius; I took Laozi as my teacher without knowing Laozi. When grown, I took the Buddha as my teacher without knowing the Buddha. Then I withdrew into the deep mountains and great marshes, practicing stillness to contemplate the mind. Thereby I came to know that the three realms are mind-only and the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. Since it is the contemplation of mind-only consciousness, then every form is the shadow of mind, and every sound is the echo of mind. Thus all sages are the tips of shadows, and all words and teachings are the smooth echoes. Because the myriad dharmas are manifested by mind alone, the language of governing the world and the means of livelihood all accord with the right Dharma. Because outside the mind there are no dharmas, every dharma is true; only the deluded cling to them so that they are not wondrous. If one awakens to one's own mind, then no dharma is not wondrous; mind and dharmas are both wondrous. Only the sage can do this.
On Acceptance and Rejection

Our Buddha's sutras all come from the Western Regions and are all from translation. The coming of the sutras began in the Han and became greatly flourishing only in the Western Jin. Among the translators of Jin, Kumārajīva alone is accounted foremost, and his disciples, the four masters Sengzhao, Daosheng, Daorong, and Sengrui, were the unicorns and phoenixes among monks, yet Kumārajīva could employ them. Of Sengzhao, however, Kumārajīva also said: in understanding I do not yield to you; in letters we must bow to each other. For Sengzhao was especially skilled in Laozi and Zhuangzi. Yet the Buddhist sutras all came from the golden mouth's proclamation, and when they reached this land their language was often dissimilar, with some sutras having several translations, so that the shallow-minded doubted. They did not know that the principle is in truth without error; the language lies in the skill or clumsiness of the translator. Hence in the canon, whatever came from Kumārajīva's hand is elegant in style, because he had the four sages at his side. Thus the Lotus is deep in principle and dense in phrasing, exhausting its wonder in every turn without depending on words; and the Vimalakīrti has a style that is graceful and grave, so that its principle is self-evident. As for Sengzhao's four treatises, they are seamless and whole; without the eye of the right Dharma one can by no means understand them. Hence the deluded criticize them, taking them as the reckless talk of the emptiness school and Laozi and Zhuangzi — which is fitting enough for them. The state preceptor Qingliang was a bodhisattva of the Avataṃsaka; when he composed his commentary on the Avataṃsaka he always cited Sengzhao's treatises, and always said 'Master Zhao,' honoring him. I have privately discussed this: if Sengzhao's views were incorrect, how could Kumārajīva have suffered him in the assembly? If Kumārajīva's eye were not clear, how could his translations be honored? If Sengzhao's treatises were not canonical, how could Qingliang have suffered them in his mouth? Through the ages there have been many doubts, yet none has gone as far as this. Why? When we look at the Avataṃsaka commentary, it cites the words of Laozi and Zhuangzi very abundantly, saying: take their style, not their meaning. Guifeng, however, said the two masters cannot trace man to his source, and the Mirror of the School refutes them even more pointedly. Yet all these masters were response-body great beings who raised the great Dharma-banner; why is their acceptance and rejection so at odds? Let me try to discuss it: perhaps each had his own emphasis. For the language of the Western Regions is plain and unadorned and moreover full of repetitions; and where a translator's learning is not good in both languages, the style is often crude and greatly burdens the principle. Now the words of the sages of China, apart from the Five Classics which are bound to the world's teaching, that carry the Way are only the single book of Laozi. But Laozi's words are ancient and terse, deeply hidden and hard to understand, and the one who unfolds the Way of Laozi is Zhuangzi alone. Master Jiao said: Laozi has Zhuangzi as Confucius has Mencius; these words are trustworthy. Yet Confucius called Laozi a dragon; if one met Zhuangzi through Mencius, would one not face him as a disciple? I have sometimes privately said that in China, from the sages down through all ages, those who bear a transcendent view, apart from Laozi, are Zhuangzi alone; and words that carry the Way, vast and free, apart from the Buddhist sutras, among all the philosophers and hundred schools, those that exhaust the study of heaven and man are the single book of Zhuangzi alone. If China had not had this man, through ten thousand ages none would know there is a true man; if China had not had this book, through ten thousand ages none would know there are wondrous discourses. For our Buddha-Dharma is vast and subtle, and translators used perilous phrasing to carry it, so that the principle must be deep and hidden — as in the Laṅkāvatāra. Hence Kumārajīva's translations are accounted foremost because he had the four sages as his support. The state preceptor's saying, 'take their style, not their meaning,' has its reason. If this land had produced words surpassing Laozi and Zhuangzi, Sengzhao would certainly have set them aside. Seen in this light, Sengzhao's use of their style in his treatises and commentaries is because Sengzhao took the Lotus as his school: what is called the good teacher of Dharma, the language of worldly truth, the means of livelihood and so forth, all accord with the right Dharma — the doing of one who has deeply penetrated the true mark. As for Guifeng's slighting and the Mirror of the School's distancing them: Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals, borrowing the command of the heavenly king to carry out reward and punishment; these two masters wielded the authority of the Dharma-king to carry out praise and blame. Qingliang, however, interfused the whole Dharma-realm, having nothing that could not be and nothing that must be; hence he accepted and did not accept. Each had his own emphasis. Hence in the Lotus I see Avalokiteśvara's thirty-two responses, where it says that one who ought to be delivered in the body of a brahmin is shown that body and taught the Dharma; and as for the two sons of Wondrous Adornment, it says your father believed and accepted non-Buddhists and was deeply attached to brahminical dharmas, and the two sons too repented of being born into this house of wrong views. For Laozi and Zhuangzi in this land are of the same kind as the brahmins of the Western Regions. Yet here the Buddha first manifests a body to teach the Dharma and then at once denounces it as the wrong view of non-Buddhists — why? It lies in attachment or non-attachment. Because Avalokiteśvara is perfect and unobstructed, he may manifest a body and teach the Dharma; because Wondrous Adornment was deeply attached, it became the wrong view of non-Buddhists. Hence when the sage teaches people he breaks only their attachment, not their dharma. Therefore all who cling to sound, form, and marks are not of right view.
On Learning and Inquiry

I often see students reading sutras and commentaries, and when they suddenly run into a citation from the philosophers or histories, it is like a tiger blocking the road: they are sure to start back in alarm. And when one teaches them to become familiar with it, they say, that is the talk of an outsider — and turn their heads away. I have also seen gentlemen who take up the words of Zhuangzi and must cite Buddhist words as a mirror, or when a phrase hits the mark, say that the whole great Buddhist canon issued from this. Alas! Can this be called thorough understanding? Weigh these two: to study Buddhism without understanding the hundred schools is not only not to know this dharma but also not to know the Buddha-Dharma; and to explain Zhuangzi while claiming to exhaust the Buddhist sutras is not only not to know the Buddha's intent but also not to know Zhuangzi's intent. This is why it is hard to understand. Hence it is said: one who looks at the small from the great does not see it all; one who looks at the great from the small does not see it clearly. I have often exhorted myself with three matters: not knowing the Spring and Autumn Annals, one cannot engage the world; not knowing Laozi and Zhuangzi, one cannot forget the world; not practicing Chan, one cannot transcend the world. Know this, and one may speak of learning.
On the Vehicles of the Teaching

Someone asked: the sages of the three teachings are originally one principle — is this really so? The answer: if one contemplates by the three realms being mind-only and the myriad dharmas consciousness-only, then not only are the three teachings originally one principle; there is not one matter or one dharma that is not established from this mind. If one contemplates by the equal Dharma-realm, then not only are the three sages originally one substance; there is not one person or one thing that is not manifested by the sovereign power of Vairocana's ocean-seal samādhi. Hence it is said: not destroying marks yet arising dependently, defilement and purity are ever distinct; not renouncing conditions yet being just true, sage and ordinary are equal. Only in what is set up is there the difference of the perfect and interfused versus the progressive, of person and dharma, provisional and real. The perfect and interfused means that all dharmas are but the one mind, with defilement and purity fused and penetrating, without obstruction or hindrance. The progressive means that the ten realms, five vehicles, and five teachings differ in shallow and deep, in principle and practice, cause and fruit. The ten realms are the four sagehoods and six ordinary destinies. The five teachings are the small, the initial, the final, the sudden, and the perfect. The five vehicles are gods and humans, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; the Buddha is the supreme One Vehicle. Yet each of these five vehicles has its own cultivation and advance, its cause and fruit, its ranks and degrees, orderly and without confusion. What is called the human is one between heaven above and earth below, within the four seas, ruled by a sovereign; the root of his cultivation is the five precepts. What is called the god is the gods of the desire realm, ruled by Indra; the root of their cultivation is the ten virtues of the highest grade; the gods of the form realm, ruled by Brahmā, and the gods of the formless realm, sustained by empty samādhi, have as the root of their cultivation the ten virtues of the highest grade together with out-flowing dhyāna and the nine successive absorptions — these two are the causes and fruits within the realm. What the śrāvaka cultivates has the four truths as its root; what the pratyekabuddha cultivates has the twelve links of dependent origination as its root; what the bodhisattva cultivates has the six pāramitās as its root — these three are the causes and fruits beyond the realm. The Buddha perfectly awakens to the one mind and wondrously accords with the three virtues; gathered, they are one, hence the perfect and interfused; scattered, they are five, hence the progressive. This purport is fully recorded in the sutras. Seen in this light, the dharmas of the five vehicles are all Buddha-Dharma, and the practices of the five vehicles are all Buddha-practice; it is simply because living beings' faculties are of greater or lesser size that the sage sets up teachings of shallow and deep, all of it responsive setting-up — what is meant by teaching not overstepping the ranks. From this one knows that Confucius is the sage of the human vehicle, and so he serves Heaven to govern humans; Laozi is the sage of the heavenly vehicle, and so is pure and desireless, leaving the human and entering the heaven. The śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are sages transcending gods and humans, and so rise above the three realms and pass far beyond the four kinds of birth, abandoning gods and humans and not entering them. The bodhisattva is the sage transcending the Two Vehicles, and so leaves gods and humans and enters gods and humans, coming and going in the three realms and saving the four kinds of birth, emerging from the real and entering the conventional. The Buddha is the sage transcending sage and ordinary, and so can be sage and can be ordinary: among gods he is a god, among humans a human, and even among other kinds he divides his form, entering everywhere. Moreover, one who can be sage and can be ordinary — how could sage or ordinary be able to do that? Observed in truth, nothing is not Buddha-Dharma and none of the three teachings is not a sage; whether person or dharma, all belong to the one mind; whether matter or principle, there is no obstruction or hindrance. This is named Buddha. Hence the perfect and interfused does not obstruct the progressive, and the ten realms are manifold; the progressive does not obstruct the perfect and interfused, and the one limit is equal — what division of this and that or dispute of right and wrong could there then be? Hence it is said: whether in the language of the borderlands or in the language of custom, one teaches the four truths. Gods and humans teach the four truths according to custom. Were those two sages not two men secretly sent by our Buddha to be forerunners of the Buddha-Dharma? Thus both the persons and the dharmas are provisional. It is simply that at the gate of establishing transformation one does not destroy the marks of cause and fruit; the learning of the three teachings all guards the student's mind, reaching the deep by way of the shallow and the far by way of the near. Therefore Confucius wished people not to behave as tigers, wolves, birds, and beasts; hence he drew them with benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, for the time being causing them to abandon evil and follow good, to go from being a thing to being a human. He cultivated the teaching of the former kings, made clear the authority of reward and punishment, composed the Spring and Autumn Annals to clarify the traces of order and disorder, rectified people's minds, settled high and low, established the distinctions of ruler and minister, father and son, and fixed the norms of human relations. His methods were strict, his teaching urgent, close to human feeling and easy to practice. But at a time when human desire runs wild, even he, pressing on, found it hard. In my view, had China not had Master Kong, few would have escaped being barbarians or beasts. Yet the traces of Master Kong are indeed thus; was his mind wholly so? Moreover he plainly said: do not be willful, do not be insistent, do not be obstinate, do not be self-centered. Consider his mind of saving the world: was he not one who taught the dharma of governing the world in reliance on the bodhisattva vehicle? That the sutras call him the Youthful Scholar has good reason. But students do not see the sage's mind and think his Way was no more than this; hence they cling to the traces of the former kings to hang up fame and profit, hardening the attachment to self, loosing greed and desire as the burden of life, until some take benevolence and righteousness as capital for robbery and open the calamity of war. Therefore Laozi pitied them, saying: this is the fault of honoring the sages and using cleverness. If one cuts off sagacity and discards cleverness, the people will benefit a hundredfold; if one breaks the measures and snaps the scales, the people will not contend. The harm of greed and desire is extreme. Hence he said: do not display what is desirable, and the mind will not be disordered. Therefore his teaching is to leave desire and be pure, to hold the mind with stillness and stability, not to busy oneself with things, to be tranquil and do nothing — this is the practice of heaven. He causes people to learn this, to leave the human and enter the heaven. Because his words are deep and profound, students find them hard to understand; hence Zhuangzi arose and greatly unfolded them. Because people's clinging is deep, his words were also urgent. As for slandering Yao and Shun and belittling Tang and Wu, these are not grand words but the meaning of cutting off sagacity and discarding cleverness. As for pushing governance back to high antiquity and the Way beyond Fuxi, these are not idle talk but the strongest statement of the harm of doing. As for reviling Confucius, it is not reviling Confucius but reviling those who study Confucius' traces; and moreover they are not literal words but words that break clinging. Hence it is said: nine in ten are fables, seven in ten are repeated words. He denounced teaching and urged separation, destroying form and obliterating cleverness, the intent being to cause people to leave the human and enter the heaven and to remove the burden of greed and desire. As for finely investigating the ways of the world and exhaustively rendering human feeling, breaking the stronghold of the attachment to self and removing the great boundary of human life, with fables spreading out and analogies marshaled in words, incisive and clear, subtle and mysterious, deep and unfathomable — this is one who teaches the dharma of gods and humans and possesses unobstructed eloquence. Is he not one who manifests the body of a brahmin and teaches the Dharma? How is his play so vast? He winnows the dusty world like chaff, sees birth and death as illusion, releases the burden of things, and roams free and easy — how great was his measure of transcendence! I have said that after the usurpations of the five feudal lords, when the unconcerned scholars voiced their arguments across the board and benevolence and righteousness were choked as a road, had not Master Meng arisen and greatly refuted them, the world and later ages would, I think, have worn their garments to the left. In the fury of the many heroes devouring one another, the whole world was dizzy and dim, perishing in things, and many raced after the fire of desire without returning; had this old man not leapt up and bared his arms among them, later ages, even with lofty and pure scholars, would not have known that caps and chariots are fetters. Weighing his merit in saving the world, how great was it? Now his work enters through stillness and stability, and his writing issues from samādhi; but later men peer at the man through the view of one bend and read his book with turbid, disordered minds, so that they are blank and do not know where it tends. If one does not see his mind but observes his words, it is fitting that one is alarmed and does not enter. Moreover he too said: after ten thousand ages, if one meets a great sage who understands his meaning, it will be as a meeting of morning and evening. And that great sage he sought — if not the Buddha, who else? If one takes him as the vanguard of our Buddha in breaking clinging, these words are trustworthy. People of the world do not even enter him; how could they enter the Buddha-Dharma?
On Practice

In our teaching the progressive practices of the five vehicles, though their activities differ, all take calm abiding and insight as the root of cultivating the mind. Hence the calm abiding and insight of our teaching include the Great Vehicle, the Small Vehicle, and the human and heavenly vehicles: the four dhyānas and eight absorptions, and the nine penetrations and clear dhyānas. Confucius also said: knowing where to rest, and then there is stability; and again: from sincerity, clarity. This is the human vehicle's calm abiding and insight. Laozi said: constantly without desire, one contemplates its wonder; constantly with desire, one contemplates its confines. And again: the myriad things all arise together, and I contemplate their return. Zhuangzi also said: nothing is better than clarity; and again: the sage does not go by it but illumines by heaven; and again: no one mirrors himself in running water but in still water; only stillness can still the stillness of others; and again: the great stability holds it. As for the hundred bones and nine openings all complete and present, whom shall I take as kin? And again: all take it for themselves; who then is the angry one? As for the Yellow Emperor's retirement, Yan Hui's fasting of the mind, the old man's catching of the cicada, and Confucius' discourse on dream and waking — these are all works of stillness and stability, releasing form and discarding cleverness, leaving desire and being pure. This is what is meant by loathing the coarse obstruction below and delighting in the pure, wondrous, and separated above, hoping to leave the human and enter the heaven. According to what the teachings make clear, this is one who abandons birth in the desire realm and is born in the first dhyāna. Hence it is said: he whose stability is vast and firm gives forth the light of heaven. This is the heavenly vehicle's calm abiding and insight. The Śūraṃgama says: all in the world who cultivate the mind, if the stain of craving is not produced, do not remain in the desire realm; such a person at a single thought becomes a companion of Brahmā. Again it says: when the habit of desire is removed and the mind free of desire appears, such a person in that hour can practice Brahmā's virtue and is named Brahmā's minister. Again: with pure prohibitions and precepts, together with clear awakening, such a person in that hour can command the hosts of Brahmā and be the great Brahmā king. Again: these three superior classes cannot be pressed by any affliction; though it is not the true cultivation of the true samādhi, in the pure mind the outflows do not stir, and it is named the first dhyāna. As for clarifying the mind until it does not move, limpid and still yet giving forth light, doubling and redoubling its excellence through the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, until subtle seeing appears before one and one molds and casts without obstruction, until one exhausts the ultimate of the group and fathoms the nature of form, entering the boundless and being named the summit of form — this is their realization. Seen in this light, the learning of Laozi, if it says the greatest calamity is none other than having a body, and so extinguishes the body to return to nothing, and that none wearies the form more than having cleverness, and so releases cleverness to sink into emptiness — this resembles the Two Vehicles. Moreover, born in a world without a Buddha, observing transformation and knowing nothingness, he resembles the solitary realizer. His fundamental tenet, emptiness and spontaneity, belongs to the non-Buddhists; but his mind of compassion in saving the world, with gods and humans both returning to him and existence and nonexistence both illumined, again resembles a bodhisattva. Spoken provisionally, he is precisely one who manifests the body of a brahmin and teaches the Dharma. Judged in truth, he is one of the human and heavenly vehicles who finely cultivates the pure life and enters empty samādhi. The reason he can save the world is that the great Brahmā king is the lord of the Sahā world, commanding the world, teaching the ten virtues and saving living beings. According to the Avataṃsaka, the bodhisattva on the grounds is a great Brahmā king, and his Brahmā hosts are all true practitioners among gods and humans, those who cultivate the heavenly practice from the human vehicle; of this kind is he. There is no doubt. Hence I say: the words of Zhuangzi exhaust purely the relation of heaven and man; they are not reckless talk.
On the Basis of Practice

It is from the one mind that the images of the ten realms appear; thus the four sagehoods and six ordinary destinies are all projections of the one mind. How could it be so only for gods and humans? Tracing the ranks of cultivation, they are in truth established from the human vehicle; hence one knows that the human is the root of ordinary being and sage. Therefore Pei Xiu said: ghosts and spirits sink in the suffering of dark sorrow, birds and beasts harbor the grief of fear and flight, the asuras rage, the gods indulge in pleasure; only the human path can order the mind and aspire to bodhi. Seen in this light, apart from the human path there is no way to establish Buddha-Dharma, and apart from Buddha-Dharma there is no way to exhaust the one mind. Thus Buddha-Dharma takes the human path as its foundation, and the human path takes Buddha-Dharma as its ultimate. Hence it is said: what bodhi takes as its object is suffering living beings; if there were no living beings there would be no bodhi. This is what that means. What is called the human path is the relation between ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, and the ordinary affairs of daily life. If ruler is ruler, minister minister, father father, son son, without scheming and without knowing, without greed and without contention, like conjured people, then this is all the superior good people gathering in one place, and this very world is a land of ultimate bliss. What need would there be of sages? Yet human beings are born of craving and die of craving, and their birth, death, and craving are wealth, beauty, fame, food, and sleep. From these five arise greedy, craving minds and the calamity of warring and contention, until ruler is not ruler, minister not minister, father not father, son not son; though the former kings' rewards and punishments were not enough to restrain their minds, they merely satisfied their own insatiable desires and bound up the immeasurable suffering of the future. Therefore our Buddha pitied them, saying: of the causes of all suffering, craving is the root; if craving is extinguished, there is nothing to depend on. Hence he manifested his body in the three realms, sharing the afflictions of the people, and taught the essential path of leaving desire and escaping suffering. And the reason he did not dwell in heaven but was born among humans is precisely to show that the marks of cause and fruit throughout the ten realms are all established from the human path. Since one dwells in the human path, one cannot but know the human path. Hence our Buddha, the sage, did not arise from empty space but took the pure Brahmā as his father and Māyā as his mother, showing that he had ruler and kin; took Yaśodharā as his wife, showing that he had husband and wife; took Rāhula as his son, showing that he had father and son. And he had to leave father and mother and go forth from home — not that he had no ruler or kin, but that he cut off the love of ruler and kin; he cast aside the glory of the state without a backward look, showing that fame and profit are a burden; he threw down wife and child and went far from them, showing the harm of craving; he entered the deep mountains and practiced austerities, showing the practice of leaving desire; he first studied the non-Buddhists' four spheres of totality, showing the leaving of the human and entering the heaven; and he abandoned these and realized the path of universal and perfect enlightenment, showing that the practices of gods and humans are not to be prized. After becoming Buddha he entered the royal palace and raised his father's coffin, and ascended to Trāyastriṃśa to teach the Dharma for his mother, showing that the Buddha-way does not abandon the way of filial piety; he taught the Dharma in dependence on the human world, showing that the human path easily aspires to bodhi; he took kings and ministers as outer protectors, showing that one who dwells in the world does not transcend the ways of the world. These are the models of our great master's manifestation in saving beings, the great norm handed down to later ages. Alas! We who are disciples of the Buddha do not know our Buddha's mind; dwelling in the human world we do not know the affairs of human relations. Discuss Buddha-Dharma with us and we are muddled about true suchness and hazy about Buddha-nature; discuss worldly dharmas with us and we are walled in by every matter, nearly like blockheads; discuss the vehicles of the teaching with us and we say these are branches and leaves, not worth esteeming; speak to us of the six pāramitās and we say the bodhisattva's practice is not something we dare to do; speak to us of the four truths and we say that is the Small Vehicle, not worth doing; speak to us of the four dhyānas and eight absorptions and we say that is what non-Buddhists practice, not worth mentioning; speak to us of the human path and we are utterly blank about the distinctions of ruler and minister, father and son, and the practices of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom. Alas! We do not know what manner of thing we are. Yet we love the high and long for the far, always borrowing from mouth and ear, never knowing that our Buddha saves people and takes them out of the world with the practice of leaving desire as the first of all. Hence it is said: freedom from desire and quiescence is foremost of all. Because I was born on the human path and do not go beyond the human vehicle, in youth I took Confucius as my teacher, knowing that human desire is the root of all suffering. Resolved on the practice of leaving desire, in youth I took Laozi and Zhuangzi as my teachers, contemplating the three realms as mind-only and the myriad dharmas as consciousness-only, and knowing that the ten realms are the projections of mind alone. Therefore I take refuge in the Buddha.
On the Tenet and Tendency

What Laozi takes as his tenet, the great Way of emptiness and nothingness, is precisely what the Śūraṃgama calls the dark and murky emptiness, the luminous essence of the eighth consciousness. For we have deluded this wondrous luminous one mind and made it the eighth ālaya-consciousness; in dependence on this there are the seventh consciousness as the root of birth and death and the sixth as the root of creating karma, transforming and giving rise to the marks of birth and death in faculty-body and world. Thus the sages and ordinary beings of the ten realms all alike do not depart from this consciousness; there is only the difference of broken or unbroken clinging, defilement or purity.
