Because the ordinary being of the desire realm does not know that the realms of the six dusts and five desires are only consciousness-transformations, he relies on the discriminations of the sixth consciousness, gives rise to greedy, craving minds, and clings stubbornly without letting go, creating all kinds of karma and receiving all kinds of suffering — what is called human desire running wild. Hence Confucius set up benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom as a dike and defense, causing thought to be without depravity and for the time being making people abandon evil and follow good; as for fixing names and ranks and rectifying high and low, his Way does not depart from discrimination. Even the works of stillness and stability he speaks of, verified by consciousness-only, are but the severing of the discriminating, depraved, and deluded thoughts of the first six consciousnesses, so as to remove the harm of contention; and what he ultimately returns to as the wondrous Way takes the seventh consciousness as its place of return — what is called the source of the living impulse, the origin of the Way. Hence it is said: generation upon generation is called the Yi. As for Laozi, who takes emptiness and nothingness as the wondrous Way, he says the valley-spirit does not die, and again that one who dies yet is not destroyed is long-lived, and again that what generates generation does not generate. Moreover his teaching takes cutting off sagacity and discarding cleverness and forgetting form and removing desire as its practice, and takes non-doing as its ultimate tenet. This is a step further than Confucius: he observes the deep pulse of the living impulse, breaks the clinging of discrimination of the first six consciousnesses, subdues the mechanism of arising and ceasing of the first seven consciousnesses, and recognizes the luminous essence of the eighth consciousness — what the Śūraṃgama calls the image-less emptiness, the subtle and refined imagining — taking it as the source of the wondrous Way. Hence he says: dim and vague, within it there is an image; vague and dim, within it there is a thing. Because this consciousness is the whole of ignorance and cannot be seen through by contemplation, he says: remote and dark, within it there is an essence. Because this consciousness-substance perfumes inconceivably and transforms inconceivably, he says: mystery upon mystery, and calls it the wondrous Way. Because heaven, earth, and the myriad things are all manifested from within it, he says: the root of heaven and earth, the gate of all wonders. Not knowing why it is so and yet it is so, Zhuangzi calls it spontaneity. Moreover Laozi was a man of China who had not seen the Buddha-Dharma, and yet his deep observation reached this far; one may call him swift and sharp of faculty. Had he once seen our Buddha and had it sealed and settled, would he not have suddenly realized the true unborn? My thought is that his journey west across the shifting sands was not without meaning. On the whole, this consciousness is deep, hidden, and hard to fathom. When the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world, the ninety-six kinds in the Western Regions took the six masters as their heads; their theses numbered a hundred or more, and there were very many who attained spiritual powers, and their books were more than the Laozi and Zhuangzi of this land. When our Buddha appeared in the world, at the assembly on Vulture Peak the outstanding men were all followers of those six masters. Yet when they saw the Buddha, some awakened without a single word, like a good horse going at the shadow of the whip — was it not that their former practice counted for something, but that the mind of false clinging was not yet forgotten? Hence their seeing the Buddha now was only a matter of a touch that transforms, to break their clinging. Therefore the Buddha's teaching of the Dharma had no redundant words but simply struck and broke them according to the clinging sentiment of living beings, what is called using a wedge to remove a wedge; fundamentally he gave no real dharma to anyone. As for the Śūraṃgama assembly, where he peeled away subtly and disputed in sequence to break the clinging to causality and spontaneity and to cut off the doubts of ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and the Two Vehicles — those who read the teachings do not examine this and merely say, that was a man of the Western Regions; this is a man of the Eastern land. If there is this and that among persons, can the Buddha-nature have two? Moreover our Buddha is the teacher of the three realms and the father of the four kinds of birth; would he teach the Dharma only for the people of that region and have no share at all for those a hundred thousand li away? Yet all living beings, in dependence on the eighth consciousness, have the clinging sentiment of birth and death and hardened self-attachment: is it only the living beings of that region who have clinging and the living beings of this region who have none? Thus this eighth consciousness, the non-Buddhists either cling to it as the dark truth, or as spontaneity, or as causality, or as the spirit-self; and cultivating the mind by stability they are born in the Brahmā heaven and cling to it as the five present nirvāṇas. Or they exhaust emptiness and do not return, entering the formless heaven, subduing the living mechanism of the first seven consciousnesses so that it does not move, and advancing in the contemplation of the nature of consciousness to the sphere of boundless space, the sphere of nothing whatsoever, and up to the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. This is cultivating the mind within the realm without departing from the nature of consciousness. Hence it is said: the student of the Way does not know the true and only recognizes the spirit of consciousness from former times; the root of birth and death through immeasurable kalpas, the fool takes as the original self. This is that. As for the śrāvakas beyond the realm, they have already extinguished the delusions of view and thought in the three realms, already cut off the suffering of birth and death in the three realms, and already realized the bliss of unconditioned quiescence; they do not even know the name of the eighth consciousness, and yet they too take it for nirvāṇa and suppose it the place of ultimate refuge. Moreover they were personally delivered by the Buddha's teaching, and yet it cost our Buddha forty years of rebuke and winnowing; and at the Lotus assembly they still doubted the Buddha's intent, thinking they were saved by the Small Vehicle. Even the bodhisattva on the grounds, having ascended to the seventh ground, only then abandons this consciousness, and still the ripened consciousness is not empty. Seen in this light, the eighth consciousness is the root of birth and death — how could it be shallow? Hence it is said: all in the world who cultivate the path and cannot accomplish supreme bodhi, and even become śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, or become non-Buddhists, gods, Māra kings, and Māra's retinues, all do so because they do not know the two roots. The first is the beginningless root of birth and death: namely that you and all living beings take the grasping mind as your self-nature. The second is the beginningless nirvāṇa, the original pure substance: namely that your essence of consciousness, originally luminous, can produce all conditions and is what conditions leave behind. This is precisely what that means. Ah! Laozi was born into the human world and appeared in a world without a Buddha, and yet he could exhaust the source of creation and observe this deeply; even his diligent practice was truly no easy thing — he had only not yet broken the pit of birth and death. The ancient worthies said: Confucius aids the precepts, because he is strict in governing the body; Laozi aids stability, because he is refined in forgetting the self. The learning of these two sages is mutually necessary with the Buddha and serves as its use — how could it be in vain? Judged in truth, those who cling to Confucius fall into causality, and those who cling to Laozi fall into spontaneity; in sum they have not departed from the nature of consciousness and so cannot exhaust the one mind. The Buddha transcends mind, intellect, and consciousness; hence he says: fundamentally not causality, not spontaneity — only then is the source of the one mind penetrated. This is the division between worldly and supramundane dharmas. What the Buddha breaks is by no means limited to this; even the supramundane Three Vehicles are all within it. People of the world, seeing only that Zhuangzi slanders Yao and Shun, belittles Tang and Wu, and reviles the followers of Confucius, take it as astonishing. What would they do if they heard the World-Honored One rebuke the Two Vehicles as scorched sprouts and rotten seeds, and grieve over the bodhisattvas of heavy defilement as icchantikas of the Buddha-Dharma? Yet the Buddha's rebuke of the Two Vehicles is not a rebuke of the Two Vehicles but of those who cling to the traces of the Two Vehicles, wishing them to abandon the small and aspire to the great. So too Zhuangzi's reviling of Confucius is not reviling Confucius but reviling those who study Confucius' traces, wishing them to cut off sagacity and discard cleverness. In sum, these are all words that send off sentiment and break clinging. If sentiment is truly forgotten and clinging ended, one will join arms and roam in the land of the wondrous Way, with no leisure even for rejoicing in supreme bliss — what need would there be for muddled confusion? The bodhisattva on the grounds in the Avataṃsaka manifests his body among those who smear themselves with ashes, serve fire, lie on thorns, and pierce themselves with needles, becoming their teacher and elder. Were it not for the Buddha-Dharma, how could they be made to enter the Buddha-Dharma? Hence the banners of clinging of those six masters could not be pulled down without the Buddha; and in my view the grand words of Laozi and Zhuangzi could not be verified and directed without the Buddha-Dharma. Truly these are playful discourses; even venerable scholars cannot free themselves from them. Now, by the contemplation of mind-only consciousness, none of them goes beyond shadow and echo.

The conception of this treatise came about when I was dwelling by the sea, in the winter of the wuzi year of Wanli, begging in the royal city; it came up in a night conversation with the layman Dongguan, who clapped his hands greatly. In the summer of the gengyin year I first put brush to it, and after storing it a long time I had never brought it out. In the winter of the jiawu year, following circumstances in the royal city, I meant to ask instruction of the Grand Astrologer Jiao Ruohou, but it did not come about. The next spring, of the yiwei year, I met with calamity for spreading the Dharma, and the draft had already been left by the sea; so I sent my attendant to search it out from among the torn slips. In autumn I received grace and was sent to Leiyang. Chan Master Daguan, coming from Mount Kuanglu with his staff, waited for me on the river; and in the eleventh month, as I was crossing the river, I met the Master at the Thatched Hut of Traveling and Lodging. Sitting at night I brought this out, and the Master read it once and sighed three times, saying: this is enough to dispel long delusion. He at once ordered his disciple Ruqi to cut it in wood to spread the gift of Dharma, and I firmly stopped him. In the summer of the wuxu year, while I was lodging in Wuyang, keeping the retreat with my disciples within the earthen walls and expounding the purport of the Śūraṃgama for the assembly, my disciple Baoqui saw it and sighed with joy, vowing to exert all his strength to complete it and finish the work. Ah! If one would know the meaning of Buddha-nature, one should observe the causes and conditions of the time. These few paltry words are truly not enough to weigh light or heavy in the Dharma-gate: conceived ten years before and completed ten years after, composed east of the eastern sea and practiced south of the southern sea — how could this be so by mere chance meeting of conditions? The Way and the time — how can they be forced? Yet this was written because of observing Laozi and Zhuangzi; hence the treatise is named after them. Written on the last day of the wuxu year of Wanli by the Daoist Hanshan, Qing, in the Laṅkāvatāra Chamber.

After my illness and the clutter of worldly affairs, I have only recently begun to read the great compilation the Caoxi General Record, together with the Treatise on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi and other works, and I am deeply moved to admiration. What is meant by: not knowing the Spring and Autumn Annals, one cannot engage the world; not knowing Laozi and Zhuangzi, one cannot forget the world; not practicing Chan, one cannot transcend the world; and by Confucius being the sage of the human vehicle, Laozi the sage of the heavenly vehicle, and the Buddha the sage who can be sage and can be ordinary, can be human and can be heavenly — sayings of this kind are theses that will not change in a hundred generations. Qiyuan bows his head once more.

blocks.text: Opening Topic of the Commentary on the Dao De Jing

inline.s: Elucidating the Tenet

What Laozi takes as his tenet is the wondrous Way of emptiness and spontaneity. This is precisely what the Śūraṃgama calls the absence of all discrimination, neither form nor emptiness, which Kauṣika and others mistook for the dark truth. This is precisely what is called the dark, empty substance of the eighth consciousness. Because this consciousness is most deeply hidden, subtle, and hard to fathom, nothing but the Buddha is sufficient to exhaust it; turned about, it becomes the great perfect mirror-wisdom. Bodhisattvas know this and break it by calm abiding and insight, yet there is still partial realization. As for the śrāvakas, not knowing it, they take it for nirvāṇa; and the brahmin ascetics of the Western Regions, not knowing it, cling to it as the dark truth. This then they take to be the wondrous Way of emptiness and spontaneity. Hence the sutra says: all who cultivate the path and cannot accomplish supreme bodhi, and even become śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, gods, non-Buddhists, Māra kings, and Māra's retinues, all do so because they do not know the two roots and practice in confusion, like boiling sand and wishing to make a fine meal: though they pass through dust-mote kalpas, in the end they cannot obtain it. What are the two? The first is the beginningless root of birth and death: namely that you and all living beings take the grasping mind as your self-nature. The second is the beginningless nirvāṇa, the original pure substance: namely that your essence of consciousness, originally luminous, can produce all conditions and is what conditions leave behind. This saying, that the essence of consciousness is originally luminous, is precisely Laozi's wondrous Way. Hence he says: remote and dark, within it there is an essence; this essence is most real. Because this substance is utterly empty and utterly great, it is not form; because it can produce all conditions, it is not emptiness. Not knowing that heaven, earth, and the myriad things are all manifested from this consciousness, one calls it spontaneity. Because of inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation, it is called wondrous; because it is most refined and unmixed, it is called real; because heaven and earth may perish but this substance does not perish, and the human body may die but this nature abides forever, it is called eternal; because the transformations of the myriad things all issue from it, it is called the root of heaven and earth, the gate of all wonders. Whenever in his book he speaks of the true, eternal, mysterious, wondrous, empty, and great Way and the like, verify it all by this, and one will have a destination of one's own; otherwise one will be as blank as one who grasps at wind and shadows. Hence this is shown first, and in the writing itself there is no need to repeat it.
Elucidating the Aspiration

In my view, one who reads Laozi and Zhuangzi must first become thoroughly familiar with the vehicles of the teaching, finely penetrate the Śūraṃgama, and fuse and comprehend our Buddha's treatises on breaking clinging, so as not to be deluded by his words. Then, finely cultivating stillness and stability, when the work is pure and ripe and the use of mind subtle, one will see this old man's work as bitter and urgent. Yet one must see truly and really that the body is the root of suffering and cleverness the root of burden, so that one can of oneself destroy form and release cleverness, and only then know this old man's true enjoyment and supreme bliss. One must further see through the affairs of the world one by one and see through human feeling one by one, dwell in the world with an empty heart, with not a hair of obstruction before one's eyes, and only then see this old man's true freedom and happiness, vast and free, plainly a man of no affairs. Then, when one has no choice but to respond to the world, one spends not a bit of strength, and serenely governs by non-doing. Observing what he taught Confucius, one may know this. The book of Zhuangzi is the commentary on Laozi; hence what I call Laozi having Zhuangzi is like Confucius having Mencius. Know therefore that what the two masters say is all true speech and not grand words. Hence he said: my words are very easy to know and very easy to practice, yet no one in the world can know them or practice them. But those in the world who discuss the two masters do not at all apply themselves to the work of their own experience; they only imitate them with literary particles of speech, and so fall far short. Moreover there are those who learn their wild and unrestrained manner, but one does not see any who enter by the work of stillness and stability. This is what is meant by those who know me being few. May those who would draw near to the two masters contemplate in this way.
Elucidating the Practice

In the book of Laozi, expositors have always taken emptiness and nothingness as the tenet, and when it comes to seeking the work of entering the Way they are blank and do not know where to lay hand. Hence in the opening chapter I take the one character 'contemplate' in 'contemplate the nothing' and 'contemplate the something' as the essential of entering the Way, so that students may easily enter. Now the work of contemplation and illumination is the greatest, and the sages of the three teachings all showed it to people. Confucius said: knowing where to rest, and then there is stability; and again: manifest the luminous virtue. Knowing and clarity is the meaning of awakening. The Buddha's calm abiding and insight includes the calm abiding and insight of the three vehicles and of gods and humans, with differences of shallow and deep. Confucius is the human vehicle's calm abiding and insight; Laozi is the heavenly vehicle's calm abiding and insight. Yet though the calm abiding and insight of the three teachings differ in depth, the sickness they undertake to cure is in every case first the breaking of the attachment to self as the first step of the work. For the people of the world all take the single character 'I' as the root of the sickness: whether wise or foolish, worthy or unworthy, they press eagerly into the field of fame, profit, and emolument, scheming for the plans of a hundred generations of descendants, exhausting their wit and cleverness, all of it a scheme for one body. As the Buddha said, of the causes of all suffering craving is the root, and all of it is for the sake of the self. Laozi also said: the great calamity is that I have a body. Because the sage Confucius was the head of the teaching of names, toward students of middle and lower capacity he did not dare speak lightly of breaking the attachment to self; only to Yan Hui did he say 'overcome yourself.' For the rest he spoke only of rectifying the mind, making the intention sincere, and cultivating the person. Yet if the mind is rectified, the intention sincere, and the person cultivated, and one applies this between ruler and minister and father and son, each fulfilling his sincerity, this itself is the Way — what is meant by setting it up for the teaching of names. As for cutting off sagacity and discarding cleverness, the purport of no-self, this is for one's own enjoyment, and he likewise did not dare lightly raise it with others, but only drew the bow without letting the arrow fly. Hence he said: if I were sage in benevolence, how would I dare? And again: do I have knowledge? I have no knowledge. A simple fellow asked me, and I was utterly empty. As for where he exerted himself most for others, he said 'overcome yourself,' and he said 'do not be willful, do not be insistent, do not be obstinate, do not be self-centered.' These four sayings lay bare his very heart and liver. Now the self is my private self; willfulness is the arising mind; insistence is the waiting mind; obstinacy is the clinging mind; self-centeredness is the mind of self. To overcome is to cut off utterly; 'do not' is a word of prohibition. He taught people to cut off utterly the sickness of these four: willfulness, insistence, obstinacy, and self-centeredness. For the sage roams the world with an empty heart, quiescent and unmoving, responding to things as they come and penetrating them in response, using the mind like a mirror: neither welcoming nor sending, so that what comes has nothing to stick to and what goes leaves no trace, body and mind both forgotten, contending with nothing. This is the sage's mind. The reason people in the world cannot be like the sage is only that they have the sickness of these four. Hence they are not free and every movement is suffering. Confucius saw that the root of the world's sickness lay here, and so had people cut it off painfully. This very teaching is the Buddha's and Laozi's tenet of no-self. Moreover the character 'do not' is a work of cutting off, the most ruthless laying on of hand, like the words 'you shall not' in the prohibitions of the legalists, making it absolutely impossible to transgress; once one transgresses, the crime admits no pardon. It is only that students do not know this. As for our Buddha's teaching of the Dharma, though vast and boundless, in sum it does not go beyond breaking living beings' coarse and subtle two attachments to self and dharma. Once the two attachments are broken one ascends the Buddha-ground; that is, the whole canon of the three baskets is the instrument for breaking these two attachments. The attachments broken are the four sicknesses of Confucius, which are still coarse attachments. People of the world do not know this and suppose there is some other mystery. As for Laozi, he goes one step beyond the people of the world, and so he established his words solely on breaking clinging, wanting people to release cleverness and forsake form, to leave desire and be pure. Now the cleverness released is private cleverness, which is willfulness and insistence; the form forsaken is obstinacy and self; the desire left is one's private self. Being pure, one is vast and unobstructed like great empty space, which is Confucius' great impartiality. Know therefore that the mind-dharma of Confucius and Laozi is never out of accord; only their gateways and settings, fencing in and guarding the world's teaching, could not but be so. Confucius was devoted to engaging the world, Laozi solely to forgetting the world, and the Buddha solely to transcending the world. Yet though their ultimate aims differ, in truth their first step alike takes the breaking of the attachment to self as the master, and their work alike enters through calm abiding and insight.
Elucidating Substance and Function

Someone said: the sages of the three teachings all teach people first to break the attachment to self, so that the substance of no-self is the same. Why then do their functions differ as engaging the world, forgetting the world, and transcending the world? Answer: both substance and function are the same; there is only the difference of shallow and deep, small and great. If Confucius truly had a self, that would be but the privacy of one man; how could he engage the world? If the Buddha and Laozi truly renounced the world, that would be self-deliverance; how could they benefit living beings? Know therefore that only by no-self can one engage the world, and only by benefiting living beings is no-self revealed; in truth they are one. When Confucius says: quiescent and unmoving, yet responsive and thereby penetrating the affairs of the world — that is function. Brightness then sincerity — that is substance. Sincerity then taking form — that is function. Mind rectified and intention sincere — that is substance. Person cultivated, family regulated, state governed, world at peace — that is function. Laozi's namelessness is substance; doing by non-doing is function. Confucius says: only Heaven is great, and only Yao matched it — vast, so that the people could find no name for it. And again: he who governed by non-doing — was it not Shun? Moreover he takes Yao and Shun as the ancestors of engaging the world: were they men of name and of doing? Only by no-self does one see the whole world as oneself; hence it is said that Yao and Shun were the same as other men. Because all people are of one substance, the only difference is the obstruction of one's private self. Because people's minds are the same mind, where minds are the same there is no obstruction of form; hence he pressed eagerly at teaching and transforming them in order to order and succor them. This is how by no-self one engages the world. Laozi says: he is always good at saving people, and so there are no abandoned people. With no abandoned people, all may become Yao and Shun; this is how by no-self one can benefit living beings. As for the sayings in his book, he acts but does not lord it over, and when the work is done he does not dwell in it — all take non-doing as the great function of engaging the world; how then was he ever one who forgot the world? As for the Buddha, his substance embraces empty space and his function pervades the sand-grain realms; he manifests bodies according to kind, and says: I accomplish perfect enlightenment within the bodies of all living beings. And again: only when all living beings are saved do I accomplish the Buddha-way. And again: if I could cause one living being to arouse the bodhi-mind, I would rather suffer the pains of hell in my own body and never weary of it. Yet are the living beings he transforms not in the world? Since he enters the world to save beings, is this not engaging the world? Moreover to endure the pains of hell without weariness for the sake of one person — is that not pressing eagerly? If there is no kind in which he does not manifest a body, can there be one fixed name for him? Liezi once said: in the West there is a great sage who is believed without words and transforms without doing. How could he have had a mind to do anything? Know therefore that the three sages' substance of no-self and function of benefiting beings are the same; only the scope of their function differs in size. Because Confucius upheld the ways of the world, he began with one body and extended to family and state and afterward to the world; hence his transformation stopped at China, and he wanted everyone to be Yao and Shun, since Yao and Shun were his ancestors. Because Laozi saw the thinness of people's hearts in his time, he thought of returning to high antiquity and took the Yellow Emperor as his ancestor; hence every phrase he spoke was unlike the ordinary, and because he saw that the great Way is hard to accommodate, he went far away across the shifting sands. As for the Buddha, his teaching covers three thousand worlds, most vast and great, without any selection. As Zisi praised the sage, saying: all who have blood and breath none fail to honor and love him. Know therefore that Confucius' substance and function were never small; he was only confined by the times and circumstances. This is precisely the dharma of responding to capacity, and hence close to human feeling. This is the distinction of substance and function. It is a pity that students of later ages each bind themselves to a teaching: those who study Confucianism are constrained, those who study Laozi are wild, and those who study Buddhism are narrow. This is the fault of students, all of it the harm of clinging to self. If one can truly break the attachment to self with strength, then one splits open the fences and is a great master.
Elucidating the Destination

I have privately thought that if the sage Confucius had not known Laozi he would certainly not have been so joyful, and if he had not known the Buddha he would certainly have been impatient; if Laozi had not known Confucius he would certainly not have said again and again that one governs by non-doing, and if he had not known the Buddha he could certainly not have taken compassion as his treasure; and if the Buddha did not engage the world he would certainly not teach living beings in the world. In my view Confucius and Laozi are transformation bodies of the Buddha. If the followers of later ages who study Buddhism do not know Laozi, they will simply go on gazing into empty space, and every dharma before them will be an obstruction, so that nothing can be liberated. If they do not know Confucius, and take the Buddha-Dharma alone into the world, they will certainly not know the ways of the world and human feeling, and on meeting anyone will speak of the mysterious and wondrous, like selling a dead cat's head, of no use whatever. Hence the patriarch also said: if the teaching does not hit the mark, it is idle talk after all. Therefore the Avataṃsaka says: whether in the language of the borderlands, one teaches the four truths. Thus the Buddha's teaching of the Dharma never merely boasted of the mysterious and wondrous. And to save beings according to custom — is that not Confucius' mind of engaging the world? The sutra also says: the sage of the fifth ground, entering the world to save beings, masters every worldly book and art, medical prescription and miscellaneous treatise, chart and seal, all kinds of dharmas without exception, and only then can he respond to capacity. Hence it is said: the language of worldly truth and the means of livelihood all accord with the right Dharma. Thus Confucianism takes benevolence as its root and Buddhism takes the precepts as its root. As for the saying that filial piety and fraternal duty are the root of benevolence, and the Buddha's saying that filial piety is named the precept — in truth they are one. Seen in this light, is the Buddha utterly without a dharma of engaging the world? Because Confucius drove out the barbarians, his teaching traveled in China alone; the Buddha taught the four truths in the language of the borderlands, and so the barbarians all followed his transformation. This is why the scope of their function differs in size. Know therefore that what the sages of the three teachings share is the mind, and what differs is the traces. To seek the mind through the traces is like measuring the sea with a gourd; to fuse the traces through the mind is like a mustard seed containing space. When mind and traces are both forgotten, the ten thousand streams flow to the source and the hundred rivers are one flavor.

To one who has things, one cannot speak of the Way. The myriad things in their profusion are not existent; it is man who makes them exist. If man did not make them exist, how could the myriad things exist? All who have things must die for things; and he who dies for things is near to losing his humanity. If the man is lost, with whom shall the Way be? Things and man — how extreme it is!

One who forgets things is not sufficient to reach the Way. One who does not have things understands things as empty; and things being empty, there is no need to forget, for they are already forgotten. Yet to say I have forgotten things, I have forgotten things, is to have something that can be forgotten, which is not true forgetting, and so it is said to be insufficient to reach the Way.

One who sinks into emptiness is not sufficient to exhaust the Way. The mind that is not empty is so because of things; when things are empty the mind is empty of itself. Mind empty and things empty: then mind is nothing and yet is; things empty and mind empty: then things are and yet are nothing. If so, what is there to stagnate on? But to insist that emptiness is emptiness and to take emptiness as the ultimate is to sink into emptiness — how could that exhaust the Way?

Forgetting and not forgetting are both forgotten; forgetting is forgotten. Yet to insist on both is hard; to forget forgetting and not insist on both is hard. Ah, how ultimate! Where shall I find one who is without forgetting yet without not-forgetting, without both yet without not-both, to speak with him of forgetting and both?

Now those who reach the Way: abiding in dust they always say movement easily alters the substance; leaving dust they always say stillness easily makes one. What is altered by movement is like a spark struck from stone; what is made by stillness is like water that can be dammed. The stone spark seems to be and the swift current seems to stop. Those who think this way do not penetrate the source of movement and stillness, the root of arising and ceasing.

To be moved by things is to have invited it myself. If there were no self, what could move? See how the long wind drums through heaven and earth, the trees break and the hollows howl — what has that to do with the great void? Hence the ultimate man has no self; he is the utmost of emptiness. Because he is empty, he is unmoved.

The substance of mind is originally true; habit and defilement make it deluded. Hence the essential of forging the Way is simply to govern habit, and the essential of governing habit is purely wisdom. Try observing one who melts ice: where fire prevails the ice melts easily; where wisdom is deep habit is easily exhausted.

I believe and others do not: it is not that others do not believe, but that their faith does not reach it. Others believe and I do not: it is not that I do not believe, but that it is not worth believing. Hence I trust in the mind of faith, and others trust in the words of faith. If the words truly meet the mind, then there is nothing not believed.

A grain's weight shifts the utmost heaviness of a thousand catties; one private thought snatches away the great impartiality one originally has. The private is the film over perfect luminosity, the stem of birth and death. Therefore gain does not lie in the small nor loss in the great; the sage is cautious and fearful in the place where nothing is seen and nothing is heard.

Toiling for profit, toiling for fame, toiling for merit, toiling for the Way: the toil is the same, but what one toils for is different. Hence where there is profit there is no fame, where there is fame there is no merit, where there is merit there is no Way; and one who has the Way, the Way accomplished, lacks nothing.

The fish on dry land does not forget to moisten its companion with foam; the caged bird does not forget to preen its feathers, because having lost its proper state it longs to return. That a man should lose his proper state and not long to return means he is not the equal of fish and birds. How sad!

Those who hasten after profit are urgent; those who hasten after the Way are slow. Profit has savor; the Way has no flavor. He who savors the flavorless turns that slowness into urgency. The flavorless — who savors it? He who savors it is called a true man.

The mind is fundamentally a limpid deep pool; by drawing in the objects before it, it muddies its own nature and gives rise to all manner of murky disturbance, oppression, and torment. Tracing it to its root, the fault lies in attachment.

With one film in the eye, empty flowers riot into being; with one mote clinging to the body, mixed thoughts fly in confusion. Understand that the film is without flowers, and dissolve the dust and cut off the thoughts.

The most fine is the greatest; the most subtle is the most manifest. The fine is easily slighted, the subtle easily overlooked. The multitude does not know this; the sage is cautious. Because of his caution, his Way is great and his merit manifest, and through ten thousand ages he has no fault.

In things there is nothing desirable; it is man who desires them, and so they become desirable. Desire is born of craving, and craving must grasp; grasping must enter, and entering means being submerged, so that the self becomes small and things great, life light and things heavy, the man lost and the thing remaining. The ancients who were good at living did not serve things, and so had no desire; though ten thousand forms were arrayed before them, it was as though the West Beauty sold her charms to deer and elk.

I observe that one who is familiar with tigers and wolves, though familiar, is always afraid, fearing they will eat him; hence he is always afraid. What are sensual desire and lust to a man but tigers and wolves? Yet men grow familiar and even play with them, and when they have eaten their fill their hearts are sweet, and they placidly do not know fear. How excessive! Tigers and wolves eat the body; sensual desire eats the nature.

Sensual desire is without rival in its power over man. Hence it is said: thank heaven there is only one such. If there were a second like it, then among all the people under heaven none could practice the Way. In my view, one who is good at opposing desire is best served by wisdom; aid wisdom by revulsion, for revulsion brings fear, fear brings distance, distance brings indifference, indifference brings forgetting. To one who has forgotten, a form is like a puppet and a flavor like chewing wax — what desire is there?

The difficult is easy, and the easy is difficult. The multitude fears the difficult and neglects the easy; the sage fears the easy and reveres the difficult. Therefore there is no Way he does not make great, no virtue he does not make broad, no merit he does not accomplish, no name he does not establish.

The world all takes merit and fame as immortal, believing they can be won by the mind, and so it wearies the mind; believing they can be won by the body, and so it wearies the body. Yet when the toil is utterly spent, one may not establish them; and if established, they may not be firm. Alas! Apart from the sage, who can make them firm? What is not firm decays; what is firm? What I call immortal is different from this: know that my own immortality is immortal.

He who glories in fame stands on tiptoe for fame; he who glories in rank stands on tiptoe for rank. Since he already stands on tiptoe, what disgrace could be added? Hence it is said: he who stands on tiptoe does not stand. He who does not stand has no root; and with no root, in the anxious scramble of name and rank for gain and loss, what glory is there?

Wealth is not great because of what it stores: where there is storing there is loss, and so it is not great. Honor does not reach its utmost because of its height: where there is height there is lowness, and so it does not reach its utmost. Know therefore that the man of penetration stores nothing, and so his wealth is the greatest; is not high, and so his honor is the utmost.

One who hides his traces is not thereby a recluse: the traces are hidden but the mind is not necessarily forgotten. One who leans on fame is not thereby illustrious: the name is illustrious but the Way is not necessarily manifest. Hence reclusion is not rectitude and prominence is not greatness. What I call hiding and manifesting is different from this: I call hiding in the substance and manifesting in the function. When the substance is hidden, one is vast as the great clarity and the ten thousand realms are still; when the function is manifest, all appears in ordered array and the one Way is equally contemplated. Thus adversity and favor accord with circumstance, and failure and success are one. Ah! He who dwells in this is a true man of greatness.

The command of ruler and father cannot be escaped; how much less the great command? Try observing one who bears a small skill and does not understand the great command: in ordinary life he is disappointed, in his proper lot he feels it a time of rejection; hence his mind leaps and stamps, and in indignation he lodges words to seek favor from the world. Ah, how excessive! To a man of penetration it is like one drunk walking at night and striking his forehead against a pillar, or holding a cloth drum and crying to heaven for rescue. Yet though the cloth drum remains, one who knows fate does not take it up.

To take scheming as secrecy is not secrecy; to take the Way as secrecy is secrecy. I have observed one who works a crossbow: perilously poised, a hundred shots and only a few hits — this is a skilled man; how much more the unskilled? One who is good at the Way can spare things: without shooting, nothing escapes him. Hence his secrecy is the greatest and his strength the utmost.

Heaven and earth revolve, a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations; birth and death have their constancy yet none can fathom it. Not fathoming their constancy, one dies for things and forgets. The sage returns to things, and so he flourishes.

What others cast away I take up. Hence what others possess, I do not possess; what I possess, others do not possess. It is not that others do not possess it, but that not knowing they possess it, they do not possess it. If they knew they possessed it, how would I differ from them?

When dust and grime soil a finger, one must wash it before being content; yet when greed and anger harm the virtue, one does not know to cleanse them away. This is to regard virtue as less than a finger. A finger's defilement harms its life; virtue's harm ruins the nature.

He who bears a heavy load is burdened; he who knows much is wearied. Long burdening injures the form; extreme weariness endangers the mind. Once endangered, the reason it is endangered is that one serves the outside. Therefore he who values life serves the inside and not the outside, follows himself and not others, and sets his will on what endures and not on what perishes.

Adapting to change — this is hard to put into words. No one but takes the pursuit of gain and the avoidance of harm as the natural way of things, yet I do not. There are also cases where gain and harm are set before one and cannot be turned aside: that is change. How then is one to penetrate it? The multitude follow it; the noble person examines it; the sage accords with it. According with it, he does not possess it. Because he does not make it his own, therefore it is not his.

People call one who steals things a thief; he is not the thief. I call one who steals the mind a thief. How true this is! Now the stealer of things: he does not necessarily take all; where there is a guard he surely cannot enter; if he enters he is surely caught; caught, he dies without pardon. Since he dies, what has he stolen? But the stealer of the mind: he loses it utterly; the more urgently you guard, the deeper he enters; if caught, he lives, and often he is let go, and there are even those who teach him. Be on your guard!

The Way flourishes in yielding; virtue flourishes in humility; things break when they reach their full. Hence the yielding grows ever stronger, the humble ever brighter, the broken ever nearer to ruin. Those of old who did not make things their affair — they alone endured.

One who is meticulous in affairs is lax in mind; one who is meticulous in mind succeeds in affairs. Thus the more meticulous the affairs, the laxer the mind; the more meticulous the mind, the more successful the affairs. If the mind is not washed, there is no way to be meticulous. Therefore the sage values the washing of the mind and withdraws, hidden in secrecy.
A single thorn in the skin makes one toss and turn, ill at ease; a host of thorns in the mind — how can one be at ease? A thorn in the skin rots the skin; a thorn in the mind destroys the mind.

Great awe is to be feared. Look at the killing severity of heaven and earth: that is great awe. Though the myriad things be many, who can withstand their withering? Therefore one who possesses awe receives it from Heaven. Heaven’s awe is perfectly impartial; human awe imitates that impartiality. Heaven’s awe loves beings; human awe gives life.

To transform others earns no merit; to transform oneself earns merit. If one is truly transformed, others are transformed without being transformed. Witness how the countenance of a person of virtue makes a man’s contentiousness melt away. How true!

To deal with adversity is easy; to deal with prosperity is hard. Adversity has a counterpart; prosperity has none by which to know it. Therefore one who knows meets adversity as sweet dew and fears prosperity as poisoned wine — the utmost of care. Because of that care, his guard is never lost. Care — is it not the mark of one whose virtue is complete?

The substance of mind is originally bright; the dust of feeling thickens day by day. As the dust thickens, the mind grows daily dimmer. Therefore the sage uses wisdom and does not use feeling. So one who would reach the Way uses wisdom to remove feeling; when feeling is forgotten, wisdom too dissolves. One who forgets feeling is near the Way.

Wisdom is vast, affairs are slight. Nothing serves to penetrate affairs like wisdom. Thus the instrument of wisdom blunts the keen and unties the tangled, all to its advantage. Just watch a fleck of snow touch a red-hot furnace, or clear frost dissolve in the blazing sun: they are overcome. So one who overcomes himself — who can withstand him?

Others use great cleverness; I use the utmost simplicity. Cleverness loses by it; simplicity gains. Therefore one skilled in the Way casts away cleverness and takes simplicity, and nothing is not gained.

What accords with me delights me; what opposes me angers me. Delight and anger alternate; likes and dislikes contend. Day by day one’s faults increase. Tracing the cause to its root, it lies in not awakening. Not awakening — that is to forget the way home.

To indulge mouth and body, to gratify ear and eye, to vie and grapple with things — people call this joy. What joy? No sorrow is greater. To cast off the body, to extinguish mind and intellect, not to herd with things — people call this suffering. What suffering? No joy is greater. Therefore one who delights in suffering deepens in suffering; one who tastes joy as bitter finds joy daily melting away. So those who would walk the Way leave that and take this.

Heaven and earth toil not, yet accomplish transformation; the sage toils and so completes merit; the multitude labors and so carries affairs through. When affairs are carried through, one may rest; when merit is complete, one retires. Hence it is said: “When merit is complete and affairs accomplished, the body withdraws — this is the Way of Heaven.” The wealthy are arrogant; the highly placed are insolent; the much-accomplished boast; the great in ambition are mad; the superior in talent are proud. The deep in virtue are lowly; the solid in the Way are yielding.

Not understanding the borrowed conditions, one arbitrarily takes and rejects. The wind of consciousness fans and blows, vast and never still. The ocean’s waters are clear, yet wind raises waves. If the wind does not rise, how are waves born? If consciousness does not arise, how do the myriad conditions exist? Therefore for one who reaches the Way: not understanding, there is birth; understanding, there is no birth. Excellent!

If the source is not far, the stream is not long; if the Way is not great, the merit is not firm. Therefore the sage’s virtue covers the myriad beings and his merit flows through ten thousand ages, because his Way is great. One who possesses the great Way — who can breach it?

The eye contains heaven and earth, yet a mote of dust can rob it of its clarity; the mind encompasses the great void, yet a single thought can block its vastness. Know then that a single thought is the root of birth and death, the source of calamity. Therefore, knowing the minute and knowing the subtle, the sage keeps his guard.

One who trusts himself — though others do not trust him, he still trusts. One who does not trust himself — though others trust him, he still does not trust. Therefore self-trust is deep sincerity; the trust of others is easily deceived. Sincerity is called purity; deception is called sinking. Wisdom illumines, consciousness deludes; delusion gives rise to a thousand differences, while illumination abides alone. Therefore one who reaches the Way uses illumination to illumine delusion, and prizes wisdom, not consciousness.

Watch a man of the marketplace walking heedlessly: he stumbles into a hollow, yet he starts, flings out his arms and swears an oath — because he dislikes the mud on his shoes. But people today dwell in inferior virtue and are wholly at ease, never startled, never swearing. They make themselves lesser than the man of the marketplace and treat their own virtue as dung and stubble. Alas!

All know change as change and change accordingly, but they do not know that within change there abides the unchanging. If one knows the unchanging, then change cannot change him. If one does not know the unchanging, then even without change, when is he ever unchanged? Just look at the sage: his body follows the myriad beings, secretly passing through the four kinds of birth; in the welter of their doings he neither leads nor welcomes. That is to dwell in the unchanging while changing. What change is there? As for ordinary men, their form is like withered wood, yet their minds are like wind-blown dust; things have vanished from their sight, yet they still moan. That is no change — yet when are they ever unchanged?

Lying down, resting, sitting, sleeping — these ease the body. Cutting off entangling conditions — this eases the mind. When the body is at ease, the will declines; when the mind is at ease, the will becomes refined. Therefore one who nourishes the Way forgets the body and takes the mind as teacher; thus the Way becomes firm.

Heaven and earth are great because their capacity to contain makes them great; rivers and seas are deep because their readiness to receive makes them deep; the sage is honored because his taking in of filth and bearing of shame makes him honored. Therefore the sage, the more he tolerates, the greater; the lower he stoops, the more honored. Thus his Way penetrates a hundred kalpas and his blessings rise through all ages, and none contends with him.

To look on the people as my people — loving the good and hating the evil may yet be partial. To look on the people as my own mind — cherishing the good and pitying the evil is never untrue. Hence it is said: “Heaven and earth share one root; the myriad things are one body.” This is what is called universal benevolence.

He who sees forms is blind; he who sees seeing is clear-sighted. He who hears sounds is deaf; he who hears hearing is keen of ear. Thus when form is complete, seeing is complete; when sound is exhausted, hearing is exhausted — nothing fails to merge. Form and sound are both not; seeing and hearing do not abide. This is called the great penetration.

The myriad thoughts surge without cease; there is no way to meet the real. If one uses thoughts to still thoughts, the more one stills them the more they will not be stilled. If one uses a single thought to still the myriad thoughts, then without being stilled they are stilled of themselves. What I call the single thought is no-thought. One who can contemplate no-thought — though thoughts go on thinking, what thought is there in the end? Yet even so, to insist on real no-thought is a superfluity; men do not even know that it is a peg.

The substance of mind is originally empty; deluded thoughts do not exist. If one understands that delusions do not exist, then though they appear, they do not exist. If one does not understand that delusions do not exist, then though they do not exist, one still takes them as existing. Therefore deluded thoughts are like flowers in the sky; their root is a film upon the eye. Once the eye-fault is understood, the flowers are no longer taken as real; the substance of emptiness is forever quiescent.

When at rest one’s inner illumination seems present, but once one meets affairs it is gone — this is simply because mind and object are not yet merged and the dust of former experience is not yet finished, and so they obstruct. Therefore one who would reach the Way: if he has not understood the former dust, then even if thoughts and imaginings all stop, he is still tending toward stillness, and so he does not attain the supreme Way.

The essence is still, the function illumines; the function does not lose the essence. In illumining itself, it is still. The essence does not depart from the function; in stillness itself, it illumines. Thus the still essence is like the great void, and its illumining function like the white sun. Hence through ten thousand changes it suffers no loss, and no darkness is unillumined.

No beginning before, no end after; ten thousand kalpas are a single thought, the six directions a single emptiness. Beings and things share one track; great and small have one form. Day and night do not alter; death and life do not shift. This is called the constant. Yet one who embodies this, though a man, is heaven — who can make fault with him?

Affairs are small, principle is great. Affairs have a thousand differences; principle has but one flavor. One skilled in principle finds nothing outside the affair at hand; hidden and manifest, being and perishing are not two. Therefore the perfected person, the more he moves, the more still he is, and nowhere does he fail to dwell.

It cannot be attained by a mindless mind, nor sought by a mind that has mind. With mind one grasps existence; without mind one clings to nothingness. Both are wrong; then one stands aloof and independent. The great person has no counterpart because nothing can take hold of his mind.

When thought exists, things exist; when mind is empty, dharmas are empty. Thus if thought is like a hollow crucible, one is at ease in every condition; if the mind is like a round mirror, coming and going are always untroubled. One skilled in this, without leaving the ordinary, sits upright in the wondrous realm.

Great forgetting neither forgets nor leaves anything unforgotten. One who forgets with intent, the more he forgets, the more he fixes. The grasping man has not understood the Way; if he truly understood the Way, what would he not forget? Hence it is said: “Fish forget one another in water; men forget one another in the Way.”

The swimming fish does not know the sea; the flying bird does not know the sky; the common people do not know the Way. If they knew the Way, how could they be common? In my view, one who skillfully embodies the Way has a body like the fish and bird and a mind like sea and sky — he is near it.

In every movement and rest, every word and silence, the lifting of a brow, the blink of an eye, in drinking and in pecking, to left and to right — at no time is he unobservant. When observation is long, thought splits open; suddenly he is self-possessed. The self-possessed know it for themselves; no one else recognizes it.

The merit of heaven and earth does not discard a single blade of grass; the moisture of the vast sea does not reject a single drop; the substance of perfect clarity does not depart from a single thought. Know then how weighty is the matter of a single thought!

The true mind is vast beyond measure, this body minute beyond measure. Therefore one who has clarified the true mind looks back on this body as a wisp of cloud drifting in the great clear sky, coming and going at will, soaring free with nowhere to lodge. Because he has nowhere to lodge, he dwells in the world as a lodger.

To act with action — one cannot act. To act with non-action — one can act. Therefore the sage does nothing and yet nothing is left undone. What I call the sage’s non-action is simply acting without possessing the act — not like cold ashes and withered wood, utterly without action.

The great void wanders within my mind like a bubble in the sea — how much more heaven and earth within the great void, the myriad things within heaven and earth, this body within the myriad things, outer things within this body! Ah, how tiny! And because it is tiny, therefore it is great.

Heaven and earth are still; the myriad things are one. Guard stillness and know oneness, and the ten thousand affairs are finished. One who dwells in this Way is never at fault; because he is never at fault, all his doings and contrivings come to no loss. One who does not lose it is called a true person.

To be aloof and without counterpart is the great sameness. Where there is no sameness, self and things are two; self and things being two, opposition of form arises. Where there is opposition of form, nothing is more beset by dependence. How then is one aloof? In my view, one skilled in reaching the Way values the forgetting of both; when both are forgotten, self and things are one. Self and things being one, the opposition of form is forgotten. The opposition of form being forgotten, on what does one depend? Being without counterpart, therefore great; being great, therefore same. The greatly same is called a sage. Hence it is said: “Who but the sage can gather the myriad things into himself?”

Mountains, rivers and the great earth are one flavor of pure truth; the mind like perfect clarity, heaven and earth are void and still. Therefore one who has penetrated this: outwardly, whatever meets his eye can engage nothing; inwardly, turning back to look, there is not a single thing. Such is emptiness; emptiness leaves no trace. Things are but words. His body lodges within the world, his mind transcends beyond appearances.

When stillness is complete, the mind penetrates; when words are forgotten, the essence is understood. Therefore the person of penetration and understanding has a mind like a hanging mirror, a mouth as if his tongue were tied, a form like withered wood, a breath like frost and snow. Ah, who indeed is such a one? I would walk with him.

His form seems constrained, his inner depth vast and empty. His eyes seem not to see, his ears seem not to hear. Dim and dull, men look at him and think him foolish; like a man who has lost himself, he does not know who accompanies him. I beg to take him as my teacher.

All that the world contains is dim as a thing in a dream. In the dream it is not absent; after waking, what remains? Therefore without awakening, how can one transcend existence? Without transcending existence, how can one leave the world? What I call leaving the world is not leaving the world; leaving the world consists in leaving the world within the world. One who leaves the world within the world is called a perfected person.

Knowledge is the beginning; the utmost end is the finish. One spurs knowledge with wisdom, and wields the utmost with expedient means. Expedient means is that which engages existence. Engaging existence, one dwells in change. In antiquity there were those who, through ten thousand changes, never lost their rectitude, because the root was preserved. But those today who, lacking the root, boast themselves skilled in change — they are like men who bind themselves and then loose others; whoever sees them will surely spit, and even a child laughs aloud at them.

Direct arrival is called sudden; secret cultivation is called gradual. Direct arrival reaches the true; secret cultivation removes the false. If the true is not reached, the false is not removed; if the false is not removed, the true is not complete. From this, look at the false: is it not the obscuring of the true, the harm of the Way, the burden of virtue?

Perfect fusion and total embrace, vast and mutually interpenetrating; wholly affair, wholly principle; hidden and manifest beyond reckoning. One and many mutually contain; many and one mutually enter. Raise one and all is gathered, yet nothing hinders their array. Small and great are not different; ordinary and sage are not divided. Ever extinguished, ever illumining; ever arising, ever still. The mind cannot think it; speech cannot discuss it. In daily use and the ordinary there is never any lack; the constant is within it, and no journey is needed. This is called the utmost.

Great words carry the Way; small words carry names. Supreme words forget words. He who carries names stays near; he who carries the Way goes far; he who forgets words penetrates. Therefore the near is easily familiar, the far is easily slandered, and the penetrating is beyond reckoning. Because it is supreme, it is beyond reckoning. One who dwells in the beyond-reckoning is called divine transformation.

A single palm does not sound; without emptiness there is no echo; without counterpart there are no words. From this we see that words arise from dependence. Yet even so: to speak the word of no-words — the word is then no-word. No-words is what words cannot reach. In my view, one who would skillfully attain no-words must let words go. Once words are let go, no-words is attained. What words are there?

Fu Guangzhai of Liaocheng said: “Among what the world calls the books of the philosophers, are not Laozi and Zhuangzi the highest? Laozi’s words are terse and his meaning profound; Zhuangzi’s speech is strange and his thought far-reaching. Those who later discoursed on the Way took refuge in them. From Xunzi and Yangzi downward, none is fit to be compared. Is this Xu Yan — Prefatory Words — not of the company of Laozi and Zhuangzi? Its writing is brilliant and lucid, yet its purport is hard to name in words. Perhaps there are even points where Laozi and Zhuangzi fall short?” A doubter says: “You go too far. How could Laozi and Zhuangzi be equaled?” I say: “Truly Laozi and Zhuangzi cannot be equaled. Yet such sayings as ‘the valley spirit’ and ‘mixing with the dust,’ and ‘the beginning of doubt’ and ‘the dark pearl,’ seem to speak and yet not exhaust, and again seem to wish to speak yet find speech difficult. The Way is truly without limit. The Western Sage had no dharma to teach, yet he taught a dharma; in him speech is exhausted. Thus, looking at Laozi and Zhuangzi, one knows that the philosophers are not complete; looking at the Western Sage, one knows that Laozi and Zhuangzi are not complete. This Xu Yan’s purport comes from the Western Sage, while its writing resembles Laozi and Zhuangzi. Hence I said, ‘Perhaps there are points where Laozi and Zhuangzi fall short.’ Yet this too is words; where there are words, it is a preface. Hence it is named Prefatory Words. Take its words and seek what it does not say — that rests with the person. Otherwise, one might say that Hanshan is a man of today; what is remarkable about his Prefatory Words? He would fall short not only of Laozi and Zhuangzi but even of the philosophers.”
The Dream Wanderings of Hanshan Deqing, Fascicles 46–50
The Dream Wanderings of Hanshan Deqing, Fascicle Forty-Six

The Master was at Mount Jing, receiving and meeting his disciples, speaking freely, talking on from sunrise — all of it the most intimate and direct guidance for benefiting beings after realization, and not to be scattered and lost. In my life I could grasp the purport but not memorize the words. The Master’s words were as deep and vast as waves, and I did not even raise this intention until ten days later, so I could no longer recall the whole. I began to set down headings in order and record the general outline; earlier talks, together with the subsequent separate instructions, are appended one by one to form the Dharma Talks at Mount Jing, so that they may be printed and given out widely and the Master’s compassionate spittle not be spent in vain. Master Danju and the great assembly are of one mind in this.
Recorded by the disciple Zhu Lu
This great matter must be discussed plainly and honestly if it is to be of use. Above all, do not crave the abstruse and wondrous; a flood of lips and tongue is called playing with the spirit.

If one does not enter this matter through investigation, one gains no strength. If one does not verify it against the teachings, one does not gain right view. If one is not forged in the crucible of conditions and circumstances, it is merely a matter of light and shadow at the gate. When the eight winds of adversity and favor come, one is shaken and carried off, unable to pass through. Enter through the Chan school, verify with the teachings, test by daily conditions — and simply be light and free amid conditions, with no mind that sticks: that is where mind-work gains strength. If one can examine oneself by conditions, one need not rely entirely on a good teacher’s words as the absolute method.

Bite firmly on the huatou — not in order to understand the huatou, but only to use the huatou to raise doubt and cut off deluded thought. The investigation must be carried on apart from the huatou itself. Only when doubt takes hold does it gain strength. The ancients said: “Three inches from the hook — why do you not speak?” Those before us set their minds on this. When doubt reaches the point where feeling and consciousness cannot arrive and words cannot reach, where it presses to the extreme, a little light and shadow bursts forth; this is called the samādhi of lightning. That is just the time to press forward, and one must not rejoice. If one takes this as it, one is satisfied with little, and one’s whole being is covered over by that speck of light and can never come forth again; whatever arises afterward, one is driven by it. Within the eighth consciousness are stored many lives’ habitual tendencies; when subtle seeds suddenly appear and no effort avails, one must borrow the power of mantra to dissolve them.

Question: Where do wisdom and consciousness differ? The very first thought, direct perception, is wisdom; as soon as it turns to the second, it is inference and falls into feeling and thought. Again: what comes tainted with feeling is consciousness; what comes untainted by feeling is wisdom. Biting firmly on the huatou is precisely seizing the road by which feeling and consciousness come, so that no second thought arises.

Investigation and awakening are not such difficult matters. Keep your breath unified for three months, and you will surely see where it settles. Above all, do not beforehand harbor a mind that awaits awakening; the moment you await awakening, you are waiting for awakening to come to you, and this very thing is a bar laid across your path, so that your practice can never enter. Again: this matter must be done by a fierce and courageous man.

One of sharp faculties has gained innate wisdom through many lives; meeting the right conditions in this life, he is finished on the spot. There are those who do not enter by investigation but need only preserve and carry it through, like the Sixth Patriarch. What of the dull-rooted? They need only consent to it themselves. The dull are not clever; they gain strength precisely from their dullness.

Bite firmly on the huatou; it is useful at every time. Even going up a mountain of knives or into a mass of fire, it is useful. There you gain the power of samādhi. If there is the slightest evasion, your whole body falls.

A Chan practitioner must not sit down on pure white ground; this is a pitfall for a thousand lives and ten thousand kalpas. Wishing to expose it for the assembly, I composed the Song of Carrying the Board.

The eye of the teachings and the eye of the school are originally not two eyes. Master Yongming, in presenting the school, took up the words of the teachings entirely to seal and confirm them, fearing that people would one-sidedly stray onto the road of no-meaning and misstep. Without the eye of the teachings, one falls into wrong views. In my commentaries on the Diamond, Lotus, Laṅkāvatāra, Śūraṅgama and other sutras, I picked out whatever burst forth where feeling and consciousness cannot reach and the road of meaning is cut off, wishing thereby to seal the school with the teachings; students should attain it for themselves.

During my time at the Eastern Sea, one evening as I sat, body and world became empty; the ocean seal emitted light and rivers and mountains quaked — I attained the corresponding wisdom. After a while I penetrated the crucial point of the Śūraṅgama, and it was suddenly before my eyes. I hurriedly lit a candle and wrote; my wrist could not pause, and by the end of the fifth watch the Śūraṅgama Hanging Mirror was complete. My attendant came out to check on me and, seeing the guttering candle on the desk, was astonished.
A bodhisattva makes benefiting beings his entire business. If he does not see through the various dharmas of the world, he cannot match the occasion and benefit beings.
In learning the Buddha’s way, first arouse the mind of great compassion, and take the breaking of self-attachment as the main thing.
Old koans, measured by people today with deluded thought, no longer meet point to point. Even if one understands and can speak of them, they lend no strength to one’s own practice.
To penetrate amid movement is easy to enter; entering amid stillness has no strength.
Entering through outer knowledge and views has no strength; entering through inner realization of one’s own nature gains strength.

Question: What of one who attains through conditions? Conditions are of two kinds: the condition of seeing and hearing is subject to regression; the condition of an actual state is not subject to regression, because the real and the insubstantial differ.
For ordinary beings, the patience of desire; for the two vehicles, the patience of birth; for bodhisattvas, the patience of non-arising; for the Buddha, the patience of quiescent extinction.

Only the one Buddha-view is right, yet there are bodhisattva-views, two-vehicle views, being-views and outsider views, all of them confused and mistaken. Therefore the World-Honored One used various expedients, solely to have them understand the one mind and enter right view, which is called the Buddha-view.
Understand that the mind of birth and death is quiescent, and you understand birth and death.
What is the upward path? There is only letting go.
The patriarchs’ words are living, every phrase. When students take them as fixed dharmas, every phrase is dead.
In daily practice, one need only see through deluded thoughts and not be used by them; there is no other place to apply the mind.
When you cannot empty anything, what then? Simply understand that it is false; then all can be emptied and all can be made light.
The bodhisattva dwells in the Land of Ultimate Bliss — what is he doing there? I want to drag him out.
The phrase “Namo Amitābha Buddha” is originally the same as a huatou; people today, however, turn it into going to the West.

That all is illusion everyone knows; one must have the capacity to master illusion before one is not turned by it. At Haiyin I once recalled the koan of the Sixth Patriarch and the man who came at midnight to cut off his head, and wished to learn his power of samādhi. Every night I opened the door and practiced visualization: if someone came to ask for my head, I would joyfully give it. So it was tonight, and so the next night. After a long time I felt a settled power of resolve. Then one night a thief was reported to have entered. I said, “Just call him in,” lit a candle and sat upright, with no fear in my heart. When the man reached the door, he crawled on the ground and dared not enter — a great tall fellow. I called out that there was nothing here, and ordered two hundred coins from the store to be given him. Had I not mastered it beforehand, I would have been thrown into panic.

Dwelling in the Wutai Mountains, the clamor was like a million men in fierce battle; there was not a single breath of peace. One day I listened where the spring rushed most violently, and after a moment I suddenly no longer heard it. The instant I raised the thought “Why?” I heard it again. So I sat for many days at the place of greatest tumult. After sitting long, the sound of the water became still. Thereafter the water’s sound never ceased, yet it was as if I did not hear it. After that I dwelt peacefully in the mountains and was never again stirred by clamor.

While I was at the Eastern Sea, the Empress Dowager sent a eunuch with a sum of silver, and I dared not refuse. I judged that I could not recklessly accept it for myself; reflecting that the region was suffering famine, I could use it to spread the Empress Dowager’s bounty. The eunuch objected. I told him I would inform the counties and have those who received the alms in that region make a register to report back; this was agreed. Later, when the two palaces heard of it, they were greatly pleased. And when I afterwards met with disaster, it was this very deed that helped me. Thus one knows that in the face of wealth one must not be careless.

When I was in Lingnan, I was not yet familiar with the ways of the people and kept a lofty distance, so that none could approach me freely; there was no one close to me. A small child wished to come near, yet always feared and ran from me. One day I learned the lion’s way of taming its cub: I forced myself to lie down and fondle him, giving him fruits and melons. Day by day he grew more familiar, and at last did not fear me. From then on people no longer shunned me, and came daily closer.

When I first went to pay my respects to a certain regional commander, I held my card in the courtyard, and for a long while he did not order me to rise and withdraw. I understood in my heart that I ought to announce my own name and present myself, yet I could not get it out of my mouth; it was as heavy as a thousand catties. When I could bear it no longer, I summoned my resolve and announced my name: “So-and-so presents himself.” Only then could I rise and leave. The next day when I came again it was the same, and for a whole year he granted me no indulgence. Others said he was a military man — how could he know to break convention in receiving a good teacher? At last, on the day we were to go together to visit the governor’s office, the commander prepared a boat with vegetarian food and fruit laid out like a guest’s seat, invited me aboard, bowed, and saluting me to the seat of honor, said: “It is not that I could not indulge you; I knew you had proud bones, and wished thereby to complete you.” We talked joyfully knee to knee before parting. Then I sighed to think how many deep-hearted men there are among officials — why ask whether they are military?

If one reads without careful personal verification, one does not get the use of it. When I was annotating Laozi, I came to “The Way of Heaven — is it not like the drawing of a bow?” I spent several more days but could not find where it fit. So I borrowed a bow and string from someone, drew it and hung it on the wall, and watched it sitting and lying. Two days later I suddenly understood that “drawing” is spoken in contrast to “slackening.” When the bow is slack, the grip stands high with slack to spare and the tips hang low and insufficient, so it is useless. When it is drawn and used, then the high is pressed down and the low raised, the grip is reduced and the tips supplied, upper and lower evenly balanced, and one can hit the mark. The Way of Heaven takes movement entirely as its function; it gives and does not receive — this fits exactly. As for the two lines “The heavy is the root of the light,” I also examined them for several years, not daring to explain them carelessly. It happened to be on the day I was traveling south, sitting alone in a boat with nothing to occupy my feelings, that the meaning of heavy and light, stillness and restlessness, appeared suddenly before my eyes. Only then did I understand the purport of the Supreme One’s words: it is seen only after one has tested it in one’s own body. One cannot say that the stale words on paper have no true flavor. Thus my one commentary on the Daodejing took thirteen years before it left the manuscript — it was no careless work.

When I compose a commentary, it must be that I gather my spirit and enter contemplation, and my understanding accords with the Buddha’s mind; only when a hint suddenly bursts forth of itself do I commit it to paper. If it involves discursive thought, it is of no use.

It is said: “If the sage does not appear in the world, ten thousand ages are as a long night.” Therefore our original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, manifested in a royal palace, left home at the Snowy Mountains, practiced austerities for six years, awakened to the Way and became Buddha, and taught at the Deer Park to save beings. Before the Buddha appeared in the world, there were ninety-six kinds of outsiders in India, each establishing its own house and gate and all claiming to be teachers. When the Buddha accomplished the Way and taught, those outsiders one by one took refuge, left home, became the Buddha’s disciples, practiced according to the teaching and realized the fruit of arhatship. Thus the assembly on Vulture Peak, twelve hundred and fifty in number, were all of the company of outsiders. At that time, those who had faith in the Buddha took refuge in Buddha, Dharma and Saṅgha and practiced as taught; those without faith were startled and doubtful, and even suffered all kinds of demonic harm and slander, falling into evil paths beyond counting. Know then that in lands today where the Buddhadharma has not spread, it is as in the time before the Buddha appeared: wise and foolish, worthy and unworthy, though their doubt and faith differ, all fail to know the original intent of our Buddha’s appearance and the graduated expedient rules for saving beings. Therefore I now briefly set out the stages of the expedient means for converting beings, so that those who have not heard and do not believe the Buddhadharma may know that we who are monks — the Dharma gate of converting beings — cannot be entered by any single deed, single practice or single gate. Hence it is said: “Expedient means have many gates; the return to the source has no second.” In sum, the forty-nine years were all in accordance with the order of faculties, great and small, shallow and deep — what is called “teaching does not skip grades.” I hope you will understand this fully and not call it common talk.
A Buddha appears in the world for the sake of one great matter: to open and demonstrate to beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and cause them to awaken and enter it. This one matter alone; there is no other. What is called the one great matter means that beings should know that birth and death are the one great matter. The Buddha’s knowledge and vision is the Buddha-nature that each and every being originally possesses. Because they are deluded about this Buddha-nature, birth and death arise. Now, to escape the suffering of birth and death, one must take the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as the first principle.
