One drop of Caoxi's water
Wanders across the rivers and lakes.
May it follow you as sweet rain,
And sprinkle the scorched and withered everywhere.
Wang Chi Visits on a Summer Day

The burning heat is poison, like fire;
The fragrance of tea is cold as ice.
Who knows that within this world of ours
All but the idle are outdone by a monk?
Farewell to Wuxin Rong, Chief Seat: Two Poems

A single flake of Jiangnan snow
Comes to cool the fever of the miasmal sea.
Now that you cross the ridge and go,
The chill of it clings to your brow.

A seven-foot staff clears overhead;
Three meals a day fill up the gourd.
When shall I, among ten thousand peaks,
Lie wearied, full, amid the clouds?
Facing the Moon

On the snow ridge a lone pine grows old;
In Caoxi a single drop runs cold.
Who knows that tonight's moon
Is still the same we watched of old?
Sailing Past Little Golden Mountain: Four Poems

Each time I come it is new once more;
Returning again, I never tire.
Only because I crave the Buddha's sun,
At times I bow to the Dharma King's own form.

The green hills never change their face;
The running water goes and comes again.
Only the moon amid the pines
Pours its clear light upon the moss.

The fishing lamps burn white in the deep of night;
The sand fowl clamor through the clear day.
The river is empty, the haunts of men are gone —
All day long the brushwood gate stays shut.

Below the steps fish and dragons rest at ease;
On the sandbar gulls and egrets take their leisure.
So brimming and full is this one stretch of water —
Yet it shuts off ten thousand ranges of hills.
Rejoicing That Huang Gongliang Has Returned from Jimen: Five Poems

No man's life reaches a hundred years;
Half of it was gone when first we met.
Then suddenly we parted three years more —
Who can reckon meeting and parting's debt?

Yesterday I rode a hollow boat;
In the night the wind and rain came down.
This morning I am overjoyed to meet you —
Far off and faint, as if in a dream.

On the frontier the grass-tips have turned white;
On Yan Mountain the maple leaves are red.
There is nothing left but the cold hue of snow,
And it still lingers on your brow.

Along the post road, a thousand rows of willow;
On rivers and lakes, ten thousand miles of wave.
Coming and going, the years are spent for nothing —
Who is it that has not idled them away?

The half-round moon over Luofu;
A single drop of Caoxi's water.
I share the taste of both with you —
There is no this or that in the flavor.
Rejoicing That Master Tanxin Qing Has Come

You have come down from the northern white,
To comfort me in this southern heat.
In the burning house we gladly look at one another —
As if facing the snows of Yan Mountain.
Inviting Master Qing to Taste Lychees

Through the long summer the fiery clouds are red;
In the fifth month the lychees ripen sweet.
I sit with you beside the Pearl River —
Day after day we tap the cold jade.
Facing Master Qing, Remembering Old Days

My hut once stood neighboring with yours;
We shared one love of water and bamboo.
Since we parted, thirty years have passed —
We look at each other, and now we are old.
Sent to the Two Princely Clans Zhen and Song of Puban and Xiangyuan: Three Poems

A single current of Yellow River water
Comes from far off in the heavens above.
On and on it flows east into the sea —
May I ask, when will it ever return?

The twin peaks of Hua Mountain stand forth;
In the high void the jade is cold.
Afar I hear the music of heaven ring —
It must be homage at the immortal altar.

The Zhongtiao Mountains are blue-green;
Morning clouds scatter bright brocade.
I know there is one who forgets the world,
Sitting alone to watch the Beginningless.
Dreaming a Visit to Tiantai: Two Poems

Suddenly I arrived at Tiantai Mountain,
And met an old man there among the clouds.
I think he must be one who fled the Qin —
His countenance is fair as this.

I flew up to the summit of Huading,
When suddenly I heard the heaven-cock crow.
Gazing far off toward Penglai Mountain,
I smoothed my beard and gave a long, long whistle.
Remembering Old Days

I dreamed I sat beneath the Dragon-Flower Tree,
And heard the Longyue bells ring out and die.
I woke within an empty valley —
A thousand ravines roared with the pine wind.
The Old Idle Monk Dwells in the Mountains

The hut is small; the hill hides a temple;
The heart is void; the mustard robe is bare.
Idly I sleep on the stone beneath the pine,
Sitting through the highest peak of all.
About to Go to Leiyang, I Take Leave of Master Tan on the River

We part beside the Hibiscus River;
Its waters in autumn are greener still.
The homeward boat goes up against the cold —
Coming and going, the heart is like woven thread.
In Praise of the Moon

On the clear sea its light seems to be;
In the cold sky its color seems to be gone.
Who knows that within a single glance
It has lit delusion's road for a thousand years?
In Praise of Clouds

A single speck, like a slender film;
Then spreading, it fills the whole vast void.
We know only that after it has risen —
We cannot see the hour before it was born.
Trying a Duan Inkstone: Three Poems

The noble man loves to wear jade,
Its warmth and mildness figuring his virtue.
This stone surpasses it even more —
Its true treasure lies in brush and ink.

The sea of words flows on ten thousand miles;
The brush's peak stands a thousand fathoms of snow.
All of it is born from within this stone —
Time and again it flies off in jade flakes.

Vast and boundless, the clear river water;
Piled and heaped, the purple stone mountain.
Who knows that the meaning of a thousand years
Lies from the first within the turbid blur?
Huacheng Hut: Two Poems

The mountain hues bring their own dusk and dawn;
The banyan's shade lies idle on the ancient road.
How many people come and go here —
The red dust stretches vast and empty on.

A well is dug upon the high plain;
The earth is deep, and water hard to find.
But when the work is carried to its utmost —
The deep spring flows and never stops.
The Chime-Stone Room

In a tiny room I hold a hidden gorge;
In poverty's company I meet the men of old.
Though I have but this inch-square patch of ground,
There is no place for clamorous dust to rest.
The Chan Devotee Ming Gives Tea

This mind from the first does not abide;
The barefoot one was never stained by dust.
From time to time he draws the fountainhead's water,
And cools the fevered, tormented in their heat.
Sent to Chentang, Chief Seat

I remember the place where you planted tea;
The whole garden soaked in spring rain.
When shall we sweep away the pine needles,
And face each other brewing a single cup?
Sent to Zongyuan of the West Hall

Caoxi's spring waters are rising;
The wild geese return to Heng Mountain.
I remember your nights of cross-legged sitting,
When the moon rose late over the pine gate.
Inscribed for the Chan Hall of Longxing Temple, Sent from Afar

The royal breath gathers in the mountains;
The sound of sutras reaches the imperial palace.
In the Dharma seat, a host of dragons and elephants —
For ten thousand ages we pray for the Yao wind.
Sent to Those Who Keep the Imperial Mausoleum Offerings

Heaven and earth opened the imperial enterprise;
Sun and moon turn the rivers and mountains about.
With incense and fire we serve the offerings diligently,
And morning and evening look up to the sacred face.
Inscribed on a Small Landscape Painting: Twenty-One Poems

Drifting clouds cover the spring hills;
A light cold freezes as if to split.
Whence does one come to tread the green?
When he returns, the moonlight is white.
Fragrant trees, early summer's growth; / a light boat on jade-green lake water. / I carry my lute to seek an old friend — / where, in clouds so deep, to find him?
Across the broken bridge a figure goes; / a little boat beneath the frosty moon. / I turn my head to the cloud-wrapped hills: / all the world of dust is shut away.
Misty trees and spring clouds, green; / river and sky, a red setting sun. / Who knows where he has gone to drink? / He will come home in the bright moonlight.
A lone boat in a night of wind and rain; / the faint, dim blur of grass and trees in spring. / A dog barks, startled, under the thatch eaves — / it must be someone crossing the river.
Fine clouds drift past the river pavilion; / a lonely village lies idle in the daylight. / A small bridge spans the wild water, / cutting off ten thousand ranges of hills.
I sit at peace in the peach-blossom hollow; / my quiet dwelling is far from the market's dust. / Only because spring's colors are fair — / not to flee the Qin.
In the tall trees the new cicadas shrill; / deep woods hide a thatched hut. / Across the broken bridge a figure goes; / white clouds fill the whole valley.
A waterfall falls beyond the cold sky; / a lone pavilion among water and stone. / The days are long, with not a thing to do — / I take a companion to look at spring hills.
Autumn water, green as jade; / far mountains congealed like cream. / Deep in the night the fish do not bite — / for whom is the bait cast?

With a patter and sigh the cold woods grow lean; / with a purl and murmur the water and stones run clear. / White clouds for a thousand, ten thousand miles — / gazing at each other, we simply forget all feeling.
Over ten thousand trees the clouds stream thick; / on a thousand peaks the setting light grows cold. / My rustic gate stays shut the livelong day; / at dusk I look to the one who shares my wine.
Far trees merge into the clear-day mist; / the river opens out, the grass pavilion cold. / I chant as I walk, one with the riverside — / only now I believe how hard it is to stay sober alone.
Old trees, grey pines grown ancient; / clear springs and white stones, rare and strange. / I carry my lute to seek a kindred soul — / far off I see a tavern's banner.
Seated in the river pavilion, I forget all contrivance; / leaning on the rail, I watch the evening light. / Someone stands waiting on the sandbar, / meaning to go home when the moon comes up.
White clouds; the sky trails silk. / The river clears, its water one with space. / Hand in hand we seek a drinking friend / and cross together east of the stone bridge.
On autumn hills the cloud-breath thins; / against red trees the dawn frost lies clear. / A single stretch of lake and sky, wide open — / left empty, waiting for the moon.
The hills are like the road to Mount Tiantai; / the blossoms hold no spring of Qin. / A fisherman sits at the mouth of the creek — / no one comes to ask the way.
Red clouds, and all four fields blotted out; / layer on layer of ice, ten thousand trees snapped. / Braving the cold, I go to visit an old friend, / trampling through the linked snow of the hills.
Ten thousand hills congealed in piled snow; / on the tall trees the light ice breaks. / Where does the cold-season plum come into bloom? / Its fragrance draws one monk after it.
Autumn hills, the new rain clearing; / far waters calm and boundless. / On the lake a recluse has his dwelling, / as high and far as the world's dust.
The Dream Wanderings of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Forty-Nine
Meeting He Xuanpu at Nanyue
We meet before the Southern Peak; / we sit facing the mid-autumn moon. / Its clear light we watch the whole night through, / wondering if it is the snow on Yan Mountain.
Yushan
At leisure I climb to the top of Yushan; / in the city I see smoke and fire. / Ten thousand rooftops crowd like clouds — / each a blue lotus blossom.
The River-Viewing Tower
Alone I climb the River-Viewing Tower; / on every side the hills are woven like cloth. / Among them lives one who feeds on cloud-haze — / we face each other, and do not know each other.
High Mountain Temple
The mountain town pillows the flowing river; / the temple rises up out of the clouds. / A bell sounds, and ten thousand doors open; / people are walking inside the lotus.
Fool's Creek
How is Fool's Creek like me? / I am the fool; the creek is not. / Its spring waters sound by day and night — / the sound of Dharma, murmuring low.
Huayan Hermitage
The hermitage stands near the Ganges' water; / a monk's robe, and the city of Sravasti. / The sound of sutras mingles with human speech: / they are always preaching the unborn.
Miscellaneous Verses, Two Poems
The white crane flies, soaring to the sky, / free and untrammelled, going or staying as it will. / Pity this unimpeded body — / it does not know the road of birth and death.
Ants crave what is rank and raw; / chasing an odor, they call to their fellows. / Hurrying, hurrying, never pausing — / and what do they gain in the end?
Impromptu, Two Poems
My Dharma companions, a thousand peak-shadows; / my livelihood, a few acres of field. / Truly I know: within this human world / such a bond is hard to make.
Green hills wait for a man's return. / I meant to seek a deep accord; / who would have thought the newcomer's heart / would clash with me in every move and stillness?
Mountain Dwelling, Thirteen Poems
A single cloud floats in the vast void; / in a moment it spreads over the whole earth. / Try to look at the state before you were born — / pure and still, without a speck of dust.
All ten thousand scenes are still by nature; / it is the mind that makes them rise and cease. / If a single thought does not arise, / where can you go to find stillness or motion?
Through the long night there is no lamp or candle; / the road ahead lies altogether dark. / Pitiful are those who sleep so soundly — / when will they wake from the great dream?
Into green mountains it is easy to enter; / pure karma is not hard to cultivate. / Only the art of stilling the mind — / there even heroes yield a step.
One pillow, the dream of yellow millet; / a thousand years of bloody merit. / Men only know such glory should endure for ever — / who believes it all turns empty in a moment?
Old snow, and grey pines grown ancient; / a monk at leisure, water and stones clear. / Sitting here, a hundred cares are forgotten; / I see this body suddenly grow light.
The fierce heat is past bearing; / a pure breeze comes down through the bamboo. / With a rustle and a sigh cool air rises — / marrow and bone are suddenly refreshed.
The wind falls still; the cicadas cry the faster. / The dragon returns, and the rain-smell is rank. / I take the cool beneath the tall trees / and idly copy the Goose-Swapping Sutra.
Where the clouds are deep there is a wild temple; / the old monk loves to lean upon his staff. / He comes back late from begging his food, / dreading to thread ten miles of pine.
Crisp air enters the sparse woods; / on ten thousand hills the autumn colors are fair. / Greedy to watch the clouds at the creek's head, / I forget the road by which I came.
I sit alone beneath the tall pine, / calm with the heart of highest antiquity. / High hills and flowing streams, such is my thought — / who is there left to understand the note?
Sun and moon, like flying birds; / heaven and earth, like a rolling ball. / This floating life is spent in busy haste — / who will look at it from within stillness?
One bowl of ever-burning lamp; / facing it at night, the heart grows stiller. / How many are the wine-sodden sleepers / whose mad dreams in sleep have never ceased?
Mountain Dwelling, Twenty Poems (Six-Character Lines)
Under the pines, a few rafters of thatch; / before my eyes, green hills on every side. / Sun and moon rise and sink without resting; / white clouds come and go, always at ease.
In the snow the plum blossom first opens; / a hidden fragrance drifts in late at night. / Just as I sit alone facing the cold lamp, / it suddenly blasts my nostrils open.
A few flakes of white cloud that will not leave; / a single round of bright moon that comes flying in. / They keep me company in the mountains' loneliness; / I laugh at the dust of the world below.

A single stretch of cold heart on a snowy night; / a few strokes of the frost bell that shatter dreams. / In the stove the incense dies to lingering embers; / beyond the window the moon climbs a lonely peak.

My whole face is covered in biting clear frost; / my whole head is white hair, sighing and thin. / In the world, empty flowers drop their shadows; / in my eyes the cataracts of illusion are wholly gone.
With a patter the spring's voice enters my ears; / bright and plain, the Ancestor's meaning comes from the West. / Unmoving, the tongue's root speaks always — / what need to sigh again, How wondrous!
In the hidden valley the orchid's fragrance is rich; / at midnight the moonlight is fair and fine. / A single stretch of clear dust stirs and swells — / and for no reason dry meditation is broken.
One thought forgets its conditions, utterly still; / a solitary brightness shines alone, wide awake. / See through it: lightning in the empty sky — / not at all the firefly before your eyes.

The clouds scatter in the vast sky, the rain has passed; / the snow melts in the cold valley, and spring is born. / I only feel this body washed as if in water; / I do not know the mind is clear as ice.
Decayed and old, one pities these weak bones; / yet looking on, I find the mind grown strong. / At midnight the backbone is like iron; / at all other hours one thought is like frost.
In the empty valley all dust is wholly dismissed; / only a single scrap of idle cloud remains. / It keeps me company as I wield my whisk by the pine roots — / how good that the deer gather in herds.
Letters are a cataract in the eye; / dhyana is a floating mote upon the mind. / Take up both, inside and out, and cast them off — / the whole body is the great chiliocosm.
In the still night the bell does not stop sounding; / on the stone bed, dreams and imaginings are all empty. / I open my eyes and do not know where I am — / I only hear my ears full of pine wind.
Pure and clear, a precious mirror holding the void; / when spring comes, the water fills Peng Lake. / It shines through to the true face of Mount Lu — / the moon is a bright pearl on the brow.

The lotus water-clock's six hours still seem short; / long incense is set to burn a hundred marks. / Day and night the true and constant flows and pours — / the conscious spirit has long been lodged in the lotus womb.
A single cloud seals the valley's mouth; / a thousand peaks split the empty sky. / Among them are a few rafters of thatch, / hiding deep a white-haired mountain elder.
How sad that green hills always remain; / how I sigh that white hair comes ever new. / We are all wayfarers within the dust — / who is the idler beyond all things?
The mountain's look is sad with last night's rain; / the pine's voice chokes cold in the clear frost. / A begging monk, like a weary bird; / the crescent moon puts on new makeup.
The world's light is like water and moon; / body and mind are bright as lapis lazuli. / I only see the ice melt at the ravine's bottom — / I do not know spring has come to the flowering branch.
Outside the gate, green hills bloom one by one; / before the window, yellow leaves rustle and sigh. / I sit alone, with nothing to say — / turning back, I see deluded thoughts wholly gone.
Immediate Matters Aboard the Boat

Empty water joins the sky, and one leaf of a boat; / I look at once on this life as a floating bubble. / A wild goose's cry shatters the dream of dependent birth; / bright moon on the reeds at the old ferry crossing.
Mount Dagu

Cloud haze her skirt, cloud her robe, the moon her arched brow; / river and lake fill my eyes, and few are the friends I know. / The cold current runs to the bottom, the heart washed clean — / ask nothing of what husband she may be.
The Pagoda on Mount Gu
A pagoda in the void, a body of water and moon; / a single mote of dust set in the vast emptiness. / The traveler's two eyes are given another speck of chaff — / how many men can recognize the real?
Baotuo Temple on Lake Poyang
A palace of glass, a platter of crystal; / on every side green hills and jade-green rails. / Within it there is one who is always preaching: / he drains the Western River, the cold night tide.
Crossing the Tong River, Mourning Zeng Jianzhai, Chief of the Imperial Table

Beneath the Dragon Flower Tree we met of old; / every night we talked until we heard the dawn bell. / Today I look for you on the Tong River's waters — / in vain I hold back tears of blood in the spring wind.
Fisherman's Songs of the Clear River, Two Poems

The water clear, the sand white, the moon a hook; / its shadow falls on the wave's heart, the line not yet drawn in. / There are endless fish that cannot swallow the bait — / in vain the fisherman hugs his deep sorrow.

A single leaf of a boat tosses after the waves; / on the Five Lakes, wind and moon are free for the feasting. / Dream and soul are always in the deepest place; / the bitterest is leaving the hook, with the water colder still.
Mooring at Hengpu

Five clouds and a single river lead into Nan'an; / a thousand folded ranges turn back through the six-and-sixty rapids. / I walk on to where the water fails and the hills run out — / countless plum blossoms to be seen from the ridge.
Climbing the Wall of Nan'an

On the city wall, petal by petal, blue lotuses spring up; / in the flower's heart fragrance holds the smoke of ten thousand homes. / My body is inside a mirror, and no one knows me — / should I seek the heavens anywhere beyond this?
Crossing the Dayu Ridge, Two Poems

A single path through cloud and haze, the plank road deep; / plum blossoms and pine rain, the air dark and heavy. / I turn it over: those who traveled this way by night of old — / how do they compare with my heart crossing the ridge today?

On the ridge the cold plum is just coming into bloom; / the branches are wrapped in clouds like an old monk's robe. / Let me try lifting my staff and holding it out again — / its fragrance follows the heaven's wind to the world's edge.
Paying Respects to the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi, Two Poems

A drop of Caoxi's water comes from a wondrous source; / it flows into the blue sea, and the waves beat the sky. / How many fish and dragons are transformed along the way — / yet the single pulse at the source is still clear and cold.

No sooner had he cast down the woodcutter's axe than a stone fell on his waist; / at Huangmei, in the dead of night, he sat in silent emptiness. / Shouldering the Dharma, he went back south with a single bowl — / and from that time on his sons and grandsons grew prouder by the day.
On the Road to Guangzhou, Two Poems

Through misty waters I journeyed south through a hundred cities; / the good teachers I met were all without feeling. / No sooner had I drawn near, meaning to stay a moment, / than they pointed to the road ahead and took their leave.

The two banks and the midstream will not suffer me to stay; / my little boat follows the waves, at the mercy of the sky's wind. / I must simply hoist the lone sail high and go — / trusting that the wave of grace is the same everywhere.
Reaching the Garrison at Leiyang

Over the miasmal sea the mist floats day and night; / dragons and serpents breathe out vapor, muddying the clear stream. / When I arrive, the whole place is the land of the unborn — / all the more I see the ruler's grace is not easily repaid.
Sent to Reverend Wuyan of Shaolin, Two Poems

On the crest of Five Teats Peak the grass and trees grow deep; / when spring comes, blossoms open all through the empty woods. / On the summit the piled snow is still a thousand feet — / who now has a heart like the one who cut off his arm?

After the Qingliang assembly, back again to Chang'an; / each time we met, each time was joy. / Since we parted I gaze from the sky's south to the sky's north; / scorching wind and northern snow look on at one another.
Setting the Boat Loose on the Boluo River

A single sail goes east, the sea's waves calm; / flutes and drums sound as if from the heavens. / Far off I see the three mountains sink beyond the sky — / and do not know I am walking inside a mirror.
Sent to Master Zhen of Little Jinshan

The heaven's wind blows me up to the Wondrous High Terrace; / at midnight I ride the tide home, carrying the moon. / Sweep clean the stones on Mount Lanka — / wait for me to come again and copy out the sutra.
Little Jinshan, Three Poems

Ten thousand miles of long waves, flowing ten thousand miles; / who set a fistful of stone to stand against the midstream isle? / Had Yu not hewn the channel open in three tiers, / the fish and dragons would surely nod their heads in assent.

A crystal palace, cut off from every trace of dust; / fragrant mist and vapor, the dew-laden air thick. / In the empty sky the bright moon floats my guest-boat; / deep in the night fish and dragons lie at the steps.

The mountain floats on the water's face, the temple rests on emptiness; / its towers and halls are void, lost in the distant haze. / This is no conjured human world — / it must rather be a Brahma-king's palace risen from the sky.
Sent to Master Miaofeng of Hedong, Three Poems

The colors of Shouyang Mountain pillow the river's flow; / you, Master, dwell at the very summit of Zhongtiao. / Hemp fields before your bed, Zhang Jing's staff in hand — / to this day its grace makes ghosts and spirits grieve.

The Yellow River, a single thread, comes down from heaven; / it flows into the Central Plain and washes the ashes of the kalpa. / Grasp the crucial pass and watch the pillar in midstream — / the ship of compassion does not count mere river-crossing talent.

I have walked to the world's end, and the road is hard; / poisonous mists and scorching winds I have taken as my full meal. / Then suddenly I remember Longmen's thousand-fathom snow — / sharply it rises, and chills me to the heart.
Answering Grand Equerry Gao, Who Sent Incense

A single petal of famous incense from the high temple; / a sealed letter sent far to the scorched wilderness. / In dreams I hear the watch-gong and take it for a chime-stone; / rising at night, I burn it myself and bow to the Dharma King.
Longing for My Old Dwelling at Longmen on Mount Wutai

Ages of ice and snow have wrapped my thatch hut round;
since we parted, full twenty years have gone by.
On Yedou Peak, beneath the moon that knows no bound,
who now, I wonder, dwells in peace beneath the sky?
Remembering Mount Kuang

Far off I think of Kuang’s Five Elders Peak,
where white clouds lock ten thousand pines in deep.
Cold moonlight bathes the waters of Peng Lake;
the falls’ roar flies with bells that chiming sweep.
Thinking of the Master of the Void-Leaning Pavilion by the Sky Pool, Mount Kuang

A tower in the air, a man therein,
at ease as among the flowers he stood;
at midnight, in the Sky Pool’s moonlit din —
I wonder who may share his solitude.
Rejoicing at Wuyang That Tan Ziwen Has Come from Jimen: Two Poems

Snow wraps the western hills; Jimen is chill.
I recall the stove, the long night wearing through.
Since we parted, silence — as if worlds apart, still
we meet, and I half doubt the sight is true.

Hot wind and northern snow alike prove vain;
this burning house is ice across the plain.
Grieve not to see my beard and temples changed —
my heart was ever a monk of Wutai’s range.
Remembering My Home Mountain and Old Companions (with Preface)

It is more than thirty years since I left my home mountain. Now I have been exiled beyond the passes. It happened that my Dharma elder, Master Ke, came with my nephew Guang to comfort me from afar. So I made three quatrains, wrote them out, and hung them again on the old wall, to show how the traces of a human life are illusion such as this.

Old tracks of mine on Chang’an’s dusty way —
night wind and morning wind have blown them thin.
Thirty years worn away since parting day;
how much, I wonder, has drained into the void within.

When we were children heaping up the sand,
a hundred games, our laughter like a flower;
though frost and wind have altered face and hand,
this heart is still at home, as in that hour.

Our temple suffered fire, and I too was far away in travel, long cherishing the thought of restoring it. Now I hear that my kind elder brother has renewed the pagoda, while the halls still lie amid brambles. My heart is caught and troubled by this, and I send these lines from afar.

I remember the kalpa-fire burning clear:
a pagoda like a lotus born in flame.
The udumbara blossoms once more here —
when shall I see Tusita’s heaven again?
Seeing Liu Yizhe Home, and to All My Old Friends: Three Poems

Three years in fevered seas, one heart we shared;
the body was not bound to sink or rise.
You sail home lone, with autumn moonlight bared,
and through cold waves my longing deeper lies.

The body toils, the mind at leisure stays;
a poor hut and the hunt-camp equal green hills’ ways.
If old friends ask what news of me there be,
say only: wandering still, his temples grey.

The world’s road is rugged, hard to tread;
how few see truly this floating life we bear.
If homeward you pass West Lake, bend your head
and mark the lotus rising from the water clear.
Thoughts Sent to Master Xugu from the Army

I lightly tossed the meditation board and took the war drum;
cross-legged sitting and the saddle ill agree.
Deep in the night the moon shines beneath the camp gate —
it seems we sit once more in the pine’s shade, quietly.
Thinking of Mount Tiantai: Two Poems

Tianmu’s cloud-glow lies thick along the sea;
half a life of dreaming has gone by in vain.
When shall I trail the staff that pokes the sky, and free
the deluded monk asleep in nirvāṇa’s chain?

On Huading’s summit moon shines doubly bright,
beneath Stone Bridge the water doubly clear.
Could I bear one drop to the burning seas’ night,
it would surpass the udumbara blooming here.
Songs of the Four Seasons at Caoxi

Four hills are veiled in thick and heavy green;
below the window wind stirs pines and stream.
In noonday sleep I snore, half lost in dream —
along the cloister rings a bell serene.

Hoe and fire are the goodly way;
when autumn comes, late rice perfumes each door.
What you cannot lay down, shoulder and bear away —
how does it compare with old Yan’s ease on Shaoyang’s shore?

Late at night I boil tea from gathered snow;
its natural taste deserves the highest praise.
And there is one more wonder I would show:
cold moonlight steeping plum trees, all the grove ablaze.
Songs from the Army: Two Poems

I doffed the dark robe for a soldier’s dress;
thus I believe: to follow karma is the Way.
Though the burning heavens blaze with fire no less,
they cannot melt a heart of ice and snow away.
Young Master Chen Studies at Tianning Temple

Lodged in Jetavana, past the world’s dust;
at night I sleep where Buddha’s close, I trust.
My dream-soul a sudden bell-stroke breaks in two —
and I believe at last: a Dharma-hearer true.
Sea-Moon Tower

Where sea and sky lie void, one tower stands;
a ten-foot cell holds boundless emptiness.
At night I rise and open wide the casement:
the bright moon out — waves, clouds my robe caress.
Young Master Liu Studies by Stone Lake

His mind is a cold spring, its color ice;
his hermit life outdoes the rock-cave monk.
At night he boils one drop from the water’s source,
and begs a flame to share the Buddha lamp.
Sent to Master Yunqi

Long brows and crane-white hair, long homed in cloud;
his fly-whisk waved above the browsing deer.
One leaf of sandalwood I send from far —
I see him lift it to the Dharma King.
Sent to the Layman Tu Chishui

Vimalakīrti’s house by White Flower stands;
through misty water, chill, the sea-seal lies.
They say Mañjuśrī has gone east again —
with whom, I wonder, will the fragrant rice be tried?
Sent to the Hanlin Scholar Feng Kaizhi, Asking for a Preface to the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra

I remember the Thousand-Flower hall, our talk face to face;
I doffed the precious robe, and long my rags hang worn.
On Laṅkā’s mountain the maṇi jewels are massed —
when shall we open the hundred-treasure casket again?
Reading Master Daguan’s Final Verse

One thought has never held concealment from the start;
his whole body never fell in the field of right and wrong.
See how, letting go, he lightly holds it forth —
then you will know the master’s warm and fiery heart.
Thinking of My Old Dwelling on Mount Wutai

On Yedou’s peak the snow has not yet gone;
since we parted, tidings long have ceased to come.
Through fevered lands and dusty dreams I walked alone —
and trail my staff across the single-plank bridge home.
Thoughts Sent from the Army to the Censor Huang Yuli: Six Poems

Ten years on war-horse through the burning waste;
I mind our roaming in the Sea-Seal’s ray.
Within the great fire I seek a place to plant my foot in haste —
yet coolest was the place I left you that day.

Gathering and parting, clouds that will not keep;
this heart has never left you since we met.
Sun and moon, two wheels, like birds that sweep
to and fro unceasing — and my dreams beset.

The great sea and the Long River are one vein;
misty waves, boundless, all are emptiness.
Though ten thousand mountains stand between,
it is an airy flower in a mirror’s stillness.

Space and the great earth may yet pass away;
how should this thought be cut off or yet stay?
Ask, in Vimalakīrti’s narrow cell:
where are all beings laid, and where do they dwell?

You went first to court, waiting the water-clock’s call;
afar you questioned the still void with the Laṅkā’s scroll.
The attendant ate his fill of fragrant rice —
and to this day not one grain has dissolved at all.

Worldly affairs are void, and idlest of all;
in heaven and earth what place has no green hill?
I know the place your true eye rests upon —
not amid sound and form, nor marks that fill.
Sent to Zou, Remonstrance Official of Nangao at Shuitian

Before his door, a robe of blessing’s field;
he snaps a pine branch for a fly-whisk now and then.
Hill hues and stream-voice ever Dharma yield —
and who, I wonder, is the one to hear it then?
Inscribed at the Purple Cloud Hermitage on Incense Burner Peak

Beneath Incense Burner Peak the purple clouds lie deep;
on terraced cliffs the pines and bamboos shade the day.
The gate leads to the Long River and the stream’s water —
clear currents wash the thoughts of the world away.

Burning summer, the day so long and slow;
I long for cool beneath the bodhi tree.
A gust of wind across the hollow sky does blow,
and bears from who knows where the scent of lotus bloom.
Thinking of Mount Jiuhua

Fair lotus peaks above the Jiujiang rise;
a belt of cloud wraps six-and-thirty crests.
Turning to the fevered land beneath the moonlit skies,
a clear dream hangs, for no cause, on cold pines’ rests.
Master Yi Comes from Hengyang to Pay His Respects

Alone he asks the way to Caoxi’s stream;
its autumn water, dustless, cold and clear.
He brings a shard of Hengshan’s moon, it seems,
still shining on the hunter band of yesteryear.
Sent to the Layman Liu Chunchi of Chaling

Meeting in person — how is it truer than not meeting?
The news that lately comes is spring upon the ridge.
Hengshan’s moonlight, the water of Caoxi:
looked at to the very bottom, they are an old friend.
Mooring on the Luo River, Visiting the Monk Master Zhong and Not Finding Him

Once I sat in the river tower and watched for snow to melt;
the Luo in spring runs faster than the tide.
Tonight I watch the moon before Egret Islet —
it seems the same companion of my solitude.
Pardoned by Grace and Returning to the Mountains

A monk since childhood, fifty years and more;
grown old, I chose to mix with worldly dust.
From now I’ll walk the road to heaven’s door,
and sleep the daylight through where peaks are thrust.
Sitting at Night
Passing the Faxing Temple in Summer: Two Poems

Beneath the bodhi tree the wind drives off the heat;
before the prajñā terrace rain brings cool.
A single cup of clear tea stills all thought complete —
where else, then, would you seek the Western Pure Land’s pool?

The bodhi tree was planted here of old,
its first intent to await the Coming Sage.
A thousand years, the robe and bowl still hold;
who mounts the ancient seat to speak in this our age?
Thinking of the Dead-Wood Hall on Mount Xuefeng

Before Dead-Wood Hall the cold is like ice;
half a thousand monks once sat within.
Afar I think of that ground of cold ash —
when shall we light the midnight lamp again?
Inscriptions on Two Paintings

The flying hills conceal the lake’s fair light;
misty trees, new-cleared, catch the setting sun.
Afar I hear the upper realm of Tusita’s height —
bells and drums fall from mid-sky, faint and wan.

A stretch of misty waves, fifteen bridges long;
cloud-hills and falling leaves, the evening’s sigh.
A lonely town half presses Wu’s river down —
and dwellers on the water hear the tide go by.
Parting from Master Tan on the River, About to Go to Leiyang
Thinking of My Old Dwelling

I once lived quietly west of the bamboo wood;
by the moonlit stream, staff in hand, I’d go.
I often think of deep night and the falling pine dew —
not knowing for whom the apes and cranes cry so.
Sent to Master Kai of the Tranquil Dwelling on Mount Fu

How fare the Nine Bands on Mount Fu today?
Looking back, the axe-helve long has rotted away.
I ask of the place where you sit cross-legged at night:
which is the more, the white clouds or the moon’s light?
Mooring at Little Golden Mountain: Reflections

Often I think how in half a month I came three times;
then all at once we parted, and five years went by.
Today I come again and sit on the summit’s heights —
and Deyun, it seems, was never of a former life.
Remembering the Plum Trees in the Mountains: Two Poems

The plum blossoms at Caoxi, whenever they come into full bloom, make one feel seated in the world of Fragrant Accumulation. This winter, because demons have been at work, I am detained by the Hibiscus River. The mountain is within a foot of me, yet I cannot sit and enjoy the fragrant offering. I write this poem to remember it.

Cold plum blossoms open on the snowy ridge;
softly, heavenly flowers fall on the lecture seat.
Would that the Fragrant Land above might bear
one bowl of it, and set it at my feet.

The fragrant plum trees heap into a wood;
their scent perfumes the heart and brings delight.
Beneath them now a lion throne is spread —
who reads the wind’s voice as the sea-tide’s might?
Receiving a Letter from My Disciple Jiang Wuyu of the Eastern Sea: Two Poems

A single sheet from an old friend, out of the blue;
ten thousand miles it comes to ask how I fare.
I answer: kin and friends are scattered, all gone too —
and a head of frost and snow but deepens care.

For fifteen years I have sat in the miasmal land;
facing the sea, I have never been able to forget.
Now and then I watch the midnight moon across ten thousand miles —
just like roaming together in the sea-seal’s light.
Ancient Buddha Pine Grove

Pine shade in layer on layer, unstained by dust;
the hills’ hue and the cloud’s light are the Dharma body’s own.
Day and night the wind-roar is the long broad tongue —
who, I wonder, has heard it to the end, and known?
The Dawn Bell of Kaiyuan

The heavenly river runs shallow, stars are few;
beneath the old temple’s eaves a hundred spirits bide.
A single dawn-bell stroke startles the great dream through —
and who, I wonder, is the one most truly awake?
The Ancient Pagoda on the Plain

What age raised this stupa toward the skies?
In Sui’s Daye years, the tale is told, it stood.
Green moss has stripped the seals, the broken stones all died;
and weeds spread over the golden field for good.
Sent to Master Yu’an

Afar I see you on the Flower Terrace preach;
the four heavens spread above the Dharma hall.
So pure the dragons and elephants your seat that reach —
do you recall the red-beard in the fevered wild, at all?
Sent to Master Caotang

From the fevered seas I come to sit at Baolin’s shade;
I long remember the old friends of the Dharma cave.
Afar I gaze on Yan Mountain’s moonlit glade —
all of it is the heart that follows karma to save.
Written at Random in Mountain Dwelling: Four Poems

A hundred years of worldly things — a flower of air;
this body and mind — a moon within the water.
Only where ten thousand hills lie deep and secret
do I sit cross-legged all day, the pine gate shut.

The red dust rolls; the world’s road stretches long.
What errand drives me to an alien land?
I turn my head — the home hills, far and dim —
and all my eyes hold cloud and the setting sun.

Amid the clamorous throng, who will step quickly free?
Since ancient days green hills shut out the market’s dust.
Do not say Peach Blossom Spring has no way in —
the falling flowers and flowing water know the ford.

Day and night the mist and glow guard the green steep;
with apes and cranes I wait, all scheming stilled.
Say not the hills are masterless in their sleep —
it is the idler will not come home, self-willed.
Seeing Off the Chan Monk Yinzhi on His Return to Shu

One chilly staff goes through the fevered land;
west of Wu Mountain thought stretches away.
On Emei’s peak, the new-autumn moon at hand —
I know you will reach the upper realm that day.
Inscribed from Afar for General Du’s Udumbara Retreat: Two Poems

Trumpets at the camp gate, yet he alone is still;
beneath the udumbara he rests in Chan all day.
Who knows that on the day the Khan bows to the king’s will,
the general breaks through being, and wins the way?

Bells, drums, and Tartar horn — all are the place of practice;
among the banners’ shadows he sits and burns his incense.
I think of you shattering the fortresses of Mara —
and of your vow: with empty mind, to behold the Dharma King.
Seeing Off Master Ci on His Return to Mount Wutai

From Mount Wutai parted, thirty years have run;
the ice and snow before my eyes remain.
You came and told me all the caves have seen and done —
and knit a bond from many lives again.
Sent to Master Kongyin

I remember Wutai’s ice, a hundred feet in height;
facing each other we sat, our bones all sharp and bare.
Musing again on thirty years and their flight —
we meet in a dream, and it seems we were never there.
Two Poems on Leaving Caoxi

To speed the Caoxi's ten-thousand-mile flow,
my heart turns home and strokes the broadsword's hilt.
I think of the snow that bathed his waist in blood —
through a thousand years the grief has never stilled.

I came to Caoxi leaning on my staff,
sat gazing at the hills, my face alight.
Today I leave for a thousand peaks away —
bird calls and stream sounds brim with endless grief.
Two Poems on Rejoicing in Snow, Newly Arrived at Hengyang

The Seventy Peaks are steeped in cold snow;
arriving here, I see this mind at peace.
Remembering the burning house where I once raced —
all now appears within an ice-jar's gleam.

In the five-heat realm a phantom body born,
for twenty years I drifted with the dust.
Today I come to the snows of Xiang —
of old, a man whose very bones were cool.
Twenty-Eight Poems on Dwelling in the Mountains

All my life I have held a passion for mist and cloud. In my early years I wandered on foot; at thirty I lived eight years among the ice and snow of Mount Wutai, and afterward dwelt twelve years by the Eastern Sea. In the year I knew my fate, the wind of karma blew me down into the land of miasma, and there nearly twenty years passed. Alas, how much is a human life? In the blink of an eye I have come and gone and am already seventy. Floating light and phantom shadow — how could they last? Lately, by the grace of His Majesty, I was granted return to my former station, and I came of purpose to the Southern Marchmount to make plans for my old age. The causes were not yet ripe, so I settled at the old Way-site east of the lake. Relying on the help of the benefactors, I built a dwelling for retreat. It was begun on the sixteenth day of the ninth month of the jia-yin year and finished by the very last days of the twelfth month — roughly completed in haste. From this time on, body and mind at last have a place of rest, like a long-wandering guest come home, setting down a heavy burden. What joy could match such ease and freedom? At once I chanted verses and had my attendant write them down, to record my hidden feelings — these are no crafted poems. When the mood came I took up the brush, with no order at all.

In Jetavana I borrowed a branch to rest;
from now I need not speak of roads made hard.
The sun is three poles high and still I lie —
no need for anyone to urge me to eat more.

Snow weighs the wicket gate; at night I hug the stove.
This body is lodged here, yet seems to be nowhere.
I do not know where sun and moon have gone;
looking back, the years of the world have passed away.

A little hut amid the tangled brush,
a stone for seat, the grasses for its shrine.
Shut in, I seem a Vimalakīrti;
ask nothing of three before or three behind.

My form a withered tree, my thoughts like ash,
snow on my crown and frost upon my cheeks.
It is not that in age I shun the world —
these eyes have nowhere left to set down dust.

Body and mind set down, I have spare ease;
my late-year life lies in ten thousand hills.
I will not let white clouds slip lightly from the vale —
let them keep the moon and guard my brushwood gate.

A cold lamp shines alone, my shadow faint;
through a sparse roof the wind blows snow across my robe.
Suddenly I recall where I sat cross-legged on Wutai —
a single brushwood door amid ten-thousand-year ice.

Cold pierces to the bone, snow on a thousand peaks;
rage buffets the man, wind through ten thousand hollows.
Wrapped head and all beneath my quilt, just woken from sleep,
I do not know this body is in the midst of stillness.

A hundred thousand worlds are shadows of a flower in air;
this body and mind the light of moon in water.
When every trick is spent, all tidings cease —
within it there is nowhere to set a thought.

The earth-stove has no fire, the stone bed is cold;
in the earthen censer the incense dies as night wears on.
Every sound of the world sinks still, the mind more still —
yet I half wonder I am gazing from within a mirror.

Cold rain falls sighing, wind fills the wood;
the lotus water-clock runs long, the night is deep.
Who knows the whole world cannot wake from its dream?
All of it is the bright light of prajñā's heart.

Deep in the night I sit alone at dry-pith Chan;
I rake the cold ash through, the fire will not catch.
Then suddenly the bell and chime sound from the tower —
one clear note fills the frosty sky.

Snow fills the world, ten thousand forms made new;
I hide myself inside a world of silver.
Sitting, I suddenly enter the storehouse of light —
and this place has never held one speck of dust.

The level lake soaks cold the garb of water-caltrop and lotus;
the blue hills above the lake are free of right and wrong.
All worldly traces melt, the human world falls far —
white clouds and gulls have both forgotten schemes.

When snow heaps at the brushwood door and I sit alone,
inch by inch the cold wood snaps its jade-like boughs.
At dawn the blue hills' color has suddenly vanished —
the plum has blossomed out and I never knew.

Spring passes, the Day of Man is gone, the snow first clears;
the new moon through sparse woods casts shadows all the clearer.
At night I rise and push the window open to the vastness —
the whole sky's stars hang from the eaves and pillars.

The clouds draw back, spring light stirs across four wilds;
from where does plum send its secret fragrance?
Staff in hand, I would go seek the hidden vale —
one branch leans aslant by the eastern wall.

A single cloud seals the pines of ten thousand ravines;
before my door the stream goes babbling day by day.
It cares not night or day, but serves my snoring sleep —
fair dreams are startled back by a bell beyond the ridge.

Deep spring, the rain has passed, the fallen blossoms fly;
softly heavenly fragrance climbs onto my robe.
A single idle heart that has nowhere to settle —
at the peak's edge I lean on my staff and watch the clouds go home.

Strolling at ease, I let my steps go where they will;
this frame of mine is like a pine in snow.
By chance I come and stand a while at the stream's head,
then follow the idle clouds across another peak

In the empty hills with deer, whom should I follow?
I will yield to the lush grass and the tall pines.
Though the red dust holds dreams hard to wake from,
the world-cutting man has never reached these myriad peaks.

Hanging white hair faces the blue hills;
this body dwells among a thousand cliffs and ten thousand gorges.
The pine gate is still, no passing guest comes by —
only white clouds wander to and fro at ease.

The blue hills do not move, thusness as it is;
morning and evening the cloud-mist rolls and spreads at will.
Though the red dust lie ten thousand fathoms deep,
not one speck has ever reached my thatched hut.

Deep among ten thousand peaks I sit cross-legged alone;
clear and distinct, the void-bright single thought stands solitary.
This body is like the bright moon hung in cold space —
only its clear shadow remains, fallen on rivers and lakes.

Waking from sleep I call the boy to brew tea;
the bamboo stove boils up, its froth like snowflakes.
Before the leaf unfurls, Māra has already withdrawn —
now I believe the groves hold true masters still.

Weary, I lean at the empty window, sitting to watch the hills;
a thousand peaks of purple and green rise from the pines.
My mind makes no claim, so let the clouds come and go —
how much more at ease is the thusness of my own being.

Moonlight and the sound of pines are all seen and heard;
the Chan mind and idle thoughts divide the sage from the common.
Melt them back to the single thought where nothing is born —
how shall I put this meaning into words for you?

Autumn water on the level lake soaks the cold sky;
old trees shed frost, red leaves fall.
On the stone path and little bridge all human tracks are cut —
a single hut is locked deep within the white clouds.
Sent to the Old Monk of Shun Hermitage
Sent to Wei Kaoshu

In quiet seclusion, just like a monk who stays at home;
one room as clear as ice in the sixth month.
Though you master emptiness and all that is comes to an end,
mountains and waters still hang upon your brow.
Written on Parting from the Friends of the East-of-the-Lake Society

The udumbara hall stands west of the bamboo grove;
far from the market's clamor, it is the best of dwellings.
Sweep the cloud-strewn ground before the steps with care —
when I return, do not let the grass run wild.

By chance I came beneath the pines and closed the brushwood gate;
you summoned the recluse to seek the world beyond.
How could I think I would drift off with the flowing water?
In parting from you my heart clings to the clouded hills.
Two Poems, Held by Wind at Yueyang

Beyond Yueyang Tower the lake soaks into the sky;
below the tower a sandbar, a boat moored for the night.
Wind-borne sails come and go, and none can be detained —
only the hills' color remains as it always was.

North wind drives the waves to beat the mountain town;
a single light sail is held back from its course.
I think it means to keep me here to watch Dongting's moon —
no wonder it shines so bright toward a traveler's side.
Passing the Cloud Grove of Yu Runfu at Jinsha

The Cloud Grove is close at hand, not far to see;
arriving, the cold air is crisp and clear.
The gate is shut and will not let the mist and cloud out —
how many a worldly thought here fades away.
Written at Random on West Lake

Hills and lake on every side, seen as in a mirror;
the great boats sink deep in the cold green waves.
I do not know this body lies within an ice-jar's shadow —
laughable, to be deep drunk with a dream not yet ended.
Mourning Master Chekong of Yellow Dragon, Mount Kuang

Formerly I dwelt with the Master amid the ice and snow of Mount Wutai for three years. Since we parted, more than thirty years have passed. Now I have come to Mount Kuang to spend my old age. I bowed once at the Master's stupa and mourned him with these poems.

I recall the days we sat facing each other at Qingliang;
hoar-frost and snow hung heavy on both our brows.
Since we parted, my dreams reach the place that breaks the heart —
a grief I cannot hold back, known only to myself.

The stupa's round shadow is embraced by ten thousand pines;
the dharma-body does not move, towering over a thousand peaks.
I know the Master always taught the Dharma of no-birth —
bird calls and stream sounds join the morning bell.
A Snowy Night in the Mountains

Snow hems a thousand peaks, I shut the gate alone;
a cold lamp in deep night lights this aging face.
The mind's ash has died out, red-dust dreams cut off —
who would believe the world holds such leisure as this?
Written on Waking from a Dream While Reading the Ten Stages Chapter of the Avatamsaka Sutra

A single leaf of a light boat and a single fishing rod;
the fragrant bait on the hook has never yet been nibbled.
You must plunge into the sea and seize your catch deep down —
do not linger on the shallow shoals among the reeds.
Two Songs of Homesickness
I left my home village at the age of twelve. Now it is sixty years. It happened that a man of my village sent word asking after me in the mountains, and so I wrote these.

Tall willows before the gate mirrored in the clear pool;
I always remember the children at play in the water.
More than sixty years, a thing like a dream —
how many times it still stirs my longing for the old garden.

A belt of blue hills winds around the river;
my home stood by the old ferry on the bank.
I left the village young and now am old —
this heart runs on unbroken as the endless water.
Thinking of the Master of Longhua in the Great Capital

Beneath the Longhua tree, a man of karmic bond;
since we parted, no one matches the closeness we once had.
How many times my dream-soul has flown to the night moon —
even if we met, it would never be real.
Entering the Mountains

Straight into a thousand peaks, never weary of the depth;
in the most secluded, uttermost place the mind can rest.
Let the pine gate gather moss as thick as it will —
from now on the people of the world will find no way to seek me.
Two Poems in Reply to Venerable Fu Wu'ang, Master of the Caoxi Hall

Since I left Caoxi, ten springs have passed;
I often long for one sip of its fragrant water.
In dreams my soul still sits beneath the pine shade —
I only fear this life is a later body still.

By the stream the plum's fragrance never fails;
how often its scented mist has damped my robe.
In recent years, whenever I come to a place to view the blossoms,
it is just as when I once sat in the Dharma Hall.
Seeing Off Master Xi of Green Forest on His Journey to the Southern Marchmount

I recall how I once climbed the Seventy Peaks,
leaning on heaven, companion to the sun, stroking the tall pines.
Through hidden crags and sheer ravines I searched out every wonder —
go now and seek the tracks my staff once left.

Deep among ten thousand peaks the green clouds are cold;
there I once built a thatched hut and studied Lazy Repose.
The fire for roasting taro is still buried in cow dung —
go stir the earthen stove and see for yourself.
Written at Random

The limpid sea, its waves becalmed, holds not one thing;
in the cold sky deep night, the moon's wheel stands alone.
Just see the ten thousand miles where not a wisp of cloud remains —
you will know your own ice-clear heart within its jade jar.
Rejoicing That My Old Mother Has Sent My Brother to Me

Kin of one blood take pity, sharing a single stem;
the lord's grace has granted me one body back.
If a day of living return should come at last,
I may still wait upon my kind mother.
Remembering My Old Home

My home stood on the shady side of Turtle Hill,
just like a bend along the Ganges.
And I remember, as a child,
how hot we were, bathing in the river.

On either bank the willow shade was thick;
at the door the southern hills were green.
With my own hands I planted a green-blossomed peach —
I do not know if it is still there.

Before the gate there was a little bridge;
as a child I saw the water wash it out.
I wanted to frame it with a single log;
the road was far and it was never done.
Remembering Friends of My Village

When we were small we studied together,
sharing one bed and one quilt.
Who would have thought that once we parted,
in a blink we would be sixty years old?

And I remember when we piled up sand,
our games together always ending in a quarrel.
I recall only a boy's face —
I cannot believe the two of us are old now.
Remembering the Hermitage in My Home Hills

My storied dwelling joined the water and the bamboo;
through long summer, clear breeze and sleep in broad daylight.
Today, beyond ten thousand miles of burning wilds,
looking back, it seems a life or two ago.
The Dream-Journey Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Fifty

blocks.text: Record of the Revival of Caoxi

inline.s: Recorded day by day by the bodhisattva-precept disciple, the monk Ben'ang, Feng Changli, and the monk Zhirong
Compiled by the official disciples Wang Anshun and Liu Qixiang
Collated by the Changchun Society disciples Chen Dixiang and Liang Sixiang
Record of the Revival of Caoxi, Part One
The Causes of the Revival

The Master said: Caoxi takes its name from Cao Shuliang of old, a descendant of Emperor Wu of Wei, who took refuge here. Its Way-site begins with the holy monk Tripiṭaka Master Jñānaphala of Liang, who came by sea from the Western Heaven and brought a bodhi tree to the Faxing Monastery of Wuyang. His prophecy ran: “In one hundred and sixty years a bodhisattva in the flesh will leave home here and save countless beings.” As he came into the range he passed the mouth of the Caoxi stream, scooped up water and drank; it was sweet and fragrant. “This is the water of my Western Heaven,” he said. “Above its source there must be a holy place.” So he followed the stream up and viewed its mountain, which looked like an elephant. “This mountain is just like Bīn-lin Mountain in my Western Heaven,” he said, and told the resident Cao Shuliang: “A monastery should be built on this mountain. In one hundred and sixty years a bodhisattva in the flesh will preach the Dharma here.” Shuliang reported it to the provincial governor, who memorialized the throne, and Emperor Wu of Liang ordered a monastery built with the plaque Baolin — this was the beginning of the mountain's founding.

In the Longshuo period of the Tang there was an adept named Lu of Xinzhou who received the robe and bowl of Huangmei and was known as the Sixth Patriarch. He returned to Caoxi, but by then Baolin had fallen into ruin. A nun named Wujin met the Sixth Patriarch and questioned him on the meaning of the Nirvāṇa Sutra; recognizing him as no ordinary man, she told her father and brothers, and they rebuilt Baolin and invited the Patriarch to dwell there. Before long someone plotted against the Patriarch; he fled for safety to Huai and Hui and hid among a band of hunters for fifteen years. Later he came to the Faxing Monastery in Wuyang, where his worth showed itself; he had his head shaved beneath the bodhi tree and returned at once to Caoxi, opening the Dharma at Baolin. By then the mountain had changed owners and belonged to the Chen family. The Patriarch taught for many years and great crowds gathered. Because the mountain is like a living elephant with tusks and trunk complete, the first monastery stood inside the great tusk of the left jaw, while the trunk lies to the right, where the ancestral graves of the Chen family already were, so the temple site was very cramped. One day the Patriarch asked the resident Chen Yaxian for the ground of one sitting-mat. Yaxian agreed, and when the Patriarch spread his mat it covered all the ridges of the four mountains. Then the Four Heavenly Kings appeared at the four corners, and Yaxian at once consented, saying: “I know the Master's Dharma-power is vast; I shall give it all. But my forebears' graves lie to the right of the temple; when you build in days to come, I beg you to keep them.” He added: “The form of this mountain is the coming vein of a living dragon and white elephant. When you build hereafter, you may level only what touches the sky, never the ground.” Then Yaxian took his family and withdrew into hiding; where he went is unknown. Thus from the time the Sixth Patriarch founded this mountain, all within the Four Heavenly Kings' ring, some tens of miles around, was one monastery, with no dwellings of laypeople. The mountain's form and its wind and air were whole and dense; even among all the ancestral Way-sites of the patriarchs from Shaolin onward, none could match its excellence. Monks always treated it as a place of hidden cultivation. Down to the beginning of our dynasty, when fields were opened, all within the ring of mountains became farmland entered on the tax registers, so monks took farming as their basic livelihood, planting, grafting, and breeding, no different from laymen. Yet there had never been lay dwellings there. In the Hongzhi and Zhengde reigns, drifters from every quarter gradually gathered in the mountains. At first they hired themselves out; in time they set up in business with capital borrowed from the monks, and the monks did not notice. Since the mountain gate led to Wengyuan and was a main road into the prefecture, the drifters gradually made it a den, spread along the roadside and opened shops and stalls. Was this only magpies seizing the magpie's nest? It would soon be wolves squatting in the lion's cave. The monks too abandoned the temple and lived on the estates, so the mountain gate grew emptier by day, the drifters gathered by day, and harm arose by day, until the monks were caught in these entanglements and could barely preserve the place at all.

In the spring of the bing-shen year I was graced with exile beyond the range. When first I entered the mountains to bow to the Patriarch, I saw how ruinous and unbearable things had become; before long the disaster indeed broke out and the monks were scattered. At once those in authority hastened to rescue the situation. At first the Commander-in-Chief Lord Chen wished me to go and set it right; before that could happen, the Surveillance Commissioner Lord Zhou of Haimen, who had great concern for the ancestral Way, was already at work on it, and presently left to offer congratulations. The Circuit Commissioner Lord Zhu then urged me most earnestly. Thereupon certain monks of the temple came one after another to take refuge, asked to receive the full precepts, and pressed their request with firm resolve; I consented. In the ninth month of the autumn of the geng-zi year I entered the mountains and took the ancestral courtyard to heart. I staked body and life on it, ordering each matter one by one and establishing them in due sequence, as listed below. In sum, all was a shattered ruin beyond repair, not to be endured a single day. Happily, relying on the spirit of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and the protection of the Dharma by those in authority, with unseen divine aid, in eight years some order was achieved. Though the work was not brought to final completion, my heart and strength were utterly spent. What was built can all serve as lasting rule; if the monks can from now on keep it carefully and not lose it, this Way-site may be preserved and be free of care for generation after generation. At that time the Master directed Changli and the others to remain in the temple to instruct the novices; everything done was witnessed by them, and every word spoken was recorded the same day. In time it became a volume, entitled Veritable Record of the Revival, following the pattern of the ten chapters of the Tongxin and arranged in ten sections; his instructions to the assembly, the pure rules, his letters, and miscellaneous writings are set out in order after them.
Nurturing the Ancestral Dragon to Complete the Site's Fengshui

When the Master first entered the mountains and saw the ancestral courtyard in ruin, he gathered his disciples and said: The Buddha taught that the great earth and its mountains and rivers are fused and formed by the One Mind alone. Though the words of geomancers are not all to be trusted, the highest principle is present in them. When Yaxian first gave up the land he said that this mountain was the coming vein of a living dragon and white elephant, and that in building hereafter one might level only what touches the sky, never the ground. This means the lie of the land must not be injured. Look at the host mountain of Caoxi: it is plainly shaped like an elephant, with four feet and six tusks, trunk and mouth complete. When Baolin was first founded the mountain's form was whole and dense, so the temple sat within the jaw, wrapped by the great tusk on the left and joined with the tusk on the right. Inside the lips was the Dragon Pool, which is the elephant's mouth. The right wall of Baolin is plainly the elephant's trunk, and the ancestral grave of Chen Yaxian was buried upon it first. In the Sixth Patriarch's day it stood just outside the Baolin wall — hence he asked for that ground and enlarged the site. The mouth is the Dragon Pool, where water gathered and a dragon dwelled. When the Patriarch subdued that dragon he cut through the point where the two tusks meet, drained the water and filled the pool in order to raise the Buddha Hall. But once the dragon had shed its form and the water was gone, the sacred energy leaked away; the Buddha Hall was complete, yet the pool was never fully filled when the Patriarch passed into stillness. To this day the space before the hall is still a deep pit — an unfinished work from former days. Thus the altar terrace reached only halfway. The Master understood the cause and filled it level. The former Arhat Tower stands where the ridge was first cut through; later men made it the mountain gate, and in time built a tower above. The Master wished to alter and repair it but had not the time. The elephant's feeding depends on its trunk, and its life lies in the trunk; the trunk should have several joints, and the Chen grave lies right at its center. So when the Sixth Patriarch entered nirvāṇa, his preserved body was first placed in a wooden pagoda built before the grave for offerings, and behind the grave the Faith-Offering Pavilion was built to house the robe and bowl. In the Chenghua period of our Ming, a certain monk removed the wooden pagoda and replaced it with brick; the interior was damp and dark, and before long the Patriarch appeared in a dream to the prefect, asking for a lodging. The prefect ordered the Faith-Offering Pavilion changed into the Patriarch's Hall, and the empty pagoda left in front became a lump of obstruction in the site's breast. Behind the Patriarch's Hall was the Cheng-Su Pavilion, built in the bing-wu year of Jiajing by the prefect Chen Baogu. When the Master arrived he saw the abbot's quarters to the left of the hall, with a path cut straight through the middle into the back mountain, slicing the elephant's trunk; and behind the hall the ground was low, prey to the north wind, so the incoming vein was injured. This was the very cause of the Way-site's decline. Examining the shape of the elephant's trunk, the Master reckoned that behind the hall there ought to be a high mound. Then an old monk told him: when I was first a novice I saw a heap behind the hall like a piled mound; when Lord Chen built the pavilion he had the monks scrape it away, and I, then a novice, was among those carrying off the earth. The Master knew this was true, so he had the monks selected as instructors in the Three Studies lead more than a hundred novices in their studies to carry ten loads of earth each day to bank it up. In three months a hill was made, as though it had always been there. Then he moved the central path to the side of the Caoxi and made it a winding corridor that curves right around the ancestral courtyard and leads into the back mountain. Only then was the site's fengshui whole. Within the mountain gate he removed every inauspicious feature, and the monks were at peace. Behind the ancestral hall there is a ravine crossed by the Flying-Tin Bridge; past the bridge is the Staff-Planting Spring, the elephant's throat. The Master led that spring into the incense kitchen. To the right of the spring a small ridge is shaped like a tongue, and right of that a hollow like a clamp — the right jaw. In old times this was the hermitage where the nun Wujin lived, she who was the chief patron of Baolin's revival; so when the Master restored the tradition he rebuilt it first of all. This was the very beginning of his work on entering the mountains.
Renewing the Ancestral Courtyard to Inspire Reverence

The ancestral courtyard was at first made by converting the Faith-Offering Pavilion, and it was exceedingly mean and cramped. Entering the gate, one could not make out the Patriarch's countenance; there was no room to array the rows for worship. In front, moreover, a worship hall joined its eaves to the roof, making it very dark. A pagoda stood tall before the grave, and beyond the pagoda the halls of the gods were layered upon one another, broken and patched together, so that at the very front there was not a crack of open ground. Near the left of the hall were monks' rooms, huddled like a fist propping up a chin; at the lower right was the household chief's kitchen, heaped with filth. The monks' quarters on either flank had sagging beams, like a thicket of thorns. Seen from outside, the buildings were jagged and gaping, with not one clear line of sight through. This is why the ancestral Way was blocked and could not flow freely. The Master saw deeply how hard it would be to open the place up; he thought day and night, yet could devise no plan to make a coherent whole. Often he climbed the pagoda and gazed out, carefully observing the whole temple's layout. To the left were the abbot's quarters, the Dharma Hall, and the Chan Hall; in front stood the bell and drum towers, flanking it into one unit. The Master said: this must have been the original arrangement when Baolin was first founded. To the right was the Buddha Hall, which the Patriarch built by filling the Dragon Pool in his own day; behind it the sutra pavilion, in front the Arhat Tower, and the Baolin mountain gate, all forming one unit. Later men made poor additions, so the Patriarch's Hall ended up in the middle with monks' quarters mixed in around it, choking the spirit path and leaving no air of reverence at all. Now, if one would sort it out thread by thread and give it a proper plan, what hand but a giant spirit's could cleave it apart?

So seeing that the hill west of the Arhat Tower was like a tiger turning its head to look back, the Master bought that hill and took its earth to fill the pool-pit before the great hall, raising the ground so as to move the monks' quarters left of the Patriarch's Hall. He also bought other houses to exchange for the monks' rooms behind the sutra pavilion, making them into public offices for the household chief, and so removed the filth at the western corner of the Patriarch's Hall. The monks of the two corridors were each given separate dwellings. The halls of the gods and the worship hall in front were demolished, and at once the ground before one was level as a palm. Then he threw himself into the work with all his strength, and everything came out as he had pictured it. So he was able to rebuild the Patriarch's Hall, lofty and fair to see, with two side halls before it to enshrine the images of the five schools from Nanyue and Qingyuan. The gate house had fifteen bays around it, meant to enshrine the patriarchs of the Lamp Transmission and their descendants, like the seventy disciples offered sacrifice alongside Confucius. But the path in front was still choked, so he bought open ground and moved three monks' quarters that stood in the way, opening a great spirit path that runs level with the Baolin gate and abreast of the Arhat Tower. He raised a three-bay Avatamsaka Tower as the head gate of the ancestral courtyard, and above it a Chan Hall where the monks copy the Avatamsaka Sutra. Thus, naturally, it became a noble prospect. Visitors today see only that all is clear at a glance, and do not know how hard the opening up of it was to accomplish.
Selecting Monks of Conduct to Nurture Talent

The monks of this temple had long been at ease living on the estates, planting and breeding, no different from laymen. Of the temple's hundred quarters, every door was barred, and once inside the gate not a soul was to be seen — only a few monks tending the incense at the Patriarch's Hall and a few in the abbot's quarters. Thus drifters ran wild at the mountain gate while the monks came and went hiding their shadows and covering their tracks. It was hateful. When the Master first arrived, he put the nurturing of talent first. He selected the whole temple's monks: those over forty were left to their own convenience; those under forty and over twenty, one or two from each quarter, were to dwell in the temple at peace, going up to the halls every day and reciting the four daily liturgies to pray for the Emperor's long life, and those who failed were fined in varying degrees. Thus more than a hundred monks gathered, and all were given the precepts. From then on bells and drums sounded at dawn and dusk, and the sound of sutras continued unbroken — a noble Way-site indeed. The monks came to know they had a proper calling, and outside insults gradually learned caution. But the monks' habits had become the custom; when a young boy left home he saw only his teacher busy with farming, no different from a layman, and never knew what the monastic calling was. Those who raised disciples sought only their usefulness in the fields, and not one word was ever said of what lies beyond the world. This had gone on so long that to hope for men of worth was impossible. At the very start of his time in the temple the Master chose from the assembly those of learning fit to be teachers — Ben'ang and two others — and urged all the monks that any novices under twenty and above eight should report their names to the abbot and be gathered in the temple; three study halls were set up with three instructors to teach the scriptures. Within a year, those who could handle two of the daily liturgies were then taught by Confucian scholars — the licentiate Feng Changli and the talented youths Long Zhang and Liang Sixiang — in the Four Books, expounding their principles and meaning. Their tuition and provisions the Master supplied himself. Thus after three years those who succeeded were shaved and ordained as monks and entered the Chan Hall to learn the rules of the monastic life, each to have his own work in cultivation, recitation, and copying the scriptures. The monks now in the Chan Hall are all talents the Master nurtured. He also said: what the Buddhadharma values is that perfuming and hearing become seeds. Lingnan had long lacked the perfuming of the Buddhadharma, and for want of seeds faith was hard to arouse. So he first had the newly ordained novices copy the great Avatamsaka Sutra: first, because the Dharma-connection is vast and makes the supreme seed; second, because the power of concentration in copying supports the beginner's contemplation and aids the provisions for entering the Way. At first there were two or three; soon everyone looked to one another and brought forth the resolve. Within ten years those who copied this sutra had completed more than ten sets. Such was the Master's work of making people — plainly evident.
Driving Out the Drifters to Wash Away the Stench and Filth

The Master saw that the ruin of the Caoxi Way-site was because drifters from every quarter had gathered in the mountains for more than a hundred years, entrenched beyond dislodging, while laymen's graves filled the valleys and were treated as their own property. It began with hired labor; in time they set up in business, borrowing capital from the monks, and outside the mountain gate they built houses and opened shops — butchery, wine-selling, gambling, and lewdness — and the harm grew daily. Yet the foolish monks did not notice, but grew intimate with them and wormed their way into their favor, each profiting from the other, so that much of what the monks raised fell into their hands. As the gnawing went deeper they turned to lawless schemes, luring men with many devices and setting wine and lust as pits and snares. Once the blind fell in, they were devoured at will and their fat and grease quite drained. Thus many of the monks' fields, mountain lands, and houses were forfeited on this account. Lately the local strongmen too cast greedy eyes that way, colluded with the yamen ruffians, and schemed together; under the pretext of harboring villains they laid accusations before the prefecture and the circuit, using it as a handle to work their swindle, alarming their superiors and shocking their hearing, until it was taken for truth. Then a petition was sent up to the military headquarters, and the order came down that the estates were all to be demolished and monks who broke the rules driven out. The men who received the order were without conscience; trusting their informants, they took it as a windfall. They came into the mountains in person to survey, and at every estate they appraised its full value, so that half had to be paid before one escaped. Thus the temple monks all fell into the net and had already lost half, while the harm was still spreading, with not a moment's peace. In the second year after the Master crossed the range, the ding-you year, he first paid his respects to the Commander-in-Chief Lord Chen and was able to lay out the monks' situation in general, whereupon the order was stayed and they were fortunate to escape. Lord Chen wished at once to send the Master to set matters right, but as he was still in mourning seclusion he did not presume to accept. The next year, wu-xu, Lord Zhou of the Salt and Grain Circuit, acting for Nan-Shao, wished to rescue the situation and asked the Master to compile a gazetteer; before long he left to offer congratulations. In ji-hai, Lord Zhu of the Nan-Shao Circuit took up his post, calling himself a wandering monk of Caoxi; grieving deeply over these abuses, he urged the Master with all his strength to set them in order. In the geng-zi year, Lord Zhu too left to offer congratulations, and on the eve of his departure gave his instructions face to face and had the temple monks earnestly invite the Master to accept the charge. So in the ninth month he entered the mountains. Seeing these men running wild, he knew they were the disease at the very heart of the ancestral courtyard: unless cured, the Sixth Patriarch's wisdom-life could never be saved. So, using the occasion of adjusting the fengshui, he blocked off the great road at the mountain gate to east and west and moved it to the streamside, running straight to the water mouth as the thoroughfare. In this way the former shops and inns were all enclosed inside the mountain gate, and travelers found food and lodging inconvenient. Yet in the end there was no means to remove them.

After three months, at the year's end, he went to pay his respects to the Commander-in-Chief Lord Dai and laid out the whole story of the harm. Lord Dai said: this is the duty of a Dharma-protector. Simply issue one order and charge the local authorities to enforce it strictly; this is the business of a single constable. On New Year's day the order went to the county, which sat watch and drove them out, not leaving a single man; the shops were all demolished, not one tile left. Thus the stench and filth gathered at the mountain gate over more than a hundred years was washed away in a single morning, and the monks' calamity was ended forever. Once the shops were torn down, the market street stood empty.
