I said: The work is great and the cost much; my strength does not reach it. He asked how much would be needed, and I answered with a certain sum. The Duke said: No difficulty; let me try to do it. On returning he told Governor-General Dai. The Duke said: How perilous! When one sees a child about to fall into a well, one must crawl to save it; how much more with Buddhas and bodhisattvas in such a dangerous place — not to be moved would be inhuman. Then he asked the cost, and the Duke was told what I had said. The Duke said: That is still not enough. He at once instructed the circuit of Nan Shao to go and survey and estimate, and also had me summoned for a face-to-face discussion. I went to see him, and the Duke was eager to build it entirely himself. I said to him: If we trouble the public funds, I fear it will not be fitting. If we follow the old practice of the Dharma gate, let me solicit from the many. The Duke instructed the circuit of Lingxi to make twelve solicitation registers, one for each of the three provincial offices, the circuit and the prefecture, to give as they wished; the sums were all gathered at the prefecture and handed over as one, without passing through the monks' hands. In this way it would be no burden and would be easily collected. The Duke followed it, and within a month nearly a thousand gold was gathered. I went in person to western Yue to select great timber, and reached Duanzhou. The governor's office kept me to repair the Baoyue Terrace, and separately appointed officials to procure the timber. In winter the Baoyue Terrace was completed and I wrote its record. The timber was all piled on the bank of the Duan River and transported in order. In the beginning of the eleventh month of winter the Annam rebels breached Qinzhou. Duke Dai asked for the imperial army to mount a distant punitive expedition, and because of this he was impeached and dismissed.
The Thirty-Seventh Year, Jiyou (1609).

I was sixty-four. In the second month of spring I was returning with the timber from the Duan River when the wind blocked us at the Antelope Gorge. I toured the Duan Stream and wrote the Record of a Dream Journey to the Duan Stream. The timber was transported to Mengjiang, and I returned to the temple. Just as I was gathering the assembly to manage the work, one or two unworthy men in the crowd stirred up trouble and made opposition, rousing the crowd to riot like rebels. Seeing it I sighed and said: This is my own heavy offense against the Buddha's teaching, the fault of grasping at appearances. While the crowd was still clamoring, I sat alone in the hall, burned incense and recited the Vajra Prajñā Sutra. Before, I had only recited the text and truly did not understand its meaning; now I suddenly had an awakening and wrote the Resolution of Doubts on the Diamond Sutra. When the draft was done, the crowd was silent. The unworthy did not believe, and my heart grew more fearful. So I brought suit at the censorate, which approved it and sent it to the judicial office. At that time I drifted out of the mountains to await judgment, living on a boat on the Furong River for two years. My funds were exhausted. Vice-Prefect Xiang Chudong, in charge of the pass at Hanguang, invited me to come. On the river we met a wind that broke the boat, and when I arrived I fell gravely ill and nearly died; the Duke called physicians who saved me with all their strength. When I returned to the prefecture I lay ill at an inn for nearly a year.
The Thirty-Eighth Year, Gengxu (1610).

I was sixty-five. That year I lay ill at the inn. In the seventh month of autumn the direct commissioner made his circuit and, reaching the prefecture, inquired about me; the judicial officer, hearing of it, then took up the case, and turned the charge back upon me. The direct commissioner strongly disapproved and rejected it, saying: This man has done great service for the Sixth Patriarch. What he gave up was intended as permanent property for the temple; now wicked monks profit and he is charged instead — is that what is called the equal Dharma gate? He again sent it to this circuit for strict investigation. Thereupon the prefecture came in person to the mountains and, following the monks' plaint, examined it item by item, and all was false speech without foundation. They falsely accused me of seizing more than eight thousand in permanent property. When I first set up the storehouse office and pure rules for the permanent property I established numbered receipts; for every receipt and expenditure of money and grain there were the supervising monk and the secretary, and every trifle that went out or came in was supported by a numbered receipt and never issued rashly. Now when the officials examined and calculated, taking the numbered receipts as the standard, not a hair was found to touch me. Then those above and below, within and without, believed that I was not reckless. The matter was thus made clear. The authorities were greatly angered at the monks and repeatedly asked me to stay in the mountains; but my heart was already weary and I firmly declined. I lodged at the Changchun Hermitage in Wuyang.
The Thirty-Ninth Year, Xinhai (1611).

I was sixty-six. In the third month of spring I dwelt at Dinghu Mountain in Duanzhou to nurse my illness. At first I had received the pardon and was awaiting the memorial; there had been no reply from the censorate, and so it was delayed until now. Again a re-examination was ordered and made clear, and only then was the case cancelled and I was free to do as I pleased. At that time scholars gathered about me seeking instruction, and I wrote the Resolution of Doubts on the Great Learning.
The Fortieth Year, Renzi (1612).

I was sixty-seven. I dwelt at the Changchun Hermitage and for my disciples expounded the Awakening of Faith and the Verses on the Eight Consciousnesses, and composed the Direct Explanation of the Hundred Dharmas. Because the text and meaning of my Rhythmic Beats on the Lotus Sutra were joined without division and hard for students to grasp, I wrote the Chapter and Section Division.
The Forty-First Year, Guichou (1613).

I was sixty-eight. I dwelt at the Changchun Hermitage. In summer, while expounding the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment for my disciples, I was only halfway through when a carbuncle broke out on my back. The physicians could not cure it and I was near death. General Wang Hanchong had already arranged my funeral affairs. A Cantonese named Liang Xingshan was a drunkard, but was known for treating sores. He happened to come and look, and said: It is grave; a little later and it cannot be saved. Be at ease, there is no harm. He gathered only herbs and applied them, and the effect followed at once, as easily as juggling balls; he fixed a time for the cure. By winter I was healed, and I wrote a piece to thank him. This carbuncle had arisen from the time I first sat in Chan; I knew it was a karmic debt. When I recited the Flower Ornament Sutra and asked leave, it would secretly break out each time I wrote or recited the Flower Ornament; with prayer it would stop. Even here in Guangdong it had twice failed to come to a head. It had been a trouble in my body for forty-eight years. When it first arose I happened to forget it, and did not know it was a carbuncle, and so it became a grave illness. Truly the repayment of karmic debt, tested upon the body, does not miss. In the tenth month my illness was cured. Earlier I had made a pact with Zeng Jinjian, a ministry official of Hengyang, to retire in old age at Nanyue, and had written more than ten letters without being able to go. Now he wrote to invite me, so I took up my staff and went, and so left Guangdong. When I first came to Guangdong several tens of disciples of Faxing followed me; over time they gradually fell away, and only Tongjiong, Chaoyi and the rest followed me through wind and waves, hardship and illness, never leaving my side. Now that I was about to go, none could bear it and all wished to come. Jiong still had entanglements, so he delayed a little and followed later with his pack. In the eleventh month of that year I reached Hudong. Earlier my disciple Fushan had taken the attendant Shenguang and gone north to visit relatives; now within a few days they too caught up with me.
The Forty-Second Year, Jiayin (1614).

I was sixty-nine. In the first month of spring I roamed Mount De and paid my respects to the Patriarch, writing four poems. I visited Duke Feng Yuancheng at Wuling and met Long Canzhi at Zhuling; I received the vegetarian feast of Prince Rong, and the monks of Dashan Temple asked to receive the precepts. Duke Feng and his companions each donated funds to build the Tanhua Retreat. In the fourth month of summer I returned to Hudong. Hearing that the Empress Dowager had passed away, I at once established a way-place of requiting kindness. There was a decree of grace, so before the spirit shrine I shaved my head again to give thanks, and resumed the monk's robe. Then I wept bitterly, saying: How sad! The benefactor is gone, and the vow for this temple is ended. Can I wait for another rebirth? As for the Surangama Sutra, from the Eastern Sea I had resolved to write a Comprehensive Commentary, and had long cherished it in my breast without leisure to set it down. Now in the fifth month of summer I first took up my brush, and in fifty days the draft was complete. In the eleventh month the retreat was finished, and I wrote poems On Dwelling in the Mountains. I gave the leaving-home ordination to the attendant Cili.
The Forty-Third Year, Yimao (1615).

I was seventy. In spring I expounded the Comprehensive Commentary on the Surangama Sutra for the assembly. In the fourth month of summer I wrote the Comprehensive Meaning of the Lotus Sutra, because although there were already two sections, the whole text was not yet fused and joined, so I set it forth again; in fifty days the draft was complete. I compiled the Brief Commentary on the Awakening of Faith. In the eighth month of autumn I roamed Nanyue, and on the Mid-Autumn day I climbed Zhurong Peak. On the ninth day of autumn Duke Feng was transferred from Wuling to be prefect of Hunan, and I accompanied him on a tour to Fangguang Temple and back. Circuit Commissioner Wu Shengbai of the censorate came to visit me at Hudong and spoke of the Surangama Sutra. Duke Wu was overjoyed and at once donated with his subordinates to have it carved. I paid homage to the portraits of the eighty-eight patriarchs, and Duke Wu greatly praised them; he had painters copy the small portraits into an album and asked me to write a biography and praise for each. Duke Feng had not been long in his post when he asked me to tour Jiuyi. In the tenth month of winter I reached Lingling and stayed the winter at Yuxi.
The Forty-Fourth Year, Bingchen (1616).

I was seventy-one. In the first month of spring I returned from Lingling. Fang Yimin had just come back from official travels and was relying on me at Hudong; I named him Fuxin Geng. Earlier, in the year after Chan Master Daguan entered extinction, my disciple Dayi asked that his spirit shrine be brought south, and monks and lay disciples made offerings to it at the Jizhao Hermitage on Jing Mountain. Now it was twelve years, and I could not forget the bond of the Dharma gate. I had long wished to go in person to mourn him, and so had not even sent incense. Just then I heard of the burial, and was determined to go. As I was about to set out, the monks of Huayao Temple asked me for a vegetarian feast and to continue the Dharma lineage. I toured the Plum and Snow Hall and mourned Chan Master Xun'an. In the fourth month of summer I left Hudong, writing poems to explain my leaving Nanyue. Kuang Muyi, Fang Yimin and He Zhongyi and others saw me off as far as the Camphor Wood Market. In the fifth month I reached Wuchang and met the Remonstrating Censor Duan Huanran; I paid my respects at the Great Buddha and roamed the Nine Peaks. In the sixth month I reached Xunyang, toured Donglin and wrote poems of remembrance of the past. I climbed Mount Kuang, mourned Chan Master Chekong, and took refuge from the heat at Jinzhu Flat, where I commented on the Zhao Lun. Seeing the mountain's secluded beauty, I had thoughts of retiring there, but on looking everywhere there was nowhere habitable. In the seventh month I toured Guizong, climbed the Golden Wheel Peak, and paid homage at the Relic Stupa, writing poems. A monk offered me the Five Milks as a quiet retreat; I climbed to view the site and found it not broad, but its setting quite secluded, and so I accepted it. The layman Xing Laici of Jiangzhou, a disciple of Master Da, wished to be my gold-giving benefactor, and so I had the thought of ending my days there. Duke Chen Chishi, a great counselor of Fuliang, came into the mountains to visit me; hearing that I had thoughts of Mount Kuang he too wished to be a protector of the Dharma. In the eighth month of autumn I left the mountain and went to Huangmei, paid my respects at the Fourth and Fifth Patriarchs' shrines, and visited Sima Wang. Entering the Purple Cloud Mountains I stayed ten days, and Duke Wang wished to be the benefactor for the building at Mount Kuang. I took leave and went to Xiangcheng, visited the Grand Historian Wu Guanwo and the Censor-in-Chief Wu Benru, who wished to build the Ruyi Hermitage to keep me. I roamed Mount Fu and crossed the river to Mount Jiuhua. In the beginning of the tenth month I reached Jinsha. The Wang clan of that place, with Chan Master Langya Yao of Dongchan, welcomed me to stay. Presently I went to Shuangjing, and the layman Yan Shengzhi of Shimen welcomed me at Wujiang, so I went to his house. He prepared provisions for the journey to accompany me. On the full moon of the long solstice month I reached Jizhao. On the nineteenth day I performed the cremation service for Great Master Da, first writing a piece to sacrifice to him. I had fixed this day beforehand and it was not missed; those who knew thought it strange. On the twenty-fifth day I gathered the sacred bones with my own hands and enshrined them at the Manjushri Terrace. My disciple Fakai built the stupa with me, and I wrote the inscription on the stupa, fulfilling the bond of the Dharma gate for a lifetime. So I stayed to see the year out, at times giving brief instruction to the monks of the meditation hall; there is the Essential Points of Chan Practice. Master Kai sought instruction on the Yogacara school, and I set forth the General Explanation of Nature and Characteristics. To those who sought instruction I each gave Dharma words, and composed the Pole-Bearer's Song. The Cantonese disciple Tong'an had taken leave earlier; only Chaoyi went with Fushan and other disciples, and the Dharma grandsons Shenguang, Guangyi, Guangshe and Ciban accompanied me.
The Forty-Fifth Year, Dingsi (1617).

I was seventy-two. In the first month of spring I went down to Shuangjing to mourn at Yunqi. At that time more than a thousand monks and lay disciples had long waited for me in the mountains and kept me twenty days. Every night they heard the Dharma in brief instruction, and each was filled with joy. I set forth the secret practices of Master Lianchi's life; hearing it, some disciples wept, saying that I revealed what others did not know. Then they asked me to write a stupa inscription. On my return, Dharma Master Xuanjin He and the officials and laymen of the whole prefecture — Censor-in-Chief Jin, Ministry Official Yu, Grand Counselor Weng and others — asked me to stay at the Zongjing Hall of Jingci. Each day several thousand fingers encircled me as I expounded the great precepts, and I wrote the Record of the Zongjing Hall. Virtuous Dharma masters from every mountain and every road all gathered on the lake to ask about the Dharma, each raising questions and objections; people said it was the greatest Dharma assembly of the southeast, such as had never been seen before. Then I roamed Lingyin, the Three Zhu Temples and the Western Hills and other famous sites, praised the three life-releasing ponds, and set out. The officials and laymen of the city prepared boats, released living creatures and gave me a farewell feast on the lake, and also drew up a petition asking me to stay at Yunqi; so there was a three-year agreement. Then I set out. All the pieces written along the way were collected by Dharma Master Xuanjin He and the scholar Tan Mengxun into four volumes of the Eastern Journey Collection and carved. Returning to Wumen, the two Dharma masters Chaosong and Yiyu asked me to enter Hua Mountain and tour the scenic spots of Tianchi, Xuanmu and Tieshan. The laymen Hanshan Zhao Fanfu, Yan Tianchi, Xu Zhongrong, Yao Mengchang, Wen Wenqi and Xu Qingzhi made offerings in the mountains; the two officials Feng Yuancheng and Shen Xuanzhu gave me a vegetarian feast at home. As I was about to set out, my disciples Dongwen and Hanyue had long been waiting. The Grand Historian Qian Shouzhi came in person to welcome me to Changshu, and so I reached Mount Yu and stayed two nights. The Grand Historian saw me off to Quhe; He Zhiren, father and son and nephew, waited at the Three-Li Hermitage at Benniu and asked me to stay in their garden for the summer retreat, but I firmly declined. They saw me off to Jingkou, and after receiving the vegetarian feast of monks and laymen at Sanshan I at once returned to Mount Kuang. On the first day of the fifth month I passed Baixia and stayed one night on the river, saw one or two old friends, and at once set sail westward. On the fifth day I reached Wuhu, where Liu Yushou, a ministry official, detained me with hospitality, and I wrote the Record of a Strange Dream. Ministry Official Cui Helou overtook me and met me on the river. On the sixteenth day of the fifth month the boat anchored at Xingzhu, and I arrived at Guizong. I had lodged there only a short while when Sima Wang, having already prepared funds beforehand, built a quiet retreat for me. On the fifteenth day of the sixth month my disciple Fushan began to break ground at the Five Milks, and by the end of the tenth month a room was at last finished, and I could settle in peace. I began expounding the Surangama Sutra for the assembly. My disciple Chaoyi shut himself in a death cell at the Golden Wheel Peak.
The Forty-Sixth Year, Wuwu (1618).

I was seventy-three. That year I built the Buddha hall and the meditation hall. In the third month Duke Chen Chishi of Fuliang entered the mountains, and with Bao Zhongsu and Xia Wozhai he formed a group of ten friends to aid the building funds. In the twelfth month of winter the halls were completed.
The Forty-Seventh Year, Jiwei (1619).

I was seventy-four. In the first month of spring my Cantonese disciple Tongjiong arrived. So I opened the hall and began the recitation of the Flower Ornament Sutra and held a long-term assembly, expounding for the assembly the Lotus, Surangama, Diamond and Awakening of Faith sutras and the treatises on Consciousness-Only. I appointed Jiong as head of the assembly. In the seventh month of autumn I made the Five Milks a permanent home for the aged from the ten directions. At the full moon of the eighth month I shut my gate and withdrew from affairs, imitating Master Huiyuan's six periods of incense in place of the water clock, and gave myself wholly to the Pure Land practice. I often thought that the Flower Ornament school would be lost to transmission, and that Qingliang's Subcommentary was feared by all for its vastness, beyond the reach of mind and intellect, so that people mostly set it aside and relied only on the Combined Treatise. But I reflected that Qingliang was the ancestor of the writings of this land; if he were abandoned, the school would lose its lineage. I resolved to set forth only the subcommentary text, drawing out its great purport so that readers might easily understand it, entitling it the Essential Outline. In the retreat I began to read, revise and cut. In winter, within the retreat, I expounded the Lankavatara and the Awakening of Faith for the assembly.
The Forty-Eighth Year, Gengshen (1620), which is the first year of Taichang.

I was seventy-five. In spring, after the recitation periods, my attendant Guangyi asked me to set forth again the Awakening of Faith and the Direct Explanation of the Perfect Enlightenment, and to annotate the seven inner chapters of Zhuangzi. In summer I was ill with pain in the feet. Duke Wu, formerly circuit commissioner of Hengyang, was transferred to the judgeship of Guangdong and entered Caoxi to pay his respects to the Patriarch; he entrusted my mountain disciples with a request for biographies and praises of the patriarchs. In my illness I compiled seventy-one biographies, each with a praise attached, and wrote them out with my own hand. Earlier, when I left Caoxi for Nanyue and dwelt at Mount Kuang, eight years had already passed, and the monks of Caoxi thought deeply of my return. The hall master Ben'ang and others came and went with inquiries more than ten times, wishing to invite me but unable to. When Duke Wu took up his post he went into the mountains on the way and, seeing the work of my revival, sighed in admiration for a long while. The monks then told him fully why they wished for my return and how they could not bring it about. Duke Wu gladly became my protector of the Dharma and at once wrote to invite me. The whole assembly of the mountain and the gentry and laymen of the province drew up a petition together, and Ang with two or three elders came to Mount Kuang to beg me in sorrow. At that time I declined on account of illness.
The First Year of Tianqi, Xinyou (1621).

I was seventy-six. In spring the Censor Wang Anshun, my disciple, entered the mountains to inquire after me. In summer the assembly asked me to expound the Lankavatara Sutra. At that time Circuit Commissioner Zhu, formerly of this circuit, was also transferred to the Guangdong Sea Circuit, and he and Duke Wu sent a letter again. I again declined on account of illness. In the winter of that year I again expounded the Lankavatara, the Zhao Lun and the Awakening of Faith for the assembly.
The Second Year of Tianqi, Renxu (1622).

I was seventy-seven. In the first month of spring my Cantonese disciples the licentiates Liu Qixiang, Chen Dixiang, Chen Dichun and Liang Sixiang entered the mountains to inquire after me. Qixiang and Sixiang stayed with me in the mountains half a year, and I expounded the Surangama, the Awakening of Faith and the Diamond Sutra. In the second month my disciple Fang Yuan from eastern Wu arrived and joined me in planning to retire. In the seventh month of autumn Censor Wang again entered the mountains and asked me in person to return to Caoxi, but I did not consent. At that time I was pressing on with the Flower Ornament, called the Essential Outline; the draft was done. Duke Wu returned from the imperial audience and again sent a letter, his meaning more earnest still. Prefect Zhang of Shaoyang specially wrote and sent the hall master Ang to me. My feelings could not be denied, and I thought I must go once. So on the tenth day of the eleventh month of that winter I left Mount Kuang and passed through Luojiao, where I met the Grand Historian Xiao Zhuoxiu, Liu Shaoye, Liu Zhuanhua, Ma Jifang, Zeng Yaochen, He Keshan and Zou Duanhou and other laymen. Passing the Qiangcheng river I met Su Xiao and Wei Qi of Ningdu and others, and feasted on the river, giving poems of parting. I crossed the ridge and passed the Jilong Hermitage, where I met Liu Jingyi and other old friends. At the full moon of the twelfth month I entered Caoxi, and the whole assembly of monks ranged incense and flowers as though welcoming a mother.
The Third Year of Tianqi, Guihai (1623).

The Master was seventy-eight, dwelling in the meditation hall at Caoxi. In the first month of spring Prefect Zhang entered the mountains to inquire after him. In the third month the disciples of Faxing in the provincial city arrived. At that time the Master's whole mind was given to the gift of Dharma. In the fourth month he expounded the precepts for the assembly and lectured on the Surangama, the Awakening of Faith and other sutras and treatises. In the seventh month of autumn he again expounded the precepts for the assembly. On the fourth day of the tenth month Duke Xiao Xuanpu, Minister of Rites, on his way north at imperial summons, entered the mountains to see the Master, and joyfully lingered; he even divined a longevity grave for the Master. They talked eagerly a day and a night in great delight. As he left the mountain the Master at once showed signs of illness. On the sixth day the attendant Guangyi returned from the provincial city, and the Master said: You have come at just the right time. Prefect Zhang of Shaoyang came in person into the mountains and called physicians to treat him. On the eighth day his disciple Chaoyi arrived, and he said: In two more days I shall not see you. The Master knew the phantom conditions were nearly exhausted and would not take medicine. At the hour of Si on the eleventh day he took leave of Duke Zhang. At the hour of Shen he drank water, bathed, burned incense and said to the assembly: All of you should be mindful that the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence swift. Then he sat upright with single mind and passed away. At that time a hundred birds cried in sorrow and the four assemblies wailed without cease; in the starry night a fine light illumined the sky, and people across the mountain all thought the temple was on fire. For three days his face was as in life, his hair had grown and his lips were red, there was slight moisture at the tip of his nose, and his hands and feet were soft as silk. When Duke Xiao heard the news he grieved long, and at once wrote to the two prefects of Nan and Shao to build a stupa for the Master and make a portrait hall. Earlier, when the Master left Mount Kuang, he had left the chief seat Tongjiong at the Five Milks to look after the assembly; now he sent letters three times urging him to return. In one he said: If you come a day earlier, that is a day earlier. This old man has not many days of strength left. Receiving the letter, Jiong hurried south. On the first day of the tenth month he reached Caoxi. The Master saw him and joy showed in his face, and he said: Good that you have come; had you been later I fear you would have regretted it. Jiong did not at first understand his meaning. Day after day he stood in attendance, and all that he heard and was admonished with was the great purport of the Buddhadharma; earnestly the Master lamented that the Dharma gate had no one. The reminders he gave were again most urgent and pointed. As for the time of his departure, it had already been revealed before Jiong returned.

The Master's Autobiographical Chronology and Veritable Record had long existed in a handwritten draft, which was kept by Tongjiong of Ji'an, the Master's chief seat. After Master Tongjiong passed away, his Dharma grandsons Jinzhao and Jinguang dwelt at Haizhuang Monastery, and the monk Huashou obtained this draft from the two monks, made a fair copy and sealed and sent it. Now it is committed to the blocks in accordance with the original draft. The Veritable Record of the third year of Tianqi, guihai (1623), was continued and recorded after the Master's entry into extinction by his foremost disciple Fushan and others, and appended and carved at the end. Because the Master was a dragon-elephant of the revival, every word and every deed of his bears on the eye of gods and men; in the text we take what can be verified, and in matters we prize the transmission of what is trustworthy. We dare not clutch at vines and creepers, nor add feet to the snake, and so invite the reproach of adding to the Dharma gate; may those who come after with the true eye be pleased to discern it. In the first month of summer in the wuxu year, on the day of the Buddha's enlightenment, the Haiyin disciple Qian Qianyi, Pantan, reverently set it down.

blocks.text: A Discussion of Master Hanshan's Rebirth

inline.s: Duke Zhuanyu Heng of Hunan wrote a biography of the revived Master Hanshan of Caoxi, speaking amply of marvels: that in a former life he was Chen Yaxian, and after death appeared again as Duke Xiao's son. Many quarters doubted this as fantastic. Duke Muchen Min of Tiantong, in his Miscellaneous Records of Things Seen and Heard, says: The Master was reborn in Tongxiang as the young son of the judicial official Yan Junyan. He did not speak for three years; one day he called his father by name and said: You — you were a disciple in my former life. When the judicial official passed the examinations and was appointed to office in Guangzhou, the boy knew all beforehand. He fell ill with smallpox and could not rise; he summoned the education commissioner Wei Huanchu to his bedside, took his hand, spoke of old times, and asked him to compose an inscription testifying to his final affairs. Reading this I was astonished in my heart. The education commissioner is a man of my own district. When the Master traveled east he never once gathered up his robes to bow at his feet; how could there have been a matter of taking hands and speaking of old times? The judicial official lived in retirement at Shimen, so I sent a letter to inquire into the details. Thereupon, in the seventh month of the second year of Chongzhen, the monks of Nanhua, Zhirong and Ben'ang, sent me the report document and the stone copy of the stupa record. The monks' document said: The second young master manifested the pure youth in a bodhisattva's house, and could cause his family to cut off the worldly ties of affection, and performed the cremation service for him. After the fire bath the crown of his head and his teeth were unbroken, and the relics were countless, the large ones like pellets, the small like beans, their color like white agate, and struck they rang with a clear sound. The whole assembly of monks together beheld and marveled. On the second day of that month, at the hour of You, the sacred bones were interred and a stupa built to the left of the former Master's stupa courtyard. The perfected man's going out into birth and entering death is a game of perfect freedom. Could it be that the former Master's cast-off shell had returned to Mount Kuang and, manifesting this golden lock, came back to guard the Patriarch's court? Or was it rather an elder of the mountain, whose former vow and power brought him to dwell in this way-place? The stupa record says: The son of the Yan family was named Zhi, his childhood name Huzi, born in the sixth year of Tianqi, in the second month of Bingyin — in fact three years after the Master's entry into extinction. He died at four. On the day of the judicial official's appointment Huzi whispered to the family: I have taken the opportunity to go to Caoxi. By this saying we know the Master came again. As for what Duke Min records of calling the name and recounting the past, I had not heard it before. The judicial official and his son turned their hearts homeward and their root of faith was firm. The layman Shengsheng often dreamed of the temple guardian spirit urging him to welcome Pindola; the next day the Master arrived, his compassionate countenance and Dharma seat exactly as in the former dream. The judicial official was then a scholar, and the Master stroked his head and gave him a prophecy. When he became a grand coordinator, he made clear the Master's rules and restored the seized fields. Huzi entered the womb through faith and sought his own parents; it was truly no accident. The manifestation of the pure youth has its own meanings. His going and coming between Wu and Yue shows that the dharma-realm is one ground. His smallpox giving off fragrance shows that defilement and purity are one suchness. His sacred bones remaining undamaged shows that the marks of the numinous are complete. His dying at four shows that he had already entered the stage of a kumara. His bones returning to the stupa courtyard shows that he relied upon the great one. This is the cultivation of accumulated kalpas, a phantom transformation in the snap of a finger, not to be measured by thought. If by these causes one proves that he was the Master come again, then I privately think it is not so. Why? From of old, when Buddhas and Patriarchs respond and transform, entering the womb and turning the wheel among men and gods, the matter is not trivial. Zaizong in a second life met the washerwoman and lodged in her; Master Xuan waited six years and relied on White Cloud to test and discern. In every case the entrustment corresponded and the response to the moment was plain. Now there is no such thing here. When the attracting conditions were ripe and the moment for tapping and pecking was the same, the incense smoke of the Twin Peaks still pointed the way, and the true body of the Five Milks had its home. I say that this child, through many lives and in this world, must have entered the Master's room, worn the Master's robe, received the Master's precepts, and been sent as a messenger to announce it to other beings. Testing the principle by the fact, there is nothing doubtful. Alas! Our Master was a teacher of gods and men, the first dragon-elephant of the Dharma's final age. His final turning of the wheel is a great cause for the Dharma gate. Monks without understanding fix their minds on incense and fire, pointing to the Dharma city as a tomb mound and taking the jeweled precinct for a memorial pillar. Little Confucians of phrases and chapters, their eyes like needle holes, glimpse Li Yuan and Yuanze and make leftover talk of before and after the body. Monks and laymen pass it by post, wake from their dreaming talk, and take the sea's shape and an ox's footprint — is it not far off? Vulgar sayings that are not true spread and become painting. I fear that later writers of monks' histories and compilers of Buddhist records will gather strange reports and so confound right faith. Since Duke Min's disciple is at hand, I have told his teacher and asked him to correct the carving, and have also written out this discussion and sent it to the monks of Nanhua to be engraved at the stupa courtyard, declaring it to later men so that they may not be misled. In the year Gengzi, on the full moon of the fourth month, the Haiyin disciple Qian Qianyi, Pantan, respectfully set it down.
Dream-Wanderings of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Fifty-Five.
The Stupa Inscription of Great Master Hanshan, Restorer of Caoxi and Heir to the Dharma, of Fayun Chan Temple at the Five Milks Peak of Mount Lu in the Great Ming, with Preface.

While I, the young Guanglun Binzhi, was in the Imperial Secretariat, I went with several fellow students to seek instruction from Master Hanshan of Mount Lao at the Longhua Retreat. Xiao Xuanpu, Minister of Rites, and my own Sima Tizhong were among them. What we heard was either the ten mysteries of Indra's net or the five leaves of the Patriarch's lamp; and the Master especially took the investigation of Buddha-recitation as the two wheels on open ground. Ten years later he entered Guangdong, and the plain cloth of Wanjiang restored me; twenty years after that he entered Wu, and through Tizhong the drum of Fudu roused me. Only then could I wander within the Master's fence and know the whole of those secret appearances, surges and sinkings, favorable and adverse, and all manner of shadow matters. Seven years later Xuanpu went north by way of Caoxi and saw the Master off at the cliff; the next year I obtained from Governor-General He the return of the Master's cast-off shell to the Five Milks. The next year the chief disciple Fushan polished stone for paper and presented the Master's own chronology, making my tongue the brush. I received and finished it three times, and the meetings at Longhua and Fudu seemed still undispersed. The Master's Dharma name was Deqing; admiring the mystery of Qingliang's dharma-realm, he styled himself Chengyin, and took the personal name Hanshan from the wonder of Mount Wutai, to signify the resting of the mad mind. His line came from the Cai clan of Jinling. His father was named Yangao, his mother of the Hong clan, who dreamed that Guanyin brought and gave her a child, and so conceived. He was born on the twelfth day of the first month of winter in the Bingwu year of Jiajing, wrapped in a white afterbirth. At ten he left home and was placed with the abbot Xilin of Bao'en Temple, who made his Dharma grandson Master Jun his teacher. At nineteen he paid his respects to Great Master Yungu of Qixia and had his head shaved and received full ordination. At twenty-six he traveled north, going in and out of Yan and Jin, and attained the samadhi of ease on Mount Tai. At thirty-eight he hid himself in the Nārāyaṇa Cave by the Eastern Sea. After long dwelling there he attained six kinds of conformity. Past fifty he was exiled to Lingnan, and as a monk turned lay devotee he greatly raised the bell of Caoxi. The imperial grace reached him again and again, and he wore the cassock once more; the Master was then sixty-nine. Three years later he returned from Wu and built a retreat below the Five Milks Peak of Mount Lu, the temple called Fayun, to support the aged of the ten directions. After dwelling there several years he went again to Caoxi. He was then seventy-eight years old, with sixty years of ordination; it was the Guihai year of Tianqi. One day before his birthday he entered extinction. In appearance the Master was full and kindly, his spirit calm and settled; seen from afar he resembled an arhat. When he first went to the outer school his mother supervised him strictly; gradually observing him, she knew he was no creature of the pond. She urged his father to tear the net of affection. And the Master's requital of boundless kindness: he declined ten yi of offerings at the Shanyin princely residence; he alone bowed to receive the gifts of Empress Xiaoding; with gold and blood he painted the Flower Ornament, gathering his two parents within the light and fragrance of the incense banners. For his visit home he spent three nights in the family quarters through the Bao'en canon-wheel, with Dharma joy and no worldly grief. The gentleman says: To give him birth and bring him to completion is called sage goodness; to fumigate and transform him is called purity. The compassion and filial piety of the world are but one bubble on that sea. His northern lectures that crossed the heavenly moat began with the Wuji exposition of the Profound Discourse on the Flower Ornament. His southern Chan that restored the old tripod began with the Buddha-recitation huatou given by Yungu. The light from the mouths of these two great beings poured together onto the Master's crown, and he was neither startled nor overflowing; his body ever sat at ease in the Huazang way-place, while the Dharma King of Clear Tranquility, like two Dharma princes, entered his pure, fierce mind as a form is mirrored. His cultivation was so single-minded that even walking in the marketplace he saw no one. Those who understood him took it that dense clouds still pass; another day he would attain what he had never had regarding Sengzhao's meaning of like a former man yet not a former man. What is called the whirlwind forever still, the rivers not flowing, he verified before his eyes and understood each thing clearly. And the doubt of birth and death that arose when he was seven melted away like ice. His verse says: Birth and death are night and day; the water flows, the flowers fall. Today at last I know the nostrils turn downward. This is the first mark of his penetration of the school. Planting his staff on Mount Tai, at the head of the narrow bridge, he heard the vital turn several times reversed, and at length did not hear the clamor of the ten thousand pipes. The ascetic of the snow cave answered with his eyes; of vegetable soup and rice water he ate a pint every ten days. Thought rested and dust was forgotten; standing, he lost himself for I know not how many mornings and evenings. His verse says: In one flash a single thought — the mad mind rests; within and without, faculties and dust are wholly clear. I turn and break through the great empty space; the myriad forms in dense array arise and cease. This is the second mark of his penetration of the school. His meeting of the mind at Mount Lao: sea and sky, snow and moon, casting mutual shadows and exchanging light; samadhi appeared before him, with no entering and no leaving. His verse says: The sea limpid, the sky clear, the light of snow and moon; herein the ordinary and the sage cut off all going and hiding. The vajra eye breaks through, the sky-flowers fall; the whole great earth returns to the ground of extinction. This is the third mark of his penetration of the school. Three years later the mechanism stirred in stillness, not arising from a thought of the mind, the meaning at the tip of the tongue. His verse says: Day after day mist and waves soak the cold sky; fish and birds roam together in one mirror. At midnight the moon beyond the sky suddenly sank; its lone brightness must be mingled with the black dragon's. What is called meeting after the moon has set — is it so or not? This is the fourth mark of his penetration of the school. From then on he turned from the true back into the worldly and made the journey to visit his parents. Miaoxi had eighteen great awakenings and countless small ones; the warmth and cold within, only the Master knew. One may suppose that the bodhisattva's root and power increased stage by stage, and that clarity, wonder, peace and joy ever corresponded with the mental factors. Hence when the Flower Ornament was at the tip of his brush, with the six-character Buddha's name his mind and hand worked together, so that not one dot passed in vain; and in dealings with host and guest his words never erred or were forgotten, his text never confused a boar for a pig. The Lotus Sutra he dedicated to the holy mother, and it was the same. At the Unhindered Assembly on Mount Tai the offerings were changed daily, with five hundred tables spread and ten thousand seated; all was secretly planned by the Master and supplied on time, with no sound of knocking. Master Miaofeng Deng, who shared the affair, never knew whence it came. In the severity of the undertaking he did not close his eyes for ninety days, and for seven days took water in place of food; he went away only when a month had passed. Call him of vigorous years, yet had he reached great age he would have outdone the households of his district. Like clouds rising and a bottle pouring, his side seldom touched the mat, and none saw him weary of diligence. Once at leisure he walked in Hainan, seeking the former traces of Zizhan and Jiyin, and looked at the vital air of the prefectural city; it alone held the western corner. He urged them to go north across the sea, and Qiongzhou was shaken by earthquake, its preservation and destruction exactly as the Master had said. Yongjia's determination of the teachings first spoke of arousing and later of accomplishing; the Master was between the two. At his awakening on Mount Tai, looking about, he had no one to consult, so he set the Surangama King before his eyes with direct perception, and for eight months had no place to apply his mind. There in the Nārāyaṇa Cave he wrote the Surangama Hanging Mirror in half a candle's time, likewise with no place to apply his mind. His disciples said: Why not have every sentence dissolved back into the contemplation of mind? The Master nodded. The Comprehensive Commentary on the Surangama began from this. Once, using the four dharma-realm contemplations, he expounded the Lotus Sutra in Lingnan, and coming to the Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa he sighed deeply and said: The Buddha's meaning essentially points out that for every person in this Saha world what lies before their eyes is the Huazang world; it requires three transformations of the pure land only to show those of dull faculties a single glimpse by degrees. From this began his Rhythmic Beats on the Lotus Sutra, his Chapter and Section Division, and his Comprehensive Commentary. Breaking a reed and singing alone, he held the tally of the Lankavatara; planting pines to carry on the revival, he kept the pact of the Diamond Sutra. The Master illumined them with the mirror of the Surangama, and so the gateless gate and the abiding that does not abide all seemed to have their locks opened. For this reason his Notes on the Lankavatara Sutra were regarded by men as the music of flowing notes, while in the Resolution of Doubts on the Diamond Sutra, though Subhuti himself came again, he must surely have looked at it and smiled. In the Flower Ornament school men often lost their way in the vastness of Qingliang and were enamored of the brevity of Fangshan, not knowing that the vast can be made brief. In one retreat at the Five Milks, through three rounds of cold and heat, he wrote the Essential Outline of the subcommentary, which will be treasured alongside the Combined Treatise. Thus all the marks of his expository penetration are spread in the records; seeing the smoke one knows the fire, and his penetration of the school is plain. Who says that he has gone with the untransmitted? And the Fayun tradition, carved in incense, counted the Buddha's name each day to several tens of thousands; perfect and sudden interpenetrate, Chan and Pure Land are both wondrous. The two great beings' earliest tying of the knot — he tucked up his robes and went straight to the mountain's brow and the sea's eye, circled his staff three times, and made a single night's awakening. Is he not truly a great man whose courage strides beyond all ages? In his early years the bound volumes and pearl cases were his vanguard; in middle years his supporting chariot; at the end his auxiliary carriage. So he wrote the Direct Pointing at the Doctrine of the Mean, the Resolution of Doubts on the Great Learning, the Heart-Method of the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals, and the inner chapters of the Daodejing and Nanhua, as skillful means of wisdom. And the conditions of ghosts and spirits were made manifest. Qiuming said: This man secretly penetrated the mind-method of Lu and India. Zhou Canzhi of Dong'ao raised the great Change's understanding the way of day and night and thereby knowing, and tested the Master with it; he said: This is what our school calls the one thing that does not belong to birth and death. The counselor leaped up, and further set forth its profound meaning for the disciples. And the Master took the Western Count as lord of the eastern feudal lords. For Elder Xilin had once dulled the Master with worldly truth, making him serve at the lecture mat, and so in the two you he hunted much. Calligraphy, rhyme and phrase, little... (the remainder of this passage is corrupt in the source).

...he simply drove them all beyond the border. Such was his requital of enmity with kindness. And earlier, when the halls and corridors of Bao'en were burned, the Master and Elder Xuelang swore to strive together for one term. When the canon was escorted back to the temple by decree, and the relic stupa put forth a bridge of light to welcome the pattra-leaves, the Master went in to give thanks, asking the holy mother to reduce her daily delicacies to fund the great beams. For long the matter had its beginnings, but it was obstructed by the island barbarians and so came to nothing. And a palace favorite who had turned the canon wheel had once suffered a slight and borne a grudge; those about the Emperor magnified it, saying he supervised Buddhist works with ornament and drew much from the treasury, and that he falsely claimed to be a Daoist priest, seizing his own affair and striking the drum of appeal to bring suit. There was a decree to arrest the Master. When the palace favorite confronted him before the prison tribunal, the Master was empty within and boldly spoke of the matter without, asking that the inner treasury be examined; and the registers of famine relief were indeed there, and nothing else could be found of any leak. The one who harbored the grudge against the palace favorite had not intended to harm the Master, and further set out the whole story in full in a formal statement, and the imperial displeasure gradually dissolved. He was sentenced for privately building a monastery and exiled to Leiyang, and all the temples that had received the holy mother's generosity, though they passed through peril, suffered no loss in the end. The former Grand Secretary Zhang Hongyang praised him for casting off what is hard to cast off and enduring what is hard to endure, and for secretly aiding the Emperor's filial piety, as merit to the state. Truly, in the fragrant light of prajñā the Master had long since been given his nostrils by Old Man Yungu; and at the parting of the ways, the pressing and prodding of Miaofeng and Elder En was not without its arm lent. When Mount Tai was accomplished, evening clouds and spring trees, pure wind sweeping the ground — where was there not an early-years brother? And what the Master sketched at the furnace of flying snow, wielding the wind's axe, the oath of the familiar host, was no less than three-armored dragons rising from nirvāṇa. Great Master Zibo rarely gave approval in the world, yet alone he lightened a thousand-li journey to the firm and solid; at the meeting at Duke Wan's stupa courtyard in Jin he sent hard questions and reasoned through them, sitting four decades in one session within the world, with Dharma joy unmatched. Though at his entry into extinction in the prison gate the demons were venomous as sand-spitters, yet what he had harbored in coming was never absent from beneath the halberds of Leiyang. Though the tour of Shuangjing was without the chief disciple Kai, he must have gone at once on his own affair, only the time was awaited; and it happened that Zibo, because the relics were moved, came to the cremation, and the inscription was written on the firm and white. This is what made them friends beyond the world. He praised Yunqi, bearing witness that our Master, Patriarch Lian, was one of those who welled up from the earth in the Lotus Sutra; and Master Langmu Zhi of Mount Fu, by the turning dhāraṇī, was also made the one who put the pupil in the eye. Then I, the young Bin, presumptuously bore the banner of the Dharma fortress and gradually rose to mount the blue clouds. The Master said that Zibo's waves were muddied and the spring was dim, and that while we two were not yet in our prime we should support each other left and right, to cleanse Caoxi — would the school then flourish? When the left thigh was wounded, a strong horse was urgently needed. So Zibo went from Caoxi to Yan, while the Master crossed the ridge and returned, his mind never elsewhere than the Patriarch's cave. He divined with Zhou Haimen, judge of the province, and the Caoxi Gazetteer was completed; he steadied it with Governor-General Dai, and the butcher and wine stalls were washed away in one sweep. The cunning with tiger caps, the soldier-slaves who made captives of our monks and ate away our lands like silkworms — in less than a morning they scattered like crows and hid like ghosts. The temple changed its face. Thereupon he bound it with the precepts, ordered it with comings and goings, guarded it with records, moistened it with the stream of Dharma, nurtured it with a charity school. Thus for several years the jeweled precinct was renewed, gradually as new. At the last he undertook the Great Hero Hall, and one or two cunning and fierce vermin of the Master's, hating that it harmed them, stirred up a great clamor and would have loosed an arrow at him; yet the Master sat at ease reciting the Vajra Prajñā Sutra and deeply understanding its meaning, joyful and calm. The clamorers were ashamed at heart, but withdrew without being reconciled. So when the governor-general was dismissed they falsely charged the Master with plundering the permanent property and appealed to the censorate. He lived in exile two years. The judicial officer gave them the belt of office; the direct commissioner did not approve, and sent it down to the prefecture to summon the keepers of the records and tally them, and not a hair was amiss. Then the plaintiff was stripped and banished, and the vermin of Caoxi were cleansed. In his youth the Master, entrusted by Elder Xilin, repaid by his own reckoning two lifetimes of debt to the amount of a thousand strings at the Unhindered Assembly, and finished by registering its surplus and giving it to the abbot Dafang of Tayuan Temple, a full ten thousand in wealth. He knew how to nourish by calm and toil by humble shepherding; he loosed the mechanism only where he could not do otherwise, and stored his use where it could not be known. The steed is praised for its virtue, yet its strength is beyond counting compared with common horses. Though the plan for Bao'en was halted by the Master's orders, and the work of Haiyin was ruined by the city's rats, and the walls of Nanhua fell to the petty traders, yet the Master's land of mind, its compassion and wisdom wondrously adorned, could never be lacking. When the costly eunuchs overflowed in their tax farming, harboring bandits and breeding villainy beyond approach, it was fortunate that some among them had a shallow admiration for the field of merit. The Master, asked by Governor-General Dai, became as an infant to them, and his response was like an echo. Thus the tax commissioner was pressed by the deadline and could not get what he wanted, and the smelting of gold and silver was carried out by the offices, so the people did not know the bite of treading on a tiger's tail. The white-sailed boats left grain to the people and drove up the Cantonese rice price; the people of the region suffered, and Duke Dai's heir was about to return to Wenling. On his way he met the white-sailed boats. At that time the tax commissioner bore a grudge against the General, and stirred up many of the market's bullies to flatter the kitchen god. The officers twice sent urgent word to the Master. The Master was at ease in his dwelling; the door was opened for him and he calmly admonished the crowd: Do you want cheap rice? Now the crime is capital; though the rice be cheap, who will eat it? The crowd's rage abated a little, and he urgently told the tax commissioner to issue an order to calm the wavering hearts, and made clear that it was not the heir's fault. The city became quiet. Thus the Master risked himself to go before the spears. Had the Master been given charge of the Great Mirror's patriarchal covenant, and had he slipped the bow of the ghost-laden, and lodged in the window of the earthenware jar, he would have had no violent knight's temper, yet he had a violent knight's merit. What is called moving the blade with utmost subtlety, so that it falls apart with a crash — he had advanced beyond mere skill. The Master's precepts were pure white, upright but not cutting; his gate stood between those of Yunqi and Zibo. The tally of his fullness of virtue: meeting him, the banner of pride breaks, the city of doubt falls, the sword of anger drops. To those who came seeking the essentials he did not begrudge setting the four-cornered truth on the ground, compassionate lest men should not possess it. His traces covered half the world, and wherever he went he mounted the ordination platform and rose to the seat of the white gavel, by tens of counts. In eastern Qi and southern Yue the Dharma teaching had long been buried and the Buddha-seed nearly cut off, but once they had the Master it was as when a gnat sees heaven and earth. Fumigated by the two adornments, sworn to the nine grades, even the Ullambana and life-releasing practices and all pure white deeds — none, capped or pinned, young or old, was not in accord. The separate transmission of the school he at times displayed with courage for those of sharp faculties, his teeth fearless, casting a mustard seed into a needle. Thus the region of Qingliang could follow the statutes of successive dynasties and be released from the land tax, and the great timber lived out its natural span as the Buddha, Dharma and Sangha property of the state. The temple master took men from the great towns, and through no disaster escaped shackles — truly the walls of the five heavens enclosing one capital. The present Emperor was reared in the Azure Palace and decreed that old, ill and wrongly implicated exiles might state their case and be pardoned. The Master had two such cases; the examination and memorial went back and forth for six years, and then he was allowed to do as he wished. And the holy mother, being Empress Xiaoding, came to Xiangdong and greatly performed Buddhist works; then he was released from Miaoxi's cap and returned to the stable of Qixian. And the one bowl and one robe the Master inscribed when he first set out on pilgrimage are matched by nothing in Fengcheng or Yanjin. The Master's intimate friends, the worthy and bold of the realm, numbered no less than a hundred, but of those who followed wind and bore frost, Duke Hu in the north and Duke Dai in the south were the greatest. In the Hudong retreat he lingered three years for Ministry Official Zeng Jinjian; at the Five Milks the ten benefactors had Sima Wang Jingfeng as their leader. At that time the famous monasteries that kept a seat empty for him were the hall at Fudu in Tongxiang and the building at Dongchan in Jinsha. For watching his whisk, Wuling and Yunqi gathered the joy of the whole realm to invite the finest of Chan and lecturing, who hollowed out their hearts and bent to him; the beauty of the southeast was exhausted, yet in the end he was shut in by the loneliness of Mount Lu and again drawn away by the songs of Caoxi. Men thought him wearied by ferrying, yet the Master had never once come down from the seat of Mount Tai. He let loose his unobstructed eloquence of joyful speech, showing the single transmission in crooked ways and melting it into the dharma-realm of a single dust mote. In his likening to Guifeng, released into the prajñā of letters, yet gaining many worldly obstacles, he resembled Juefan. In marshaling the ten thousand practices with the one mind as their source, and adorning the land of non-arising and of rebirth, he again resembled Yongming. Though the correct command was desolate, and he seemed somewhat too warm of grandmotherly heart, perhaps he was observing the times and meeting the faculties, unable to bear that the grass before the Dharma hall should grow a fathom deep. The first stem was Xin, to change the face; the second stem was Bing, to make the pattern flourish. The Stupa Inscription of Great Master Hanshan of Haiyin in the Great Ming, at the Five Milks Peak of Mount Lu.

Our Emperor Shenzong, the Manifest Emperor, grasped the golden wheel to rule the world and extended the will of the holy mother Empress Dowager Cisheng, honoring and supporting the Three Treasures to deepen her care and nurture. In the prime of his years the Emperor had no heir shining before him, and the holy mother took it as her sorrow. She established a way-place for praying for an heir on Mount Wutai, and Master Miaofeng Deng and Great Master Hanshan were in fact its principals. Emperor Guangzong, the Chaste Emperor, was then born at the appointed time. Thereupon the two masters' names were heard in the ninefold palace, like the udumbara flower appearing at the edge of heaven. Miaofeng did not leave the city of Rajagriha but greatly performed Buddhist works, while the Master had his journey to Leiyang. Where the causes and conditions led, appearing sideways and thrusting out — truly it is not to be measured by ordinary feeling. When the Master passed away at Caoxi, Duke Xiao Xuanhua, Grand Minister of Rites, saw the marvels with his own eyes and told me of them. Afterwards Chen Dixiang of Nanhai brought the record of his conduct and asked me to write the stupa inscription. I said: My teacher Duke Xuanhua is here; another day let him be asked to write the second stele. The next year, Yichou, his disciple at Mount Lu, Fushan, brought the whole body back to the Five Milks and left hair and nails at Caoxi, and sent a letter to tell me, saying: When the Master traveled east and got you he rejoiced, saying: The banner pole need not fear falling. When the lamp's wick sputtered and the moon set, his talk was tireless, and what he entrusted was most deep. The inscription before the stupa — who but you is fit to write it? How dare I again decline? I respectfully record that the Master's name was Deqing, his clan the Cai, a man of Quanjiao. His father was Yangao, his mother of the Hong clan, who dreamed that the Great Being brought and gave her a child, and so he was born. At seven his uncle died and lay on the bed; he asked his mother where he had gone, and so took up the doubt of birth and death, of coming and going. At nine he could recite the Universal Gateway Chapter. At twelve he left his parents and entered Bao'en Temple, relying on Elder Xilin. Duke Zhao Wensu of Neijiang stroked his head and said: This child will one day be a teacher of gods and men. At nineteen he shaved his head and received full ordination from a certain Master Wuji. He heard the Profound Discourse on the Flower Ornament expounded, and when he came to the ten mysteries, to the passage where the ocean-seal's dense array ever abides, he awakened to the purport of the dharma-realm's perfect fusion without end. Admiring the life of Qingliang, he styled himself Chengyin. With Elder Yungu of Yungu he bound Chan at Tianjie Temple and roused himself to investigation. A carbuncle broke out on his back; he prayed to the temple guardian spirit, vowing to recite the Flower Ornament ten times, asking for three months' leave to finish the Chan term. When the prayer was done he slept soundly, and rising in the morning the illness was quite gone. Within three months he was as if in a dream. Walking in the marketplace he was as though seated in Chan, and saw not one person in the market. Elder Xuelang En was one year older than the Master, and they relied on each other as Asanga and Vasubandhu. In the Bingyin year of Jiajing the temple was destroyed by fire, and they vowed to store virtue and await the time, hoping for its revival. The Master then rose towering into the world, while Xuelang in the end became a great lecturer and repaired the old stupa, somewhat requiting the vow. The Master once heard a lecture at Tianjie; the privy was swept clean and there was no trace of anyone, and he thought the one in charge of the eastern privy must be no ordinary man. He sought him out: a sallow-faced sick monk, his gaze darting. So they made a pact to call on masters together; at dawn he had already gone. It was Master Miaofeng Deng. The Master, thinking the Jiangnan habit soft and warm, resolved to enter a place of winter ice and summer snow, of bitter cold beyond bearing, to file and sharpen himself. So he drifted north. In heavy snow he begged in the market of Guangling, saying: My single bowl is enough to make ten thousand bushels light. Reaching the capital, Miaofeng came in coarse cloth to visit; his beard and hair were matted like a merchant of Heshuo. The Master looked at his pupils and knew him; they looked at each other and smiled. He called on Bianrong Zhen; Rong said nothing, only opened his eyes and gazed straight. He also called on Xiaoyan. Yan asked from what quarter he had come. He said: From the south. Yan said: Do you remember the road by which you came? He said: Once past, and it is done. Yan said: Then your place of coming is clear. He roamed Mount Pan and reached the stone chamber of Thousand Images Peak, where he saw the monk who did not speak, and so they gathered firewood and drew water together and passed the summer. It was the Guiyou year of Wanli, the first year. The next year he spent the winter with Miaofeng at Puban and read the Treatise on the Non-Movement of Things. Coming to the passage where the Brahmin left home, he suddenly understood the purport of the whirlwind stilling the peaks. He wrote a verse: Birth and death are night and day; the water flows, the flowers fall. Today at last I know the nostrils turn downward. Seeing it, Feng at once asked what the Master had attained. The Master said: Last night I saw two iron oxen in the river, fighting as they went into the water; to this day there is no news of them. Feng said: I am glad you have the capital to dwell in the mountains. He met Chan Master Faguang of Mount Niu and sat in practice seeking instruction. Faguang's voice came forth like a heavenly drum, and the Master was deeply in accord. Seeing the Master off to Wutai he wrote a poem: The lion in the snow, ride it here to see; the hidden dragon in the cave, let it go and rest. And he said: Do you understand this meaning? I want you not to grasp a dead snake. The Master dwelt at Longmen on the North Peak, in a few rafters of an old hut amid ten thousand mountains of ice and snow. At the meeting of spring and summer the melting ice rushed and struck, and in the stillness it was like the sound of ten thousand horses galloping. He asked Miaofeng about it. Feng cited the ancients' words: Hear the sound of water for thirty years without turning the faculty of mind, and you shall realize Guanyin's perfect penetration. The Master agreed. Each day he sought a log bridge across the stream and sat upright upon it. At first the sound of water was clear and distinct; after a long time he suddenly forgot his body, all sounds were still, and the water no longer clamored in his ears. One day after the gruel, as he walked in meditation, he suddenly stood still: radiance like a great perfect mirror, in which the mountains, rivers and great earth appeared as reflections. When he came to, body and mind were serene and he could not find them at all. He spoke a verse in praise. He roamed Yanmen. The military commissioner Hu asked him to compose poems; just as he began to ponder, poetic lines pressed and filled his throat and lips, and all that he had ever recited, seen and heard appeared in an instant before him. His whole body was mouths, yet he could not pour it all out. The Master said: This is what Faguang called the Chan sickness; only sound sleep can dissolve it. Wrapped in his robe he sat cross-legged and sat five days and nights. Duke Hu shook him and he did not move; he sounded the small gong several times, and then he came out of samadhi. Sitting silently he looked back: it was like breathing in and out. Dwelling in the mountains and walking on pilgrimage were all matters of dream. Its joy was beyond all comparison. Returning to the mountain he pierced his finger and wrote the Flower Ornament Sutra in blood, dotting the brush and reciting the Buddha's name, never neglecting his responses; reciting with the mouth and painting with the hand, everything clear and distinct. The neighboring monks thought it strange and led their followers to pester him; in the end they all sighed in praise and left. Once he dreamed that he and Miaofeng attended Great Master Qingliang as he gave instruction in the contemplation-realm of the perfect fusion of the first entry into the dharma-realm: as he expounded, the realm appeared. Again he dreamed of ascending the tower of Maitreya and hearing the Dharma: Discrimination is consciousness; non-discrimination is wisdom. Relying on consciousness, there is defilement; relying on wisdom, there is purity. Defilement has birth and death; purity has no Buddhas. From then on the division between consciousness and wisdom was clear in his mind and eye. After the Master had established the way-place for praying for an heir he fled far to Mount Lao by the Eastern Sea. The holy mother ordered the monk Rui'an of Longhua Temple to search him out and find him, and sent envoys to summon him twice without being able to bring him. She bestowed three thousand in gold from the inner treasury, and he firmly declined again. The envoy dared not report back. The Master said: Of old there was the case of forging a decree to relieve famine; Shandong has a bad year — would it not be well to spread the holy compassion to the starving thereby? The envoy took the relief registers back and reported. The holy mother sighed in admiration and had the whole palace donate gold to build a temple, granting the name Haiyin. The Master went to the capital to give thanks and asked for the canon for Bao'en Temple. The Emperor ordered him to escort it, and so he conveniently returned to visit his parents. The temple stupa emitted light for many days; on the day of welcoming the sutras the light was like a floating bridge crossing north, and the sutras traveled within the stupa's light. On his return the Master memorialized the whole story of Bao'en, saying: I beg that a hundred in gold be reduced daily from the delicacies, and in ten years the work can be undertaken. The holy mother consented. In the year Yiwei the calamity of the Daoists arose. The Master had dwelt in the mountains thirteen years, speaking the Dharma in expedient ways, and the mleccha land of the Eastern Sea all turned to the Three Treasures. But the Daoist priest, over the seizure of the cloister, sent up a flying memorial with false charges, and there was a decree to arrest him and take him to the prison tribunal. Earlier the holy mother, honoring and trusting the Buddha vehicle, had sent imperial envoys out in the four directions, and the palace men slandered and framed, always speaking of burdensome expense; the Emperor did not inquire into it. But their words were much heard in the outer court, and the offices concerned made the Master a rare commodity, wishing thereby to implicate the holy mother's attendants and also to examine the alms given before and after, treasury gold to the amount of several hundred thousand. He was tortured to the utmost, and the Master said nothing at all. Then he calmly raised his head and answered: It would be easy for you, sir, to make me confess falsely. When the case is made, where will you put the holy mother? The several hundred thousand you examine is but a trifle to the Emperor. His Majesty is purely filial and would not, for a trifle, wound the holy mother's heart. After the case is made, I fear there will be no way to answer the holy mother. If you, sir, prosecute this case to the end, where will you go? The one in charge gaped and could not close his mouth. So the case was made and submitted. What was listed was only three thousand in gold for famine relief, verifiable in the inner treasury registers. The holy mother and the Emperor were both greatly pleased. He was sentenced for privately building a temple and exiled to Leizhou; it was not the Emperor's intention. Master Daguan Ke, urgent over the Master's trouble, was about to go to the capital gate when they met on the river. The Master said: It is the ruler's command; how can it be defied? He wrote for him the Discourse on Expelling the Guest and they parted. The Master crossed Yu Ridge, entered Caoxi, and reached Wuyang, where in red prison garb he saw the general of Yue...
